Chapter 4

← Chapter 3 · Home · Chapter 5 →

Summary

For years after the disappearance, Vera grieves by the shore. Her hair is cropped and her body heavy, and she drifts in sleep and dreaming. She tries to write a book, lights fires on the beach, and questions fishermen and sailors. Catherine decides her daughter is losing her mind and offers the only cure she knows: opium and a dreamless paradise of eternal youth. Vera refuses, and years later travels west by train from Grand Central Station and then by bus, stopping short of Miss MacIntosh’s Iowa in Indiana. She recalls a young woman who jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge on her way to be married, clutching the suitcase that held her wedding veil. On the train, a fat, soft-faced lady warns her that the Middle West is desolate, a place of old people who are deaf because they do not wish to hear.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · The Search for Meaning · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Fire · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Moon and Stars · Opium · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The House · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Ecclesiastes · Edgar Allan Poe · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Romantic Poets · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Vera begins by describing a long period dominated by the dream of Miss MacIntosh, a lost and beloved figure whose disappearance profoundly affected her. She is trapped in a somnolent, vacant state, disconnected from reality, with her mother interpreting this as a loss of sanity. This passage highlights themes of grief, memory, and the struggle to hold onto reality after loss. The dream is both a refuge and a prison, reflecting Vera’s internal conflict.
  • Catherine’s response to Vera’s mental state is a complex act of love and resignation. She accepts Vera’s “death in the midst of my life,” urging her to remain still and give up on living fully, which symbolizes a surrender to despair and the avoidance of life’s harsh realities. This acceptance also suggests a generational transmission of defeat and illness, emphasizing the themes of mortality, mental illness, and the desire for oblivion.
  • Vera recounts her mother Catherine’s promises of eternal youth and beauty, describing a fantastical vision filled with precious jewels, supernatural servants, and luxurious attire. These images contrast sharply with Vera’s own physical decline and sorrow, underscoring the tension between illusion and harsh reality. The mention of the “opium paradise” and “sleeping wakefulness” evokes a state of escapism, where illusion replaces the world.
  • Despite years of despair, Vera has not given up searching for Miss MacIntosh, symbolizing a search for meaning, connection, and a normal life. The dream of a simple, domestic, and ordinary life with knitting needles in the sand, building a house of driftwood, and lighting a fire on the beach stands in stark contrast to her actual existence. This passage expresses the human longing for stability, belonging, and the “other America” of routine and community.
  • Vera recalls Miss MacIntosh’s descriptions of Iowa, a place of cold, ordinary, and finite life, filled with hardships and community ties. This reflection points to the inescapability of origin and the harsh realities that contrast with dreams of escape. The cold imagery of frozen ears, frozen horses, and frozen smoke symbolizes emotional and spiritual freezing, a life stunted by environment and circumstance.
  • A fat, soft-faced lady warns Vera about the desolation awaiting her destination. She describes it as a place “out of this world,” devoid of social life, communication, human contact, and filled with decay and death. This forewarning encapsulates themes of isolation, the death of community, and the futility of Vera’s quest. It also reflects the fear of entering a place where life is “chilling,” “numbing,” and where the “golden bowl was broken.”
  • The chapter recounts the tragic end of a young woman who jumped from the Brooklyn Bridge clutching her suitcase, her veil packed inside, disappearing into the dark waters. This vivid and haunting image captures the despair and finality of fate, especially those of the lower classes, and reinforces themes of loss, hopelessness, and the elusive nature of identity and love.
  • Toward the end, Vera expresses a yearning for a life filled with ordinary joys like family picnics, blossoming orchards, laughter of children, and a natural death after a long life. This vision contrasts with the dark hallucinations and self-deception that have plagued her. It symbolizes hope, renewal, and the possibility of healing from eternal mourning.
  • Vera questions whether she has made the “wrong choice” or if there is no real choice at all, reflecting on the many “turnings” and “windings” of her journey. This existential doubt touches on themes of destiny, free will, and the search for meaning amid confusion and despair.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Catherine offers Vera “my death in the midst of my life” and promises that “The years should bring me youth.” Why does she think stillness is the kindest gift she can give?
  • Vera dreams “of nothing but a shoemaker’s awl, an old tramp’s shoe which needed mending, a hammer, a nail.” Why does a rich girl dream of tools?
  • Vera tries to write a book but cannot compete with “four snails crawling across the open pages,” whose “writing was more beautiful than mine.” Why does she leave the book by the tide?
  • Miss MacIntosh’s Iowa is all frozen, down to the farmer brought ashore with his hands frozen to the reins. Then Vera says, “But this was not Iowa.” Whose Iowa is it?

Characters

  • Catherine’s offer is called “my mother’s greatest act of love, the only sign that she had a child.” How can a gift of oblivion be love?
  • The dead girl accepts the proposals of men she has never seen and describes herself differently to each. How is she like Vera, who sets out for a life she has read about in seed catalogues?
  • The fat lady on the train calls the Middle West “the jumping-off place, the end of the world.” Is she a false prophet, or does she know something Vera does not?

Connections

  • Vera calls herself “a Lazarus of these awakening joys.” Who or what does she hope will call her out of the tomb?
  • The chapter promises “the silver, the golden, never the leaden bells.” How do bells mark the stages of a life here and in the chapters before?
  • Miss MacIntosh “had given her life to prove that dreams were false,” yet Vera now lives by dreaming of her. How does the chapter turn the nursemaid herself into a dream?

Reflection

  • Vera says she came “because only of the unknown, because only of that which I had reached for, life, the unreachable.” Can a person set out for a place they have only imagined?
  • The old people are deaf because “they did not wish to hear,” their ears filled with “the roarings of the world inside.” What do people stop hearing when grief or age fills them?
  • “Time died when my love died.” How does grief change a person’s sense of time?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Deeply affected by Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance or death.
  • Battles between despair, illusions, and the desire for a meaningful life.
  • Struggles with her mother Catherine’s perception of her sanity.
  • Embodies themes of mourning, hope, and transformation.

Miss MacIntosh

  • The lost love, symbolizing a “normal life” and idealized domesticity.
  • Her disappearance is mysterious and traumatic.
  • Associated with innocence and unattainable dreams.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Acts as both caretaker and enforcer of oblivion.
  • Seeks to protect Vera by encouraging a withdrawal from life.
  • Represents acceptance of death in life and resignation.

Fat, soft-faced lady on the train

  • Provides a warning about the desolation of Vera’s destination.
  • Symbolizes the voice of experience and harsh reality.
  • Contrasts with Vera’s hope and romanticism.

Research: Themes

Loss and Mourning

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Vera is consumed by the loss of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Grief manifests as a somnolent, almost catatonic state, with Vera’s body described as “slothful and immense” and her mind “employed by nothing but the dream” of normalcy.
  • The loss is so profound that time seems to stop and Vera experiences a “long sleep of empty years.”

Reality vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine believes Vera is losing her sanity and attempts to have Vera “stilled and put away” through opium or drug-induced sleep, offering her an “opium paradise” as an escape from reality.
  • Catherine creates a vision of immortal beauty and oblivion for her daughter, likening her eventual state to an “embalmed corpse” or a nymph in a fairy grotto as a metaphor for eternal stasis and escape from pain.
  • Vera contrasts this illusion with her own experience, becoming “the creature of my own sorrow,” a “fat, stupid, indolent girl” whose sorrow isolates her from life.

Search for Meaning and Life

See: The Search for Meaning

  • Despite despair, Vera clings to memories and symbols of Miss MacIntosh, such as the ivory knitting needles found in the sand, and lights a fire on the beach to signal her lost love.
  • Vera undertakes a physical quest, talking to fishermen and sailors, symbolizing a search for connection and understanding in the vastness of the sea and life.
  • Ultimately, Vera seeks to reconcile with life, imagining a “charmed life” in a familiar, ordinary world of nature, community, and simple joys, such as family picnics, wildflowers, and children’s laughter.

The Burden of the Past and Hope for Renewal

See: Memory and the Past

  • Vera acknowledges the haunting presence of past memories and illusions but expresses hope for a new life free from these obsessions.
  • She envisions a future where the “dead past would be buried,” and she would awaken to the “blessed events” of life, including natural death after a long life filled with love and community.
  • The chapter returns again and again to the need to turn away from the insubstantial past toward the reality of life, even though it is fraught with disappointment and loss.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Red Hair and Red Rooster’s Wing

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Birds

  • Symbolizes vitality, passion, and the vividness of Miss MacIntosh’s presence.

Opium Paradise and Dream States

See: Opium

  • Represents escape from pain and reality.
  • The “sleeping wakefulness” blurs lines between life and death, reality and illusion.

Driftwood House and Fire on the Beach

See: The House · Fire

  • Symbolize Vera’s fragile hope and attempt to reach out to Miss MacIntosh or the lost past.

Frozen Iowa and Dead Star

See: Moon and Stars · Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Iowa represents the harsh, ordinary, and ultimately unwelcoming origin.
  • The “dead star” metaphor suggests a point of no return or a lost opportunity.

Nature’s Cruelty and Funeral Wreaths

See: Roses and Flowers · Weddings and Funerals

  • The natural world is depicted not as nurturing but cold and indifferent.
  • Funeral wreaths and deaf old people symbolize death, silence, and abandonment.

Further notes from the text

  • Catherine’s offer to Vera comes with a whole philosophy of not living: it is better to think of walking than to walk, better to think of dancing than to dance, and Vera should lie still as “the companion corpse of her eternal illness,” with an immortal beauty as her reward.
  • Years after the disappearance Vera finds Miss MacIntosh’s ivory knitting needles in the sand. She searches by sailboat and questions fishermen drying their nets, lobstermen red as the lobsters they trap, and codfish fishermen back from the Grand Banks.
  • Vera names herself formally here: daughter of Catherine Helena Cartwheel, née Snowden, “and of a father unknown, perhaps of many fathers.” She explains her own name, Vera, as standing for truth, and imagines the Midwest as a place where everyone will greet her by it.
  • Before she reaches Iowa she imagines it frozen: birds dying on crystal branches, smoke frozen in the chimneys, a farmer whose wagon went through the ice of a lake and who came ashore in spring with his hands frozen to the reins and his four horses rising through the foam. Then she admits this was not Iowa at all.
  • The bride who jumps from the Brooklyn Bridge had lost her father at three and was traveling a thousand miles to marry a stranger with a waxed mustache. She fell clutching her straw suitcase with her crushed veil inside. The waxed mustache links her to Vera’s dream bridegroom in Chapter 10.
  • The fat lady on the train adds folk consolations to her warnings: there are as many fish in the sea as were ever caught, and “there was a second husband for everybody.”

Research: Resources

  • “For those who died in the midst of life would never die”: The burial service of the Book of Common Prayer says, “In the midst of life we are in death,” from the medieval Latin chant Media vita in morte sumus. Catherine turns it around: Vera must accept “my death in the midst of my life.”
  • “She twirled her white umbrella in her swan boat”: The swan boat in the Boston Public Garden is real and has been in service since 1877. See Swan boats (Ch 4).
  • “Sometimes the sound of the sea was faded to a single cicada’s cry”: Periodical cicadas spend 13 or 17 years underground and then emerge by the millions in the same spring, filling the woods of the Middle West with their shrill song.
  • “not even if I walked on stilts like the stilt birds”: The black-necked stilt is a slender shorebird of marshes and salt pans whose very long pink legs let it wade deeper than other birds. See Birds.
  • “a poor invalid sleeping in a charity ward or under the roofless heavens”: Catherine repeats a fear from Chapter 2, where “Sometimes she thought she was a poor patient sleeping in a charity ward.” See the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “the inexhaustible jewels of Golconda”: Golconda, in southern India, was the market for the diamond fields that produced the Koh-i-Noor and the Hope diamond, and its name came to mean any source of endless wealth.
  • “filagreed coral reefs, sapphire pavements”: In Exodus 24:10 the elders of Israel see the God of Israel, “and there was under his feet as it were a paved work of a sapphire stone, and as it were the body of heaven in his clearness.” See The Bible.
  • “like a nymph in a mountain cave . . . the fairy grotto where the lone traveller is lured”: In Keats’s “La Belle Dame sans Merci” (1819), a knight is lured by a fairy lady to “her elfin grot” and wakes alone on a cold hillside. See Romantic Poets.
  • “the opium paradise which should bring the power of wakeful sleep”: Thomas De Quincey’s Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821) described the dreams and torments of opium, and Charles Baudelaire’s Artificial Paradises (1860) took up the same theme. See Opium.
  • “I should be the greatest debutante of any season”: A debutante was a young woman formally presented to society, usually at a ball at the start of the winter season, to show that she was ready for marriage. Her “coming-out party” was the great event of a rich girl’s youth.
  • “white satin slippers with paper soles such as are worn by the dead who have not far to travel”: Undertakers sold burial slippers with soles of cardboard or paper, made only to be seen in the coffin.
  • “or perhaps a thousand canaries blown here by the storm and singing in the candle flames”: In Chapter 2 Catherine’s canary Marco Polo flew out through an open transom into a thunderstorm. See the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “the routine of Monday following Sunday, Tuesday following Monday, the washings on the lines . . . baking day”: The old household week ran by a fixed round of chores, washing on Monday, ironing on Tuesday, mending on Wednesday, and baking later in the week, as in the nursery rhyme, “They that wash on Monday / Have all the week to dry.”
  • “knitting for the mission at some far Arctic post”: Church women across America knitted mittens, sweaters, and hoods for missions such as the Grenfell Mission of Labrador and Newfoundland, founded by the doctor Wilfred Grenfell in the 1890s.
  • “I did not dream I lived in marble halls, for I lived in marble halls”: The line turns the song “I Dreamt I Dwelt in Marble Halls” from Michael Balfe’s opera The Bohemian Girl (1843), in which a lost noble girl raised by Gypsies dreams of the riches she was born to.
  • “the red-faced lobster-trappers red as the lobsters they trapped”: Live lobsters are a dark greenish brown. They turn bright red only when cooked, as the heat frees the red pigment that a protein in the shell had kept hidden.
  • “codfish fishermen returning from the Great Banks”: The Grand Banks off Newfoundland were for centuries the richest cod grounds in the world. In Young’s day the schooners of Gloucester and Boston still sailed to the Banks for cod, and many never came home.
  • “to sailors of the deep, to all who were wayfarers of the sea”: Psalm 107:23-24 reads, “They that go down to the sea in ships, that do business in great waters; These see the works of the Lord, and his wonders in the deep.”
  • “the night shrouded the night of the soul”: The phrase recalls “the dark night of the soul,” from the poem of the sixteenth-century Spanish mystic Saint John of the Cross, the soul’s passage through darkness and desolation toward God.
  • “that was why she wore ear muffs”: Earmuffs were invented in 1873 by Chester Greenwood of Farmington, Maine, a fifteen-year-old whose ears froze while he skated. Miss MacIntosh wore hers against Iowa winters so cold that “the children’s ears were frozen.”
  • “when the great boomers were booming”: The ice of a frozen lake booms and groans as it cracks and shifts with the changing temperature, especially in spring as it begins to break up.
  • “the promised land of which I had read in catalogues of wild flowers and seed catalogues”: The Promised Land is the land God promised Israel, “a land flowing with milk and honey” (Exodus 3:8). Seed catalogues such as W. Atlee Burpee’s, begun in 1876, brought pictures of gardens and orchards to farm families across the country. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “There would be cherry and apple and peach and persimmon trees”: The wild persimmon grows across southern Indiana, where its fruit, sweet only when fully ripe, often after the first frost, is made into persimmon pudding. Mitchell, Indiana, has held a Persimmon Festival since 1946.
  • “old rail fences broken down by the wild mares”: Split-rail fences, built of logs split lengthwise, zigzagged across the frontier Midwest. Abraham Lincoln grew up in southern Indiana from 1816 to 1830, and his campaign of 1860 sold him as “the rail-splitter.”
  • “All people would greet me by my name, Vera, that which stands for truth”: Vera means “true” in Latin and “faith” in Russian. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “I would be a Lazarus of these awakening joys”: Lazarus of Bethany, brother of Martha and Mary, was raised from the dead by Jesus after being dead for four days. This miracle is a central event in the Gospel of John (John 11). The story of Lazarus’s raising highlights the close relationship between Jesus and his friends, as well as Jesus’s power over death. The miracle was a powerful sign of Jesus’s divine authority and his identity as the Messiah as well as a symbol of the promise of eternal life through faith in Jesus. Lazarus in this context represents Vera’s yearning for a new beginning, a restored life beyond the illusions and failures of the past, where she can experience reality as it is lived by ordinary people, with the natural rhythms of life and death, love, and community. See Lazarus of Bethany (Ch 4).
  • “births and weddings and wedding anniversaries, natural death at the end of a long life, the silver, the golden”: Silver and golden weddings mark the twenty-fifth and fiftieth anniversaries of a marriage, a custom that began in Germany, where a wife was given a wreath of silver or of gold.
  • “the silver, the golden, never the leaden bells”: Bells in this chapter symbolize the presence of death and the funeral rites permeating the house, the relentless passage of time and the cycle of life and death, a link between the material and spiritual worlds, calling attention to the unseen and the spectral, the deep, underlying melancholy that shadows the characters’ lives and the house itself. Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “The Bells” (1849) moves through the same stages of life, from silver sleigh bells and golden wedding bells to brazen alarm bells and the iron bells of the funeral. See Bells (Ch 4) and Edgar Allan Poe.
  • “the burning brimstone butterfly and the pebble moth”: The brimstone butterfly is named for its sulfur-yellow wings, and some think the butter-colored brimstone gave the word butterfly its name. The pebble prominent is a grey-brown moth of willows and poplars. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “a ribbon to the youngest baby, a medal to the oldest citizen”: County fairs and the Indiana State Fair, held since 1852, gave ribbons for babies, livestock, pies, and quilts, and the small-town celebration honored its oldest citizen.
  • “from the insubstantial fabric of old days, old nights”: The phrase returns from Chapter 3, where Miss MacIntosh “dismissed the insubstantial fabric of the dream,” an echo of Prospero in The Tempest. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “because of a dead girl’s love letters strewn on the floor of a room like a cell”: The dead girl first appears in Chapter 1, where Vera lists her among the reasons for her journey. Here her story is told in full. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “each accepting the proposal of a man she had never seen”: Matrimonial newspapers and lonely hearts clubs printed letters from men and women seeking marriage, often farmers in remote country, and many couples married after corresponding without ever having met.
  • “marriage, the union of body with soul, children, chickens, a little farm with a vine-covered gate”: The reality for women at that time was they had to be married or they were nothing. There were no other prospects. Marriage and a family was the most important event in a woman’s life and a wedding was every girl’s dream until very recently in the United States.
  • “waxen brides in their wedding gowns with their long trains and veils”: The white wedding gown became the fashion after Queen Victoria wore white satin at her wedding in 1840. The dead girl has “no father who would give her away,” the old custom in which the bride passes from her father to her husband.
  • “who wore a waxed mustache, an old-fashioned handlebar”: The stranger’s handlebar matches the one in “her portrait at the age of three in the arms of her father who had worn an old-fashioned handlebar.” She is going a thousand miles to marry a man who looks like the father she lost.
  • “her mother who had been an Irish wash woman”: Irish immigrant women, many of them fleeing the famine of the 1840s, made up a large share of the laundresses and domestic servants in nineteenth-century American cities.
  • “under a shower of rice and old shoes”: Guests threw rice at a wedding couple as a wish for fertility and plenty, and old shoes were thrown after them or tied to their carriage for luck.
  • “for Grand Central Station”: The Chapter 2 resources tell the history of Grand Central. See Grand Central Station (Ch 4).
  • “she had jumped from Brooklyn Bridge”: The first man known to jump from the Brooklyn Bridge, Robert Odlum, died doing it in 1885, two years after the bridge opened, and many have taken their lives there since. Hart Crane, whose long poem The Bridge celebrates it, drowned himself in 1932 by leaping from a ship in the Gulf of Mexico. See The Brooklyn Bridge (Ch 4) and Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “she would go to Boise or Reno, where she had gone to get her divorces”: In 1931 Nevada cut the residency required for a divorce to six weeks, and Idaho soon matched it. Reno became the divorce capital of America, and its “divorce ranches” housed women waiting out their weeks. See Women, Gender, and Marriage.
  • “there were just as many fishes in the sea as ever were caught”: The old proverb, “There are plenty more fish in the sea,” is the usual consolation for a lost love.
  • “there were bats in every broken belfry”: To have bats in the belfry, an American expression from about 1900, is to be crazy, the bats flitting about in an empty head.
  • “there were funeral wreaths hanging on all the doors”: A wreath or a band of black crepe hung on the front door announced a death in the house and asked passersby for quiet. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “The voice of the turtle-dove was not heard in all that land, for the golden bowl was broken and the wheel broken at the cistern”: The lady reverses the Song of Solomon, “the voice of the turtle is heard in our land” (2:12), and quotes Ecclesiastes 12:6, “or the golden bowl be broken, or the pitcher be broken at the fountain, or the wheel broken at the cistern.” That chapter of Ecclesiastes describes old age and failing senses, “and all the daughters of musick shall be brought low,” which fits the deaf old people. Henry James took the title of his novel The Golden Bowl (1904) from it. See Ecclesiastes.
  • “Nobody knew what time it was, for all the clocks were stopped”: An old custom stopped the clocks of a house at the moment of a death. In Dickens’s Great Expectations, Miss Havisham stopped every clock at twenty minutes to nine, the moment she was jilted on her wedding day. See Clocks and Watches.
  • “carrying old-fashioned ear trumpets which they did not turn on”: Before electric hearing aids, the hard of hearing held horn-shaped ear trumpets to their ears to gather sound. Beethoven used them as his deafness grew. See Silence and Deafness.
  • “their ears were mere empty shells filled with no roarings of the outside world”: The image recalls the Chapter 3 entry on the roar heard in a shell, the sound of the room caught inside. Here the shells are empty. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “they had taken quinine to cure their malaria”: Quinine is an alkaloid, a naturally occurring compound, extracted from the bark of the cinchona tree. Quinine was historically and remains an important medication for treating malaria. Quinine’s bitter taste makes it a component of tonic water and some other beverages. Historically, this usage originated from mixing medicinal quinine with soda and sugar to mask its bitterness for malaria prevention in tropical regions. Quinine here is both a literal reference to the antimalarial drug and a symbolic element illustrating unintended suffering and the complex nature of healing and illness in the novel’s landscape. Large doses of quinine cause cinchonism, whose symptoms include ringing in the ears and hearing loss, so the cure really could have deafened them. See Quinine (Ch 4).
  • “caused by the festerings in the river bottoms, the marsh butterflies”: Malaria, called the ague, plagued the river bottoms of nineteenth-century Indiana and Illinois. People blamed the bad air of the marshes until Ronald Ross showed in 1897 that mosquitoes carry the disease. The Chapter 3 resources explain malaria’s name, mal aria, “bad air.”

Vocabulary

Awl
A small pointed tool for piercing leather, used by shoemakers.
Belfry
A bell tower, or the room in a tower where the bells hang.
Brackish
Of water: slightly salty, as where a river meets the sea.
Brimstone
Sulfur. The brimstone butterfly is named for its sulfur-yellow wings.
Cat’s eye
A gemstone, such as chrysoberyl, with a band of light across it like the slit of a cat’s eye.
Cistern
A tank for storing water, often underground.
Crow’s feet
The small wrinkles at the outer corners of the eyes.
Debutante
A young woman making her formal entrance into society.
Diadem
A jeweled crown or headband worn as a sign of royalty.
Ear trumpet
A horn-shaped tube held to the ear to help the hard of hearing.
Ermine
The white winter fur of the stoat, used to trim the robes of kings and nobles.
Ethereal
Light, airy, and delicate, as if not of this world; heavenly.
Festering
Rotting and oozing; growing more corrupt.
Filigree
Delicate ornamental work of fine twisted wire. Young writes “filagreed.”
Fire opal
A red, orange, or yellow opal with flashes of color.
Fishmonger
A seller of fish.
Foolhardy
Recklessly bold.
Freighter
A ship that carries cargo.
Handlebar
A mustache with long ends curled upward like the handlebars of a bicycle.
Hawking
Hunting with trained hawks or falcons.
Hectagonal
Young’s word, probably a slip for hexagonal (six-sided) or heptagonal (seven-sided). Quartz crystals grow in six-sided columns.
Hoar-frost
White frost formed as feathery ice crystals.
Husbanded
Kept carefully; conserved.
Ice floe
A sheet of floating ice.
Imperceptibly
So slowly or slightly as to go unnoticed.
Indolent
Lazy; avoiding effort.
Lapis lazuli
A deep-blue stone, ground by painters to make the pigment ultramarine.
Matrimony
Marriage.
Moonstone
A milky, pearly-blue gemstone.
Née
Born; used before a woman’s maiden name. Young writes “nee.”
Negligee
A woman’s light, flowing dressing gown.
Noxious
Harmful or poisonous.
Oblivion
The state of being forgotten, or of being unaware of everything.
Owlishly
Like an owl; staring wide-eyed and solemn.
Prism
A clear piece of glass with flat sides that splits light into the colors of the rainbow.
Scudding
Moving fast before the wind.
Slumberous
Sleepy; inducing sleep.
Somnolent
Sleepy; causing sleep.
Spar
A pole used as a ship’s mast, boom, or yard. Spar is also the name for certain shiny, easily split crystalline minerals, such as Iceland spar.
Squall
A sudden, violent gust of wind, often with rain or snow.
Tallow
Animal fat used for candles and soap. Tallow-colored is a dull, yellowish white.
Tributary
A stream or river that flows into a larger one.
Turtle-dove
A small wild dove. The “turtle” of the Bible’s “voice of the turtle” is this bird.
Undulating
Rising and falling in waves.
Vapid
Dull and empty of life or interest.
Vaunted
Boasted of; praised highly.
Wayfarer
A traveler, especially on foot.
chapter-62:
Chapter 62

← Chapter 61 · Home · Chapter 63 →

Summary

Mr. Spitzer dreams of rowing down a river that turns from fire to ice. He rewrites his will, leaving his music to the world. He learns the full story of the silent violinist from the library steps, and remembers a clarinetist who killed himself, leaving a note that he was going to join a greater orchestra. Crossing Louisburg Square, he is startled to learn he is in Boston and not Philadelphia.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · The Old Horn-Blower · The Old Violinist · The Pack Rat

Concepts present

Symbols: Eyes and Blindness · Fire · Fireflies · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica

Allusions: Astronomy · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Music and Composers · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Mr. Spitzer dreams of rowing down a river that transforms from molten fire to frozen ice, surrounded by fantastical imagery: old walruses, seals with diamond necklaces, seagulls turning into musicians, and a great water orchestra. This symbolizes the fluid, transformative nature of reality, music, and life itself, flowing, burning, freezing, and shimmering between states, much like the elusive nature of perfect sleep and death which he never attains. This dreamscape is laden with surreal and symbolic images that represent the merging of reality and illusion, life and death, music and silence.
  • Mr. Spitzer rewrites his will meticulously, with instructions reflecting his eccentric personality and his deep connection to his music and to the world around him. The will includes bequests of his musical works to the world "even to indifferent ears and even to deaf ears and even to dead ears and to sea conches"; this shows his acceptance of obscurity and his desire for his music to endure beyond his earthly life. The will also contains poetic and mysterious instructions, such as leaving secretive eggs and milk, and canceling subscriptions, which reflect his detachment from worldly affairs but attachment to ritual and symbolism. The will is an act of final artistic and existential expression, blending legal formality with poetic imagination.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on how music, like life, is fleeting and imperfect, filled with unplayable notes, paradoxes, and silent chords. He contemplates how his compositions incorporate sounds of nature, cosmic events, and the elusive music of the dead or music that can never be fully realized or heard. This passage explores the metaphysical nature of music as both creation and loss, as something that connects the living and the dead, the real and the imagined. He acknowledges that no music is ever played exactly as composed, and that silence may be the truest form of music, an idea that profoundly illustrates the fragility and mystery of artistic expression.
  • The story of the old horn-blower who has tuberculosis caused by his relentless playing of his instrument is a poignant metaphor for the physical and spiritual toll of devotion to art. Despite his suffering, the horn-blower cannot stop because music is both his love and his torment. Mr. Spitzer’s sympathy and sorrow for the horn-blower highlight the paradox of artistic creation that it can be both life-giving and life-destroying. The horn-blower’s determination to "blow on" even unto death embodies the tragic dedication of the artist.
  • Mr. Spitzer recounts the tragic suicide of a clarinetist who felt "out of tune" despite reassurances of his perfection. This introduces the theme of alienation and despair among musicians who cannot reconcile their inner experiences with external reality. The clarinetist’s note about joining a "greater orchestra" evokes the hope or belief in a transcendent musical realm beyond this life. It also inspires Mr. Spitzer’s thoughts about an orchestra that includes all lost and unheard music, suggesting an eternal, cosmic harmony that surpasses earthly limitations.
  • This surreal image of an old violinist silently playing an invisible violin with imaginary bow gestures symbolizes pure artistic expression divorced from physical constraints. Mr. Spitzer recognizes this as perhaps the "best music", the music of silence, the unplayed and unplayable music that expresses the ineffable. The violinist’s story of having been a second violinist who never actually touched his strings, and who was dismissed after accidentally producing a "false note," highlights themes of illusion, invisibility, and injustice in the artistic world. It represents the paradox of the artist’s life: the tension between visibility and invisibility, reality and performance, acceptance and rejection.
  • Mr. Spitzer muses on the nature of memory and time, suggesting that events must happen twice to be real, that memory is inherently inaccurate, and that past and present coexist in complex ways. This philosophical reflection ties into the themes of music and life as cyclical, ephemeral, and intertwined with illusion and reality. The idea that memories may come from an "alien source" adds a mystical dimension to his understanding of self and art.
  • In the closing sections, Mr. Spitzer contemplates the ultimate silence that surrounds all music and life. He considers silence not as mere absence but as a profound presence, "more silent than the grave." The chapter ends with a scene of Mr. Spitzer almost applauding the silent music of the old violinist and his recognition that music may never fully be heard or understood but still holds profound beauty and meaning. The passage also touches on his existential confusion and isolation, highlighted by the moment he forgets where he is, symbolizing disconnection from reality.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Joachim Spitzer

  • A retired lawyer and musician, described as a composer and conductor of a unique “water music.” He is deeply reflective, often dreaming and contemplating his life, music, and the cosmos. He appears to be a symbol of the artist’s struggle and existential quest.

The Old Horn-Blower

  • A tragic figure who blows his horn despite having tuberculosis, symbolizing devotion to art even unto death.

The Old Violinist

  • A member of the Philadelphia Symphony who never touched his strings, symbolizing the paradox of illusion and reality in art.

The Pack Rat

  • A metaphorical figure that steals scraps but returns something in exchange, symbolizing the cycle of loss and gain in creativity or life.

Research: Themes

  • The elusive nature of sleep and death.
  • The interplay between reality and illusion.
  • Music as a metaphor for life, death, and cosmic order.
  • The struggle of the artist to realize and communicate his vision.
  • The persistence of memory and identity beyond physical existence.
  • The concept of silence and the unplayable music of the spheres.
  • The loneliness and alienation of the creative genius.
  • The inevitability of loss and the quest for immortality through art.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Water and Rivers

See: The Sea and Water

  • Metaphors for the flow of life, time, and reality. The river transforms from fire to ice, representing change and the cyclical nature of existence.

Music and Instruments

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represent creation, communication, and the ineffable aspects of life. Music is described as complex, sometimes unplayable, and deeply tied to natural phenomena like waves, wind, and stars.

Stars and Celestial Bodies

See: Moon and Stars

  • Symbols of eternity, the unknown, and the cosmic order. The constellation Orion and others are referenced as markers of time and existence.

The Pack Rat

  • Symbolizes the artist’s daily struggle, the exchange between loss and gain, and the persistence of creativity.

The Old Oil Lamp with Bull’s-Eye

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Eyes and Blindness

  • Represents the faint, fragile light of consciousness and creativity amid darkness.

Silence

See: Silence and Deafness

  • A recurring motif representing the ultimate music, the space before and after sound, and the mystery of existence.

The Firefly

See: Fireflies

  • Symbolizes fragile life and the fleeting nature of existence and memory.

Dream of the River of Fire and Ice

See: The Sea and Water · Snow, Ice, and Winter · Fire

  • Reflects the shifting states of reality and consciousness, the tension between light and darkness, life and death.

Mr. Spitzer’s Will

  • Symbolizes the artist’s legacy and the desire to give all his music freely to the world, with an emphasis on the music being played only on water, highlighting the connection between music and nature.

The Old Horn-Blower’s Lament

See: Music and Instruments

  • Highlights the tragic devotion to art despite physical decline, embodying sacrifice and the inevitability of death.

The Suicidal Clarinetist

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represents the torment of the artist who perceives himself as “out of tune” with the world, and the concept of a “greater orchestra” beyond life.

The Old Violinist Who Never Touched Strings

See: Music and Instruments

  • A powerful metaphor for the paradox between appearance and reality in art, and the pain of exclusion for breaking the illusion.

Music of Silence and Memory

See: Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness

  • Explores the impossibility of perfect memory and the idea that music, like life, is ephemeral and incomplete, and that silence may be the truest form of music.

Mr. Spitzer’s Final Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Contemplate the nature of truth, memory, and existence, emphasizing that all experiences may be repetitions or illusions, and the loneliness intrinsic to human life and creativity.

Research: Resources

  • “Sometimes Mr. Spitzer wondered if he had ever really slept.” This is a richly symbolic and dreamlike meditation on the nature of sleep, death, and reality as experienced by Mr. Spitzer. It expresses his profound uncertainty about whether he has ever truly experienced perfect sleep or death, suggesting that both are illusions that elude him personally. This sets a tone of existential questioning and disorientation that pervades much of the novel. Mr. Spitzer’s dreams are vivid and surreal, featuring intense transformations of natural elements. These images evoke a fluid boundary between opposites such as life and death, warmth and cold, light and darkness. The river of fire and river of ice symbolize continual change and the merging of contradictions, reflecting the novel’s themes of flux and ambiguity. The imagery creates a haunting, otherworldly scene. The juxtaposition of natural arctic animals with opulent, human settings blends the real with the surreal, the living with the symbolic, underscoring the theme of blurred boundaries between reality and illusion. The final reflection that all these rivers might be one great river of reality flowing and transforming encapsulates the novel’s exploration of existence as a continuous, mutable process rather than fixed states. The image of a "burning star in the frozen cloud" as another star above ice pinnacles suggests a cosmic dimension to this ongoing transformation, linking the personal experience of Mr. Spitzer to universal cycles of life, death, and rebirth. This paragraph encapsulates key motifs of the novel: the elusive nature of sleep and death, the interplay of opposites and transformation, and the blending of dream imagery with reality to explore profound philosophical questions about existence. It conveys Mr. Spitzer’s inner turmoil and his attempt to make sense of a world where boundaries are fluid and certainty is impossible.
  • Arcturus is the brightest star in the northern constellation of Bootes.
  • The instruments serve as a rich symbolic network that conveys the novel's deep meditation on the nature of existence, the limits of human understanding, the transient beauty of life and art, and the enduring but often silent music of the soul. The musical imagery ties together themes of memory, loss, death, creativity, and the eternal quest for meaning amidst chaos and silence
  • viola da gamba is a bowed, fretted string instrument that was popular during the Renaissance and Baroque periods and is held between the legs. It belongs to the viol family, is distinct from the cello, and typically has six or seven strings tuned in fourths with a major third in the middle. Key features include frets on the fingerboard to aid intonation, a softer and brighter sound than a cello, and a flat back with sloping shoulders.
  • violoncello (or cello) is a large, bowed string instrument in the violin family, played sitting down with the instrument held between the knees.
  • naiads - In Greek mythology, the naiads, sometimes also hydriads, are a type of female spirit, or nymph, presiding over fountains, wells, springs, streams, brooks and other bodies of fresh water.
  • piccolo - is a type of small, shrill woodwind instrument. The instrument is a small version of a flute played an octave higher.
  • hautboy - is an oboe or similar treble double reed instrument.
  • harpsichord - is a keyboard instrument that produces sound by plucking strings with a plectrum when a key is pressed, unlike the piano which strikes strings with hammers. It was a dominant keyboard instrument during the Renaissance and Baroque eras and is known for its distinctive sound.
  • Hyperborean means a member of a people in Greek mythology who lived in perpetual sunshine.
  • phaeton - Phaëton was the son of the sun god Helios (or Phoebus) in Greek mythology. He asked to prove his parentage by driving his father's sun chariot, but his lack of skill caused the horses to run wild, burning the earth and creating deserts. Zeus eventually struck him with a thunderbolt to stop him. Horse-drawn light, open, four-wheeled carriage popular in the 18th and 19th centuries. It was owner-driven (no outside driver's seat) and often had a folding top. An open-style car without fixed weather protection, similar to its horse-drawn predecessor.
  • Paraselene or Moon dog or mock moon is an atmospheric optical phenomenon which consists of a bright spot on one or both sides of a full moon.
  • largo - is an Italian term that means "slow and broad" and indicates a very slow tempo.
  • barcarolle - is a folk song of Venetian gondoliers, which is imitated in classical music to create a gently rocking rhythm, often in 6/8 or 12/8 time. The most famous examples are Jacques Offenbach's "Barcarolle" from the opera The Tales of Hoffmann and Frédéric Chopin's Barcarolle, Op. 60 for solo piano.
  • The Boston Evening Transcript was a daily afternoon newspaper in Boston, Massachusetts, published from 1830 to 1941. It is no longer in publication, with its final issue printed on April 30, 1941.
  • sea gannet - is a large seabird, most commonly referring to the Northern Gannet, known for its spectacular plunge-diving to catch fish. These birds are white with black and gold markings and spend their lives at sea, only coming to land to nest.
  • Pasteurized milk is milk that has been heated to kill harmful bacteria and other pathogens, making it safe to drink without risk of serious illness from harmful microbes. This process, named after Louis Pasteur, involves heating milk to a specific temperature for a set time, such as 145 degrees for 30 minutes or 161 degrees for 15 seconds, before cooling it down and packaging it. Pasteurization significantly extends shelf life and is the gold standard for milk safety, with most commercially available milk being pasteurized.
  • Pledge of Allegiance - is a patriotic recited verse that promises allegiance to the flag of the United States and the republic of the United States. The first version was written in 1885 by Captain George Thatcher Balch, a Union army officer in the Civil War who later authored a book on how to teach patriotism to children in public schools. In 1892, Francis Bellamy revised Balch's verse as part of a magazine promotion surrounding the World's Columbian Exposition, which celebrated the 400th anniversary of Christopher Columbus' arrival in the Americas. Bellamy, the circulation manager for The Youth's Companion magazine, helped persuade then-president Benjamin Harrison to institute Columbus Day as a national holiday and lobbied Congress for a national school celebration of the day. The magazine sent leaflets containing part of Bellamy's Pledge of Allegiance to schools across the country and on October 21, 1892, over 10,000 children recited the verse together. Bellamy's version of the pledge is largely the same as the one formally adopted by Congress 50 years later, in 1942. The official name of The Pledge of Allegiance was adopted in 1945. The most recent alteration of its wording came on Flag Day (June 14) in 1954, when the words "under God" were added. However, Bellamy's authorship has been contested, as evidence has come out contradicting his claim. Several countries have a form of national pledge or oath, though the practice of daily, mandatory recitation in schools (as commonly associated with the US) is unusual by international standards. In many nations, oaths are typically reserved for specific occasions like citizenship ceremonies or for public officials.
  • "golden cock-of-the-rock and dance of the golden cock-of-the-rock" It is a metaphor for a powerful, transformative force, both earthly and cosmic that embodies life’s vitality, the passage of time, and the spiritual or mystical dimensions underlying existence. This interpretation aligns with the novel’s broader themes, where imagery of birds, especially cocks and roosters, recur as symbols of time, change, and the boundary between life and death. The golden cock-of-the-rock's dance may thus represent the dynamic, sometimes mysterious forces that govern the characters’ experiences and the novel’s dreamlike atmosphere. The phrase symbolizes a potent, golden, life-affirming yet elusive force expressed through dance, evoking awakening, cosmic rhythms, and transformation within the novel's complex symbolic universe.
  • Northwest of Ursa Major, the Great Bear, is the constellation Camelopardalis. Camelopardalis is a large, faint constellation that borders the northwestern part of the Great Bear.
  • Harvard University's history began in 1636 when the Massachusetts Bay Colony founded it as New College to train clergy. It was renamed Harvard College in 1639 after its first major benefactor, clergyman John Harvard, and has since grown into the oldest institution of higher learning in the United States, renowned for its academic prestige, wealth, and influence.
  • At Harvard, graduating magna cum laude is a distinction awarded to students with "great distinction," typically those in the top 15% of their class. It is a Latin honor determined by a combination of departmental recommendations for High or Highest Honors and college-wide GPA cutoffs, which are set annually.
  • The New England Conservatory of Music (NEC) was founded in Boston, Massachusetts, in 1867 by Eben Tourjée, making it the oldest independent music school in the United States. From its beginnings in a few rented rooms above the Boston Music Hall, the conservatory grew into a major music institution with a celebrated venue, Jordan Hall, which was granted National Historic Landmark status jointly with the NEC in 1994. Over its history, NEC has become a global leader in music education, known for its innovative approach and for attracting influential musicians as faculty and students.
  • Pop concert in the Great Shell - may refer to Edward A. Hatch Memorial Shell, commonly referred to as the Hatch Shell, is an outdoor concert venue on the Charles River Esplanade in the Back Bay section of Boston, Massachusetts. Built in 1939–1940, it is one of the city's prominent examples of Art Deco architecture. The Hatch Shell is best known for hosting the Boston Pops annually for the Boston Fourth of July celebration, but is also used for free concerts most weekends and many weeknights during the summer months. The grass pavilion in front of the stage has no permanent seating. There is a memorial nearby to Arthur Fiedler, first permanent conductor of the Pops.
  • Haydn’s Creation or The Creation is an oratorio written by Haydn and considered to be one of his masterpieces. It is a celebration of the creation of the world as in the Book of Genesis.
  • Johann Strauss’s Boston Dreams may refer to 1872 when Strauss visited America and Boston built a stadium that sat 100,000 people.
  • Gustave Pick’s Fiacre Song may refer to Gustav Pick’s Fiakerlied which is a Viennese song.
  • “old trot, trot sheet music” may refer to Trot, an old-style Korean pop music genre that emerged in the early 1900s, characterized by a repetitive, simple beat and ornamented, emotive vocals. It was influenced by Western dance styles like the foxtrot, Japanese enka, and Korean folk melodies, blending them into a unique style that expresses emotions like sadness, endurance, and hope.
  • gondolieri - is the Italian word for the gondola boatmen of Venice.
  • emoluments - a salary, fee, or profit from employment or office.
  • mortmain - is a French term meaning "dead hand," is a legal concept referring to the perpetual, inalienable ownership of land by a corporation, such as a church or charity. Historically, this practice was disfavored because it removed land from the feudal system and deprived lords of valuable feudal incidents. To curb this, Statutes of Mortmain were enacted to regulate or prohibit the transfer of land to corporations without a license.
  • Orion - Orion is a constellation visible globally and features the famous Orion's Belt. The Orion Nebula, a stellar nursery within it, is one of the brightest in the sky. In Greek myth, Orion was a giant and mighty hunter. His death story varies, but most legends involve his death by the bow of Artemis or a scorpion's sting, after which he was placed in the heavens.
  • Taurus - In astrology, Taurus (April 20–May 20) is the second sign of the zodiac, representing the bull and associated with being grounded, practical, and sensual. As a constellation, it's one of the oldest and most recognizable in the night sky, visible in the Northern Hemisphere and home to the Pleiades and Hyades star clusters.
  • wentletrap - Wentletraps are small, often white, very high-spired, predatory or ectoparasitic sea snails, marine gastropod mollusks in the family Epitoniidae. The word wentletrap originated in Dutch, and it means spiral staircase. These snails are sometimes also called "staircase shells", and "ladder shells".
  • Pleiades - also known as the Seven Sisters, refers to both a prominent star cluster in the constellation Taurus and the seven daughters of Atlas and Pleione in Greek mythology. The star cluster is about 100 million years old and consists of thousands of stars, with six or seven visible to the naked eye. Its bright blue stars and visibility in the winter night sky have made it a significant feature in cultures around the world for centuries.
  • Hyades - the mythological sisters were associated with rain, and after their brother Hyas died, they were transformed into the star cluster, which also became known as "the Rainy Ones". The star cluster is the closest one to Earth, appears as a V-shape that forms the face of Taurus, and includes the bright star Aldebaran (though Aldebaran is not a true member).
  • fritillaries - are a type of butterfly and a genus of flowering plants known for their checkered patterns.
  • Coronachs are a song or hymn of mourning composed or performed as a memorial to a dead person.
  • coradicorn - may refer to a Cormorant which is an aquatic bird.
  • Cocytus is the river of wailing in the underworld in Greek mythology.
  • old Polish kings - spans from the first crowned king, Bolesław I the Brave, in 1025, to the last elected king of the Polish– Lithuanian Commonwealth. Key dynasties include the Piast dynasty, which ruled from the kingdom's founding until 1370, followed by the Jagiellonian dynasty after 1386. A significant aspect of Polish monarchy was the elective monarchy, where kings were chosen by the nobility, a unique system in Europe from the 16th to the 18th centuries.
  • old Laplander emperors - There is no historical record of "Laplander emperors" because Lapland (Sápmi) was never an independent empire with its own emperors. The term "Laplander" is outdated, and the indigenous Sámi people are historically part of the regions now known as Finland, Sweden, Norway, and Russia. Historically, the region was loosely governed by various authorities, and as part of larger empires like Sweden and Russia, its administration was managed by those states.
  • old Siberian kings - There was no unified "Siberian monarchy" or single line of "Siberian kings" in the modern sense. Instead, Siberian rulers were organized into various khanates, with the most prominent being the Khanate of Sibir, ruled by competing dynasties like the Taibugids and Shaybanids. The most famous "Siberian king" in this context was Khan Kuchum, the last ruler of the Khanate of Sibir, who was defeated by the Cossack Yermak Timofeyevich, leading to the Russian conquest of the region. The House of Sibirsky was the foremost of many Genghisid families formerly living in Russia. It traced its descent from Kuchum, the last of the Siberian khans. Kuchum's sons were captured by Yermak's Cossacks and brought to Muscovy, where they were settled in Yaroslavl and other towns and were authorized to style themselves Tsarevichs of Siberia. Kuchum's grandson Alp-Arslan was even installed as a puppet khan of Kasimov between 1614 and 1627. In 1591, the son of Kuchum, Abul Khayir was the first of his dynasty to convert to Christianity. His conversion was followed by the conversion of his entire family who eventually assimilated into the Russian nobility. In 1686, the tsar decreed that the dynasties of the king of Imeretia in the Caucasus along with the princes of Siberia and Kasimov were to be entered into the Genealogical Book of the Russian nobility. The tsarevichs married into the best Russian families. One of their princesses was the wife of Peter the Great's maternal uncle, another married a son of the Georgian king.
  • Queen Victoria in her youth - Queen Victoria's youth was marked by a highly isolated upbringing under the "Kensington System," a set of strict rules designed to keep her under the control of her mother and her advisor, Sir John Conroy. Despite her controlled childhood, she pursued hobbies like painting, drawing, writing in her diary, and singing.
  • Leaning Tower of Pisa - construction started in 1173 on the bell tower for the Pisa Cathedral. Construction halted for nearly a century, a delay that allowed the soil to settle and prevented its early collapse. The tower was completed in 1372 after architects attempted to compensate for the lean by making the upper floors taller on one side. Modern efforts in the 1990s stabilized the tower and reduced its tilt to about 4 degrees, a lean that is now intentionally preserved.
  • "Russian Imperials" refers to the Russian Empire, a vast Eurasian state that existed from 1721 to 1917, ruled by autocratic emperors known as "czars" or "tsars".   • "Kolokol" is a Russian word for "bell" and can refer to several things, including the historical newspaper Kolokol edited by Alexander Herzen, the Kolokol Group of volcanoes in Russia's Kuril Islands, the Tsar Bell (also called Tsar Kolokol) in the Moscow Kremlin, or an incapacitating agent known as Kolokol-1.
  • "Crowned griffins" may refer to a symbol of power in heraldry and art, an emblem used for regions like Kashubia, or a creature with a crown in a specific context like a game or a piece of jewelry.   • first flight of the Wright brothers - The Wright brothers made the first controlled, sustained flight of a powered, heavier-than-air aircraft on December 17, 1903, at Kill Devil Hills near Kitty Hawk, North Carolina.   • Nineveh - Nineveh was a major ancient city and the capital of the Neo-Assyrian Empire, located on the eastern bank of the Tigris River, across from modern-day Mosul, Iraq.   • Galatea - In Greek mythology, Galatea was the name of the following figures: 1) a Nereid who loved the shepherd Acis, and was loved by the cyclops Polyphemus. 2) the post-antiquity name given to the statue of a woman created by Pygmalion and brought to life by Aphrodite. 3) daughter of Eurytius, son of Sparton.   • aubade - is a song or poem that greets the dawn, traditionally a morning love song about lovers parting at daybreak.   • Uranus - Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun, a tilted "ice giant" with at least 28 moons and faint rings. People born under this sign are known for being adventurous, optimistic, honest, and freedom-loving, though they can sometimes be impatient and blunt.
  • Southern Cross - is an asterism of the Crux constellation, made up of four or five bright stars that form a distinctive cross shape. It is one of the smallest and most easily recognized constellations in the southern night sky.
  • fugacious - tending to disappear; fleeting.

  • The names of all Mr. Spitzer’s elegies uses these musical titles and images as metaphors for the interplay of life, death, memory, and creativity.   • star coral - can refer to several types of reef-building stony corals, such as the mountainous, lobed, or boulder star corals, or to other less common corals like the ORA Asterospicularia or Northern Star Coral.   • dogwinkle - dog whelk, dogwhelk, or Atlantic dogwinkle is a species of predatory sea snail, a carnivorous marine gastropod in the family Muricidae, the rock snails. Nucella lapillus was originally described by Carl Linnaeus in his landmark 1758 10th edition of Systema Naturae as Buccinum lapillus.
  • Crusader scallop or seashell - The scallop shell is the traditional emblem of St. James the Great, one of the apostles of Jesus and the patron saint of Spain and pilgrims. In medieval times, pilgrims who completed the journey to the shrine of St. James at the Cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, Spain, would collect a scallop shell from the coast as a souvenir and proof of their accomplishment. They would wear the shell on their hat or cloak. The scallop shell is widely used today as a wayfinding symbol along the Camino de Santiago routes, often painted in yellow on a blue background on milestones and signs to guide pilgrims to their destination. The shell's grooves, all converging at a central point, are seen as a metaphor for the many different paths pilgrims take from all over the world, all leading to the single destination of St. James' tomb. The shell was also used by pilgrims as a practical utensil for gathering water to drink or as a makeshift bowl for food, which they might request from homes along the way. The red cross often painted on the shell is the Cross of Saint James (Cruz de Santiago), which is linked to medieval crusaders and Spanish military orders. Chapter 26

← Chapter 25 · Home · Chapter 27 →

Summary

Mr. Spitzer's field of law is the dead: wills, deeds, archives, and lost heirs. One case involves two Boston spinsters, each believing she is Cleopatra. One left her fortune to her Siamese cats under his supervision, and the cats seem likely to live forever. He asks what Peron would have done had their places been reversed. He concludes that Peron would never have been faithful to Catherine's bedside, but would have dragged her into the living sunlight even if it killed her. He reflects that to reach the upper world one must first travel through the lower.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Philosophy: Hinduism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Schopenhauer

Allusions: Astronomy · Dante · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Music and Composers · Suicide in History and Literature · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Mr. Spitzer’s role is described as one dealing with "the dead," wills, deeds, secret archives, and old houses haunted by ghosts: both literal and metaphorical. He has encountered many baffling situations, such as lost heirs and numerous wills designed to confuse even the most conscientious attorney. This has led him to doubt the very idea of inheritance and continuity through generations, extending even to physical traits like hair and eyes, which he likens to "properties... of a dream" that fade while observed. This passage underscores the theme of uncertainty and the fragile, illusory nature of identity and legacy.
  • Mr. Spitzer recalls an eccentric case of an old Boston lady who believed herself the reincarnation of Cleopatra and left her estate to her numerous Siamese cats, with the caretaker to live in the house as long as the cats lived. The cats are described almost mystically, with "nine lives," prowling the house and garden as if they owned it, playing piano keys, and embodying a kind of magical, surreal presence. This passage conveys a haunting atmosphere and illustrates Mr. Spitzer’s encounters with the bizarre and uncanny elements of death and legacy. It also reflects his cautious and conservative approach to administering such an unusual estate.
  • This is a deeply poignant section where Mr. Spitzer recalls the shock of identifying his dead brother in a morgue among the homeless and faceless corpses. He reflects on how his life has since been shadowed by this event, feeling as if he lives his brother’s life and dies his brother’s death. The passage reveals Mr. Spitzer’s internal struggle with grief, memory, and the passing of time. It also illuminates the contrast between the brothers: Mr. Spitzer’s “cosmic serenity” versus his brother’s impatience, competition, and instability. This reflection on personal loss and identity is central to the chapter’s emotional core.
  • Mr. Spitzer expresses a belief in a future beyond the law and human institutions where a future of “silent music” and “heavenly harmonies” is fixed beyond time’s fluctuations. He contemplates the idea that perfect life should be perfect death, where there is no rivalry, no immortal derangement, but complete oblivion rather than memory. This is contrasted with Catherine’s opium-induced desire for complete memory. These meditations reveal Mr. Spitzer’s somber, even nihilistic, outlook on existence, death, and what, if anything, lies beyond.
  • The chapter contrasts Mr. Spitzer’s faithful, solemn devotion to Cartherine and the dead with his brother Peron’s impetuous love of life, fear of death, and competitive nature. Mr. Spitzer doubts that his brother would have been so faithful or so enduring in grief, emphasizing Peron’s preference for the “great crowds of Derby Day” and his inability to face death or prolonged farewell. This contrast highlights different ways of confronting mortality and loss, and the complex dynamics of family loyalty and love.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates Catherine’s opium-induced visions and her tendency to “narcotize” her memory to avoid facing reality, creating an opaque inner world filled with imaginary beings. He serves as a guardian of her property and life, yet his presence is often ignored or rejected, and he is caught in a paradox of faithfulness and absence. This passage captures the theme of elusive truth, memory, and perception, and the isolating burden of care and love.
  • Toward the end, Mr. Spitzer reflects that to reach the upper world (perhaps a metaphor for peace, truth, or heaven), one must first pass through the lower world: the streets and alleys inhabited by thieves and painted street women. This metaphor suggests a journey through all aspects of life, including its sordid or painful parts, before reaching any transcendence. It ties into the chapter’s exploration of death, memory, and the complexity of existence.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Joachim Spitzer (Peron’s twin brother)

  • Family lawyer, guardian of the dead’s legacy.
  • Scrupulous, conservative, somber, introspective.
  • Struggles with the paradox of his profession and personal grief over his twin brother. He is caught between duty and emotional turmoil.
  • Believes in a final peace beyond life and law, emphasizing oblivion rather than memory after death.
  • His work involves dealing with the hidden past, dusty archives, and eccentric clients, many of whom create baffling legal puzzles through multiple wills or lost heirs.
  • This career, entered reluctantly due to family expectations, keeps him continually close to death and the mysteries of inheritance.
  • A notable case in Mr. Spitzer’s youth involved an elderly Boston lady who believed she was Cleopatra reincarnated. She left her estate and numerous Siamese cats to an ancient caretaker, with Mr. Spitzer supervising. The cats are described almost as immortal beings, with a mysterious presence that haunts the house, symbolizing the blurred lines between life and death, reality and illusion.
  • He also considers Catherine's narcotic-induced oblivion as a form of escape from reality, pondering the value of memory and oblivion in death.
  • Mr. Spitzer philosophizes on the necessity of traveling through the "lower world" (a metaphorical space of moral and social darkness) before reaching the "upper world" or enlightenment. This journey includes encountering thieves, street women, and the underbelly of life, suggesting his awareness of the complex layers of existence beyond his legal profession.

Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s twin brother)

  • Impulsive, competitive, and distrustful of the law.
  • Impetuous, restless, afraid of death.
  • His relationship with Joachim is that their lives and deaths intertwine metaphorically; Peron’s death haunts Joachim.
  • Represents the chaotic, fleeting nature of life and human memory.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Bedridden and addicted to opium.
  • Mr. Spitzer handles her estate.
  • Represents illusions of grandeur and the persistence of the past into the present.
  • Her estate is managed by Mr. Spitzer.
  • Central to Mr. Spitzer’s personal life, her illness and narcotic use create a complex emotional dynamic.
  • Embodies memory, oblivion, and the tension between awareness and escape.

Research: Themes

  • Mortality and the Legacy of the Dead The chapter explores how death shapes the living through legal, emotional, and mystical legacies. The dead control the living via wills and memories, but these connections are uncertain and fraught with paradox.
  • Memory vs. Oblivion Mr. Spitzer contrasts Catherine’s desire for memory with his own preference for oblivion after death, questioning what form of afterlife or peace is truly desirable.
  • Illusion and Reality The recurring motif of illusions, reincarnations, the cats’ seeming immortality, and fragmented memories, highlights the fragile, dream-like quality of existence. This is similar to the Catherine’s canary at the beginning of the book.
  • The Law and Its Limits The law is portrayed as an imperfect, sometimes arbitrary system that tries to impose order on the chaos of life and death. Mr. Spitzer hopes for a future beyond law, where harmony replaces discord.
  • Duality of Human Nature Through the contrast between Joachim and his twin brother Peron, the duality of restraint vs. impulsiveness, order vs. chaos, and life vs. death is examined.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • The Siamese Cats Symbolize mystery, immortality, and the blurred boundary between life and death. Their dominance in the Boston lady’s house reflects ongoing life amid death.
  • The Pyramid and the Sphinx Represent ancient legacies, riddles of existence, and the enigmatic nature of identity and memory.
  • The Dead Brother A symbol of lost potential, memory, and the haunting presence of the past in the present.
  • Opium and Narcotics Reflect escape, oblivion, and the tension between retaining memory or seeking peace through forgetfulness.

Research: Resources

  • In the US, property can be passed down through generations in perpetuity through methods (Heirs’ Property, Perpetual Trusts, Family Limited Partnerships, Buy-Sell Agreements, Limited LIability Companies (LLC), Living Trusts, Irrevocable Trusts) ensuring a lasting legacy. Promoting Inequality: A significant critique of inherited wealth is that it exacerbates economic inequality, enabling wealth acquisition without labor and hindering social mobility. Critics of these methods create a "Virtual Aristocracy". These unrestricted perpetual trusts, can hold wealth indefinitely, and could lead to the concentration of wealth in the hands of a few families, potentially creating a privileged class. Inherited wealth can create a "glass floor," preventing children from privileged families from falling below a certain economic level, regardless of their own efforts. Inheriting wealth without earning it can undermine a sense of accomplishment and make inheritors feel like mere placeholders for future generations. Support for these methods state passing on wealth to kin is considered a deeply ingrained human desire and is seen as an essential aspect of individual freedom within a system of private property rights. It makes estate tax deductions for charitable bequests easier and provides an incentive for wealthy individuals to donate to charities. Perpetual trusts, when properly structured, can protect assets from potential legal challenges and distributions that may not be in the long-term interest of beneficiaries. The US has a history of enacting estate and gift taxes, though their reach and rates have fluctuated over time, often tied to war financing or efforts to curb wealth concentration. There is ongoing debate about the role and impact of these taxes, with some advocating for their repeal and others for their reform. Traditional legal principles like the Rule Against Perpetuities aimed to prevent perpetual trusts, but many states have modified or abolished this rule, leading to renewed debate about the implications of trusts that can last indefinitely. Other viewpoints have called for the complete abolition of inheritance, asserting that it is incompatible with a fair and equitable society.
  • Women's property rights have expanded over time in the United States, but they have been restricted by gender stereotypes and laws.In medieval times, married women's land became their husbands' property. In 1718, Pennsylvania allowed married women to manage their homes while their husbands were away. In 1848, New York passed the Married Women's Property Act, which allowed women to keep their property when they married. Other states passed similar laws in the 1850s. By 1900, most states recognized women's property rights. However, women of color were not included in these rights. Women faced barriers to accessing credit and mortgages without a male co-signer. In 1974, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act was passed, which helped to address these barriers. Women can apply for home loans and take out lines of credit, which has made it easier for them to become homeowners. Gender stereotypes and ideologies have historically been barriers to women's property rights.

  • “elegiac song” is a funeral song and that is the music that Mr. Spitzer plays or writes or listens to.
  • There were cases of pets/animals inheriting estates: Gunther VI German Shepherd, a Poodle in 1931 which turned out to be a hoax, and Blackie a cat who is the wealthiest according to the Guiness Book of World Records.
  • “perpetual grief” and two other quotes above may refer to the philosophy of Arthur Schopenhauer who believed that death is a natural part of life and a return to a state of non-existence that existed before birth. He thought that individual consciousness is impermanent and that the life of an individual is meaningless. His key ideas are will-to-live (the driving force behind our attachment to life and our fear of death), knowledge (shows the meaninglessness of life and the worthlessness of living), suicide (pointless because it affirms the will-to-live), palingenesis (suggest that the mind has always existed and will continue to exist), redemption (that death is an opportunity for redemption through the negation of the will). The portrayal of Mr. Spitzer's lifelong sorrow, his recognition of life as a series of losses and unfulfilled desires, and his contemplation of the illusory nature of reality all echo Schopenhauerian themes. The passage reflects a worldview where grief and suffering are continuous and intrinsic to life.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s belief that people need to travel though the lower world to reach the upper world mirrors Pilgrim’s Progress and/or Dante’s writings. There are 7 levels of purgatory with 7 vices. There are 7 virtues. Hell has 9 circles and Heaven has 9 levels of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, Sun, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the fixed stars, and the primum mobile. According to Dante the cosmos depends on God, who exists in the Empyrean, and immaterial heaven beyond space and time. The Empyrean is made up of God’s love and light, and is home to angels, the blessed, and the souls of the faithful. Interesting note that the woman with the Siamese cats believes she was the reincarnation of Cleopatra and Dante meets Cleopatra in the circle of Hell called Lust.
  • Catherine is expecting a man to save her, which is the damsel in distress. This is a narrative device in which one or more men must rescue a woman who has been kidnapped or placed in other peril. The "damsel" is often portrayed as beautiful, popular, and of high social status; she is usually depicted as a princess in works with fantasy or fairy tale settings. Kinship, love, lust or a combination of those motivate the male protagonist to initiate the narrative. Critics have linked the helplessness of these women to societal views that women as a group need to be taken care of by men and treated nicely. Throughout the history of the trope, the role of the woman as the victim in need of a male savior has remained constant, but her attackers have changed to suit the tastes and collective fears of the period: "monsters, mad scientists, Nazis, hippies, bikers, aliens..."
  • “Musica Universalis” is a metaphysical principle by Boethius that uses mathematical relationships to express ‘tones’ that could be heard by the soul. The "Musica Universalis" here symbolizes the harmonious and eternal cosmic order that underlies the apparent chaos of mortal life and death. It is depicted as a sublime, transcendent music that governs the movements of the stars and planets, reflecting a divine harmony beyond human perception. Mr. Spitzer, a semi-retired lawyer and composer of "silent music," embodies this principle as someone who is attuned to the "music of the spheres" or the eternal, silent harmonies that exist beyond earthly sounds. His compositions, unheard by living ears and played only for the dead or in the celestial realm, metaphorically represent this cosmic music. The chapter emphasizes the contrast between earthly, temporal music and this higher, immutable harmony, suggesting that the tangible world is but a fragment or shadow of a greater metaphysical reality. Catherine's opium dreams expand this theme by blurring the boundaries between the real and the illusory, the living and the dead, reflecting the ineffable nature of the universal music that ties all existence together. The "Musica Universalis" is not just an abstract concept but a living presence in her visions with images of angels harping, celestial choirs, and cosmic rhythms permeating her consciousness. The chapter suggests that this music is intertwined with suffering and mortality (the "music of the perfect silence beyond the chance of the brittle and falling stars") highlighting a metaphysical view where life, death, and cosmic order are inseparable parts of a greater whole. The "Musica Universalis" is used to articulate a metaphysical principle that all existence, from the smallest earthly details to the vast cosmos, is bound by a harmonious, eternal music. This music transcends the limitations of physical reality and human understanding, offering a vision of unity amid fragmentation and a cosmic order beneath the apparent chaos of life and death.
chapter-02:
Chapter 2

← Chapter 1 · Home · Chapter 3 →

Summary

Vera describes her mother, Catherine. She is an opium addict who has lain in bed for years among jewels and phantoms and treats her hallucinations as more real than the world. The chapter traces how she came to this. There was a brief marriage to Jock Cartwheel, and a love triangle with twin brothers: Catherine loved Peron Spitzer, who did not love her, while his brother Joachim loved Catherine without return. Joachim, Mr. Spitzer, is the family lawyer and visits her bedside every evening. An Egyptian sailor arrives looking for the dead Peron and mistakes Joachim for him, and Catherine gives the sailor elaborate directions through her labyrinthine house.
