  • “they were going to Alaska, that cold place”: The United States bought Alaska from Russia in 1867 for $7.2 million, a purchase mocked as “Seward’s Folly,” and it became a state in 1959. In its far north the summer sun barely sets, “the sun dipping below the horizon and immediately arising again,” and in winter it barely rises. See Snow, Ice, and Winter.
  • “Home, James”: The order to a coachman, and later a chauffeur, comes from the old catchphrase “Home, James, and don’t spare the horses,” which became the title of a popular song in the 1930s. In Catherine’s mouth it becomes a question: “for where is home?”
  • “this same barber pole”: The red and white stripes of the barber pole go back to the barber-surgeons of the Middle Ages, who let blood as well as cut hair. The pole stood for the staff a patient gripped, and the stripes for the bandages.
  • “served an unjust sentence breaking rocks for a state highway”: Into the twentieth century, convicts in many American states, especially in the South, were chained together in gangs to quarry stone and build and repair roads.
  • “only a yellow canary with a glassy eye and ruffled wing”: The canary is a finch from the Canary Islands, the Azores, and Madeira, kept as a caged songbird since the 1600s. Coal miners carried canaries underground, since the birds would sicken from poison gas before the men did, and British mines used them until 1986. Catherine’s canary, “all that had ever stood between her and tides of death,” is a miner’s canary in reverse. See Birds.
  • Juniper, Tulip, Cellini, Solomon, Methuselah, Marco Polo, Admiral Peary, Shackleton, Dante: Catherine names her canary “depending on her moods and her position in space,” as when she is “voyaging between two stars,” and the names run from plants to kings, long life, artists, poets, and the great explorers of the earth’s far ends.
    • Benvenuto Cellini was an Italian goldsmith and sculptor of the sixteenth century, known for his bronze Perseus with the Head of Medusa in Florence, his golden saltcellar for King Francis I, and his boastful autobiography.
    • Solomon was the wise king of Israel who succeeded his father, King David, and built the first Temple in Jerusalem.
    • Methuselah was a biblical patriarch and said to have lived 969 years. His name is synonymous with longevity (Genesis 5:27).
    • Marco Polo was an Italian explorer who traveled through Asia along the Silk Road between 1271 and 1295, and spent years at the court of Kublai Khan.
    • Admiral Robert Peary was an American explorer and US Navy officer who made several expeditions to the Arctic. He claimed to have reached the North Pole in April 1909, a claim still disputed. See Exploration and the Poles.
    • Sir Ernest Shackleton was an Anglo-Irish Antarctic explorer, born in County Kildare in 1874. When his ship Endurance was crushed by the ice in 1915, he led all twenty-eight of his men to safety.
    • Dante Alighieri was an Italian poet who wrote the Divine Comedy. See Dante.
  • “a hurricane blowing off the Canary Islands”: The Canary Islands, off the northwest coast of Africa, were not named for the birds. The Roman writer Pliny the Elder said the name came from the Latin canis, “dog,” for the large dogs found there, and the birds were later named for the islands.

A bedspread.

A designer and maker of fine clothes for women.

A bedspread, usually a light one.

The sky or the heavens, imagined as a solid dome overhead, as in Genesis 1.
Four-flusher
A bluffer or cheat. In poker, a four flush is a worthless hand of four cards of one suit passed off as five.

Slang for a detective, from the soft rubber-soled shoes that let one follow quietly.
Hanging gardens
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: terraced gardens said to have been built by King Nebuchadnezzar II. No trace of them has ever been found.
Heraldic
Of heraldry, the coats of arms and emblems of noble families.
Imploring

Ineffable

Carefree; unconcerned.

A two-masted sailboat with the smaller mast set behind the main mast.
Labyrinthine
Like a labyrinth; intricate and confusing.
Laundress
A woman who washes and irons clothes for a living.
Listlessly
Without energy or interest.
Livid
Bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Also furiously angry.
Lorgnette
A pair of eyeglasses held up to the eyes by a long handle.
Lute
A plucked string instrument with a rounded back shaped like half a pear, popular in Europe from the Middle Ages through the 1700s.
Maelstrom
A powerful whirlpool; any violent, confused situation.
Malingering
Pretending to be ill to avoid work.
Medusa
A jellyfish in its free-swimming, bell-shaped stage, named for the Gorgon of Greek myth whose hair was snakes.
Mercantile
Of merchants and trade; commercial.
Mercurial
Quick and changeable in mood. From the swift Roman messenger god Mercury and the liquid metal named for him.
Mesa
A flat-topped hill with steep sides. Young writes of a “mesa of snow.”
Metropolitan
In the Orthodox churches, a bishop who presides over the other bishops of a province.

A maker or seller of women’s hats.

Tiny. Young’s form of minuscule.

An optical illusion, common in deserts, in which hot air bends light so that distant water or cities seem to appear.

A small amount.
Moleskin
A heavy cotton fabric with a soft, short nap like the fur of a mole.
Morosely
Gloomily, sullenly.

The shining, rainbow-colored lining of some shells, used for inlay.

To travel by dogsled; also the command that starts sled dogs running.

Ne’er-do-well

A woman’s light, flowing dressing gown.

The act of making something unclear or obscure.

The state of being forgotten, or of being unaware of everything.

A person in their eighties.

All-knowing.

Able to be touched or felt; plain to see.

Writing material the ancient Egyptians made from the stems of the papyrus reed.
Parasol
A light umbrella carried for shade from the sun.
Phantasmagoric
Like a phantasmagoria, a shifting series of dreamlike or nightmarish images. A phantasmagoria was an eighteenth-century magic-lantern ghost show.
Piebald
Of a horse: with irregular patches of two colors, usually black and white.
Promontory
A high point of land jutting out into the sea.
Protean
Able to change shape or form readily, like the sea god Proteus.
Rabbit warren
A network of rabbit burrows. Figuratively, a crowded building full of small, maze-like rooms.
Refulgent
Shining brightly; radiant.
Regatta
A series of boat races.
Rice powder
A fine face powder made from rice, used to whiten the skin.

A woman’s outfit for riding horseback.
Ritualist
One devoted to the strict observance of rituals.
Roan
Of a horse: with a solid-colored coat sprinkled with white hairs.

Rose-colored. Also hopeful or overly optimistic.

A stone coffin, often carved, placed above ground. The plural is sarcophagi.
Sentient
Able to feel and perceive.
Sexton
A church officer who looks after the building and churchyard and often digs the graves.
Shade
A ghost; the spirit of a dead person. The underworld is “that dark abode of shades.”

A sailboat with one mast.
Smelling salts
A strong-smelling mixture, chiefly ammonium carbonate, sniffed to revive someone who feels faint.

One who claims to foretell the future.

An unmarried woman, especially an older one. The word first meant a woman who spun thread.

An icicle-shaped formation of minerals hanging from the roof of a cave.

Chapter 31

← Chapter 30 · Home · Chapter 32 →

Summary

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer admire Cousin Hannah, whose great deeds made their own lives seem unfulfilled. Her secret grief is circled but never named: the mirrors of her house draped in black, her failed battle to rescue Catherine from opium, her indifference to both Spitzer brothers. Mr. Spitzer remembers his long faithfulness to her, knocking at a door that never opened. He struggles to write her epitaph, drafting and discarding version after version.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past

Philosophy: Existentialism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ecclesiastes · Judaism · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer indulges Catherine’s moods as long as they are not of reality, believing reality would kill her as it had killed her canary, which she imagined flying over the waves. This suggests a delicate balance between fantasy and harsh reality in her life.
  • Their mutual admiration for Peron (who gambled his life away) and Cousin Hannah, an adventurer whose own life made their adventures seem unfulfilled, hints at the complex relationships and ideals binding these characters.
  • Cousin Hannah is described as direct, fierce, and adventurously restless, having fought losing battles with shadows and enduring harsh physical and emotional challenges, including suffrage campaigns and desert treks. She embodies "forlorn romance" and is portrayed as a great captain metaphorically armored by suffrage and armed with swords of ice and fire.
  • Her refusal to marry and the whispered secret of her life shadowed by grief add mystery and depth to her character. Her life is marked by dramatic adventures and a stoic endurance of suffering.
  • Despite her strength and battles, she could not "rescue herself," and her death is framed as a "domestic war," contrasting with the grand battles she fought. This passage suggests a tragic dimension to her life and death.
  • She sought to "carry" Vera’s mother away from opium dreams, fighting her losing battle with shadows, showing her as a protective but ultimately tragic figure.
  • She ignored Joachim, the lawyer, after Peron’s death, refusing any recognition or mourning, which underscores her complex relations and possibly her disdain for what she considered weak or insubstantial men. Also Mr. Spitzer may not be who he seems to be/
  • Mr. Spitzer’s persistent but unanswered visits to Cousin Hannah’s empty house symbolize a futile effort to maintain connection and control over the past. His rituals of knocking, leaving calling cards, bringing important papers contrast with the silence and absence inside, emphasizing themes of loss and the elusiveness of presence.
  • Cousin Hannah’s adventures in deserts and mountains serve as metaphors for her restless spirit and unattainable quests, with imagery of desert storms, Islamic kingdoms, and un-climbable alpine peaks creating a mythical aura around her.
  • The desert beauty’s mirror she brought is a symbol of the transience of human life, reinforcing the chapter’s meditation on mortality.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s efforts to compose an epitaph for Cousin Hannah, his hesitation and inability to decide on words reflect his sorrow and the difficulty of capturing a complex life and character in simple terms. His proposed epitaphs evoke her warrior spirit, her suffering, and her ultimate solitude and death at home rather than on a battlefield.
  • The meditation on death and memory adds philosophical depth to the narrative.
  • His own uncertain status between life and death, as suggested by bureaucratic errors listing him dead, parallels the ambiguous boundary between presence and absence that permeates this chapter.
  • Cousin Hannah’s scorn for Vera’s mother’s love for a "shadow," a fleeting and unsubstantial man, contrasts with Catherine’s belief that death is necessary to her love. This conflict highlights different understandings of love, reality, and illusion.
  • Cousin Hannah’s rejection of the external man and her suspicion of phantoms as rivals underscore the chapter’s theme of the elusive and often illusory nature of relationships and human connections.
  • The repeated imagery of knocking on doors, peering through keyholes, and the sensation of being watched by hidden eyes evokes a haunting atmosphere, symbolizing the barriers between people, the mysteries of identity, and the unseen presences that linger in memory and imagination.

  • Catherine’s love is for an elusive, intangible presence rather than a real man.

Chapter 38

Summary

Catherine's memories of Hannah are vague and clouded by her dreams of an immortal love. She has reinterpreted Peron's neglect as a devotion too large to express. We learn that Catherine never believed in women's suffrage, the cause of the woman who tried hardest to save her. Mr. Spitzer adds his anecdotes, and Hannah appears in memory with keys and jeweled sword. Vera names the house for what it has become: a loony bin by the sea.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clouds and Storms · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Pearls and Jewels · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology · Heraclitus and Flux · Hinduism · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Dante · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens by portraying Cousin Hannah as a formidable, almost mythic figure who never reconciled with life and whose identity remains blurred in memory. This passage sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of memory, identity, and legacy. It emphasizes Hannah’s singularity and the elusive nature of her life and spirit, framing her as a person who lived on the outermost edges of experience.
  • Catherine is described as indefinite, clouded by dreams of immortal love and escape, living in a world of opium-induced fantasies and unawakened romance, in contrast to Cousin Hannah’s stark reality and fiery spirit. This contrast highlights two modes of existence: one engaged with harsh realities and causes (Hannah), and the other retreating into beautiful but unreal dreams (Catherine).
  • The chapter repeatedly emphasizes Cousin Hannah’s adventurous spirit and her sacrifices for the suffrage movement, portraying these efforts as both heroic and, from Catherine’s perspective, somewhat futile or unworthy of Hannah's potential. This passage reveals Catherine’s ambivalence (envy mixed with guilt) as she reflects on Hannah’s committed activism versus her own life of dreams and withdrawal.
  • Catherine’s reflections on love are poignant and laden with sorrow. She imagines a love greater than any realized affection, a "dead love which never was and never would be real," expressed in silence and absence rather than presence. She interprets Peron’s neglect as a form of love out of fear of her power, suggesting a profound but unspoken emotional tension. This theme of unattainable love permeates the chapter.
  • There are vivid passages describing Catherine’s dreams of travel and escape to exotic places (Egypt, Italy, the land of the Kurds) and her missed opportunities for a different life. These passages symbolize longing, regret, and the tension between the dream of freedom and the reality of confinement, both physical and psychological.
  • Catherine’s mind is portrayed as wandering and unreliable, filled with illusions and shifting memories. The narrative suggests that her dreams, though inaccurate, might hold a deeper truth than conventional reality. This raises philosophical questions about the nature of truth, memory, and perception.
  • Cousin Hannah is depicted as "sharp-witted, dashing, wild and reckless," a figure of masculine virtues and relentless energy, "like a finely tempered blade" who never stopped despite adversity. This passage celebrates her fortitude and contrasts it with Catherine’s frailty and passivity.
  • The chapter discusses mysterious, mystical elements: the whisperings of the dead, the music of the spheres, and spectral visions, suggesting a world where life and death intermingle and where memory and existence are fluid. Cousin Hannah’s belief that the dead are silent and that her battles were with the living underscores the existential tension between life’s visible struggles and the ineffable beyond.
  • Despite her admiration for Cousin Hannah’s strength and purpose, Catherine is disappointed that Hannah is not the romantic hero she imagined, a knight or prince who could awaken her from her dreams. This passage reflects Catherine’s deep yearning for connection and meaning, mingled with a sense of loss.
  • The chapter closes with reflections on the instability of time and identity, suggesting that even the most certain facts of time, place, person may be illusions or dreams. Mr. Spitzer’s observations about disorientation and the blurring of reality and illusion reinforce the chapter’s overarching meditation on perception

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • Described as a "great captain of extremes," a resolute and brave suffragette who sacrificed much for her cause.
  • Adventurous and daring, having traveled "to the outermost reaches of space," symbolizing exploration beyond physical and societal boundaries.
  • Exhibits masculine virtues: sharp, shrewd, incisive, relentless and compared to a "finely tempered blade."
  • Seen as singularly devoted to her cause, seemingly indifferent to love or personal attachments.
  • Her presence is associated with powerful imagery: whistling sounds, iron keys, jeweled swords, and snow storms.
  • A figure of mystery and paradox; she weeps for subtle reasons (e.g., a snowflake touching her hand), showing a hidden emotional depth.
  • Her life is characterized by perpetual motion and battle, never fully reconciled with peace or rest.
  • Represents strength, fortitude, and the harsh realities of activism and sacrifice.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Portrayed as dreamy, opium-addicted, lost in illusions and fantasies of an "immortal love" and lost romances.
  • She envies Cousin Hannah’s adventures but remains passive, bound to memories and dreams rather than action.
  • Her mind is clouded, veiled by dreams that are as much about escape as about longing.
  • She imagines herself as a great courtesan with many imaginary lovers, embodying a spectral beauty trapped in time.
  • Her love life is described as unfulfilled, marked by silence and absence, especially in relation to a man named Peron.
  • She distorts reality, unable to fully grasp or engage with the present moment.
  • She has a sense of guilt about her withdrawal and dreams, contrasted with Cousin Hannah’s active life.
  • Her life is marked by isolation and a yearning for an "unearthly romance" free from mortal change.
  • Represents passivity, longing, and the desire for transcendence.

Mr. Spitzer

  • His mind is clouded and dwells on abstract, cosmic music and metaphysical concepts.
  • Symbolizes a detached intellectual or mystical observer, contrasting with the passionate activism of Cousin Hannah and the dreamy passivity of Catherine.
  • His perspective reflects on the limitations of human understanding and the ineffability of life’s mysteries.

Research: Themes

Memory and Reality

  • The novel blurs the lines between memory, dream, and reality.
  • Catherine’s recollections are described as "inaccurate," "clouded," and "untrustworthy," reflecting the elusive nature of truth.
  • The narrative questions the reliability of memory and whether dreams may contain a deeper accuracy than factual truth.
  • Time is fluid, with events and identities slipping and merging, e.g., Catherine confusing visitors or historical periods.

  • Cousin Hannah embodies sacrifice for a cause, dedicating her life to suffrage and battling societal "ogres."

Research: Resources

  • Musica Universalis (music of the spheres) concept incorporates the metaphysical principle that mathematical relationships express qualities or “tones” of energy that manifests in numbers, visual angles, shapes and sounds which are all connected within a pattern of proportion. This has been explored by Pythagoras, Plato, Aristotle (he rejected the idea), Boethius developed three categories of music (musica mundana, musica humana, and musica quae in quibusdam constituta est instrumentis), Keppler expounded on the idea and cherry picked data to support his claims. They have since been refuted. Boethius developed imagery to go with his writings and I believe Young took inspiration from these illustrations for the novel. Musica universalis serves as a profound metaphor for the cosmic order, the spiritual unity beyond earthly fragmentation, and the haunting, silent music that connects life, death, memory, and the infinite. It highlights the novel’s exploration of metaphysical questions about existence, identity, and the search for meaning beyond the limits of human perception and experience.
  • Human Will or Free Will is the capacity of humans to make choices and decisions independently of external forces. Philosophy has debated the existence and nature of free will with arguments for and against. Determinism is the opposite of free will. Religions grapple with the concept of free will and attempt to reconcile it with divine sovereignty and predestination. Free will is closely linked with moral responsibility which is used to hold individuals accountable for their actions. Self-determination is part of free will where individuals choose their thoughts, words, and deeds. The environment a person is surrounded by also strongly influences human actions as well as instincts and inherited dispositions. The act of will allows individuals to direct and control their thoughts and actions and help them formulate and work towards fulfilling goals. In the chapter the significance of human will or free will is explored in a complex and nuanced manner, reflecting the novel’s broader themes of illusion, fate, and the limits of human understanding. Humans are not the architects of fate or destiny, and their freedom is limited by the ordered, but often harsh, conditions set by a God or nature. Individuals should "mind their own knitting" and live in the present moment, carefully attending to their responsibilities without chasing impossible dreams. At the same time, the chapter acknowledges the tension between this acceptance and the human desire for freedom and change. Miss MacIntosh is depicted as someone who neither denies the reality of suffering nor yields to despair; rather, she embraces labor, self-forgetfulness, and service to others as the true expression of human will within the bounds of mortal existence. Her will is not about imposing arbitrary control over life’s uncertainties but about perseverance and making the best of one’s circumstances. The novel also suggests that the illusion of complete free will is just that, an illusion. The individual is bound by the web of life’s circumstances, time, and fate, and the ultimate truth might be that the "individual is the one illusion". This idea challenges the notion of absolute free will, instead positing a universe where human wills are intertwined and limited within a grand cosmic logic that often eludes understanding. Human will or free will is significant as it embodies the struggle between acceptance of life's inevitable limitations and the desire for autonomy and meaning. Miss MacIntosh represents the choice to embrace reality with clear eyes and firm resolve, finding dignity and purpose in the acceptance of one’s mortal condition, while the narrative acknowledges the profound ambiguity and complexity of free will within the greater cosmic order. Human will is real but bounded, expressed best through practical endurance, moral clarity, and service, rather than through fantasies of absolute freedom or control over fate.

It can be understood as representing the eternal, unchanging spiritual realms or dimensions, where the soul and spirit exist beyond physical mortality and temporal constraints. Heraclitus’s philosophy in this context conveys that the world and ourselves are never static but perpetually evolving, and this continuous movement is both the source of life’s mystery and its challenge. The chapter meditates on how characters like Mr. Spitzer and Vera’s mother (Catherine) experience this flux (caught between reality and dreams, life and death, presence and oblivion) highlighting the fragile, transient, and often ambiguous nature of human existence.
  • Parmenides and the Paradox of Motion - Parmenides, an ancient Greek philosopher, argued that change and motion are illusions and that reality is unchanging and indivisible. This paradox (the question of how motion and change can exist if reality is fundamentally fixed and eternal) echoes the novel's exploration of the fluid boundaries between life and death, reality and illusion, presence and absence. In this chapter, the narrative reflects on the elusive nature of being, the difficulty of grasping a stable self or reality amid constant flux and transformation. The novel discusses how perceptions and memories shift, how the self might be divided or multiple, and how time and space themselves seem unstable or illusory. The paradox of motion in the context of the novel underscores the characters' struggles with their own existence, the impermanence of life, and the search for meaning in a world that seems to continuously dissolve and reform, much like Parmenides' philosophical dilemma. The mention of Parmenides and the paradox of motion highlights the novel's deep engagement with questions about the nature of reality, the illusion of change, and the elusive quest for permanence amidst inevitable flux.
  • Philosophical debate around perpetual motion explores the limits of human knowledge, the nature of reality, and the relationship between theory and practice. The chapter presents the idea that life and death are intertwined in a kind of endless cycle or flow, with no clear boundaries or finality. The chapter also reflects on the paradoxes of identity and existence, the relations between body, soul, and spirit, and the elusive nature of reality and perception. This is analogous to the concept of perpetual motion in that the philosopher or thinker is caught in an unending process of motion and change, never reaching a final resolution. The chapter discusses how music, as a metaphor for life and the universe, is a continuous flow that never fully resolves or ends, akin to perpetual motion. The novel philosophically explores the themes of endless cycles, the ambiguity of beginnings and ends, and the continuity of existence, all of which resonate with the concept of perpetual motion as an unceasing process without final rest or resolution.
  • Zeno’s paradoxes - the finite can contain the infinite. Neil deGrasse Tyson “there are an infinite number of steps to a finite destination”. Young discusses Zeno's paradoxes in the context of the characters’ reflections on life, death, and existence. They are trying to understand the idea of progress and the nature of time, for example, by questioning how two parallel lines might meet or how one might justify sorrows if one had experienced nothing. The chapter conveys a sense of confusion about the continuity of life and death and the elusive nature of reality. It refers to Zeno's paradoxes by highlighting the puzzlement about motion and the passage of time, such as the difficulty in knowing if one has truly moved forward or if one is caught in an endless cycle, like walking in circles or being lost between two polarities. They reflect on the idea of being between two worlds, the living and the dead, and the uncertainty of identity and existence, which echoes the philosophical challenge posed by Zeno's paradoxes regarding infinite divisibility and the nature of motion. This discussion illustrates the novel's broader themes of ambiguity, the interplay between reality and illusion, and the complexity of human consciousness and experience.

Chapter 25

← Chapter 24 · Home · Chapter 26 →

Summary

Vera considers Mr. Spitzer, whom Catherine accuses of being dead, or of being his own dead brother. We learn how Peron died. He fell through a fourteenth-floor window, perhaps by suicide, perhaps mistaking the window for a door. Joachim himself once walked through a glass wall in another lawyer's office without noticing, and his valet later found glass behind his ears. Bills for the wall followed. When Joachim finally tried to collect damages for his discomfort, a clerk told him that Mr. Spitzer had died several years ago.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Roses and Flowers · Silence and Deafness · The House · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Buddhism · Existentialism · Hinduism · Nietzsche · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Schopenhauer · Stoicism

Allusions: Astronomy · Greek Mythology · Suicide in History and Literature

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter immediately introduces Mr. Spitzer through Vera's perspective, but filtered through Catherine's eyes. He is described as "useless as regret," having missed much of life but content with it. The most striking aspect presented is Catherine's conviction that he is already dead, buried, or married to the worm or his brother. His living flesh does not convince her; she sees him as a "dead brother" and a "pale version of himself." This passage is crucial because it establishes the central theme of the blurred line between life and death, particularly concerning Mr. Spitzer's identity. It also highlights Catherine's unique, perhaps delusional or enchanted, perception of reality, setting the stage for the surreal atmosphere of their interactions. Her ability to see beyond his physical presence, even if seemingly inaccurate, is presented as a form of "omniscience".
  • The description of Mr. Spitzer's appearance and behavior reinforces Catherine's perception of his unreality or partial presence. He wears a "white tuberose or the white carnation" or perhaps just a "door knob" on his lapel, suggesting the ambiguity of his form or Catherine's perception of it. His "inane apology," "vapid face," and habit of "only half listening" and "only half seeing" by closing one eye contribute to the sense of his being only partially present or engaged with the living world. This passage is important because it provides details that embody the abstract idea of his state of being. His actions, like blotting out half his vision and hearing "perhaps to please her," suggest a passive resignation or even an attempt to conform to her reality.
  • The chapter contrasts Mr. Spitzer's partial state with Catherine's heightened, albeit unusual, perception. Her "omniscience, though he was dead, was only half of hers, for she was both living and dead, and she could see everything and much more besides". She is described as an "excellent judge of reality, that which was so unreal, an infinitesimal particle". This passage is vital for understanding the dynamic between the two characters and the narrative's exploration of reality and illusion. Catherine isn't just mistaken; her perception is presented as a different, perhaps deeper, form of knowing, one that encompasses both life and death and sees the unreality inherent in reality itself. Her ability to perceive Mr. Spitzer as "not the Mr. Spitzer she saw" but a "ghostly person" underscores her unique perspective and his ambiguous status.
  • Despite Catherine's fantastical claims (tables being coffins of stars, chairs set above a sea of clouds, bumble bees in the bedroom, a rose being a lady's ear, Mr. Spitzer being a tower of water or a duchess), Mr. Spitzer is "not inclined to deny completely the interesting possibility" and is "rather willing to concede that there was doubtless some right in her point of view". This passage is important because it reveals aspects of Mr. Spitzer's character: his passivity, his inability to argue, and his acceptance of the "mortal chaos" where identity and reality are fluid. It contrasts sharply with his later description as a lawyer, highlighting the transformative effect of Catherine's presence or his own internal state. His concession suggests either a profound uncertainty about reality or a deep empathy/indulgence towards Catherine.
  • The motif of the twin is introduced early and becomes central to Mr. Spitzer's identity. Catherine accuses him of being married to his brother, and later he is described as a "soul divided" because he is this twin, "and one was dead, and one lived". The confusion between Peron and Joachim is a key element, suggesting a merging or confusion of their identities. This passage is crucial for understanding Mr. Spitzer's internal conflict and his perceived state of living death where he embodies the dead brother, making him a divided soul. The ambiguity surrounding which twin is which (Peron the gambler vs. Joachim the lawyer/musician) adds to the sense of confusion and blurred identity.
  • Mr. Spitzer agrees with Catherine that "Time... was like her opium illusions". His memory is vague, especially of the "immediate moment or image, even when it was presumably real". His mind is described as "watery and vague," even his own face not being real to him. This passage reinforces the theme of the dissolution of conventional reality. His difficulty grasping time and immediate reality contributes to his passive state and his acceptance of Catherine's surreal world. It suggests that his internal state mirrors the external chaos he perceives.
  • The passage where Mr. Spitzer reflects on his past and what might have been is significant. He remembers having loved Catherine, even with his "dying breath," and believes he found "a refuge from the unreal world, a safe harbor beyond the storms of life" with her. He contemplates how different his life might have been "if ever she had accepted his passive hand in marriage and his undying love". This passage introduces a layer of pathos and regret to Mr. Spitzer's character. It reveals a past desire for a conventional life and love, which was apparently unfulfilled, contributing to his current state of perpetual waiting and "living death." His current life is explicitly described as a "life of patience and of waiting".
  • The chapter delves into the circumstances surrounding the brother's death and Mr. Spitzer's ongoing relationship with this event. The confusion over the brother's identity (Peron/Joachim) and the nature of his death (suicide or accident) is central. Mr. Spitzer feels a "heavy sense of woe, this stain of immortal guilt". He continues to think "too much of the dead brother, of Peron's tastes, his attitudes, likes, dislikes, furies and regrets", suggesting that the dead brother lives on through him. The passage describing the brother's death (falling from the fourteenth floor of an office building) is a concrete (though surreal) event in a chapter full of abstraction. This event is the catalyst for Mr. Spitzer's current state, his divided soul, and his perpetual meditation on death. The brother's suicide (or accident) is presented as final and decisive, contrasting with Mr. Spitzer's "hesitant suicide" or "perpetual and unconsummated suicide".
  • The anecdote about Mr. Spitzer walking through a glass wall is one of the most important and extended passages in the chapter. It serves as a metaphor for his inability to perceive or interact with conventional reality. He didn't notice the wall, thinking it was "nothing, a transparency as thin as air or thinner". This accident, which he recounts hesitantly and almost boasts about, is linked to his absent-mindedness, his perpetual grief, and his inability to distinguish between real obstacles and illusions. The fact that he only learned of it from his valet noticing glass particles and receiving bills underscores his detachment from physical reality. This passage is crucial because it provides a concrete example of Mr. Spitzer's state of being: someone physically present but mentally elsewhere, prone to blurring the lines between the tangible and the intangible, mirroring his brother's fatal fall through what looked like clouds. It also leads to the final, poignant revelation that, according to an "obtuse desk clerk," Mr. Spitzer is already dead.
  • The chapter culminates with Mr. Spitzer attempting to collect compensation for his glass wall "injury" and being told by a desk clerk that he is dead, having "departed this mortal life several years ago". This passage is the most significant as it brings Catherine's initial perception into a different, external context. It confirms (or at least presents as a bureaucratic fact) Mr. Spitzer's state of being dead, rendering his arguments and claims void. This final interaction encapsulates the chapter's core themes: the unreality of life, the reality of death (or vice versa), the confusion of identity, and the ultimate futility of navigating the living world when one is already perceived, or actually is, among the dead. His arguments falling upon "empty air" is a powerful final image of his non-existence in the eyes of the living world.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Joachim Spitzer (Peron’s twin brother)

  • Described as "useless as regret," a man trapped in liminality, between being alive and dead, reality and illusion, a “soul divided”.
  • Portrayed with physical and psychological frailty: fat, slow, hesitant.
  • He embodies indecision and ambiguity, unable to commit or fully engage with life.
  • Haunted by his brother Peron’s death and his own survival, which he views as a “living death.”
  • Experiences illusions and confusion; his senses and memory are unreliable.
  • Visits Catherine regularly, where his ambiguous existence is both challenged and sustained.
  • His life is marked by routine, melancholy, and a lack of clear purpose, yet he retains a faint spark of life and pride.
  • Mr. Spitzer's ambiguous existence and his nightly visits to Catherine..
  • Reflections on his brother Peron’s mysterious death.
  • An episode where Mr. Spitzer physically walks through a glass wall without injury, symbolizing his tenuous grasp on reality.
  • The ongoing conflict involves legal claims and correspondence.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s internal conflict regarding his unresolved life and death.

Peron (Joachim’s twin brother) Spitzer

  • The deceased twin, described as quick, impetuous, and decisive.
  • Committed suicide by falling through a window; his death is enveloped in mystery and doubt.
  • Contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s hesitant survival.
  • Represents a life fully lived and a death fully embraced.
  • His legacy haunts Mr. Spitzer, who often thinks in his brother’s voice or perspective.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A strong, discerning woman who sees through Mr. Spitzer’s facade.
  • She maintains a complex relationship with Mr. Spitzer, accusing him of falsehood yet drawing him into her dreamlike world.
  • Serves as a bulwark for Mr. Spitzer’s fragile existence.
  • Her bedroom is depicted as a magical, enchanted space where reality blurs and transformations occur.

Research: Resources

  • The will-to-live by Schopenhauer could be used to rationalize why Mr. Spitzer did what he did and how Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim and Peron are all the same person. Mr. Spitzer’s actions (his tireless searches, his care for others, and his internal conflicts) are driven by this fundamental will, compelling him to persist despite loss and disintegration. The multiplicity of characters such as Jock, the Black Coachman, Joachim, Peron, and Mr. Spitzer symbolically represents different manifestations of this singular will struggling within one being, blurring the lines between self and other, life and death, reality and illusion. “In psychology, the will to live is the drive for self-preservation, usually coupled with expectations for future improvement in one's state in life. The will to live is an important concept when attempting to understand and comprehend why we do what we do in order to stay alive, and for as long as we can. This can be related to either one's push for survival on the brink of death, or someone who is just trying to find a meaning to continuing their life. Some researchers say that people who have a reason or purpose in life during such dreadful and horrific experiences will often appear to fare better than those that may find such experiences overwhelming. Every day, people undergo countless types of negative experiences, some of which may be demoralizing, hurtful, or tragic. An ongoing question continues to be what keeps the will to live in these situations. People who claim to have had experiences involving the will to live have different explanations behind it.”
  • The push and pull between silent music and the music of the spheres or harmonious music form much of Mr. Spitzer’s tale. Particularly how Schopenhauer considers music the highest form of art. The philosophy of silence in music is that silence can be a powerful tool for making a statement, conveying emotion, and organizing structure. The novel embodies Schopenhauer’s belief in music as the highest art through its intricate portrayal of Mr. Spitzer’s silent and profound music, the use of musical metaphors to explore existential themes, and the depiction of music’s transcendence beyond the physical and intellectual world. The novel’s deep engagement with music as both expression and mystery reflects the Schopenhauerian vision of music as the direct and ultimate language of the will.
  • “where angels fear to tread” - may refer to the book, Where Angels Fear to Tread by EM Forster. This line can be interpreted as highlighting the existential and spiritual uncertainties faced by the characters, especially Vera and Miss MacIntosh, as they encounter realms (both literal and metaphorical) that transcend ordinary human experience and comprehension. It underscores the delicate balance between life and death, reality and illusion, and the profound, often frightening, mysteries that lie at the boundaries of human understanding.
  • Archimedes of Syracuse was an ancient Greek mathematician, physicist, engineer, astronomer, and inventor. He is known for his contributions to mathematics, physics, and engineering, and is often considered one of the greatest scientists and mathematicians of all time.
  • The concept of heaven “as a state of mind” originates from interpretations of Jesus’ teachings, particularly the phrase the “Kingdom of Heaven is within you,” Luke 17:21, which suggests that a state of peace, love and spiritual fulfillment can be achieved here on Earth through one’s mindset and actions, rather than being solely a place one goes to after death; this interpretation is often associated with mystical or spiritual traditions that emphasize inner consciousness and personal transformation.   • Fate refers to a predetermined destiny where events are beyond one’s control, while “self-determination” means actively shaping one’s own life through choices and actions.
  • Proving existence through denial refers to a philosophical concept where the act of actively denying something’s existence can inadvertently reveal its presence, often used in arguments where the very act of trying to refute something implies its reality, particularly in discussions about abstract concepts like God or the nature of consciousness. In philosophy, the most well-known example of this is Anselm’s Ontological Argument, which attempts to prove God’s existence by arguing that if you can conceive of a being greater than which nothing can be conceived, then that being must exist because the idea of a “greater being” inherently implies existence. This concept can be misused to manipulate arguments by implying that simply denying a claim equates to its truth, which is a logical fallacy.
  • Friedrich Nietzsche proposed the “will to power” as a driving force behind human behavior, instead of the “will to life” of his predecessor Arthur Schopenhauer. Will to life - an irrational force drives humans to strive endlessly. Will to power - a dynamic force drives humans to overcome resistance and become who they truly are. Nietzsche believed that the will to power is more useful than the will to life for explaining human behavior. He used the will to power to explain both life-affirming and life-denying impulses, as well as master and slave morality. He believed that the will to power is the expression of self-realization, and that it is a condition for growth. He believed that the will to power is a perpetual struggle against life, and that it is never done. In the chapter it reflects Nietzsche's "will to power" through its exploration of internal conflict, the striving for control amid chaos, the tension between life and death, and the dynamic, creative force underlying human existence, as embodied in Mr. Spitzer’s character and experiences.
  • Joachim and Peron (Jock Cartwheel) Spitzer may refer to Castor and Pollux, also known as the Dioscuri, as twin brothers in Greek and Roman mythology. Hinduism sees a soul (atman) that is reborn into various forms, while Buddhism views rebirth as a continuation of consciousness, not a soul, and focuses on Nirvana as a path to end suffering, not a destination for the soul.
  • The philosophy of death explores the meaning of death, our relationship to it, and the various ways it impacts human existence and understanding. It delves into questions about what happens after death, the nature of consciousness, and the ethical implications of death, including suicide and capital punishment. The Nature of Death: Dualism (the soul continues to exist after death, potentially in a separate realm or afterlife), Materialism (death is the permanent cessation of all bodily functions, including consciousness), Annihilationism (death is the end of all conscious experience, and nothing exists after death). Philosophical Perspectives on Death: Stoicism (death is not something to be feared, as it is a natural part of life and a release from suffering), Existentialism (like Kierkegaard and Heidegger, emphasized the importance of confronting our mortality to understand our own existence and the meaning of life), Nietzsche (proposed that individuals have the freedom to define their own death, suggesting it could be a conscious choice rather than an inevitable fate). Ethical Considerations: Suicide (philosophy engages with questions about the moral permissibility of suicide, including whether it's ever justifiable), Capital Punishment (the death penalty raises complex ethical questions about state-sanctioned killing and the value of human life), Euthanasia (issues related to assisted dying and the right to choose one's own death). The Meaning of Life: some philosophers argue that the awareness of our mortality can give deeper meaning to life, prompting us to live more fully and intentionally; others suggest that facing death head-on can help us appreciate the present moment and the beauty of existence. Fear of Death: the philosophy of death explores the psychological and emotional impact of fearing death, including its effects on our choices and behaviors; some philosophers believe that the fear of death is irrational and stems from our ignorance of what happens after death. Implications for Living: many philosophical perspectives on death suggest that accepting our mortality can lead to a more fulfilling and meaningful life; by contemplating death, we may be better equipped to appreciate the present moment, make conscious choices, and live a life aligned with our values.
  • Nietzsche's quote, "If you gaze long into an abyss, the abyss gazes also into you," is a famous aphorism warning against becoming consumed by the things you are confronting. It suggests that prolonged engagement with negativity, suffering, or challenging ideas can have a transformative effect on the person observing them, potentially altering their perspective and even their character. Mr. Spitzer as a man whose prolonged confrontation with death, identity, and existential uncertainty has led to a profound internal transformation shows in the novel how the abyss he peers into ultimately gazes back, shaping and haunting his very being.

Chapter 55

Summary

The twins had opposite mottos: Peron's "carpe diem," seize the day, and Joachim's "hoc opus, hic labor est," this is the work, this the labor. Joachim had planned a quiet life of music and stamp collecting in their twin house of mirrored rooms. Peron borrowed, forged his brother's checks, and left debts. When Peron died, Joachim paid for the funeral and the debts, went bankrupt, and lost the house. He now lives in a beachcomber's shack, still wondering whose funeral it was.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Eyes and Blindness · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness · The House · Twins and Doubles

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates how he might have lived had his brother died earlier. It describes his orderly, carefully planned life dedicated to music, philately, and collecting rare artifacts. It shows his desire for certainty, order, and a calm pursuit of immortality through art, contrasting with the chaos brought by his brother. This sets up the fundamental tension between the brothers’ lives and personalities.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s conservative financial choices are described in detail. This symbolizes his attempt to secure an immutable future for his music and life, despite the apparent futility, reflecting his cautious and meticulous nature opposed to his brother’s recklessness.
  • The contrast between Joachim (Mr. Spitzer) and Peron are deeply explored as to their opposing characters. Joachim is altruistic, restrained, careful, and Peron was egotistical, reckless, and dismissive of Joachim’s order and sacrifices. It highlights Peron’s irresponsibility, including borrowing and forging checks in Joachim’s name, which caused Joachim’s financial ruin. The passage reveals Joachim’s feelings of invisibility, neglect, and resentment toward Peron, who never acknowledged or appreciated him.

The passage is a powerful summation of the chapter’s themes of loss, memory, and the fragile persistence of life

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer (Joachim)

  • A man of order, methodical, cautious, and devoted to a grand musical project he calls his “opus” or “dirge.”
  • Represents stability, intellectual rigor, and a desire for certainty in an uncertain world.
  • Lives a life of sacrifice, burdened by his brother’s recklessness and debts.
  • Suffers from physical and mental impairments, including distorted vision and a fragile body, symbolic of his fragile mental state.
  • Haunted by his brother’s absence and the loss of a shared past, struggling with identity and reality.
  • Symbolizes the rational, structured side of human nature, trying to impose order on chaos.

Peron (Mr. Spitzer’s Brother)

  • A gambler, extrovert, and embodiment of chaos, risk, and unpredictability.
  • Lives a life of abandon, irresponsibility, and indifference to consequence.
  • His death leaves Joachim to bear the burdens and debts he left behind.
  • Represents the impulsive, irrational, and destructive forces in life, contrasting sharply with Joachim’s order.
  • His laughter and ghostly presence continue to haunt Joachim.

Research: Themes

Duality and Mirror Imagery

See: Duality and Doubles

  • The chapter repeatedly emphasizes twins, mirrors, and reflections: twin portraits, twin gardens, twin portraits of historical figures, and the divided house.
  • Symbolizes the split between order (Joachim) and chaos (Peron), reason and passion, life and death.
  • The mirroring extends to the psychological level where the brothers are halves of one whole, each incomplete without the other.

Memory and Identity

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • Joachim’s identity is fragmented; his memory is unreliable, altered by grief and loss.
  • He questions whether he is himself or his brother, and whether he is awake or dreaming.
  • His life is a continuous search for meaning in the past and the present, often blurred and confused.

Order vs. Chaos

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Joachim’s life is governed by plans, maps, and precise arrangements designed to exclude chance and disorder.
  • Peron’s life is the antithesis: reckless, chaotic, and unpredictable.
  • The tension between these forces creates conflict and tragedy, illustrating the human struggle to balance these aspects.

Mortality and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Joachim views his music as a tomb, an immortal legacy that will outlive his physical existence.
  • Peron’s death and presumed freedom contrast with Joachim’s struggle to survive and find meaning.
  • The chapter meditates on death, mourning, and the desire for lasting significance.

Alienation and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Joachim feels alienated from himself, others, and reality.
  • His impaired vision and mental confusion symbolize his estrangement from the world.
  • He lives in a liminal state, neither fully awake nor fully asleep, caught between life and death.

  • Wealth, like many other things in the story, is portrayed as a form of illusion or "counterfeit," reflecting the transient and unstable aspects of life and human experience that the characters grapple with.The history of money is a journey from direct barter to symbolic representations of value, including commodity items, metal coins, paper notes, and modern digital currencies. This evolution was driven by the need for a more efficient and reliable medium of exchange as societies grew more complex. For most of early human history, transactions were based on barter or the direct exchange of goods and services. Early societies began to use easily tradable items with inherent value, known as commodity money. Around 9000– 6000 B.C., cattle, sheep, and camels were among the first forms of money. They were both a medium of exchange and a symbol of wealth. From around 1200 B.C., cowrie shells became the most widely and longest-used currency in history, particularly in Asia and Africa. Their durability, size, and scarcity made them a popular choice. Salt, grain, and even whale teeth were used as currency in various cultures. The use of precious metals marked a significant step in money's history, offering a more durable and standardized medium of exchange. As early as the 3rd millennium B.C. in Egypt and Mesopotamia, standardized weights of gold, silver, and other metals were used for trade. The Lydian kingdom (in modern-day Turkey) is widely credited with issuing the first standardized and officially stamped coins around 650–600 B.C.. Made from electrum (a gold and silver alloy), these coins featured a royal symbol that guaranteed their weight and value. Around the same time, Chinese mints produced metal coins in the shape of spades and knives. The invention of paper money was a solution to the inconvenience of carrying heavy metal coins for large transactions. Chinese merchants would deposit their metal coins with goldsmiths and receive a paper receipt, which they then used for purchases. This early system was known as "flying money". During the Song Dynasty (1020s), the Chinese government took control of the system, issuing the first official paper currency. Inspired by Marco Polo's accounts of Chinese paper money, Europeans began adopting it in the 17th century. Sweden was the first to introduce European-style banknotes in 1661. The formal backing of currency evolved from commodities to government decree. To control inflation and ensure stability, governments in the 19th and early 20th centuries adopted the gold standard, where they issued paper money redeemable for a fixed amount of gold. After World War II, many countries pegged their currencies to the US dollar, which was, in turn, fixed to gold. In the 1970s, this system was abandoned, and money became a fiat currency. Its value is not derived from a physical commodity but from a government decree and public trust in the issuing authority. The rapid evolution of technology has pushed money into the digital realm, from traditional systems to decentralized networks. Starting in the 1950s, modern credit cards allowed for cashless purchases, with the first successful general-purpose card being the Diners Club Card in 1950.

The business of counterfeiting money is nearly as old as money itself: plated copies (known as Fourrées) have been found of Lydian coins, which are thought to be among the first Western coins. Before the introduction of paper money, the most prevalent method of counterfeiting involved mixing base metals with pure gold or silver. During World War II, the Nazis forged British pounds and American dollars. Today, some of the finest counterfeit banknotes are called Superdollars because of their high quality and imitation of the real US dollar. There has been significant counterfeiting of Euro banknotes and coins since the launch of the currency in 2002, but considerably less than that of the US dollar. Some of the ill-effects that counterfeit money has on society include a reduction in the value of real money; an increase in prices (inflation) as a result of an increase in money being circulated in the economy; a decrease in the acceptability of paper money; and losses, when traders are not reimbursed for counterfeit money detected by banks, even if it is confiscated. Traditionally, anti-counterfeiting measures involved including fine detail with raised intaglio printing on bills which allows non-experts to easily spot forgeries.   • The extensive list of royalty, animals, insects, famous buildings, and notable historical figures serves multiple symbolic and thematic purposes. The variety of figures represents the vast, interconnected, and layered nature of existence. It suggests that human life, history, and nature are woven together in a complex tapestry that transcends time and space. The mention of these figures alongside celestial and natural imagery emphasizes the novel's theme of blurred boundaries between life and death, reality and dream. The dead are portrayed as continuing presences, their memories, and legacies lingering in the world and in the consciousness of the living, especially in the mind of Mr. Spitzer, the family lawyer who acts as a keeper of memory and history. The passage references metamorphosis explicitly and the transformation of earthly figures into ethereal or symbolic forms. This imagery aligns with the novel’s preoccupation with change, impermanence, and the fluidity of identity. The characters and elements listed symbolize various stages, states, and aspects of being, emphasizing that nothing remains fixed, and all life is subject to transformation. By mixing images of grandeur with decay, the list underscores the inevitability of death and the fading of all earthly glory. It stresses that all humans, regardless of status, are subject to mortality, a recurring theme in the novel. The cataloging of historical and mythical figures alongside ephemeral things like butterflies and moths, and symbolic references points to the fragility of memory and the losses that accumulate over time. Mr. Spitzer’s role is to navigate this complex legacy, but even he is often overwhelmed by the incompleteness and elusiveness of memory. The list contributes to the novel’s dreamlike and mythic quality. It mirrors the fragmented, layered storytelling style, where history, myth, and personal memory intertwine. This technique immerses the reader in the same blurred reality experienced by the characters, where time is non-linear and identities are fluid. The list is not meant to be read as a mere inventory but as a symbolic meditation on the themes of the novel: the passage of time, mortality, transformation, memory, and the intertwined nature of life and death. It reflects the complexity of existence that Mr. Spitzer faces as he attempts to make sense of the lives and legacies of those around him.
  • “Lady Hamiltons” Dame Emma Hamilton, known upon moving to London as Emma Hart, and upon marriage as Lady Hamilton, was an English maid, model, dancer and actress. She began her career in London's demi-monde, becoming the mistress of a series of wealthy men, culminating in the naval hero Lord Nelson, and was the favourite model and muse of the portraitist George Romney. In 1791, at the age of 26, she married Sir William Hamilton, British ambassador to the Kingdom of Naples, where she was a success at court, befriending the queen who was a sister of Marie Antoinette, and meeting Nelson.
  • “George Washingtons fording the twin Delawares” Washington Crossing the Delaware is the title of three 1851 oil-on-canvas paintings by the German-American artist Emanuel Leutze depicting General George Washington's crossing of the Delaware River with the Continental Army on the night of December 25–26, 1776, during the American Revolutionary War. Washington's covert crossing the Delaware River that night was the first of several moves, leading to a surprise attack and victory against Hessian forces at the Battle of Trenton in New Jersey on the morning of December 26. The original was part of the collection at the Kunsthalle in Bremen, Germany, and was destroyed in a bombing raid in 1942, during World War II. Leutze painted two more versions, one of which is now in the Metropolitan Museum of Art in New York City. The other was in the West Wing reception area of the White House in Washington, D.C., but in March 2015, was purchased and put on display at the Minnesota Marine Art Museum in Winona, Minnesota. In April 2022 Christie's announced that the smaller painting would be sold at auction the following month, for a pre-sale estimate of $15 million to $20 million. It sold for $45 million.
  • “Duchesses of Devon” There have been many Duchesses of Devonshire throughout history, including Georgiana Cavendish (1757–1806), a famous socialite and political activist known for her style and charisma, and Deborah Cavendish (1920–2014), a member of the well-known Mitford family and a writer and socialite. Other notable Duchesses include Mary Cavendish (1895–1988), who served as Mistress of the Robes to Queen Elizabeth II, and Amanda Cavendish (born 1944), the current wife of the 12th Duke.
  • “President Monroes” James Monroe was an American Founding Father who served as the fifth president of the United States from 1817 to 1825. He was the last Founding Father to serve as president as well as the last president of the Virginia dynasty. He was a member of the Democratic-Republican Party, and his presidency coincided with the Era of Good Feelings, concluding the First Party System era of American politics. He issued the Monroe Doctrine, a policy of limiting European colonialism in the Americas. Monroe previously served as Governor of Virginia, a member of the United States Senate, U.S. ambassador to France and Britain, the seventh secretary of state, and the eighth secretary of war. During the American Revolutionary War, he served in the Continental Army. Monroe studied law under Thomas Jefferson from 1780 to 1783 and subsequently served as a delegate to the Continental Congress as well as a delegate to the Virginia Ratifying Convention. He opposed the ratification of the United States Constitution. In 1790, Monroe won election to the Senate where he became a leader of the Democratic-Republican Party. He left the Senate in 1794 to serve as President George Washington's ambassador to France but was recalled by Washington in 1796. Monroe won the election as Governor of Virginia in 1799 and strongly supported Jefferson's candidacy in the 1800 presidential election. As President Jefferson's special envoy, Monroe helped negotiate the Louisiana Purchase, through which the United States nearly doubled in size. Monroe fell out with his longtime friend James Madison after Madison rejected the Monroe– Pinkney Treaty that Monroe negotiated with Britain. He unsuccessfully challenged Madison for the Democratic-Republican nomination in the 1808 presidential election, but he joined Madison's administration as Secretary of State in 1811. During the later stages of the War of 1812, Monroe simultaneously served as Madison's Secretary of State and Secretary of War. Monroe's wartime leadership established him as Madison's heir apparent, and he easily defeated Federalist candidate Rufus King in the 1816 presidential election. During Monroe's tenure as president, the Federalist Party collapsed as a national political force and Monroe was re-elected, virtually unopposed, in 1820. As president, he signed the Missouri Compromise, which admitted Missouri as a slave state and banned slavery from territories north of the 36°30′ parallel. In foreign affairs, Monroe and Secretary of State John Quincy Adams favored a policy of conciliation with Britain and a policy of expansionism against the Spanish Empire. In the 1819 Adams–Onís Treaty with Spain, the United States secured Florida and established its western border with New Spain. In 1823, Monroe announced the United States' opposition to any European intervention in the recently independent countries of the Americas with the Monroe Doctrine, which became a landmark in American foreign policy. Monroe was a member of the American Colonization Society which supported the colonization of Africa by freed slaves, and Liberia's capital of Monrovia is named in his honor. Following his retirement in 1825, Monroe was plagued by financial difficulties and died on July 4, 1831, in New York City: sharing a distinction with presidents John Adams and Thomas Jefferson of dying on the anniversary of U.S. independence. Historians have generally ranked him as an above-average president.
  • “Monroe Doctrine” was a U.S. foreign policy statement in 1823 by President James Monroe that opposed European colonialism and interference in the Western Hemisphere. It essentially divided the world into two spheres of influence: Europe and the Americas, with the U.S. pledging not to interfere in European affairs in exchange for European powers staying out of the newly independent nations of the Western Hemisphere. While initially not taken seriously by Europe, it evolved into a cornerstone of American foreign policy and was later extended by Theodore Roosevelt's Corollary to justify U.S. intervention in Latin America.
  • “British Red Coats” refers to soldiers of the British Army, particularly those who wore distinctive red coats, primarily during the 17th to the early 20th centuries. The term gained notoriety in the United States due to their role as the opposing force during the American Revolution. While the red coat is strongly associated with the British, it was also adopted by other armies and has a history tied to practicality and symbolism.
  • “the twin belles of old New York” may refer to The Dolly Sisters. Hungarian-American identical twins Rosie and Jenny Dolly were well-known dancers, singers, and actresses in New York City's vaudeville and theater scene in the 1910s and '20s. They were famously successful on Broadway and became international celebrities. Their lives were later turned into the 1945 film The Dolly Sisters. There is also a popular Greenwich Village legend that tells the story of two feuding twin sisters who were the original inhabitants of the twin antebellum houses at 39 and 41 Commerce Street. According to the story, a sea captain built the identical houses for his twin daughters, giving them a shared garden but few windows facing each other to keep them apart. This version of the houses' history is not supported by evidence. The houses were actually built in the 1830s by a New Jersey milkman as an investment property. In the early 20th century, identical twins Caroline and Margaret Bailey were well-documented by their local Bronxville newspaper, which once called them the "Village's most famous twins".
  • “twin President Garfields” James Abram Garfield (November 19, 1831 – September 19, 1881) was the 20th president of the United States, serving from March 1881 until his death in September that year after being shot two months earlier. A preacher, lawyer, and Civil War general, Garfield served nine terms in the United States House of Representatives and is the only sitting member of the House to be elected president. Before his candidacy for the presidency, he had been elected to the U.S. Senate by the Ohio General Assembly, a position he declined when he became president-elect. Garfield was born into poverty in a log cabin and grew up in northeastern Ohio. After graduating from Williams College in 1856, he studied law and became an attorney. He was a preacher in the Stone– Campbell Movement and president of the Western Reserve Eclectic Institute, affiliated with the Disciples. Garfield was elected as a Republican member of the Ohio State Senate in 1859, serving until 1861. He opposed Confederate secession, was a major general in the Union Army during the American Civil War, and fought in the battles of Middle Creek, Shiloh, and Chickamauga. He was elected to Congress in 1862 to represent Ohio's 19th district. Throughout his congressional service, he firmly supported the gold standard and gained a reputation as a skilled orator. He initially agreed with Radical Republican views on Reconstruction but later favored a Moderate Republican–aligned approach to civil rights enforcement for freedmen. Garfield's aptitude for mathematics extended to his own proof of the Pythagorean theorem, which he published in 1876. At the 1880 Republican National Convention, delegates chose Garfield, who had not sought the White House, as a compromise presidential nominee on the 36th ballot. In the 1880 presidential election, he conducted a low-key front porch campaign and narrowly defeated the Democratic nominee, Winfield Scott Hancock. Garfield's accomplishments as president included his assertion of presidential authority against senatorial courtesy in executive appointments, a purge of corruption in the Post Office, and his appointment of a Supreme Court justice. He advocated for agricultural technology, an educated electorate, and civil rights for African Americans. He also proposed substantial civil service reforms, which were passed by Congress in 1883 as the Pendleton Civil Service Reform Act and signed into law by his successor, Chester A. Arthur. Garfield was a member of the intraparty "Half-Breed" faction who used the powers of the presidency to defy the powerful "Stalwart" Senator Roscoe Conkling from New York. He did this by appointing Blaine faction leader William H. Robertson to the lucrative post of Collector of the Port of New York. The ensuing political battle resulted in Robertson's confirmation and the resignations of Conkling and Thomas C. Platt from the Senate. On July 2, 1881, Charles J. Guiteau, a disappointed and delusional office seeker, shot Garfield at the Baltimore and Potomac Railroad Station in Washington. The wound was not immediately fatal, but an infection caused by his doctors' unsanitary methods in treating the wound killed Garfield on September 19. Due to his brief tenure in office, historians tend to rank Garfield as a below-average president or omit him entirely from rankings, though he has earned praise for anti-corruption and pro-civil rights stances.
  • “Roman senators” In the 3rd century BCE, Roman senators were members of a life-long, elite body that held significant power by advising magistrates and the Roman people. Membership was exclusive, initially consisting of patricians but later expanding to include plebeians who had held senior magistracies. The Senate's authority stemmed from the collective prestige of its members, who were typically from wealthy, landowning families, and the Senate's advisories (senatus consulta) were often followed in practice. The senate then numbered around 300 members. Famous Roman senators of the 3rd century BC include Marcus Claudius Marcellus, a renowned general and consul, and Cato the Elder, a staunch conservative statesman and military leader. Another key figure was Gaius Flaminius, a consul and politician known for his land reforms and his death at the Battle of Lake Trasimene.
  • “Roman senates” In the 3rd century BCE, the Roman Senate was a powerful and influential body, though its exact number of members is debated but likely around 300, and was composed of former and current magistrates drawn from the wealthy equestrian and patrician classes. The Senate held significant advisory power, with its decrees, called senatus consulta, generally implemented by magistrates. This period, known as the Middle Republic, saw the Senate's authority at its height, influencing Roman policy through its collective prestige.
  • “St. Bernard dogs” became famous for rescuing alpine travelers by working with monks at the Great St. Bernard Hospice in the Alps, where they were bred for their strength, endurance, and keen sense of smell to find people buried under snow and avalanches. Working in pairs, one dog would locate and provide warmth and comfort to the stranded individual while the other returned to the hospice to alert the monks. The most famous of these dogs was Barry, credited with saving over 40 lives, with his preserved body now at the Natural History Museum of Bern.
  • “Queen Isabellas of Spain” Isabella I, also called Isabella the Catholic, was Queen of Castile and León from 1474 until her death in 1504. She was also Queen of Aragon from 1479 until her death as the wife of King Ferdinand II. Reigning together over a dynastically unified Spain, Isabella and Ferdinand are known as the Catholic Monarchs. Her reign marked the end of Reconquista and also the start of the Spanish Empire and dominance of Spain over European Politics for the next century. Isabella's marriage to Ferdinand of Aragon in 1469 created the basis of the de facto unification of Spain. With Ferdinand's help, she won the War of the Castilian Succession, securing her position as Queen of Castille. Isabella reorganized the governmental system, brought the crime rate down, and unburdened the kingdom of the debt which her half-brother King Henry IV had left behind. Her reforms and those she made with her husband had an influence that extended well beyond the borders of their united kingdoms. Isabella and Ferdinand are known for being the first monarchs to be referred to as the queen and king of Spain, respectively. Their actions included completion of the Reconquista, the Alhambra Decree which ordered the mass expulsion of Jews from Spain, initiating the Spanish Inquisition, financing Christopher Columbus's 1492 voyage to the New World, and establishing the Spanish Empire, making Spain a major power in Europe and the world and ultimately ushering in the Spanish Golden Age. Together with her husband, Isabella was granted the title of "Catholic Monarch" by Pope Alexander VI, a Spaniard. Her sainthood case was opened in 1958, and in 1974 she was granted the title of Servant of God in the Catholic Church.
  • “Christopher Columbus” was an Italian explorer and navigator, sponsored by the Spanish monarchs, who led four transatlantic voyages between 1492 and 1504, opening the door for widespread European colonization of the Americas. His expeditions began a new era of European exploration, but also brought disease and conquest to the Indigenous populations of the Americas.
  • “Chrysler Building” is a 1,046-foot-tall, Art Deco skyscraper in the East Midtown neighborhood of Manhattan, New York City, United States. Located at the intersection of 42nd Street and Lexington Avenue, it is the tallest brick building in the world with a steel framework. It was both the world's first supertall skyscraper and the world's tallest building for 11 months after its completion in 1930. As of 2019, the Chrysler is the 12th-tallest building in the city, tied with The New York Times Building. Originally a project of real estate developer and former New York State Senator William H. Reynolds, the building was commissioned by Walter Chrysler, the head of the Chrysler Corporation. The construction of the Chrysler Building, an early skyscraper, was characterized by a competition with 40 Wall Street and the Empire State Building to become the world's tallest building. The Chrysler Building was designed and funded by Walter Chrysler personally as a real estate investment for his children, but it was not intended as the Chrysler Corporation's headquarters (which was located in Detroit at the Highland Park Chrysler Plant from 1934 to 1996). An annex was completed in 1952, and the building was sold by the Chrysler family the next year, with numerous subsequent owners. When the Chrysler Building opened, there were mixed reviews of the building's design, some calling it inane and unoriginal, others hailing it as modernist and iconic. Reviewers in the late 20th and early 21st centuries regarded the building as a paragon of the Art Deco architectural style. In 2007, it was ranked ninth on the American Institute of Architects' list of America's Favorite Architecture. The facade and interior became New York City designated landmarks in 1978, and the structure was added to the National Register of Historic Places as a National Historic Landmark in 1976.
  • “old Flatiron Building", originally the Fuller Building, is a 22-story, 285-foot-tall steel-framed triangular building at 175 Fifth Avenue in the Flatiron District neighborhood of Manhattan in New York City. Designed by Daniel Burnham and Frederick P. Dinkelberg, and sometimes called, in its early days, "Burnham's Folly", was opened in 1902. The building sits on a triangular block formed by Fifth Avenue, Broadway, and East 22nd Street (where the building's 87-foot back end is located) with East 23rd Street grazing the triangle's northern (uptown) peak. The name "Flatiron" derives from its triangular shape, which recalls that of a cast-iron clothes iron. The Flatiron Building was developed as the headquarters of construction firm Fuller Company, which acquired the site from the Newhouse family in May 1901. Construction proceeded rapidly, and the building opened on October 1, 1902. Though the building was originally 20 floors, a "cowcatcher" retail space (a low attached building so called for its resemblance to the device on rail locomotives) and penthouse were added shortly after the building's opening. The Fuller Company sold the building in 1925 to an investment syndicate. The Equitable Life Assurance Society took over the building after a foreclosure auction in 1933 and sold it to another syndicate in 1945. Helmsley-Spear managed the building for much of the late 20th century, renovating it several times. The Newmark Group started managing the building in 1997. Ownership was divided among several companies, which started renovating the building again in 2019.
