Jacob Garlick agreed to acquire the Flatiron Building at an auction in early 2023, but failed to pay the required deposit, and three of the four existing ownership groups took over the building. In October 2023, the building's owners announced that it would be converted to residential condominiums; the project is planned to be complete by 2026. The Flatiron Building's facade is divided vertically into three sections, similarly to the components of a classical column. The three-story base is clad with limestone, while the upper stories are clad with glazed terracotta. The building's steel frame, designed by structural engineering firm Purdy and Henderson, was intended to withstand four times the maximum wind force of the area. Called "one of the world's most iconic skyscrapers and a quintessential symbol of New York City", the building anchors the south (downtown) end of Madison Square and the north (uptown) end of the Ladies' Mile Historic District. The neighborhood around it is called the Flatiron District after its signature, iconic building. The building was designated a New York City landmark in 1966, was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 1979, and was designated a National Historic Landmark in 1989.
  • “old Fishback Building” may refer to the building in Indianapolis it was the start of Frank Fishback’s coffee roasting business in the late 1880s and by the 1910s it also sold Virginia Sweet brand foods. The company closed in the 1930s. The Fishback family is a family in America that can be traced back to John Fishback, an immigrant from Germany in 1714 who settled in Virginia with Governor Spottswood's colony. Extensive genealogical records, including the 1914 book Genealogy of the Fishback Family in America, document the family's history and its descendants' migration across the United States, with significant populations historically in Kentucky and other states.
  • “Boston Common” is a public park in downtown Boston, Massachusetts. It is the oldest city park in the United States. Boston Common consists of 50 acres of land bounded by five major Boston streets: Tremont Street, Park Street, Beacon Street, Charles Street, and Boylston Street. The Common is part of the Emerald Necklace of parks and parkways that extend from the Common south to Franklin Park in Jamaica Plain, Roxbury, and Dorchester. The visitors' center for the city of Boston is located on the Tremont Street side of the park. The Central Burying Ground is on the Boylston Street side of Boston Common and contains the graves of artist Gilbert Stuart and composer William Billings. Also buried there are Samuel Sprague and his son Charles Sprague, one of America's earliest poets. Samuel Sprague was a participant in the Boston Tea Party and fought in the Revolutionary War. The Common was designated as a Boston Landmark by the Boston Landmarks Commission in 1977.
  • “old Third Avenue El” may refer to the now defunct IRT Third Avenue Line. The IRT Third Avenue Line, commonly known as the Third Avenue Elevated, Third Avenue El, or Bronx El, was an elevated railway in Manhattan and the Bronx, New York City. Originally operated by the New York Elevated Railway, an independent railway company, it was acquired by the Interborough Rapid Transit Company (IRT) and eventually became part of the New York City Subway system. The first segment of the line, with service at most stations, opened from South Ferry to Grand Central Depot on August 26, 1878. Service was extended to Harlem in Manhattan on December 30. In 1881 this line already began 24/7 service. Service in Manhattan was phased out in the early 1950s and closed completely on May 12, 1955. The remaining service in the Bronx was designated as part of the 13 route until it was discontinued on April 29, 1973. The Third Avenue El was the last elevated line to operate in Manhattan, other than the 1 train on the IRT Broadway–Seventh Avenue Line (which has elevated sections between 122nd and 135th Streets and north of Dyckman Street), and was a frequent backdrop for movies. Service on the Second, Sixth, and Ninth Avenue elevated lines were terminated in 1942, 1938, and 1940, respectively.
  • “Chinatown” U.S. Chinatowns were ethnic enclaves, primarily in the West, established in the mid-19th century by immigrants drawn by the Gold Rush and railroad jobs, but were devastated by the 1882 Chinese Exclusion Act which banned further immigration and caused populations to decline. By the early 20th century, Chinatowns were predominantly male-dominated communities centered on social societies, gambling, and opium dens, but after the 1943 Magnuson Act repealed the exclusion laws, populations began to rise again, leading to changes in the established communities.
  • “Old-time Hoboken ferry boats” may refer to the Hoboken Ferry Company, which began operations in 1822, offering the sole connection across the Hudson River for nearly 90 years. The Hoboken Ferry operated until 1967 and saw significant developments like the 1907 opening of the Delaware, Lackawanna & Western Railroad's Hoboken Terminal, which the ferry served, and the introduction of various ferryboats like the double-ended, vehicle-carrying Binghamton in 1905. The ferry system transported thousands of commuters daily and remained the primary mode of transport for many years, only eventually facing competition with the arrival of the PATH train in 1908.
  • “Jersey shore” the Jersey Shore was a popular resort destination known for its boardwalks, amusement parks, and seaside attractions like Atlantic City's Steel Pier, with fashion evolving from long dresses to modern bathing suits by the 1930s. It was accessible via new bridges and tunnels from major cities, becoming an iconic vacation spot that attracted families, celebrities like Marilyn Monroe, and even hosted the Miss America pageant. The landscape featured classic smaller motels, especially in the Wildwoods, and the area was a hotbed for classic Americana before the emergence of more modern developments.
  • Maxwell autos may refer to Maxwell Motor Company which ran from 1904 to 1925 and which later became Chrysler.
  • Peron’s motto was carpe diem. Carpe diem is Latin for seize the day.
  • Joachim’s motto was “hoc opus, hic labor est —for this is the truly difficult thing.” Hoc opus, hic labor est is Latin for - this is the task, this is the labor. The line is from Aeneid, a Latin epic poem written by Vrigil.
  • There are now three different mottos hinting at three different personalities in this chapter. Peron is carpe diem; seize the day. Joachim is hoc opus, hic labor est; this is the task, this is the labor. Mr. Spitzer’s is semper fidelis, semper idem, semper paratus; always faithful, always the same, always ready.
  • Gambling or betting or gaming is the wagering of something of value on an event with an uncertain outcome with the intent of winning something else of value. Gambling dates back to the Paleolithic period, before written history. Financial Investments are generally not considered gambling when they meet certain criteria. Studies show that though many people participate in gambling as a form of recreation or to earn an income, gambling, like any behavior involving variation in brain chemistry, can become a behavioral addiction. Behavioral addiction can occur with all the negative consequences in a person's life minus the physical issues faced by people who compulsively engage in drug and alcohol abuse. Problem gambling has multiple symptoms. Gamblers often gamble to try to win back money they have lost, and some gamble to relieve feelings of helplessness and anxiety. Gamblers may exhibit a number of cognitive and motivational biases that distort the perceived odds of events and that influence their preferences for gambles. Addiction by Design by Natasha Dow Schull shows how the manipulation of gambling pulls players into a trancelike state in which daily worries, social demands, and even bodily awareness fade away. Once in the zone, gambling addicts play not to win but simply to keep playing, for as long as possible, even at the cost of physical and economic exhaustion. Gamblers seek to lose themselves while the gambling industry seeks profit. Schull describes how the industry designs systems to profit from the maximum amount from gamblers and manipulates human psychology.
  • “Swiss bell ringers” refers to both a popular form of American entertainment in the 19th and early 20th centuries, featuring musical performances with handbells and cowbells, and the generic term for handbell choirs that became popular as a result of these shows. These performing groups, which were not necessarily actually from Switzerland, brought a unique sound and visual spectacle to audiences, contributing to a lasting tradition of handbell music. In the 1840s Swiss bell-ringing acts, likely featuring family troupes, gained popularity in the United States after appearing in larger entertainment shows, like P.T. Barnum's American Museum. Groups like the Spaulding Brothers' Swiss Bell Ringers and the Peak Family Swiss Bell Ringers created elaborate performances, often including other musical instruments and vocalists. The name "Swiss" added a touch of exotic charm and a connection to the romanticized imagery of the Swiss Alps, influencing their popularity.
  • “plinths” is a supportive block, base, or foundation for a variety of objects, including statues, columns, vases, and even entire structures in engineering. The term can also refer to a decorative or functional element at the bottom of cabinetry, a base for electronic enclosures, or the lowest part of an architrave. The primary purpose of a plinth is to provide stability, elevate an object, or serve as a structural foundation.
  • “little black boys with golden turbans” The earliest versions of lawn jockeys, used as hitching posts, were created in the 1850s or early 1860s. There are several legends about the black lawn jockeys. The Jim Crow Museum of Racist Memorabilia writes that "there is very little, if any, primary source material for the claim that lawn jockeys were used as signaling devices for escaping slaves on the Underground Railroad." It is featured in two stories: Raymond Chandler’s 1942 Philip Marlowe novel, The High Window, and a short story by Flannery O’Connor in 1955, The Artificial Nigger. The story suggests that people are not intrinsically racist: rather, racist views are handed down from generation to generation because some people stand to profit from racism. O'Connor said that it was her favorite story she had written.
  • “porte cochère” is a French-derived architectural element consisting of a covered, roofed entrance structure large enough for vehicles to pass through, providing shelter for passengers disembarking or arriving. Historically used for horse-drawn carriages and now for automobiles, these structures are often found at grand estates, luxury hotels, and other buildings to offer protection from the elements and create a welcoming, sheltered entryway into a courtyard or the building's interior.
  • pagoda is a Hindu or Buddhist temple or sacred building, typically a many-tiered tower, in India and East Asia.
  • viol is a musical instrument of the Renaissance and baroque periods, typically six-stringed, held vertically and played with a bow.
  • "avant-courier" is someone or something that goes ahead of others, like a scout or herald, to announce or prepare for an arrival. The term comes from French, where "avant" means "before" and "coureur" means "runner" or "courier". While originally referring to military scouts, it now describes anyone who precedes another, providing an advance warning or notice of what is to come.
  • “Aeolian harp” (also wind harp) is a musical instrument that is played by the wind. Named after Aeolus, the ancient Greek god of the wind, the traditional Aeolian harp is essentially a wooden box including a sounding board, with strings stretched lengthwise across two bridges. It is often placed in a slightly opened window where the wind can blow across the strings to produce sounds. The strings can be made of different materials (or thicknesses) and all be tuned to the same pitch, or identical strings can be tuned to different pitches. Besides being the only string instrument played solely by the wind, the Aeolian harp is also the only string instrument that plays solely harmonic frequencies. They are recognizable by the sound which is a result of this property, which has been described as eerie and ethereal. The Aeolian harp, already known in the ancient world, was first described by Athanasius Kircher (1602– 1680) in his books. It became popular as a household instrument during the Romantic era, and Aeolian harps are still hand-crafted today. Some are now made in the form of monumental metal sound sculptures located on the roofs of buildings and windy hilltops.
  • “sub specie aeternitatis, under the aspect of eternity, in its essential or universal form” This reflects a philosophical viewpoint regarding the nature of existence and identity beyond the limitations of time and individuality. This Latin phrase, traditionally used by philosophers like Spinoza, means to consider something "under the aspect of eternity," i.e., from a timeless, eternal perspective rather than a temporal or limited one. In the context of the chapter, it suggests looking at the self or existence not just as a particular individual bound by time, but as part of a universal, timeless whole. Mr. Spitzer is reflecting on his own identity and existence, recognizing that he is more than the sum of his temporal experiences. He contemplates that he may have been "retailored" or transformed in ways that transcend ordinary perception, and that his "essential or universal form" is something beyond his individual, physical self. The passage conveys his awareness of the fluidity and multiplicity of identity and existence, moving beyond the confines of linear time and fixed boundaries. It means considering oneself or one’s being from the perspective of eternity, seeing beyond the limited, changing self to a more fundamental, universal essence that is not confined by time or space.
  • It is an honorific expression denoting what is considered to be universally and eternally true, without any reference to or dependence upon temporal facets of reality. The Latin phrase can be rendered in English as "from the perspective of the eternal". More loosely, it is commonly used to refer to an objective (or theoretically possible alternative) point of view. Spinoza's "eternal" perspective is reflected in his Ethics (Part V, Prop. XXIII, Scholium), where he applies Euclid's method (with the use of geometry) to philosophical inquiry, starting with God and nature, before moving to human emotions and the human intellect to reach an understanding of moral philosophy. By proceeding sub specie aeternitatis, Spinoza sought to arrive at an ethical theory that is as precise as Euclid's Elements. In the history of philosophy, this way of proceeding may be contrasted with Aristotle's. Aristotle's methodological differentiations in his "philosophy of human affairs" and his natural philosophy are grounded in the distinction between what is "better known to us" and things "better known in themselves", or what is "first for us" and what is "first by nature", a distinction that is deliberately discarded by Spinoza, and also by other modern philosophers.
  • “Newport polka” refers to several 19th-century musical compositions, notably Carl Bergmann's "Midday Polka" and "Fillmore House Polka," which celebrated Newport, Rhode Island's social scene. These are notated instrumental pieces, with the "Midday Polka" from 1854 and the "Fillmore House Polka" from 1856 dedicated to the grand hotels of the city. The term can also refer to notated music sheets or other polka compositions from or related to Newport.
  • “schottische” is a 19th-century German partnered country dance, similar to a slower polka, that involves sidesteps and a slow turn, or sometimes a hop. Also known as the "Scottish dance," it originated in Bohemia and became a popular European and American folk dance, influencing various regional styles and music like Argentina's chotis and Finland's jenkka. It is typically performed to music in 4/4 time and is still a part of folk dance traditions worldwide.
  • “polka” is a lively, 19th-century Bohemian (Czech) dance and dance music genre characterized by couples dancing to music in 2/4 time with a basic pattern of quick steps and a hop. Popularized across Europe and the Americas, the name likely derives from the Czech word "půlka," meaning "half-step," though it has also been mistakenly linked to Polish women due to the similar-sounding Czech word.
  • “minuet” is a social dance of French origin for two people, usually written in 3/4 time. The English word was adapted from the Italian minuetto and the French minuet. The term also describes the musical form that accompanies the dance, which subsequently developed more fully, often with a longer musical form called the minuet and trio, and was much used as a movement in the early classical symphony. While often stylized in instrumental forms, composers of the period would have been familiar with the popular dance.
  • “mother-of-pearl Venus comb” is a species of large predatory sea snail, a marine gastropod mollusk in the family Muricidae, the rock snails or murex snails. The shell of this Indo-Pacific species has a very long siphonal canal and numerous spines. Perfect specimens of the shell are not easily found because of the fragility of the numerous long spines.
  • “Mozart” Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart was a prolific and influential composer of the Classical period. Despite his short life, his rapid pace of composition and proficiency from an early age resulted in more than 800 works representing virtually every Western classical genre of his time. Many of these compositions are acknowledged as pinnacles of the symphonic, concertante, chamber, operatic, and choral repertoires. Mozart is widely regarded as one of the greatest composers in the history of Western music, with his music admired for its "melodic beauty, its formal elegance and its richness of harmony and texture". Born in Salzburg, Mozart showed prodigious ability from his earliest childhood. At age five, he was already competent on keyboard and violin, had begun to compose, and performed before European royalty. His father, Leopold Mozart, took him on a grand tour of Europe and then three trips to Italy. At 17, he was a musician at the Salzburg court but grew restless and travelled in search of a better position. Mozart's search for employment led to positions in Paris, Mannheim, Munich, and again in Salzburg, during which he wrote his five violin concertos, Sinfonia Concertante, and Concerto for Flute and Harp, as well as sacred pieces and masses, the motet Exsultate Jubilate, and the opera Idomeneo, among other works. While visiting Vienna in 1781, Mozart was dismissed from his Salzburg position. He stayed in Vienna, where he achieved fame but little financial security. During Mozart's early years in Vienna, he produced several notable works, such as the opera Die Entführung aus dem Serail, the Great Mass in C minor, the "Haydn" Quartets and a number of symphonies. Throughout his Vienna years, Mozart composed over a dozen piano concertos, many considered some of his greatest achievements. In the final years of his life, Mozart wrote many of his best-known works, including his last three symphonies, culminating in the Jupiter Symphony, the serenade Eine kleine Nachtmusik, his Clarinet Concerto, the operas The Marriage of Figaro, Don Giovanni, Così fan tutte and The Magic Flute and his Requiem. The Requiem was largely unfinished at the time of his death at age 35, the circumstances of which are uncertain and much mythologised. His elder sister, Maria Anna Walburga Ignatia "Marianne" Mozart, nicknamed Nannerl, was a highly regarded musician from Salzburg, Austria. In her childhood, she developed into an outstanding keyboard player under the tutelage of her father Leopold. She became a celebrated child prodigy and went on concert tours through much of Europe with her parents and her younger brother Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart. At age 17, her career as a touring musician came to an end, though she continued to work at home teaching piano and performing on occasion. At age 33 she married, moved to a village six hours by carriage from Salzburg, and there raised her own and her husband's children. On her widowhood in 1801, she returned to Salzburg and resumed teaching and performance. She is known to have composed works of music, though no manuscripts survive. In her later years she contributed to the biographical study of her late brother.
  • “hieroglyph” a stylized picture of an object representing a word, syllable, or sound, as found in ancient Egyptian and other writing systems.
  • “siste viator” is a Latin phrase meaning "Stop, traveler," commonly used as an inscription on Roman roadside tombs. The phrase itself is an epitaph, a warning to passersby, encouraging them to pause and consider mortality and their own inevitable end. It invokes themes of mortality, transience, and the universality of death, a common motif in Roman funerary practices.
  • “morceau” is a short literary or musical composition.
  • “alack and a day” is an archaic interjection used to express sorrow, regret, grief, or a sense of misfortune, essentially meaning "woe to the day!" or "shame to the day!" the event occurred. It's a longer form of the word "alack," which itself functions similarly to "alas".
  • “playing the bones” can have several meanings, depending on the context. It could refer to using a musical instrument called the "bones", or it could be a slang term related to gambling, mob culture, or even sexual activity.
  • “parimutual” is a betting system in which all bets of a particular type are placed together in a pool; taxes and the house-take, or vigorish, are deducted, and payoff odds are calculated by sharing the pool among all winning bets. In some countries it is known as the tote after the totalisator, which calculates and displays bets already made. The parimutuel system is used in gambling on horse racing, greyhound racing, jai alai, and other sporting events of relatively short duration in which participants finish in a ranked order. A modified parimutuel system is also used in some lottery games. Parimutuel betting differs from fixed-odds betting in that the final payout is not determined until the pool is closed, in fixed-odds betting, the payout is agreed at the time the bet is made. Parimutuel gambling is frequently state-regulated, and it is offered in many places where gambling is otherwise illegal. Parimutuel gambling is often also offered at off-track facilities, where players may bet on the events without actually being present to observe them in person.
chapter-24:
Chapter 24

← Chapter 23 · Home · Chapter 25 →

Summary

Vera's thoughts move through the household. The servants have absorbed Catherine's dreams so completely that they argue whether it is Roman in the morning and Greek in the afternoon, and assign rooms to famous phantom guests. Catherine plans her own funeral, calls Athens on a telephone wired only to the servants' quarters, and tries to reach Cousin Hannah on a number long disconnected. Mr. Spitzer will come again in the evening with his vague certainties about heaven. Vera asks herself to whom she can turn with her questions about love, marriage, birth, and death, and finds no one.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Music, Sound, and Silence · Time

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Plato and Platonism · Spinoza

Allusions: Music and Composers · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The servants in the household are described as deeply immersed in the dream-like atmosphere created by Vera’s mother. They engage in elaborate fantasies, imagining themselves serving imaginary guests: historic figures, fictional personages, and legendary characters. This passage illustrates how the servants reflect and perpetuate Catherine’s opium-induced dreams, blurring the line between reality and illusion. For example, the old valet believes he serves Wellington, and the gardener imagines himself the spouse of Potiphar, while the Irish housemaid speaks only to herself to avoid confusion. The servants’ acceptance of this unreal environment underscores the theme of escapism and how the household is trapped in a timeless, surreal bubble.
  • The descriptions of the house being filled with imaginary guests sleeping "tier above tier" according to rank and station, the lighting of fires for guests who will never arrive, and the arrangement of Renaissance chairs for intimate conversation depict a grand but empty social world. This passage powerfully conveys Catherine’s craving for social connection and grandeur, yet it is all sustained by illusion. The “mad lady retouching her make-up” and the drunken second butler stumbling over her train amplify the eerie, ghostly quality of the household’s existence.
  • Catherine is obsessed with planning her own funeral and other grand events involving the dead returning to life, a motif that symbolically represents her preoccupation with mortality and the afterlife. Her social secretaries, invitations to ambassadors of Heaven and Hell, and the presence of fashionable dogs highlight her attempt to impose order and meaning on a world that is inherently chaotic and illusory. This passage reveals her complex psychology of wanting to be in control, her detachment from reality, and her engagement with the fantastic.
  • Catherine’s attempts to communicate by telephone with historical figures, relatives, and distant acquaintances only bring frustration and confusion. She calls Athens but reaches Rome, leaves messages for Emperor Hadrian who is never there, and receives only “a cackle of old hen voices” when calling Boston. The telephone is later revealed to be connected only to the servants’ quarters, emphasizing the isolation and breakdown of real connection. This passage poignantly illustrates Catherine’s alienation and the futility of her attempts to reach beyond her own dream-world.
  • Mr. Spitzer, described as a “roundhouse of the trains which run no more” and a “ghost ship with broken mainmasts,” symbolizes the unreliability and futility of seeking certainty or solace in Catherine’s world. He is a poor companion to her “eternal illness,” representing the failure of rationality or conventional comfort in the face of her decaying mental state. His presence contrasts with Vera’s desire for answers about life, love, and death, highlighting the gap between illusion and reality.
  • The chapter ends with Vera contemplating to whom she might turn for answers or to profound personal questions. This passage captures the existential uncertainty and search for meaning that underpin the narrative, emphasizing that even amidst the surreal, Vera seeks some grounding or truth.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Central figure, caught in opium dreams, presiding over an imaginary world filled with historical, mythological, and invented guests.
  • She is practical in some ways but fully immersed in her visionary, dream-like state, discussing grand affairs and social invitations as if real.
  • She is aware of her illusionary world but maintains a clever detachment, placing faith only in the unreal.
  • Her attempts to reach historical or imaginary figures and the failure of these calls reveal her isolation and the limits of her dream world

Miss MacIntosh

  • Practical, grounded, and coarse-grained, she offers contrast to Catherine and the servants’ fantastical world.
  • She is a companion to Vera and represents the voice of reality amidst chaos.

The Servants

  • Immersed in Catherine’s dreams, they adopt roles and beliefs reflecting the surreal environment.
  • Some believe they serve historical figures (e.g., Wellington), others think they live in impossible settings (a forest of cuckoo clocks).
  • They maintain the household’s illusion by preparing for imaginary guests and engaging in conversations about impossible events.
  • The servants’ conversation about imaginary guests and their roles within the dream world encapsulates the blending of fantasy and reality.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A mysterious and somewhat unsatisfactory companion to Catherine, embodying confusion and lost memories.
  • He represents uncertainty about earthly matters while espousing nebulous spiritual certainties about an ultimate Heaven.
  • His characterization as uncertain, evasive, and disconnected from his own memories contrasts with Catherine’s intense visionary life, highlighting themes of memory and reality.

Research: Themes

Reality vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The chapter immerses the reader in a world where the boundaries between real and imaginary are fluid. Catherine’s opium dreams populate the house with imaginary guests, servants who believe in elaborate fantasies, and environments that shift unpredictably.
  • The servants interact with these illusions as if real, discussing imaginary dignitaries, polishing imaginary shoes, and setting places for guests who never arrive. This highlights how illusion can become a shared reality in certain states of mind.

Madness and Sanity

See: Madness and Sanity

  • The novel delves into how prolonged exposure to Catherine’s dreams affects the servants, leading some to lose their grip on reality and adopt bizarre identities or behaviors (e.g., thinking they serve Wellington or living among cuckoo clocks).
  • This theme raises questions about the fragile line between sanity and madness in a closed, surreal environment.

Time and Space Distortion

See: Time

  • The house is timeless and spaceless in a conventional sense, populated by figures from different centuries, places, and mythologies simultaneously.
  • Imaginary guests from various epochs co-exist, and the servants debate the time of day as Roman or Greek, reflecting a dislocation from normal temporal experience.

Isolation and Communication

See: Isolation and Connection · Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Catherine attempts to communicate with distant or deceased figures through a telephone that only connects to the servants’ quarters, symbolizing her isolation and failed attempts at meaningful contact.
  • This motif underscores the theme of disconnection between Catherine’s inner world and external reality.

Death and the Afterlife

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine’s dreams include discussions about her own funeral rites and arrangements for the dead returning to life, blending death with ongoing social rituals.
  • The presence of flowers associated with death and the continual reference to the “dead horses” and “black coachman” suggest a liminal space between life and death

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Imaginary guests and historical figures represent the blending of past, present, and fantasy, showing how Catherine's mind holds vast, impossible histories simultaneously.
  • Black and white horses and coachman symbolize the passage between realms, possibly life and death, or reality and illusion. Earlier Catherine said the white horses were her will and the coachman her conscious.
  • The telephone is a device meant for communication but only connecting to servants’ quarters, symbolizing failed outreach and isolation.
  • Bronze chrysanthemums are flowers for the dead, symbolizing mourning and death’s persistent presence.
  • Cuckoo clocks and elephants represent distorted time and impossible realities within the servants’ transformed perceptions.
  • Snow crystals and halos are visual symbols of the dreamlike, kaleidoscopic nature of Catherine’s world, with multiple suns, moons, and shapes reinforcing the surreal atmosphere.

Research: Resources

  • In the 1800s, servants were an essential part of households, performing a variety of tasks, including cooking, cleaning, and caring for children. They were often treated poorly, with low wages and long hours. In the early 1900s, servants worked in large households of wealthy families, performing a variety of tasks. They were expected to follow strict rules and hierarchies, and had little personal freedom.
  • Catherine and the servants made me think of Audre Lorde who talked about how you cannot dismantle the master’s house using the master’s tools. Here is another expansion on that thought, “You can hang decorations in the master’s house. You can spray slogans about freedom on its walls. You can create altars of equality in its gardens. But the master’s house will still be a prison for everyone but the master himself. What price do we have to pay for staying in the metaphorical master’s house? Why fight for a seat at its tables? Why uncritically celebrate blackface positions in imperialist structures or “woman-face” patriarchs? The only way to be free is to get out of the master’s house.”
  • Beau Brummell is a Regency Era figure who later became associated as a dandy, with fashion, and anything of good quality.
  • Duke of Wellington was a leading figure in 19th-century Britain.
  • Admiral Robert Peary: see Chapter 2, Resources, for the full entry.
  • Plato’s boat might refer to the Ship of State by Plato. It is a metaphor comparing governing a city-state to being the captain of a ship and only philosopher kings should rule.
  • Sir Christopher Wren was a highly acclaimed English architect as well as other professions.
  • Jenny Lind was a Swedish opera singer in the 19th century.
  • Spinoza was a Dutch philosopher. Shakespeare was a famous British playwright.
  • Before 1900, the typical opiate addict in America was an upper-class or middle-class white woman. As long as the opium user was a sick old lady there was no push to punish users.
  • Bishop of Hippo is Saint Augustine who was also a theologian and philosopher.
  • Emperor Hadrian was a Roman emperor from 117 to 138.
  • King Canute or Cnut the Great was King of England, Denmark, and Norway.
  • The Duchess of Spode may refer to an English brand of pottery.
  • Check online for the symbolism of trains in literature.
chapter-11:
Chapter 11

← Chapter 10 · Home · Chapter 12 →

Summary

In this short chapter, Vera wonders how she will bear her isolation. She cannot live on illusion as her mother does, and she trusts herself to know where the dream ends and reality begins, as Miss MacIntosh taught her. She imagines how far her mother has traveled through her opium dream, which runs by the alphabet. The P’s must be past by now. The Q’s are hard company: the Queen Charlotte Islands, and the Queen Maud Mountains, who visits as a frigid, silent house guest in a lace skirt five hundred miles long. The R’s are the charming ones, guests who never met in life: Mr. Res Tacamah, the drug bottle; a pharaoh who unwraps into Rameses I, II, and III; Roland, Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, Rhadamanthus, and Sir Walter Raleigh, who takes off his head with his plumed hat. Mr. Spitzer has missed them all, and Catherine will tell him so.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Mr. Res Tacamah

Concepts present

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Mountains · Opium · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Bus and the Journey · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Sir Walter Raleigh · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Everything Catherine sees in this chapter is Vera’s guess. “She must have reached,” “Perhaps my mother had already passed on.” Vera, who prides herself on knowing where the dream ends, spends the chapter dreaming her mother’s dream for her.
  • The chapter opens with Vera pondering how to endure isolation, recognizing that unlike her mother Catherine, mere illusions are insufficient. She is aware of the boundary between dream and reality, a lesson imparted by Miss MacIntosh, who denies the existence of what does not exist. This sets the thematic framework of the chapter, highlighting the tension between illusion and reality, and the difficulty of coping with solitude without resorting to self-deception.
  • Catherine is described as being in a “wakeful coma,” journeying through an opiate-induced voyage through various symbolic “places” starting with the letter P (Pericles, Penelope’s web, the Pleiades, penguins) and moving onto the Q’s and R’s. This voyage represents a surreal and metaphorical experience, suggesting that Catherine’s consciousness moves through layers of history, mythology, geography, and fantasy. These symbolic names imply a vast, intricate mental landscape, blending real and imagined elements.
  • The Q’s include the Queen Charlotte Islands, Queen Maud Mountains, and a naval battle, each representing different aspects of isolation, coldness, and distance. Queen Maud Mountains, in particular, is portrayed as an imperious, frigid visitor to Catherine’s bedroom, embodying a chilling and overwhelming presence that silences and immobilizes. The description of her skirt as “five hundred miles long and made of pure Brussels lace” evokes a surreal and vast majesty, emphasizing Catherine’s awe and envy.
  • Catherine’s mental journey perhaps continues to the R’s, a group connected by “silken relationships” despite never having met in reality. This assembly includes historical, mythical, and symbolic figures such as Mr. Res Tacamah (a drug bottle), the Egyptian pharaoh Rameses I, II, III (representing fragmented selves and layered identities), runes, royal masts, Roland, Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, and others. The richness of this imagery suggests a complex and paradoxical inner world where time, space, and identity blur.
  • Mr. Spitzer appears as a figure who perpetually misses Catherine’s gatherings of extraordinary company, including great composers, painters, and mythological judges like Rhadamanthus. There is a tone of irony and loss here, as Mr. Spitzer is condemned for forgotten crimes and fails to witness Catherine’s vibrant and mysterious social realm, underscoring themes of absence and missed connection.
  • Among the remarkable guests, Sir Walter Raleigh stands out, described in a lavish white satin suit and associated with a society devoted to atheistic propositions, such as man existing before Adam and God being an idea or even “dog spelled backward.” This philosophical and irreverent note introduces questions about belief, existence, and the nature of divinity, adding a layer of intellectual challenge to Catherine’s dreamlike world.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Catherine’s calculations admit “no theory of loss in the universe where all things were lost.” Who is right, Catherine or Vera?
  • Queen Maud Mountains hides her face behind a parasol “which happened to be my mother’s.” What does Catherine see when she looks at her guest?
  • The pharaoh learns he “had been partitioned into many selves without his knowing it.” Who else in the novel has been divided this way?

Characters

  • Vera says no “mere illusion would suffice me,” then imagines her mother’s dream in detail. How sure is she of the line between them?
  • Catherine is “this great hostess who was in exile.” What is she exiled from?
  • Rhadamanthus finds Mr. Spitzer “guilty of many forgotten crimes.” What crime might Catherine charge him with?

Connections

  • Mr. Res Tacamah was “the drug bottle with ears” in Chapter 2. What has changed in him?
  • Mr. Spitzer’s silent music in Chapter 2 meets Rimski-Korsakov’s music “which was not altogether silent.” Why does Catherine compare them?
  • Raleigh asks to be called “Ocean or Water.” How does the sea keep entering Catherine’s closed room?

Reflection

  • Is there a kind of loneliness that imagination makes worse rather than better?
  • Catherine never leaves her bed, so the mountain comes to her. What is gained and lost by living this way?
  • Can a person know where her own dreams end?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Reflects on isolation and the difficulty of enduring it without resorting to illusions.
  • Maintains a clear boundary between dream and reality.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s Mother)

  • Existing in a semi-conscious, dreamlike coma.
  • Her mental state is depicted as a voyage through symbolic landscapes and figures.
  • Acts as a hostess to a surreal assembly of historical, mythological, and symbolic guests.
  • Denies loss, existing in a universe where things are lost but preserved in other forms.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Absent from every gathering; Catherine will remind him afterward of all he missed.
  • Tied to legal errands and earthly concerns, contrasted with Catherine’s ethereal dream world.
  • Judged by Rhadamanthus in the dream for forgotten crimes, symbolizing guilt and judgment.

Miss MacIntosh

  • Her denial of “those things which did not exist” is the lesson Vera leans on to tell dream from reality.

Research: Themes

Isolation and Endurance

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Vera contemplates how to endure isolation, contrasting herself with her mother, who copes differently through dreams and illusions.
  • Vera is grounded in reality, aware of the dividing line between dream and reality, unlike her mother who dwells in a liminal, dreamlike state.

Dream versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Catherine inhabits a dream world where places and people symbolize different stages or elements of her mental and emotional journey.
  • Her dream is a voyage through alphabetic symbolic “stations” (P’s, Q’s, R’s), each representing complex ideas, places, or characters.
  • Catherine’s dream reflects a universe where loss is denied or transformed rather than accepted.

Memory and Loss

See: Memory and the Past · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Catherine’s dream denies loss, imagining a universe where things are lost but not lost forever.
  • This suggests a coping mechanism for dealing with grief or fading consciousness.

Identity and Multiplicity

See: Identity and the Self

  • Catherine’s dream involves figures like Rameses I, II, and III, representing fragmented selves and layered identities.
  • The dream hints at disjointed time and space, and the coexistence of past and present selves.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Alphabetical Journey (P’s, Q’s, R’s)

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • Represents a symbolic progression or mental voyage.
  • P’s include Pericles, Admiral Peary, Penelope’s web, the Pleiades, and formal penguins.
  • Q’s include Queen Charlotte Islands, Queen Maud Mountains, and a naval battle.
  • R’s include a wide array of figures and concepts: Mr. Res Tacamah (a drug bottle, Catherine’s opium/laudanum), Egyptian pharaohs (Rameses I-III), runes, roulades, rubrics, royal masts, rose windows, Roman numerals, riddles, red-caps in Grand Central Station, Roland, Rimski-Korsakov, Sir Joshua Reynolds, the Great Ram constellation, Rhadamanthus, Sir Walter Raleigh, and more.

Queen Maud Mountains

See: Mountains

  • Personified as a cold, snobbish, imperious houseguest, symbolizing perhaps a harsh, distant presence.
  • The detail of her five-hundred-mile-long Brussels lace skirt evokes grandeur, coldness, and isolation.

Mr. Res Tacamah

See: Mr. Res Tacamah · Opium

  • A symbolic figure representing a drug bottle and shifting identities, suggesting notions of altered consciousness or dependency.

Rameses I, II, III

See: Ancient Egypt

  • Symbolize fragmented identities and the confusion of time within the dream.
  • The pharaoh unwrapping himself reveals the layered nature of self and memory.

Sir Walter Raleigh

See: Sir Walter Raleigh

  • Imagined with a white satin suit embroidered with pearls and gems.
  • His decapitation and request to be called “Ocean or Water” suggest themes of transformation, fluidity, and martyrdom or sacrifice.
  • Raleigh was beheaded in 1618.
  • Represents atheistic propositions and philosophical skepticism within the dream.

Research: Resources

  • “entertaining the P’s, the Q’s, the R’s”: “Mind your P’s and Q’s,” the old warning to watch one’s manners, suits a hostess who greets every guest by letter.
  • “her opiate voyage through nowhere”: Thomas De Quincey’s opium dreams in Confessions of an English Opium-Eater (1821) carried him to Egypt and the East: “I was buried, for a thousand years, in stone coffins, with mummies and sphinxes.” See Opium, The History of Opium, and the Chapter 4 resources.
  • “Pericles”: Pericles (c. 495-429 BC) led Athens in its golden age and had the Parthenon built. See Shakespeare.
    • Shakespeare’s Pericles, Prince of Tyre (c. 1608) is a voyage play. Its hero loses his wife, buried at sea in a chest, and his daughter, and finds both again.
  • “Admiral Peary”: Robert E. Peary claimed the North Pole in 1909 and was made a rear admiral in 1911. Matthew Henson, the Black explorer beside him, by his own account reached the spot first and got little credit for decades. In 1897 Peary brought six Inuit from Greenland to New York for the American Museum of Natural History, and four died within months. The museum staged a fake burial for the boy Minik while it kept his father Qisuk’s skeleton. See Exploration and the Poles, Society, Class, and Race, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “Penelope’s web”: In the Odyssey, Penelope weaves a shroud for Laertes by day and unravels it by night to hold off the suitors. See Homer’s Epics and the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “the Pleiades”: The Pleiades are the seven daughters of Atlas, set in the sky as a star cluster in Taurus. They return at the end of the chapter in Ronsard’s Pléiade. See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “a naval battle, an island, and a continent”: The battle is never named. Quiberon Bay (1759) is the famous Q: Admiral Hawke chased the French fleet into a rocky bay off Brittany in a November gale.
  • “Queen Charlotte Islands”: The Queen Charlotte Islands, off the Pacific coast of Canada, were named in 1787 for the ship Queen Charlotte, which was named for George III’s queen. They are the home of the Haida and are now called Haida Gwaii. See Birds.
    • The gyrfalcon is the largest of the falcons, a bird of the Arctic. White gyrfalcons were gifts for kings, and Catherine kept falconer’s gloves in Chapter 2.
    • Goldeneyes are diving ducks called “whistlers” for the sound of their wings in flight.
  • “a wild swan absent, one wild swan more”: In Andersen’s “The Wild Swans” (1838), eleven brothers are turned into swans, and their sister weaves nettle shirts to free them. The last shirt is unfinished, and the youngest is left with a swan’s wing. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “the proud, cold, utterly snobbish Queen Maud Mountains”: The Queen Maud Mountains rise at the head of the Ross Ice Shelf, on the south edge of the Ross Sea. Roald Amundsen found them in 1911 on his way to the South Pole and named them for Queen Maud of Norway, a daughter of King Edward VII of England. Queen Maud Land is a different region of Antarctica, claimed by Norway. See Exploration and the Poles, Mountains, and Snow, Ice, and Winter.
    • The Ross Sea, a deep bay of the Southern Ocean, is named for James Clark Ross, who sailed into it in 1841.
  • “colder than Boston society”: John Collins Bossidy’s toast (1910): “And this is good old Boston, / The home of the bean and the cod, / Where the Lowells talk only to Cabots, / And the Cabots talk only to God.” See Society, Class, and Race.
  • “coming like the mountain to Mahomet”: The proverb comes from Francis Bacon’s essay “Of Boldness” (1625). Mahomet called a hill to come to him, and when it would not, he said, “If the hill will not come to Mahomet, Mahomet will go to the hill.” Here the mountain comes to Catherine, who never leaves her bed. See Mountains.
  • “made of pure Brussels lace”: Brussels lace is well known for its delicacy and beauty. Originally it was only made from the finest spun linen thread, which was spun in dark damp rooms to keep the thread from becoming too brittle. Only one ray of light was allowed into the room, and it was arranged so that it fell upon the thread. See Clothing, Hats, and Skirts.
  • “pyramid-shaped ices”: Ices were molded into shapes for grand dinners. The pyramids Catherine serves come just before the pharaoh arrives. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “Mr. Res Tacamah who was the drug bottle”: His name may join Rx to tacamahac. Rx stands for the Latin recipe, “take,” at the head of a prescription, and tacamahac is an aromatic resin used in ointments and incense. In Chapter 2 he was “the drug bottle with ears to hear her ravings.” See Mr. Res Tacamah, Opium, and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “Rameses I, II, III”: The royal mummies were found in 1881 in a hidden tomb at Deir el-Bahri, where priests had moved and rewrapped them, some in other kings’ coffins. Shelley’s “Ozymandias” (1818) takes its name from the Greek form of Ramesses II’s throne name, User-maat-re. See Ancient Egypt, Romantic Poets, and the Chapter 2 resources.
    • Menpehtyre Ramesses I (or Ramses) was the founding pharaoh of ancient Egypt’s 19th Dynasty. The dates for his short reign are not completely known but the timeline of late 1292-1290 BC is frequently cited as well as 1295-1294 BC. While Ramesses I was the founder of the 19th Dynasty, his brief reign mainly serves to mark the transition between the reign of Horemheb, who had stabilized Egypt in the late 18th Dynasty, and the rule of the powerful pharaohs of his own dynasty, in particular his son Seti I, and grandson Ramesses II.
    • Ramesses II, commonly known as Ramesses the Great, was an Egyptian pharaoh. He was the third ruler of the Nineteenth Dynasty. Along with Thutmose III of the Eighteenth Dynasty, he is often regarded as the greatest, most celebrated, and most powerful pharaoh of the New Kingdom, which itself was the most powerful period of ancient Egypt.
    • Usermaatre Meryamun Ramesses III was the second pharaoh of the Twentieth Dynasty in ancient Egypt. Some scholars date his reign from 26 March 1186 to 15 April 1155 BC, and he is considered the last pharaoh of the New Kingdom to have wielded substantial power. He took Ramesses II’s throne name and modeled his temple at Medinet Habu on Ramesses II’s, one king dreaming another’s dreams.
  • “partitioned into many selves without his knowing it”: The Egyptians held that a person was made of many parts: the ka, the life force; the ba, the soul that flies from the tomb; the name; the shadow; and the heart, weighed at judgment. See Ancient Egypt and Identity and the Self.
  • “runes, roulades, rubrics, royal masts, rose windows, Roman numerals, many riddles, many red-caps in the Grand Central Station”: Catherine’s R’s run from letters and songs to ships, churches, and numbers.
    • Runes are letters from ancient Germanic alphabets, also called runic alphabets or futharks, which were used primarily to write Germanic languages before the adoption of the Roman alphabet. They are also recognized as symbols with mysterious or magical significance, often used in divination and fortune-telling. Runes were typically carved into wood, stone, or bone.
    • A roulade is an elaborate embellishment of several notes sung to one syllable.
    • A rubric is a word or text written in red ink for emphasis. In the Book of Common Prayer, the rubrics are the instructions printed in red, the stage directions of the services in Chapter 10.
    • A royal mast is the topmost section of a sailing ship’s mast, above the topgallant.
    • A rose window is a round window of stained glass found in churches and cathedrals.
    • Roman numerals are a numeric system created by ancient Romans. They number Rameses I, II, III.
    • A red-cap is a railroad porter. Grand Central’s red caps were mostly Black men from 1909 on. The terminal did not pay them, and they lived on tips until the 1940s. In 1937 red caps organized the International Brotherhood of Red Caps.
    • Grand Central, officially Grand Central Terminal (1913), stands at 42nd Street and Park Avenue in Midtown Manhattan.
  • “Roland who was killed at Roncevalles”: Roland was a military leader under Charlemagne who died at the Battle of Roncevaux Pass in 778, when Basques ambushed Charlemagne’s rear guard. The Song of Roland (c. 1100) turns them into Saracens and has Roland blow his horn too late. In Dante’s Divine Comedy, Roland is named Orlando and placed in the Heaven of Mars with others who fought for the faith (Paradiso 18). See Dante.
  • “Rimski-Korsakov who never came except in Mr. Spitzer’s absence”: Rimski-Korsakov was a prominent Russian composer, a member of the Mighty Handful, five composers who drew on Russian folk music, and a significant figure in shaping Russian classical music. He is known for his operas, orchestral pieces like Scheherazade (1888), named for the bride who tells a tale night after night to stay alive, and Capriccio Espagnol. He sailed around the world as a young naval officer. See Music and Composers and Fairy Tales and Folklore.
    • “music which was not altogether silent”: Mr. Spitzer has written “only silent music, that which, for many years now, no one else had ever heard” (Chapter 2).
  • “Sir Joshua Reynolds”: Sir Joshua Reynolds (1723-1792) was an English painter who specialized in portraits. He promoted the “Grand Style” in painting, which depended on idealization of the imperfect. He was a founder and first president of the Royal Academy of Arts and was knighted by George III in 1769.
  • “the constellation known as the Great Ram”: The Great Ram is Aries, the first sign of the zodiac, the golden ram whose fleece Jason sought. See Astronomy and Greek Mythology.
  • “Raphael’s tomb”: Raphael (1483-1520), the Italian painter, is buried in the Pantheon in Rome. Pietro Bembo’s epitaph reads, “Here lies Raphael, by whom Nature feared to be outdone while he lived, and when he died, feared that she herself would die.”
  • “the songs of Ronsard”: Ronsard was a prominent French Renaissance poet, born in 1524. He was often called the “prince of poets” and was influential in developing the French sonnet and other poetic forms. Ronsard, with his friend Joachim du Bellay, founded the group of poets known as La Pléiade, which aimed to elevate the French language through poetry inspired by classical works. His most famous works include Les Odes (1550) and Les Amours (1552), which helped establish him as a leading poet. His sonnets are particularly admired, with “Mignonne, allons voir si la rose” being one of his most famous poems. He is credited with perfecting the 12-syllable Alexandrine line of French verse and is known for his rich imagery, classical references, and exploration of themes like love, beauty, and the fleeting nature of life. Ronsard also served as a poet and chaplain to King Charles IX and was a major literary figure during the French Renaissance. He continued to revise and publish his works throughout his life. The group took its name from the Pleiades, the seven stars among Catherine’s P’s. Ronsard wrote his poems to be sung, and composers set them in his lifetime.
  • “Tracing a lost heir to no property”: Mr. Spitzer has “practiced law in only the most desultory fashion, often without fee, preferring the lost causes” (Chapter 2). See Joachim Spitzer and the Chapter 2 resources.
  • “Rhadamanthus”: Rhadamanthus, son of Zeus and Europa and brother of Minos, was a king of Crete who became a judge of the dead. In Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 6), he forces the dead to confess the crimes they hid on earth, as he finds Mr. Spitzer “guilty of many forgotten crimes.” He returns in Chapter 14. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the sister ravens, the brother doves”: The Grimms’ “The Seven Ravens” and Giambattista Basile’s “The Seven Doves” (1634-36) both tell of brothers changed into birds and a sister who saves them. Young makes the ravens sisters. See Fairy Tales and Folklore and Birds.
  • “Sir Walter Raleigh in his marvelous white satin suit embroidered with seed pearls”: Sir Walter Raleigh (c. 1552-1618) was an English statesman, soldier, spy, writer, poet, and explorer. He was famous at Elizabeth’s court for the pearls and jewels on his clothes, even his shoes. See Sir Walter Raleigh and Exploration and the Poles.
    • Raleigh’s poetry is known as the plain style. His writing contains strong personal treatments of themes such as love, loss, beauty, and time. Most of his poems are short lyrics that were inspired by actual events. In poems Raleigh expresses a contempt-of-the-world attitude more characteristic of the Middle Ages than of the dawning era of humanistic optimism. But his lesser-known long poem, The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, expresses a melancholy sense of history. The poem was written during his imprisonment in the Tower of London. Raleigh answered Christopher Marlowe’s “The Passionate Shepherd to His Love” with “The Nymph’s Reply to the Shepherd.” Raleigh gives an almost line-for-line refutation of Marlowe’s sentiments. Centuries later, William Carlos Williams added “Raleigh Was Right” (1940) to the conversation. It begins, “We cannot go to the country / for the country will bring us / no peace.”
  • “when he removed his white plumed hat, removed also his head”: Raleigh was beheaded at Westminster on October 29, 1618. Of the axe he said, “This is sharp medicine, but it is a physician for all diseases.” His widow kept his embalmed head for the rest of her life. The poem he wrote the night before begins, “Even such is Time, that takes in trust / Our youth, our joys, our all we have, / And pays us but with earth and dust.” See Sir Walter Raleigh.
  • “his intimate name, Ocean or Water”: Elizabeth called him “Water.” Spenser named him “the Shepherd of the Ocean” in Colin Clouts Come Home Againe (1595), and Raleigh wrote The Ocean’s Love to Cynthia, with the Queen as the moon who rules the tides. See Sir Walter Raleigh and The Sea and Water.
  • “a society of night devoted exclusively to atheistic propositions”: “The school of night” comes from Love’s Labour’s Lost (4.3): “Black is the badge of hell, / The hue of dungeons and the school of night.” The phrase became a name for Raleigh’s circle with Thomas Harriot and Christopher Marlowe, men accused of doubting Genesis and God. In 1594 an inquiry at Cerne Abbas examined charges of atheism against Raleigh’s circle. See Sir Walter Raleigh, Shakespeare, and Genesis.
    • “man had existed before Adam”: The Baines note (1593) charged Marlowe with saying that ancient authors “have assuredly written of above 16 thousand years agone whereas Adam is proved to have lived within 6 thousand years.” See the Chapter 9 resources on pre-Adamites.
    • “God is dog spelled backward”: The word read backward is the last of the R’s “many riddles.”

Chapter 12

← Chapter 11 · Home · Chapter 13 →

Summary

It is after ten at night, and Vera lies beside the Big Ben alarm clock, the one reliable clock in a house of stopped clocks. Restless, she slips out into a garden her grandfather planted for his blind wife, made to be touched and smelled rather than seen. She moves through it with closed eyes in near ecstasy and meditates on Miss MacIntosh and all she taught. The chapter closes on Catherine's suspicion that Mr. Spitzer sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother, betting on phantom horses he could know nothing about.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Dreams and Imagination · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Freedom and Escape · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Love · The Search for Meaning · Time

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Eyes and Blindness · Fog and Mist · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Roses and Flowers

Philosophy: Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Shakespeare · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a meditation on time, describing the Big Ben alarm clock as "Old Reliable," contrasted with other clocks in the house that have stopped at different hours, symbolizing a suspended or fragmented perception of time, linked with Catherine's gradual withdrawal from the world. This symbolizes the tension between the objective measurement of time (servants’ clocks) and subjective experience (stopped clocks), reflecting how personal grief or change distorts time.
  • Vera’s unplanned visit to Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom is described as a sporadic, almost dreamlike moment that is “blurred” in memory and “told only through a veil of oblivion,” emphasizing the elusive nature of memory and how absence reveals what is hidden. This passage sets the tone for the exploration of consciousness and the limits of human understanding.
  • There is a lengthy and lyrical reflection on the human senses and the body’s design underscores the unity and beauty of nature. The eye is described as the organ of sight placed perfectly in the skull, with hair acting as a protective and sensory element, and the skin as a “drum of all our senses.” This passage celebrates the human body as a masterpiece of nature and highlights the interconnectedness of all living things.
  • Vera finds herself in a garden created for a blind person, her grandmother, and reflects on how this place, though designed for the absence of sight, paradoxically influences her own vision. The garden is full of sensory experience beyond sight: textures, smells, and forms without color. This metaphor illustrates the theme of perception beyond the visible, and the coexistence of joy and sorrow, as the garden’s sadness contrasts with Vera’s boundless happiness.
  • Vera contemplates how her earlier dreams and visions experienced as musical discourses with ghosts, reincarnations, and fantastical experiences contrasts with the harsh reality taught by Miss MacIntosh. The nursemaid’s admonition to accept that "nothing had happened" and that mortals are not omniscient introduces a sobering perspective. This tension between dream and reality, imagination and practicality, is a central philosophical conflict in the chapter.
  • Miss MacIntosh represents a grounded, no-nonsense worldview where she emphasizes moral clarity, the distinction between what is real and unreal, and the rejection of dreaming. Her views on love are practical, seeing it as “greatest love which could see another’s face in daylight and hear another’s voice.” She embodies endurance, frugality, and a refusal to indulge in illusions, contrasting with Vera’s imaginative tendencies.
  • The chapter ends with reflections on human limitations in the face of divine mystery. The world is described as a flawed creation, with God having “been filled with the greatest remorse” over the imperfections. Humans are advised to focus on their own lives and not “meddle in His remote business,” highlighting themes of humility and acceptance of the unknowable.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Reflective, imaginative, and sensitive.
  • Struggles between embracing imagination/dreams and confronting reality.
  • Experiences moments of joy and freedom but also faces the harsh truths of life and mortality.

Miss MacIntosh

  • The practical, no-nonsense caretaker who keeps the "Old Reliable" clock.
  • Represents pragmatism, moral clarity, and a grounded worldview.
  • Cautions against illusion and flight of fancy; emphasizes duty and reality.
  • Her perspective contrasts with Vera’s imaginative nature.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Catherine is mentioned as retiring slowly from the world, symbolized by the stopped clocks.

Vera’s grandfather and grandmother

  • The grandfather who planted the garden for his blind wife represents the effort to create a world accessible through other senses.
  • The grandmother’s blindness and her practical nature are contrasted with Vera’s imaginative vision.

Mr. Spitzer (Joachim)

  • A figure with an ambiguous nature and identity.
  • Catherine suspects he sometimes imagines himself to be his dead brother (Peron), blurring reality and fantasy.

Research: Themes

The Illusion and Reality of Time

See: Illusion and Reality · Time

  • Vera reflects on time as both a practical necessity and an illusion.
  • The Big Ben alarm clock symbolizes reliable, practical time, set for servants who must rise at certain hours.
  • Other clocks in the house are stopped at different times, symbolizing frozen moments or hesitation in the past, especially linked to Catherine’s retreat from the world.

The Life of the Imagination vs. Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Vera contrasts a "life of the imagination" with the waking world, pondering the significance of dreams and whether they hold more truth than reality.
  • Dreams are described as limitless and bridging life and death, whereas waking life is governed by cause and effect.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic attitude opposes Vera’s dreamy perspective, emphasizing practical reality and cautioning against illusions.

The Role and Limits of the Senses

See: The Search for Meaning

  • There is an extended meditation on the human senses (sight, hearing, taste, smell, and touch) as the means by which humans experience reality.
  • Vera highlights the design and function of eyes, eyelashes, eyelids, and hair as protective and sensory mechanisms.
  • The garden of the blind symbolizes a world without vision, emphasizing other ways of perceiving such as touch (Braille, texture), and questioning how place and perception influence sorrow and happiness.

Freedom, Innocence, and Joy

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Freedom and Escape

  • There is a moment of profound joy and freedom as Vera walks out into the night, celebrating the beauty and unity of nature.
  • This freedom is described as innocence and clarity of vision, untainted by past sorrow or fear.
  • Vera feels connected to the natural world, sensing stars, flowers, and animals as real and meaningful.

The Limits of Human Understanding and Divine Mystery

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · The Search for Meaning

  • Vera reflects on the limitations of human knowledge, emphasizing that humans are not omniscient and should not try to tamper with God's mysteries.
  • God is portrayed as remorseful over creation’s imperfections, but humans are advised to focus on their own lives rather than cosmic mysteries.

Love and Human Relationships

See: Isolation and Connection · Love

  • Miss MacIntosh’s perspective on love is pragmatic and grounded; love is about seeing and hearing another in daylight and tested by harsh experience.
  • She is portrayed as a plain and practical woman, devoid of romantic illusions or flights of fancy.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Clocks and Time

See: Clocks and Watches · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Clocks stopped at different hours symbolize frozen moments, hesitation, or the past lingering in the present.

The Garden of the Blind

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • Represents a sensory world without sight, emphasizing the importance and limitations of perception.

Eyes and Eyelashes

See: Eyes and Blindness

  • Represent the function and fragility of vision and perception; Vera meditates on their biological and symbolic significance.

Moonlight and Mist

See: Fog and Mist · Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The pregnant moonlight and mist create an atmosphere of mystery, illumination, and ambiguity.

Hair

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Symbolic of protection and sensitivity; also connected to historical and biblical references.

Flowers

See: Roses and Flowers

  • Sensual, tactile flowers in the garden illustrate the blending of senses and the threshold between perception and imagination.

Research: Resources

  • “The wisest man was a fool in God’s eyes, and there was a fool bound in the heart of every child.” - Proverbs 22:15 The phrase captures the paradox of human existence: our striving for knowledge and meaning amid inherent limitations and the acceptance that all are bound to folly in the grander cosmic scheme
  • Big Ben is the nickname for the Great Bell of the Great Clock of Westminster, and, by extension, for the clock tower itself, which stands at the north end of the Palace of Westminster in London, England. Originally named the Clock Tower, it was renamed Elizabeth Tower in 2012 to mark the Diamond Jubilee of Queen Elizabeth II. The clock is a striking clock with five bells.
  • The theme of shadows runs through the novel. It brings to mind Plato’s work, The Allegory of the Cave, or Plato's Cave. It is an allegory presented by the Greek philosopher Plato in his work, Republic. The Cave, describes a group of people who have lived chained to the wall of a cave all their lives, facing a blank wall. The people watch shadows projected on the wall from objects passing in front of a fire behind them and give names to these shadows. The shadows are the prisoners' reality, but are not accurate representations of the real world. The shadows represent the fragment of reality that we can normally perceive through our senses, while the objects under the sun represent the true forms of objects that we can only perceive through reason. The philosopher is like a prisoner who is freed from the cave and comes to understand that the shadows on the wall are actually not the direct source of the images seen. A philosopher aims to understand and perceive the higher levels of reality. However, the other inmates of the cave do not even desire to leave their prison, for they know no better life.
  • Mona Lisa is a half-length portrait by Leonardo da Vinci.
  • Chanticleer is a male ensemble featured in fiction (Chanticleer and the Fox).
  • Julia Arthur and Maude Adams did a production of Romeo and Juliet in 1899.
  • Tramontane is a classical name for a northern wind.

Chapter 41
