Summary

Catherine believes only a hair's breadth separates life from death. Her selves leave her body and may not return, furniture drifts, and windows face different seas. She imagines herself an engineer, a builder of cities, a traveler across deserts, yet she cannot walk. Mr. Spitzer complains that she never saw him as a unique person, and so he never learned who he was. Catherine does not envy Hannah's single, steady purpose.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Duality and Doubles · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Pearls and Jewels · Silence and Deafness · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The House

Philosophy: Aristotle · Hinduism

Allusions: American Writers · Exploration and the Poles · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Vera relates Catherine's conviction that there is no true difference or only an infinitesimal difference between life and death. This passage sets the tone for the entire chapter, establishing Catherine’s liminal state between existence and non-existence, and the fluidity of identity and time.
  • Catherine’s spirit is described as moving outside her body, with multiple selves that come and go, one of which may be immortal and lost. This idea reflects the fragmentation of identity and the mystical uncertainty about what constitutes the “self.”
  • A powerful metaphor emerges with Catherine being lost inside her own ear, described as a vast continent filled with echoes, voices, and labyrinthine paths. This can be interpreted as symbolic of mental disorientation, isolation, and the struggle to find meaning or escape from her internal world.
  • Catherine imagines traveling by night train through surreal, impossible landscapes: Alpine mountains, the Gobi Desert, cities without lights, accompanied by mysterious figures. This passage highlights the surreal, dreamlike quality of her consciousness and the dislocation from ordinary reality.
  • The chapter describes the old house where Catherine resides as a place that moves and changes, with furniture shifting, mirrors lopsided, and windows looking out on different seas or streets. This emphasizes the instability of her environment, mirroring her unstable mental state and the blurring between inner and outer worlds.
  • Despite her frailty, Catherine is described as having almost supernatural control over natural phenomena (winds, waves, stars, tides) and as a “great engineer” and “mathematical genius”.This passage elevates her to a mythic stature, emphasizing her complex inner life and imagination.
  • It is revealed that Catherine cannot physically walk and that her life has become largely a dream or internal experience, one that others perceive as her “absence”. This underscores the theme of illusion vs. reality and the isolating effects of her condition.
  • Catherine reflects on the absence of sorrow in her life as a sorrow itself and compares herself to others who have suffered or died tragically, such as Cousin Hannah and Mr. Joachim Spitzer. These passages delve into the psychology of grief and emotional existence.
  • The narrative describes strange phenomena in the house, objects appearing and moving mysteriously, footprints, feather fans, riding gloves, which suggests the presence of invisible guests or spirits. This contributes to the surreal, haunted atmosphere and the blurring between the real and the spectral.
  • Toward the end, Catherine’s ability to vanish, to be many persons simultaneously, and to fail to recognize herself is emphasized:

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Central character, portrayed as a dreamer, visionary, and tragic figure embodying the liminal state between life and death.
  • She is both powerful and vulnerable, with an intricate inner life of dreams and illusions.
  • Her physical immobility contrasts with her spiritual and imaginative wanderings.

Joachim Spitzer

  • A figure who represents rationality, optimism, and unrequited love.
  • He struggles with his own sorrow and identity, often diminished in comparison to Catherine’s grandeur.
  • He serves as a foil to Catherine’s mystical and dreamlike existence.

Cousin Hannah

  • A suffrage captain and historical figure in Catherine’s memories and imagination.
  • Represents a more practical, tragic, or "honest" life, contrasted with Catherine’s dreamlike and evasive existence.

Peron Spitzer

  • A figure symbolizing tragic melancholy and finality in death.

Research: Themes

Life and Death as Intertwined States

See: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles

  • Catherine insists there is little difference between life and death, "only an infinitesimal difference… a hair’s breadth".
  • Her spirit moves beyond the physical body, engaging in multiple selves and journeys that may never return, implying immortality is linked to loss and absence.
  • Death is not final; rather, it is a transformation or continuation of life in another form or realm.

Dreams and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Dreams are not substitutes but the only reality; Catherine never truly moves physically but travels extensively in her dreams.
  • The house itself is a shifting, surreal place, moving through time and space, inhabited by invisible guests, spirits, and echoes.
  • Time collapses; events are timeless or simultaneous, reflecting Catherine’s fractured perception.

Isolation and Estrangement

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Catherine is isolated, physically immobile but mentally and spiritually wandering widely.
  • She experiences a profound estrangement from the living world, which no one notices because of her pervasive absence and contradictory behavior.
  • The lack of sorrow, paradoxically, is itself a sorrow, highlighting emotional detachment.

The Power of Imagination and Creation

See: Dreams and Imagination

  • Catherine wields quasi-miraculous powers over natural elements: controlling winds, tides, stars, and raising the spectral dead.
  • She is portrayed as a "great engineer" and "mathematical genius" who constructs bridges, cities, and controls cosmic forces.
  • Despite her powers, she is vulnerable to exhaustion and fears losing her imaginative faculties.

Memory, Identity, and Self

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • Identity is fluid; Catherine can be many persons at once, sometimes failing to recognize herself.
  • Memories and past experiences collapse into moments without clear distinctions between past and present.
  • She grapples with who she is, where she is, and what form she might take after death.

The Ear as a Metaphor for Consciousness and Entrapment

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Catherine describes the ear as a vast, labyrinthine continent, a "doorway to the soul," where she is lost and wanders endlessly.
  • The ear symbolizes the inner world of sound, memory, and consciousness, filled with echoes, voices, and spectral presences.
  • She pleads to be let out of her ear, symbolizing a desire to escape mental imprisonment.

Illusion, Appearance, and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Personality and human form are mere appearances, like shadows or reflections on water.
  • Catherine’s physical appearance is marked by “blemishes” she tries to conceal with beauty spots, illustrating the tension between surface and essence.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Pearls and Planets

See: Pearls and Jewels · Moon and Stars

  • Pearls counted by Catherine symbolize worlds, memories, or selves; counting them leads to loss or dissolution.

Snow and Winter

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Snow imagery recurs throughout, symbolizing purity, coldness, death, and mystery.
  • Catherine walks naked through snow and blizzards that are warm and opalescent, blending opposites.

The House

See: The House

  • A living, shifting entity with invisible servants, moving through time and space.
  • Represents Catherine’s mind or inner world, harboring ghosts, memories, and dreams.

The Ear

See: Silence and Deafness

  • A labyrinthine metaphor for consciousness, entrapment, and the soul’s journey.

Mirrors and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Used to explore identity, illusion, and self-recognition.

Animals and Mythical Creatures

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Elephants, rabbits in lace veils, falcons, and spectral figures populate Catherine’s dream world, symbolizing various aspects of memory, power, and mystery.

Research: Resources

  • Sunt lacrimae rerum means there are tears for things or life is tragic.
  • Whetsaw owls may refer to the Saw-whet owl found in North America and one of the smallest owl species.
  • Catherine describes the groundhog seeing its shadow like the custom in the US called Groundhog Day, yet she mentions it is like Candlemas Day also known as the Feast of the Presentation of Jesus Christ and is a Christian Holy Day. Both happen on February 2nd.
  • Caesar’s campaign could refer to the Gallic War or Caesar’s civil war.
  • The War of the Roses was a series of civil wars fought over control of the English throne.
  • Mad Antony’s love may refer to Mark Anthony’s obsession with women. He had five wives and fathered many children.
  • Helen of Troy: see Chapter 23, Resources, for the full entry.
  • Aristotle was a Greek philosopher.
  • Balboa may refer to Vasco Nunez de Balboa who was a Spanish explorer who discovered the Isthmus of Panama to the Pacific Ocean.
  • Ritz may refer to one of the luxury hotels owned by the Ritz-Carlton Company.
  • The Gobi Desert is a large desert in East Asia.
  • Tory is a person who holds a political philosophy that is based on the British version of traditionalism and conservatism.
  • A peruke is a wig popular in the 17th to 19th century.
  • A crinoline is a stiff petticoat.
  • Ravens are often considered a mediator between life and death.
  • Pallida morte futura means to burst into the future.
  • Catherine asks “...were there not many roads to the crown of her head?” This seems to mimic part of a Hindu proverb, there are hundreds of paths up the mountain, all leading to the same place, so it doesn’t matter what path you take. The only person wasting time is the one who runs around the mountain, telling everyone his or her path is wrong. The phrase poetically reflects the intricate, often challenging, and layered nature of character and existence, highlighting the idea that the self is reached or shaped through many trials and paths rather than a single, direct line.
  • It seems at varying times that Catherine and Mr. Spitzer are describing powers of omniscience, omnipresence, and omnipotence.
  • Nepenthe is a fictional medicine for sorrow that is mentioned in Greek literature and mythology.
  • Tergiversation is an evasion of straightforward action or a clear-cut statement.
  • Saracen refers to Arab Muslims, Turks, and Persians or other Muslims.
  • La lutte finale may refer to a line from The Internationale which is a left-wing anthem used in anarchist, communist, and socialist movements.
  • “pale, pale, pale” It symbolizes both a literal description of physical appearance and a deeper metaphor for human frailty, loss, and the dissolution of life and identity as one approaches death.
  • “a nowhere train” may reference Anita Leslie’s, A Train to Nowhere, about WWII and her extraordinary role as a woman in it. She hated being surrounded by mediocre men. It evokes the existential condition of wandering through life’s uncertainties, the elusive quest for self-understanding, and the blurring of boundaries between reality and illusion that permeate the novel.
  • “immortal beauty” is part of Emerson’s Nature essay. The idea is that beauty is not just a sensory experience but a reflection of the spiritual and universal order of the universe. It is to be found in the interconnectedness of nature, the inherent goodness of the natural world, and the human ability to perceive and experience it. Beauty is not just about physical appearances but inhabits spiritual and moral qualities. Emerson emphasizes the role of the intellect in understanding the underlying harmony and beauty of nature. Emerson encouraged people to reconnect with nature and art. It captures the idea of a timeless, enduring essence of beauty and spirit that survives beyond physical life, reflecting the novel’s exploration of mortality, identity, and transcendence.
  • Mr. Spitzer complains that Catherine doesn’t see him as the “unique individual”. If she did, “He would have known his identity.” Which is called the “looking-glass self” theory by Charles Horton Cooley. Our self-perception is influenced by how we believe others see us. People in theory develop a sense of self by observing and internalizing how others react to a person, therefore, a person defines oneself based on those perceptions. While this can be powerful there are also self-assessment, internal reflection, values, interests, and passions. Oftentimes our perceptions can be inaccurate and lead to a distorted self-image. This complaint is both literal and symbolic: it underscores Mr. Spitzer's yearning for personal acknowledgment and his existential predicament of living in the shadow of his brother and in the liminal space between life and death, reality and illusion.
  • Mr. Spitzer is stuck in the cycle of grief and/or stuck in a depression. Common stages of cycling through the grief process: denial, anger, bargaining, depression, loneliness, acceptance. People who cling to sorrow or make it a central part of their identity find it difficult to move on from grief or other painful experiences. They may become trapped in a cycle of sadness. People may use this as a way to cope with the pain of loss or trauma. Trauma and memory can form a strong emotional attachment.
  • Present society is a product of romanticism developed in the late 1800s. Alain de Botton is a current philosopher who goes into this topic. His philosophy of love says people revolve around the concept that often idealizes love, finding meaning and purpose in relationships rather than focusing on the work and effort involved in maintaining them.
  • If Catherine really woke up she would rapidly age and die which may refer to a type of woman using magic tropes. Magic: The story often revolves around a character who has been gifted with some form of magical ability, such as the power to change shape, heal, or control nature. Loss of Magic: The magic is eventually lost or used up, often due to a specific event, mistake, or a consequence of their actions. Rapid Aging: The character's physical appearance begins to change dramatically, they may start to look older, their hair may turn grey, and they may experience a decline in physical health. Themes of Responsibility: The story may explore themes of responsibility, the consequences of choices, or the price of magic. Moral Lessons: These folktales can be seen as cautionary tales, highlighting the consequences of using magic irresponsibly or the price of taking shortcuts. Exploration of Mortality: The rapid aging can be a way to explore the theme of mortality and the inevitable passage of time. Symbolic Representation: The loss of magic and the subsequent aging can symbolize the decline of power, the fading of youth, or the exhaustion of a particular resource.
  • Cousin Hannah is given this oxymoron title “patriarchal suffrage captain” Patriarchy as a system of social organization where men hold the primary power and authority versus suffrage which is the fundamental right of all to vote which would lead to all citizens having the power to influence political decisions and hold leaders accountable. The paradox is suggesting that someone who holds patriarchal power but is also advocating for or leading a movement that challenges this very power structure.
chapter-58:
Chapter 58

← Chapter 57 · Home · Chapter 59 →

Summary

On the library steps, Mr. Spitzer meets an old violinist with shaking fingers who plays an imaginary violin. Mr. Spitzer recognizes the silent piece at once, a forgotten minor composition, and hears what is not there. He admits he distinguishes less and less between reality and his dreams, and suspects this may be his only wisdom.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · The Old Violinist

Concepts present

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Music and Composers

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer watches an old violinist who plays invisible notes on an imaginary violin. Despite the silence, Mr. Spitzer "knew immediately what music he was playing" and recognized it as an obscure minor composition from childhood, something almost lost to modern ears. This passage establishes the mystical and imaginative nature of the music. It exists purely in the mind and memory, evoking nostalgia for a past that is fading. The description of the old musician’s expert emotional gestures and Mr. Spitzer’s empathetic response shows a deep connection between memory, art, and the ineffable experience of music beyond sound.
  • The narrative elaborates on the qualities of the music and the sounds of nature, city life, and ephemeral sensations woven seamlessly into the violinist's silent performance. Mr. Spitzer experiences a profound detachment from his corporeal self and is deeply moved, his soul almost slipping from his body. The music is described as "pre-musical music," existing before human consciousness or after it no longer perceives sound, suggesting a timeless, transcendent art form. This passage highlights the boundary between reality and imagination, sound and silence, life and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates how the old violinist might have been many other figures (an athlete, a gentleman, a fisherman, a king) if only the instruments and tools in his hands had changed. This reflection suggests the fluidity of reality and identity, how reality is "made up of just so many sticks and not one stick more." The passage explores the transformative power of imagination and the interchangeable roles people might play, blurring boundaries between art, sport, and life.
  • Mr. Spitzer recalls his brother and old sportsmen, tying these memories to ideas of death, legacy, and continuing influence. This section reveals his obsession with memory and how past lives and experiences persist beyond physical death, transforming but never disappearing. It also contrasts Mr. Spitzer's sensitivity to silent, subtle music with Peron's preference for the rougher, more physical world of sports, highlighting differing responses to life's challenges and art.
  • Mr. Spitzer questions whether the old musician is alive or dead, a dream or reality, reflecting on the ambiguous boundary between life and death. The violinist’s wild, convulsive movements are seen both as music’s highest expression and possibly a sign of illness or death. This ambiguity deepens the chapter’s themes of mortality, the unknowability of existence, and the persistence of art and spirit beyond physical life.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on himself as a "silent composer" and "walking score board," someone who carries music and memory within but whose music is intangible and largely unheard. This passage underscores his isolation and the internal nature of artistic creation, the idea that much of life’s music is invisible or unperceived by others but deeply real to the creator.
  • The chapter closes with Mr. Spitzer’s reflection that he no longer distinguishes clearly between reality and dreams, life and death. This indistinction, while sometimes embarrassing, is also his "only wisdom," a protective cloud through which he moves. The metaphor of his black cape and drifting shadow emphasizes his liminal state between worlds, carrying the darkness as a cloak.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is a large, reflective man, draped in a black cape, who is a silent composer and connoisseur of music. He is caught between life and death, reality and imagination. His deafness contrasts with his profound musical understanding, highlighting a spiritual or metaphysical connection to music beyond sound. He embodies melancholy, wisdom, and a deep sense of loss, especially connected to his dead brother and the passing of time.

The Old Violinist

  • The Old Violinist is an enigmatic figure with white hair and shaking fingers, who plays silent music on an imaginary violin. His physical condition suggests age and wear, but his music transcends physical limitations, becoming a symbol for the persistence of art and spirit beyond bodily decay. He may represent forgotten or marginalized artists, or even symbolize the border between life and death.

Research: Themes

  • Music in this chapter exists beyond audible sound. The old violinist plays silent, imaginary music that Mr. Spitzer "hears" through intense observation and imagination. This silent music is described with rich auditory imagery (whispers, sobs, bird calls, and natural sounds) suggesting music as a universal language transcending physical constraints.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s reflections evoke buried childhood memories and a past nearly lost to time. His thoughts on his dead brother and old sportsmen convey a deep sense of mourning and nostalgia. The music, described as an old, nearly forgotten waltz, symbolizes this connection to the past and the fading of cultural memory.
  • The chapter blurs the lines between living and dead. Mr. Spitzer contemplates whether the old violinist is alive, dying, or already dead, and imagines music existing before consciousness and after hearing ceases. The text wrestles with existence, identity, and what remains after physical death.
  • Mr. Spitzer draws analogies between music and sports, imagining the violinist as a baseball player, a billiards player, or other figures, emphasizing how art and life are intertwined and fluid. Reality itself is depicted as made from “sticks” or tools, with identity shaped by perspective and imagination.
  • Mr. Spitzer admires the violinist with a mingled feeling of pity, reflecting on the loneliness of the artist and the fragility of human endeavor. This ambivalence highlights the complex human response to suffering and greatness.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • The violinist’s “imaginary bow” and “imaginary strings” represent art beyond the physical realm, emphasizing creativity as a spiritual act. The music is described with natural and cosmic imagery: “singings of blind moths,” “bird calls,” “sea shells buzzing like bees,” and “sparks sparking on the strings”.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s attire symbolizes his somber, reflective nature and his boundary state between darkness and light, life and death.
  • The hour-glass of the heart is a metaphor for the passage of time and the reversal or renewal of life, connected to the emotional impact of the music.
  • Baseball, billiards, croquet, polo, fishing, and even kingship are used metaphorically to describe potential alternate lives or identities for the violinist, highlighting the fluidity of reality and identity.
  • Frequent references to the sky, clouds, stars, and celestial bodies evoke a cosmic scale and the mystery of existence.

Research: Resources

  • Pearl-buttoned spats were a popular, elegant fashion accessory for both men and women from the late 19th century to the 1920s. Originally designed to protect footwear from dirt on unpaved roads, they became a symbol of social status and high fashion, especially during the Victorian and Edwardian eras. The trend began to fade in the late 1920s with the rise of more casual styles and shorter hemlines, which made intricate footwear and decorative buttons more visible.
  • “minor composition” This may refer to Paul Lincke’s Luna Waltz from 1911. Carl Emil Paul Lincke was a German composer and theater conductor. He is considered the "father" of the Berlin operetta. His well-known compositions include "Berliner Luft" ("Berlin Air"), the unofficial anthem of Berlin, from his operetta Frau Luna; and "The Glow-Worm", from his operetta Lysistrata. Luna Waltz is an instrumental piece adapted from the 1899 operetta Frau Luna and published in the United States in the early 20th century. The waltz, originally a dance tune within the original operetta, became a popular, standalone composition that showcased Lincke's success as a composer of Berlin operettas, a genre he helped define with this work.
  • “pre-musical music” The earliest musical instruments demonstrate that early humans possessed abstract thought, symbolic expression, and sophisticated cognitive and social skills. These instruments, made from bone, shell, and ivory and dating back over 40,000 years, show that music played a crucial role in rituals, communication, and social bonding, helping to unite communities, convey spiritual beliefs, and even coordinate collective work or warfare. The existence of these complex tools indicates that early humans were innovators, capable of abstract thought and creating objects with symbolic and functional meaning beyond mere survival needs.
  • “prided himself that music and baseball were fused in his psychology” and ‘intuitive understanding to this relation of music to sports” Music and baseball (sports) are similar in their shared need for practice, discipline, teamwork, and performance. Both fields involve individual roles within a collective, rely on rhythm and coordination, cultivate passionate fanbases, and have rich, evolving traditions and narratives that contribute to their cultural significance.
  • “Te Deums” may refer to Te Deum laudamus which means Thee, O God, we praise. It is a Latin Christian hymn.
  • “loggerhead turtle” The loggerhead sea turtle is a species of oceanic turtle distributed throughout the world. It is a marine reptile, belonging to the family Cheloniidae. The average loggerhead measures around 90 cm in carapace length when fully grown. The adult loggerhead sea turtle weighs approximately 135 kg (298 lb), with the largest specimens weighing in at more than 450 kg (1,000 lb).
  • “hawk moth” The Sphingidae are a family of moths commonly called sphinx moths, also colloquially known as hawk moths, with many of their caterpillars known as hornworms. It includes about 1,450 species. It is best represented in the tropics, but species are found in every region.
  • “...playing on and on as if, as he had never begun, he could not stop. Mr. Spitzer had heard ringings in his ears for several days—almost to the extent that he had almost forgotten his own troubles, which were not inconsiderable.” This conveys a sense of endless, continuous, and perhaps futile musical performance. The music is portrayed as persistent and unceasing, embodying a kind of immortal or eternal quality that transcends ordinary experience of time and completion. This ongoing music creates a haunting atmosphere where the boundaries between beginning and end blur, much like a dream that persists indefinitely. Mr. Spitzer's experience of "ringings in his ears for several days," to the point that he almost forgot his own troubles, highlights the overwhelming impact of the music on his consciousness. The ringing in his ears symbolizes not only the literal auditory effect but also the emotional and psychological immersion in the music, which momentarily distracts him from his personal hardships and sorrows. His troubles, though significant, are temporarily overshadowed by the profound effect of the violinist's performance. This passage suggests both the haunting, unending nature of the music and its power to momentarily transport Mr. Spitzer beyond his own suffering, providing a brief escape or solace. It also reflects the novel’s broader themes of time, memory, and the elusive nature of reality and art.
  • The idea of doing something without being able to stop has occurred in history with the Dancing plague of 1518 where 50 to 400 people danced until they dropped exhausted then got up and continued until they were taken to a hospital.
  • In Greek mythology, Orpheus was a Thracian bard, legendary musician and prophet. He was also a renowned poet and, according to legend, travelled with Jason and the Argonauts in search of the Golden Fleece, and descended into the underworld to recover his lost wife, Eurydice.
  • “neap tide” is a tide just after the first or third quarters of the moon when there is least difference between high and low water.
  • “ebb tide” is the period when the tide is going out, or the water level is falling from high to low, with water flowing away from the shore. It is the opposite of a flood tide, which occurs when the water level is rising. The term can also refer to the seaward flow of water in estuaries or tidal rivers during this lowering water phase.
chapter-43:
Chapter 43

← Chapter 42 · Home · Chapter 44 →

Summary

In silk hat and black cape, Mr. Spitzer keeps watch, unsure whether he himself is living or dead. Hannah's dying becomes a dance of death. She raves through deserts, mountains, and snow, speaks to Caesar, a blacksmith, and a figure she calls her love, asks for a mirror, and longs for silk skirts and parasols she scorned all her life. She asks whether she is the anvil or the hammer, and at the end she cries out for a lost beloved under the snow.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Fireflies · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Buddhism · Freud and Jung · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Shakespeare · The Bible · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with vivid descriptions of Cousin Hannah’s struggle through dreamlike, stormy landscapes symbolizing her life’s battles and approaching death. The imagery of crossing deserts, climbing mountains, and clouds emphasizes the arduous journey of life and death, and the suffragette’s wild screams indicate confusion and loss of self-identity near death.
  • It is revealed that even this great lady “wept if a wandering snowflake touched her hand” and was “fragile as were all mortal things,” prone to “wild dreams, visions, fantasies, presentiments, forebodings, fears of the unknown.” This humanizes her, showing vulnerability despite her public strength and ideals.
  • Mr. Spitzer himself is uncertain of his own state, “not sure who he was, whether living or dead,” and reflects on the confusion about who is dying and the nature of death. His belief that “the dead cast no vote” and his abstention from voting reflect his detachment from worldly affairs.
  • The narrative explores death as both an ending and a beginning, a “great crucible” where opposites meet, and where “death was that which blew us all along.” It describes Cousin Hannah’s cries and visions as part of a larger metaphysical process, suggesting death is not peace but a storm or dance of contradictory forces.
  • Cousin Hannah speaks to various mythic and historical figures like Caesar, a blacksmith, a golden archer, a blackamoor, asking profound questions about identity and fate (“Am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?”). This symbolizes her grappling with agency, power, and the unknown as life fades.
  • The blackamoor, a mysterious figure she calls her love, and the “great lamp-lighter” who might light her way, appear repeatedly in her delirium. This imagery suggests a guide or companion in the transition from life to death, blending cultural and mystical symbols.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on how Cousin Hannah’s ravings mix ancient history, myth, and personal memories, with cities, armies, and landscapes blending into a timeless dreamscape. There is uncertainty whether these are real memories, dreams, or hallucinations, emphasizing the blurred boundary between life and death, past and present.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Cousin Hannah cannot decide “whether the lid was lowering or raising.” What does the chapter gain by leaving the direction of the lid unresolved, and how does the question change when the lid becomes the lid of the sky?
  • Hannah asks the blacksmith, “Am I the anvil which is struck or the hammer which strikes?” In what ways has the suffrage captain been both over her life? Which does she seem to be at the end?
  • Hannah’s visions travel to Ur, Nineveh, Crete, and Babylon. Mr. Spitzer prefers that she speak of the remote past, things “made safe by their remoteness,” rather than of tomorrow’s weather or the next election. Why might the far past feel safer than the near future at a deathbed?
  • Near its end the chapter turns to the image of an old ship coming apart, and Mr. Spitzer thinks that “not even the greatest calker could calk her now.” How does this sinking ship compare with Hannah’s own question, “Where’s my figurehead?”, and with Catherine’s figurehead in Chapter 40?
  • Mr. Spitzer calls vanity “that which took longest dying” and finds it “in woman’s heart as in man’s heart” and perhaps “in the heart of God.” Is Hannah’s cry for her mirror and her skirt a betrayal of her cause, a last joke, or simply a human frailty the chapter refuses to blame her for?

Characters

  • Mr. Spitzer keeps his “attitudes of dignity, remorse, patience” because “someone must maintain spiritual equilibrium.” Is his calm a gift to the dying woman, a defense for himself, or both?
  • Mr. Spitzer admits he is “perhaps not the best of all possible witnesses to death-bed scenes” and has “a tendency to keep things alive after they were gone.” How does an uncertain witness change the weight of Hannah’s last words?
  • Mr. Spitzer suspects the Black Moor “might be a man and not a woman,” and Hannah searches for “my nymph, my lovely girl.” What does the chapter suggest about the love Hannah denied, and why might it surface only at the end?
  • Mr. Spitzer notices “pawn figures moving not only from dream to dream of the dreamer but from dreamer to dreamer,” so that the Black Moor resembles the black coachman of Catherine’s opium dreams. What would it mean for dreams to be shared, and how does this connect to his sense that “no one could simply be himself”?

Connections

  • Hannah spent her life refusing feminine frivolities, yet she cries for the skirt “which I took off so long ago.” How does the skirt work as a symbol of the self she set aside for the cause? Does the chapter mourn that choice or honor it?
  • In Hannah’s heaven “the white hen crows,” and “none shall stop her.” How does this reversal of the barnyard order echo the work of the suffrage movement? See Women’s Suffrage.
  • Hannah says, “Then put out the light,” and asks whether the turban-winder has come to strangle her. If she is casting herself as Desdemona, what does that reveal about how she has understood love and the men she fought against? See Shakespeare.
  • The chapter is titled “The Dance of Death” in the reading guide. How does Hannah’s “mad dance” on “a lonely mountain top” compare with the medieval dance of death, in which Death leads every rank of person to the grave? See On the danse macabre (Ch 43).

Reflection

  • Mr. Spitzer’s understanding “always came too late,” arriving “like a gift freely given to one who could not express his appreciation.” When does understanding arrive too late in ordinary life, and is it still worth having?
  • “When nothing was possible, all things were made possible.” In what situations does the loss of every option open something new?

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A somber, enigmatic figure who carries a high silk hat and black cape, symbolic of mourning and ritual.
  • He is both witness and participant in the suffragette’s dying experience.
  • Reflects deeply on life, death, identity, and the nature of existence.
  • Struggles with his own sense of being alive or dead, voting or not voting, and the meaning of his presence.
  • His observations are philosophical, often pondering the illusions of life and the mysteries beyond death.

Cousin Hannah

  • A once powerful figure, now fragile and approaching death.
  • Engaged in a fierce, chaotic battle against death, manifested in vivid, surreal visions.
  • Experiences wild dreams, hallucinations, and shifting identities in her final hours.
  • Struggles with recognition of self and the meaning of life and death.
  • Exhibits vanity, fear, ecstasy, confusion, and moments of clarity.
  • Her final moments are a “dance of death,” a paradoxical mix of seriousness and frivolity.

Research: Themes

Life, Death, and the Transition Between

See: Death and Mortality

  • Death is depicted not as an end but a complex transformation, a journey through storm, cloud, snow, and desert.
  • The suffragette’s battle with death is fierce and confusing; death is both a closing and an opening (“Oh, is the lid raising, lowering?”).
  • The ambiguity of death and existence is central, with Mr. Spitzer unsure if he or the suffragette is alive or dead.
  • Death is associated with loss, revelation, and paradox, often blending into life’s experiences.

Memory, Identity, and Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self

  • The suffragette’s past is fragmented and elusive, mixing real and imagined events.
  • Both characters wrestle with who they are and who others have been.
  • Dreams and memories flow outside of linear time, suggesting the permeability of identity.
  • Reality and illusion are intertwined; the suffragette’s visions may be symbolic rather than literal truth.

Vanity and Human Frailty

See: Decay and Ruin

  • Despite the gravity of death, vanity persists (“vanity of silken skirts,” “great parasols fringed by gold”).
  • The suffragette clings to images of beauty and love even as she fades.
  • The fragility of human existence is highlighted, especially in the face of death.

Love and Loss

See: Love · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • The suffragette expresses deep, eternal love in her delirium, though the identity of lover and beloved is unclear.
  • Love and death blur together, raising the question of whether death extinguishes love or transforms it. Her last whispered words ask, “should love be extinguished by death?”
  • The paradox of love’s endurance beyond death is a poignant motif.

The Role of the Observer

  • Mr. Spitzer’s role as witness is complicated by his own uncertain status.
  • He balances grief with detachment and observation with participation.
  • He questions the reliability of memory and perception, acknowledging possible error.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

High Silk Hat & Black Cape (Mr. Spitzer)

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbols of mourning, ritual, and his ambiguous status between life and death.

Storm, Snow, Desert, Mountains

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Mountains · Clouds and Storms

  • Represent the suffragette’s internal struggle and the vast unknown of death.

Skirt of Clouds and Waters

See: The Sea and Water · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms

  • Symbolizes beauty, identity, and the suffragette’s fading presence.

Black Moor / Blackamoor

  • A mysterious figure, possibly a lover or phantom, representing the suffragette’s complex relationships and desires.

Crystal Casket / Mirror

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Symbols of self-reflection, identity, and the enigma of existence; the mirror is sought but elusive.

Music (Lute, Harp, Bells)

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represents the ethereal, transcendent aspects of life and death; the music continues even as life fades.

Firefly Light / Star

See: Fireflies · Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Symbolizes hope, guidance, and the fragile spark of life amid darkness.

Bellrope / Bells

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represent the passage of time, calling, and the inevitability of death.

Iceberg / Frozen Elements

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Emphasize coldness, isolation, and the slow crumbling of life.

Further notes from the text

  • Mr. Spitzer carries his high silk hat, “almost his only God,” and keeps watch unable to help, since he is as one already dead.
  • He wonders whether Hannah’s sudden longing for feminine frivolities is a last great joke, a parody of life at the moment life is fading. See Comedy in Chapter 43.
  • He had supposed that bodily death and real death would come together. Watching her, he begins to doubt it, and wonders whether the person dying now is someone he has not really seen since his forgotten youth.
  • Hannah’s delirium crosses the ancient world, Ur of the Chaldees, Nineveh, Crete, Babylon, and asks for her little boat and her figurehead, linking her dying to Catherine’s image of the figurehead in Chapter 40.
  • She cries out to the Black Moor, “beloved of woman,” the figure Mr. Spitzer later connects with the black coachman of Catherine’s dreams.
  • Her ravings repeat a paradox that sums up the novel’s method: look not into the things that are, to see the things that are not.
  • Near the end he pictures her going down like a ship in a whirlpool, and he is certain he will be on the other shore, not where the wreckage lands. The chapter closes on her whisper that death might be “her life, her love,” and her question, “should love be extinguished by death?”

Research: Resources

  • High Silk Hat - used to be a clear symbol of authority and status in society. It represented wealth and prestige. Culturally it also represented capitalism, enterprise, and ambition. The first top hats were made of beaver fur felt. From the 1840s silk plush replaced beaver, which gave the silk hat its name. For Mr. Spitzer the hat is “almost his only God.”
  • “this great emir of suffrage”: Emir comes from the Arabic amir, meaning commander or prince. It was the title of military leaders and rulers across the Islamic world. Calling Hannah an emir makes her a desert commander, which fits the armies, tents, and camel bells of her deathbed visions.
  • “Oh, is that you, great lamp-lighter?”: Before electric street lights, a lamplighter walked the streets at dusk with a long pole, lighting each gas lamp, and came back at dawn to put them out. Hannah greets Mr. Spitzer this way when he arrives, and later asks whether “the great lamp-lighter” has come “to light her way through worlds of darkness.” Mr. Spitzer, who has “always tapped at every lamp-post” on his walks, becomes a guide for the dying, yet “not even the great lamp-bearer could light this darkness.” See The lamp-lighter (Ch 29) and On the lamplighter and The Little Prince (Ch 48).
  • “So like a palmer she had wandered through this world”: A palmer was a medieval pilgrim who had traveled to the Holy Land and carried back a palm frond as proof. Some palmers had no home and spent their lives traveling between holy sites. The word suits Hannah, whose great cause kept her always on the road and never settled.
  • “the auk’s egg”: The great auk was a large flightless seabird of the North Atlantic. Hunters killed the last confirmed pair on the island of Eldey, off Iceland, in June 1844. After its extinction, its eggs became prized collector’s items that sold for large sums at Victorian auctions. Placing the egg among Hannah’s vanities joins beauty to extinction. The Iceland connection also ties it to Mt. Hekla, which appears later in the chapter.
  • “the glass barouche”: A barouche was a fashionable four-wheeled carriage of the nineteenth century. It had a folding half-hood and two double seats facing each other, and it was built for being seen in. A barouche made of glass could not exist, which puts it among the vanities that veil and display at once.
  • “something almost spontaneously starting up outside of the scheme of time, whether future or past”: Eternalism (philosophy of time) is an approach to the ontological nature of time, which takes the view that all existence in time is equally real, as opposed to presentism or the growing block universe theory of time, in which at least the future is not the same as any other time. Some forms of eternalism give time a similar ontology to that of space, as a dimension, with different times being as real as different places, and future events are “already there” in the same sense other places are already there, and that there is no objective flow of time. It is sometimes referred to as the “block time” or “block universe” theory due to its description of space-time as an unchanging four-dimensional “block”, as opposed to the view of the world as a three-dimensional space modulated by the passage of time. Mr. Spitzer half suspects that Hannah’s past is not memory at all but a time outside time, and that “one life might contain all.”
  • Don Juan is a legendary, fictional Spanish literature character. He first appeared in a 1630 play, Tirso de Molina’s The Trickster of Seville, and probably most famously in the opera Don Giovanni by Mozart. He was a libertine, womanizer, arrogant, unrepentant, and was punished for these sins. Mr. Spitzer wonders whether Hannah had always been “this pale Don Juan beneath her mask,” the great seducer hidden inside the woman who refused love. See The Pale Don Juan.
  • “the next horse race at Churchill Downs when the track was muddy”: Churchill Downs is the racetrack in Louisville, Kentucky, that opened in 1875 and has hosted the Kentucky Derby ever since. A muddy track favors certain horses and upsets the odds, which is exactly the uncertainty that drew Mr. Spitzer’s gambling brother. Mr. Spitzer judges that this talk of the future would be tactless at a deathbed. See On the Kentucky Derby and Black Jockeys (Ch 80).
  • “join the vast majority, just as the Romans said”: The Romans used the phrase “abiit ad plures,” meaning “he has gone to the many,” as a polite way to say someone had died. It appears in Petronius’s Satyricon. The English poet Edward Young used the same idea in his 1721 play The Revenge: “Death joins us to the great majority.” Mr. Spitzer turns the saying around and thinks the city of the dead might be “a smaller city.”
  • “Watchman, what hour?”: This is a version of Isaiah 21:11, “Watchman, what of the night?” In the prophecy, someone calls out from the darkness asking how long the night will last, and the watchman answers that “the morning cometh, and also the night.” The verse inspired John Bowring’s 1825 hymn “Watchman, Tell Us of the Night.” Hannah asks it as an old clock strikes, as if the hour of her death were a question someone on the wall could answer.
  • The twelve apostles included Judas Iscariot, who betrayed Jesus. Matthias was chosen to take his place (Acts 1:26), and Paul, who came later, is often called the thirteenth apostle. Jesus and the twelve made thirteen at the Last Supper, one root of the old superstition that thirteen at table is unlucky, and Hannah’s “hooded thirteen apostles” picketing the town clock carry that ominous number. In the Eastern tradition there may have been as many as seventy apostles.
  • Moors was a term first used by European Christians to designate the Muslim inhabitants of Maghreb, Iberian Peninsula, Malta, and Sicily during the Middle Ages. The Black Moor becomes a black rooster.
  • In ancient Greece Hephaestus was the god of blacksmiths and was disabled either at birth or because of his fall from Mount Olympus.
  • In Isaiah 41:7 the craftsmen are encouraged with a job well done when the hammer and anvil work together to make an object. In context the object is an idol, and the prophet is mocking people who build their own gods. There are seven other bible verses that talk about the hammer being used for making things, war and murder.
  • “winding, unwinding your turban, the turban moon in the cloud”: A turban is a long cloth wound around the head. Turbans have been worn since around 2350 B.C. Hannah sees the moon itself as a turban wound and unwound in the clouds.
  • “what lazar demanding alms”: A lazar is a beggar with a disease, especially leprosy. The word comes from Lazarus, the beggar covered with sores in Luke 16, and it gave its name to the lazaretto, a hospital for contagious diseases. Lazarus of Bethany, who was raised from the dead, also haunts Mr. Spitzer’s world of the living dead. See Lazarus of Bethany (Ch 4).
  • “gardens of beautiful odalisques”: An odalisque was a servant woman in an Ottoman harem. The word comes from the Turkish odalık, meaning chambermaid. European painters turned the odalisque into a fantasy of the reclining, veiled woman, most famously in Ingres’s Grande Odalisque of 1814. These are women no man sees “unless he died,” hidden the way Hannah has hidden herself.
  • Mt. Hecla or Mt. Hekla is a stratovolcano in Iceland. In medieval Europe it was known as the gateway to Hell. Mr. Spitzer calls it “the iceberg burning with inner fire” and thinks Hannah was always nearer to it than to “the burning desert sand,” fire hidden under ice.
  • “came but with the neap tide”: A neap tide happens twice a month, when the sun and moon pull at right angles to each other at the first and third quarter moon. Neap tides have the smallest difference between high and low water. Young reverses this: Hannah’s “highest tide” arrives with the weakest tide of the month, and her life follows its own rhythm, “harnessed to no moon.”
  • Young described the characters in this book as the spokes of a wheel coming out from Miss MacIntosh in the center of the story. In this chapter Mr. Spitzer lets “the spokes of the wheel” extend as far as possible before they reach “the clouded rim of doubt.” See The Wheel and the Spokes.
  • Emperor Tiberius or Tiberius Caesar Augustus was the second Roman emperor. He ruled from A.D. 14 to 37, Jesus was crucified during his reign, and he spent his last years withdrawn on the island of Capri. Hannah sees him in “his trailing purple robes,” the color reserved for emperors.
  • Ur of the Chaldees or Ur Kasdim is a city mentioned in the Bible as the birthplace of Abraham. It stood in southern Mesopotamia, in what is now Iraq. Unlike the cities Mr. Spitzer imagines “buried under the desert sand and never exhumed,” Ur was dug up: the archaeologist Leonard Woolley excavated it between 1922 and 1934 and found its royal tombs.
  • Nineveh was an ancient Assyrian city of Mesopotamia and the capital of the Assyrian Empire. In the Bible, God sends Jonah to preach there. It was destroyed in 612 B.C.
  • Crete is the largest and most populous of the Greek islands. It was the home of the Minoan civilization, and in Greek myth it held the labyrinth of the Minotaur.
  • Babylon was the capital of the Babylonian Empire. It was said to hold the Hanging Gardens, it is linked with the Tower of Babel, and the people of Judah were carried there in exile in the 500s B.C.
  • “ram’s horn”: The shofar is a trumpet made from a ram’s horn and blown in Jewish worship, especially at Rosh Hashanah. In Joshua 6, priests blow seven ram’s horns and the walls of Jericho fall. Hannah’s “great angel blowing his horn upon a lonely mountain top” also recalls the angels with trumpets in Revelation 8, who announce the end of the world. See On the Battle of Jericho (Ch 59).
  • “Was she the burning phoenix or the star?”: The phoenix is the mythical bird that lives for centuries, burns itself on a pyre, and rises again from its own ashes. Herodotus wrote that the Egyptians said it came to Heliopolis every five hundred years. Christians later took it as a symbol of resurrection. For Hannah, who believed in no future life, the question of rising again stays open.
  • “Then put out the light”: This echoes Othello, Act 5, Scene 2, where Othello stands over the sleeping Desdemona and says “Put out the light, and then put out the light,” before smothering her in her bed. Several things in Cousin Hannah’s deathbed cries point to the play: she calls to a “Black Moor, beloved of woman,” she asks whether the turban-winder has come “to strangle me so that I cannot cry out,” and she lies in a bed that has become a deathbed. The suffrage captain, who spent her life refusing the role of wife, casts herself at the end as Shakespeare’s most famous murdered wife. See Shakespeare.
  • “None should see the face of love and live”: This echoes Exodus 33:20, where God tells Moses, “Thou canst not see my face: for there shall no man see me, and live.” Hannah replaces God with love, which suggests that for her, love was the force too great to look at directly.
  • “Comes he not to the dying king?”: In 1 Samuel 16:23, the young David plays the harp for King Saul, and the troubling spirit leaves the king. Hannah calls for her court musician to come with “great gold harp strings,” which places her in the role of a tormented king in need of music. Mr. Spitzer, the musician who hears “the music of the dead,” sits beside her unrecognized.
  • Triton is a god of the sea in Greek mythology, the son of Poseidon. He blows a conch shell to calm or raise the waves, which is why Hannah asks, “Who blows this great Triton’s shell?”
  • Triton shells are a marine mollusk. They are large sea snails named for the god, and their shells have long been blown as trumpets.
  • Ramadan is the ninth month of the Islamic calendar and a Muslim month of fasting, prayer, and reflection.
  • Shiraz is a dark-skinned grape used to produce red wine. Shiraz is also a city in southern Iran, long celebrated as the city of poets, roses, and gardens. The great Persian poets Hafez and Saadi are buried there, which suits Cousin Hannah’s “Shiraz or the sandalwood and the jewel and the incense of a dream.” See Shiraz.
  • Cousin Hannah asks whether the jewel gleaming in her love’s forehead is “the third eye.” Third eye is a mystical and esoteric concept of a speculative invisible eye on the forehead which provides perception beyond ordinary sight. In Hindu tradition the god Shiva has a third eye in the center of his forehead, and when it opens it destroys. In one story Shiva burns Kama, the god of love, to ash with it. The forehead point is also the ajna chakra, the seat of inner sight, which the bindi marks. The question ties her lost love to both vision and destruction. See Hinduism.
  • Eighth day of the week may refer to Burmese Theravada Buddhism where the week has eight days. Wednesday is divided into two parts. Early Christian writers also called the resurrection the “eighth day,” the day after the seven days of creation, and Augustine ends The City of God with the seventh day of rest leading into “the eighth and eternal day.” It is a time outside ordinary time. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • The thirteenth month of the year may refer to the International Fixed Calendar that has thirteen months of 28 days each and the day of the week is constant. A thirteenth month also exists in lunar calendars that add a leap month to catch up with the solar year, such as the second month of Adar in the Hebrew calendar. Like the eighth day, it is a time outside ordinary time.
  • “In heaven the black rooster lays the egg, and the white hen crows”: An old proverb says “A whistling woman and a crowing hen are neither fit for God nor men.” It was used against women who spoke out of their expected place, which makes a crowing hen a fitting image for a suffragette. A rooster laying an egg was considered unnatural and dangerous. Medieval legend held that a rooster’s egg hatched the basilisk, and in Basel in 1474 a rooster accused of laying an egg was tried and burned. Hannah’s heaven reverses the order of the barnyard. The hen crows, “and none shall stop her.”
  • Forbidden East may refer to the Forbidden City in Beijing, the palace of the emperors of imperial China, built in the early 1400s.
  • “the men wore skirts, and the ladies wore trousers or bloomers”: Pants were first worn by women and men by Scythians around 3,000 years ago. The Scythians were horse riders of the steppes, and the Greeks thought trousers fit only for barbarians. Mr. Spitzer’s “forbidden east,” where the men wear skirts and the ladies wear trousers, turns the customs of his own country upside down.
  • Bloomers are divided women's garments for the lower body. They were developed in the 19th century as a healthful and comfortable alternative to the heavy, constricting dresses worn by American women. They take their name from their best-known advocate, the women's rights activist Amelia Bloomer. It became a symbol of women's rights in the early 1850s.
  • “pawn figures moving not only from dream to dream of the dreamer but from dreamer to dreamer”: Carl Jung believed that dreams reveal more than they conceal. They are a natural expression of the imagination and speak in the most straightforward language the mind has: mythic narratives. The parts of a person’s mythic life keep a similar structure across the whole lifespan. His idea of a collective unconscious refers to the psychological constants shared by all societies, such as rites of passage into womanhood, or the growing fascination with death after middle age. Mr. Spitzer’s sense that the same figures pass from one dreamer to another is close to Jung’s collective unconscious.
  • “Is there no meeting place, place where two parallel lines meet?”: Euclid’s fifth postulate held that parallel lines never meet. In the nineteenth century, mathematicians such as Lobachevsky and Riemann built non-Euclidean geometries in which that rule no longer holds, and in projective geometry parallel lines meet at a point at infinity. Hannah’s question asks whether two lives that ran side by side without touching, like hers and her lost love’s, can meet at the end.
  • “walk like the cripple healed by some great, sudden miracle”: In John 5, Jesus tells a man who had been unable to walk for thirty-eight years, “Rise, take up thy bed, and walk,” and in Acts 3 Peter heals a man lame from birth at the temple gate. Mr. Spitzer half expects Hannah, who never gave up a fight, to rise from her deathbed the same way, but “she lay prone as an everlasting horizon.”
  • “Is that the tent-maker? Is that the tent?”: The name of the Persian poet Omar Khayyam means “tentmaker.” Edward FitzGerald’s 1859 translation of his Rubáiyát made him famous in English as a poet of mortality, and in one quatrain the body is “but a Tent where takes his one day’s rest / A Sultan to the realm of Death addrest.” The apostle Paul was also a tentmaker by trade (Acts 18:3), and he called the body “our earthly house of this tabernacle,” a tent that will be taken down (2 Corinthians 5:1). Hannah, whose visions are full of desert tents, asks where the tent-maker sets his tent “upon what star or cloud” as her own tent is being struck.
  • “Look not into the things that are to see the things that are not”: This inverts 2 Corinthians 4:18, “While we look not at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen: for the things which are seen are temporal; but the things which are not seen are eternal.” Paul is urging faith. Hannah, who believed in no afterlife, is giving a warning.
  • “you like Mr. Chandelier moving through clouds”: Mr. Chandelier comes from Catherine Cartwheel’s opium dreams in Chapter 2, the chandelier imagined as her companion with “seven lighted candles in his seven crystal hands.” Hannah’s calling on him is another dream figure passing “from dreamer to dreamer.” See Mr. Chandelier.
  • Bacchus, the Roman name for the Greek god Dionysus, is the god of the grape-harvest, winemaking and wine, fertility and orchards. Hannah asks whether it is “Bacchus and his crew of satyrs crowned by flowers.”
  • Satyrs in Greek mythology are male nature spirits, part goat or horse, who follow Dionysus.
  • Nymphs in Greek folklore are minor female nature deities.
  • Pierrot is a stock character of pantomime and comedy in the late seventeenth-century Italian troupe of players performing in Paris. He is the sad clown, with a whitened face and loose white clothes, forever lovesick, usually for Columbine, who leaves him for Harlequin. The mime Jean-Gaspard Deburau made Pierrot famous in Paris in the 1820s and 1830s. Mr. Spitzer sees in Hannah’s “somersaultings like Pierrot” a lovesick clown hidden under the warrior.
  • “not even the greatest calker could calk her now”: A calker, now usually spelled caulker, forces fibers soaked in pitch or tar into the seams between a wooden ship’s planks to make it watertight. Mr. Spitzer’s “maritime memories derived from a remote forefather” turn Hannah’s dying body into an old ship coming apart at its seams.
  • Southern Cross or Crux is a constellation of the southern sky that has four bright stars in a cross-shape.
  • Northern Cross is an astronomical asterism in the northern hemisphere of the celestial sphere and is much larger than the Southern Cross. It is part of the constellation Cygnus, the Swan.
  • “if this earth were totally abandoned, would not a bee zoom in a meadow of wild flowers . . . a leaf fall?”: If a tree falls in the forest does anyone hear it? The question challenges the notion that perception is essential for reality. Some philosophers argue that the sound requires a conscious observer because it is a form of perception. Others argue that sound is an objective physical phenomenon that exists independently of perception. The question touches on perception (how the world is experienced), reality (what the world is like apart from human perception), existence (whether something must be perceived in order to exist), and the role of the observer in shaping an understanding of the world. It can also suggest that life goes on without humans there to witness it, which decenters the human point of view.
  • “was there not the white of edelweiss embroidered upon the hem?”: Edelweiss appears as a detail embroidered on the hem of the white skirt Cousin Hannah cries for. It is an alpine flower that grows in high-altitude habitats, and it carries a good deal of symbolism. It has been associated with courage and bravery, resilience and survival, nobility and purity, luck and good fortune. It grows on high, dangerous cliffs, and climbers risked their lives to gather it, which is why it came to stand for courage, a fitting emblem for Hannah.
  • Asphodel may refer to the Asphodel Meadows. It is a section of the underworld in Greek mythology where ordinary souls are sent to live after death.
  • Pleiades, also known as The Seven Sisters or Messier 45, is an open star cluster in the night sky visible in virtually every part of the globe.
  • “Is it the will-o’-the-wisp”: A will-o’-the-wisp is a ghostly light seen at night over marshes and bogs. It is also called ignis fatuus, Latin for “foolish fire.” In folklore it leads travelers off safe paths and into the swamp. It is now thought to come from burning marsh gases. Hannah asks whether she “must follow her who followed me,” which makes her lost love a light that is both a guide and a lure.
  • “Do I come again to that dark tower? Is that the winding horn?”: These questions recall Robert Browning’s 1855 poem “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came,” whose title comes from a line Edgar speaks in King Lear. Roland crosses a ruined wasteland to the dark tower where all the knights before him were lost, and the poem ends as he raises his horn: “Dauntless the slug-horn to my lips I set, / And blew.” Hannah, too, has come to the end of a long quest where others fell. See Childe Roland to the Dark Tower.

Vocabulary

Acclimatized
Grown used to a new climate, place, or situation.
Acme
The highest point of something; the peak.
Adventitious
Happening by chance; not essential or built in.
Ambrosial
Divinely fragrant or delicious. From ambrosia, the food of the Greek gods, which gave them immortality.
Amorphous
Without a clear shape or form.
Amphitheatre
A round or oval open-air arena with rising tiers of seats around a central space, used in ancient Rome for gladiator contests and public spectacles.
Anvil
The heavy iron block on which a blacksmith hammers hot metal into shape.
Apparition
A ghost, or a ghostlike image of a person.
Arcanum
A mysterious or specialized knowledge, language, or information accessible or possessed only by the initiate. From the Latin arcanus, hidden or closed. Plural: arcana.
Armorer
A maker or repairer of armor and weapons.
Astral
Having to do with the stars.
Auk
A diving seabird of northern seas. The great auk, a large flightless species, became extinct in 1844. More under Resources.
Balloon fish
A pufferfish, which swallows water to swell its body into a spiny ball when threatened.
Barnacled
Crusted with barnacles, small shelled sea creatures that cling to rocks, pilings, and the hulls of ships.
Barouche
A fashionable four-wheeled carriage with a folding half-hood and two seats facing each other. More under Resources.
Blackamoor
An old term for a Black African or any dark-skinned person, common in European art and in decorative figures of Black servants. It is now considered offensive.
Breastplate
A piece of armor covering the chest.
Caliph
The title of the chief Muslim ruler, understood as a successor to the Prophet Muhammad.
Calker
Also caulker. A worker who seals the seams of a wooden ship to make it watertight. More under Resources.
Carousel
A merry-go-round. Earlier, a tournament in which horsemen performed exercises and displays.
Casket
A small, often ornate box for jewels or valuables. In American usage, also a coffin, so Young’s “casket containing no jewel” carries both meanings.
Centaur
In Greek mythology, a creature with the head and upper body of a man and the body and legs of a horse.
Centurion
An officer in the Roman army who commanded about a hundred soldiers.
Chimerical
Imaginary, fanciful, or wildly unrealistic. From the Chimera, the fire-breathing monster of Greek myth made of a lion, a goat, and a serpent.
Citadel
A fortress, usually on high ground, that protects a city.
Clapper
The hanging metal tongue inside a bell that strikes it to make it ring.
Cockle
A small saltwater clam with a ribbed, heart-shaped shell. A cockleshell boat is a small, flimsy one.
Colonnade
A row of columns, usually holding up a roof.
Combers
A nautical term for long, curling waves that roll in and break on a beach or reef.
Conch
A large sea snail with a spiraled shell that can be blown like a horn. Held to the ear, it seems to hold the sound of the sea.
Consummation
The completion or fulfillment of something.
Cosmography
A description or map of the whole universe, both heavens and earth.
Crow’s-nest
A lookout platform high on a ship’s mast.
Crucible
A heat-resistant pot for melting metals. Figuratively, a severe test that changes a person.
Crusader
A soldier in the Crusades, the Christian military campaigns to take the Holy Land, fought between 1096 and 1291.
Crystal-gazer
A fortune-teller who looks into a crystal ball to see the future.
Crystal-hunter
A prospector in the Alps who climbs into rock clefts to find quartz crystals.
Cup-bearer
A servant who poured and served wine to a king, a position of great trust. Nehemiah was cup-bearer to the Persian king Artaxerxes, and in Greek myth the youth Ganymede was cup-bearer to Zeus.
Dance of death
Also danse macabre. A medieval image of Death leading people of every rank, from pope and king to child and beggar, in a dance to the grave. See On the danse macabre (Ch 43).
Deference
Polite respect, or yielding to someone else’s wishes or judgment.
Disembodiment
Separation from the body; existing as a spirit without a body.
Dopester
A person who predicts the outcome of horse races, elections, or other contests from inside information, or “dope.”
Emir
A commander or prince in the Islamic world. More under Resources.
Empearled
Adorned with pearls, or having a pearly sheen.
Enigma
A mystery or puzzle; a person or thing that is hard to understand.
Eunuch
A man who has been castrated. Eunuchs were employed for centuries to guard harems and to serve as officials in royal courts in the Middle East, China, and Byzantium. See The eunuch (Ch 35).
Fallacy
A mistaken belief, or a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument unsound.
Figurehead
A carved figure, often a woman, mounted on the bow of a sailing ship. See On the figurehead and intuition (Ch 40).
Firmament
The sky or the heavens, imagined as a solid dome overhead, as in Genesis 1.
Flounced
Trimmed with flounces, wide strips of gathered or pleated fabric sewn to a skirt or dress.
Forebodings
Feelings that something bad is about to happen.
Forecastle
The forward part of a ship below the deck, where the crew lived. Pronounced “FOHK-sul.”
Frivolities
Silly, trivial, or lighthearted things.
Gondolier
The boatman who rows a Venetian gondola, standing at the stern with a single oar.
Halcyon
Calm and peaceful. From the halcyon, a mythical bird said to calm the sea while it nested on the waves in winter.
Halo
A ring of light around the sun or moon, caused by ice crystals high in thin clouds.
Hanging gardens
The Hanging Gardens of Babylon, one of the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World: terraced gardens said to have been built by King Nebuchadnezzar II. No trace of them has ever been found.
Helm
The wheel or tiller that steers a ship.
Ibis
A long-legged wading bird with a downward-curved bill, sacred in ancient Egypt to Thoth, god of writing and wisdom.
Immured
Shut in or imprisoned, as if walled up.
Imponderable
Something that cannot be measured, weighed, or judged.
Inscrutable
Impossible to understand or interpret.
Inveterate
Long settled in a habit and unlikely to change, as in “inveterate gambler.”
Keel and list
To keel over is to capsize, with the keel, the ship’s backbone along the bottom, turning upward. To list is to lean to one side, usually from water taken on.
Lagoon
A stretch of shallow water separated from the sea by a reef or sandbar.
Lazar
A diseased beggar, especially one with leprosy. More under Resources.
Lethargy
Sluggishness, drowsiness, a lack of energy.
Livid
Bluish-gray, the color of a bruise. Also furiously angry.
Lunar month
The time from one new moon to the next, about 29.5 days.
Lute
A plucked string instrument with a rounded back shaped like half a pear, popular in Europe from the Middle Ages through the 1700s.
Maharajah
A great king or prince in India. From the Sanskrit for “great king.”
Mandarin
A high-ranking official of imperial China.
Medusa
A jellyfish in its free-swimming, bell-shaped stage, named for the Gorgon of Greek myth whose hair was snakes.
Mercurial
Quick and changeable in mood. From the swift Roman messenger god Mercury and the liquid metal named for him.
Metamorphic
Having to do with a change of form. In geology, rock that heat and pressure have changed.
Mica
A mineral that splits into thin, shiny, nearly transparent sheets and makes rock glitter.
Minaret
A tall, slender tower of a mosque, from which the call to prayer is given.
Mirage
An optical illusion, common in deserts, in which hot air bends light so that distant water or cities seem to appear.
Monsoon
A seasonal wind in South Asia that brings months of heavy rain.
Mosaic
A picture or pattern made by setting small pieces of colored stone, glass, or tile together.
Nag
An old or worn-out horse.
Neap tide
The tide with the smallest difference between high and low water, twice a month at the quarter moons. More under Resources.
Negligee
A woman’s light, flowing dressing gown.
Nepenthe
In Homer’s Odyssey, a drug from Egypt that Helen puts in the wine to banish grief and sorrow. Anything that brings forgetfulness of pain. See On Nepenthe (Ch 82).
Odalisque
A servant woman or concubine in a Turkish harem. More under Resources.
Pagoda
An Asian tiered tower with multiple eaves, usually a Buddhist temple or shrine.
Palmer
A medieval pilgrim who brought back a palm frond from the Holy Land. More under Resources.
Paradox
A statement or situation that seems to contradict itself and yet may be true.
Parasol
A light umbrella carried for shade from the sun.
Parterre
An ornamental garden of flower beds laid out in a pattern. A parterred floor is inlaid in patterned sections.
Perambulations
Walks or strolls, especially leisurely ones.
Peregrinations
A journey, especially a long or meandering one.
Phantasmal
Ghostly; like a phantom or an illusion.
Pinnacle
The highest point; a tall, pointed mountain peak or the slender spire on a building.
Portfolio
A flat case for carrying loose papers and documents.
Presentiment
An intuitive feeling that something is about to happen.
Principality
A territory ruled by a prince.
Prism
A clear piece of glass with flat sides that splits light into the colors of the rainbow.
Promontory
A high point of land jutting out into the sea.
Roseate
Rose-colored. Also hopeful or overly optimistic.
Rubicon
A small river in northern Italy. Julius Caesar crossed it with his army in 49 B.C., starting a civil war, so “crossing the Rubicon” means passing a point of no return. See Crossing the Rubicon (Ch 23).
Sandalwood
A fragrant wood from India and the Pacific, burned as incense and used in perfume.
Sartorial
Having to do with clothing, tailoring, or style of dress.
Seer
A person who sees the future; a prophet.
Shah
The title of the king of Persia, now Iran.
Shell game
A swindle in which a pea is hidden under one of three shells or cups and shuffled, and bettors guess where it is. The operator usually palms the pea, so no one can win.
Skiff
A small, light boat for rowing or sailing. Young’s “skiff moon” is a crescent shaped like one.
Spar
A pole used as a ship’s mast, boom, or yard.
Steeplechase
A horse race over fences, ditches, and water jumps, first run cross-country from one church steeple to another.
Suffragette
A woman who campaigned for women’s right to vote. The word was coined by a London newspaper in 1906 for militant British activists. Most American activists called themselves suffragists. See Women’s Suffrage.
Sultanate

Chapter 33
