Summary

A Boston newspaper once referred to Catherine as "the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel," and Mr. Spitzer never told her. The same paper reported Peron seen walking on Benevolent Street, and Mr. Spitzer walked there the next evening. Catherine cannot remember her wedding or her groom, and sometimes thinks she married Death in her sleep. Mr. Spitzer decides that her dreaming is no farther from reality than the routines of people who punch clocks. The chapter ends with him rising to open a door she has asked a human-sized blackbird to open.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Jock Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Time

Symbols: Birds · Horses and Carriages · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · The House · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: American Writers · Judaism

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, it is revealed that a Boston newspaper mistakenly referred to Vera’s mother as deceased, calling her “the late Mrs. Catherine Cartwheel” despite her still being alive. Mr. Spitzer chooses not to correct this error, believing it trivial and possibly benevolent, as Catherine lives in a realm of “starry illusions” due to her opium addiction. This passage introduces the theme of blurred boundaries between life and death, truth and illusion, and the idea of allowing one’s illusions to persist rather than disturbing them.
  • Catherine’s refusal to acknowledge her marriage (Jock Cartwheel) to Mr. Spitzer and her preference for imagining multiple, shifting, and fantastical bridegrooms underscores her dissociation from reality and her embrace of poetic, surreal identities. This passage highlights her mercurial memory and the fluidity of her self-identity, as well as her rejection of conventional social realities in favor of dreamlike existences.
  • Catherine’s fragmented and vague recollection of her wedding, surrounded by “spirits in the air,” “glassy pebbles rolling on the shore,” “swords of fire, swords of ice,” and “wild, ethereal wedding music,” creates a surreal, almost otherworldly atmosphere. This passage amplifies the motif of memory as unreliable and the blending of reality with fantasy. It suggests that her perception of life events is filtered through a dreamlike, fractured consciousness.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s role as the observer and caretaker is critical. He reflects on Catherine’s addiction, her detachment from time, and her illusory world, concluding that she is “probably no more enslaved than others were by their predisposition toward illusion.” His philosophical musings on consciousness, unconsciousness, and the nature of life and death add depth to the narrative, portraying a compassionate understanding of human frailty and the necessity of illusions. His own struggle with reality, his brother’s ruin, and his meticulous attempts to grasp the elusive mirror Catherine’s own fragmented existence.
  • A striking passage describes Catherine talking to invisible or imagined persons showing her living in a world where the usual distinctions between presence and absence, reality and fantasy, are dissolved. Mr. Spitzer’s action of opening the door when she asks, despite the door being closed and her talking to a blackbird, demonstrates his gentle indulgence of her illusions and the poignancy of her condition.
  • References to the “dead lute-player in the garden,” “formal king penguins,” “melancholy seals,” and “tinkling duchesses” contribute to the surreal and symbolic texture of the chapter. These images reinforce the theme of a world where music, memory, and myth intermingle, and reality is perceived through a kaleidoscope of unusual and poetic visions.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A once-famous beauty and socialite who has long been out of public view.
  • A complex figure, described as living in illusions and opium-induced dreams.
  • Her memories, especially of her wedding(s), are fragmented, poetic, and unreliable.
  • She refuses to accept certain realities, such as her supposed death or marriage to Jock (Catherine’s late husband).
  • She interacts with imaginary figures and experiences reality as a blend of dream and fact.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A close, faithful friend of Catherine.
  • He understands her illusions and indulges them, choosing not to correct her perceptions.
  • He is practical but also philosophical, contrasting his own conscious precision with Catherine’s dreamlike state.
  • He is involved in artistic creation like writing harp music inspired by the wind and bridges.
  • Carries a burden of familial and financial complications (his brother’s debts).
  • He represents a grounding figure, yet he is also caught in Catherine’s world of illusion.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s thoughts include existential questions about reality, illusion, death, and time.

Research: Themes

Memory and Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

  • Catherine’s memories are described as “beautifully inaccurate,” blending fact with fantasy.
  • She often confuses time, place, and people, exemplifying the fragility of human memory.
  • Memories of her wedding are surreal involving images like bats, owls, icy landscapes, and ambiguous bridegrooms.
  • The narrative suggests memory as a form of dream or illusion that can persist beyond life.

Death and Existence

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine is believed dead by society but is alive in her own dream world.
  • Death is portrayed ambiguously, sometimes as a wedding to Death itself or as slipping into an eternal unconsciousness.
  • The boundary between life and death is blurred, raising questions about what it means truly to live or die.

Time and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Time

  • Time is fluid and unreliable in Catherine’s experience; she confuses noon and midnight, beginnings and endings.
  • Mr. Spitzer attempts to keep time (symbolized by his watch) as a measure of reality, but even he is caught between illusion and fact.
  • The novel questions the nature of reality itself and how much is defined by perception.

Music and Sound

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Mr. Spitzer’s harp music inspired by wind and bridge cables symbolizes the blending of natural forces and artistic creation.
  • Music serves as a metaphor for the ephemeral, invisible forces shaping human experience and memory.

Isolation and Companionship

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Despite Catherine’s isolation in her illusions, Mr. Spitzer remains a constant companion, albeit one often rejected by her.
  • Their relationship is marked by a tension between reality and fantasy, presence and absence.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Wedding and Bridegroom(s)

See: Weddings and Funerals · The House

  • Catherine’s ambiguous wedding(s) symbolize transitions, possibly to death or between states of consciousness.
  • The multiple, shifting bridegrooms (white camel, church steeple, wind) reflect the fluidity of identity and reality.

The Black Coachman and Carriage

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize passage, possibly death or transition.
  • The carriage on the streets of Boston, after years of absence, signals a disruption of normal order.
  • Catherine also said the Black Coachman was her conscious and the carriage was her body.

The Blackbird and the Door

See: Birds · Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Catherine talks to a human-sized blackbird and instructs to open a door that is actually closed.
  • These images portray the overlap of the real and the imaginary.

Stars and Celestial Imagery

See: Moon and Stars

  • Stars and heavens often represent unreachable or eternal realms.
  • Catherine refuses to marry Mr. Spitzer “not while the stars shone in the glassy heavens,” linking love and fate to cosmic forces.

The Newspaper Mistake

  • The misreporting of Catherine’s death and Mr. Spitzer’s decision not to correct it sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of truth vs. illusion.

The Wedding Memories

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Catherine’s hazy, fantastical memories of her wedding illustrates the blurred line between reality and fantasy.

Mr. Spitzer’s Harp Music

See: Music and Instruments

  • His artistic endeavor is inspired by natural sounds and symbolizes the attempt to impose order or meaning on chaos.

Catherine’s Conversations with Invisible Figures

  • Demonstrates her detachment from consensus reality.

  • Causality is influenced by which one event, process, state, or object (a cause) contributes to the production of another event, process, state, or object (an effect) where the cause is partly responsible for the effect, and the effect is partly dependent on the cause. In general, a process has many causes, which are also said to be causal factors for it, and all lie in its past. An effect can in turn be a cause of, or causal factor for, many other effects, which all lie in its future. Some writers have held that causality is metaphysically prior to notions of time and space. Causality is an abstraction that indicates how the world progresses, so basic a concept that it is more apt as an explanation of other concepts of progression than as something to be explained by others more basic. The concept is like those of agency and efficacy. For this reason, a leap of intuition may be needed to grasp it. Accordingly, causality is implicit in the logic and structure of ordinary language. The topic of causality remains a staple in contemporary philosophy. The chapter presents causality as unstable and enigmatic, entwined with the themes of illusion, memory, and subjective reality. The traditional, linear cause-effect relationship is replaced by a vision of interwoven, reversible, and often contradictory events, reflecting the novel's broader exploration of reality as mutable and uncertain.

Chapter 22

← Chapter 21 · Home · Chapter 23 →

Summary

At an unusually festive breakfast of fine china and white roses, Miss MacIntosh reads the newspaper aloud: rebellions, Wall Street, storms, strikes, the price of eggs. She fires questions at Vera, complains about dust and unmatched socks, and talks about shipwrecks off the coast. Vera is irritated by her cheerfulness, asks twice about the ruined dress, and is deflected. Almost in passing, Miss MacIntosh remarks that baldness is no cure for sorrow. Vera begins to wonder whether her nursemaid is as dreamlike as everyone else.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Richard MacIntosh

Concepts present

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s seething irritation and physical discomfort, describing scratches, aches, and a nameless fatigue that suggests both physical and spiritual malaise. This sets the tone of discontent and existential questioning that permeates the chapter. The sea is described as a mysterious, almost otherworldly presence, "an astral light as of some other planet".
  • Vera’s feeling of disconnection from the usual routine and Miss MacIntosh’s cheerful insistence on continuing the day’s affairs despite Vera’s obvious distress highlight a fundamental tension between resignation and rebellion.
  • Miss MacIntosh reads aloud the morning newspaper, which is water-stained and blurred, symbolizing the blurred and unstable condition of the world and their lives. The newspaper covers a wide range of topics from international politics and economic troubles to mundane notices like shipments of coconuts and sports scores, reflecting the chaotic and fragmentary nature of modern life.
  • Her manner is repetitive and insistent on routine knowledge and memorization of things such as: biblical creation days, current events, and housekeeping duties. This shows her belief in order and discipline as a defense against chaos and despair.
  • The sea is a recurring symbol representing memory, oblivion, and the unknown. Miss MacIntosh doubts that the sea has memory, questioning "What does the sea remember when it swallows the ship?" This reflects Vera’s own questioning of existence and loss.
  • The house is depicted as a decaying, almost haunted place filled with relics, broken items, and ghosts of the past. The chapter describes the house’s vast but unused wealth (silver services, fine china) and its gradual ruination, symbolizing the decay of old values and failed dreams.
  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed as brusque, pragmatic, and somewhat harsh, focused on housekeeping, moral discipline, and maintaining order. She criticizes Vera’s laziness and failure to perform her duties, insisting on sewing, cleaning, and learning practical skills for any future husband.
  • Her voice is described as grating and rasping, likened to rusted hinges and drowning sounds, emphasizing her toughness and weariness but also her refusal to indulge in illusions or sentimentalities.
  • The chapter is punctuated by Miss MacIntosh’s rapid-fire questions about the creation days, geography, history, sports, and the meaning of life and death. These questions serve as a kind of catechism, an attempt to impose order and knowledge on a world that feels chaotic and uncertain to Vera.
  • Vera reflects on the futility of these lessons and the disconnection between the external facts of the world and her internal sorrow and longing.
  • While Miss MacIntosh insists on routine and practical concerns, Vera is lost in a dreamlike state, haunted by memories, illusions, and phantasms. There is a growing sense of alienation and sorrow, Vera’s desire for “perfect happiness” contrasting with Miss MacIntosh’s grounded, if harsh, realism.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s dismissal of ghosts and phantoms as nonsense, and her readiness to confront any imaginary specter with her black umbrella, symbolizes her rejection of fantasy and acceptance only of the tangible and practical.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Tired, disillusioned, and inwardly restless, she struggles with a profound sense of sorrow and alienation.
  • She questions the value of the tasks imposed on her and longs for a life beyond repetitive lessons and duties.
  • She exhibits moments of defiance and yearning for joy (“I shall dance again”).

Miss MacIntosh

  • A forthright, practical woman with a strong sense of duty, she is Vera’s caretaker and disciplinarian.
  • She is resistant to illusions and ghosts, skeptical of sentimentality, and focused on maintaining order.
  • Despite her harshness, she harbors her own doubts and vulnerabilities, reflected in her philosophical musings and physical frailty.

Richard, Miss MacIntosh’s brother (Mentioned)

  • A missionary who died trying to convert tribes to Christianity. Miss MacIntosh describes him as having red hair.

Research: Themes

  • Routine vs. Inner Turmoil Vera experiences deep emotional fatigue and existential questioning, feeling trapped in repetitive, meaningless tasks imposed by Miss MacIntosh’s rigid routine. The contrast highlights the human struggle between external order and internal chaos.
  • Memory and Forgetfulness The sea, a recurring motif, is described as both full of “wrinkles” and yet possibly without memory. This paradox symbolizes the blurred lines between remembering and forgetting, life and oblivion.
  • Illusion vs. Reality Miss MacIntosh dismisses phantoms and ghosts as nonsense, emphasizing the importance of facing reality and practicality, whereas Vera’s experience is haunted by memories, dreams, and elusive presences.
  • Mortality and Loss References to death, the “angel of death,” and shipwrecks evoke the fragility of life and the inevitability of decay. Vera is preoccupied with the absence of new life (no children) and the presence of old, broken things, symbolizing lost hopes.
  • Knowledge and Education The insistence on memorizing Biblical genealogies, current events, geography, and sports reflects a traditional, perhaps oppressive, approach to learning as a way to impose order and meaning in a chaotic world.
  • Isolation and Connection Vera feels isolated, disconnected from the external world and even from Miss MacIntosh, who seems unable to perceive Vera’s sorrow. There is a tension between their companionship and emotional distance.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • The Sea Represents memory, oblivion, and the passage of time. It is both a life source and a graveyard, swallowing ships and memories alike.
  • The Breakfast Table The ornately set table contrasts with the characters’ modest lives, symbolizing lost grandeur or unrealized potential.
  • Phantoms and Ghosts Symbolizes Vera’s inner fears and the past’s haunting presence. Miss MacIntosh’s dismissal of them reflects a pragmatic worldview.
  • Broken and Sunken Objects Shipwrecks, broken crockery, and old estate remnants symbolize decay, loss, and the impermanence of human endeavors.
  • Black Umbrella Miss MacIntosh’s protective and practical tool, symbolizing her grounded nature and defense against both literal and figurative storms.
  • Symbolism The chapter abounds with symbolic references to ships, storms, and phantoms, enhancing themes of memory and loss.
  • Stream of Consciousness Vera’s thoughts flow freely between observation, memory, and philosophical reflection, emphasizing her inner turmoil.
  • Allusion Biblical references to creation days, historical figures (Emperor Constantine, King Canute), and literary figures (Jeremiah) deepen thematic complexity.
  • Contrast Between Vera’s emotional state and Miss MacIntosh’s external cheerfulness and routine.

  • The Dream and the Illusion: The unfinished creation ties into the novel's recurring theme of life as a dream or illusion, where the boundaries between reality and fantasy blur. God's "unfinished" work parallels the incomplete and often contradictory experiences of the characters, especially in relation to memory, identity, and mortality.
  • Theological Ambivalence: The theme also conveys a theological ambivalence or doubt.   • Call to Moral and Practical Action: Because creation is incomplete, the characters, particularly Miss MacIntosh, emphasize the importance of practical, honest living in the present world rather than dreaming of distant, perfect worlds or afterlives. The unfinished world demands human effort and self-discipline, and moral clarity, rather than escapism or fantasy. The significance of God leaving things uncreated or unfinished is to highlight the imperfection and incompleteness of existence, the limits of human understanding, the blurred boundary between reality and illusion, and the call for grounded, practical living amid uncertainty. In 1947, after Rickey broke the color line by signing Jackie Robinson to the Dodgers, there were rumors that southerners playing for the Cardinals were planning to boycott games against the Dodgers, although the players later denied it. In general, the Cardinals were latecomers to integration. Front-office executive Bing Devine said the owner from 1947 to 1953, Fred Saigh, refused to sign black players. There was a widespread belief that St. Louis was, in many ways, a Southern city. In the mid-1950s many of its stores and restaurants refused to serve black customers. The Cardinals, with baseball's largest radio network blanketing the Midwest and South, had cultivated white Southern fans. Their ballpark was also the last in the majors to abolish segregated seating. Because of their lack of black players, the Cardinals' play suffered on the field tremendously in the 1950s. Meanwhile, with the success of Robinson, the Dodgers doubled down on the opportunity to sign players of color from the Negro leagues. In the subsequent years after their pennant-winning season in 1947, they would sign Don Newcombe, Roy Campanella, and Jim Gilliam from the Negro leagues, adding to an already tremendous team. The Dodgers made the World Series in 1949, 1952, 1953, 1955, 1956, and 1959 (winning championships in 1955 and 1959) and were a historic pennant race away from making it in 1951, in part because they were the first to accept African American players. The 1951 season included a 14-game winning streak for the Dodgers against the Cardinals, the longest such streak in the rivalry.

  • Islands of the Blessed may refer to the Islands in Greek mythology which were a semi-legendary place in the western ocean where the souls of heroes and worthy people went after death. They were also known as the Fortunate Isles or Elysian Fields.

  • “Man is man’s wolf” - Homo homini lupus. It implies that without social order or moral restraint, humans naturally act in their own self-interest, often to the detriment of others. In the context of the novel, this phrase underscores Miss MacIntosh’s practical and often harsh perspective on life and human relationships. She critiques illusions about human goodness or harmony and points to the fundamental struggles and hostilities that characterize human existence. Her reflections on the difficulties of marriage and human relationships further illustrate this theme of conflict and mistrust among people. Miss MacIntosh’s worldview is grounded in realism and common sense, and she frequently expresses skepticism about the idealized notions of love and trust, viewing human nature as frail and prone to betrayal and disappointment. The phrase encapsulates this somber viewpoint on the inherent challenges in human connections and the social order
  • “The sheep cannot guard the sheep against the thief.” - John 10:1 This conveys a profound truth about human vulnerability and the limits of self-protection within a community or among similar individuals. This metaphor suggests that those who are alike or in the same vulnerable position (the "sheep") cannot effectively protect each other from external harm or threats (the "thief"). It highlights the inherent helplessness and fragility of individuals who, despite being part of a group or society, remain exposed to dangers they cannot fully defend against. It also resonates with the novel’s exploration of isolation and the limits of trust and protection among people, even those closely connected. The phrase is part of a larger discourse on human frailty, the inevitability of suffering, and the need for resilience and acceptance of one’s condition in life.
  • “We must catch the old Devil by the tail” - is an idiom that means to be struggling or barely scraping by with limited financial resources. This metaphorical expression conveys the urgency and necessity to confront and overcome the forces of evil, temptation, and corruption that pervade human existence. Miss MacIntosh uses this phrase to emphasize that evil (personified as the "old Devil") must be actively confronted and controlled rather than ignored or allowed to run rampant. Catching the Devil by the tail suggests grabbing hold of these negative forces firmly before they can cause harm or spread further. The phrase fits into the broader themes of the novel regarding the struggle between good and evil, the moral challenges people face, and the importance of maintaining integrity and common sense amidst life's confusions and illusions. It reflects Miss MacIntosh’s stern belief in the necessity of moral discipline and the fight against the "powers of darkness" in a world full of suffering and temptation.   • “The first thrashing had its origin, I have no doubt, in heaven, and one fell.” - Genesis 50:10 It is a symbolic expression reflecting the theme of a cosmic or spiritual fall that initiates suffering and disorder in the world. It signifies that the troubles in human life are reflections or consequences of this primordial "fall" or "thrashing" in heaven, marking the beginning of a long history of struggle between good and evil, order and chaos.   • “He was fallen from morning until seven o’clock” - is the exact opposite of Luke 10:18 where he fell “like lightning from heaven.” It is a poetic and somewhat enigmatic expression reflecting a complex perception of time, existence, and death. The phrase reflects the novel’s meditation on the fugitive and mysterious aspects of time, death, and the human experience or a temporal window marking the moment of irreversible change, the transition from life to death, and the attempt to grasp and give meaning to this transition within the novel’s dreamlike, layered narrative.

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter is one of the hardest in the novel: Esther describes being raped by the Chicago detective, and the chapter deals with racism.

Summary

Esther dreads a trial before a jury. The Chicago detective has come three times in three disguises, collecting clues for murders no one else notices. He is also the man who raped her. He cares only about the deaths of white children. Esther's speech begins to repeat words in threes, and she hints at an old, hidden death from her youth. Her own childhood reproaches her.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · The Chicago Detective · Esther’s Father

Concepts present

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Fear and Courage · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Exploration and the Poles · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery

Key passages

From the research

  • Esther expresses her dread and isolation as she anticipates a courtroom trial, where she will be accused and misunderstood by a crowd of women who will judge her harshly without truly understanding her. It underscores her loneliness and the societal scrutiny she faces, as well as the impossibility of defending herself against accusations about her maternity and morality.
  • The detective’s repeated, disguised appearances and his cold, investigative demeanor create a haunting, almost spectral presence in Esther’s life. He is both the biological father of her stillborn children and the figure who pursues her legally, embodying both intimacy and threat.
  • The narrative of the detective’s rape of Esther is described with a mixture of detached observation and emotional complexity. The experience is both a physical violation and a symbolic act that precipitates her ongoing “pregnancy” with stillborn children, both literal and metaphorical.
  • The motif of being “always pregnant” with stillborn children recurs throughout this chapter, symbolizing loss, unfulfilled potential, and the burden of expectation and judgment placed upon her. This is also tied to her physical and emotional condition, which isolates her further.
  • Esther contrasts her own suffering and social condemnation as a woman with the freedom and impunity of men, highlighting societal hypocrisy and the loneliness of her position.
  • The chapter frequently invokes imagery of death, murder, and stillbirth as metaphors for Esther’s lost hopes and emotional wounds. The “murder of her heart” is a poignant expression of her deep psychological pain and the cumulative effect of her tragic experiences.
  • Despite the external pressures, accusations, and her own confusions, Esther claims a mysterious, almost radiant identity, self-sufficient and brooding, unwilling to explain herself to anyone.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • The protagonist, a woman who is perpetually pregnant yet burdened with loss and mystery.
  • She is introspective, lonely, and caught between hope and despair.
  • She fears legal prosecution and societal judgment but is also fiercely protective of her own narrative and secrets.

The Chicago Detective

  • The father of Esther’s children, a figure who has repeatedly found Esther in vulnerable states.
  • He is investigating murders but is ironically implicated in Esther’s personal tragedy through his actions.
  • He represents authority, suspicion, and the complexities of truth and guilt.

Esther’s Father (the Policeman)

  • Symbolizes familial and societal surveillance and judgment.
  • His passive role highlights Esther’s isolation and the inescapability of the small-town environment.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Loss

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther experiences repeated pregnancies that result in stillbirths, symbolizing loss, unfulfilled potential, and emotional trauma.
  • Her womb is described as swollen with “empty waters,” a metaphor for hope and despair coexisting.

Societal Judgment and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Society, Class, and Race

  • Esther fears the court trial, anticipating gossip, blame, and misunderstanding from the community.
  • She is alienated and misunderstood, with the jury and townspeople serving as a metaphor for harsh societal judgment.

Mystery and Ambiguity

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative blurs reality and memory. Esther’s story is full of mysteries: the paternity of her children, the nature of her pregnancies, and the actions of the detective.
  • The repeated motif of “stillborn” children and the detective’s ambiguous role deepen this theme.

Powerlessness and Defiance

See: Fear and Courage

  • Despite her vulnerability, Esther exhibits moments of defiance, especially against unfair accusations and societal expectations.
  • Her internal world remains rich and complex, even as she is perceived as “crazy” or “mulish.”

  • Esther Longtree in this chapter is portrayed as a profoundly tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of loss, mystery, maternal suffering, and societal judgment. Her character is marked by an overwhelming burden of perpetual pregnancy and stillbirths, an existence both physically and emotionally laden with pain and unanswered questions. Esther’s situation is unique and unprecedented in the legal realm, as she faces the threat of arrest and trial for the disappearance or death of her children: children who may never have been born or who remain unseen by others. She is caught in a web of suspicion and gossip, misunderstood and condemned by her community and the justice system, yet she remains deeply isolated, bearing her sorrow silently and without defense. This isolation is compounded by her physical condition (repeatedly pregnant yet without the relief of childbirth) and by the haunting presence of her absent children, described metaphorically as her “tears” and “stillborn” who haunt her mind and body. Her relationship with the Chicago detective, who is implicated as the father of her lost children, adds layers of complexity and darkness to her narrative. The detective’s repeated appearances (disguised as various characters) are both invasive and inscrutable. Esther’s encounters with him are marked by violence, mystery, and a sense of inevitability: she is raped by him, yet the experience is described with a strange passivity and detachment, as if she were “sleeping in the grass” and indifferent. This rapist-father figure represents a brutal intrusion into her life, one that leaves physical and psychological scars, but also a tangled mystery of conception, conception without life, and lost pregnancies. Esther’s internal world is rich with symbolism and metaphor: the “stillborn” children, the “broken gooseberry bushes,” the “buzzard hanging rounded like a period” all evoke a landscape of death, loss, and unfulfilled potential. Despite her suffering, Esther is radiant and self-sufficient in a strange way, carrying her burden with a stubborn dignity. She is aware of the social judgments (accusations of insanity, immorality, or deceit) but she resists these with a fierce inner knowledge of her own innocence and the mystery of her condition. She embodies a tragic maternal figure whose story is one of loss made visible and invisible, a woman burdened by an unexplainable condition and an unresolvable mystery.   • “his eye-glasses, his footprints, too, his calling card… a thread” These are all clues used in famous mystery novels. The Golden Age of Detective Fiction (roughly 1913–1939) was an era between the World Wars defined by polite, "whodunit" puzzle mysteries, primarily featuring British writers like Agatha Christie, Dorothy L. Sayers, Margery Allingham, and Ngaio Marsh. These stories favored intellectual, fair-play clues over violence, often set in closed circles like country houses, focusing on solving the murder rather than dark, psychological grit. Iconic characters from this time period: Hercule Poirot, Miss Marple, Lord Peter Wimsey, Perry Mason, and Philip Marlowe. E.C. Bentley's Trent's Last Case (1913) is often cited as the beginning, with Christie's The Mysterious Affair at Styles (1920) setting the standard. The Detection Club, founded in 1930, established "rules" for the genre, such as no faked clues or supernatural solutions. The stories offered escapism, featuring a return to order after a "sanitized" version of murder, often reflecting a desire to move past the trauma of World War I. While often associated with the British "cozy" style, the era also saw the rise of American "hard-boiled" fiction. American hard-boiled detective fiction is a gritty, unsentimental subgenre emerging in the 1920s–30s, defined by cynical private eyes, urban corruption, fast-paced dialogue, and brutal violence. Pioneered by Dashiell Hammett and perfected by Raymond Chandler, these stories moved away from genteel puzzles to realistic crime, often published in pulp magazines like Black Mask.

Summary

Mr. Spitzer admits that he may be only another of Catherine's hallucinations, and that he truly lives only during these evenings in her room. He recalls the butterfly collection he abandoned after Peron's funeral, his correspondence with fellow collectors, and the births and deaths of butterflies he watched. If one were called away at the crucial moment, he observes, one could never tell whether one had seen a beginning or an end.

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening passage describes Mr. Spitzer’s nightly visits as a kind of faithfulness, drawing “him each evening here as to a brilliant star,” despite his life feeling like a “dark and empty plain” except for these “delusive evenings.” This passage highlights the blurred boundary between his corporeal reality and the narcotic, hallucinatory world of Catherine. He is portrayed as a “living ghost” caught between life and death, reality and fantasy, which underscores the chapter’s exploration of existence, memory, and identity. The imagery of “the vastness of this trembling flesh enclosing his feeble spirit like a flame” poignantly captures the fragility of his being.
  • There is a significant reflection on Mr. Spitzer’s dead twin brother, who had a very different approach to life. While Mr. Spitzer was thinking “only of the impossible future,” his brother “had loved the cruelty of actual life” and seemed to live only in the present moment. The brother’s death profoundly affected Mr. Spitzer, dividing his soul almost to lunacy. This contrast illuminates themes of mortality, memory, and the divergent ways individuals confront existence and loss. It also sets up a tension between rationality and passion, foresight and immediacy.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s passion for collecting butterflies is portrayed not merely as a hobby but as a meditative and symbolic pursuit. The butterflies are described with poetic richness. This imagery conveys a mystical quality, indicating that these ephemeral creatures represent moments of beauty, transformation, and perhaps spiritual truth. His care for butterflies is contrasted with Catherine’s visions of “imaginary sea bishops,” “mermaids,” and other fantastical figures, suggesting a shared yet distinct engagement with the invisible or transcendent world.
  • The chapter notes that after Peron’s “devastating funeral,” many aspects of Mr. Spitzer’s life ended, including his butterfly collecting and his “own capacious heart.” Peron’s pragmatic, earthly interests are contrasted with Mr. Spitzer’s more spiritual and impersonal passions. This marks a turning point, emphasizing loss not only of a person but of a way of life and a kind of inner vitality. Peron’s skepticism about the afterlife and the significance of spiritual phenomena positions him as a foil to Mr. Spitzer’s contemplative nature.
  • The closing passage reflects on the indistinguishability of birth and death moments: “if one were suddenly called away in the midst of these proceedings, one should never know whether it was death or birth, beginning or end.” This philosophical observation encapsulates a central motif of the chapter, the fluid boundary between beginnings and endings, life and death, seen through the metaphor of the butterfly’s emergence and expiration. It also explains the impetus for Mr. Spitzer’s studies: the search for meaning in “impalpable butterflies,” or elusive spiritual truths.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Peron Spitzer (Joachim’s Twin Brother)

  • A loudmouthed, pragmatic man who embraced the cruelty of actual life and seemed indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts.
  • His untimely death deeply affects Mr. Spitzer’s psyche and way of life.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Peron is portrayed as a man focused on the immediate, material world, indifferent to spiritual or afterlife concepts, and unconcerned with the delicate beauty Mr. Spitzer values.
  • Peron’s death, seen as a suicide, marks a turning point for Mr. Spitzer, leading to the end of many of his pursuits and a deepening of his introspection.

  • The chapter opens with a profound reflection on whether the protagonist, Mr. Spitzer, is truly a musician or merely a gambler who has deluded himself into believing in a lost musical career. This internal conflict is central where he is haunted by the "germinal music in his head," yet increasingly obsessed with gambling. The imagery of cards (ace of clubs, spots on dice) and horse races evokes a chaotic, chance-driven world contrasted with the ordered art of music. The passage poses the question of identity and authenticity and whether his essence is musical or rooted in worldly, mundane obsessions like gambling. This sets the tone for the chapter's exploration of perception and self-delusion.
  • The chapter highlights Mr. Spitzer’s narrow focus: he reads only the sporting page, ignores international, financial, and high society news, and has never attended concerts or engaged with refined cultural matters. This suggests a man disconnected from broader social and cultural contexts, reinforcing his isolation and the ambiguity of his self-identity. His ignorance of “the value of a sand dollar or a Boston dollar or an English pound sterling” metaphorically implies his detachment from worldly values and economic realities.
  • There is a symbolic and surreal moment where Mr. Spitzer practices moose calls in the city at dusk, only to hear the answering call of an actual moose which is an extraordinary, almost hallucinatory experience. The moose’s antlers are described as “looming like tree boughs through the blowing purple fog,” blending natural imagery with urban and cosmic elements (traffic lights, the Pleiades). This encounter blurs the boundary between reality and imagination, the natural and the supernatural, highlighting Mr. Spitzer's liminal state between sanity and hallucination, music and noise, life and death.
  • The climax of the chapter is the vision of the wild ducks flying overhead: exotic “beautiful Asiatics” with crested heads and golden eyes, described in luminous, almost otherworldly colors. Mr. Spitzer perceives their honking calls as a “wild sonata,” a natural music that becomes his elegy. The ducks’ flight is metaphorically linked to transcendence, migration, and perhaps the soul’s journey. He imagines himself metamorphosed into wings, a silent observer caught between earth and sky. The passage conveys a sense of awe, mystery, and the dissolution of boundaries between self and nature, music and silence, sound and chaos.
  • Near the end, the chapter suggests that Mr. Spitzer’s elegy (the music he cannot write or remember) may be embodied in the calls of the wild ducks. This is a powerful metaphor for artistic creation as something wild, natural, and perhaps uncontrollable, rather than composed or intellectual. The elegy is not just a lament but an acceptance of the wild, untamed forces that accompany him “through the long reaches of the silence”

  • cubistic dream player - refers metaphorically to Mr. Spitzer’s fragmented and multifaceted perception of himself and his life. The term "cubistic" evokes the art movement Cubism, where objects are depicted from multiple viewpoints simultaneously, resulting in fragmented and abstracted forms. The "cubistic dream player" suggests a person whose identity and experiences are fractured, seen from various angles that do not form a coherent whole, much like a cubist painting. Mr. Spitzer feels that he is composed of many disjointed parts or "selves," and his memories and perceptions are scattered and overlapping, not fitting together into a unified reality. This fragmentation reflects his inner confusion and the blending of dream and reality that permeates the novel. This image captures Mr. Spitzer’s sense of dislocation and the complexity of his existence, as he struggles with his identity, the loss of his brother Peron, and the elusive nature of truth and memory. It is a symbolic way to portray the multiplicity and ambiguity of Mr. Spitzer’s consciousness and life experience, emphasizing the novel’s themes of fractured identity and the interplay of illusion and reality.
  • The Cubist art movement, pioneered by Pablo Picasso and Georges Braque in the early 20th century, revolutionized art by rejecting traditional single-point perspective and instead depicting subjects from multiple viewpoints simultaneously. Notable women Cubist artists are:
  • Marie Laurencin: A French painter who studied with Georges Braque and developed a distinct style with soft, pastel colors and graceful, flowing figures. Her work offered a lyrical and feminine counterpoint to the more traditional Cubist aesthetic.
  • María Blanchard: A Spanish painter who moved to Paris and became a significant figure in the Cubist movement. Despite being an important painter, she was often overlooked in historical accounts of the era, which were dominated by male artists.
  • Sonia Delaunay: While also known for her work in Orphism, Delaunay's style was heavily influenced by Cubism and she was a key figure in the avant-garde.
  • Natalia Goncharova: A Russian avant-garde artist who, along with her partner Mikhail Larionov, was a founder of the Rayonist movement. Her work engaged with many modernist styles, including Cubism.
  • Lyubov Popova: A leading figure of the Russian avant-garde, Popova's work moved through various phases of modernism, including Cubo-Futurism.
  • Aleksandra Exter: Studied art in Kiev and became a prominent avant-garde artist whose work became increasingly radical, mixing Cubist influences with other modernist ideas.
  • Mary Harriet Jellett: An Australian artist who was a pioneer of modern art in Australia and was heavily influenced by the Cubist style.This approach resulted in paintings and sculptures that appear fragmented into abstract, geometric forms, emphasizing the flat, two-dimensional surface of the canvas.
  • The central idea of Cubism was to show objects as the mind comprehends them in their totality, rather than from a single, fixed viewpoint. This involved breaking down and reassembling objects into an abstract form to suggest their three-dimensional structure and their movement through time and space. Artists reduced figures and objects to fundamental geometric shapes such as cubes, spheres, and cones. This fragmentation of forms challenged traditional naturalistic representation. Cubists rejected the illusion of depth created by traditional perspective, instead highlighting the flatness of the canvas. Background and foreground often merge in their compositions. Cubism was significantly influenced by the late work of Post-Impressionist painter Paul Cézanne, who simplified nature into geometric forms, and by the abstract, stylized forms of African tribal masks and Iberian sculpture.
  • The chapter explores Mr. Spitzer’s deep existential and artistic struggles through metaphoric natural imagery and philosophical reflection.   • A "fugue" has two main meanings: a complex musical composition where a theme is repeated and interwoven by multiple voices, and a temporary mental state of amnesia and wandering, often associated with dissociative disorders. Musically, it involves a single theme being introduced by one voice and then imitated by others in a structured, imitative style. Psychologically, a dissociative fugue is a condition where an individual forgets their past and may travel, only to have no memory of the period later.
  • “Antiphonies” are a type of responsive singing or music between two groups, creating a "call and response" effect. The term can also refer to a verse sung before and after a psalm or hymn, often used in religious services.
  • “Winding horns” are a type of wind instrument, historically made from animal horns or metal, used for signaling over long distances in activities like hunting, battle, and ceremonies. Also known as blowing horns or war horns, they produce a single note, and different meanings are conveyed through rhythms and speed.

These pilgrims evoke a feeling of journeying beyond ordinary experience, aligning with the novel's recurring themes of transition between worlds, dreams, and the mystical or spiritual journey. This description is part of Mr. Spitzer’s reflections on butterflies, moths, and celestial or spiritual beings, blending natural imagery with poetic and symbolic language to suggest a realm beyond the mundane.

Chapter 42

Summary

Catherine rides in a glass carriage behind four alabaster horses, driven by the black coachman, through the sleeping house toward Hannah's deathbed. Mr. Spitzer, a keeper of lists of lost ships, keeps vigil beside the dying suffragette. He finds her crippled, wrapped in an old army coat, sobbing and delirious in a white tent of a room. He wonders what her battles truly won, and she cries out to be hidden from the eyes of men.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Love · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · The Search for Meaning · Time

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche

Allusions: Astronomy · Greek Mythology · Napoleon and Wellington · The Bible · The Civil War · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a dreamlike passage describing Catherine’s journey in a glass carriage driven by a black coachman with alabaster horses, passing through surreal landscapes of mirrors, fountains, tapestries, and sleeping cities. This journey is symbolic of transition, memory, and farewell, as she travels to visit Cousin Hannah in a realm beyond ordinary time and space. Catherine’s visit is described as hallucinatory, almost otherworldly, blending dream and reality, emphasizing the fluidity of time and the nature of farewell as something that transcends physical existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer is preoccupied with lists of sunken and lost ships, the mystery of their disappearance, and the elusive nature of time and memory. This section metaphorically ties the fate of lost ships to the human experience of loss, disappearance, and the unknowability of final destinies. His meditation on finding coordinates, lost passengers, and the ocean’s endless mysteries parallels the chapter’s broader themes of searching for meaning amid oblivion.
  • Much of the chapter is devoted to Mr. Spitzer’s detailed remembrance and reflection on Cousin Hannah, the fading suffrage captain. Her life is portrayed as one of militant energy, passion, and struggle by leading crusades, breaking conventions, and battling societal and personal constraints. Yet now, in her old age, she is reduced to a fragile figure, almost unrecognizable, lying in a vast, tent-like death chamber filled with memories and trophies of battles past. The contrast between her former fiery strength and present weakness is poignant, illustrating the inevitability of decline and the loneliness of a warrior’s final moments.
  • Mr. Spitzer speculates on the hidden personal life of Cousin Hannah, suggesting a secret and perhaps tragic love life that contrasts with her public image of fierce independence and detachment. There is mention of a mysterious bridegroom who was left at the church door and rumors of a secret man or caliph who supported her cause. This passage explores the tension between public persona and private vulnerability, and the elusive nature of love and companionship even for the strongest figures.
  • The closing passages focus on Mr. Spitzer’s visit to Cousin Hannah’s death chamber, where he confronts her mortality and the enigma of her spirit. The imagery of snow, white curtains, desert tents, and the blending of life and death create a surreal atmosphere. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the nature of death as a journey and the dissolution of identity. Despite her indifference and silence, he remains faithful, accompanying her in her final hours, contemplating the mystery of the soul, the possibility of resurrection, and the universal fate that awaits all.
  • Throughout the chapter, there are numerous philosophical reflections on time, memory, identity, and the interconnectedness of life and death. Mr. Spitzer’s musings on eternal recurrence, the blending of opposites, and the fragile boundary between dream and reality deepen the emotional and intellectual impact of the narrative. His lament over forgotten heroes and lost loves, and his sense of being a witness to fading glory, add a layer of melancholic grandeur

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah (C. H. Freemount-Snowden)

  • A formidable, militant suffrage leader whose life was dedicated to battling the conventions of love, society, and gender roles.
  • She is depicted as a warrior, storm king, and mystic figure, feared and revered but ultimately isolated and sorrowful in her final days.
  • Her identity spans multiple cultural representations (Hannah in Boston, Hamid in the East, and the Great Moor) symbolizing a universal warrior figure.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • She journeys in a glass carriage driven by spectral horses and a coachman, making a dreamlike farewell visit to Cousin Hannah.
  • Her journey transcends time and space, emphasizing the fluidity of reality and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer An observer and quasi-legal figure who researches lost ships, heirs, and ancient records.
  • He represents the search for meaning, order, and connection amid chaos and oblivion.
  • He reflects on his own precarious existence and the mysteries surrounding Cousin Hannah.
  • The Unknown Bridegroom A mysterious figure tied to Cousin Hannah by rumor and symbolism.
  • He represents lost love, abandonment, and unfulfilled relationships, adding a layer of personal tragedy to Hannah's public life.

Research: Themes

The Fluidity of Time and Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Time

  • The narrative challenges linear notions of time. Catherine’s journey is described as transcending death and time, visiting Cousin Hannah when both are bed-ridden or dead. Dreams and waking reality blur, reflecting a mystical view of existence where farewell is "a matter of opinion as to the time, the place, the person"

Death and the Afterlife

See: Death and Mortality

  • Death is portrayed as both an end and a transformation or a continuation into another dream or realm. The chapter explores death's mysteries, the dissolution of identity, and the hope or doubt surrounding resurrection and eternal life.

Memory and Legacy

See: Memory and the Past

  • Cousin Hannah’s fading fame and forgotten battles symbolize how history erases even the greatest struggles. Mr. Spitzer’s reflections reveal the tension between public recognition and private sorrow, as well as the difficulty of preserving true legacy.

Love and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection · Love

  • Despite her militant exterior, Cousin Hannah harbors hidden loves and intimacies. The narrative hints at secret lovers, lost opportunities for human connection, and the loneliness of a life lived in opposition to societal norms.

Identity and Transformation

See: Identity and the Self

  • Hannah's multiple identities (Hannah, Hamid, Al Hamid, Great Moor) and her shifting roles reflect the multiplicity of self and the transformative power of myth and legend. Mr. Spitzer’s own uncertainty about his identity parallels this theme.

The Search for Meaning Amid Chaos

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline · The Search for Meaning

  • Mr. Spitzer’s obsession with lost ships and records symbolizes humanity’s quest for order and meaning despite the inherent chaos of existence. The lost ships, passengers, and forgotten histories mirror Cousin Hannah’s own forgotten life.

Glass Carriage and Alabaster Horses

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize the ethereal, dreamlike journey between worlds or states of being. The horses’ heads turning like foam and their journey through clouds evoke a passage beyond the physical.

Mirrors and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • The house with rooms of mirrors and endless reflections represents the multiplicity of perspectives and the elusive nature of truth and self.

White Tent and Desert Imagery

  • Cousin Hannah’s death chamber is likened to a desert tent or pagoda, blending Eastern and Western symbols of the sacred and transient. The desert and snow imagery evoke isolation, purity, and the harshness of the final journey.

Lost Ships and Stars

See: The Sea and Water · Moon and Stars

  • Ships represent journeys, lost hopes, and the passage of souls. Stars symbolize guidance, memory, and the unreachable. Mr. Spitzer’s cataloging of lost ships parallels the attempt to map lost lives and loves.

Snow and Ice

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Metaphors for death, stillness, and the crystallization of time and memory. The persistent snow on Cousin Hannah’s face and body symbolizes the inevitability of death and the fading of life’s passions.

  • Represent unfulfilled love and abandonment, contrasting with Cousin Hannah’s militant independence and loneliness.

Further notes from the text

  • Catherine’s carriage ride through the sleeping house is full of driving directions: turn right, turn left, follow the winding road, watch for the road’s edge and the clouded void. “One could sometimes hear her directing the wind.”
  • Mr. Spitzer keeps lists of lost ships, some vanished long before his birth, some sunk in calm seas for reasons never known. Hannah’s dying is set among these lost vessels.
  • He travels back and forth “between two dying ladies,” Catherine and Hannah, past sundials with their numbers blotted out by fog.
  • Hannah’s past is drawn as a military epic: armies riding into war with silken petticoats for flags, camp followers, ladies who left home and husband to follow her. “Always by indirection, she had broken the hearts of many men.”
  • The town gossips about an abandoned bridegroom from Hannah’s past: some say he died early of grief clutching withered flowers, others that he lived to a great age and never married.
  • Finding her wrapped in a white sheet, Mr. Spitzer first thinks he has come too late and is in her tomb, then remembers that in the East sleepers cover their faces. He decides he must behave as if he has crossed a far frontier.
  • He sees himself as the blind lighthouse keeper, the deaf bell-ringer, the star that does not see its own light, the gatekeeper who does not know which gates he keeps.

Research: Resources

  • Mr. Spitzer complains of being “victimized by routine itself” and “valued his dignity perhaps more than his life.” He is the old, traditional, for appearances sake symbol. This also paralyzes him because he can do nothing. He’s stuck as all conservative thinking leads to is the center must hold, the line must not be crossed. These phrases portray Mr. Spitzer as a deeply complex figure burdened by the weight of his responsibilities and the shadow of his brother, struggling with the constraints of his life and the decay of his own identity. His routine existence and his concern for dignity underscore the novel's themes of mortality, identity, and the tension between appearance and reality.
  • Nietzsche calls it the “moment”. There is an eternal path ahead of us and behind us and what we have is this moment. He wrote about it in Thus Spoke Zarathustra. If one had to live this life over again for all eternity with all its ups and downs, pains and pleasures, would it be tolerable? Would one still choose life, to live? It is a thought experiment for self-reflection and a test of how life affirming a person really is. Nietzsche had the idea of “amor fati” (love of fate). One would come to love one’s fate, the life that one has led. A willingness to accept all aspects of one’s life. The Ubermensch is Nietzsche’s concept of a higher type of human or humanity that is connected to eternal recurrence. A person is capable of loving their life, even in its entirety, is more likely to reach this state. Nietzsche also believed that eternal recurrence would force us to confront the meaninglessness of conventional morality and encourage us to create our own values. (i.e. Do what you will, harm none.) By contemplating eternal recurrence, Nietzsche hoped to spark an interest in personal values which would lead to a more authentic and fulfilling life. The chapter presents the “moment” as an eternal path stretching both ahead and behind us, with the present moment being the only certainty and the profound locus of all experience, mystery, and transformation.

Dreams are often considered symbolic reflections of our subconscious thoughts, emotions, and experiences. Dreams could be a mirror of our waking life where concepts, themes, and memories are explored in a different way. It explores life as a dream by philosophically questioning the nature of reality, identity, and mortality, using spiritual metaphors and emphasizing the fluid, elusive qualities of existence.   • There are different views on immortality and what that looks like. Many beliefs and religions focus on the individual’s soul or spirit after death. Non-personal immortality is where philosophers and thinkers believe there may be a collective consciousness with or without an individual component. Symbolic immortality is where immortality lies in one’s legacy, impact, and memory is what is remembered after death. This forms a sort of immortality through history. Chapter 47

Summary

Mr. Spitzer remembers Hannah's last words about the mountains moving, and lays her skirt over her body. He wonders whether her love was that skirt, covering her wound. He reflects on what he owes his twin, on materialism and spirit, on everything in the world seeming conscious, and on the rejected possibility, the life that was never lived. He decides it is better that lost things sink whole than drift scattered.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Roses and Flowers · Silence and Deafness · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Plato and Platonism · Schopenhauer · Spinoza · Wittgenstein

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Judaism · Shakespeare · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Mr. Spitzer reflects that Cousin Hannah, like himself, "had deferred her life to the next life" and that her death blurs the boundary between life and afterlife. He questions whether their love and existence end or begin anew, pondering the symbolism of reveille or taps in bugle calls. This passage underscores the theme of death as a transition rather than an end, and the ambiguity surrounding the afterlife and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s relationship with his twin brother is a recurring motif. He muses on owing much to his brother, both financially and spiritually, and imagines their mutual presence across the divide of death, forming a “Welcoming Committee of One” on the other side. This reflects the intertwining of identity, memory, and fate, and how death and life are shared continuums rather than isolated events.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a pervasive sense of death as a profound mystery, “this shrouded mystery, it seemed to him, this veil of gossamer which none should lift,” emphasizing the inscrutability of death and the impossibility of fully comprehending it. Mr. Spitzer’s uncertainty about whether the suffrage captain was the bride or bridegroom, or had passed beyond recognition, highlights death’s ambiguity and impenetrability.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates the interdependence of love and death, asserting “Death was ever this dying love,” and that transience is the essence of beauty and love. The mourner, like Mr. Spitzer himself, exists only to mourn, suggesting that love outlives life but is always shadowed by mortality. This passage poignantly links grief, memory, and the human condition.
  • Mr. Spitzer is troubled by the limits of memory and identity. He questions whether he can truly know himself or others, acknowledging his own forgetfulness and the “factor missing” in all attempts to capture reality or the self. This theme emphasizes the fragility and partiality of human understanding.
  • Music recurs as a metaphor for existence. Mr. Spitzer imagines “music written never to be played,” encompassing all sounds, silences, and lost notes, symbolizing life’s incompleteness and the ineffable nature of experience. Music embodies the complexity, beauty, and loss inherent in life and death.
  • A striking symbolic image is the suffrage captain’s skirt, which Mr. Spitzer lays over her body. He speculates that "perhaps her love was her skirt hiding her great wound, her disappointment, her bleeding heart." The skirt or veil represents both concealment and protection, underscoring the theme of hidden truths and the mysteries of love and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer meditates on marriage as a metaphor for union, often equated with death or the end of possibility. He contrasts his own fear of commitment with his brother’s more reckless embrace of chance, reflecting on the paradox that marriage might herald death or vice versa, and the loneliness of the single and the unmarried in life and beyond.
  • The chapter closes on the image of Cousin Hannah as a wanderer, “crying at many gates... forever crying for the image of her love who had gone before her into the darkness.” This suggests that death does not end longing or quest; the dead carry “unfinished business” and infinite frustration, wandering through liminal spaces between life and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s fear of change is a subtle but important passage. He fears the transformation that death brings, of beauty fading or returning briefly before complete dissolution, reflecting human anxiety about impermanence and loss.
  • Lastly, there is the image of Mr. Spitzer as a keeper of old papers, lawsuits, and memories symbolizing human attempts to impose order and meaning on life and death, even as all eventually sink beneath the waves. This suggests the futility yet dignity of human effort in the face of mortality and oblivion.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A meditative figure, possibly a twin or double, who embodies contemplation, loss, and the attempt to reconcile opposites (life/death, love/loss).
  • His identity is fluid, reflecting confusion and multiplicity; he is both mourner and wanderer, seeker and lost soul.

Also listed as: Mr. Spitzer’s Brother (Joachim)

  • A contrast to Mr. Spitzer, more impulsive and superstitious, who had a different view of love and death.
  • His death catalyzed Mr. Spitzer’s deep reflections and mourning.

The Old Suffrage Captain (Cousin Hannah)

  • A symbolic figure representing a lost love, death, and unresolved mystery.
  • Her death and legacy inspire Mr. Spitzer’s reflections on love, mortality, and memory.
  • Her “skirt” symbolizes her love, her wound, her identity veiled and hidden.

Research: Themes

Love and Death as Intertwined Realities

See: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Love

  • Love is portrayed as transitory and dying, yet death is equated with a dark lover who embraces and consumes the beloved.
  • The idea that death is not an end but a transformation or continuation, possibly into another life or state.

Memory, Identity, and Loss

See: Memory and the Past · Identity and the Self · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with memory and identity, feeling lost between two worlds, unable to anchor himself or find certainty.
  • The elusive nature of memory and the impossibility of fully capturing or commemorating a lost love.

The Transient and Illusory Nature of Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Images and forms blend into one another (fishes into flowers, walls into sands) highlighting the fluidity and impermanence of existence.
  • The world is described as illusory, clothed by dreams and veils, with reality fragmented and difficult to grasp fully.

The Passage Between Life and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates whether there is a boundary between life and death or if the two overlap or are one.
  • The metaphor of voyaging between two shores or worlds both ephemeral and non-existent which emphasizes ambiguity and liminality.

The Role of Music and Silence

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Music is a metaphor for life and memory, incomplete and elusive, containing unplayed notes and unuttered words.
  • Silence and the “music of the dead” symbolize absence, loss, and the unspeakable aspects of death and grief.

The Symbolism of Nature and Celestial Imagery

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Frequent references to mountains, waves, stars, moons, clouds, snow, and sea creatures evoke the vastness and mystery of existence (throughout).
  • These images underscore the themes of impermanence, transformation, and the cosmic scale of human experience.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Interplay of Memory and Forgetting

  • Mr. Spitzer is caught in a tension between remembering and forgetting, with memory fragmented and unreliable.

Death as a Process, Not an Event

  • Death is portrayed less as a definitive end and more as a transformation, continuous with life and love.

The Ambiguity of Identity and Time

See: Clocks and Watches

  • Mr. Spitzer’s reflections reveal confusion about who he is, when he is, and how identity persists or dissolves across time and death.

Symbolism of Clothing and Veils

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • The recurring motif of skirts, shrouds, and veils points to concealment, mystery, and the social/cultural framing of death and identity.

The Role of Nature and the Cosmos
