Research: Resources

  • Another of philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein contributions was silence. “Whereof one cannot speak, thereof one must be silent.” Language has logical limits, and when we try to use it to express things that are beyond these limits (like metaphysical or ethical truths), we should be silent. Silence for him was a space for potential meaning and understanding, a recognition of the limits of language, and a way of acknowledging what lies beyond the grasp of words. Wittgenstein's statement in this chapter is a thematic anchor underscoring the novel's exploration of the ineffable aspects of human existence. It implies a humility before the mysteries that lie beyond speech and reason, advocating silence as a form of respect or acknowledgment when words fail. This emphasis on silence and the limits of language permeates the novel’s meditations on death, reality, and the spiritual unknown.
  • “no distinction between the living and the dead, the past and the present, the lover and the loved.” seems to mirror mystical interpretations from Sufism and Christian Theology and signifies the ultimate unity and interconnectedness of love, the person experiencing love, and the object of that love. In Sufism, the phrase highlights the journey of the soul towards union with the divine. The lover seeks to merge with the Beloved and in that ultimate union the distinction between the two dissolves. In Christian Theology the Father can be seen as the Lover, the Son as the Beloved, and the Holy Spirit as the love that binds them. In philosophy the phrase emphasizes the interconnectedness of all things and the illusion of separation. This reflects the novel’s broader meditation on the illusory nature of individuality and the interconnectedness of all beings, suggesting that what we perceive as separate states or identities are part of a single, fluid existence.
  • “good-night, sweet prince” - Hamlet by Shakespeare. It signifies a final, loving farewell to a cherished figure who has endured great trials and is now moving beyond mortal existence. It reflects themes of mortality, transition, and the enduring nature of love even beyond death. This farewell is both personal and universal, blending sorrow with a quiet hope for peace in the beyond.
  • “Good-night, my lady” may refer to a folk song from 1867 by Edwin Pearce Christy. It is a reverent and intimate goodbye marking the end of an earthly presence and symbolizing the transition to whatever lies beyond, embodying both sorrow and hope.
  • “God rest ye merry gentlemen” - The song dates back to the 15th century and its historic meaning is “may God grant you peace and happiness” or “God keep you mighty, gentlemen” It appears in two Shakespeare plays and Charles Dickens’s, A Christmas Carol. It symbolizes a blending of mourning and celebration, highlighting the tension between mortality and the desire for comfort or joy beyond death. It underscores the novel’s theme that life and death are inseparable and intertwined, and that even in the face of death, there may be a call to continue the “dance” of existence, however enigmatic or elusive that may be.
  • Peron and Joachim as materialism and immaterialism. In philosophy, materialism says that everything that exists is fundamentally physical, composed of matter and energy. All phenomena, including consciousness, are ultimately reducible to physical processes. They point to the success of science in explaining the physical world and that consciousness can be explained by brain activity. Physicalism is similar in that everything can be explained by physics. Immaterialism believes there is an existence of entities or properties that are not physical, such as minds, consciousness, or spiritual realms. Non-physical entities or properties exist alongside or instead of the material world. Idealists believe that only minds and their perceptions are real, while the material world is a construction of the mind. Peron symbolizes the external, material world with its pleasures, follies, and impermanence, while Joachim represents the internal, immaterial realm of thought, memory, and spiritual seeking. Their contrast embodies the novel’s exploration of human existence as oscillating between these poles, neither fully attainable nor entirely separable, but always entwined in the complex dance of life and death.
  • “This tendency of an image to repeat an image, perhaps with variations, was something to be considered, weighed, taken into account.” It refers to the idea that images, memories, or experiences tend to recur in life or in the mind, not always exactly the same but often with subtle differences or variations. This repetition suggests that what we perceive or remember is not a one-time event but part of a continuing pattern or cycle that reappears over time. The variations in repeated images imply that while the core essence may be the same, our perception or the circumstances around it might change slightly, affecting how the image or memory manifests. The character’s reflection here invites the reader to consider that life, memory, and identity are not static but fluid and evolving, shaped by recurring motifs and experiences that are never identical yet connected. This idea ties into the novel’s broader themes of illusion, memory, and the elusive nature of reality, where nothing is fixed and the past and present intermingle.
  • “Among all things possible, there was the rejected possibility.” It suggests a profound philosophical reflection on existence and choice. It means that within the vast range of possible outcomes or realities, there exists at least one possibility that is consciously or unconsciously excluded or denied. This "rejected possibility" embodies the idea that not everything that could happen or be is accepted or realized; some potentialities remain unchosen or unacknowledged. If one were to eliminate all mistakes or errors from life, one might also lose the essential "seed of truth" those mistakes contain. Thus, the rejected possibility is not merely an absence but a meaningful part of the whole: the unactualized potential that shapes reality and experience. It points to the complexity and ambiguity of life, where certainty is elusive, and truth includes its negations and contradictions.
  • extraordinary apostrophe is a figure of speech where a speaker or writer directly addresses someone or something that is not present or cannot respond.
  • “Simultaneities” is the concept of simultaneity, or events happening at the same time, it is not absolute, particularly when considering events at different locations. It encapsulates a key thematic concern in the novel: the dissolution of clear boundaries between states of being and the coexistence of multiple temporal and existential planes, contributing to the novel's exploration of illusion, memory, and the nature of reality.
  • “there was no Savior upon these waters” - Matthew 14:22-33 This phrase carries thematic weight across the novel, which often explores the fragility of life, the absence or ambiguity of divine aid, and the painful solitude of human suffering amid forces beyond control. It underscores the stark reality that sometimes there is no rescue, no reprieve, no saving grace, only the merciless, indifferent "waters" that engulf all.
  • “I am the Ethiope” may refer to A Midsummer Night’s Dream by Shakespeare. The phrase is embedded in a passage describing various mystical and spectral figures, blending historical, mythical, and symbolic references. It reflects the theme of multiplicity and transformation of self, the blending of identities across time and space, and the difficulty of pinpointing a single, fixed identity or reality. The declaration “I am the Ethiope” symbolizes one aspect of this fluid, shifting self: an identity that is part of a broader cosmic and spiritual transformation, often with connotations of being an outsider or other.
  • “Should it include the road not taken or the road taken?” The Road Not Taken by Robert Frost. This line invites reflection on how we understand our lives and legacies: Do we honor only the choices we make, or do we also acknowledge the possibilities we forgo? And what bearing does this have on memory, identity, and the way we make sense of our existence? It exemplifies the novel's philosophical and often ambiguous approach to life, death, and meaning.
  • “wedded before one is bedded” historical wedding traditions had a bedding ceremony that was practiced where newlyweds were publicly accompanied to their marital bed by wedding guests. It refers to the traditional or ideal sequence in marriage where the formal union (wedding) takes place before the couple begins their sexual life together (being bedded). It highlights a customary expectation that marriage is a prerequisite to sexual relations. However, this phrase is used in a reflective and somewhat ironic context in the novel, suggesting that for some characters or situations, this order might be reversed or disrupted. It points to complexities and ambiguities in relationships and life, where social or formal conventions do not always align with lived realities.
  • “he was agonized by attributing consciousness to everything” - may refer to panpsychism which suggests that a mind, or mind-like aspect, is a fundamental and widespread characteristic of reality. It says that the subjective experience associated with human consciousness exists, in some form, throughout the universe, even in its most basic elements. It has its roots in ancient Greek philosophy with Thales and Plato and later with Spinoza, Leibniz, and Schopenhauer. It reflects Mr. Spitzer's profound and troubling awareness of the pervasive presence of consciousness or life-like qualities in all things around him. This means that Mr. Spitzer experiences a kind of existential distress or mental anguish because he perceives consciousness, intention, or awareness not just in people but extending to inanimate objects, natural phenomena, and abstract concepts. He senses life, emotion, or meaning in things that are traditionally considered lifeless, such as clouds, stars, waves, or even shadows and this blurs the line between what is truly alive and what is not. This overwhelming and almost mystical perception causes him suffering because it challenges ordinary reality and makes his own sense of self and understanding of the world unstable and confusing. This agonizing attribution is part of Mr. Spitzer's broader struggle with reality, illusion, memory, and identity. It underlines his sensitivity to the ambiguities and mysteries of existence, where the boundaries between life and death, the living and the non-living, and reality and dream are not distinct. His mind is burdened by this expansive and unsettling sense of interconnectedness and animation of all things, which he cannot easily reconcile or control. The phrase captures Mr. Spitzer's deep philosophical and emotional turmoil as he contemplates a universe filled with consciousness beyond human life, contributing to the novel’s themes of illusion, perception, and the elusive nature of reality.
  • “corpo santo” (holy body) is an archaic term referring to St. Elmo’s fire, a weather phenomenon where luminous plasma is created by a corona discharge from pointed objects during electrical storms. St. Erasmus (St. Elmo) is the patron saint of sailors. Sailors sometimes viewed it as a good omen. It carries the connotation of a body that is holy or consecrated, embodying the intersection of human mortality and divine mystery, a key motif in the novel’s meditation on the nature of being and transcendence.
  • “for more than life or death he feared change, change of any kind.” This refers to the character Mr. Spitzer’s deep and profound fear of change itself, beyond even his fear of life or death. This indicates that Mr. Spitzer is so unsettled and troubled by the instability and unpredictability that change brings, that it causes him greater anxiety than the ultimate certainties of life and death. Change here represents not just physical or external alterations but also internal transformations: of identity, perception, and existence. Mr. Spitzer is caught in a state of flux and ambiguity, struggling with his shifting self, memory, and reality. His life is marked by uncertainty, fragmentation, and a blurred distinction between past, present, and future, as well as between life and death. Because of this, change threatens his fragile sense of self and his attempts to find order and meaning. This fear of change is tied to his larger existential condition: he is a man already profoundly altered by the death of his brother and by his own uncertain identity, living "between two worlds," never fully anchored in either. For him, change threatens to dissolve what little stability or continuity he has, making it more terrifying than even death itself. The phrase captures Mr. Spitzer's core existential crisis: he fears the loss of self and the unknown transformations that might erase or radically alter his identity, which is a deeper fear than the finality of death.
  • “should one be held accountable for one’s entire life or for one moment of unforeseen and unforeseeable transmutation, perhaps a change taking place beyond all consciousness or memory or desire?” It reflects a profound philosophical meditation on personal responsibility and identity. This question raises the issue of whether a person should be judged or held responsible for all their actions and choices throughout life, or whether there might be some singular, transformative moment that escapes conscious control or awareness. This moment could represent a radical change in one's nature or being that occurs beyond the reach of conscious thought, memory, or even desire. Through this reflection, it suggests that human identity and moral accountability are complex and possibly unstable. There may be pivotal experiences or changes that redefine a person in ways they neither foresee nor fully comprehend themselves. Hence, it questions the fairness or possibility of holding someone accountable for such a moment, as it may be beyond their conscious control. This theme ties into the novel’s broader exploration of illusion, memory, identity, and the blurred boundaries between life and death, consciousness and unconsciousness. The characters grapple with the elusive nature of reality and selfhood, where life is seen as a series of fragmented, shifting images and experiences, and where the individual self may itself be an "illusion" or subject to sudden, profound change. This passage invites readers to consider the mystery of human change and the limits of judgment, emphasizing the ambiguity and complexity of personal transformation within the novel’s dreamlike, introspective narrative.
  • “Death was the Orient whether it was heaven or earth” may refer to Murder on the Orient Express where Agatha Christie by putting an act of vigilantism at the heart of the mystery story reverses the roles of criminal and victim. This phrase suggests that death is like the Orient in the sense that it can be perceived as both a kind of heaven and a kind of earth or a place beyond ordinary understanding, where familiar dualities merge or dissolve. Death is portrayed as a realm that transcends the usual boundaries between life and afterlife, material and spiritual existence. It is a space that is both real and unreal, tangible and intangible, familiar and utterly unknown. The passage reflects on death as a kind of journey or transition, much like the mystical and often enigmatic idea of the Orient in Western imagination. It is a place where conventional distinctions blur: there is no heaven separate from earth, just as there is no clear division between life and death. The imagery evokes a liminal space where opposites converge, and the soul or spirit moves beyond the limitations of mortal life. It encapsulates the novel's theme of death as a profound, ambiguous, and ineffable state: neither fully this world nor the next, but a complex passage that holds mystery, transformation, and the blurring of boundaries
  • “But time could not tell him the time.” It reflects the profound confusion and disorientation experienced by Mr. Spitzer. Although time as a concept exists, and clocks or calendars mark its passage, to Mr. Spitzer, these markers are unreliable or meaningless. He cannot grasp or "tell" the exact moment or hour in his life because his perception of time is fractured: his memory and consciousness are impaired, and the usual order and progression of time seem disrupted or illusory. This line symbolizes how Mr. Spitzer lives in a state where time has lost its usual significance; it is an abstraction that fails to provide him with certainty or clarity about his existence or experiences. Time is no longer a steady, measurable flow but something ambiguous, elusive, and perhaps even cyclical or fragmented in his reality. It means that although time passes, Mr. Spitzer cannot understand or locate himself within it. The phrase captures his existential uncertainty and the novel’s broader themes of disintegration, memory loss, and the elusive nature of reality and identity.
  • “a great rajah’s jewel” is foreshadowing for a subplot later on in the book with Mr. Spitzer.
  • “He rescued all ladies but one he had imprisoned, leaving her to rot.” Given the novel's themes of complex and often painful relationships between men and women, and the recurring motif of loss, abandonment, and unfulfilled love, this line points to the paradoxical and tragic nature of such relationships. The man may have been a rescuer to many, but in this one critical case, he failed utterly, leaving the woman isolated and doomed.
  • “oh, how he hated these urban changes caused by the population growth” Mr. Spitzer in general is a conservative character wanting to preserve tradition. It reflects Mr. Spitzer’s lament over the transformations in the city and society brought about by increasing population and modernization. This sentiment expresses a nostalgic resistance to the loss of the familiar, orderly world he once knew. The urban changes symbolize not only physical alterations to the cityscape, such as new buildings replacing old ones, changes in neighborhoods, or the disappearance of landmarks but also deeper social and cultural shifts that disrupt established ways of life, traditions, and personal identities. Mr. Spitzer, who is described as a man deeply attached to order, precision, and the continuity of the past, finds these rapid and sometimes chaotic changes troubling. They represent a break from the stability and clarity he had valued, contributing to his sense of disorientation and loss. His dislike is tied to both the physical environment and the social fabric, as population growth often brings about overcrowding, new social dynamics, and a fading of old communities and familiar faces. This feeling is part of the larger themes in the novel dealing with change, memory, loss, and the struggle to hold on to identity amidst a shifting world. Mr. Spitzer’s lament is not just about city planning but about the inevitability of change and the personal and collective dislocation it causes. The phrase captures Mr. Spitzer’s sorrow and frustration at a world in flux, a world moving away from the ordered past he had known toward an uncertain and often alien present.
  • “Good-night and good-morning—simply to imply that she would live beyond the night enfolding her as if it were the night of love which makes no distinction between the living and the dead, the past and the present, the lover and the loved.” There is an Arabic phrase for the “Good-night and good-morning.” “The lover and the loved” may refer to Rumi or Sufism that also have similar sayings. The phrase emphasizes an understanding of existence in which love creates a unity that transcends time and mortality. It suggests that the separation we perceive (between life and death, or between selves in relationship) is ultimately illusory within this “night of love.” The continuity of love persists beyond physical life, blurring the lines that normally divide existence. This interpretation aligns with the novel’s larger thematic exploration of blurred realities, the coexistence of dream and wakefulness, and the merging of opposites like life and death, as seen in the characters’ experiences and reflections throughout the novel.
  • Moses is an important prophet in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, Druze faith, Baha’i faith and other Abrahamic religions. He is significant as a liminal figure embodying the journey through mortality and the blurred boundaries between life and death, guiding both the living and the reader through the novel’s complex interplay of reality, memory, and dream.
  • “lived, moved, gathered weight…” - Acts 17:28 It signifies the ongoing process of existence that is simultaneously rich and fragile, substantive and elusive, embodying the novel’s themes of transformation, mortality, and the elusive nature of reality.

This "dead self" that "heard no heartbeat" suggests a profound emptiness or loss inside her, where life has failed to take hold or continue. Chapter 52

Summary

Going through Hannah's estate, Mr. Spitzer opens trunk after trunk of wedding gowns, with no bride's slippers among them. He finds letters in languages he cannot read, her lost skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots, and evidence that she lived as Hannah in Boston and as Hamid in the East. Her book lies open to the tale of Tristram and Iseult. He resolves to keep her secret. He closes her eyes and weights them with two pennies, one for the sun and one for the moon.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Concepts present

Philosophy: Existentialism · Heraclitus and Flux · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Spiritualism and the Occult · Taoism and Zhuangzi

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Greek Mythology · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Civil War · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a complex metaphorical description of mystery, time, and identity. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the suffragette’s lost love and her elusive, shadowy identity, "No name, no face told him her identity in cloud fusions as none told him who he was now". This sets the tone of searching for meaning in a life shrouded in ambiguity.
  • Mr. Spitzer sees himself as connected to her through shared duplicity and duality, unable to condemn her without condemning himself.   • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a figure who chased a lost love, symbolized by the lost skirt on a mountain peak, a metaphor for incomplete or thwarted love: "the old suffragette had returned without her love who had gone to retrieve her skirt, surely no dog would ever find".   • Mr. Spitzer’s research reveals her as a woman of many paradoxes and adventures: a mountain climber, balloonist, flyer, traveler through deserts and Holy Lands, who lived beyond time and space: "She had gone to Holy Lands as to Death’s seraglio guarded by eunuchs black and white where were locked so many beautiful girls with their faces veiled".   • The chapter meditates on the nature of time, memory, and existence.   • Mr. Spitzer’s physical search through her estate, opening trunks, examining keys, finding wedding gowns, veils, and other artifacts, symbolizes an attempt to unlock the mysteries of her life and, metaphorically, the mysteries of love and existence itself.   • Mr. Spitzer questions not only her identity but his own, reflecting on the blurred lines between reality and illusion, living and dead: "He questioned who he was as he questioned who she was, and doubtless this would always be the case".   • The suffragette is likened to a bride who has hidden away or been lost, a figure of unfulfilled destiny and love: Perhaps "she had abandoned the bridegroom at the church door". This symbolizes the elusiveness of love and the human condition of searching for something lost or unattainable.
  • There is a recurring tension between what is real and unreal, the dream and reality, memory and oblivion.   • The chapter closes with a meditation on the limits of language and knowledge: "He was not certain of the book’s title now when all writing had faded ... no language contained truth, for the truth was that which could not be expressed". This encapsulates the chapter’s theme of the ineffability of the greatest mysteries of life and love.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A reflective, almost spectral figure who is both narrator and investigator. He embodies duality and duplicity, often questioning his own identity and existence, blurring lines between life and death, reality and dream. His role is to manage and close the estate of the old suffragette, but his journey is deeply philosophical and metaphysical.

The Old Suffragette

  • A mysterious woman shrouded in symbolism; she is a traveler, a rebel, and a figure of lost love and elusive identity. Known for her suffrage activism, she is also depicted as a wanderer through physical and metaphysical realms of mountains, deserts, and clouds. She carries the paradox of being both bride and bridegroom, representing the complex intersections of gender, love, and death.

Research: Themes

  • Mystery and Identity The chapter is permeated with questions of identity, both Mr. Spitzer’s and the suffragette’s. Mr. Spitzer struggles to know who he is or whether he is a ghostly twin. The suffragette’s identity remains veiled, indicated by symbols like veils, masks, and cloud fusions.
  • Love and Loss Central to the narrative is the motif of lost love, symbolized by the suffragette’s lost skirt and her search for love that may never be found or may be forever elusive. Love is portrayed as inseparable from death, an eternal quest that transcends time.
  • Life, Death, and the Afterlife The chapter explores the boundaries between life and death, suggesting that death may multiply uncertainties and dissolve distinctions, such as gender roles and personal identities. Death is not an end but a continuation or transformation, with echoes of the past and shadows of lost loves lingering.
  • Time and Timelessness Time is fluid and ambiguous; events are reported out of chronological order, and the notion of “when” is elusive. The suffragette’s life and death exist in a timeless realm where beginnings and ends blur.
  • The External vs. Internal Worlds The suffragette’s adventures traverse both external landscapes (mountains, deserts, clouds) and internal, psychological realms. Reality and dream intertwine, with the external world mirroring internal emotional and spiritual states.
  • The Search and the Unattainable Mr. Spitzer’s search through the suffragette’s estate, her memories, and her secrets is a metaphor for the human quest for meaning, often futile and always incomplete. The imagery of keys, trunks, and locked doors symbolizes mysteries that cannot be fully unlocked.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Clouds and Snow Represent mystery, concealment, and transformation. They are often described as moving, shifting, and obscuring identity and reality.
  • Skirts and Veils The suffragette’s lost skirt embroidered with forget-me-nots symbolizes lost love and identity. Veils and skirts also signify the blurred boundaries of gender and self.
  • Keys, Locks, and Trunks These represent the attempt to unlock secrets, memories, and truths. Mr. Spitzer’s fumbling with keys and trunks underscores the impossibility of fully understanding or revealing the suffragette's life.
  • Stars, Moons, and Celestial Bodies Used to depict guidance, mystery, the unreachable, and the eternal. The moon, often mirrored or sunken, symbolizes reflection and illusion.
  • Birds and Butterflies Symbols of transformation, fleeting beauty, and the soul’s journey. The butterfly sailing out of the ear (a door) suggests escape or transcendence.
  • Music and Silence Music represents life’s rhythm, emotion, and unspoken realities; silence and muteness indicate death, absence, or the ineffable.

  • Mr. Spitzer wonders if doubt should move mountains “which faith had not moved." This is a direct inversion of the common saying that faith can move mountains. This highlights a core philosophical tension between believing in something despite a lack of evidence (faith) and questioning everything (doubt). - Matthew 17:20. The image of the suffragette searching for a lost skirt, leading to the death of her lover, suggests the absurdity of human pursuits. The pursuit of something seemingly trivial (the skirt) leads to tragic consequences, mirroring the existentialist idea that life is inherently meaningless, and humans create their own meaning through their actions. The description of the skirt as "white lace gleaming through snow and its little flowers which were like the memories of little loves" blurs the lines between reality and memory. It suggests that our perceptions of reality are shaped by our past experiences and emotions, leading to a subjective and potentially distorted understanding of the world. The mention of the suffragette crying "Long live woman! Vive la femme! Viva la donna!" in many languages, "perhaps even in Sanskrit which was the language written upon a silent snowflake," touches on the philosophy of language. It suggests that language can be a powerful tool for expressing universal concepts (like the importance of women) but that there are also limits to what language can convey. There are "secret languages never to be translated into words," implying that some truths are beyond the reach of verbal expression. The reference to, "the suffragette who had lost her apostle" could also be referencing the loss of an ideal form. Platonism is the belief that everything we see is a shadow or "lesser" version of a perfect form. The loss of her apostle, who could be a student or follower, is also the loss of what the suffragette sees as a perfect version of herself. The next paragraph emphasizes the individual's choice and action in the face of an indifferent or absurd universe. The suffragette's decision to dress as a man can be seen as an assertion of her freedom and rejection of societal norms. The fantastical images of footmen and golden stairways highlight the human tendency to create meaning and beauty in a world that may ultimately be meaningless. The contrast between Cousin Hannah's practical clothing and the elaborate attire of other climbers could be interpreted as a reflection of the philosophical debate between idealism and materialism. The suffragette's focus on functionality suggests a more materialistic worldview, while the other climbers' emphasis on appearance could be seen as representing idealism. The repeated blurring of the lines between mountains and clouds, and the shifting perceptions of the moon, raise questions about the nature of reality and the limitations of human perception. The statement, "the moon had floated most amazingly distending worlds," suggests that reality is not fixed but is shaped by our individual perspectives. The image of the footman cutting a golden stairway from a frozen lake to the mountains of the moon could be an allusion to Plato's Allegory of the Cave. The stairway could represent the philosopher's ascent from the darkness of the cave (the material world) to the light of the sun (the realm of Forms). The mountains of the moon could symbolize a higher realm of knowledge and understanding. The paragraph's emphasis on nature, individual experience, and the search for spiritual meaning aligns with the themes of Transcendentalism. The suffragette's mountain climbing could be seen as a metaphor for the individual's journey to transcend the limitations of the material world and connect with a higher power or truth. The mention of "horizons unknown as the stars floated" could also be interpreted in a nihilistic way, suggesting that there are no ultimate goals or destinations and that all human endeavors are ultimately meaningless. At first it's a whimsical and imaginative description of mountain climbing, then, beneath the surface, it explores fundamental philosophical questions about freedom, reality, perception, and the meaning of life which invites the reader to think about their own philosophical reflections.

  • Coverture was a legal doctrine in common law systems where a married woman's legal existence was subsumed into that of her husband's, essentially making her a legal non-entity. Coverture was gradually weakened and eventually eliminated through legislation and legal reforms in the United States.   • The 1850s and 1860s in the US were a period of intense national division and conflict, culminating in the Civil War. The decade of the 1850s saw escalating tensions surrounding slavery, with political compromises failing to resolve the issue and the nation moving closer to the brink of war. The Civil War itself, fought from 1861 to 1865, resulted in the end of slavery and Northern victory, but at a tremendous cost in human lives and national unity. Compromise of 1850 attempted to address the issue of slavery in newly acquired territories, but ultimately failed to quell the growing divide. Major battles like Gettysburg and Vicksburg marked turning points in the war. Emancipation Proclamation (1863) declared enslaved people in Confederate-held territory to be free. New York City draft riots (1863) discontent with the draft laws during the Civil War led to violent protests. The 13th Amendment (1865) officially abolished slavery in the United States.   • The period from 1850 to 1860 in American news was dominated by the escalating tensions over slavery and the eventual outbreak of the Civil War. The rise of the penny press and the increasing use of correspondents, especially during the war, marked significant developments in the news industry. The debate over slavery intensified, with the Compromise of 1850, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, and the Dred Scott decision significantly impacting the political landscape and fueling sectionalism. Newspapers became powerful tools for disseminating views on these issues, often aligning themselves with specific political parties. The penny press, exemplified by newspapers like the New York Herald, gained popularity by offering affordable, mass-circulation papers with a focus on local news, crime stories, and human interest pieces. This shift in business model and content helped make newspapers a mass medium. While colonial newspapers were typically one-person operations, the 1850s saw a growth in the number of journalists and correspondents, particularly with the outbreak of the Civil War. The war itself became a major news event, with newspapers deploying reporters to cover battles and casualty lists. These correspondents, including some who were soldiers themselves, provided eyewitness accounts of the war, often facing censorship and logistical challenges. Newspapers played a role in shaping public opinion on social issues, including the abolitionist movement. For example, Harriet Beecher Stowe's "Uncle Tom's Cabin", serialized in a newspaper, significantly influenced public perception of slavery. Western and Southern newspapers, often personal enterprises, emphasized local news, particularly about crops, land, and Native American relations. The Wide Awakes political organization, which arose in the late 1850s, relied heavily on newspapers to spread their message and organize supporters, demonstrating the power of the press in social and political mobilization. Legendary editors like Horace Greeley and James Gordon Bennett rose to prominence, shaping the landscape of American journalism.

The paragraph questions whether our senses provide a complete picture of reality. The idea that "Even the closed door was not closed, for should death be better known than love? The image of the butterfly escaping through the ear, "even when it was a door of the silence," implies that even in the absence of sound, there are avenues for experience or existence. The description of Mr. Spitzer as a night watchman in the "starry universe" raises questions about the nature of reality. Is he a real figure, or is he merely a figment of someone's imagination? His light awakening "other sleepers, those he never knew" suggests the interconnectedness of existence, even if we are unaware of it. The suggestion that he perhaps "had intended to lock and not to unlock" introduces the possibility that his actions may have unintended consequences, highlighting the limits of human control and the role of chance. The final lines emphasize Mr. Spitzer's role as the "only mourner among men," suggesting a profound sense of isolation and the burden of grief. His mourning for himself implies a recognition of his own mortality and the inevitability of loss. This connects to existentialist themes of individual responsibility and the search for meaning in a seemingly meaningless world.
  • Mr. Spitzer's meticulous accounting and listing is directly tied to his struggle with his identity, particularly his relationship with his deceased brother. He seeks a perfect balance, a mirrored reflection where everything in his life corresponds to his brother's, suggesting a desire to understand himself through this dualistic lens. The fear of "no differing counterpart" speaks to the existential anxiety of lacking a defined self, relying on another for definition. This resonates with philosophical concepts of identity formation, the "self" versus the "other," and the influence of external relationships on self-perception. Thinkers like Sartre and Simone de Beauvoir explored similar themes in existentialism. Spitzer's obsessive listing and indexing of even the most mundane objects (pearl buttons, rusted nail heads, etc.) reflects a deep-seated need to impose order on a chaotic world. He's trying to find patterns, connections, and a "common denominator" to make sense of existence. This aligns with the philosophical pursuit of metaphysics: trying to understand the fundamental nature of reality. The futility of Spitzer's efforts mirrors the inherent difficulties in finding absolute order or meaning in a world often perceived as absurd or chaotic (a key theme in existentialism and absurdism). The questions about the sail ("Was the sail unwinding the same as the winding sail?") touch on the philosophical problem of identity over time. Does something remain the same if its state changes? This is further complicated by the cyclical nature of the tides and the wagon wheels, implying a sense of eternal return or repetition. This connects to Heraclitus's famous saying, "No man ever steps in the same river twice," emphasizing the constant flux and change in the universe. The paragraph also hints at Nietzsche's concept of eternal recurrence. Spitzer's attempts to capture reality through lists and measurements are ultimately limited. His fear that "all the weight, as he had often complained, was on this weightless star" alludes to the disparity between the tangible and intangible, the concrete and abstract. He can list the physical properties of objects, but he cannot capture their essence or meaning. This is related to epistemology, the study of knowledge and its limitations. The paragraph suggests the impossibility of fully knowing or representing reality, as there will always be something missing or lost in translation. The description of Spitzer's actions creating "division as in division there was creation," suggests that in every act of creation, there is also an act of destruction. This mirrors the belief that every action has an equal and opposite reaction. This is connected to the concept of the "Tao" which states that everything is composed of two opposites, and that without the other, it cannot exist.
  • “She would be found when she was dust and ashes and ruined silks and shrouds split by the blowings of no winds more fierce than the blowings of winds” The passage opens with a description of a body found after death, surrounded by decaying remnants of life. There is an ambiguity regarding the identity of the deceased ("the bride who might almost have been the bridegroom"), which suggests a blurring of traditional roles and identities in death. This reflects a philosophical concept that death transcends or dissolves the constructs of identity and societal norms that define life. The description of "Lost Atlantis which drifted now like a continent or life raft above with birds where no birds had ever set their feet and flowers and cities carried away while man slept and woman loved" suggests that reality is subjective and dreamlike. This alludes to philosophical idealism, which posits that reality is fundamentally mental or consists of ideas rather than material substances. The image of a world carried away "while man slept and woman loved" implies a critique of human consciousness, suggesting that profound changes occur beyond waking awareness. The passage details instances of conception occurring through unconventional means ("born by the ear of the dead," "because the wind blew," "because another woman had shouted at her"). These examples challenge traditional notions of causality and creation, suggesting a universe where events occur through mysterious, non-linear processes. This aligns with philosophies that emphasize the interconnectedness of all things and the potential for events to arise from unexpected sources. The recurring theme of challenging traditional dichotomies, such as life and death, male and female, and reality and illusion, reflects a broader philosophical inclination to question binary oppositions. This is evident in the description of the skull face of the bride who might almost have been the bridegroom. The passage suggests that these oppositions are fluid and that meaning can be found in their blurring. The emphasis on events occurring in the absence of traditional senses ("born by the ear of the dead," "whisper shaking a cloud where there was neither life nor light nor sound") suggests that significant forces operate beyond the realm of human perception. This implies a belief in the power of the unseen, unheard, and unconscious to shape reality.
  • “Perhaps he was like that Spanish don who, when his bride abandoned him to be the bride of Christ” - It evokes the image of a man whose bride leaves him not for another man but for a religious life, specifically to become a nun, symbolically marrying Christ. This metaphor reflects a situation of abandonment and loss, where the expected earthly partnership is replaced by a spiritual or unattainable one. Within the context of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer is deeply engaged in unraveling the mysteries surrounding the old suffragette, whose life and identity are filled with ambiguities, contradictions, and elusive truths. The reference to the Spanish don and his bride underscores themes of loss, unfulfilled love, and the elusive nature of identity and relationships. Just as the don’s bride chooses a spiritual path over a worldly marriage, the suffragette seems to have abandoned traditional roles and attachments, embarking on solitary, mysterious journeys and quests that defy conventional understanding. This simile highlights the emotional and existential solitude Mr. Spitzer perceives, not only of the suffragette but perhaps of himself as well, caught between realities, lost loves, and the search for meaning in a world of illusions and faded dreams. It suggests a profound sense of departure and transformation, where love is redefined, lost, or redirected beyond the earthly realm.
  • It may refer to José Zorrilla's play "Don Juan Tenorio," Don Juan makes a bet that he can conquer more women than Don Luis. Don Luis challenges Don Juan to conquer a woman about to take her vows as a nun, and an engaged woman. This brings us to the Spanish don whose bride became a nun. In the play, Don Juan's target, Doña Inés, is a novice nun whose innocence captivates him and leads him to contemplate redemption.
  • Mr. Spitzer's search through the house and trunks represents a quest for knowledge and understanding of the suffragette's life. The fact that he searches for "he knew not what" suggests that the nature of knowledge itself is uncertain. The "magnetic doors" that open on their own imply that some knowledge is revealed passively, not through active seeking. The idea that there were many differences between the suffragette's last sleep and her first sleep suggests a changing reality, shaped by experience and time. The "tumultuous life" alters the nature of her being. The reference to a "windowless seraglio or cave or darkened tower" relates to the mind as a prison or a space of limited perception. The idea of the "supernumerary love, a wife unknown" introduces the concept of hidden aspects of the self or unconscious desires. The paragraph delves into the nature of love and its mysteries. The "blind god of love" refers to the idea that love is irrational and indiscriminate. The image of the "turban-winder winding fields of consciousness" suggests that love can lead to a loss of individual identity and a merging of consciousnesses. The phrase "in the unwinding there should be no memory and no woman and no man" implies a fading of individual existence and a potential descent into nothingness. This reflects themes of nihilism and existentialism where existence is seen as meaningless and absurd. The individual's fading suggests a loss of self and meaning.
  • The entire scene is dreamlike, blurring the line between reality and illusion. Mr. Spitzer finds himself entangled in wedding gowns, which transform into seas, sails, and shrouds. This reflects a questioning of what is real and what is merely a construct of the mind. The passage suggests that the material world might be less substantial than the dreams and ideas that inhabit it. This aligns with metaphysical idealism, which posits that reality is fundamentally mental or spiritual. Mr. Spitzer's inability to discern whether there is one moon or many mirrored moons, or even no moon at all, highlights the limitations of human knowledge. He is trapped within his own "hypothesis," which he cannot prove. This underscores the theme of uncertainty and the difficulty of attaining objective truth. The census-taker reference is interesting because census-takers are about collecting data to create an idea of a population, Mr. Spitzer fears the census-taker because he fears the idea of ultimate knowledge. The passage touches on existential themes of meaninglessness and the search for purpose. The old maid's rejection of marriage and her call to "divest themselves of excess luggage" can be interpreted as a rejection of societal norms and a pursuit of individual freedom. However, her obsession with wedding gowns suggests an underlying longing for connection and meaning, even in the face of her conscious rejection of it. Mr. Spitzer's role as a "dead man coming to mourn for her" reinforces the sense of existential angst and the confrontation with mortality. The imagery of carousels of brides where there is no bride, and a spiral staircase finding through clouds where constellations sleep, underscores the absurdity of existence. Mr. Spitzer is caught in a world of contradictions and paradoxes, where meaning is elusive and reason fails to provide answers. The reference to a world of mirrored moons and the difficulty in knowing which is real is reminiscent of Plato's Allegory of the Cave. The world we perceive may be a mere reflection of a higher, more authentic reality. The wedding gowns themselves are rich in symbolism. They represent not only marriage but also societal expectations, lost dreams, and the weight of the past. The fact that Mr. Spitzer is "trapped" by them suggests that he is burdened by these forces, unable to break free from the constraints of tradition and memory. Mr. Spitzer likens himself to Charon's ferry boat. Charon is a figure in Greek mythology who carries souls of the newly deceased across the river Styx that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead.
  • Mr. Spitzer's reflections are deeply rooted in skepticism and a sense of the limitations of human knowledge. The paragraph centers around the idea that "no language contained truth, for the truth was that which could not be expressed." This alludes to the philosophical concept of the ineffable or the idea that some experiences or realities are beyond the capacity of language to capture. This is related to mystical traditions and certain schools of philosophy that emphasize intuitive or non-rational forms of knowledge. The "word never written, the name never told" represents a truth that is forever elusive and beyond human grasp. Mr. Spitzer's "unretentive mind" is described as being "like a sieve," unable to hold onto definitive knowledge. This symbolizes the limitations of human memory and the unreliable nature of perception. This skepticism extends to the external world as well as he walks on and on "coming to no end", suggesting the world has no fixed state or endpoint. His experience aligns with skepticism, which questions the possibility of attaining certainty. The image of the suffragette reading a romance about "lovers never mated" (Eloise et Abelard) speaks to the theme of unfulfilled longing and the tragic nature of human relationships. Mr. Spitzer's inability to determine which character she identifies with (Tristram or Yseult) highlights the ambiguity and complexity of human identity and desire. The weighted eyes with pennies, "one in memory of the sun, one in memory of the moon," symbolizes the end of perception, the inability to see or experience the world, and the finality of death. The description of the world as "one level of sheeted silver and gold" suggests a flattened, perhaps illusory, reality. This relates to philosophical ideas about the nature of appearance versus reality, and the possibility that the world we perceive is merely a construct or a shadow of a deeper truth. Mr. Spitzer's reluctance to awaken the dead for fear they might die again connects the idea that it is better to leave things be than to interfere with the natural order of life and death. This connects to philosophical concepts of acceptance and the inevitability of death.

Chapter 70

← Chapter 69 · Home · Chapter 71 →

Summary

In the quiet, Vera tells of Mrs. Hogden, whose name keeps shifting and whom Vera admits she never actually saw. Mrs. Hogden sold her Dutch windmill home and arrived at Catherine's house with birdcages, temple bells, and a letter of employment as arithmetic teacher that Catherine denied writing. Lisa Lunde, Catherine's new companion, suspected her at once. Mrs. Hogden lived for months in the abandoned playroom, playing chess against herself. She finally left her wig on a crab at the water's edge and a blackboard message reading "All a's are b's."

Characters present

Mrs. Hogden · Vera Cartwheel · Catherine Cartwheel · Lisa Lunde

Concepts present

Themes: Decay and Ruin · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Time

Philosophy: Existentialism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • Vera describes the mysterious and unsettling arrival of Mrs. Hogden, a corporeal yet ghostly figure who invades Vera's dreams and memories, contrasting sharply with Miss MacIntosh, the former nursemaid. Mrs. Hogden is portrayed as a confusing and contradictory figure (fat, over-dressed, and intrusive) acting almost like an apparition haunting the household and Vera’s psyche. This passage sets the tone of ambiguity and surrealism, highlighting the blurred lines between reality and dream, presence and absence.
  • Mrs. Hogden arrives unexpectedly, burdened with numerous packages and personal belongings, having sold her Dutch windmill home to take up a position supposedly offered by Vera’s mother. Despite her chaotic appearance and peculiar behavior, she is convinced of her rightful place in the household, promising to teach arithmetic and “reflect my mother’s every mood.” The tension between Mrs. Hogden's assured intrusion and the household's skepticism is introduced here, particularly through Lisa Lunde’s suspicion and Catherine’s disbelief and rejection.
  • A key passage details the growing argument between Mrs. Hogden and Vera’s mother, who denies ever inviting her. Despite this, Mrs. Hogden knows intimate details of Catherine’s life, suggesting a mysterious or imagined connection. Catherine’s refusal to accept Mrs. Hogden, calling her a liar and impostor, contrasts with Mrs. Hogden’s unwavering optimism and strange knowledge. This conflict symbolizes themes of reality versus illusion, sanity versus madness, and the intrusion of unwanted presences into private life.
  • Mrs. Hogden’s life in the playroom (a place full of forgotten objects and memories) is described in detail. She is isolated, eccentric, and increasingly despondent yet strangely content with her condition. Her behavior of talking to herself, playing chess alone, drinking secretly, and dressing and undressing depicts a tragic figure clinging to illusions of importance and social connection. The portrayal evokes themes of aging, mental decline, and the human need for companionship and recognition.
  • As Mrs. Hogden feigns or experiences illness, taking to her uncomfortable bed, Catherine’s revulsion grows. Catherine refuses to tolerate a “rival invalid” and orders her removal through Mr. Spitzer, the lawyer. Mrs. Hogden’s persistence and Catherine’s harshness underscore the breakdown of relationships and the cruelty often directed at the vulnerable or unwanted. This passage reflects the themes of illness, dependency, and social rejection.
  • Eventually, Mrs. Hogden is expelled from the house with a generous financial settlement arranged by Mr. Spitzer. The aftermath reveals the house’s return to emptiness, the closure of the playroom, and the lingering mystery of Mrs. Hogden’s identity and presence. Vera contemplates Mrs. Hogden’s role as both a real and dreamlike figure, a substitute for lost connections, and a symbol of the fragile boundary between memory and imagination.
  • The chapter closes with the image of the little three-legged blackboard left behind by Mrs. Hogden, inscribed with a cryptic message in red chalk: “All a’s are b’s, it read—all b’s are c’s—and therefore, dear heart, all a’s are c’s. You know me.” The message itself, though logically sound in its first part, becomes ambiguous with the personal address. It's a statement of universal truth followed by a claim of personal recognition, forcing a re-evaluation of what "knowing" entails in a world where appearances are constantly deceiving. The sentence uses a foundational logical principle only to immediately subvert it with a personal claim of recognition, deeply resonating with the novel's central themes of illusion, identity, and the elusive nature of truth and self-knowledge.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mrs. Hogden/Logden/Fogden/Dogden/Bogden

  • Fat, corpulent, with bleached, plastered curls.
  • Wears multiple coats stacked over each other, eccentric hats, and carries a variety of odd objects (empty birdcage, packages, temple bells).
  • Her face is blandly expressionless except for an aggressive chin and abnormally large, unfocused eyes.
  • Smells of over-ripe apples and is associated with decay and disorder.
  • Wears a water-stained yellow satin nightgown, black fur slippers, and a frilled white night-cap with an aggressive chin bow.
  • Optimistic despite her apparent destitution and displacement.
  • Talks to herself and answers her own questions, which others interpret as madness.
  • Displays a strange serenity and is described as the "least critical human being."
  • Has an air of maudlin dignity and commands a dubious respect.
  • Exhibits contradictory behavior: vain but neglected, hopeful but delusional.
  • Plays chess alone, often crying over imagined victories or defeats.
  • Has a strong attachment to visual education and arithmetic, though she never succeeds in teaching.
  • Claims to be descended from notable historical figures (Daniel Boone, William the Conqueror, Alexander Graham Bell).
  • Sold a Dutch windmill home to come to Catherine’s house based on a letter of employment that Catherine denies writing.
  • Possibly a shoplifter or of dubious character as viewed by Lisa Lunde, but not confirmed.
  • Mysterious in origin, with no known relatives or friends, disappearing without trace after leaving.

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera emerges as a deeply introspective, highly imaginative, and somewhat detached individual whose internal world often blurs with external reality. Her character is defined by a profound engagement with dreams, a complex relationship with her past, and a unique way of perceiving and constructing reality.
  • She explicitly states that Mrs. Hogden, a central figure in this chapter, is someone she "never saw", but rather a "trick of my imagination, this substituting of the one for the other". Vera acknowledges Mrs. Hogden as a "substitute... for the dream life I wanted" and even calls her "my mind’s betrayal of my mind". This self-awareness about her mental constructs highlights her active internal world, where figures like Mrs. Hogden go “waddling in and out of my dreams.” She can "see" Mrs. Hogden by simply "closing my eyes, by concentrating". This constant blurring of waking life, dreams, and imaginative constructs suggests that Vera's consciousness is the primary lens through which the narrative unfolds, making her a subjective and unreliable, yet compelling, narrator.
  • Vera's character is also deeply shaped by her past and the figures who influenced her upbringing, particularly Miss MacIntosh and her mother. Miss MacIntosh, Vera's former nursemaid, "brought me up to understand that my mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman such as she saw me becoming, a woman like herself, simple and average and clear-eyed". This suggests that Miss MacIntosh tried to instill a sense of conventionality in Vera, despite Vera's inherent imaginative tendencies (Miss MacIntosh "would have disapproved of, most ardently" of night-dreaming). Vera's "escaped from my mother’s house" further indicates a strained relationship with her mother, who is portrayed as eccentric and prone to "frenzied dreaming". Vera's ongoing comparison of Mrs. Hogden to Miss MacIntosh, even after Miss MacIntosh's death, shows her lingering attachment to these formative figures and her effort to understand her own identity through their contrasting influences.
  • Despite her imaginative immersion, Vera demonstrates a keen observational and analytical mind, though often applied to her internal world. She meticulously describes Mrs. Hogden's outlandish appearance and actions, down to the "smashed hat with a wilted ostrich feather" and the "row of Javanese temple bells". She also notices the "evidence left by Mrs. Hogden" in the playroom, such as "derelict whiskey bottles, empty coat hangers, withered apple cores, broken egg shells, dead flies", distinguishing even an "artificial eyelash". Her philosophical reflections, such as her belief in a "small, warped flower growing... outside the consciousness of God", reveal a mind that questions universal truths and finds significance in anomalies.
  • Vera also conveys a sense of loneliness and a search for meaning or connection. She explicitly states, "The life I required was the life which required, like his, a lost companion —not merely this self-centered affliction of the right hand loving the left". Her observation that "Everybody is lonely" suggests a deep, shared human experience she identifies with. Mrs. Hogden, as an imagined companion, could be seen as Vera's attempt to fill this void, even while acknowledging the illusion
  • Vera's identity appears somewhat fluid and permeable. Mrs. Hogden mistakenly supposes Vera to be Lisa Lunde, and Vera herself often blurs the lines between her own experiences, her mother's dreams, and the fabricated reality of Mrs. Hogden. This fluidity contributes to the dreamlike atmosphere of the chapter and underscores Vera's role as a narrator whose self is not rigidly defined, but rather an evolving construct shaped by memory, imagination, and the enigmatic characters she encounters, both real and imagined.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Catherine, Vera's mother, is a profoundly eccentric, wealthy invalid whose grasp on reality is tenuous and fragmented. Her character is defined by a series of contradictions, delusions, and a self-centered, often manipulative, approach to those around her.
  • Initially, Vera establishes Catherine as an unconventional figure, noting that Miss MacIntosh, Vera's former nursemaid, raised Vera to understand that her "mother’s way of life was far from average and was not to be imitated by a good woman". Catherine is also revealed as the "true subject of [Vera's] dreams," indicating her deep, almost obsessive, significance to Vera.
  • Catherine's disconnection from reality is a dominant trait. She "dreamed that she was poor," contrasting with Lisa Lunde's mother who "dreamed that she was rich". Her physical and mental state is described as one of profound invalidism, often sinking into "deeper and deeper coma" and experiencing hallucinations, such as "a huge toad was eating my mother’s face" or "the balloon fish floating over my mother’s head", and "shadowy figures stepped out of the walls. There were moths with human faces". She herself admits to having "lost my mind several times" and declares, "I am not responsible for my actions". Her identity is fluid; she believes she has "killed her former self and that my mother’s former self was walking through the house while my mother lay with her hair streaked out like twilight on a pillow, for my mother was dead—added, subtracted, multiplied, divided".
  • Despite her profound mental disarray, Catherine exhibits moments of surprising shrewdness and practicality, particularly concerning financial matters. She can display a "shrewd gleam in her eyes, the absolute efficiency with which she inquired into her financial concerns, past and present," even seeking to collect "Old loans which she had forgotten making" from dead parties. Her instruction to meticulously inspect the house for missing items after Mrs. Hogden's departure further underscores this trait.
  • Catherine's interactions with Mrs. Hogden, her newly arrived companion, highlight her manipulative and self-centered nature. Initially, she feigns "profound, glazed astonishment," denying any knowledge of Mrs. Hogden or having sent an invitation, calling her an "impostor, a liar, a day-dreamer, a thief". Despite Mrs. Hogden possessing intimate details of Catherine's life like "the head of Alcibiades was in the drainpipe" or "a whale swimming into my mother’s bedroom" which only Catherine could have divulged, Catherine still refuses to see her. She employs elaborate excuses, claiming to be "gone to Boston to see a podiatrist" or "to the North Pole". She blames Lisa Lunde for Mrs. Hogden's presence and attempts to discourage Mrs. Hogden by assigning her an uncomfortable "deserted playroom" and a "hospital cot" that was "too short and too narrow". Her ultimate directive to Mr. Spitzer to "push her off a high building or throw her into the ocean" to get rid of Mrs. Hogden reveals a cruel and extreme impulse.
  • Catherine's desire for an arithmetic teacher who would teach "Two and two always making four...over and over again" suggests a yearning for simple, undeniable truths in a chaotic personal reality. However, she rejects Mrs. Hogden's attempts to teach, deeming her "mad as a loon" for repeating the lesson. She views Mrs. Hogden as a "rival invalid" and a "gross, stinking parody" of her own "distended world of shimmering, loosely woven textures", indicating a fierce protectiveness over her unique inner world.
  • Catherine's memory and awareness fluctuate. After Mrs. Hogden's departure, she is "disappointed now that she had not been taught arithmetic and blamed Lisa Lunde", even considering hiring another "lonely old woman" to teach her. This cyclical nature underscores her persistent detachment from the consequences of her actions and her inability to learn from past experiences.

Lisa Lunde

  • Lisa Lunde is introduced as Vera's mother's "young companion who took my place when, carrying a large suitcase, I escaped from my mother’s house". This immediately establishes her as a replacement for Vera and suggests a practical, perhaps less privileged, background. Indeed, she is described as a "would-be physicist working for her living in order to help support her mother who was poor and mad and dreamed that she was rich", highlighting her sense of responsibility and pragmatic drive, contrasting with the opulence and delusion of Vera's mother's household.
  • Lisa Lunde is characterized by her analytical, skeptical, and often blunt nature. She "prided herself on seeing immediately through Mrs. Hogden’s pretensions" and quickly assesses Mrs. Hogden as a "very dubious character, a shoplifter or something equally vicious". Her scientific inclination is evident in her desire to "shatter all illusions at one blow," as when she cruelly declares "Res Tacamah... is nothing but a drug bottle". She struggles with Mrs. Hogden's evasiveness, conceding "she was perhaps not a shoplifter... but she did not look like a school-teacher either—there was something so evasive about her, something that evaded definition". This reflects her need for clear categories and her frustration with ambiguity.
  • Despite her initial skepticism and clear-sightedness, Mrs. Hogden's unwavering self-assurance eventually sways Lisa Lunde, causing her to "began to believe that she had come because she was invited". This suggests a slight vulnerability to the pervasive illusions of the house, or perhaps a weariness from constantly battling them.
  • Her role in the conflict between Vera's mother and Mrs. Hogden is notable. When Vera's mother blames her for Mrs. Hogden's presence and demands she "get rid of her," Lisa Lunde reveals a more complex, almost vindictive side. "Lisa Lunde, revengeful, began to enjoy the embarrassing situation. She ran back and forth with meaningless messages between the two, and she would do nothing to interpret either character to the other". This shows a passive-aggressive streak, where she derives satisfaction from the escalating absurdity, perhaps as a form of rebellion against her demanding employer or simply a release from her own constrained life.
  • Lisa Lunde also acts as a voice of conventional sanity, remarking that talking to oneself is fine, "but when you get to answering your own questions—then you are crazy as a loon". This pragmatic, somewhat judgmental perspective contrasts sharply with the eccentricities of Mrs. Hogden and the delusions of Vera's mother.
  • Lisa Lunde serves as a grounded, albeit sometimes resentful, observer and participant in the surreal events of the household. She is a foil to the dreamers and the deluded, attempting to apply reason and practicality in a world that largely defies both. Vera's mother, however, consistently blames Lisa Lunde, even for "keeping Mrs. Hogden out of sight", underscoring Lisa Lunde's thankless position as the companion trying to manage an unmanageable reality.

Research: Themes

Illusion vs. Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Mrs. Hogden blurs the line between dream and waking life, reality and hallucination.
  • Her presence challenges the boundaries between sanity and madness.
  • Symbol of the mind’s betrayal of itself, a substitute for lost or desired figures (such as Miss MacIntosh).

Loneliness and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Mrs. Hogden is depicted as profoundly lonely, coming from a desolate life in a cold windmill.
  • The Arctic tern’s repeated, inexplicable visits symbolize persistent isolation.
  • Despite her eccentric behavior, she is a figure of tragic solitude.

Decay and Disorder

See: Decay and Ruin · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Her physical smell and appearance evoke decay (rotted apples, dead flies).
  • The disorder she brings contrasts with the previously orderly household.
  • Symbolizes the intrusion of chaos into a controlled environment.

Madness and Sanity

See: Madness and Sanity

  • Mrs. Hogden’s behavior is perceived as madness, yet she retains a shrewd awareness and control.
  • The narrative questions who is truly mad: the woman or those rejecting her.
  • Madness is portrayed both as a social stigma and a complex psychological state.

Time and Permanence

See: Time

  • Mrs. Hogden talks about time running backward and forward, dreams of a motorboat, and eternal social seasons.
  • Her presence represents a temporary permanence, a fixture in a house and life otherwise transient.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Mrs. Hogden herself is a complex symbol. She represents a kind of spectral presence, both corporeal and ghost-like, who invades the household and disturbs the established order. She is described as a "fat, corporeal, moon-eyed" woman who is not beautiful and who waddled "in and out of my dreams". She embodies the intrusion of chaos and unwanted reality into a fragile, dreamlike world maintained by Vera's mother and the memory of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Mrs. Hogden is also symbolic of decay and disorder, her physicality is often described in grotesque and unsettling terms, such as "rolling of loose, misshapen flesh," "wrinkled breasts hanging like bags of whey," and "a huge mold of greenish, bluish jelly". She contrasts sharply with the idealized past represented by Miss MacIntosh and the house itself.
  • Miss MacIntosh and Mrs. Hogden, in their stark contrast, explore different facets of the novel's central themes. Miss MacIntosh, the champion of stark reality, ultimately reveals a hidden life of profound vulnerability and disillusionment, making her a complex figure of "imperfection" that Vera comes to love. Mrs. Hogden, on the other hand, is a figure of superficial optimism and self-deception, a "grotesque parody" who inadvertently reveals the emptiness and shared nature of the very illusions she seems to embody. Through these two women, Young delves into the intricate relationship between outward appearance and inner truth, the nature of human suffering, and the pervasive power of imagination in shaping individual realities. Vera's journey of understanding and acceptance, particularly regarding Miss MacIntosh, becomes a quest to reconcile the perceived and the concealed, the dream and the truth.
  • The playroom is a central symbolic space. It is "closed for so many years" and filled with "useless or forgotten objects," old trunks, umbrellas, and boxes. This room represents a liminal space where the past and present collide, and where forgotten memories and decayed hopes reside. Mrs. Hogden inhabiting this space symbolizes the intrusion of decay and madness into the sanctuary of childhood memories and order. The moonlight that "lit her up" and the "silvery walls" that "shone around her like curled water" give the playroom an eerie, otherworldly quality, blurring the line between reality and dream.
  • Mrs. Hogden's teaching of arithmetic is symbolized by the apples she brings, some of which are wormy, and later by buttons as substitutes. Physical decay is a pervasive image

  • wormy apples, rotted fish-like faces, dirty and torn clothes, dust, dead flies, and foul smells. This imagery creates a sense of entropy and decline, reflecting the mental and physical deterioration of characters and the household.
  • The repeated emphasis on arithmetic, especially "two and two making four," functions as a symbol of order, logic, and certainty. Yet it is juxtaposed against the madness and chaos that Mrs. Hogden and the household embody, highlighting the tension between reason and irrationality.
  • Catherine and Mrs. Hogden, though seemingly antithetical, are deeply intertwined through their relationship with illusion and Vera's perception.
  • Catherine creates illusions to escape a painful reality, while Mrs. Hogden accepts the house's illusions as her own reality, finding profound happiness within them. Catherine is the "genuine unbeliever" in reality, while Mrs. Hogden is the "least critical human being".
  • Catherine is a fading, beautiful ghost, a "dead beauty", while Mrs. Hogden is an overwhelmingly corporeal, even grotesque, presence. Mrs. Hogden's physical reality is a "stinking parody" of the house's dreams.
  • Mrs. Hogden acts as a "substitute" for Miss MacIntosh in Vera's mind and directly mirrors Catherine's dreams, often speaking them aloud. Catherine even mistakes Mrs. Hogden for her dead Cousin Hannah, highlighting the fluidity of identity within the house's dreamscape.
  • Mrs. Hogden's character serves to "universalize" and "vulgarize" the "rare and individual and hidden" aspects of the house's dreams, making them commonplace through her uncritical embrace.
  • Both characters, in their distinct ways, explore the novel's central themes of reality, illusion, memory, and identity, offering different facets of a world where the boundaries between the living and the dead, the real and the imagined, are constantly dissolving.

  • Mrs. Hogden is a complex, multifaceted figure who embodies disorder, decay, misplaced optimism, and the collapse of old certainties. She is a grotesque presence in the household after Miss MacIntosh's departure, representing a stark contrast to the grounded, practical, and clear-eyed Miss MacIntosh. Mrs. Hogden is described as corpulent, overburdened with possessions, dressed in layers of ill-fitting clothes, and surrounded by chaos, both physical and mental. She clings to illusions of social status, authority, and control, despite her evident disarray and marginalization. She is simultaneously comic and tragic, a figure who inhabits a liminal space between reality and dream, presence and absence, sanity and madness. Symbolically, Mrs. Hogden could be seen as representing aspects of American society and history, especially those tied to the decline of certain old social orders and the ambiguous transition to modernity. Mrs. Hogden’s sale of her Dutch windmill, her carrying all her worldly goods in a two-door Ford, and her clinging to relics such as the beaded bag, the birdcage, and the Javanese temple bells evoke the image of a once-privileged class now reduced to decay and disarray. She could symbolize the fading of old American aristocracy or the genteel upper-middle class, who struggled to maintain dignity and status in a changing social landscape. Her presence in the house, with its priceless chairs and frozen grandeur, underscores the tension between fading grandeur and the disorder of decline. Mrs. Hogden’s peripatetic arrival, her confusion about places and people (mixing up Mr. Res Tacamah, a drug bottle, with a gentleman visitor), and her life of loneliness parallel the broader social dislocations in America, including the effects of the Great Depression, the migration from rural to urban areas, and the alienation of individuals in modern capitalist society. Her sense of being unwanted yet persisting reflects the experience of many who were left behind by rapid social and economic change. As a middle-aged woman burdened by social pretensions and personal illusions, Mrs. Hogden represents the constrained roles available to women before the feminist advances of the 1960s. Her role as a supposed "teacher of arithmetic" who never fulfills this role and instead devolves into a caricature of herself suggests the limitations and frustrations imposed on women whose identities were often tied to domestic service or caretaking roles, without autonomy or recognition. Mrs. Hogden’s refusal to acknowledge reality fully: her constant smiling despite ruin, her endless dressing and undressing, her imagining social events and parties in an empty house, and her inability to accept her own decline can be read as a metaphor for American society’s denial of its underlying problems. This denial includes racial segregation, economic inequality, and social injustice that persisted before the civil rights movements and social reforms of the 1960s. Mrs. Hogden may symbolize the marginalized individuals who existed on the peripheries of American prosperity, those who were invisible or ignored by mainstream narratives of progress. Her ambiguous identity (Mrs. Hogden, Logden, or Fogden), her lack of family or friends, and the servants’ refusal to acknowledge her expectations all point to a persona that is both part of and apart from society. Mrs. Hogden symbolically represents the decaying remnants of a bygone American social order, burdened by illusions of grandeur and authority, and caught in the liminal space between past certainties and an uncertain modern future.** She embodies the contradictions of persistence and decline, presence and invisibility, sanity and madness, reflecting the complex historical and social transformations experienced in the United States, including the decline of old aristocratic values, the dislocations of modernity, the constrained roles of women, and the societal denial of persistent inequalities.

Lisa’s critical view of Mrs. Hogden and the fanciful world around Vera’s mother points to the tension between dream and reality, illusion and fact, an important theme in American culture, especially as the country grappled with modernity, the aftermath of the Great Depression, war, and social change. Lisa’s skepticism toward the older generation’s illusions (including those of Vera’s mother and Mrs. Hogden) may symbolize the younger generation’s disillusionment with the promises of the American Dream, especially in the years before the social upheavals of the 1960s. Her practical, sometimes harsh demeanor reflects a cultural shift toward realism and away from romantic or fanciful ideals that had dominated earlier eras. Symbolically, Lisa Lunde represents the scientifically educated, pragmatic, socially aware young American woman before 1965 who challenges illusions and embodies the tensions of modernity, class struggle, and generational change in the United States. She is a figure of rationality and skepticism standing in contrast to the dreamlike, unstable figures around her, reflecting broader cultural and historical shifts in American society during the early to mid-20th century.

Chapter 39
