Chapter 66

← Chapter 65 · Home · Chapter 67 →

Summary

Dressed for a long voyage in whaler's hat and sea boots, Miss MacIntosh teaches Vera through a storm. She fires questions about geography, finance, and the body, describes her imaginary raids on the Stock Exchange, which she calls a palace of evil, and her Arctic explorer, and speaks of her removed ovaries. Then, one cold September morning, she walks into the sea. Her clothes are found on the beach and her red wig is torn in the sand, while old Friday, the sheep dog, barks at the waves.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel · Mr. Titus Bonebreaker · Old Friday · Lorena

Concepts present

Themes: Fate and Chance · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Clouds and Storms · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Exploration and the Poles · Gambling and Playing Cards · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • At the outset, Miss MacIntosh is described as dressed for a long voyage (whaler’s hat, sea boots) ready for protection amid a storm, though she insists they are not going anywhere. Her booming voice and strong presence contrast with the child narrator’s perception of her eccentric normalcy. She expresses pity for fishermen, sailors, fishes, and even stars, acknowledging nature’s cruelty toward the weak. This passage sets a tone of resilience, foreboding, and her deep connection with nature’s harshness.
  • Despite the storm and darkness, Miss MacIntosh insists on continuing lessons, asking questions about the heart, geography, history, and more. She shows impatience but also a dedication to education. Vera later reflects that these lessons were far from orthodox and took on new significance after Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance, hinting at her mysterious fate and the deeper layers beneath her teaching methods.
  • A turning point is the revelation that Miss MacIntosh was bald all her life, wearing a red wig that Vera had not noticed before. This physical detail symbolizes her alienation and difference. Her loneliness is profound; she loathes children despite being a nursemaid, yearns for adult companionship, and feels disconnected even in bustling cities like New York. This passage humanizes her, exposing vulnerability behind her strong exterior.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s interactions with a nameless wooden-legged Arctic explorer at the Stock Exchange are important. She admires Captain Cook, debates the discovery of the North Pole, and contemplates socialism and finance. The explorer’s persistent proposals to take her to the Arctic, contrasted with her preoccupation with finance and her own cautious independence, reveal two isolated souls longing for escape and meaning. This dialogue also highlights themes of isolation, survival, and the clash between harsh reality and dreams.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections about her amputations (physical and metaphorical), her lost femininity (due to baldness and removed ovaries), and her unfulfilled love life deepen the sense of tragedy. She contrasts her fate with old traditions and societal expectations of women, expressing a complex relationship with identity and desire. Her hope for a world without colonialism, extravagance, and selfishness reflects her idealism and disillusionment.
  • The chapter culminates with a haunting depiction of her disappearance: her clothes strewn on the beach, the red wig torn, and only remnants left behind. Vera contemplates the metaphor of amputated feet walking on their own, the sea as her coffin, and the endless cycles of nature and memory. The chapter closes with the image of old Friday (the dog) barking by the sea, symbolizing continuity amid loss and the enduring mystery of Miss MacIntosh’s life and death.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • A strong, eccentric woman who dresses for storms and long voyages, symbolizing her preparedness for life's harshness. She is bald, always wearing a red wig, which is a hidden truth only discovered later. Her voice is booming and manly, and she exhibits contradictory traits: a resolute socialist with disdain for wealth and extravagance but also an astute student of finance.
  • Represents resilience, the burden of loneliness, and the struggle for self-identity. Her baldness symbolizes vulnerability and a unique form of naked truth.
  • She harbors dreams of love, adventure, and escape from societal norms, but also suffers from deep isolation and self-awareness of her physical and emotional amputations.
  • Acts as a strict, demanding teacher who pushes Vera to learn relentlessly, even amid storms and symbolic death.

The Arctic Explorer at the Stock Exchange

  • A wooden-legged, talkative man with a haunting past who invites Miss MacIntosh to join him on an expedition to the North Pole. His character is mysterious and symbolic of isolation, survival, and the lure of the unknown.
  • Embodies the exploration of the unknown, physical and emotional scars, and the harsh reality beyond civilization.
  • A complex connection based on shared loneliness and amputations; he proposes a life of silence and isolation, contrasting with Miss MacIntosh’s attachment to her worldly concerns.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • She is described as being "pent up in bed" and dreaming in an "over-heated room". This suggests she is physically unwell and possibly confined to her bed for an extended period.
  • Vera mentions that her mother sometimes dreams "opium dreams" and entertains "too many hallucinations" for her health's sake. This implies a detachment from reality and a possible reliance on drugs or other means to escape her physical condition.
  • Vera notes that her mother has strange dreams where she never recognizes living men, only the dead ones. This indicates a preoccupation with the past and a possible inability to connect with the present.
  • Miss MacIntosh criticizes her mother for lacking common sense, specifically citing the gift of an Eskimo cookbook as an example. This suggests a disconnect between the mother's actions and practical reality.
  • The gifts Vera's mother gives Miss MacIntosh (a silk nightgown and the Eskimo cookbook) point to a certain level of wealth and privilege.
  • Vera wonders if her mother always knew Miss MacIntosh was bald, despite it being a secret. If true, this could indicate a deeper understanding or perception than she lets on.

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera is deeply influenced by Miss MacIntosh, to the point of reflecting her moods and taking on "every color except my own". This suggests a lack of a strong, independent identity in her childhood, making her highly susceptible to Miss MacIntosh's unusual worldview.
  • Vera is often confused by Miss MacIntosh's lessons and pronouncements. She admits to being "very stupid, undeveloped" and unable to answer basic questions. However, this also implies a certain level of intellectual curiosity, even if she struggles to grasp the concepts.
  • As a child, Vera takes Miss MacIntosh's eccentricities for granted, considering them "commonplace". This acceptance highlights her innocence and the way children often normalize the unusual behavior of adults in their lives.
  • The narrative is framed as a recollection from "long years after Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance". This distance allows Vera to view the lessons with "a new light," recognizing their unorthodox nature. The nostalgic tone suggests that Miss MacIntosh, despite her strangeness, had a significant impact on Vera's life and development.
  • Vera seems haunted by Miss MacIntosh's disappearance and the circumstances surrounding it. The recurring imagery of storms, drowning, and the sea suggests a deep sense of loss and unresolved questions. She can still hear Miss MacIntosh's voice "roaring above the storm" 829, indicating a lasting psychological impact.
  • Vera's observation that Miss MacIntosh wished to tell her all her secrets during the last month of her life suggests a growing awareness and understanding of her nursemaid's complexities. She begins to perceive Miss MacIntosh's loneliness, her longing for adult companionship, and her hidden vulnerabilities, such as her baldness.
  • Even as a child, Vera seems to possess a keen eye for the absurd. She notices the incongruities in Miss MacIntosh's behavior, such as her wearing a whaler's hat during lessons or receiving an Eskimo cookbook as a gift when she never cooks. This suggests an underlying sense of humor and an ability to recognize the strangeness of the world around her.
  • In retrospect, Vera reflects on her own shortcomings and tendencies, such as her proneness to hallucinations and her lack of a distinct identity. This introspection suggests a desire to understand herself and her relationship with Miss MacIntosh on a deeper level.

Mr. Bonebreaker

  • Miss MacIntosh reflects that Mr. Bonebreaker belonged to an old religion where women must kneel before men, similar to the customs of What Cheer, Iowa, where women wash men's feet. She contrasts this with her own situation, noting her baldness and lack of traditionally feminine features, which prevent her from fulfilling such a role.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker seems to represent a lost opportunity for love and connection in Miss MacIntosh's life. He is associated with the idea that she could never kneel before a man, implying a rejection of traditional gender roles and a sense of isolation.
  • It is said that Mr. Bonebreaker fled leaving his umbrella behind.
  • Miss MacIntosh's baldness is a significant factor in her perception of her relationship with Mr. Bonebreaker. She believes her lack of hair and other physical attributes made her unattractive and contributed to the failure of their relationship.
  • Mr. Bonebreaker is mentioned as one of the people who knew Miss MacIntosh was bald.

Old Friday (pet dog)

  • Old Friday is consistently present at Miss MacIntosh's heels, even after her disappearance. He barks "much as if he might still be aware of her, a moving shadow, a shadow of a black umbrella moving over water and sand– as if perhaps she had never gone or had returned". This suggests that Old Friday retains a memory of Miss MacIntosh and remains loyal to her, even when others have moved on.
  • The text implies that Old Friday might perceive something beyond what others can see. Vera questions, "had he not known the denudation and the dream, the reality and the illusion, how each must live by some pretense?". This suggests that Old Friday is aware of the underlying truths and illusions that define Miss MacIntosh's existence.
  • Even after Miss MacIntosh's apparent drowning, Old Friday continues to bark by the sea, suggesting a continuation of life and memory even in the face of loss. The waves return "with all but her, waves swollen with winds, the waves like sheep with a thousand bells, aye, while she and the shores and sounding waves wash far away in echo and response".
  • Old Friday's barking by the sea after Miss MacIntosh's disappearance can be interpreted as a symbol of inconsolable grief and mourning. He is a constant reminder of her absence.

Lorena

  • Lorena appears only briefly but her presence is significant in relation to Miss MacIntosh and the broader themes of the novel.
  • Lorena is mentioned as a beautiful dancing girl with dark hair, described as fat, who ran away and became a strip-tease dancer. This characterization contrasts sharply with Miss MacIntosh’s practical, no-nonsense, and grounded nature. Lorena represents a more sensual, flamboyant, and perhaps socially transgressive aspect of femininity, set against Miss MacIntosh’s sobriety, austerity, and emotional reserve.
  • Lorena’s knowledge of Miss MacIntosh’s baldness before Vera discovers it suggests an intimacy or at least a closer social awareness of Miss MacIntosh’s vulnerability and true self.
  • Lorena’s laughter behind her fan and her awareness of this physical fact highlight the difference in how women in the novel perceive and interact with each other, often marked by a mixture of judgment, awareness, and perhaps envy or pity.
  • Lorena helps underscore Miss MacIntosh’s loneliness and isolation. While Lorena embodies escape, sensuality, and perhaps a more conventional form of social engagement (albeit in a marginal way), Miss MacIntosh remains solitary, bald, and burdened by her practical concerns and emotional detachment. Lorena’s figure acts as a foil to Miss MacIntosh, illuminating the nursemaid’s deeper struggles with identity, acceptance, and the harsh realities she faces.

Research: Themes

Isolation and Loneliness

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh’s baldness and social detachment highlight profound loneliness, despite her physical presence among others.
  • The Arctic explorer’s life and invitation symbolize a complete withdrawal from society into the harsh, silent wilderness.
  • Vera, as a child, reflects this isolation by absorbing the moods and eccentricities of Miss MacIntosh without fully understanding them.

Truth and Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh claims to always speak the "bald truth," a pun on her physical baldness and metaphorical truthfulness.
  • Her imaginary financial dealings on the Stock Exchange represent the illusion of control and wealth in a chaotic world.
  • The explorer’s tales mix reality with fantasy, blurring the lines between truth, myth, and personal delusion.

The Harshness of Nature and Fate

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Fate and Chance

  • The recurrent imagery of storms, drowning, and the sea as a coffin symbolize the inevitability of death and nature’s indifference.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s preoccupation with the fishermen, drowned sailors, and drowned things on the beach emphasizes vulnerability.
  • The Arctic setting and references to icebergs, glaciers, and the North Pole evoke an unforgiving environment that mirrors internal struggles.

Identity and Physical Amputation

See: Identity and the Self

  • Both Miss MacIntosh and the Arctic explorer carry physical and emotional amputations (her baldness and removed ovaries; his lost leg), symbolizing loss and survival.
  • Their shared disabilities forge a silent kinship and mutual understanding of alienation.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s lost hair and wig symbolize the loss of traditional feminine identity and seduction.

Education and Knowledge

See: The Search for Meaning

  • Miss MacIntosh’s relentless questioning, despite her indifference to answers, reflects a ritualistic pursuit of knowledge.
  • Vera’s difficulty in answering symbolizes innocence and underdevelopment, contrasting with Miss MacIntosh’s eccentric wisdom.
  • Subjects range from geography and history to biology and social science, showing a broad but fragmented understanding of the world.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Hurricane Lamp

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Clouds and Storms

  • Represents fragile knowledge and guidance amid darkness and storms.

The Sea and Waves

See: The Sea and Water

  • Symbolize the passage of time, death, and the subconscious.

The Black Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • Miss MacIntosh’s shield against the world; her barrier protecting her from close human contact.

The Red Wig

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • A mask hiding her baldness, symbolizing concealment of vulnerability.

Stock Exchange

  • A place of illusionary wealth and human folly; also a site where she confronts capitalism and socialism.

Iceberg and North Pole Imagery

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Symbolize isolation, the unknown, and the emotional coldness of the characters.

The Amputated Foot and Head

  • Metaphors for loss, survival, and the persistence of the dream or spirit beyond physical destruction.

While it existed in antiquity, the modern era of colonialism, driven by European powers from the 15th to the 20th century, saw empires expand across the Americas, Africa, and Asia. The Spanish and Portuguese initiated colonization in the Americas, followed by the French and British who established empires in North America, the Caribbean, and other parts of the world. This process frequently involved violence, the subjugation of indigenous populations, and the imposition of the colonizer's culture, language, and economic systems, with lasting negative impacts still felt today.
  • The history of Jewish return to Palestine is marked by two major periods: ancient exiles and returns, and the modern Zionist movement. Ancient returns occurred after the Babylonian exile around 538 BCE and were driven by religious and political events. The modern era saw a mass return fueled by the late 19th-century Zionist movement, which aimed to establish a Jewish homeland in Palestine amidst rising antisemitism, culminating in the establishment of the State of Israel in 1948. Around 587 BCE, the Babylonians destroyed the First Temple in Jerusalem and exiled many Jews. In 538 BCE, Cyrus the Great of Persia conquered Babylon and allowed the Jews to return to Judah and rebuild the Temple, which was completed in 515 BCE. The Romans destroyed the Second Temple in 70 CE during the First Jewish-Roman War, leading to a major Jewish diaspora and the loss of sovereignty. The Zionist movement, which began in the late 19th century, aimed to re-establish a Jewish homeland in Palestine. Organized immigration to Palestine began in 1882, with immigrants motivated by a combination of religious ideals and practical/economic considerations, though not yet modern Zionism. The movement gained momentum due to rising antisemitism and pogroms in Europe, which led to increased Jewish immigration to Palestine throughout the 1930s. The British limited Jewish immigration to Palestine with the "White Paper of 1939," which disappointed Zionists, though many Jews still arrived during this period. Following World War II and the liberation of concentration camp survivors, the United Nations partitioned Palestine. On May 14, 1948, the modern State of Israel was proclaimed, re-establishing Jewish sovereignty after nearly 2,000 years.
  • “She hoped that there would be an end to the Tong wars. She hoped that China, the Sleeping Dragon, would awaken”
  • The Tong Wars were a series of violent disputes beginning in the late 19th century among rival Chinese Tong factions centered in the Chinatowns of various American cities, in particular San Francisco. Tong wars could be triggered by a variety of inter-gang grievances, from the public besmirching of another Tong's honor, to failure to make full payment for a "slave girl", to the murder of a rival Tong member. Each Tong had salaried soldiers, known as boo how doy, who fought in Chinatown alleys and streets over the control of opium, prostitution, gambling, and territory. In San Francisco's Chinatown district, the Tong Wars lasted until 1921, with the various criminal Tongs estimated between nineteen and as many as thirty at the peak of the conflict, though the actual number is uncertain, with frequent splintering and mergers between the various Tongs. While a loose alliance, consisting of the Chinatown police, Donaldina Cameron, the courts, and the Chinese community itself tried to stem the tide of the fighting Tongs, it was the 1906 San Francisco earthquake and subsequent fires caused by the earthquake that was the death knell for the Tongs in San Francisco, as it destroyed the brothels, gambling dens, and opium houses that the criminal organizations had used for the majority of their revenue. Recovery was slow for most Tongs, so they abandoned the old Chinatown.
  • China has been referred to as “the sleeping Dragon.” In China, the dragon stands for power, strength, and good luck. In the past, the Chinese emperor was referred to as the Dragon. China’s economy covers thousands of years with cycles of prosperity and decline. "Let China sleep, for when she wakes up, she will shake the world." - Napoleon Bonaparte.
  • “She once knew two dwarves who begot a normal-sized child.” it's possible and actually quite common for two parents with dwarfism, especially achondroplasia, to have an average-sized child, as there's a 25% chance for a child to inherit a "normal" height gene from each parent, resulting in an average-sized stature, while still having a 50% chance of a dwarf child like themselves, and a 25% chance for a severe, often fatal, form of dwarfism (homozygous).
  • “She did hope that, before she died, the King of England would lose his crown” Attempts to overthrow the English monarchy span centuries, from medieval power struggles like the Anarchy and Wars of the Roses, to the successful republican revolution during the English Civil War (leading to Charles I's execution and the Commonwealth), the Glorious Revolution (limiting monarchical power), and the Jacobite Risings seeking Stuart restoration, all demonstrating persistent challenges to royal authority.
  • Hysterectomies are rarely performed on women younger than thirty-five years old. It is a mystery as to what happened to Miss MacIntosh’s ovaries and difficult to pinpoint her age or anyone’s age except Vera in the novel.

  • "although there had been more than one man in her life, of course, and there had been a rival love" refers to Miss MacIntosh's complex and somewhat troubled romantic past. It also underscores her loneliness and the barriers she faced in forming lasting intimate relationships, especially given her physical condition (she was bald and had an amputated breast and ovaries removed) and her guarded nature. The "rival love" hints at unresolved emotional tensions or losses in her past, which may have contributed to her solitary lifestyle and her resignation to a life without conventional love or marriage.
  • “But Mr. Bonebreaker had belonged to that old religion” This passage critiques patriarchal traditions by illustrating the extreme expectations placed on women to be subservient to men, using vivid, almost grotesque imagery of kneeling and hair used as a towel for washing men's feet. “that old religion” and its description here refers to patriarchy of which Christianity is a part and instances of the changes from a matrilineal society and traditions to a patrilineal one are in the Bible (Marilyn French from Eve to Dawn). Patriarchy entitles men to admiration, sex, consent, and domestic labor from women. Men also receive better medical care and pain management and overall focus of health science for their bodies. Men also are able to practice bodily control which is often and routinely denied women. Misogyny and sexism go hand in hand with patriarchy although it is possible for men to practice one or the other and both need not be present at the same time. Sexism is the theoretical and ideological branch where beliefs, ideas and assumptions are used to rationalize and naturalize patriarchal norms and expectations. Misogyny is the “law enforcement” branch of patriarchy which policies and enforces gendered norms and expectations for girls and women (Kate Manne Entitled). Gerda Learner documented men’s withholding knowledge and power from women through denying education for centuries (Creation of a Feminist Consciousness). Young upends many of these gendered norms in the novel.

  • American tin history spans from 17th-century colonial tinsmiths, making decorative and functional "tinware" like pierced lanterns, to the 19th-century "Tin Can Revolution" driven by Civil War needs, which fostered mass production of inexpensive, lightweight containers for food, transforming household goods and expanding food distribution. Later, tin became crucial for electronics and architecture (tin ceilings). Cans became central to American life, enabling global food distribution and connecting the frontier with the industrialized East. Tin ceiling tiles emerged as an affordable alternative to ornate plaster, symbolizing affordable elegance in buildings.   • “Great Dane” is a German breed of large mastiff-sighthound, which descends from hunting dogs of the Middle Ages used to hunt bears, wild boar, and deer.   • “Wilderness Scout” in the U.S. wasn't a formal program but emerged from early youth groups like Ernest Thompson Seton's Woodcraft Indians (1902) and Daniel Carter Beard's Sons of Daniel Boone (1905), which emphasized nature skills and American Indian lore, eventually merging into the Boy Scouts of America (BSA), which itself developed older youth programs like Senior Scouts and Explorers (1935) for advanced wilderness camping and challenging outdoor pursuits, exemplified by trips to Philmont and Canadian wilderness canoe expeditions. Wilderness scouts, frontiersmen, and explorers frequently wore fringed garments, like the "hunting frock" or buckskin jackets, because the fringe served practical purposes, shedding rain and helping the leather dry faster, in addition to being a cultural style adopted from or shared with Native Americans, making it ideal for frontier life.
  • “Ah, my dear, said he, they would both have done better as fiction writers.” Polynesian voyagers, who predate the Maori people, may have reached Antarctica as early as the 7th century, long before Europeans like Cook and Peary. This evidence includes oral histories, legends like that of Hui Te Rangiora, and archaeological findings on subantarctic islands. Maori oral traditions speak of Polynesian explorers like Hui Te Rangiora, who sailed to the southern ocean in the 7th century and encountered areas of ice and a "dark, misty, foggy place". Archaeological evidence, such as artifacts from ancient ovens and middens found on subantarctic islands, suggests Polynesian presence in waters further south than previously understood. The study argues that these oral histories and traditional records, often overlooked by Western scholars, provide evidence that Polynesians were the first humans to see Antarctica. European exploration of Antarctica was not confirmed until the 19th century, with Cook and Peary's expeditions occurring much later than the proposed Maori voyages.
  • "He just knew that they had something in common—their differences from others—and their amputations and their sense of having killed something young and helpless" This passage suggests that both Miss MacIntosh and the explorer share a profound sense of isolation and loss that sets them apart from ordinary people. But more importantly, these amputations symbolize emotional or existential wounds, each carries a deep internal absence or sacrifice. The phrase "their sense of having killed something young and helpless" reflects a psychological or spiritual burden they both bear, perhaps guilt or sorrow over lost innocence, lost potential, or something vulnerable within themselves or their past. This shared feeling of having caused or endured damage to something fragile adds to their alienation and mutual understanding.

Chapter 34

← Chapter 33 · Home · Chapter 35 →

Summary

Catherine recalls being married both in white and in black, with a dog reciting the ceremony in Latin and a St. Bernard giving her the last sacrament. Then she remembers Hannah's presence in her room: iron keys at her belt, a metallic energy, sharp wit, contempt for mortal men, and total indifference to Mr. Spitzer. In Hannah's company Catherine felt both flirtatious and guilty, sensing a love she could not name. Hannah always predicted that Joachim would fail Catherine at the crucial moment, as Peron had by his suicide.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Fear and Courage · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Time · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Birds · Dogs · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Mirrors and Reflections · Mountains · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Genesis · Greek Mythology · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a surreal and haunting depiction of Catherine’s marriage, described as both a wedding and a funeral, veiled in white and black, with multiple conflicting versions of what happened. This passage highlights Catherine’s uncertain, fragmented memory and symbolizes the blending of beginnings and endings, life and death, love and loss. It evokes the mysterious, almost mythical quality of her experience and sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of elusive reality.
  • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a powerful, almost otherworldly woman. She challenges Catherine’s fantasies and illusions about love and men, urging her to face the harsh realities of life without illusions. This passage contrasts Cousin Hannah’s stark realism with Catherine’s dreamy, romantic visions and introduces the theme of female independence and existential struggle.
  • The golden cock, which causes Cousin Hannah to dance and emit “showers of metallic sparks,” is a striking symbol associated with awakening and revelation. This passage links to themes of awakening from dreams or illusions and the harsh truths of reality. The cock’s crowing also connects to cultural and geographical references, such as Moroccan courtyards and veiled women, adding layers of meaning about visibility, secrecy, and awakening.
  • Catherine’s desire to learn arithmetic and geometry so she can understand who "the geometer" is (whether sane or insane) symbolizes her quest for order, meaning, and clarity in a chaotic and mysterious world. This passage encapsulates the chapter’s central tension between rationality and imagination, reality and dream, and reflects Catherine’s struggle to make sense of her life and the illusions that surround it.
  • The chapter contains a profound meditation on human existence, describing man as “a nine days’ wonder,” “a falling star,” “a broken sea shell,” emphasizing transience, fragility, and the illusory nature of life. This philosophical reflection deepens the chapter’s existential themes and Catherine’s skepticism about men, love, and reality.
  • Throughout the chapter, Catherine both resists and admires Cousin Hannah, who tries to provoke her and break down her defenses. Catherine’s flirtation, guilt, and fascination highlight the interplay of imagination, memory, and identity. Cousin Hannah’s relentless energy and refusal to submit contrast with Catherine’s vulnerability and dreams, illustrating different responses to life’s hardships.
  • The final passages consider Cousin Hannah’s distrust of men, her “perpendicular” strength compared to Catherine’s “horizontal” invalidity, and Catherine’s wavering faith both in men and women. The chapter ends on a note of ambiguity, with references to death, sorrow, and the slow passage of time, underscoring the unresolved tensions and mysteries that permeate Catherine’s life.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Catherine

  • A complex character caught between dreams and reality, longing for love but resigned to solitude.
  • Her memories and fantasies reveal her inner turmoil and sense of loss.
  • She is reflective, romantic, and somewhat nostalgic, haunted by unanswered questions about love and life.

Cousin Hannah

  • A formidable, almost mythical figure symbolizing strength and independence.
  • She challenges Catherine’s illusions and urges her to face reality.
  • Known for her fiery spirit, sharp wit, and relentless energy, she is both a source of inspiration and tension.
  • Her distrust of men and disdain for conventional womanhood provide a counterpoint to Catherine’s experiences.

Research: Themes

Marriage and Loss

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • Catherine’s reflections on her marriage are fragmented and surreal. She imagines multiple versions of her wedding (married in white, black, at a funeral, by a dog, or not at all) signifying confusion, loss, and the elusive nature of commitment and love.
  • Marriage is portrayed as a metaphorical death of the soul, supported by Cousin Hannah’s cynical view that marriage leads to sacrifice and the wasting of a woman’s talents.

Illusion vs. Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine struggles to distinguish between dreams, memories, and reality. Her imagination creates a world where events happen simultaneously or not at all, where identities and places blur into one another.
  • The mirrors, illusions, and dreams symbolize the instability of perception and the human desire for clarity and understanding.

Identity and Loneliness

See: Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection

  • Catherine feels isolated, spouseless, and robbed of love, reflecting a deep sense of loneliness and alienation.
  • Cousin Hannah represents a contrasting figure of strength and defiance, yet also one marked by solitude and an almost otherworldly existence.

Death and Time

See: Death and Mortality · Time

  • Death is a recurring motif, intertwined with marriage, dreams, and memory. Catherine contemplates the inevitability of death and the fading of beauty and life’s passions.
  • Time is fluid and fragmented, with references to sleep, awakening, and timelessness, emphasizing Catherine’s disoriented state.

Female Strength and Defiance

See: Women, Gender, and Marriage · Fear and Courage

  • Cousin Hannah embodies resilience, independence, and courage. She is portrayed as a warrior-like figure, unyielding and untamed, contrasting with Catherine’s vulnerability.
  • Cousin Hannah’s disdain for men and her distrust of Catherine’s whimsical nature highlight different approaches to womanhood and survival.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

White and Black in Marriage

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • White symbolizes innocence and first marriage; black signifies death, mourning, and second chances or loss.

The Funeral and the King of France

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Represents grandeur, loss, and the blending of significant life events into one confusing memory.

The St. Bernard Dog

See: Dogs

  • A prophetic figure in Catherine’s dreams, symbolizing guidance, loss, and perhaps spiritual rites.

Mirrors and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Symbolize self-perception, illusion, and the fragmented nature of identity.

Mountains and Avalanches

See: Mountains

  • Represent obstacles, permanence, and sudden destruction in life and relationships.

The Golden Cock Crowing

See: Birds

  • Symbolizes awakening, sovereignty, and perhaps the harsh reality that disrupts illusions.

Iron Keys

See: Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Worn by Cousin Hannah, symbolize access, control, and the discordant music of life’s complexities.

This was a symbolic act of power and control. In the book the Dialectic of Sex a quote from Carrie Chapman Catt estimates that: “to get the word ‘male’ out of this country 52 years of pauseless campaign… During that time they were forced to conduct 56 campaigns of referenda to male voters, 480 campaigns to get legislatures to submit suffrage amendments to voters, 47 campaigns to get state constitutional conventions to write woman suffrage into state constitutions, 277 campaigns to get state party conventions to include woman suffrage planks, 30 campaigns to get presidential party conventions to adopt woman suffrage planks in party platforms and 19 successive campaigns with 19 successive Congresses. Thus defeat was so frequent, and victory so rare - and then achieved by such bare margins - that even to read about the struggle for suffrage is exhausting, let alone to have lived through it and fought for it.” In light of this Cousin Hannah’s relentless energy is seen as not disproportionate to the women’s suffrage movement. Cousin Hannah’s attitude to marriage and men (at least the outward appearance) would reflect the fundamental struggle. Again from The Dialectic of Sex “To make both women and children totally independent would be to eliminate not just the patriarchal nuclear family, but the biological family itself.”

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes the murder of mothers and newborns and deals with racism.

Summary

Esther asks who killed the heavens and the earth and love itself. The detective sends her an old clipping about a mass murderess, an abortionist who killed unmarried mothers and their newborns. She was caught after killing a woman who was pregnant only in her dreams. Esther reveals that her first child was fathered by a Black man, which makes the detective's indifference to Black children personal. Sterile salesmen keep sending gifts for babies who may be dead.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · The Chicago Detective · Justice O’Leary · The Old Woman Abortionist

Concepts present

Themes: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Butterflies and Moths · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · Shadows

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Genesis · Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter begins with a profound meditation on who "had killed the heavens," the earth, and love itself images symbolize the destruction of innocence, life, and hope. Esther Longtree, the "stillborn mother," embodies silent suffering and unanswered cries, reflecting a deep personal and universal grief. This sets the tone for the chapter's exploration of death and loss, both literal and metaphorical.
  • Esther is described as pregnant but in a strange, watery, almost void-like condition: "pregnant with death," carrying something intangible rather than a living child. This paradoxical pregnancy symbolizes sterility and sorrow, emphasizing her unique, mysterious condition. Her physical state is intertwined with her emotional and psychological torment. Her isolation is emphasized by her work in the restaurant and her efforts to forget the "moths" and "stillborn who came to her at night".
  • The detective who pursues the mystery of children's deaths but only those of white children, ignoring the black children, whom he deems too many and unimportant. This racial divide in justice and attention highlights societal neglect and racial injustice. The detective's selective interest and fear of "black mysteries" contrast sharply with Esther's own encompassing sorrow that transcends race.
  • Esther recalls a faded newspaper clipping about an old woman abortionist who killed poor unmarried mothers and babies under her care. The story is haunting, especially the detail about a pregnant woman who was only "pregnant in her dreams," leading to a fatal mistake that exposed the murderer. This story resonates with Esther's own experience of pregnancy, loss, and the theme of death hidden beneath appearances.
  • Esther reflects on sending letters to the detective, possibly as a way to confront or taunt him. She recalls being raped by him, left for dead, and how since then murder has "grown upon this landscape." This passage reveals deep personal trauma and implicates the detective as both pursuer and perpetrator which adds complexity to their relationship and to the themes of guilt and accusation.
  • Throughout the chapter, there are repeated images of shadows, blackbirds, and stillborn children, symbolizing death, mystery, and things that never fully manifest. Esther sees the landscape as perhaps the "world unborn," hovering on the threshold of realization, reflecting her own liminal existence between life and death, birth and loss.
  • The passage listing exhibits A through U as letters standing for objects, feelings, and accusations (e.g., A for agony, M for murder, N for Negro, S for shadow) is a powerful symbolic enumeration of all the elements that accuse or haunt Esther. It illustrates the complexity of her guilt, the societal judgment upon her, and the intertwining of personal and collective tragedy.
  • Despite all her suffering and the detective's threats, Esther asserts her preference for silence, mystery, and the void over explanation or judgment. She wants to remain enigmatic, outside the reach of "old human laws" and inquisitions, embracing her unique condition and sorrow as a "great serenity".
  • The chapter ends with Esther questioning who should be responsible for the deaths and losses she embodies. She acknowledges the many "fathers," the salesmen, census-takers, and others, but ultimately feels her own stubbornness and sorrow are unique. She cherishes the natural world and wonders why she should be punished for "a few mistakes" when she has already suffered so much.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • The protagonist; a pregnant woman symbolizing loss and mystery.
  • Complex, haunted by past pregnancies and the deaths of children, real or imagined.
  • Her perspective is lyrical, introspective, and fragmented, blending reality and metaphor.

The Chicago Detective

  • Represents societal judgment and racial bias.
  • Obsessed with solving murders of white children but indifferent to black children’s deaths.
  • Seen by Esther as both a threat and possibly the real murderer.

Old Doctor

  • A figure who once tried to aid Esther, representing medical authority and perhaps failed understanding.
  • He recognizes Esther’s exceptional nature and mystery.

The Miller

  • The Miller is a symbolic and tragic figure embedded in the narrative’s broader themes of loss, death, and the elusive nature of identity and legacy.
  • The Miller is described in the context of a flour miller who experiences epileptic seizures, during which he falls into the flour bin, covering himself in flour that then falls from his hat and clothes like snow. This imagery evokes a surreal, almost ghostly presence as people mistakenly believe it is snowing when it is actually flour. The miller’s role and condition emphasize themes of fragility and the blurring between life and death, reality and illusion.
  • The Miller is burdened with the expectation that a secret "thumb print" (a unique mark or identity) will be passed down from father to son, symbolizing lineage and continuity. However, this expectation is shattered when the old miller dies, and the son realizes that no one can truly pass on such a mark upon intangible things like the sunset, starlight, or water. This failure to transmit identity or legacy underscores the sense of loss and futility pervasive in the chapter and in the novel. The son’s epileptic fits may symbolize the psychological and physical turmoil resulting from this loss of meaning and continuity.
  • The Miller represents the human desire for permanence and identity amid the ephemeral and often cruel realities of life. His character evokes the tension between hope and despair, the tangible and the intangible, and the tragic consequences when the expected inheritance of identity and belonging is denied or impossible.
  • The narrative situates the Miller within a landscape of death, mystery, and unanswered questions, linking his personal tragedy to the larger themes of stillbirth, lost children, and the "quiet murders" of existence that haunt Esther Longtree and the novel’s world. The Miller Boy’s condition and the symbolism of flour as falling snow contribute to the chapter’s atmosphere of haunting ambiguity, where the boundaries between life, death, and memory dissolve.
  • The Miller is a poignant emblem of lost legacy and identity, reflecting the novel’s meditation on mortality, memory, and the ineffable mysteries of human existence as presented through Vera’s lyrical and fragmented narration.

The Little Boy

  • The Little Boy character emerges as a poignant and symbolic figure deeply intertwined with Esther Longtree’s complex emotional and psychological landscape.
  • The Little Boy is described as an exception among the many stillborn or lost children that haunt Esther. He is distinct because he “grew and cast his shadow,” unlike the others who remained stillborn or unmanifested. His crying is described as “like the night wind, like the falling leaves,” evoking a mournful, haunting presence that unsettles Esther. She desires to “reach him once with her hands” and to “still him,” but she cannot, as he mistrusts her, his own mother, and actively obstructs her path, causing her to stumble, fall, and suffer further losses.
  • This mistrust and obstruction suggest a fractured or troubled relationship, symbolizing perhaps Esther’s guilt, grief, and inability to fully reconcile with the loss or absence represented by her children. The Little Boy’s role as an accuser is implicit; he embodies the accumulated sorrow and unanswered questions about motherhood, loss, and abandonment that weigh heavily on Esther. The chapter intimates that he is part of the “evidence of sadness” in her life, a living shadow of the grief that has shaped her existence .
  • The Little Boy's shadow symbolizes the tangible imprint of loss and memory, as well as the burden of the past that follows Esther. His presence amplifies the themes of mystery and guilt that pervade the narrative. While Esther is “always pregnant,” carrying death and loss within her, the Little Boy serves as a manifestation of that sorrow made visible, a constant reminder of what is lost and unresolved.
  • The Little Boy character in this chapter is a complex symbol of loss, accusation, and the haunting persistence of grief in Esther Longtree's life. He is both a real and spectral figure who represents the emotional weight of her stillbirths and unfulfilled motherhood, embodying the tension between memory, guilt, and the desire for reconciliation that Vera, the narrator, carefully unfolds.

The Old Woman Abortionist

  • Mentioned in an old newspaper clipping; accused of killing unmarried mothers and babies.
  • Symbolizes institutional cruelty and hidden atrocities.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Loss

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther is "always pregnant," but the pregnancies are metaphorical and literal, filled with loss and the absence of children (stillborn or never born).
  • The grief of lost children haunts her, symbolized by "little bones," a "little book," and the shadow of death inside her womb.
  • Her pregnancy represents both creation and sterility, life and death simultaneously.

Guilt and Innocence

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Esther feels guilt for the "murder" of her children, though this guilt is ambiguous - is she guilty or a victim of fate or society?
  • The detective’s pursuit symbolizes societal judgment and the invasive quest for truth. Esther fears exposure but also wishes for some form of public trial to assert control over her narrative.

Racism and Social Injustice

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Society, Class, and Race

  • The white Chicago detective is interested only in the deaths of white children, ignoring black children’s deaths, revealing racial prejudice and societal neglect.

Mystery and the Unknown

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The nature of Esther’s pregnancies, the deaths, and the detective’s role create a pervasive sense of mystery.
  • The chapter explores the limits of understanding and the unknowable facets of human experience.

Nature and Cosmic Imagery

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Constant references to stars, clouds, birds, leaves, and celestial phenomena frame the narrative in a cosmic context of creation and destruction.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Pregnancy and Stillbirth

See: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • Not just physical but symbolic of potential, loss, and unfulfilled possibility.
  • Esther's "watery pregnancy" and "wild pregnancy" evoke fragility and chaos.

The Little Book (ABC’s)

  • Symbolizes innocence, learning, and memory.
  • Its presence in the grass where no child is physically found evokes haunting loss.

Birds (Robins, Blackbirds, Moths)

See: Butterflies and Moths · Birds

  • Represent life, death, innocence, and societal neglect.
  • Blackbirds especially tie to racial themes and death ignored by authorities.

Shadows and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Shadows

  • Recur throughout as metaphors for hidden truths, guilt, and fear.
  • Esther’s shadow and the detective’s shadow symbolize identity and the unknown.

Newspaper Clippings

  • Represent external judgment, historical atrocities, and persistent societal violence.
  • Esther Longtree's parents are portrayed as a mismatched, barren couple who never consummated their marriage, representing a union without real love, flesh, or genuine connection. The father is a large, lumbering, passive policeman (symbolizing authority but with a lonely, ineffectual life) while the mother is a small, delicate, child-like woman, proud of her fragile appearance but emotionally distant and incapable of nurturing.
  • Symbolically Esther's parents might represent the fraught and dysfunctional relationship between dominant societal forces and marginalized or oppressed groups in America, especially in terms of race and gender relations.
  • The father, a "passive policeman" who is "big—her mother, small," could symbolize the established power structures (law enforcement, government authority) that are large and imposing but ineffective or disconnected in truly addressing human needs or justice. His passivity and loneliness may reflect institutional failure or indifference.
  • The mother, fragile and child-like, might represent the traditional, constrained role of women or the idealized but ineffective domestic sphere, unable to assert real agency or nurture true growth. Her narrowness and coldness can symbolize limitations imposed on women or the societal denial of genuine human connection.
  • Together, their "unnatural conception" of Esther Longtree, where the "third person" (a go-between woman) carries a silver spoon between them to enable conception, reflects a forced, artificial union that produces a complicated, burdened offspring (Esther), who embodies both the failures and contradictions of this relationship.
  • Given the racial elements in Esther's story, her first child born of a black man, and the tensions around race and identity, the parents can also be seen as symbolic of the racial divisions and unfulfilled promises of American society prior to the Civil Rights Movement of the 1960s. The father as authority and the mother as fragile tradition suggest the racial and social dynamics that left many marginalized and created fractured identities.
  • Esther's parents symbolize the fractured, unequal, and dysfunctional societal foundations of America, marked by racial segregation, gender inequality, and institutional failures. This interpretation is supported by the detailed symbolic narrative of their personalities and relationship, reflecting broader social and historical themes.
  • Esther's parents symbolize the divided and dysfunctional social order in America, embodying the tensions between authority and vulnerability, racial and gender divides, and the consequences of an artificial, loveless union producing a troubled next generation.

Research: Resources

  • Esther Longtree in this chapter is portrayed as a deeply tragic and complex figure, embodying sorrow, loss, mystery, and a profound connection to themes of fertility, death, and motherhood. Esther is described as a large, pregnant waitress, often weighed down not only by her physical condition but by the immense emotional burden of repeated stillbirths and lost children she carries within her memory and body. Her pregnancy is symbolic, described as “watery” and “wild,” with her body “pregnant with death,” indicating a continuous cycle of creation and loss intertwined in her existence. She is caught between hope and despair, weighted down "by the death of a small thing," her body swollen but also fragile, her spinal column curved by the weight of memory. Esther represents the paradox of fertility and sterility simultaneously. Though she is repeatedly pregnant, the children are stillborn or lost, rendering her motherhood incomplete and haunted by absence. This condition makes her a symbol of the "Song of Songs of the sterility which is the creation," where creation is intertwined with loss and death. Her pregnancy is not just physical but metaphysical, involving the vastness of the universe, stars, and the earth, all of which seem to be "killed" or destroyed, mirroring her personal tragedy. Her mental state is marked by suspicion, confusion, and a profound sense of mystery. She contemplates who might have "killed the heavens," the earth, and love itself, reflecting a cosmic grief that parallels her personal losses. She imagines a detective who is both a pursuer and a murderer, embodying the threat of exposure and judgment, while the children she once had or never had remain elusive, "the child that never was". Esther’s relationship with the detective is complex: she suspects him of having raped her and leaving her for dead, yet he is also the one who threatens to uncover her secret sorrows. Her narrative includes a haunting sense of being pursued and judged unfairly, and she is both victim and accuser in her own story. The chapter also touches on racial issues through the detective's selective interest in "white" deaths while neglecting "black" ones, revealing societal biases and injustices. Esther, being associated with the "quiet, black mystery," is marginalized and ignored by official justice, highlighting themes of racial invisibility and systemic neglect. Esther is haunted by old murders, tragedies, and lost children, both personal and historical. She reflects on a mass murderer, abortionist and other cases of maternal and infant death, drawing parallels to her own suffering and guilt. These old stories serve as a backdrop to her present torment and sense of isolation, deepening the theme of a past that refuses to be forgotten. Despite her suffering, Esther shows moments of defiant acceptance and even joy, laughing in her sleep and finding some beauty in the natural world and her own strange, wild condition. She is stubborn, proud, and insists on her innocence in the face of accusation. Her condition is "no dream" but a persistent reality, and she prefers the mystery and silence of her pain to exposure or judgment. Esther Longtree is a figure of immense sorrow and mystery, embodying the tragic intersection of life and death, fertility and sterility, hope and despair. She is pregnant with loss, carrying both physical and metaphysical burdens, haunted by memories, accusations, and societal neglect, especially in the face of racial injustice. Her story is a poignant, symbolic exploration of motherhood, tragedy, and the human condition.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes a tragic and complex history of motherhood, loss, and social neglect in the United States, especially reflecting the fates of unmarried or marginalized women and their children. Her story evokes the suffering of countless women who experienced stillbirths, miscarriages, or the loss of children under harsh social conditions. She is "always pregnant" yet often gives birth to "nothing," representing the grief of "stillborn" children and the immense sorrow that accompanies such loss. This condition is described as a vast, mysterious, and diffused crime or guilt that is both personal and cosmic in scale, involving death and sterility in creation itself. Esther Longtree's narrative intertwines with the grim history of illegal or dangerous abortions, as suggested by the story of the old woman abortionist who killed unmarried mothers and their babies in a hospital disguised as care. This history reflects the brutal reality many women faced in times when reproductive rights and safe medical care were inaccessible. The abortionist's killing of a woman who was "pregnant in her dreams" but had no child underscores the terror and stigma surrounding female reproduction and the societal condemnation of women’s bodies. Esther’s interactions with the white detective reveal the racial and social divisions in America’s history of violence and injustice. The detective focuses only on the deaths of white children, ignoring the countless black children lost or murdered: a commentary on racial indifference and systemic racism. Esther’s world is described as a "quiet, black mystery," where black children's deaths are overlooked, symbolizing the historical neglect and invisibility of black lives in American social and legal systems. Her burden of loss and the constant shadow of death she carries symbolize not only individual grief but also a collective history of women’s suffering, social marginalization, racial injustice, and the silencing of certain kinds of pain. Esther Longtree is a figure embodying the intersection of these historical realities: motherhood, loss, racial discrimination, and societal neglect in the US.
  • Who Killed Cock Robin is a common association with the mythology of Lugh, a warrior, a king, a master craftsman and a savior. He is also associated with Mercury and Baldr in Norse mythology. He was killed by Bran the Blessed, the god of winter in the form of a raven. Lugh is believed to have been given a Chirstian continuation through Saint Mologa in Ireland. Cock Robin appears seven times in Esther Longtree’s chapters. "Who killed Cock Robin?" repeatedly asked in the novel is not just about a single culprit but a symbol of the pervasive and inscrutable nature of death, loss, and guilt. It is a question without a definitive answer, reflecting the novel's exploration of mystery, suffering, and the silent tragedies that haunt Esther and the world she inhabits.
  • Young reminds us that the jury will consist of men. It was not until 1968 that all states in the US were required to let women serve on juries and not until 1975 that the Supreme Court decision made it federal law.
  • The idea of women dreaming or fantasizing about being raped comes from a long history supported by male dominated institutions where women are trained to be rape victims which is still being challenged today. The rape fantasy in women is man-made. Women use the rape fantasy to find their sexuality within the context of male sexuality or power drive.
  • The Song of Songs is an erotic poem. It is unique within the Hebrew Bible in that it celebrates sexual love. The two are in harmony, each desiring the other and rejoicing in sexual intimacy. Jewish tradition reads it as an allegory of the relationship between God and Israel In Christianity, it is treated as an allegory celebrating the love between God and Church or Christ and his bride, the Church. The Christian church's interpretation of the Song is evidence of God's love for his people, both collectively and individually. Over time a moral element and the bride as Virgin Mary were added. It is unique in that these conclusions are not found in the overtly theological books of the Bible. Those books reveal an imbalance in the relationship between God and man, but Song of Songs is a theological metaphor in which the two partners are equals, bound in a committed relationship. In modern times the poem has attracted the attention of feminist biblical critics, with Phyllis Trible's Depatriarchalizing in Biblical Interpretation and the Feminist Companion to the Bible series edited by Athalya Brenner and Carole Fontaine.
  • Mary Janes originated in the early 1900s, named after a character in Richard Outcault’s Buster Brown comic strip (1902), and were popularized by the Brown Shoe Company. Originally, brown or black, low-cut strap shoes were worn by both young boys and girls as formal attire. They transitioned into popular women's fashion in the 1920s-30s and became a 1960s mod icon.
  • Abortion has been used to separate good women from bad women. This stigma punishes the bad woman in society. Even if the abortion is necessary to save a woman’s life, religion often stipulates that a woman must sacrifice herself. It is better to die than live with the stigma of having an abortion. The only good heroine is a dead one. When Young was writing this over eighteen years, abortion and contraception were not legal.
  • “But he only dealt with the deaths of little white children, for the deaths of the little black children were not his business, there being so many and so unimportant.” When Young wrote this the civil rights movement had been going on since 1954.
  • The Chicago detective sent Esther a “yellowed newspaper clipping” that read “Mass Murderess Apprehended Accused by Dead Mothers and Dead Children.” There was nothing about the fathers. It was a “...woman abortionist and her timid little assistant…” who had killed “...all the poor, unmarried mothers and their babies, too, in a hospital which she ran for that purpose.” The mothers were described as well treated right up until their delivery. It said the fathers sent bouquets. When the mother was supposed to deliver, mother and baby were killed “...by the cruel, old abortionist, a large woman, weighing almost three hundred pounds.” The babies were buried with lime.
  • Lime is used at mass grave sites to capture the scent of decay and keep soil pH high. Low pH soil is an indicator for a mass grave as the decomposition products are acidic and lower the soil pH. Adding lime reduces this acidity.
  • The newspaper was dated as happening during the “horse and buggy age.” The “old woman abortionist” kept at her trade until she murdered a “...woman who was not, who never could have been a mother.” This story may have its roots in real events.
  • Baby farming is the historical practice of accepting custody of an infant or child in exchange for payment in late-Victorian Britain and, less commonly, in Australia and the United States. Some baby farmers adopted children by paying lump-sum payments, while others cared for infants for periodic payments. There are several women or couples in the past that murdered or allowed the adopted children to die through starvation. Even the Catholic run Bon Secours Mother and Baby Home in Ireland illegally adopted children without their mother’s consent and the Home had an abnormally high child death rate with malnourished, emaciated babies. A significant amount of children’s remains were discovered in a septic tank on the property. There was also mistreatment and abuse of the mothers.
  • One of the most famous baby farming child murderers was Amelia Dyer. She murdered infants in her care over a thirty-year period during the Victorian era in the United Kingdom. Trained as a nurse and widowed in 1869, Dyer turned to baby farming to support herself. She initially cared for the children legitimately, then began directly murdering children she took in, strangling at least some of them, and disposing of the bodies to avoid attention. She was caught because the body of a child was found in the river. The “timid assistant” may refer to Dyer’s 23-year-old daughter Polly who assisted in the child murder of Doris Marmon.
  • “...was natural and a mother should suffer—she would just deliver the child then in such a way that it would be born dead —and would kill the mother—but only after it had been the agony of birth.” This may refer to Genesis 3:16 as Eve and women’s punishment for being cast out of the Garden of Eden.
  • Esther may be suffering from False pregnancy or pseudocyesis. It is the appearance of clinical or subclinical signs and symptoms associated with pregnancy although the individual is not physically carrying a baby. The mistaken impression that one is pregnant includes signs and symptoms such as tender breasts with secretions, abdominal growth, delayed menstrual periods, and subjective feelings of a moving fetus. False pregnancy has a prominent psychiatric component as well as physical manifestations of pregnancy. It can be caused by physical or mental trauma, a chemical imbalance of hormones, and some medical conditions.
  • Esther thought he only solved the “white mysteries.” Esther guessed it might be dead brides or the missing father where the children played with the skull judging by the newspaper clippings the Chicago detective sent her. The missing father may refer to the story Madge told Homer during the bus ride in Chapter 7 about Mr. and Mrs. Tidings.
  • Once when he thought he was dreaming he “delivered a real baby...and said—Oh, I see it all now! Life is a dream, and I have been wrong and much wronged, and I must give up this practice!” This line may refer to a play by Pedro Calderon de la Barca called Life Is A Dream. Barca was a Spanish dramatist, poet, writer and knight of the Order of Santiago. Life Is A Dream is a philosophical allegory regarding the human situation and the mystery of life. The play's central themes are the conflict between free will and fate, as well as restoring one's honor. Other themes include dreams vs. reality and the conflict between father and son.
  • “Not she… so lonely, reaching out to love, to death which is another form of love. She was always right.” There are several characters, like Miss MacIntosh and Mrs. Hogden, that have manipulated their arguments so they are never wrong or never appear to be wrong.

Chapter 72
