This created resentment and gave rise to stereotypes of Jews as greedy and obsessed with money, which later fueled secular conspiracy theories about Jewish wealth and control. In the 19th century, antisemitic ideas evolved from religious prejudice into modern political and racial theories of antisemitism, giving rise to more elaborate conspiracy narratives. German novelist Hermann Goedsche published Biarritz, which featured a fictional scene of a secret rabbinical cabal meeting in a Jewish cemetery to discuss a plot for world domination. This work was a commercial success and was later plagiarized to create The Protocols of the Elders of Zion (circa 1903), this fabricated document is the most infamous antisemitic text. It was a forgery created by the Russian secret police to stir up antisemitism and deflect from public discontent with the Tsarist regime. The Protocols claim to be the minutes of secret meetings held by Jewish leaders outlining a plan to take over the world. Though repeatedly exposed as a hoax, it continues to circulate and influence conspiracy theories to this day. Antisemitic conspiracy myths played a central role in the rise of Nazism and the Holocaust. Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party adopted the Protocols as proof of a "Jewish world conspiracy". They used it to justify their persecution and extermination of six million Jews. They falsely claimed that Jews were behind communism, capitalism, and Germany's loss in World War I. The American industrialist Henry Ford distributed massive quantities of antisemitic material, including articles based on the Protocols, through his newspaper, The Dearborn Independent. He later retracted and apologized for his publications following a lawsuit, but the damage was already done. Following the Russian Revolution, an antisemitic conspiracy theory known as "Jewish Bolshevism" or Żydokomuna claimed that Jews controlled the Soviet Union and international communist movements. This false notion was promoted by anti-communist factions and heavily used by Nazi propaganda. In the modern era, antisemitic conspiracy theories have adapted to contemporary fears and platforms, continuing to spread hatred. "ZOG" theory (Zionist Occupation Government) theory, promoted by some white nationalists, claims that Jews secretly control Western governments. "Great Replacement" theory is a white nationalist conspiracy theory, which has influenced mass shootings, and claims that Jews are orchestrating a demographic "replacement" of white people through immigration. At the 2017 Charlottesville rally, participants chanted "Jews will not replace us". The internet and social media have facilitated the widespread dissemination of antisemitic conspiracy theories, with groups like QAnon promoting versions of the myth. These online forums and platforms amplify old lies and connect them to new global events, continuing the cycle of prejudice and misinformation.
  • The history of the Jewish rubber business is marked by individual entrepreneurial success, particularly in products like condoms, alongside the forced seizure of Jewish-owned businesses during the Nazi era. A prominent example is Julius Fromm, a Polish-German chemist who invented the modern condom and founded a successful rubber products company, only to have his factory stolen by the Nazis before he fled to England in 1939.
  • The shipwreck described in this chapter is a powerful and symbolic event that carries deep thematic weight. The shipwreck is recounted primarily through the perspective of the little toy salesman, who is portrayed as the lone survivor of a catastrophic maritime disaster during a fierce storm at sea.
  • The storm and subsequent sinking of the ship represent a cosmic upheaval, described as "a wild, raging storm between the cracking Poles," with the sea rising "in billows to the dark heavens hammering," and the moon and stars falling like sparks and rain of blood. This imagery evokes an apocalyptic vision of the world’s end, suggesting the collapse of order and the overwhelming power of nature and fate.
  • The little toy salesman survives the wreck, sitting alone in a rubber life boat while all others perish, including the captain, crew, women, children, and even celestial bodies like the moon and stars. His survival is depicted ambiguously; he is both pitied and condemned as a "murderer" because he did not drown with the others and thereby "killed" them by surviving. His survival seems almost accidental or unwilling; he "had wanted to do so," but was upheld by "swollen bladders" and "heaving breasts".
  • After the storm, the salesman experiences a prolonged "calm" that is described as worse than the storm itself, filled with loneliness, disorientation, and existential dread. He is surrounded by floating debris and bloated bodies, with a haunting "dead child's hand" that clings to him, symbolizing his inescapable connection to death and loss. This hand, which wears a gold ring like his own, is a spectral reminder of the dead children and the burden of survival.
  • The little toy salesman loses his memory, taste buds, tear ducts, and reason during the storm and the aftermath, which symbolizes a loss of self and disconnection from reality. His mind "cracking" and being "lost between the Poles like a leaf falling nowhere" reflects the disintegration of identity and the fragility of human existence in the face of overwhelming catastrophe.
  • The narrative critiques human selfishness and cruelty during the disaster: the old German sea captain orders men to jump into the sea while women and children take the lifeboats, reflecting societal and gendered survival biases. The passengers are described as conceited and snobbish, oblivious to their impending doom. The little toy salesman's survival contrasts with the collective fate, emphasizing themes of exclusion and difference.
  • The shipwreck is accompanied by powerful, almost liturgical imagery: "leaden church bells," "mourning bands," "a golden flood of music more beautiful than Bach, Beethoven, or Brahms," and the captain conducting as he goes down with the ship. This suggests the shipwreck as a kind of requiem or cosmic ritual. The black mourning band in the sky spanning horizon to horizon intensifies the sense of universal mourning.
  • The little toy salesman’s story parallels Esther Longtree’s ongoing "everlasting pregnancy" with the "little shadow boxer," symbolizing themes of birth, death, and hope amidst despair. The shipwreck and the salesman’s survival underscore Esther’s loneliness and the burden of nurturing life in a world shadowed by loss and uncertainty.
  • “He had dreamed in an everlasting silence. He had thought that his mother had killed him…” in the desert. This echoes stories about Cousin Hannah’s travels in desert countries.
  • “He whispered into her ear that there would be a great war and that the bad men would blow up the world some day of calm just for fun, that all the men and all the women and all the children would be killed, and…” everything would be poisoned and disappear forever.” This may refer to the proliferation of nuclear weapons during the Cold War. The Cold War saw a rapid nuclear arms race that saw the U.S. and Soviet Union build massive arsenals, which fueled the proliferation of nuclear weapons to other nations like the UK, France, and China. This escalation was driven by mutual suspicion and doctrines like Mutually Assured Destruction (MAD), but was tempered by arms control efforts such as the Partial Test Ban Treaty and the Non-Proliferation Treaty (NPT). The period is also marked by dangerous standoffs, such as the Cuban Missile Crisis, which underscored the need to prevent nuclear conflict. Little Boy was the codename for the type of atomic bomb dropped on the Japanese city of Hiroshima on 6 August 1945 during World War II. It was the first nuclear weapon used in warfare. Carl Jung had visions and dreams about carnage and thought he was going insane. From his journals it is considered a premonition of World War I.
  • The Gobi Desert is a vast, arid region in northern China and southern Mongolia. It's known for its dunes, mountains and rare animals such as snow leopards and Bactrian camels. In the Gobi Gurvansaikhan National Park, the Khongoryn Els sand dunes are said to sing when the wind blows. The park also features the deep ice field of Yolyn Am canyon. Dinosaur fossils have been found at the red "Flaming Cliffs" of Bayanzag.
  • The Arabian Peninsula, or Arabia, is a vast, arid region in Southwest Asia, bordered by the Red Sea, Persian Gulf, and Arabian Sea. As the birthplace of Islam and Arab culture, it comprises Saudi Arabia, Yemen, Oman, UAE, Kuwait, Qatar, and Bahrain. The region is historically known for its nomadic Bedouin traditions, significant oil resources, and rapid 20th-century urbanization.
  • The "English-only" movement in the US was characterized by waves of nativism and forced Americanization, peaking around World War I to target immigrants and minority languages. While English was the dominant language, it was not legally official, but rather enforced through laws, school policies, and cultural assimilation, aiming to eliminate bilingual education and marginalize non-English speakers, particularly German speakers. Although English predominated, early America was multilingual. However, English was established as the primary language of political, economic, and social life. Following a surge in immigration, President Theodore Roosevelt supported English-only efforts in 1907, promoting the idea that immigrants should become Americans, not "dwellers in a polyglot boarding house". World War I sparked intense hostility against German-Americans, leading many states to ban German in public spaces, schools, and even conversations. By 1919, 15 states mandated English as the sole language of instruction. Restrictions extended to foreign-language newspapers and, in some areas, required non-citizens to pay special taxes. By the 1940s, bilingual education had been virtually eliminated due to policies focused on rapid, forced assimilation. Explicit English-only policies were used to systematically eliminate indigenous languages in government-run boarding schools.
  • Chinese money evolved from ancient cowrie shells to the world's first paper currency (7th–15th centuries) and a dual system of copper "cash" and silver. Key developments included the Song dynasty’s invention of paper money, the Yuan dynasty’s reliance on paper notes, and later, the Qing dynasty’s shift toward silver, culminating in modern currency reforms in the early 20th century, culminating in the Renminbi's emergence.
  • Bathsheba was an Israelite queen consort. According to the Hebrew Bible, she was the wife of Uriah the Hittite and later of David, with whom she had all of her five children. Her status as the mother of Solomon, who succeeded David as monarch, made her the Gebirah of the Kingdom of Israel.
  • Siberia is a massive region covering over 5.2 million square miles (13.5 million square km) across Northern Asia, constituting about three-quarters of Russia's total territory. Known for its extreme, long, and cold winters, it features vast tundra, coniferous forests (taiga), and major mountain ranges, including the Ural and Altai. It contains Lake Baikal, the world's deepest lake, and is resource-rich, while being sparsely populated and historically significant for its indigenous communities and Russian expansion.
  • The Holy Land is a sacred region in the Southern Levant, primarily located within modern-day Israel and Palestine. It is revered by Jews, Christians, and Muslims as the setting for key biblical events, including the life, ministry, and death of Jesus Christ, as well as the birthplace of the Jewish people.
  • Kewpie is a brand of dolls and figurines that were conceived as comic strip characters by American cartoonist Rose O'Neill. The illustrated cartoons, appearing as baby cupid characters, began to gain popularity after the publication of O'Neill's comic strips in 1909, and O'Neill began to illustrate and sell paper doll versions of the Kewpies. The characters were first produced as bisque dolls in Waltershausen, Germany, beginning in 1912, and became extremely popular in the early 20th century.
  • A bandy-legged man has legs that curve outward at the knees, creating a bow-like shape where the knees are farther apart than the ankles when standing straight. Also known as bow-legged or genu varum, this condition often causes the legs to appear arched. The term refers to a physical, often congenital, alignment where the legs bend outward.
  • Ulster is one of the four historical provinces of Ireland, located in the north of the island. It traditionally comprises nine counties: six form Northern Ireland (Antrim, Armagh, Down, Fermanagh, Londonderry, and Tyrone), which is part of the United Kingdom, while three (Cavan, Donegal, and Monaghan) are part of the Republic of Ireland.
  • “The captain was crazy, too” This may refer to Wilhelm Furtwängler, a renowned German conductor. Furtwängler was known for his intense and passionate conducting style, despite having a paralyzed left arm from a childhood accident, which he often kept low or used minimally. He was considered one of the greatest conductors of his time. The novel's reference to him as a "German captain" could also subtly allude to his controversial position during World War II, when he remained in Germany under the Nazi regime.
  • “four ugly gamblers” may refer to the "Big Four" Allied powers during World War II, who led the fight against the Axis, were the United States, the United Kingdom, the Soviet Union (USSR), and China. These nations formed the core of the alliance, with China fighting Japan since 1937 and the others joining later.
  • “a woman who thought that she was two women” may refer to France who was also a major Allied power, particularly before its occupation and later during liberation.
  • Johann Sebastian Bach was a German composer and musician of the late Baroque period. He is known for his prolific output across a variety of instruments and forms, including the orchestral Brandenburg Concertos; solo instrumental works such as the cello suites and sonatas and partitas for solo violin; keyboard works such as the Goldberg Variations and The Well-Tempered Clavier; organ works such as the Schübler Chorales and the Toccata and Fugue in D minor; and choral works such as the St Matthew Passion and the Mass in B minor. He is known for his mastery of counterpoint, as heard in The Musical Offering and The Art of Fugue. Felix Mendelssohn precipitated the Bach Revival with a performance of the St. Matthew Passion in 1829. Ever since, Bach has been known as one of the greatest composers of classical music.
  • Ludwig van Beethoven was a German composer and pianist. One of the most revered figures in the history of Western music, his works rank among the most performed of the classical music repertoire and span the transition from the Classical to the Romantic era. Beethoven's early period, during which he forged his craft, is typically considered to have lasted until 1802. From 1802 to around 1812, his middle period showed an individual development from the styles of Joseph Haydn and Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart, and is sometimes characterised as heroic. During this time, Beethoven began to grow increasingly deaf. In his late period, from 1812 to 1827, he extended his innovations in musical form and expression.
  • Johannes Brahms was a German composer, virtuoso pianist, and conductor of the mid-Romantic period. His music is noted for its rhythmic vitality and freer treatment of dissonance, often set within studied yet expressive contrapuntal textures. He adapted the traditional structures and techniques of a wide historical range of earlier composers. His œuvre includes four symphonies, four concertos, a Requiem, much chamber music, and hundreds of folk-song arrangements and Lieder, among other works for symphony orchestra, piano, organ, and choir.
  • “the German captain went down with the ship” Captain Hans Langsdorff is the most famous German captain who went down with his ship metaphorically in WW2. After ordering his ship, the pocket battleship Admiral Graf Spee, to be scuttled in Montevideo on December 17, 1939, to save his crew, he died by suicide on December 20, 1939, in Buenos Aires. Hans Langsdorff chose to take his own life to prove that he acted with honor, ensuring his crew's safety after the Graf Spee was trapped by British cruisers. He is often cited for his moral courage and for prioritizing the lives of his crew over the strict, often suicidal, orders of the Nazi regime.
  • An antiphon is a short, often scriptural chant or verse sung as a refrain in Christian liturgy, particularly within Catholic Mass (Entrance, Offertory, Communion) and the Liturgy of the Hours (Lauds, Vespers). It acts as a thematic focal point for a specific day or season, usually accompanying psalms or canticles. Historically rooted in early Christian worship and favored by St. Ambrose, they were originally performed in a call-and-response style between two choirs.
  • Antipodes are points on Earth diametrically opposite to one another, representing the maximum distance apart on the globe. Most landmasses have their opposite point in the ocean, as 70% of Earth is water. The US mainland aligns with the Indian Ocean, Australia with the North Atlantic, and New Zealand with Spain/Portugal.
  • Nimbus primarily refers to a dark gray rain-bearing cloud (often associated with nimbostratus) or, traditionally, a luminous cloud/halo surrounding a deity or saint. Derived from Latin for "cloud," it represents an aura, atmosphere, or a specialized cloud type that produces rain.
  • Aureole is a circle of light or brightness surrounding something, especially as depicted in art around the head or body of a person represented as holy.
  • “the little rubber salesman, a victim of the Jews” may refer to Arthur Miller's play Death of a Salesman. The play features a character, Willy Loman, who is a failing salesman. While Arthur Miller was Jewish, the play itself is often considered a universal American tragedy about the failure of the American Dream, and Willy's Jewish identity is a long-debated topic among literary critics. Some productions and analyses have framed Willy as a Jewish character whose assimilation makes him vulnerable to societal pressures. The rubber pipe that Willy uses to commit suicide is a key symbol in the play. This is also a representation of the character's antisemitism, prejudiced and paranoid worldview within the fictional narrative.
  • Mongolians are an East Asian ethnic group native to Mongolia, China (primarily Inner Mongolia), and parts of Russia, numbering around 10 million in total. Known for a historical, enduring, and nomadic pastoralist tradition, they are closely linked to the Mongol Empire founded by Genghis Khan. They primarily speak Mongolian languages and practice Tibetan Buddhism and shamanism.
  • “The burning, sunlight was blackening his skin” may refer to the damage done by a nuclear bomb.
  • When the stranger, identified as the little toy salesman, recovers consciousness on the shore, the items he sees symbolize America as a landscape of accumulated detritus, lost potential, and the complex interplay of natural decay and human impact.
  • “purple oyster sponges, crab shells, jellyfish like glass, and bones of dead fish”: These natural elements represent the raw, indifferent cycles of nature, where life and death are constantly intertwined. The "glassy" jellyfish can also hint at the blurred lines between reality and illusion that permeate. This aspect of America is ancient, untamed, and a vast receptacle for the remnants of countless lives, both human and non-human.
  • “little carcasses of other little children”: This deeply tragic image symbolizes the profound loss of innocence and unfulfilled potential within the American experience. It resonates with Esther Longtree's story of stillbirth fantasies and lost children, suggesting a hidden sorrow or the casualties of a harsh reality that often goes unacknowledged.
  • “playing cards”: Playing cards in the novel are often associated with chance, fate, and the illusions of control, as seen in scenes with gamblers. Their presence on the shore suggests America as a place where fortunes are gambled, where outcomes are subject to unpredictable forces, and where the remnants of failed risks are left behind.
  • “old junk”: This broad category signifies the accumulation of discarded material, reflecting a society of consumption and the inevitable detritus of progress. It speaks to America as a land that produces and discards, where forgotten objects bear witness to past lives and aspirations.
  • “rubber tires”: As specific man-made discards, rubber tires represent the waste product of modern industry and transportation. They highlight the impact of human activity on the natural landscape, suggesting a departure from a pristine wilderness towards an environment marked by the remnants of ceaseless movement and consumption. This also connects to the little toy salesman's later identity as a "rubber salesman".
  • “birth control devices”: The inclusion of these items is particularly striking, pointing to themes of sexuality, control over reproduction, and perhaps the anxieties or deliberate choices related to creating or preventing life. In a novel deeply concerned with motherhood, loss, and the nature of existence, these devices symbolize attempts to manage or deny natural processes, or the consequences of such interventions in the American context.
  • Collectively, these items portray America not as a land of simple, idealized dreams, but as a complex, often melancholy landscape where the natural world is inextricably mixed with human-made refuse and the poignant echoes of lives lived and lost. It is a place of stark reality, littered with the tangible evidence of decay, chance, and the profound, sometimes tragic, consequences of human existence, leaving the returning "stranger" with a sense of alienation and a confrontation with a less glamorous truth.
  • “there would be a great war and that the bad men would blow up the world some day of calm just for fun” may refer to the Cold War. The Cold War was a period of international geopolitical rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union and their respective allies, the capitalist Western Bloc and communist Eastern Bloc, which began in the aftermath of the Second World War and ended with the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991.
  • "red haw" most commonly refers to the Red Hawthorn, a small, thorny deciduous tree or shrub native to North America known for its white spring flowers and bright red fruits. It is also referred to as Downy Hawthorn or Scarlet Hawthorn.

Chapter 5

← Chapter 4 · Home · Chapter 6 →

Summary

Night falls on the bus. The roads are flooded and there are no stars or signposts. The bus waits at a Pennsylvania Railroad crossing while Madge moans in her sleep, accusing every man but her husband. Moses sings, drinks, and holds forth. He refuses ever to cut his hair. He rails against the Democrats and the New Deal, though he never has time to vote. He lives with his old mother, has never married, and talks constantly of pregnant women and of old Doc O’Leary, who once delivered babies and has now lost his mind. Birth and death fill his talk. The chapter leaves open whether Moses is driving the bus or only dreaming that he drives it.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Moses Hunnecker · Justice O’Leary · Miss Pebbles · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Fear and Courage · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Birds · Clouds and Storms · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Pregnancy, Birth, and Children · The Bus and the Journey

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Edgar Allan Poe · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Civil War · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with the depiction of the bus-driver, Moses Hunnecker, losing his way, driving through a landscape of washed-out roads, fallen trees, and empty air. This journey seems endless and cyclical, capturing a sense of existential disorientation and decay. The imagery of “no stars, no sign-posts now,” and “a crazy bus-driver losing his way that he knew too well” evokes a world without guidance or hope, emphasizing the theme of wandering and searching for meaning.
  • A large portion of the chapter focuses on the bus-driver Moses’s refusal to cut his hair. His hair is described as growing continuously, becoming intertwined with his identity and his “immortal” self. It is his “only virtue,” his “angel,” his connection to life amid desolation. The hair is also political as a symbol of his resistance to the Democrats and the societal changes he despises, representing his claim to personal freedom and his soul. His hair grows like “golden tassels tossing in the wind,” full of “burning eyes like the eyes of Argus,” symbolizing watchfulness, memory, and vitality amidst decay.
  • The bus-driver, Moses, is portrayed as a lifelong Republican, openly hostile to the Democrats whom he blames for the country’s ruin (“running this old country straight into its grave.”) He links his hair to his political identity, refusing to let the government control or “tax” even that last piece of himself. His tirades against political corruption, free public projects, and the decline of society are interwoven with his personal narrative and symbolic hair.
  • The chapter outlines a tension between the bus-driver, Moses, and an old, senile doctor, Old Doc/Justice O’Leary, who persists in imagining a world of birth and vitality or a world that no longer exists. The doctor’s practice is described as a delusion, with “no patients but the stormy petrels in a land where were no stormy petrels.” The bus-driver mocks the doctor’s illusions and refuses his medical help, reflecting a conflict between life and death, reality and imagination. This interplay highlights themes of denial, madness, and the persistence of hope or delusion in a dead country.
  • The chapter contains intense imagery of death and desolation from the flooded graves, dead fish, drowned seeds, barren trees, to the wild mares dreaming of pregnancy but carrying only death. Yet, paradoxically, it also speaks of rebirth and cyclical renewal (“you died every minute that you lived... and you were born every minute that you died”) though this cycle appears to be trapped in despair and futility. This duality underscores the existential and metaphysical concerns of the chapter.
  • Towards the end, the bus-driver, Moses, questions his own reality and wonders if he is truly driving or merely dreaming in his four-poster bed. He contemplates death, resurrection, and the meaning of existence. His long hair, the enemies (the Democrats), the old doctor’s empty practice, the empty hotel, and the desolate landscape all blend into a hallucinatory vision of a world on the brink of oblivion. His repeated references to his mother, his hair, and his political stance deepen the sense of personal and societal collapse.
  • The closing passages have the bus-driver, Moses, singing and murmuring amidst the rain, addressing the old doctor and his imaginary patients, declaring the futility of birth and renewal in a dead land. He embraces his identity as the bus-driver, calls old Doc “the bringer of pain,” and expresses a bitter, resigned acceptance of the endless, repetitive journey through a world without stars or hope.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • Moses says his hair “was his angel, his dead mother who lived in him, his dream of life.” Why does a man who has kept nothing else keep his hair?
  • Old Doc sees “the breath on the mirror where there was no breath, the feather move where there was no feather.” How does the chapter keep turning the signs of life into signs of death?
  • The road keeps “passing the same things again and again.” Why might the novel make Vera’s journey a circle?

Characters

  • Moses insists he is “my mother’s son and not my mother’s daughter,” yet says he is “Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses.” What is he afraid of becoming?
  • Moses and old Doc are mirror images, two bearded men who never married. Why does Moses need an enemy so like himself?
  • Madge accuses “every man but her husband who slept at her side.” What does this reveal about her before her story is told?

Connections

  • In Chapter 4 the fat lady warned of “the jumping-off place,” and here Moses uses the same words. How does the Middle West begin to take shape out of other people’s warnings?
  • Moses calls the passengers “four angels at four bed-posts, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John.” What changes when a bus ride becomes a bedtime prayer?
  • The chapter returns to Moses’s politics again and again. How is his hatred of the Democrats really about fear of losing himself? See The New Deal (Ch 5).

Reflection

  • “There may be only one way to get into this world . . . but there is more than one way to get out of this world.” How does this chapter blur the line between birth and death?
  • Moses swears never to cut his hair “as long as the Democrats were running us.” What vows do people keep long after the reason is gone?
  • Moses says, “I never saw life come, but I have seen life go.” What does it mean to know death better than birth?
  • Is Moses driving the bus or dreaming that he drives it? Does it matter to the passengers?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Vera watches the bus-driver and the other passengers, including Madge, capturing their physical and emotional states with a keen, almost clinical eye. She notes Madge’s moaning and accusing, Moses’s erratic behavior and long hair, and the desolate landscape outside. Her observations are detailed, conveying a sense of decay, confusion, and suspended time.
  • Vera’s narration is imbued with philosophical undertones. She reflects on themes of life and death, creation and destruction, reality and illusion.
  • She engages with the bus-driver’s thoughts and conversations, especially his long monologue about his hair, politics, and existential musings.
  • Vera seems to understand the symbolic weight of the bus-driver’s hair as a metaphor for identity, resistance to corruption, and his connection to life amid death.
  • Vera’s narration conveys a sense of uncertainty about the reality of their situation. The bus-driver himself seems caught between dreaming and waking, life and death, and Vera shares this ambiguity.
  • She hints that the bus-driver may be dead or dreaming, trapped in a liminal space where time loops and places vanish. This uncertainty colors her perspective, making her more contemplative and less definitive in her judgments.
  • Vera is empathetic to the people around her. She also maintains a certain detachment. She does not intervene or change the course of events but rather records them with a mixture of sorrow, irony, and resignation. Her tone suggests an understanding of the tragic absurdity of their journey and the existential plight of the characters.
  • Vera functions as a bridge between the reader and the symbolic, almost hallucinatory world of the chapter and for the rest of the novel. Through her narration, the reader gains access to the bus-driver’s inner turmoil, the desolate landscape, and the metaphysical questions raised.
  • Vera’s bus trip exists in a liminal space between reality and dream, serving as a profound metaphor for her search for life and truth amid the illusions and uncertainties that surround her.

Moses Hunnecker (The Bus-Driver)

  • Central figure, described as wild-eyed, drunken, and somewhat erratic.
  • His long hair and beard symbolize his identity, freedom, and resistance to external control.
  • He is a life-long Republican, openly hostile to Democrats, whom he blames for the country’s decay.
  • He is a caretaker figure for his mother and is caught between delusion and reality, possibly dead or dreaming while driving an old bus.
  • His internal monologue reveals a deep existential crisis and philosophical reflection on life, death, and meaning.

Justice O’Leary (Old Doc)

  • Represents a figure of lost hope and failed medical practice.
  • He is senile, long-bearded, and imagines he is still delivering babies and practicing medicine in a dead world.
  • Symbolizes a dying or decayed authority, clinging to illusions and the past.
  • Moses criticizes him for bringing misery and being out of touch with reality.

Miss Pebbles

  • She is a figure embodying deafness and detachment from reality, both literally and metaphorically.
  • Her physical deafness also isolates and makes her unable to engage fully with the world around her.
  • This deafness symbolizes a disconnection from the living world and the ongoing turmoil and a futile or incomplete attempt to connect or listen.
  • Her perceptions and experiences are filtered through dreams or illusions rather than reality which further emphasizes her detachment and perhaps a coping mechanism against the bleakness surrounding her.
  • She complains to the desk clerk about being kept awake by noises that are in fact spectral or imaginary. These hauntings reflect a world where the boundaries between life and death, reality and illusion, have blurred, and Miss Pebbles exists trapped in this liminal space.
  • Her character serves as a poignant contrast to the bus-driver’s chaotic, vivid awareness of the world’s decay and the surreal events transpiring around them. While the bus-driver wrestles with his drunken consciousness and the metaphysical implications of his journey, Miss Pebbles is insulated, unable or unwilling to fully confront these realities. Her state can be seen as symbolic of denial or the human tendency to retreat into subjective realities when faced with overwhelming despair and madness.

Madge Capehorn and Homer Capehorn

  • Madge is a figure of tragic endurance and profound emotional pain, trapped in a loveless and alienating marriage with Homer, who is depicted as passive, innocent, and disconnected. Their relationship embodies the novel’s exploration of despair, loss, and the elusive nature of human connection, with Madge’s pregnancy serving as a potent symbol of both life and death, hope and despair.

The Pregnant Women (Imaginary Patients)

  • Appear as spectral or hallucinated figures in the old doctor’s dreams.
  • Symbolize the barren or dead future, as none are truly alive or giving birth.
  • Their cries and suffering are echoes of lost hope and the cyclical nature of life and death.

Research: Themes

Death and Resurrection

See: Death and Mortality

  • The bus-driver’s journey is metaphorical, possibly representing a passage between life and death.
  • References to being buried alive, resurrection, and dying twice highlight the blurred line between existence and nonexistence.
  • The cyclic nature of life and death is emphasized by imagery of birth cries, death moans, and eternal return.

Identity and Resistance

See: Identity and the Self · Fear and Courage

  • The bus-driver’s refusal to cut his hair symbolizes holding onto personal identity and autonomy despite external pressures.
  • Hair represents a personal dream, a physical manifestation of selfhood that remains even when everything else decays.

Political and Social Decay

See: Decay and Ruin · Society, Class, and Race

  • The bus-driver’s tirades against Democrats reflect frustration with political corruption and societal decline.
  • The country is depicted as a “dead country,” with broken roads, empty towns, and lost hopes.

Illusion vs Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The narrative questions what is real and what is imagined: the bus-driver might be dead, dreaming, or trapped in a cycle of madness.
  • The old doctor’s practice is a hallucination; the pregnant women are ghosts of a lost future.

Isolation and Loneliness

See: Isolation and Connection

  • The bus-driver is isolated, both physically on his journey and mentally in his state of drunken delirium and existential despair.
  • No one else truly communicates or understands him; the old doctor is never there when Moses rails at him, and the passengers sit silent behind him.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Bus and the Journey

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • The bus is a metaphor for life’s journey, fraught with obstacles, detours, and a lack of clear direction.
  • The journey may represent the soul’s passage through life and death or a psychological odyssey.

Hair

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Symbolizes identity, resistance, and the last vestige of personal freedom.
  • The bus-driver’s hair grows uncontrollably, reflecting his wild imagination and refusal to conform.

Old Doctor’s Instruments

  • Rusted forceps, broken stethoscope, and apothecary weights symbolize decay and the death of old certainties.

Pregnant Women and Birth Imagery

See: Pregnancy, Birth, and Children

  • Represent potential and hope but also pain, suffering, and the cycle of life and death.
  • Their ghostly presence emphasizes barrenness and lost futures.

Stormy Petrels, Woodpeckers, Red-winged Blackbirds

See: Birds · Clouds and Storms

  • Represent chaos, disturbance, and the persistence of nature amid decay.

Four Passengers / Angels (Matthew, Mark, Luke, John)

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • Suggest a spiritual or religious dimension to the bus-driver’s journey, hinting at judgment or salvation.

Research: Resources

  • “Oh, the old grey mare, she ain’t what she used to was”: The “Old Gray Mare” song is believed to have originated as a campaign ditty in the 19th century, specifically as a political jab at seven-term Baltimore mayor Ferdinand Latrobe by Democratic political operative Thomas Francis McNulty. The tune itself comes from J. Warner’s minstrel song “Down in Alabam’” (1858). The tune has been adapted for various purposes, including Civil Rights songs and as a way to underscore the decline of aging. This song reflects the bus-driver’s weary, somewhat erratic state as he navigates the flooded roads, facing obstacles and detours, mirroring the theme of decline and weariness pervasive in the narrative. The old gray mare can be seen as a metaphor for the bus-driver himself, his vehicle, or even the broader journey of life marked by fatigue, struggle, and a sense of things not being what they once were.
  • “all the glass-blowers, the night watchman”: Natural gas found in east-central Indiana in the 1880s drew glass factories, among them Ball Brothers in Muncie (1887), and glass-blowers were among the best-paid skilled workers of the day.
  • “We were stopped by the shunting cars of the Pennsylvania Railroad”: The Pennsylvania Railroad was once the largest railroad in America by traffic and revenue, and it called itself “the Standard Railroad of the World.”
  • “Three shakes of a dead dog’s tail”: The bus-driver gives a grim twist to the old phrase “two shakes of a lamb’s tail,” meaning in no time at all.
  • “It’s the jumping-off place. It’s where creation stops”: The fat lady on the train used the same words in Chapter 4. See the Chapter 4 resources.
  • “seeing the breath on the mirror where there was no breath, the feather move where there was no feather”: Holding a mirror or a feather to the lips was the old test for death. King Lear, holding the dead Cordelia, calls, “Lend me a looking-glass; / If that her breath will mist or stain the stone, / Why, then she lives,” and then, “This feather stirs; she lives!” See Shakespeare.
  • “the elegiac music of the spheres or with those heavenly harmonies no mortal ears could hear”: Pythagoras taught that the planets make music as they move, a harmony too constant for human ears to notice. See Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres.
  • “the great dolphins uplifting the stone boats of the dead upon the turbulent waves”: In Greek myth and funeral art dolphins carry souls across the sea and rescue the drowning, as they saved the poet Arion when sailors threw him overboard.
  • “coming like all the furies”: The Furies, or Erinyes, were the Greek goddesses of vengeance who hunted down wrongdoers. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the Burma-Shave signs, the broken rail fences”: The Burma-Shave sign series first appeared on U.S. highways in 1926 and remained a major advertising component until 1963. It was usually a series of six consecutive signs along the edge of highways. See Burma-Shave signs (Ch 5).
  • “his memory of the polar star”: Polaris, the North Star, stays nearly fixed above the North Pole, and travelers have long steered by it.
  • “holy Lucifer and Lucifer matches”: Friction matches were sold as “Lucifers” from 1829, and the name stuck to matches for a century.
  • “so that he might hide himself away from the face of God”: Adam and Eve hid “from the presence of the Lord God amongst the trees of the garden” (Genesis 3:8), and the murderer Cain says, “from thy face shall I be hid” (Genesis 4:14).
  • “His hair had grown three inches since he left Persia at sunset”: Persia is a real small town in western Iowa. Midwestern towns often borrowed faraway names, such as Peru, Lebanon, Cairo, Moscow, and Athens. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “the sky had been filled with red-winged blackbirds”: The red-winged blackbird is one of the most common birds in North America, and in winter it gathers with grackles and cowbirds in flocks of millions. See Birds.
  • “turning her broken earphones off and on”: Early electric hearing aids, with a microphone, a battery, and an earphone, came into use in the early twentieth century and replaced the ear trumpets of Chapter 4. See the Chapter 4 resources.
  • “full of burning eyes like the eyes of Argus if he had lived, full of eyes like the peacock’s burning tail”: Argus Panoptes is a many-eyed giant in Greek mythology. This is known to have generated sayings like the eyes of Argus, which means to be subject to scrutiny of one’s actions to an invasive degree. The “eyes of Argus” metaphorically convey the idea of a penetrating, multifaceted vision or insight or seeing many facets or truths simultaneously, reflecting the novel’s themes of layered realities and the complex perceptions of its characters. Hera set Argus to guard Io, and after Hermes lulled him to sleep and killed him, Hera set his hundred eyes in the tail of her peacock. See Argus Panoptes (Ch 5).
  • “this womb of time”: Iago says, “There are many events in the womb of time which will be delivered” (Othello 1.3). See Shakespeare.
  • “he could always, if things got too much for him, hang himself by the hair of his head”: King David’s son Absalom was caught by the head in an oak, by tradition by his long hair, and was left hanging until he was killed (2 Samuel 18:9). Moses’s vow never to cut his hair is also the Nazirite vow, “there shall no razor come upon his head” (Numbers 6:5), and Samson lost his strength when his hair was cut (Judges 16).
  • “the way the Democrats were running this old country straight into its grave”: The New Deal faced opposition due to concerns that it strayed too far towards socialism, expanded presidential power unconstitutionally, and potentially redistributed wealth. Some critics believed the government was not doing enough to combat the Great Depression, while others argued the New Deal’s policies hindered private enterprise and individual liberty. Many critics, including the American Liberty League, saw the New Deal as a step towards socialism, arguing it involved excessive government intervention in the economy. Opponents, like Robert A. Taft, argued that Roosevelt was exceeding his constitutional authority and expanding the powers of the presidency. Some feared that the New Deal policies would lead to a massive and potentially detrimental redistribution of wealth. Critics, like Herbert Hoover, argued the New Deal would create a bloated bureaucracy, intrude on business, and limit personal liberty. Some believed the New Deal’s policies, such as increased business taxes and Social Security excise taxes, harmed businesses and discouraged hiring. Critics also questioned the New Deal’s effectiveness in addressing the Great Depression, arguing it didn’t create enough jobs or revive the economy. The reaction of Moses to the New Deal policies symbolizes the broader social and economic upheavals of the era, seen through the eyes of a common man who feels alienated and distrustful of political leaders and their solutions. The chapter uses his perspective to illustrate the anxieties and conflicts within American society at that historical moment. See The New Deal (Ch 5).
  • “What with all these free-lunch counters”: Saloons once set out a “free lunch” of ham, pickles, and bread for anyone who bought a nickel glass of beer, the salt in the food keeping customers drinking.
  • “They say we are all equal in the sight of God”: The Declaration of Independence holds that “all men are created equal,” and Paul writes, “ye are all one in Christ Jesus” (Galatians 3:28). Moses answers that God “did not create us all alike.”
  • “an old retriever, a dog with a bird in its mouth. It’s a wild duck”: In Henrik Ibsen’s The Wild Duck (1884) a wounded wild duck dives to the bottom to die and is brought up by a clever dog. The family keeps it in their attic, and the play turns on the illusions people need in order to live.
  • “the bus-driver was no fly to be caught in that spider’s web”: Mary Howitt’s poem “The Spider and the Fly” (1829) begins, “Will you walk into my parlour?” said the Spider to the Fly.
  • “to sleep in the country churchyard”: Thomas Gray’s “Elegy Written in a Country Churchyard” (1751) mourns the humble dead of a village, where “The rude forefathers of the hamlet sleep.”
  • “will cover me with a coat of hair like the wild asses that live in the desert places”: In Job 39:5-8 God asks, “Who hath sent out the wild ass free?” and says that he scorns the city. Jacob says of his brother, “Esau my brother is a hairy man” (Genesis 27:11).
  • “all those Brain Trusters were busted with their W.P.A. projects”: Brain Trust was a term for a group of close advisers, most associated with the advisers to Franklin Roosevelt. A newspaper gave the name in 1932 to Roosevelt’s circle of professors, chiefly Raymond Moley, Rexford Tugwell, and Adolf Berle.
  • “their W.P.A. projects and their public parks and their marble bird baths and their rotten roads and their free skating rinks”: WPA (Work Projects Administration) was an American New Deal agency which employed millions of mostly unskilled men to carry out public works projects to provide employment during the Great Depression. It began in 1935 as the Works Progress Administration and was renamed in 1939. Its workers, about 8.5 million in all, built parks, roads, and skating rinks and ran nursery schools, which is why Moses complains of “free kindergartens.”
  • “why don’t you just close their wombs, tie the knots?”: Indiana passed the first eugenic sterilization law in 1907, and in Buck v. Bell (1927) the Supreme Court upheld forced sterilization. Tens of thousands of Americans were sterilized under such laws.
  • “the barber who was once a blood-letter, too”: Bloodletting, practiced since ancient times, reached its height in the 18th and 19th centuries, with various instruments and techniques developed to facilitate the process. Leeches were also used to draw blood, and lancets and scarificators were employed to create incisions for blood removal. Prominent physicians and surgeons, including John Hunter, endorsed bloodletting for various conditions. In 18th and 19th century America, physicians, barber-surgeons, and even barbers could practice bloodletting. While physicians often recommended bloodletting, barbers and barber-surgeons, who also performed minor surgeries and grooming services, frequently carried out the procedure. In America Benjamin Rush bled patients heavily during the Philadelphia yellow fever epidemic of 1793. The “bloodletting” in the chapter symbolizes obsolete medical practices and, by extension, the ineffectiveness of attempts to control or cure the pervasive decay and suffering in the world depicted in the novel. See the Chapter 3 resources on the barber pole.
  • “is the blood of Abel crying from the ground that I should live to see these bloody flowers?”: This may refer to the story of Cain and Abel in Genesis 4:10, where God says, “the voice of thy brother’s blood crieth unto me from the ground,” and where Abel’s blood carries a power that doesn’t let Cain settle again on the earth. The first human death could symbolize the future violence which pollutes the earth. God uses a flood later on in Genesis to purify the earth. This phrase encapsulates Moses’s anguished contemplation of human suffering’s enduring cry through history and its impact on her perception of life and the world around her.
  • “have we elected a king or a congress? What’s the senate doing?”: This could be referring to the presidency of Franklin D. Roosevelt (FDR) who was elected to a record four terms as president before the Twenty-second Amendment, ratified in 1951, limited a president to two terms. His 1937 plan to add justices to the Supreme Court led critics to charge that he wanted to rule like a king.
  • “remember that you are a good Republican and that we shall never have free medicine”: Roosevelt left health insurance out of the Social Security Act of 1935 for fear of the American Medical Association, and when Truman proposed national health insurance in 1945, the AMA fought it as “socialized medicine.” The universal healthcare discussion in this chapter serves to underscore one of the novel’s key themes: the tension between the ideal and the practical, between dreams and reality, and the social ethics of care and responsibility. It represents a call for tangible, practical action in a world marked by suffering and deprivation.
  • “He would not trust himself in that secret box”: The secret ballot, printed by the government and marked in private, came to the U.S. from Australia, and the states adopted it between 1888 and the 1890s. Before that, voters often cast party tickets in public view.
  • “his White Horse, his Long John, his Johnnie Walker, his fire water”: The different whiskeys represent both Moses’s personal struggles and the broader themes of despair, escape, and the search for meaning in the novel’s interior American setting. Prohibition ended in December 1933, Roosevelt’s first year in office, after the Democrats ran on repeal, so Moses drinks freely under the party he hates.
    • White Horse Scotch Whisky is a blended Scotch whisky from Edinburgh, first produced by James Logan Mackie in about 1890.
    • Long John Whisky may refer to Long John Macdonald, a bootlegger who took out a license and founded the Ben Nevis distillery at Fort William in 1825.
    • Johnnie Walker is a brand of Scotch whisky now owned by Diageo that originated in the Scottish burgh of Kilmarnock in East Ayrshire. The brand began with the grocer John Walker, who opened his Kilmarnock shop in 1820 and was selling whisky by 1825. The Johnnie Walker name and the Striding Man logo came from his grandsons’ rebranding in 1908 and 1909.
    • Firewater is a strong alcohol and may also be called moonshine. Some sources suggest that “firewater” may have originated as a term used by Native Americans to describe alcohol. The term “firewater” is thought to be a translation of the Algonquian Indian word “scoutiouabou,” which means the same thing.
  • “old fool gives up his sceptre and his crown of stars and his golden throne”: The “old fool” is Roosevelt. Moses swore not to cut his hair “until Roosevelt got out of the White House,” so the sceptre, crown, and golden throne mock the president’s long hold on office. Scepter is a staff or wand held in the hand by a ruling monarch as an item of royal insignia. A crown of stars is a circle of stars often representing unity, solidarity and harmony in flags, seals, and signs and is also in motifs related to the Woman of the Apocalypse (Revelation 12:1) and Baroque allegorical art depicting the Crown of Immortality. The Crown of Immortality is a metaphorical symbolic representation of eternal life, often depicted in art and literature. It’s a traditional symbol of honor, achievement, and immortality, often associated with religious or spiritual concepts. It can be visualized as a laurel wreath or a circle of stars. A golden throne symbolizes divine authority, high status, and opulence. In various cultures, it represents the power and majesty of rulers, deities, or figures of significance. The use of gold, a precious and revered metal, further enhances this symbolism, connecting it to concepts of wealth, divinity, and triumph. The phrase captures a theme of resistance to inevitable change, the stubbornness of old power figures, and the futility of clinging to decaying authority in a world that moves on. It underscores the chapter’s atmosphere of decay, entrapment, and social criticism expressed through the bus-driver’s bitter, drunken monologue.
  • “in a dark night of the human soul”: The phrase comes from the Spanish mystic Saint John of the Cross, whose poem “The Dark Night” (1500s) describes the soul’s passage through darkness to God. The Dark Night of the Soul has been described as a type of evolution where it has been recognized that those things that are limited need to be set aside and to press forward with patience and perseverance. In this chapter, the “Dark Night of the Soul” signifies the profound inner crisis of confronting the shadow side of existence (birth and death, loss and love, illusion and reality) captured in Moses’s night of screaming women and his question whether it was “his birth or his death he was living through once again”. See the Chapter 4 resources and The Dark Night (Ch 5).
  • “stormy petrels in the way of the old bus-driver”: The petrel may be named for Saint Peter, since it seems to walk on the water. Sailors took the storm petrel as an omen of bad weather, and “stormy petrel” came to mean a troublemaker. See Birds.
  • “Jezebel!”: Jezebel is in the Book of Kings in the Hebrew Bible. She is known for violently purging the prophets of God from Israel and instituting the worship of Baal and Asherah. She was later put to death by defenestration or being thrown from a high place or window. In the Book of Revelation (2:20) she is symbolically associated with false prophets. Before her death Jezebel “painted her face, and tired her head” (2 Kings 9:30), dressing her hair, a fitting curse in a chapter so taken up with hair. “Jezebel” in this context represents a symbol of moral judgment and inner conflict within the bus-driver’s troubled psyche during a moment of dark reflection and suffering.
  • “the woodticks ticking like old town clocks”: The deathwatch beetle bores into old timbers and taps its head against the wood to call a mate. The ticking, heard in quiet rooms at night, was long taken as an omen of death. Moses’s woodticks ticking “like old town clocks that went on after they had stopped” carry the same omen.
  • “he was Penelope weaving this web, not Ulysses who wandered over the wide seas”: Penelope is a character in Homer’s Odyssey. The reference to Penelope highlights themes of waiting, fidelity, and steadfastness amid uncertainty and absence. Penelope, the faithful wife of Odysseus in Greek mythology, is renowned for her patience and loyalty, waiting many years for her husband’s return from the Trojan War while warding off numerous suitors. She put off her suitors by weaving a shroud for her father-in-law Laertes by day and unraveling it each night.
  • “his immortal hair was the part of him that was immortal, that would never die, that would keep on growing”: Hair and nails do not continue to grow after death. While it may appear that way due to dehydration and skin shrinking, it’s an optical illusion. The actual growth of hair and nails requires complex hormonal regulation and the continued production of new cells, which ceases upon death. Hair and nails symbolize the fragile boundary between appearance and reality, life and death, strength and vulnerability, serving as potent metaphors for the characters’ inner lives and existential conditions.
  • “He had been told of people buried alive and crying in their graves”: While there appears to be an overestimation of the number of people buried alive accidentally in this chapter, in 1885 a victim was found inside his coffin with much of his hair pulled out. The fear was widespread in the nineteenth century. Poe’s story “The Premature Burial” (1844) turns on it, and inventors patented “safety coffins” with bells, air tubes, and flags so that anyone who woke underground could signal. See Edgar Allan Poe.
  • “not even if Gabriel should blow his horn to resurrect us all”: Gabriel is an archangel first described in the Hebrew Bible (Daniel 8:16). The reference to Gabriel serves to mark the bus journey as not merely physical but spiritual, underscoring the novel’s exploration of mortality, transcendence, and the search for meaning beyond the material world. The Bible does not name the angel of the last trumpet, only “the trump of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16); tradition gave the horn to Gabriel.
  • “There would still be those rusted forceps of his”: Obstetric forceps for delivering babies were invented by the Chamberlen family in England, who kept them a family secret for more than a century.
  • “the apothecaries’ weights that he used for paper weights”: Druggists weighed medicines in grains, scruples, drams, and ounces, the apothecaries’ system, until the metric system replaced it.
  • “bare footprints in the dust, long and light, some with webbed toes”: Syndactyly affects 1 in 2,000 to 3,000 births and most frequently in white males where there is webbing (extra skin between the toes and/or hands). Throughout history, people with birth defects, including those with syndactyly, faced stigma and marginalization. In some cultures, birth defects were seen as a sign of divine displeasure or as having supernatural origins, leading to fear or even infanticide. In this chapter the webbed toes belong to old Doc, who goes about in “his long white nightgown with his webbed toes,” and to the bare footprints in his office, “some with webbed toes, footprints of things unhuman.”
  • “That same stream which a child could wade in was that same river which a man could drown in”: Pope Gregory the Great wrote that Scripture is like a river, “shallow enough here for the lamb to go wading, but deep enough there for the elephant to swim” (Moralia in Job).
  • “you died every minute that you lived, got a new skin every seven years”: The popular belief that the body renews itself every seven years is a myth. Skin in fact replaces itself in about a month, though some cells last a lifetime.
  • “as if he had been old Father Time himself”: Father Time is the old man with a long beard, a scythe, and an hourglass, the figure of passing time and death.
  • “you remembered only the last thing you saw”: In the nineteenth century some believed the eye of a dead person kept the last image it saw, and police photographed the eyes of murder victims hoping to see the killer. The idea was called optography.
  • “the undertaker . . . had done an excellent sidetrade in the furniture business”: In nineteenth-century America the town cabinetmaker often made coffins as well as tables and beds, and many furniture dealers became undertakers. Embalming, the undertaker’s art “to paint the dead and make them seem alive,” spread after the Civil War, when soldiers were embalmed to be sent home and Lincoln’s embalmed body was carried across the country. See The Civil War.
  • “no credit in the book of human life, none by the recording angel”: In Jewish and Christian tradition an angel records every deed of a person’s life. In Laurence Sterne’s Tristram Shandy the recording angel drops a tear on a sinful oath and blots it out forever.
  • “old Doc with his broken stethoscope”: The French doctor René Laennec invented the stethoscope in 1816, at first a simple wooden tube, so that he would not have to put his ear to a patient’s chest.
  • “these shotgun weddings”: A shotgun wedding was a marriage hurried along because the bride was pregnant, as if her father stood behind the groom with a gun.
  • “imagining he was drunk on ether and starlight”: In the nineteenth century people breathed ether for fun at “ether frolics” before doctors used it to put patients to sleep. See the Chapter 1 resources on ether.
  • “in his second childhood”: In Shakespeare’s As You Like It, Jaques’s seven ages of man end in “second childishness and mere oblivion.” See Shakespeare.
  • “He should have been a horse-and-buggy doctor”: The country doctor who drove his buggy to farmhouses at all hours was celebrated in Arthur Hertzler’s bestselling memoir of practice in Kansas, The Horse and Buggy Doctor (1938).
  • “not a cent with which to pay old Charon when they crossed the river in a leaking boat”: Charon in Greek and Roman mythology is the ferryman to Hades or the underworld. Charon symbolizes the passage through death or the threshold between life and death, reinforcing the novel’s exploration of mortality, memory, and the liminal spaces of existence. The Greeks put a coin, an obol, in the mouth of the dead to pay the ferryman, so the dead without “a cent” cannot cross. See the Chapter 3 resources.
  • “It was a dead country”: Moses’s dead country of the empty box factory, “the foundry that had no bricks and no fires and the bell-tower that had no bells,” and “the filling station that was always closed” is the small-town Middle West emptied by the Depression. The decline of rural America is a multifaceted issue with roots in the 19th century and continuing into the present day. It’s driven by factors like industrialization, urbanization, and economic shifts, leading to population loss, declining infrastructure, and increased poverty. As the U.S. industrial sector grew, urban areas became magnets for jobs and economic opportunities, drawing people from rural areas. This shift began in the late 18th and early 19th centuries, and continued into the 20th century. Technological advancements in agriculture led to increased efficiency and the displacement of farm workers, further contributing to out-migration from rural areas. Rural areas struggled to keep pace with industrialization and urban growth, often experiencing higher poverty rates and fewer opportunities compared to cities. From the mid-20th century on, rural areas lost manufacturing jobs as factories closed and industries moved to urban centers. Rural areas often have older populations, with fewer young people choosing to stay and contribute to the workforce.
  • “four angels at four bed-posts, Matthew, Mark, Luke, John”: Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John are the authors of the first four books of the New Testament, collectively known as the Gospels. These books provide accounts of the life, teachings, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. They are not simply historical accounts but are also theological interpretations of Jesus’ life. Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John in the chapter symbolize the four passengers as spiritual or angelic figures, evoking the Four Evangelists and thus linking the narrative to themes of spiritual journey, life, death, and cosmic judgment. Moses is reciting the old bedtime prayer known as the White Paternoster, recorded in the 1600s: “Matthew, Mark, Luke, and John, / Bless the bed that I lie on. / Four corners to my bed, / Four angels round my head.”
  • “Conceived on boxwood, born on cedarwood, died on wormwood”: These three woods form a thematic triad reflecting the novel’s exploration of reality versus illusion, preservation versus decay, and comfort versus bitterness. Boxwood and cedarwood evoke the desire for stability and lasting truth, as embodied by Miss MacIntosh and the grounded aspects of Vera’s search for reality, while wormwood represents the bitterness, loss, and spiritual malaise that haunt Vera’s life and her mother’s opium-induced coma.
    • Boxwood has several meanings in the bible: 1) In Isaiah 41:19, boxwood is listed among trees God will plant in the desert, symbolizing divine provision and the restoration of Israel. 2) Isaiah 60:13 mentions boxwood as part of the adornment of God’s sanctuary, representing beauty and God’s presence. 3) The use of boxwood in prophetic visions symbolizes resilience and God’s ability to shape creation with purpose and care.
    • Cedarwood has several meanings in the bible: 1) Cedar wood, known for its strength and resistance to decay, is associated with the construction of sacred spaces like the Temple of Solomon, symbolizing endurance, holiness, and divine presence. 2) The cedars of Lebanon symbolize the flourishing and prosperous life of the righteous, often associated with grandeur and splendor. 3) The use of cedar in palaces and homes represents security and shelter. 4) Cedar can also symbolize human pride and the subsequent downfall, as seen in Ezekiel 31:3.
    • Wormwood has several meanings in the bible: 1) Wormwood, known for its bitter taste, is used metaphorically to represent bitterness, affliction, remorse, and punitive suffering. 2) Wormwood symbolizes the bitter consequences of turning away from God, like idolatry, disobedience, and injustice. 3) In Revelation 8:10-11, the falling star called “Wormwood” symbolizes a catastrophic event, divine judgment, and the consequences of spiritual infidelity. 4) In Lamentations, wormwood is used to describe the profound grief and suffering caused by God’s judgment.
  • “don’t come after me with those old pruning hooks”: Isaiah 2:4 foresees a time when nations “shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks.”
  • “Take away your bellows. There’s no living spark”: God breathed into Adam “the breath of life” (Genesis 2:7). In the eighteenth century the humane societies founded to rescue the drowned tried to revive them by blowing air into their lungs with bellows.
  • “Go play your double flutes somewhere else”: The aulos, the double pipe of ancient Greece, was the instrument of satyrs, of Dionysian revels, and of funerals.
  • “as long as I’m my mother’s son and not my mother’s daughter”: In this time period writers like Ernest Hemingway and others were concerned about the masculine point of view in their writing. Through recorded time there has been a fear of the feminization of men and boys that will bring about the downfall of society. For all the hysteria that successive waves of feminism have wrought, the patriarchy continues to fight back with the rise of authoritarianism and fascism. Both fully constrict women and children to their assigned “natural roles.” Choice for women and children is restricted or completely eliminated.
  • “the angels crying, crying like loons”: The common loon’s wailing call carries for miles across northern lakes at night, and its wild sound gave rise to the phrase “crazy as a loon.” Moses calls old Doc “crazy as a loon” a few lines later. See Birds.
  • “you black Republican”: Historically, the term “Black Republican” has had different meanings: 1) Before the Civil War, it was used as a derogatory term for abolitionist members of the Republican Party. 2) During Reconstruction the term was also used for Republicans who supported legislation that favored African Americans. 3) During and after the Civil War the term was used to refer to members of the Negro Republican Party, a faction of the Republican Party in the South that was predominantly made up of Black Americans. 4) From the 1870s to the 1960s it was associated with the “black-and-tan faction” of the Republican Party in the South, which opposed the segregationist “lily-white movement”. Moses, a life-long Republican, hurls his own party’s name at old Doc as an insult, as he did moments before with “you damned Republican trying to fleece me.”
  • “mad enough to go off his beam”: In the 1930s pilots flew along radio range beams, and a pilot who strayed heard the signal change. “Off the beam” came to mean off course or wrong.
  • “It ain’t going to rain no more, no more”: “It Ain’t Gonna Rain No Mo’,” Wendell Hall’s comic song of 1923, was one of the great hits of the decade.
  • “The old grey goose is dead. Died in the morning”: The folk song “Go Tell Aunt Rhody” (also known as “The Old Gray Goose is Dead”) has a rich history rooted in both European and American traditions. The melody originated as a gavotte in Jean-Jacques Rousseau’s 1752 opera Le Devin du Village. An English version of the opera was produced in London in 1766, and the tune subsequently inspired various English lyrics, including “Sweet Melissa”. Around 1825, the tune began appearing in U.S. hymnals, and the Aunt Rhody version, a common American folk song, has appeared in numerous song anthologies. The lyrics tell the story of a gray goose that is being saved to make a feather bed, but dies. The song’s lyrics are often interpreted as expressing grief or loss, specifically the death of a loved one, but it’s also been suggested that the goose’s death is a matter of gain for those who need feathers for their beds. “The old gray goose is dead” symbolizes the pervasive presence of death and the fragility of life in the narrative. It underscores the chapter’s mood of desolation, the cyclical nature of existence, and perhaps the inevitability of loss that haunts the characters on their journey. See Go Tell Aunt Rhody (Ch 5).
  • “the cigar store Indian puffing his pipe”: Carved wooden figures of Native Americans stood outside tobacco shops from the nineteenth century, because Europeans had learned tobacco from Native peoples. The figures were a stereotype and have mostly disappeared.
  • “You know me, Moses Hunnecker, the bus-driver”: Like the Moses of Exodus, the bus-driver leads his people through a wilderness toward a promised land, and the biblical Moses saw the Promised Land from Mount Nebo but never entered it (Deuteronomy 34). See Moses Hunnecker’s name carries Biblical freight (Ch 5).
  • “A doctor ought to bury his secrets, bury his mistakes”: An old saying holds that doctors bury their mistakes. Frank Lloyd Wright gave it a twist in 1953: “The physician can bury his mistakes, but the architect can only advise his clients to plant vines.”
  • “maybe he should have let that excellent old doctor look at him”: Moses refuses old Doc again and again and only at the end wonders whether he should have let him look. Men have long avoided doctors and medical help because of fear and feeling vulnerable.
