Chapter 82

← Chapter 81 · Home

Summary

Vera thinks of all she could have confessed to Esther. Her mother is dead. The sea swept away the house with its golden towers, leaving chandeliers strewn along the shore, and only the string of pearls she wears remains to her. She is mourning three deaths. At the end, Catherine rose from her bed and walked. Mr. Spitzer carried her into the garden by the sea and declared his love. He told her he was really Peron, and that it was Joachim who had died. But Catherine had already died in his arms before he spoke. He also lost his old valet, the clam-digger, in the storm. Vera sees Miss MacIntosh anew: "Whatever is average is the dream. Whatever is hidden is the revealed." At dawn in the hotel corridor she meets a stone deaf man, who lost his hearing at fourteen. They become lovers, and he whispers that their child will be his ear. They plan to marry and invite everyone, the flowers and birds and Esther Longtree, who hangs a misspelled sign in the restaurant window, "Owt to luntsch. bee bak in a whale."

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Esther Longtree · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · The Old Clam-Digger · The Stone Deaf Man · Lucie Bell

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Music, Sound, and Silence · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Time

Symbols: Dogs · Fog and Mist · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Pearls and Jewels · Silence and Deafness · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Deafness and Sign Language · Exploration and the Poles · Homer’s Epics · The Bible · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Vera reflects on the death of her mother, Catheine, the destruction of the house with its golden turrets and towers by the sea, and the scattering of chandeliers along the shore. This passage sets a tone of mourning and the dissolution of past grandeur and illusions. The only remaining possession is a string of pearls worn by Vera, symbolizing a fragile connection to her lost heritage and memories. Vera mourns "three deaths" and is "in love with an older love than memory provided".
  • A significant section meditates on the experience of deafness as a metaphor for exile and loss. Vera compares the deaf to marble statues who perceive much but miss the vital auditory dimension of reality. The silence is described as a cold, alien world, yet it also holds a unique, possibly more beautiful mode of communication beyond speech. This passage deepens the theme of isolation and the limits of human perception, emphasizing that even those who hear do not perceive everything, while the deaf may be haunted by imagined sounds or the absence of words.
  • The narrative details Catherine's gradual return from a drug-induced dreamlike state to a fragile awareness before her death. Mr. Spitzer, who had loved Catherine secretly and faithfully, waited for a moment to confess his love, which ultimately came too late. The image of Mr. Spitzer carrying Catherine in his arms into the garden by the sea, speaking of his long-buried love as the sea and nature respond around them, is poignant and symbolic of unfulfilled love and the mystery of death. Catherine dies as Mr. Spitzer speaks, underscoring the bittersweet timing and the intersection of life, death, and love.
  • Mr. Spitzer reveals that he is actually Peron/Jock, not the dead brother Joachim, introducing a complex identity theme and the idea of living with the memory of a lost self. His grief over Catherine’s death and the loss of the old clam-digger valet is profound. The old clam-digger, a loyal companion who drowned in the storm, symbolizes the loss of grounding and connection in a world slipping into chaos and dissolution.
  • The descriptions of the old clam-digger’s habits (burying himself in the sand, being mistaken for part of the landscape, developing nervous tics) serve as a metaphor for the human condition in the face of time and loss. Despite physical preservation, there is a spiritual or intellectual departure, resulting in a "living corpse." This passage contemplates the nature of life, death, and decay in a subtle, haunting way.
  • Toward the end of the chapter, Vera hears the voice of a stone deaf man who, though unable to hear, speaks and sings in a world of silence. His voice, full of longing, loss, and fragmented thoughts, expresses the paradox of communication without sound. Vera falls in love with this silent traveler, highlighting a theme of love transcending conventional senses and communication. The deaf man’s reflections on missed sounds and the imaginary world emphasize the elusive boundary between reality and dream.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a recurring motif of life as a dream, of love preceding words, and of silence having its own language. Vera and the stone deaf man imagine a wedding attended by wildflowers, birds, and nature itself, a symbolic union beyond earthly conventions. The chapter closes on a note of tender acceptance and mystery, with Vera embracing love and silence as intertwined realities.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Vera

  • Reflective and deeply emotional, Vera grapples with mourning, love, and the nature of existence.

Esther Longtree

  • Mentioned as someone Vera might have confided in but who perhaps would not fully understand or be interested. Represents a contrasting perspective on loss and endurance.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A complex figure who reveals his true identity as Peron, the brother of Joachim. He has waited years to confess his love and to close a chapter on the past. His grief is profound, encompassing the loss of Catherine, the old clam-digger, and his own illusions.

Catherine

  • Once beautiful and dreamlike, she lived in a state between life and death, sustained by drugs and illusions. Her death and the destruction of her home symbolize the dissolution of a dream or an era.

The Old Clam-Digger (Valet)

  • A loyal servant and companion to Mr. Spitzer, embodying endurance and the passage of time. His disappearance in the storm represents another loss for Mr. Spitzer.

The Stone Deaf Man

  • A poignant figure who cannot hear but communicates and experiences the world through other senses. He is symbolic of isolation yet profound inner life and love beyond words. The woman he is with when Vera first meets him is Lucie Bell.

Lucie Bell

  • She appears as a complex and symbolic figure intertwined deeply with themes of love, silence, and loss. She is depicted not merely as a character but almost as an embodiment of elusive and silent love within a world fraught with communication barriers and existential solitude. Lucie Bell is portrayed as a "silent girl" who is intimately connected to silence and absence of speech. The narrator, Vera, hears a man's voice repeatedly calling out to her, lamenting that Lucie Bell be "a little bird girl with such a small, pecking face and such long, thin legs" who "make[s] too much noise" and is "not my love" because she cannot answer him or give love in return through words. This man’s voice speaks of a deep yearning for a silent love, one that transcends verbal communication, which reflects the novel’s broader preoccupation with the limits and possibilities of communication. Lucie Bell represents a love that exists beyond spoken language, a theme emphasized by the stone-deaf man's narrative. He explains how he hears not with ears but with his eyes and fingers, experiencing the world through a different sensory reality. Lucie Bell’s silence and absence echo the deaf man’s experience, symbolizing a love that must be understood through nonverbal means, through "the tongues of silence speaking the name of love". Her silence is not emptiness but a different form of communication and connection, one that is accessible only through deep empathy or alternative perception. The man who calls out to her also expresses feelings of abandonment and unfaithfulness, suggesting that Lucie Bell left him or was "fickle," loving a jukebox or a "tired marathon skater" more than him. This reflects a tension between presence and absence, fidelity and loss, which permeates the narrative. Lucie Bell’s departure before Vera arrives adds to the sense of missed connections and unfulfilled love in the novel. Although Vera never sees or hears Lucie Bell directly, she deeply loves the deaf man who loved Lucie Bell, indicating that Lucie Bell serves as a bridge or catalyst for Vera’s understanding of love in a silent, fragmented world. Lucie Bell’s absence and silence foreground Vera’s own quest for connection amidst loss and the failure of conventional communication. Lucie Bell can be seen as part of the novel’s meditation on sensory loss, altered perception, and the mysteries of human connection. Just as the narrator reflects on the deafness, blindness, and the nature of communication beyond the ear and eye, Lucie Bell embodies the challenge of loving and being loved when traditional modes of interaction fail or are absent.

Research: Themes

Loss and Mourning

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Vera mourns not only Catherine but also the loss of a dreamlike past, the family estate, and symbolic “pearls.” Mr. Spitzer’s layered grief includes his brother Joachim, Catherine, and the old clam-digger.

Illusion vs. Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine’s life was sustained by dreams and drugs, blurring the line between waking life and sleep, life and death. Vera questions what is real and what is dream.

Silence and Communication

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Extensive meditation on deafness, silence, and the limitations and beauty of communication beyond words. The stone deaf man represents the world of silence yet full of inner sound and love.

Time and Timelessness

See: Time

  • Time is experienced unevenly, accelerating at moments and suspended in others. Catherine’s slow death, Mr. Spitzer’s long wait, and the clam-digger’s timeless endurance reflect different relationships with time.

Love Beyond Death

See: Death and Mortality · Love

  • Mr. Spitzer’s confession of being Peron and his love for Catherine after her death touches on eternal love transcending mortality.

Nature and the Sea

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The sea is a powerful force of destruction and transformation, symbolic of change, loss, and perhaps renewal. It carries away the house and treasures but also represents the boundary between worlds.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Sea

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represents overwhelming change, the passage of time, and the erasure of the past. It is both nurturing and destructive.

Pearls

See: Pearls and Jewels

  • The only remaining inheritance of Vera after the storm. Symbolize lost treasures, memories, or purity.

The Old White Horse and Surrey

See: Horses and Carriages

  • Symbolize the passage toward death and the journey between worlds. The horse turning into silver, blue, green, and gold hints at transformation and transcendence.

The Silent Dog and Barking

See: Dogs · Silence and Deafness

  • Represent intuition and knowledge beyond human perception, especially about death.

Music and Silence

See: Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness

  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity as Peron and his music represent communication beyond words and the connection between the living and the dead.

The Stone Deaf Man

See: Silence and Deafness

  • Symbolizes isolation, alternate perception, and the power of love and inner sound beyond physical hearing.

Fog and Moonlight

See: Fog and Mist · Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Indicate ambiguity, the boundary between clarity and obscurity, life and death, dream and reality.

Further notes from the text

  • Vera’s mourning begins with the house: the sea has swept over the opium paradise, the divan upheld by dolphins dreams under the flood, and no lawyer will be needed for the estate, because nothing is left to administer.
  • Catherine’s last hours are framed as a paradox Mr. Spitzer understood: she would die if her enchantment continued, and she would die if she rose and walked again. She rises, takes a few steps, and dies.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s declaration, that he was really Peron, comes with his usual rolling periods, as if to assure himself that what he says is true, or not quite true. Vera does not decide which.
  • The old clam-digger, Mr. Spitzer’s valet, used to bury himself in the sand with only a hole for his mouth and nose, so that the herring gulls mistook him for a moss animal or a rock. The storm takes him with the house.
  • Left alone like an old barnacled boat, Mr. Spitzer asks how he will pass his time, and the novel turns to Miss MacIntosh’s creed of the average and the middle way, which Vera now sees anew.
  • The songs and hymns of the chapter gather the book’s images, the Rock of Ages, the lighthouse beam for the wanderer, the waters that have gone over the soul, and repeat its oldest line: my beginning was my end, and my end was my beginning.
  • The stone deaf man’s ears are in his fingertips. His former love, Lucie Bell, left him before Vera came. Vera loves him “as a mother might love a child” and as a woman loves a man, and they plan a wedding to which everyone is invited, Esther Longtree included.

Research: Resources

  • Nepenthe is a mythical, ancient Greek potion or drug used to induce forgetfulness of pain, sorrow, or grief. It is famously mentioned in Homer's Odyssey as a gift to Helen of Troy to ease her suffering.
  • Scaling refers to the adjustment of size, scope, or intensity, with meanings ranging from enlarging/reducing dimensions in mathematics and design to increasing business operations, or removing deposits from teeth. It fundamentally involves changing the scale of a subject.
  • A jackdaw is a small, highly social bird in the crow family, known for its striking pale-gray eyes and a distinctive silver-gray "shawl" on the back of its head. It is commonly found in urban areas, farmland, and woodlands across Europe, Asia, and North Africa.
  • Tatterdemalion describes a person wearing ragged, torn, or disreputable clothing, or refers to something in a state of decay, filth, or disrepair. Originating in the early 1600s, this term often used for a "ragamuffin" implies a shabby, unkempt appearance. As an adjective, it means ragged or dilapidated.
  • Gannets are seabirds, closely related to boobies. They are known as 'solan' or 'solan goose' in Scotland. A common misconception is that the Scottish name is 'guga' but this is the Gaelic name referring to the chicks only.
  • The Arctic tern is a tern in the family Laridae. This bird has a circumpolar breeding distribution covering the Arctic and sub-Arctic regions of Europe, Asia, and North America.
  • “beach cherry” Eugenia reinwardtiana is a shrub to small tree in the family Myrtaceae. Native to tropical forests in Indonesia, the Australian state of Queensland, and many Pacific Islands, its common names include Cedar Bay cherry, beach cherry, Australian beach cherry, mountain stopper, nīoi, and a'abang.
  • “eel grass” Zostera is a small genus of widely distributed seagrasses, commonly called marine eelgrass, or simply seagrass or eelgrass. The genus Zostera contains 15 species.
  • The hymns Miss MacIntosh sings reveal a profound spiritual dimension to her character. While she often dismisses religious belief as "mockery of faith" or "human exaggerations", these songs from her childhood represent an enduring, if conflicted, faith. They expose her inner struggles with vulnerability, physical and emotional wounds, and the existential human condition of being lost and in need of guidance. These moments of singing, even as she performs mundane tasks, highlight the tension between her practical life and her deep, unarticulated spiritual longings, demonstrating that her common sense and brusqueness are often a defense against profound personal suffering and a search for meaning in a chaotic world.
  • "Lo, she would lift her eyes to the hills from whence cometh help." This references Psalm 121, often the basis of hymns about looking to the hills for help.
  • "Thou didst turn Thy face from me, and I was troubled" echoes lament or penitential psalms.
  • "For Thou art my strong rock and my castle, so also be my guide." This refers to God as a "strong rock and castle," a common biblical metaphor used in hymns.
  • "Thou hast covered me, and Thou hast numbered the hairs of my head, and Thou hast closed the wound of my side. Thou hast plucked out the arrows." These lines evoke biblical imagery associated with God’s protection and healing, reminiscent of hymns about divine care and salvation.
  • "Song of the shepherd who would lead all sheep home, losing none in narrow defiles" alludes to the Good Shepherd theme common in Christian hymns.
  • "Song of the Rock of Ages cleft for me" directly mentions the famous hymn "Rock of Ages."
  • "Songs of the Rugged Cross" refers to the hymn "The Old Rugged Cross," focused on the crucifixion.
  • Songs of the shaded valley, of the still stream" evoke traditional hymn imagery of peaceful pastoral scenes symbolizing God's care.
  • "Songs of those who reel to and fro and stagger like a drunken man, of the lost soul, of the pinioned wings" suggest hymns that address human frailty, being lost, and spiritual struggle.
  • Songs "of the lighthouse beam which lights the way to the poor wanderer tossed upon the rolling waves far from any harbor" is a metaphor often used in hymns about guidance and salvation.
  • "Awake, thou lute and harp, she sang. I myself will awake right early." This references the hymn "I Will Awake and Watch with Tears," based on Psalm 59.
  • "The waters have drowned us. The stream has gone over our soul." echoes lament themes of being overwhelmed, common in many hymns.
  • “When the white girls turned their faces away from him, an old Negro woman down the road said to him, And what difference, little boy, for you be a man, don’t you, and you dream on! You be like us now. All must suffers for something that be not their fault, you because your skin be white and we because our skin be black…” This sudden inclusion of a Negro woman plays into the Magical Negro trope in cinema, television, and literature. The character often has no past but simply appears one day to help the white protagonist. They usually have some sort of vague magical power. The character is patient and wise, often dispensing various words of wisdom. Racism historians traced the trope to the late fifteenth century and early sixteenth century. The Magical Negro stereotype serves as a plot device to help the white protagonist get out of trouble, typically through helping the white character recognize his own faults, overcome them and teaching him to be a better person. Although the character may have magical powers, their magic is used to help and enlighten a white male character.
  • Vera comes to terms with the other adults in her life:
  • Catherine: Vera’s view of her mother changes drastically by the end of the novel. While Vera used to see her mother as a beautiful lady sleeping in her swan boat, Vera comes to terms with her mother's death and sees her mother as poor, as if she had been evicted from her house long before she died and wandered like a beggar through the streets. This is vastly different from the beautiful woman Vera once idolized.
  • Mr. Spitzer: Vera learns the truth about Mr. Spitzer's identity, that he was Peron, not Joachim, and that his life had been a "celestial joke". She understands his love for her mother, a love hidden and unfulfilled for many years. Vera sees him as someone who has lost everything and is living in the past. She recognizes his grief over the loss of the old clam-digger was greater than that of her mother.
  • Miss MacIntosh: Vera acknowledges that her love for Miss MacIntosh came late, only when she saw beyond the surface of her character. Vera realizes that Miss MacIntosh's apparent mediocrity hid a phantasmagoric dream. Vera understands that despite Miss MacIntosh's seemingly sensible nature, she was drawn to the ocean's depths and eventually drowned.
  • Vera says, "Esther Longtree would be me," this holds deep symbolic and thematic significance. This statement reflects Vera's identification with Esther Longtree as a representation of a universal, enduring love and connection to all forms of life and experience, especially those that are broken, silent, or marginalized. Throughout the narrative, Vera contemplates profound themes of loss, silence, death, and the complexities of human love and perception. Esther Longtree emerges as a figure who embraces life and love despite her own hardships, embodying a kind of maternal, nurturing spirit who "loved us all and all things hurt or silent or broken or dead or living". Vera’s final identification with Esther suggests a merging of identities, where Vera aspires to embody Esther’s compassion, endurance, and openness to the multiplicity of loves and sufferings that define human existence. Esther is not presented as a traditional role model in terms of success or societal status but rather as a symbol of the "average," the "hidden," and the dream-like qualities of life and love that transcend ordinary perception. Vera recognizes in Esther a power and enchantment beneath the surface that she had been too wrapped up in herself to fully perceive earlier. Esther represents a bridge between the ordinary and the extraordinary, the visible and the hidden, the living and the dreaming. By choosing Esther as her role model, Vera acknowledges the importance of embracing the "average" and the "hidden" aspects of life, which can "crumble into the most phantasmagoric dream that man has dreamed" and that "all the shining waters dream beyond the surface cold and bare". Esther’s figure embodies the theme that through acceptance of loss, silence, and the unseen dimensions of existence, one can attain a deeper, more inclusive love and one that is not dependent on words or conventional communication but flows through "tongues of silence" and "all our loves". Vera’s statement is not merely an adoption of Esther’s persona but a profound recognition of the values Esther symbolizes: compassion for the silent and broken, an embrace of the unseen dimensions of reality, and a love that transcends ordinary understanding. It marks a transcendence of Vera’s earlier isolation and mourning toward a more universal, interconnected understanding of love and existence and an acceptance of the dream-like, silent world that Esther inhabits and loves. Vera chooses Esther Longtree as her role model because Esther represents the enduring, silent love that encompasses all life’s contradictions, sufferings, and mysteries, and through this identification, Vera finds a way to affirm her own place in the continuum of love and loss that the novel so poignantly explores.
  • The final chapter marks a significant shift in Vera's narrative. After recounting the stories of Esther Longtree, Miss MacIntosh, Mr. Spitzer and her mother, Vera turns her attention to her own experiences and a newfound love with a stone deaf man. This signals a move towards personal redemption and finding meaning amidst the chaos and illusions that permeate the novel.
  • Vera's relationship with the stone deaf man highlights the theme of communication beyond conventional means. Since he cannot hear, their connection relies on visual cues, touch, and unspoken understanding. This echoes the novel's broader exploration of how people connect despite their individual limitations and the illusory nature of reality.
  • The stone deaf man's perspective offers a unique insight into the world of silence. He claims that all the waters of creation had smashed against his ears, leaving him stone deaf. He is bombarded by loud noises in his mind, but it is a silent world. Silence allows Vera and her lover to connect on a deeper level, transcending the superficiality of spoken words. The silence also seems to be a way for him to be closer to death.
  • The stone deaf man's experiences also emphasize the importance of imagination. Having lost his hearing at fourteen, he lives in a world where sounds are memories or creations of his mind. This reinforces the novel's recurring motif of the power of imagination to shape reality and find beauty in the face of adversity.
  • The relationship between Vera and the stone deaf man shows an acceptance for one another. He accepts that she can hear and she accepts that he cannot. This can be compared to the acceptance that Miss MacIntosh has for death and Vera has for her mother's opium addiction.
  • Recurring Themes
  • The line between illusion and reality continues to blur in this chapter. The stone deaf man's perception of the world is shaped by his unique sensory experience, highlighting the subjective nature of reality. He says that life is imaginary and this is an imaginary world.
  • Vera's loss of her pearls symbolizes the shedding of material possessions and the pursuit of deeper meaning. Her relationship with the stone deaf man offers a path towards redemption, as she finds love and connection in unexpected circumstances.
  • The chapter explores different facets of love – maternal love, romantic love, and universal love. Vera's love for the stone deaf man transcends physical limitations and societal norms, representing a pure and unconditional form of affection. She feels elegiac even before her love arrives.
  • The thought of death, especially Vera's death, is brought up many times. The stone deaf man cannot hear the silent horn that Gabriel will blow.
  • Concluding Thoughts
  • The ending remains ambiguous, leaving the reader to ponder the ultimate meaning of Vera's journey. The novel does not offer easy answers but instead celebrates the complexities and contradictions of human existence.
  • The final chapter reinforces the novel's celebration of the unconventional and the marginalized. Vera's choice to embrace a relationship with a stone deaf man challenges societal expectations and highlights the beauty of finding love in unexpected places.
  • The final chapter suggests that the power of imagination and the capacity for love can transcend the limitations of reality. Despite the losses and disillusionments Vera has experienced, she finds solace and meaning in her connection with the stone deaf man, embracing a world where silence speaks volumes and love knows no bounds.
  • Vera and the stone deaf man plan to get married, and they plan to invite everyone. The stone deaf man believes that their procreation will provide life that can transcend his limits. There is hope because the next generation will lead the way. I explore Marguerite Young's work on Substack.

Chapter 67

Summary

The bus reaches an Indiana tavern and cannot park between a leaking milk truck and a hearse. Moses curses at old Doc, whom he believes is blocking the space with his ghost car. The passengers rock wearily in their seats. Madge laughs breathlessly, and Homer recalls a fun house of mirrors with no doors, wondering which door Jacqueline found.

Characters present

Moses Hunnecker · Justice O’Leary · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Key passages

From the research

  • Moses curses and talks to old Doc, an unseen presence whom children shoot at with bean-shooters. This dialogue reveals a sense of loneliness and grandiosity, as Moses argues with someone who cannot respond. Moses feels that old Doc should move his "old ghost buggy" to let the bus park, suggesting a metaphorical traffic conflict between the living and the dead, or between progress and stasis. Moses’s speech about traffic rules (chalk lines, detour signs, slow turns) symbolizes the need for order in life and relationships, but also the impossibility of such order in this surreal setting.
  • Moses’s exhaustion is palpable as he drapes himself over the steering wheel, singing softly and lamenting his situation. Homer and Madge are caught in an "infinite weariness," reluctant to leave the bus, suggesting a deeper existential fatigue or a reluctance to face reality. Moses’s talk of increasing the town’s population by three contrasts with old Doc’s apparent failure to contribute positively, adding layers of irony and social commentary.
  • Moses describes Old Doc’s "old ghost buggy" as an old Ford without essential parts, and accuses Doc of being dead "from the shoulders down." This blurring of lines between life and death deepens the surreal atmosphere. Moses threatens to scatter "heathen Chinee" inside Doc’s buggy and warns of a "hot time in the old town tonight" with buzzards arriving, intensifying the ominous tone. This passage may symbolize the clash between vitality and decay, or between the living’s struggle to move forward and the dead’s hold on space and memory.
  • Vera briefly contemplates that old Doc might be the undertaker in the hearse, blending the roles of doctor and death. This ambiguity deepens the theme of mortality and the thin boundary between life and death. The undertaker as "the best doctor" implies a dark irony or that death is the ultimate end, beyond complaint or cure.
  • The passengers’ rocking back and forth, Madge’s high, thin laughter, and Homer’s absent-mindedness contribute to a dreamlike, nightmarish atmosphere. Madge describes their stalled situation as being trapped in a crazy house with mirrored walls and no doors, evoking feelings of entrapment and confusion. Homer’s mention of "Jackie" and tuberculosis introduces a note of illness and impending loss, heightening the emotional tension.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Bus-driver

  • A long-haired, possibly drunk or deeply weary man who curses and talks aloud to "old Doc," an unseen figure. He embodies frustration, loneliness, and a struggle against an unyielding obstacle.

Old Doc

  • Moses sees him in an old "ghost buggy" (car), who occupies a parking space and seems to symbolize obstruction, death, or the past. As a doctor he may represent death or stagnation.

Madge

  • Laughs breathlessly at Moses's misery, indicating a detachment or acceptance of the surreal situation.

Homer

  • Impatient and absent-minded, dreaming of a bride he fears his wife might never know.

Vera

  • Observes and reflects on the scene, feeling tired and dreamlike.

Research: Themes

  • Loneliness and Communication with the Unseen Moses talks to old Doc, who is unseen and possibly a ghost or symbolic figure. This "conversation" reflects the human need to vent frustration and to communicate even when no one is listening or present. It highlights isolation and the internal battles people face.
  • The Struggle Between Life and Death Old Doc’s "ghost buggy" and the hearse symbolize death or the past, while the bus and its passengers represent life moving forward. Moses’s frustration in trying to park reflects the tension between these forces, with death obstructing the path of life.
  • Rules and Order vs Chaos Moses imagines traffic rules (chalk lines, detours, traffic lights) as metaphors for social order and fairness. The chaotic reality, with obstacles like old Doc’s ghost buggy, represents life's unpredictability and unfairness.
  • Existential Weariness and Dreamlike Reality Vera and passengers feel an "infinite weariness," and the situation is likened to being stuck on a ferris wheel or in a crazy house with mirrored walls and no exits. This surreal imagery evokes the feeling of being trapped in life’s endless struggles and the confusion about how to move forward.
  • The Passage of Time and Memory Moses references the past ("the past was the past") and the inevitability of time moving on. Old Doc’s presence and the image of buzzards returning evoke decay and the cyclical nature of life and death.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Moses pleads repeatedly with Doc to move over, symbolizing the desire for obstacles (death, the past, inertia) to yield to life and progress.
  • “I can’t give you anything but love, baby,” sung by Moses, contrasts the harshness of his situation with a tender expression, perhaps hinting at the human capacity for care amid struggle.
  • Moses’s comment about the passengers in old Doc’s buggy suggests confusion or denial about the nature of life, lineage, or reality.
  • It’s “like being stalled on a ferris wheel at the top of the sky.” Madge’s description captures the surreal, trapped feeling of the moment.

Further notes from the text

  • The bus finally parks between a milk truck leaking from its cans and a hearse, birth and death on either side of the passengers. See Comedy in Chapter 67.
  • Moses’s cursing of old Doc becomes a comic theory of marriage and traffic: perhaps there should be a chalk line down the middle of every bed, with signs for detours, narrow shoulders, and steep inclines, or a man might be ditched.
  • He boasts that he is bringing in real business, increasing the population of the town by three, more than Doc can say, and calls Doc’s car an old ghost buggy that could be parked on a postage stamp.
  • His report of the buzzards that have staged a return and brought their relatives, eighty or ninety seen over Rush Creek at sundown, ends with a cheerful jab: the generations of buzzards go on.
  • Vera says the passengers stay in their seats out of infinite weariness: “we had come home to no home,” and perhaps they wished to prolong the journey.
  • Madge’s laughter is high and thin, at the driver’s misery and Doc’s, while Homer dreams of a bride his wife might never know. Vera expects a bird to fly out of the bus-driver’s beard.

Chapter 29

Summary

Mr. Spitzer speaks at length about butterflies. He compares the difficulty of telling butterfly from moth to telling brother from brother, and happiness from sorrow. He names species by the hundreds and dwells on the butterfly as psyche, the soul. He describes Peron's funeral, crowded with gamblers and merry mourners, and the one person who saw his grief, an old lamplighter weeping on a street corner. He wonders whether a sock darned again and again until no original thread remains is still the same sock. The chapter ends with him as a dark atheist who knows more of the life beyond the grave than of this one.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Butterflies and Moths · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Silence and Deafness · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Bus and the Journey

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Descartes and Dualism · Hinduism · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche · Phenomenology · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Stoicism

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Dante · Deafness and Sign Language · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Homer’s Epics · Judaism · Music and Composers · Napoleon and Wellington · Revelation and the Apocalypse · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens by discussing the difficulty of distinguishing butterflies from moths, creatures that exist on a boundary line, symbolic of the blurred lines between happiness and sorrow, day and night, life and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s observations on butterfly and moth behavior are presented as metaphors for life’s uncertainties.
  • The mystery of night-flying butterflies and oceanic migrations suggests the theme of wandering souls or psyches, with butterflies representing spiritual voyagers seeking reunion with immortal love.
  • The transformation of the caterpillar into the chrysalis and then the butterfly is described with deep symbolism: death and rebirth, the chrysalis as a shroud or mummy, and the butterfly as an epitome of immortality within mortality.
  • The enduring and recurring memories of butterflies in Mr. Spitzer’s mind serves as a metaphor for memory, identity, and the persistence of the soul beyond physical death.
  • The chapter elaborates on the spectacular colors of butterflies, which are illusions created by light on scales, not pigmentation, paralleling the illusory nature of life and perception.
  • The idea that male butterflies emit perfumes to attract scentless females introduces a sensual, almost spiritual dimension to the butterfly’s existence, with Mr. Spitzer even imagining he can smell these perfumes as extensions of his own thoughts or memories.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on the unknowability of life beyond death, the multiplicity of gods and spirits, and the possibility that butterflies may have originated beyond Earth, highlighting the vast unknown and the limits of human reason.
  • The metaphor of the “bipart soul” and the questioning of selfhood and identity are central to the chapter’s existential inquiries. Who really owns a soul, and can one be alive and dead simultaneously?
  • The death of Mr. Spitzer’s brother Peron and the impact of that loss loomed large. The chapter contrasts Peron’s early death and wild life with Joachim’s (Mr. Spitzer’s) long survival marked by grief, memory, and the pursuit of meaning through butterflies.
  • The funeral scene with its bizarre, lively crowd reflects the complexities of social death and memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s mental state and his ongoing internal struggle with grief and identity are woven through the reflections on butterflies and memory.
  • Despite his age and diminished faculties, Mr. Spitzer retains and even deepens his knowledge of butterflies, from common species to exotic and mythical varieties, associating them with gods, myths, and celestial bodies.
  • The chapter gives a sense of the butterfly as a cosmic and spiritual symbol, embodying life’s fragility and transcendence.
  • The analogy of Mr. Spitzer’s patched socks and tattered coat illustrates the human condition of decay and endurance, the fragility of identity, and the process of continual repair and reinvention.
  • The regal butterflies, despite their vulnerability, symbolize dignity and persistence amid mortality.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • An old, reflective lawyer and butterfly collector.
  • He embodies melancholy, wisdom, and the quest for understanding life through the metaphor of butterflies.
  • His thoughts are clouded by grief and age, yet his butterfly knowledge grows even in mental decline.

Also listed as: Joachim Spitzer (twin brother to Peron who allegedly lived)

  • Vera who observes Mr. Spitzer’s life and mental state.
  • Reflects on grief, memories, and symbolic connection to butterflies.
  • The profound, almost hidden grief after his brother’s death and how it shapes his worldview.

Peron Spitzer (twin brother to Joachim who is allegedly dead by suicide)

  • A mysterious, volatile figure who lived a fragmented life.
  • His death profoundly impacts Mr. Spitzer, whose mourning colors his worldview.
  • Peron’s character contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s logical nature; he is seen as a greater mystery.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Mentioned as a figure who has her own mystical and dreamlike experiences.
  • Imagined alongside Mr. Spitzer’s butterfly reflections, creating a shared atmosphere of mystery.

Research: Themes

Butterflies as Symbols of the Soul and Immortality

  • They symbolize transformation, immortality, and the elusive nature of life and death.
  • Despite their mortality, butterflies are portrayed as perfect images of immortality, transcending their ephemeral physical existence.

The Boundary Between Life and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • The novel explores the liminal space between life and death through Mr. Spitzer’s reflections.
  • His own existence is depicted as an oscillation between these states, likened to butterflies fluttering between light and darkness.
  • The chapter meditates on memory, loss, and the persistence of the soul or consciousness beyond physical death.

Memory, Loss, and Mourning

See: Memory and the Past · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Mr. Spitzer mourns his dead brother Peron, whose life was full of mystery and volatility.
  • His butterfly memories serve as a means to keep his brother’s essence alive, reflecting the human struggle to grasp and preserve fleeting moments.
  • The grief is profound yet hidden, affecting Mr. Spitzer’s mental state deeply.

The Mystery of Origin and Existence

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The chapter speculates on the origins of butterflies and existence itself.
  • Questions arise about whether butterflies predate time and space or came from cosmic or otherworldly realms.
  • This reflects broader metaphysical inquiry into creation, existence, and the nature of the divine.

The Role of God and the Divine

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates the nature of God, presenting a multifaceted and paradoxical image of divinity.
  • God is both light and darkness, creator and destroyer, and elusive beyond human comprehension.
  • The divine is intertwined with the symbolism of butterflies and the cosmic order.

Ephemeral Beauty and the Illusion of Permanence

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Life’s fleeting moments are compared to bubbles, transient, yet significant.

Butterflies

Colors and Patterns on Wings

On Butterfly and Moth Distinctions and Flight Times (Day vs Night)

Research: Resources

  • The philosophical exploration of happiness and sorrow are intertwined, with sorrow often seen as a necessary component for experiencing the depth of joy and vice versa rather than as simple opposites. It can be viewed in a number of ways: a dialectical relationship (yin and yang-complementary forces where one cannot exist without the other); the contrast highlights the value of positive experiences; a catalyst for growth, introspection, and a deeper understanding of life’s complexities. Philosophical perspectives are found in Buddhism, Christianity, Hinduism, Stoicism, Utilitarianism, Hedonism, Life Satisfaction Theory. Plato and Aristotle’s eudaimonia where flourishing and well-being are achieved by living a virtuous life, not simply experiencing happiness. Nirvana is a state of liberation from suffering and the cycle of rebirth. Equanimity is the ability to remain calm and balanced in the face of both pleasure and pain. The philosophical exploration of happiness and sorrow is presented through the reflections of Mr. Spitzer, who contemplates the ambiguous and intertwined nature of these emotions. The chapter discusses how happiness and sorrow seldom occur in pure, disassociated states; rather, happiness is often tinged with sorrow due to the fear of its temporality, and sorrow is tinged with happiness from the knowledge that it may endure. Mr. Spitzer observes the delicate distinctions between butterflies and moths, using them as metaphors for the subtle and elusive qualities of emotions like happiness and sorrow. Butterflies, associated with daytime and vibrant colors, contrast with moths, which fly by night and evoke muted and exaggerated perceptions. This imagery reflects the nuanced interplay of light and darkness, joy and pain, in human experience. The chapter touches on the fleeting and ephemeral nature of life and emotions, highlighting that moments of happiness are brief and often overshadowed by sorrow. Mr. Spitzer’s meditations suggest that both happiness and sorrow are transient, yet deeply interconnected aspects of existence that shape the human condition. It philosophically portrays happiness and sorrow not as opposites but as closely related states, each containing elements of the other, and both integral to the complexity of life’s experiences. This exploration is woven into the natural and symbolic imagery of butterflies, moths, and the rhythms of day and night, emphasizing the fluid and often paradoxical nature of these emotions.
  • Immortality within the framework of mortality is a philosophical exploration of extending life, potentially indefinitely, while acknowledging the inherent limitations of our biological existence. Collective immortality suggests that while individuals are mortal, their legacy and impact on others can create a form of enduring existence. Some argue that immortality could strip life of its meaning and urgency, while others believe it could offer an opportunity for greater exploration and purpose. Exploring the concept of death and its implications for our understanding of life and existence is central to the discussion of immortality. Mortality can also be a source of meaning and value, as it can make experiences more precious and urgent. Immortality is explored as a concept deeply intertwined with mortality rather than separate or opposed to it. Mr. Spitzer reflects on the ambiguous boundary between life and death, the transient nature of existence, and the paradoxes of human identity and experience. The chapter discusses butterflies and moths as symbols at the boundary between life and death, day and night, tangible and intangible. Butterflies, which live briefly and beautifully, represent the fleeting moments of life that nonetheless embody a form of immortality through their delicate and recurring patterns. Moths, often nocturnal and mysterious, suggest the hidden, unconscious aspects of existence. The imagery of metamorphosis, from caterpillar to chrysalis to butterfly, serves as a metaphor for transformation beyond physical life, hinting at a form of life that transcends mortality. Mr. Spitzer, as a character caught between life and death (being the surviving twin of a deceased brother), embodies this tension. His reflections reveal that mortality and immortality are not simply opposites but exist in a dynamic relationship where life contains elements of death and death contains elements of life. He perceives that the "dead did not return except in our thoughts," suggesting that immortality may reside in memory, legacy, or a spiritual continuation beyond physical life. The chapter also touches on the idea that time and individuality are illusions or constructs, and that existence may be cyclical or layered with overlapping realities. The "immortal invalid" and the "deathless dead" are motifs illustrating beings who exist in this liminal space, neither fully alive nor fully dead. Immortality within the framework of mortality signifies the persistence of being beyond physical death, not as an escape from mortality but as a transformation and continuation in memory, spirit, or cosmic cycles. It highlights the paradox that while human life is ephemeral and marked by loss and change, there is a form of enduring existence that transcends bodily death, embodied in symbols like the butterfly, the moth, and the music of the spheres that Mr. Spitzer contemplates. This nuanced view challenges simple dichotomies, emphasizing that mortality and immortality are deeply connected, and immortality is found within the very experience of mortal life and death rather than beyond it.
  • Butterflies feature prominently in mythology across various cultures. They often symbolize the soul, death, rebirth and transformation and to some good luck and messengers from the spirit world. Psyche in Greek mythology as a goddess of the soul, is often depicted with butterfly wings, symbolizing her connection to the soul and transformation. They symbolize the complex interplay of life, death, transformation, and the soul's journey, embodying the novel's central motifs of illusion, fleeting beauty, and the search for meaning beyond the physical world. They are a poetic representation of the transient yet enduring nature of existence as seen through Mr. Spitzer's meditative perspective.
  • Moths have a rich history in folklore and mythology and are often associated with death, the afterlife, and even messengers from the spirit world as well as good fortune and cleansing. Black moths can symbolize mortality, divinity, and universal secrets. White moths can symbolize death or ill wishes. Brown moths symbolize the need for a purification and the slow, unseen destruction of things. Moths in Matthew 6:19-21 are something that destroys treasures on earth so treasures in heaven should be created instead. Moths serve as a complex metaphor for transformation, the interplay of light and shadow, life and death, and the elusive boundaries of identity and existence. They embody the novel’s themes of impermanence, mystery, and the search for meaning beyond the visible world.
  • Nietzsche’s frog is a way to metaphorically understand perspective and belief. Nietzsche believed that all knowledge and values are perspectival, meaning they are shaped by our individual experiences and values. This is reflected in the idea of a "frog's perspective," which can be understood as a belief system that is constantly changing and shifting. The term "frog's perspective" can also be associated with the idea of narrow-mindedness or being unable to see the bigger picture. Another metaphorical expression, "swallowing the frog" can refer to confronting unpleasant realities or difficult emotions in order to grow or achieve a higher level of understanding. This aligns with Nietzsche's emphasis on confronting difficult truths and embracing the "unpleasantness" of life. The frog can also symbolize a sense of "being in the muck," referring to the lower aspects of oneself that need to be overcome in order to reach a higher level of awareness. Frogs appear symbolically connected to themes of life, death, transformation, and communication beyond ordinary human experience. Mr. Spitzer encounters a mute man who uses a frog as a musical instrument, training it to croak and even mimic human speech. This mute and his frog symbolize profound voicelessness and the struggle to communicate in a world that is largely silent or deaf to certain truths. The frog’s croaking becomes an emblem of fragile, ephemeral voice amid silence, reflecting the broader motifs of mortality, loss, and elusive knowledge that permeate the novel. The frog also represents vulnerability and the liminal state between life and death. Its death mourned by Mr. Spitzer as a loss greater than many others. The mute’s deep grief over the frog's death underscores a shared human sorrow for lost expression and connection, heightening the novel’s meditation on mortality and the persistence of memory or spirit beyond physical life. Nietzsche’s frog metaphor, often interpreted as symbolizing awakening or transformation, where the frog must endure discomfort to emerge anew, parallels the frog’s role in the novel as a creature caught between states (mute yet singing, alive yet dying). The frog’s croaking in the mute’s mouth, its death, and burial evoke themes of metamorphosis, suffering, and the fragile boundary between existence and oblivion, which are central to Nietzschean philosophy of overcoming and transformation. It relates symbolically to liminality, transformation, and the struggle for voice and meaning amid silence and death. This aligns conceptually with Nietzsche’s frog as a figure of existential change and awakening, though Young’s usage is more focused on fragility, loss, and the ineffable aspects of human experience. The frog in the novel is a potent symbol of voicelessness, transformation, and mortality, echoing themes akin to Nietzsche’s idea of the frog as an emblem of awakening and existential transition.
  • Mystical Metamorphosis generally refers to a transformative process that involves a shift or change, often with a mystical or spiritual element. It can be applied to various contexts, including artistic creations, self-discovery, and the transformative nature of life itself. The term can evoke the natural process of metamorphosis, like that of a caterpillar transforming into a butterfly, which is seen as a symbol of change and transformation. It can also be used to describe the mystical journey of self-discovery and spiritual growth. It is a central symbol in the novel, encapsulating the transformational processes that characters undergo, both literally and metaphorically, and emphasizing the fluid, mysterious nature of life and the soul's passage through different states of being.
  • Transfiguration refers to a significant transformation, often involving a shift in understanding, perspective, or even a change in one's self or the world. This can occur through introspection, intellectual exploration, or exposure to new ideas, leading to a transcendence of previous beliefs or realities. Transfiguration can involve a profound change in one's understanding of the self, the world, or their place in it. This can be a result of deep self-reflection, intellectual discovery, or encountering new perspectives. It often signifies a move beyond limitations, old habits, or accepted truths, leading to a more profound or enlightened understanding. Nietzsche viewed transfiguration as an aesthetic process, where individuals can transform their brokenness and misfortune into a form of artistic creation and redemption. Transfiguration is a powerful symbol of the mutable, ephemeral nature of identity and existence. It reflects the novel’s philosophical inquiries into the self, mortality, and the interplay between reality and illusion, using the metaphor of the butterfly and moth to articulate the continuous process of becoming and passing away.
  • The philosophy of conversion explores the concept of a significant and transformative change, often in belief, behavior, or identity. It can be viewed within religious, philosophical, and psychological contexts, examining the nature of this change, its motivations, and its implications for individuals and societies. Religious Conversion Christian conversion, Jewish conversion, Islamic conversion, Hinduism doesn't have a formal conversion process. In Plato's philosophy, the concept of conversion is represented in the allegory of the cave, where a prisoner's awakening involves turning away from shadows and towards the light of truth. Philosophical conversion can also refer to an existential change in the individual, adopting new moral standards or making a fundamental shift in their understanding of reality. Moral conversion involves a change in an individual's moral beliefs, values, and actions, often driven by a critical self-reflection and a new understanding of moral principles. Philosophers like Descartes and Husserl are considered to have undergone a form of philosophical conversion in their pursuit of universal science and phenomenology, respectively. The philosophy of conversion is significant as it encapsulates the novel’s central concerns with change, the instability of identity, and the interplay of life and death. Conversion is not merely a religious or moral act but a profound existential process that embraces ambiguity, transformation, and the continual search for meaning amid uncertainty and flux. This philosophy enriches the novel’s exploration of human consciousness and the elusive nature of reality.
  • The list of ways that refer to God and/or Jesus holds deep symbolic and thematic significance. It encapsulates the multifaceted nature of the divine as understood within Christian theology and mysticism. The significance of this enumeration lies in its portrayal of God/Jesus as an entity with many aspects and attributes, each reflecting different dimensions of spiritual truth and human experience. It emphasizes the complexity and paradox inherent in the divine nature: simultaneously merciful and just, immanent and transcendent, suffering and triumphant. This multiplicity mirrors the novel’s broader themes of ambiguity, multiplicity of selves, and the intertwining of life and death. The list serves to underscore the novel's exploration of spiritual reality versus human perception. The divine is depicted not as a singular, easily definable being but as a presence that manifests in diverse and sometimes contradictory ways, much like the fragmented identities and overlapping realities experienced by the characters such as Mr. Spitzer and Vera’s mother, Catherine. This reflects the novel’s preoccupation with the elusive nature of truth, the complexity of existence, and the blurred boundaries between reality and illusion. By invoking these various titles, the text taps into a rich tradition of Christian symbolism, inviting readers to contemplate the depth of spiritual meaning behind everyday experiences and the mysterious workings of grace, suffering, and redemption. It situates the characters' personal struggles within a cosmic framework, suggesting that their lives are part of a larger divine narrative that encompasses both the mortal and the eternal. This list also contrasts with the practical, grounded character of Miss MacIntosh, who embodies common sense and reality, as opposed to the more mystical and dreamlike experiences of other characters. The divine names remind us of the novel's tension between the earthly and the spiritual, the seen and the unseen, the real and the illusory. The list is a poetic and theological meditation on the nature of divinity, serving as a thematic focal point that enriches the novel’s exploration of identity, faith, and the search for meaning amidst uncertainty and paradox.
  • True Vine - is an allegory or parable in John 15:17 where Jesus’s disciples are described as branches of himself, who is described as the “true vine” and God the Father as the “husbandman”.
  • Bread of Life - John 6:35 a statement by Jesus signifying that he is the source of spiritual nourishment and eternal life, not just physical sustenance.
  • Gate and Door - John 10:9 are often used metaphorically to represent opportunities and access to God’s presence and salvation, with Jesus himself being referred to as both.
  • Wine symbolizes joy, God’s blessings and provisions, and even the blood of Jesus Christ, but it also warns against the dangers of excessive drinking and intoxication. Can represent the fullness of God’s Kingdom (Isaiah’s prophecy).
  • Mediator - is a go-between or intercessor who reconciles two parties, particularly God and humanity, with Jesus Christ being the one and only mediator, bridging the gap between the divine and human. Moses was also a mediator between God and Israel. Kings, priests, and prophets also acted as mediators in the Old Testament, representing God to the people. 1 Timothy 2:5, Hebrews 8:6, Hebrews 9:15.

  • The soul is the purported immaterial aspect or essence of a living being. It is typically believed to be immortal and to exist apart from the material world. Anthropologists and psychologists have found that most humans are naturally inclined to believe in the existence of the soul and that they have interculturally distinguished between souls and bodies. In philosophy, the soul has been the central area of interest since ancient times. Socrates envisioned the soul to possess a rational faculty, its practice being man's most godlike activity. Plato believed the soul to be the person's real self, an immaterial and immortal dweller of our lives that continues and thinks even after death. Aristotle sketched out the soul as the "first actuality" of a naturally organized body: form and matter arrangement allowing natural beings to aspire to full actualization. The soul holds profound significance as a complex and elusive entity intertwined with themes of identity, mortality, and the metaphysical boundaries between life and death. Vera, through Mr. Spitzer’s reflections, presents the soul not as a singular, fixed entity but as something multifaceted and possibly plural. The soul is described as comprising body, soul, and spirit, each with distinct but interconnected roles, and these components may exist simultaneously or sequentially, blurring the lines between life and death, self and other. This ambiguity reflects the novel’s broader theme of fragmented identity and the elusive nature of selfhood. The soul is portrayed as engaging in a continuous interplay with life and death. Mr. Spitzer contemplates how the soul might live beyond death, or how life and death might be inseparable, with moments of existence overlapping in ways that defy linear time. The soul’s journey is likened to traversing between worlds, sometimes indistinguishable from shadows, clouds, or reflections, emphasizing the thin veil between existence and non-existence. The soul is connected to natural and cosmic imagery (clouds, stars, moths, butterflies, and sea creatures) suggesting that it is part of a larger, universal process of transformation and transmutation. This imagery conveys the soul’s ephemeral and yet eternal qualities, linking human experience to the rhythms of nature and the cosmos. Mr. Spitzer’s meditations reveal the soul as a source of both wonder and confusion. He acknowledges his limited understanding of the soul, its origins, and its destiny. The soul’s elusive nature challenges certainty and invites contemplation about the limits of human knowledge, the nature of existence, and the possibility of immortality or reincarnation. The chapter discusses the relationship between soul and memory, suggesting that memory might be a manifestation or extension of the soul. Memory, like the soul, is imperfect and fragmentary, and the dead may live on through memories or echoes rather than physical presence. This concept supports the novel’s recurring theme of the persistence of identity beyond physical life. The soul is significant as a symbol and concept embodying the novel’s exploration of identity, mortality, and the metaphysical uncertainties of human existence. It is neither wholly present nor absent but exists in a liminal space between being and non-being, connected intimately to the natural and cosmic order, and enveloped in mystery and ambiguity.

  • The white-veined blacks are a common butterfly found in northwest Africa and Asia.
  • The black-veined marble white was a large butterfly in Europe.
  • Lapwing is a ground nesting bird found in Europe.
  • Tropic of Cancer (Northern Tropic) is the most northerly circle of latitude on Earth.
  • The Tropic of Capricorn (Southern Tropic) is the circle of latitude closest to the equator.
  • Aurora Borealis is the northern lights.
  • Aurora Australis is the southern lights.
  • The emerald (Papilio palinurus) butterfly is found in Southeast Asia.
  • The amethyst may refer to the Purple emperor butterfly found in Europe and Asia.
  • The "coxcomb red" most likely refers to the Coxcomb Prominent moth (Ptilodon capucina). This moth is named for the white tuft of scales on its head, which resembles a coxcomb or the crest of a rooster. It's a fairly common moth in Britain and is known for its camouflaged appearance when at rest, resembling a dead leaf. The moth's caterpillar is green with two red projections and has a unique defense mechanism of curling its head back when alarmed.
  • The red admiral is a butterfly found on five continents.
  • The white admiral is a butterfly found in North America.
  • The checkered skipper is a butterfly found in the US.
  • The silver-spotted skipper is a butterfly found in North America.
  • The grizzled and dingy skippers are butterflies found in Europe and Asia.
  • The greylings is a butterfly found in Europe.
  • Adonis blues butterflies are found in Europe and Asia.
  • Wood white butterflies are found in Europe.
  • Io was one of the mortal lovers of Zeus in Greek mythology.
  • Cabbage white butterflies are found in Europe and North America.
  • The painted lady is a butterfly found in North America.
  • Swallowtail butterflies are found mostly in tropical regions but are found on every continent except Antarctica.
  • Young is describing a hyperfixation where a person is completely engrossed by something, to the point where it becomes all-consuming and disrupts day-to-day functioning. It gets hard to focus on anything other than the object of hyperfixation. With hyperfixation, passion can turn into obsession. The object of interest takes up so much time, it comes at the cost of personal wellbeing, relationships, and responsibilities. It can even be a symptom of an underlying mental health condition.
  • Mr. Spitzer has applied the philosophical question of the Ship of Theseus to his socks. Ship of Theseus is a thought experiment that questions if an object that has had all of its components replaced remains fundamentally the same object. There have been three proposed solutions: there is no identity over time, four-dimensionalism, and according to cognitive science it is an example of extreme externalism - the assumption that what is true in our minds is true in the world. In philosophy of mind, the ship is replaced by a person, whose identity over time is called into question. The Ship of Theseus metaphor and the image of Mr. Spitzer's socks together articulate the tension between change and sameness, the fragility of identity, and the inevitable passage of time that leaves physical and existential marks on the individual. They highlight the novel’s preoccupation with the mutability of self and the paradox of persistence through transformation.
  • Bindlestiff is a hobo or one who carries his clothes or bedding in a bundle.
  • Queen butterflies are found in North and South America.
  • King butterfly is another name for a Monarch butterfly.
  • Cardinal butterflies are found in Europe and Asia.
  • Gregorian chant is a form of monophonic, unaccompanied sacred song in Latin of the Roman Catholic Church.
  • Mr. Spitzer considers himself a dark atheist. A negative atheist is someone who does not believe in the existence of deities but does not explicitly assert that there are none. Mr. Spitzer calling himself a "dark atheist" signifies his profound struggle with the mysteries of existence, death, and faith. It captures his skeptical yet deeply reflective nature, his confrontation with loss and absence, and his place within the novel’s broader themes of illusion, reality, and the search for meaning amid chaos.
