Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children.

Summary

Esther's parents never consummated their marriage. For seven years a large, dark woman in men's clothes came to their house at night with a tiny silver spoon, until Esther and Rosemary were conceived. An uncle, a boxer, told her the story, laughing. On her seventh birthday, Esther's mother took her to visit the dying, blind go-between, and Esther saw in her the father she never had. Ever since, every day has been her birthday.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Esther’s Mother · Esther’s Father · Rosemary

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Clocks and Watches · Clouds and Storms · Moon and Stars · Roses and Flowers · Shadows · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Spiritualism and the Occult

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Ancient Egypt · Don Quixote · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Esther is described as "illusive," a natural woman born of barren parents who never consummated their marriage. Her conception was not ordinary but happened "across distance," involving a third person, an "old concubine" or "other woman," who carried a silver spoon used to impregnate her mother. This section emphasizes the unnaturalness and mystery surrounding her birth, portraying Esther as a being born out of doubt and separateness rather than love or union of flesh and soul. Her parents' marriage was arid, with no conjugal love, and Esther’s existence itself is framed as a "terrible joke" on nature.
  • The "other woman," a large, dark, and somewhat menacing figure, acted as a go-between for Esther's parents who could not physically unite. She carried the silver spoon, symbolizing the method of conception, and her presence is shadowy and powerful. This woman’s cold, almost androgynous characteristics and her role in the conception add a mysterious and somewhat sinister tone to Esther’s origins. The chapter notes that this took place over many years, with the "other woman" visiting regularly, setting an alarm clock, and performing ritualistic acts to ensure the conception would succeed.
  • Esther’s mother’s feelings of fear, pain, and hopelessness during the prolonged and unnatural conception are described in detail. The husband's passive role contrasts sharply with the other woman’s active involvement. The mother’s suffering is emphasized, including her physical pain and emotional torment. Esther is born kicking and afraid, a product of a "long honeymoon" that never became a true marriage night. The birth is marked by difficulty and instruments, symbolizing the unnaturalness and struggle of Esther’s arrival into the world.
  • Esther’s mother repeatedly reminds her of the stillborn child (Rosemary), whom Esther is supposed to have "killed" in the womb with her "big feet." Esther’s innocence is corrupted early by the family’s dark secrets and the community’s scorn. The chapter highlights the emotional neglect and psychological burden Esther endures, including being called "Little Jackass" by her father and teased by her uncle. The tragedy of Rosemary's stillbirth and Esther’s survival is a source of lifelong guilt and alienation.
  • On Esther’s seventh birthday, she and her mother make a difficult journey to visit the other woman, who had helped bring Esther into the world. This visit is symbolic, portraying the harsh reality behind the fantasy of a "golden palace." The other woman is found dying, blind, and monstrous, yet still the "father" figure in Esther’s story. This episode underscores the unnatural triangle and the burden of Esther's existence, as well as her mother’s complex feelings of gratitude, regret, and unresolved pain.
  • The chapter closes with a poignant meditation on Esther’s gradual death, a metaphor for her lifelong suffering and alienation. Despite her physical presence and vitality, Esther is portrayed as a "happy dead," burdened by the weight of her origins and the absence of natural love. Her connection to nature, to other selves, and to dead creatures highlights her liminal state between life and death, presence and absence.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • The protagonist, described as a large, muscular, and natural woman, yet burdened by the unnaturalness of her conception and birth. She embodies both physical strength and emotional vulnerability.
  • She is “illusive,” caught between life and eternity, haunted by the shadow of her stillborn twin Rosemary.
  • Known as “Little Jackass,” a nickname signifying her struggle with identity and acceptance.
  • She experiences loneliness and rejection but has a deep maternal heart.
  • Esther’s internal conflict is central, revealing layers of shame, defiance, and longing.
  • Her mother’s contradictory feelings of desire, regret, and hope illustrate the emotional complexity of motherhood under duress.

Esther’s Mother

  • A small, delicate, and fragile woman who yearned for a child but was unable to conceive naturally.
  • She endured the long, torturous process of conception mediated by the “other woman.”
  • Often blames Esther for the barren landscape of their lives and the shadow of Rosemary.

Esther’s Father (The Policeman)

  • A large, distant man who never consummated the marriage and remained emotionally aloof.
  • He is passive, absorbed in his own interests, such as reading old baseball scores.
  • His relationship with Esther’s mother is marked by distance and lack of physical union.

The Other Woman (The Go-Between / The Concubine)

  • The "other woman" who assists with Esther Longtree's conception is a complex and symbolically rich character, embodying themes of alienation, unnatural intervention, and the blurring of gender and human roles.
  • The other woman is portrayed as a large, dark, and somewhat grotesque figure, physically contrasting with Esther's small, delicate mother. She is described as immense and misshapen, with a dimpled chin like Esther's, yet her body smells of manure and old tulip bulbs rotted by rain, evoking an earthy, almost animalistic presence. She wears men's shoes, a man's hat, and coat, casting a shadow "like a man's shadow" on the wall, blurring gender lines and emphasizing her liminal status between man and woman.
  • She functions as a go-between or intermediary in the conception process: carrying a tiny silver spoon, the instrument used to impregnate Esther's mother. This spoon symbolizes the unnatural and clinical intervention in what would typically be a natural act of conception. The process is slow, torturous, and prolonged, spanning seven years of visits, during which the other woman comes at night, sometimes knocking or whistling to announce her arrival. She is methodical, patient, and calm, yet possesses a "slow anger." Her presence is both cruel and necessary, a facilitator of life born out of barrenness and absence of conjugal love.
  • Unlike the natural union of man and woman, the conception of Esther occurs "across a great, arid distance," facilitated by the other woman’s spoon. This reflects the barrenness and emotional coldness of Esther's parents' marriage, emphasizing estrangement and the failure of traditional love and procreation.
  • Her wearing of men's clothes and casting a male shadow suggests a hybrid or ambiguous gender identity, symbolizing the breakdown of conventional roles. She holds power over the creation of life, yet is an outsider, "a foreigner, someone who spoke with a strange accent," possibly exiled or carrying a "crime," which adds a sense of otherness and ostracism.
  • She is associated with both life-giving and ominous death imagery, such as carrying a funeral wreath and walking among frozen boughs and songless birds. Her hands are described as large, flat, and dark, capable of warming Esther’s mother but also marking the child with the shadow of her intervention. This duality underscores the paradox of creation: birth emerging from pain, alienation, and sacrifice.
  • While she is described as cruel "as a child," she is also "more wonderful, more beautiful than either of her parents," suggesting a mysterious, inscrutable depth beneath her harsh exterior. She slaps and pinches Esther's mother to arouse life, indicating a brutal but necessary form of care.
  • The other woman operates in secrecy, moving "back and forth" between Esther’s parents, whose marriage is unconsummated. She is the physical manifestation of the "shadow" that lies over Esther’s family history and conception, highlighting themes of hidden trauma, secrets, and the unnatural origins of Esther’s being.
  • The other woman’s intervention results in Esther’s conception, an event described as unnatural and painful, but also miraculous in producing a child with a "big heart" and intense life force despite the barrenness of her parents' union. Esther's identity is deeply shaped by this conception, as she is "the child of the unnatural mating," simultaneously mulish and vulnerable, burdened by loneliness and the weight of her origins.
  • Her presence and role also deepen the novel’s exploration of family dysfunction, the failures of traditional marriage, and the ways in which life asserts itself against bleakness and despair. The other woman, though harsh and alien, becomes a symbol of the persistence of life and the complexities of identity born from fractured beginnings.
  • The other woman is a potent symbol of the unnatural, intermediary force enabling Esther’s conception amid a loveless and barren marriage. She embodies ambiguity, cruelty, and hidden power, bringing to life themes of alienation, gender fluidity, and the paradoxical relationship between life and death. Her character is crucial to understanding Esther’s origins and the larger thematic fabric of the novel.

Rosemary

  • Esther’s stillborn twin, whose spirit and memory haunt Esther.
  • Symbolizes what might have been and the loss that shadows Esther’s life.

Esther’s Uncle

  • The uncle is portrayed as a complex and somewhat enigmatic figure within the narrative of Esther Longtree's conception and family history. He is described as a pugilist who died of cancer and left his estate to an old spiritualist medium, a tall, thin-cheeked man in contact with astral forces, star bodies, and influences. This detail suggests that the uncle was connected to both the physical and metaphysical realms, bridging the earthly and the astral, which resonates with the novel's themes of spiritual and existential ambiguity.
  • His role in Esther’s life is marked by a peculiar mix of cruelty and candor. He mockingly informs Esther that her conception was "unnatural" and that she was called "Little Jackass" by her father because of this unnaturalness. His laughter until his face turned purple while telling her this indicates a harsh and mocking attitude, perhaps reflecting the family's broader discomfort or denial regarding the circumstances of Esther's birth. The nickname "Little Jackass" itself is symbolic: implying stubbornness, mule-like qualities, and an outsider status that Esther internalizes as part of her identity.
  • The uncle’s death and bequest to a spiritualist medium also suggest his fascination or involvement with the occult or unseen forces, emphasizing the novel's recurring motifs of mystery, otherworldliness, and the blurred lines between life and death. His character embodies a link to the past and the mystical, adding layers to Esther's tangled family legacy and the shadowy "third person" involved in her conception.
  • The uncle functions as a symbolic figure who exposes the unnatural and painful origins of Esther's life through his teasing and his association with spiritualism, reflecting the novel’s themes of alienation, the supernatural, and the complex intersections of family, identity, and fate.

Research: Themes

Unnatural Conception and Birth

See: Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther’s birth is the result of an unnatural process involving a silver spoon, a third person, and years of effort without conjugal love or union.
  • The story contrasts the natural processes of life and love with a barren, mechanical, and painful conception.
  • This theme explores the impact of artificiality on identity and human connection.

Loneliness and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Esther lives a life marked by emotional and physical isolation, born from a marriage devoid of love.
  • She is described as “mulish,” resisting all constraints but trapped by her origins.
  • Loneliness pervades her family and her own experience.

Identity and Acceptance

See: Identity and the Self

  • Esther struggles with her identity, labeled “Little Jackass” and burdened by the legacy of her birth.
  • Her physical and emotional differences set her apart, and she grapples with feelings of shame, rejection, and the desire for love.
  • The story probes how origins influence self-perception and social acceptance.

Nature and Symbolism

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Nature imagery (clouds, stars, flowers, birds) contrasts with the barren and mechanical nature of Esther’s conception.
  • Esther’s heart is described as “starlight, wind, water,” suggesting a connection to natural forces despite her unnatural birth.
  • The passage uses symbolism to reflect emotional states and existential questions.

Memory and Trauma

See: Memory and the Past · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • The narrative shows how trauma from birth and family secrets shapes Esther’s life.
  • The long seven-year process of conception and the presence of the other woman haunt the family.
  • Esther’s mother’s feelings of guilt and regret color their relationship.

Death and Life

See: Death and Mortality

  • The birth of Rosemary (stillborn) alongside Esther highlights the proximity of life and death.
  • Esther’s life is described as a slow death, a gradual fading even as she lives.
  • The passage reflects on mortality, loss, and the fragility of existence.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Silver Spoon

  • Symbolizes the unnatural means of conception, coldness, and mechanical intervention.
  • Represents the emotional barrenness and distance in the parents’ relationship.

The Other Woman

  • Embodies the intrusion of unnatural forces, the shadow of death and life intertwined.
  • Her dual nature (wearing men’s clothes, having a shadow like a man) symbolizes gender ambiguity and the breaking of natural roles.

The Fence

  • A metaphor for the boundary between life and eternity, natural and unnatural existence.
  • Esther stands “arms akimbo, legs astraddle” at this fence, caught between worlds.

Nature (Clouds, Stars, Flowers)

See: Moon and Stars · Roses and Flowers · Clouds and Storms

  • Contrasts with the harshness of Esther’s birth, representing purity, innocence, and the natural cycle of life.
  • The “clouds filled with holes” evoke fragility and vulnerability.

The Shadow

See: Shadows

  • Rosemary’s presence as a shadow symbolizes loss and absence.
  • Esther’s own shadow represents the duality of her existence.

Social Commentary

  • The passage critiques societal expectations of marriage, conception, and family.
  • It exposes the cruelty of imposed roles and the stigma of non-traditional origins.

Symbolic Use of Time

See: Clocks and Watches

  • The seven-year conception period symbolizes prolonged suffering and anticipation.
  • The anniversary visit to the other woman reflects attempts to reconcile past trauma.

Interpersonal Relationships

See: The Sea and Water

  • The coldness between Esther’s parents contrasts with the strange intimacy involving the other woman.
  • Esther’s relationship with her parents is fraught with misunderstanding and blame.

Research: Resources

  • Esther Longtree is a deeply tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of unnatural conception, loneliness, maternal suffering, and existential isolation. Her characterization is rich with symbolism and psychological depth, revealing a woman who is both physically imposing and emotionally vulnerable. Esther is described as a large, muscular, wind-burned woman with dark skin and crossed eyes that reflect a dazzling inner light where there is no actual light. Her body is often swollen due to pregnancy, yet she carries a profound sadness and a sense of being out of place in the world. She is mulish, stubborn, and somewhat vulgar, traits that stem from her difficult origins and emotional turmoil. Despite her toughness, her heart is described as "big and leaking," full of regrets, expectations, and memories, highlighting her emotional complexity and capacity for deep feeling. Esther’s origins are central to her character. She was conceived in a way that defies the natural order, her parents never consummated their marriage physically, and instead, a third person, an "old concubine," using a silver spoon, facilitated her conception across a great emotional and physical distance between her parents. This unusual conception symbolizes the emotional barrenness and alienation in her family. Her parents’ marriage is described as arid and loveless, lacking the fundamental union of flesh and soul. Esther’s conception is painful, slow, and unnatural, taking seven years and involving this mysterious third woman who serves as a go-between. The figure of the "other woman," the old concubine who carries the silver spoon and physically intervenes in the conception, is a haunting presence in Esther’s story. This woman is physically and symbolically powerful and described as large, dark, and foreign, with masculine traits. She embodies the harsh reality and cruelty of Esther’s conception and birth. She is portrayed as both cruel and strangely beautiful in an inner, invisible way, representing an essential but unsettling force in Esther’s life and origin. Esther was born kicking and afraid, a difficult birth requiring instruments. She is the only one to survive; her twin, Rosemary, was stillborn. This loss haunts Esther, who is burdened by her mother’s guilt and neglect, and by a sense of having caused harm. She carries the memory and presence of Rosemary as a kind of shadow or ghost, which deepens her loneliness and feeling of being an unnatural offspring. Esther’s relationship with her parents is fraught with pain and misunderstanding. Her mother is distant, delicate, and childlike herself (never truly matured or fulfilled) and she often blames Esther for the darkness and barrenness of their world. Her father is large, passive, and somewhat detached, calling Esther "Little Jackass," a nickname that reflects both affection and cruelty. Both parents are emotionally unavailable, and Esther is left to navigate the world as an awkward, oversized child of a loveless union. Esther stands as a symbol of isolation born of a union that never was, a child who bridges eternity and life but belongs fully to neither. She is "cloud-like," "illusive," and driven to the edge of existence, a creature shaped by absence and distance. Her physical largeness contrasts with the emotional barrenness around her, making her a living paradox and a figure of existential struggle. Despite her tragic origins and the neglect she suffers, Esther has a "maternal heart" and a deep desire for love and motherhood. Yet she repeatedly experiences loss (stillbirths, shadows, unborn children) and carries the burden of these losses within her. She is a woman perpetually pregnant with doubtfulness and sorrow, embodying both fertility and barrenness simultaneously. On her seventh birthday, Esther and her mother undertake a difficult journey to visit the "other woman," the go-between who had helped conceive Esther. This journey is symbolic, marked by hardship, loss of clothing, and the harshness of the natural and social world. The visit reveals the death and decay underlying Esther’s origin: the go-between is dying, blind, and stained by darkness, and Esther perceives her as a kind of paternal figure despite her appearance and gender. Esther is caught between life and death, reality and shadow, natural and unnatural. Her death is "gradual," tied to her continuous experience of loss and alienation. She tries to be good despite the hatred and misunderstanding she faces, and she is marked by a profound loneliness that aligns her with the natural world’s shadows and ghosts. Her character embodies the tragic consequences of emotional and physical disconnection within a family and society. Esther Longtree in this chapter is a richly drawn figure representing the painful intersection of unnatural conception, family dysfunction, loneliness, maternal longing, and existential grief. She is a living paradox: large yet vulnerable, natural yet unnatural, maternal yet burdened by loss. Her story is woven with symbolism and mythic resonance.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes a deeply troubled and complex history of barrenness, failed unions, and unnatural origins that can be read as a metaphor for certain aspects of American history, especially related to its cultural and social foundations. Her life story is marked by the unnatural conception and barren marriage of her parents, who never consummated their union in the usual way. Instead, Esther was conceived through an intermediary, a dark, fierce go-between woman who carried a silver spoon between her parents over many years of painful, slow attempts at conception. This act was carried out without love, intimacy, or unity between the parents, symbolizing a broken or forced foundation rather than a natural, loving creation. Esther herself is born kicking, burdened by the shadow of a stillborn twin, Rosemary, representing loss, failure, and the cost of this unnatural origin. Symbolically, Esther’s story reflects a history of disconnection, loneliness, and suffering born from a society or culture that lacks genuine union and affection at its core. The barren marriage, the long and cruel struggle to bring life into being without real love, and the presence of the mysterious third figure (the go-between woman) who acts almost like a dark force intervening between the natural order, all suggest themes of alienation and forced creation. Esther’s immense physical presence, her repeated pregnancies of stillborn children, and her ultimate loneliness and marginalization reflect the burdens of a history that is both prolific and deeply wounded. Esther Longtree can be seen as symbolizing the nation’s own troubled birth and development: a land born of separateness and conflict, of broken promises and harsh realities underneath the surface of prosperity and growth. Her story recalls the suffering of those who have been marginalized, neglected, or burdened by the consequences of historical injustices and the failures of foundational relationships, whether racial, cultural, or familial. Esther Longtree embodies the tragic history of a people born out of a fractured union, carrying within them the scars of that origin and the weight of unfulfilled hopes and lost futures. Her life’s anguish and resilience mirror the broader American narrative of creation through suffering, alienation, and the struggle for identity and belonging.
  • The intermediary woman who facilitated Esther Longtree’s conception is a complex and symbolically potent figure whose role resonates deeply when analyzed alongside the historical context of Black Americans’ civil rights struggles in the United States. This woman is described vividly and somewhat grotesquely as a large, dark, misshapen figure with broad, earth-stained hands, wearing men’s shoes, a man’s hat, and coat. She is a foreigner, someone with a strange accent, and carries an aura of mystery and hardship, possibly linked to an old crime or exile. She is neither kind nor gentle but is methodical, fierce, and patient, walking back and forth between Esther's parents with a silver spoon, the instrument used to impregnate Esther’s mother over the course of seven years. This woman embodies a liminal, almost mythic figure: part man, part woman, part shadow crossing boundaries between genders, generations, and roles. She is the "go-between" in a domestic and biological triangle that is itself fractured and barren, symbolizing the failure of natural union and the intrusion of a painful, unnatural process. The intermediary woman’s outsider status (foreign, dark, and stigmatized) can be read as emblematic of the marginalized Black American figure during the civil rights era. Like the go-between, Black Americans were often seen as "other," standing apart from the mainstream, burdened by historical injustices and systemic exclusion. Yet, this figure is also crucial to the creation of life, a bearer of possibility and transformation despite the cruelty and hardship she embodies. Similarly, Black Americans’ struggle was against a backdrop of oppression but also one of profound resilience and the potential to create new social realities. Esther’s conception through an intermediary and a silver spoon, rather than through a natural marital union, parallels the forced and unnatural social conditions imposed upon Black Americans (segregation, disenfranchisement, and systemic violence) that distorted natural human relations and family structures. The intermediary's role in bridging a distance or barrier between two barren parents mirrors the social barriers (legal, racial, and cultural) that Black Americans sought to overcome in their fight for civil rights. The intermediary woman’s presence between Esther’s parents and her shadow-like figure evoke the heavy legacy of slavery, segregation, and historical trauma that Black Americans carried. Esther herself, born of this unnatural and painful process, embodies the complex identity born from a fractured past. The intermediary’s shadow, her "darkness," and the violence implicit in the conception process reflect the historical violence and the pain of inheritance that civil rights activism sought to confront and transcend. The intermediary woman subverts traditional gender and familial roles by acting as the agent of conception in an unconventional way. This subversion can be seen as analogous to the civil rights movement’s challenge to established power structures and norms. The movement demanded recognition and redefinition of identity, agency, and rights, much as the intermediary woman’s presence disrupts the conventional narrative of family and birth. The intermediary is simultaneously a figure of cruelty and care, oppression and agency. She is paid for her role, yet wields a strange power over the life created. This duality reflects the complex dynamics in civil rights struggles, where oppressed communities both suffered under systemic injustice and exercised profound agency in shaping their destinies. The intermediary woman in Esther Longtree’s conception is a richly layered symbol and explores themes of alienation, unnaturalness, and painful mediation that resonate powerfully with the historical and social conditions of Black Americans fighting for civil rights. She embodies the barriers to natural unity imposed by history and society, yet also the endurance and complexity of life born from hardship and estrangement. Her figure invites reflection on the intersections of race, gender, power, and identity in a fractured world.
  • Modern Spiritualism is widely considered to have begun in March 1848 in Hydesville, New York, following the claims of the Fox sisters, Margaret and Kate, who reported hearing mysterious rappings that they believed were spirit messages. The movement originated in an area of upstate New York known as the "Burned-over District," which was already a center for religious fervor and movements like Millerism and Mormonism during the Second Great Awakening. The movement quickly spread, with early adherents seeking direct communication with the spirits of the deceased. By the 1850s, it had spread across the country and internationally. In the 1850s, the movement attracted the attention of scientists who began investigating the reported supernatural occurrences. The credibility of the movement was challenged, especially in 1888 when the Fox sisters confessed to faking the original rappings. However, many believers continued their faith, and the movement adapted. Influential figures like Emma Hardinge Britten, a medium and lecturer, used the platform of Spiritualism to advocate for social causes like women's rights and temperance. Spiritualism experienced a major revival after World War I, as many people sought to connect with loved ones who had died in the war. The movement continued to develop organizations and gather followers, with communities like Cassadaga, Florida, becoming known as centers for spiritualist activities. Throughout the mid-20th century, Spiritualism persisted, adapting to new generations and social changes, and leaving a lasting impact on American religious and cultural history.
  • Spiritualism is the metaphysical school of thought opposing physicalism and also is the category of all spiritual beliefs from ancient to modern. They believe that spirit mediums are gifted to carry on such communication, but that anyone may become a medium through study and practice. They believe that spirits are capable of growth and perfection, progressing through higher spheres or planes, and that the afterlife is not a static state, but one in which spirits evolve. The two beliefs, that contact with spirits is possible, and that spirits may dwell on a higher plane, lead to a third belief, that spirits can provide knowledge about moral and ethical issues, as well as about God and the afterlife. Many believers speak of spirit guides or specific spirits, often contacted, and relied upon for worldly and spiritual guidance. According to Spiritualists, anyone may receive spirit messages, but formal communication sessions are held by mediums, who claim thereby to receive information about the afterlife. Spiritualism developed and reached its peak growth in membership from the 1840s to the 1920s, especially in English-speaking countries. By 1897, spiritualism was said to have more than eight million followers in the United States and Europe, mostly drawn from the middle and upper classes.
  • In classical mythology, Cupid is the god of desire, erotic love, attraction and affection. He is often portrayed as the son of the love goddess Venus and the god of war Mars.
  • The Immaculate Conception is the belief that the Virgin Mary was free of original sin from the moment of her conception. Original sin is the Christian doctrine that holds that humans, through the fact of birth, inherit a tainted nature in need of regeneration and a proclivity to sinful conduct. According to Christian apocryphal and Islamic tradition, Saint Anne was the mother of Mary and the maternal grandmother of Jesus. Saint Anne appears as the mother of Mary in the late 2nd-century Gospel of James. Saint Anne and her husband, Joachim, are infertile, but God hears their prayers and Mary is conceived. The conception is claimed to occur without sexual intercourse between Saint Anne and Joachim, which fits well with the Gospel of James' persistent emphasis on Mary's sacred purity, but the story does not advance the idea of an immaculate conception. The Orthodox Church claims that Mary was conceived by her parents in the same way everyone is conceived. Anne (Hannah in Arabic) is recognized as a highly spiritual woman and as the mother of Mary. In the Quran she is described as childless until her old age. One day, Hannah saw a bird feeding its young while sitting in the shade of a tree, which awakened her desire to have children of her own. She prayed for a child and eventually conceived. Joachim (Imran in Arabic) died before the child was born. Expecting the child to be male, Hannah vowed to dedicate him to isolation and service in the Second Temple. However, Hannah bore a daughter instead, and named her Mary. Her words upon delivering Mary reflect her status as a great mystic, realizing that while she had wanted a son, this daughter was God's gift to her. She said - My Lord! Truly, I brought her forth, a female. And God is greater in knowledge of what she brought forth. And the male is not like the female. So her Lord received her with the very best acceptance. And her bringing forth caused the very best to develop in her. Joachim was a rich and pious man, who regularly gave to the poor. At the temple, Joachim's sacrifice was rejected, so the couple's childlessness was interpreted as a sign of divine displeasure. Joachim consequently withdrew to the desert, where he fasted and did penance for 40 days. Angels then appeared to both Joachim and Anne to promise them a child. Joachim later returned to Jerusalem and embraced Anne at the city gate, located in the Walls of Jerusalem. An ancient belief held that a child born of an elderly mother who had given up hope of having offspring was destined for great things. Joachim is named as the patron saint of fathers, grandfathers, grandparents, married couples, cabinet makers, and linen traders.
  • “Her parents had never consummated their marriage but had only dreamed of heaven as something far away.” Purity culture is a movement emphasizing abstinence until heterosexual marriage, strict gender roles, and modesty, often creating intense sexual shame and anxiety. It uses rituals like purity balls, rings, and pledges to control sexual expression, placing the burden of sexual responsibility on women and girls to prevent male lust. Many raised in this culture report anxiety, fear, and difficulties with intimacy, even after marrying. There is a growing movement of former adherents who are deconstructing these teachings and addressing the trauma caused by them. Its influence persists through different ministries and a continued focus on "biblical womanhood".
  • Gas jets, or gasoliers, provided prominent indoor and outdoor lighting in the US from the early 19th century until being largely replaced by electric light, with remnants existing in specialized, theatrical, or rural settings. These systems utilized coal gas, manufactured gas, or, by the late 19th century, acetylene and natural gas to provide bright, steady illumination via burners, often employing mantles for increased efficiency.
  • Concubinage in the U.S. was primarily defined by the sexual exploitation of enslaved Black women by white owners, alongside localized systems like plaçage in Louisiana. These coerced, non-marital relationships were driven by power imbalances, racial prohibitions on marriage (anti-miscegenation laws), and the economic value of offspring.
  • The gramophone, invented by Emil Berliner in 1887, is an early, mechanical, analog sound reproduction device that plays flat, spirally-grooved discs (shellac records). It uses a stylus and horn to amplify sound mechanically, without electricity. As a precursor to the modern turntable, it revolutionized music by allowing mass production of recordings, distinguishing itself from cylinder-based phonographs.
  • “green cherries” have been a part of candied fruit recipes for generations.
  • Esther Longtree claims she is Jesus Christ as part of her complex self-perception, intertwined with her tragic and sorrowful life marked by endless pregnancies and stillbirths. She is a character burdened by a profound sense of loss and unfulfilled motherhood, feeling perpetually pregnant with children who never fully came to life. This identification with Jesus Christ seems to symbolize her own suffering, sacrifice, and bearing of pain, much like the figure of Christ who endured suffering for humanity. Esther's claim is connected to her experience of being "always pregnant," carrying the weight of loss, sorrow, and the burden of unrealized hopes. Her life is marked by a sense of being different, isolated, and carrying an immense internal burden: a "pregnancy which was more than the memory provided for." She is aware of her uniqueness and the vastness of her suffering, and by likening herself to Jesus Christ, she expresses the depth of her endurance and the sacrifice implicit in her condition. Esther’s self-identification with Christ also reflects her feeling of being misunderstood and unrecognized, much like the biblical Christ who was often rejected and not understood by those around him. She is conscious of her pain and her role as a bearer of suffering, and this claim may be a manifestation of her grappling with her identity and the meaning of her life amidst her hardships.
  • According to Christian theology, Mary was not impregnated by a literal bird like a dove, but rather conceived Jesus through the power of the Holy Spirit. While artistic depictions sometimes show a dove (a symbol of the Holy Spirit) during the Annunciation, this is a symbolic representation.
  • “an old coat made of old fruit bags” likely refers to garments created from repurposed cotton mesh citrus bags (orange, grapefruit, or lemon sacks), or more commonly, patterned cotton flour/feed sacks used for clothing during the Great Depression and World War II, which often featured bright, fruit-themed, or floral prints.
  • Women historically pinched their cheeks and bit their lips to induce a natural, rosy flush of color, particularly during the Victorian era (19th century) and the Elizabethan era (16th century). This practice was used to enhance beauty without the stigma of wearing obvious makeup, which was often considered improper, associated with actresses, or linked to low morals.
  • “woman carrying candle, book, bell, funeral wreath” The phrase "bell, book, and candle" refers to a Latin Christian method of excommunication by anathema, imposed on a person who had committed an exceptionally grievous sin. Evidently introduced by Pope Zachary around the middle of the 8th century, the rite was once used by the Latin Church. This form of excommunication was inflicted on Robert II of France by Pope Gregory V for his marriage to Bertha of Burgundy in the year 996, because Bertha was his second cousin. He was later reconciled with the Church after negotiations with Gregory's successor Pope Silvester II.
  • Sexton beetles, commonly known as burying beetles, are large, orange-and-black insects that act as nature’s undertakers by burying small, dead animals (like mice or birds) to feed their larvae. They are among the few insects that display active parental care, with both parents preparing the carcass, removing hair, and feeding their young.
  • The idiom, to be born with a silver spoon in their mouth, means someone born into a wealthy family or someone who has a prosperous background or is of a well-to-do family environment, often with the connotation that the person does not fully realize or appreciate the value of his or her advantage, its having been inherited rather than earned. It first appeared in print in English as early as 1719, in the translation of the novel Don Quixote.
  • In vitro fertilization was not successful in humans until 1977. Prior to the development of IVF in humans, a physician and professor was doing research on reproduction in animals in 1891. In 1934, IVF was tried on rabbits. In 1948, research was expanded on IVF. In 1958, mouse embryos were grown in vitro and transferred into female mice. In 1959, research proved fertilization in vitro was capable of producing a live birth of a rabbit.
  • A treacling mill may refer to treacle mining which is a joke about mining of black treacle or molasses in a raw form similar to coal. The subject purports to be serious but is an attempt to test credulity. Thick black treacle makes the deception plausible. The topic has been a joke in British humor since the mid-19th century.
  • A "dark woman" who assisted with births ,may refer to the following: 1) the Biblical midwife Shiphrah, who was a Nubian woman mentioned in the Book of Exodus. Shiphrah, along with her colleague Puah, defied the Pharaoh's order to kill newborn Hebrew males. 2) Biddy Mason, who was born into slavery, was a midwife and advocate for other enslaved people in 19th-century California. After gaining her freedom, she became a successful entrepreneur and philanthropist. 3) Margaret Charles Smith was an African American midwife in Alabama who delivered over 3,000 babies during a career spanning over 30 years, often in rural areas with limited healthcare access. 4) Mary Francis Hill Coley was a midwife from Georgia who delivered over 3,000 babies during her career. Her work was featured in the 1952 documentary, All My Babies. 5) Susie Carey was a third-generation midwife featured in a photograph at the National Museum of African American History and Culture. 6) Sarah Hudson Grant was a Black Southern midwife whose work is remembered today.
  • Artificial insemination is the deliberate introduction of sperm into a female's cervix or uterine cavity for the purpose of achieving a pregnancy through in vivo fertilization by means other than sexual intercourse or in vitro fertilisation. It is a fertility treatment for humans, and is common practice in animal breeding. The first recorded case of artificial insemination was John Hunter in 1790, who helped impregnate a linen draper's wife. The first reported case of artificial insemination by a donor occurred in 1884 when William H. Pancoast, a professor in Philadelphia, took sperm from a handsome student in his class to inseminate an anesthetized woman without her knowledge. The incident was not published until twenty-five years later in a medical journal. The sperm bank was developed in Iowa starting in the 1950s in research conducted by University of Iowa medical school researchers Jerome Sherman and Raymond Bunge. In the United Kingdom, the British obstetrician Mary Barton founded one of the first fertility clinics to offer donor insemination in the 1930s. Mary Barton and her first husband were medical missionaries in pre-partition India, then still ruled by Britain. She witnessed the way in which women would be punished or even killed for being childless. At the time, it was taboo to suggest that it might be the husband, and not the wife, who was infertile - not only on the Indian subcontinent but also in the United Kingdom. Barton understood that both men and women could be infertile and in 1943 was the lead author on an article for the British Medical Journal. It was signed by many of the researchers active in the field in Great Britain at that time. With her second husband, Bertold Wiesner, Mary Barton successfully inseminated an estimated 1500 women, the majority with sperm provided from Wiesner, some 100-200 from neuroscientist Derek Richter as well as an unknown number from as yet unidentified donors. It is estimated that Wiesner is the biological father of around 600 children born following these procedures, although some believe this figure could be as high as 1000. When Barton and Wiesner published their paper on the procedure it was publicly condemned by the Pope who called it a sin, and the Archbishop of Canterbury who called for the British parliament to make human artificial insemination illegal. Although it was not criminalized it was not legalized either and therefore the status of artificial insemination was ambiguous. Consequently, the activities of Barton and Wiesner at the fertility clinic were conducted in secrecy and all inseminated women were instructed to tell nobody about it.
  • Instruments to assist with childbirth have evolved from rudimentary tools for destructive purposes in antiquity to sophisticated instruments like forceps and vacuum extractors today. Early interventions included destructive tools for delivering stillborn fetuses and instruments for procedures like symphysiotomy, a painful procedure to widen the pelvis. Modern forceps, introduced by the Chamberlen family in the 16th century, were a breakthrough for delivering living infants, and their use, along with vacuum extractors, remains a vital part of modern obstetrics.
  • Vera’s birthday and Esther Longtree’s birthday are portrayed with contrasting atmospheres and underlying thematic significance, reflecting their differing life circumstances and symbolic roles.
  • Vera’s birthday, her fourteenth, is described with a sense of ritual and expectation, though tinged with loneliness and unrealized celebration. Vera receives a formal party dress, a filmy white creation, somewhat too mature for her, chosen by Mr. Spitzer in a moment of abstraction linked to the memory of Vera’s mother. Despite the preparation, there are no guests, no grand party, and only Miss MacIntosh, her nursemaid, and Vera herself are present. The absence of guests and the muted atmosphere emphasize Vera’s isolation and the unrealized joys of childhood. Miss MacIntosh insists on simplicity and adherence to routine, asking Vera to take care of her duties, underscoring the austere and disciplined environment Vera inhabits. Vera is caught between the innocence and hope of youth and the harsh, confining realities imposed by her surroundings and caretakers. The birthday marks a threshold of maturity but also a loss of innocence, as Vera is trained for domesticity and marriage, and the celebration itself becomes a subdued, private event rather than a joyous public occasion. The birthday is also symbolic of Vera’s gradual awakening to the complexities and burdens of life. It is described as a moment on the edge of life’s "beginning of the end," a turning point where the dreams and illusions of childhood begin to confront reality. The party dress and the preparations seem almost a costume for a role Vera must play rather than an expression of genuine celebration. The atmosphere is one of quiet resignation and subdued hope, with Vera realizing she has "but one" life and must face the responsibilities and limitations of her social role.
  • Esther Longtree’s birthday, by contrast, is enveloped in sorrow, mystery, and the burdens of an "everlasting pregnancy," symbolic of a life marked by loss, unfulfilled hopes, and complex emotional struggles. Esther is the "passive policeman’s only daughter," a big, awkward woman whose life is overshadowed by repeated stillbirths and the mysterious fate of her children. Her birthday is less a celebration and more a reflection on her difficult existence, her isolation, and her maternal suffering. She is surrounded by the imagery of loss and death: stillborn children, shadows, ghosts, and spiritual burdens. Her pregnancy is portrayed as both a physical and metaphysical state, representing ongoing grief and hope intertwined. Esther’s birthday is not a moment of public recognition or joy but a private, almost secretive experience filled with anxiety and anticipation of an uncertain future. She is burdened by the expectations and mysteries of motherhood, the absence of fathers, and the threat of legal and social accusations. The narrative emphasizes her loneliness and the complexity of her emotional and physical state, weaving natural imagery (flowers, birds, snowflakes) with the harsh realities of her life.
  • Vera’s birthday is marked by a subdued, almost melancholic celebration within a structured, disciplined environment, while Esther’s birthday is enveloped in sorrow, mystery, and the physical and emotional weight of repeated loss. Vera’s day is a threshold into maturity, Esther’s a reflection of enduring struggle.
  • Vera’s birthday symbolizes the fragile transition from innocence to experience, the imposition of societal expectations, and the tension between dreams and reality. Esther’s birthday symbolizes endurance, maternal sacrifice, and the haunting presence of loss and unfulfilled potential.
  • Vera’s birthday occurs within the protective but confining care of Miss MacIntosh, reflecting themes of control, preparation for societal roles, and the looming responsibilities of adulthood. Esther’s birthday reflects marginalization, survival amid hardship, and the complexities of maternal identity in a world shaped by absence and loss.
  • Vera’s birthday carries a quiet hope and the bittersweet nature of growing up alone. Esther’s birthday carries a profound sense of isolation, struggle, and the interplay of hope and despair.

Chapter 45

← Chapter 44 · Home · Chapter 46 →

Summary

Reading Hannah's faded letters by candlelight, Mr. Spitzer vows to keep her great secret until long after her death. He sees that her public and private lives cannot be fitted into one portrait. He recalls her asking whether she was always falling, and her sense that she aspired higher and so fell farther. He considers what her grave should say, and how public memory turns the greatest lives into monuments and loses the secret heart.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Identity and the Self · Love · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Symbols: Butterflies and Moths · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Fireflies · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Existentialism · Hinduism · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Nietzsche · Spinoza

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Gambling and Playing Cards · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Music and Composers · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates the paradox that Cousin Hannah, devoted to the cause of suffrage and seemingly a great authority on love, had never truly experienced love in the conventional sense. He muses that "if one knew all hearts, one should know none," and that love is essentially an unreachable image, a vision that, if grasped, leads to its death. Cousin Hannah’s life is described as a "double life, perhaps a triple life," full of ambivalence, contradictions, and secrecy. This had left Mr. Spitzer disappointed and uncertain about her true nature and feelings.
  • The imagery of cold mountains, snow, clouds, and icy landscapes recurs throughout the chapter as metaphors for the suffrage captain’s inner life and death. She is depicted as "sleeping under waters and clouds," her head "wrapped in veils and clouds and pillowed on stone," symbolizing her isolation and the inscrutability of her existence. The harshness and coldness of these natural elements reflect the emotional barrenness and the "heart of darkness and mystery" that Mr. Spitzer perceives.
  • The novel frequently explores the intertwined relationship between love and death. Cousin Hannah’s dying words and hallucinations evoke a sense of loss, betrayal, and eternal searching for a “dead love,” a love that was "killed" by her own actions or fate. Passages where she cries out about losing her love, wandering through mountains and deserts, and questioning her own identity ("Was I always falling?") emphasize the tragic dimension of her life and the universal human experience of love’s fragility and mortality.
  • Mr. Spitzer is portrayed as a melancholic witness to this woman’s life and death, struggling to reconcile the public image of the suffrage captain with the hidden truths he uncovers. He reflects on the fleeting nature of memory and fame, lamenting that she will be forgotten or remembered only for her public deeds, while her "secret heart" remains obscured. His meditations on pigeons as symbols of souls and memory, and his sorrow at man’s loss of remembrance, highlight the theme of oblivion and the limits of legacy.
  • In the final passages, Cousin Hannah’s delirious but poignant utterances reveal her inner torment and longing. She speaks of betrayal, lost love, and the breaking of a bond that "never was," wandering through cosmic and earthly landscapes in search of forgiveness and reunion. Her invocation of celestial and natural symbols (the moon, stars, snowflakes, sea shells) creates a dreamlike atmosphere where the boundaries between reality and vision blur. Mr. Spitzer hears and tries to interpret these "last remarks," recognizing the deep sorrow and ambiguity they contain.
  • Throughout, there are philosophical interludes where Mr. Spitzer reflects on the nature of existence, suggesting that life and death are continuous, that identity dissolves into "waters and clouds," and that memory is fragile and transient. He considers death as a form of love and vice versa, and entertains the idea that perhaps only the smallest, most delicate perceptions like butterflies, snowflakes, or ripples of water are free to escape fate. These reflections frame Cousin Hannahs’s story within a broader existential context.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A reflective figure.
  • He has witnessed the suffragette's life and death.
  • He is a skeptic yet compassionate observer, wrestling with doubt about love, death, and memory.
  • His perspective is melancholic and filled with symbolic musings.

Cousin Hannah

  • A heroic figure involved in suffrage, labor strikes, and adventurous exploits.
  • Her private life was a mystery, marked by lost love, guilt, and spiritual wandering.
  • She died with a sea shell at her feet, symbolizing her connection to the sea and the unknown.
  • She is described metaphorically as a "sleeping beauty," a "dead star," and a "great betrayer of woman," reflecting her complex legacy.

Research: Themes

Love and Its Ambivalence

See: Love

  • Love is portrayed as an unattainable ideal.
  • Cousin Hannah’s love life is marked by loss, guilt, and a yearning for a final answer that never comes.
  • Cousin Hannah’s lamentations at her deathbed emphasize her betrayal of love (whether by herself or by fate) and her eternal search for her lost love.

Memory, Identity, and the Passing of Time

See: Memory and the Past · Time · Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with memory’s frailty, likening it to fleeting natural phenomena.
  • The chapter meditates on the dissolution of identity.
  • Cousin Hannah’s secret life and true self remain ambiguous, veiled in clouds and mystery, reflecting the difficulty of truly knowing another person, especially after death.

Death and Transition

See: Death and Mortality

  • The narrative frequently returns to images of death as a form of journey or transformation.
  • Death is intertwined with love; “Death is love, and love is death.”
  • Cousin Hannah’s death is surrounded by symbolic natural elements which serve as metaphors for her passing and the mystery surrounding it.

Public vs. Private Life

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • Cousin Hannah was a public hero, a suffragette with noble deeds and a fiery spirit, yet her private life was marked by confusion, betrayal, and unfulfilled love.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on how public memory tends to forget the complexity of individuals, often reducing them to symbols or monuments.
  • Cousin Hannah had a "double life," perhaps even a "triple life," that no one truly understood.

Mysticism and Symbolism

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The chapter is rich with symbolic imagery: mountains, clouds, snow, stars, fireflies, sea shells, the moon, and butterflies.
  • These symbols often blur the boundary between reality and hallucination, reflecting Mr. Spitzer’s and Cousin Hannah’s fractured consciousness.
  • The narrative suggests the possibility of existence beyond physical death, through memory, spirit, or cosmic forces.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Clouds and Snow

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Clouds and Storms

  • Ambiguity, transition, death, and the veil between life and afterlife.

Mountain Peaks

See: Mountains

  • Obstacles, spiritual heights, isolation, and the vast unknown.

Sea Shell/Sea

See: The Sea and Water

  • Memory, the call of the unknown, the eternal sea of life and death.

Fireflies and Stars

See: Fireflies · Moon and Stars

  • Fleeting Beauty, lost souls, and unreachable ideals.

Butterflies

See: Butterflies and Moths

  • Transformation, fleeting perceptions and the fragility of life and consciousness.

Bell/Bells

See: Music and Instruments

  • Calls to attention, spiritual awakening, and auditory hallucinations connected to death and memory.

Skirt/Flounces

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • The lost love or spirit, something elusive that the suffragette seeks but cannot find.

Moon

See: Moon and Stars

  • Mystery, guidance, and the shifting nature of reality and perception.

Research: Resources

  • Young may have taken inspiration for the character Cousin Hannah from Susan B. Anthony and her sister, Hannah. Mr. Spitzer described Cousin Hannah as “this great father of suffrage”. Susan B. Anthony’s father was the first one in the family to become interested in the women’s suffrage movement. She was interested in social reform. She was a teacher and was paid less than her male counterparts (then as now). Anthony said, “I wasn’t ready to vote, didn’t want to vote, but I did want equal pay for equal work.” The family started out as Quakers and Anthony claimed to be a Quaker but the father moved away from the order to join the Unitarian Church. They were abolitionists and temperance advocates and had the likes of Frederick Douglass speak at their house. She formed a partnership with Elizabeth Cady Stanton and Lucy Stone. Stanton kept a room for her at her house where she also spent most of her life working with her. Anthony and Stanton went on to write the History of Woman Suffrage. Anthony said this kind of work, "makes me feel growly all the time... No warhorse ever panted for the rush of battle more than I for outside work. I love to make history but hate to write it." Anthony did not believe in her writing skills which mostly went to Stanton. Most of her quotes come from speeches and lectures. Anthony did not live to see the ratification of the 19th Amendment or equal rights. "There have been others also just as true and devoted to the cause—I wish I could name every one—but with such women consecrating their lives, failure is impossible!" "Now, after 40 years of agitation, the idea is beginning to prevail that women were created for themselves, for their own happiness, and for the welfare of the world." Back to her religion. It is a mixed bag in that they moved to being Unitarian although proud of her Quaker roots. She was involved with the Friends of Human Progress that included “Christians, Jews, Mahammedans, and Pagans.” She tried to start her own Free church where all were welcome. She later, according to Stanton, became agnostic. "Work and worship are one with me. I can not imagine a God of the universe made happy by my getting down on my knees and calling him 'great.'" When Anthony's sister Hannah was on her deathbed, she asked Susan to talk about the great beyond, but Anthony later wrote, "I could not dash her faith with my doubts, nor could I pretend a faith I had not; so I was silent in the dread presence of death." Hannah was known for her domestic nature, but also for her full sympathy with the reforms championed by her sister. As a teen, Anthony went to parties, and she had offers of marriage when she was older, but there is no record of her ever having a serious romance. Anthony loved children, however, and helped raise the children in the Stanton household. As a young worker in the women's rights movement, Anthony expressed frustration when some of her co-workers began to marry and have children, sharply curtailing their ability to work for the understaffed movement. When Lucy Stone abandoned her pledge to stay single, Anthony's scolding remarks caused a temporary rupture in their friendship. It was a bit more than a temporary rupture. They both formed separate suffrage movements. Anthony wanted a federal constitutional amendment. Stone wanted a more gradual state-by-state approach. Anthony opposed the 15th Amendment because it did not grant everyone the right to vote. Stone supported it as a stepping stone. It was 20 years before their two organizations worked together again. Stone worked out with her husband a separate but equal marriage where Stone retained rights to her property and finances and her personal liberty. Lucy Stone wore bloomers. She also kept her name. They publicly declared their commitment to equality and rejected the idea of a wife’s legal subordination. Journalists repeatedly asked Anthony to explain why she never married. She answered one by saying, "It always happened that the men I wanted were those I could not get, and those who wanted me I wouldn't have.” To another, she answered, "I never found the man who was necessary to my happiness. I was very well as I was.” To a third she said, "I never felt I could give up my life of freedom to become a man's housekeeper. When I was young, if a girl married poor, she became a housekeeper and a drudge. If she married wealth she became a pet and a doll. Just think, had I married at twenty, I would have been a drudge or a doll for fifty-nine years. Think of it!" In a speech in 1877, Anthony predicted "an epoch of single women. If women will not accept marriage with subjugation, nor men proffer it without, there is, there can be, no alternative. The woman who will not be ruled must live without marriage."
  • Twelve Miles - is what Mr. Spitzer thinks about putting on Cousin Hannah’s gravestone. There are some famous 12 Mile Markers in the US. There are also some in unincorporated communities in Indiana. It can also refer to a territorial waters limit. Twelve Miles can be understood as a symbolic measure of travel through life and time, marking a stage or a point that carries personal or spiritual significance in the midst of complexity and ambiguity. It is less a literal distance and more an emblematic representation of passage, progress, or endurance on the journey of life and memory in the novel's broader themes of time, existence, and spiritual quest.
  • “mountaineers lost long ago stared out from behind great crystal walls.” There are many dead bodies weighing hundreds of pounds that have not been carried off of Mount Everest and other mountains, plus there is an enormous amount of trash that is left at the campsites. The phrase conveys the persistence of memory and the haunting presence of the past, while emphasizing the fragile, elusive nature of existence in the novel’s dreamlike world.
  • “pigeon poler” - It may refer to poker (Peron Spitzer) where it is a player who is perceived as a weak or inexperienced player, easily manipulated or exploited. Some poker players might intentionally act like a “pigeon” to deceive other players. It symbolizes a guardian or guide navigating others, in this case pigeons, through uncertain or liminal spaces, much like Mr. Spitzer’s own role as a watcher and intermediary between worlds.
  • “he was become his brother.” may be a full confession by Mr. Spitzer that he is not Joachim but Peron/Jock. It encapsulates the novel’s exploration of identity, loss, and the haunting persistence of the past within the present self.
  • “She knew her Carthage.” may refer to Dido, the legendary founder and queen of Carthage. Dido, whose name also appears as Elissa, is a figure from Phoenician and Roman history and mythology. She is known for founding the city of Carthage and for her tragic love story with the Trojan hero Aeneas. In Virgil’s Aeneid, Dido is depicted as a wise and ambitious leader who built Carthage into a prosperous city, according to some accounts. It means she was no stranger to hardship, defeat, and the costs of struggle, embodying the resilience and tragic grandeur associated with such historical and symbolic ruin.
  • “Who is that dwarf, a turret on his head, a rose at his collar? It is the rose of consciousness.” May refer to Nietzsche where the dwarf represents self-doubt and the limitations of conventional thought. Zarathustra’s journey involves overcoming the dwarf, symbolizing the overcoming of self-doubt and the embrace of his philosophy, including the concept of eternal recurrence. Young gives him the rose of consciousness. According to Thomas Reid sensory information, particularly in relation to movement, contributes to our subjective experience of the world. This framework suggests that consciousness might be closely tied to our ability to interact with and act upon the world. Sensation vs Perception - Thomas Reid (which I’ve mentioned before) saw sensation as a primitive feeling or awareness, while perception was the process of interpreting these feelings and associating them with external objects. The ability to distinguish between sensation and perception is linked to consciousness. The turret is typically a small tower, often ornamental, that juts out from a building. It is typically found on castles, large houses, etc. The passage poetically captures consciousness as a guarded, precious, and living presence within the self, one that both defines identity and is shaped by the ongoing flux of life and perception.
  • “Shall love be infinitely postponed? If infinitely postponed, then it is love.” may refer to Hegel. To deny something is to determine it, and to determine something is to negate it. Spinoza’s principle is “every determination is negation”. Hegel takes this one step further by suggesting that negation itself is a process of creation, and is even the essence of positive being. By denying a certain trait or characteristic, one is implicitly acknowledging the possibility of its opposite or the existence of a different reality. For Hegel, this power of the negative, or the act of negation, is what drives progress and development. Denying a particular concept allows for the possibility of a new one to emerge, incorporating both the original concept and its negation. This is often explained through the concept of the negation of the negation, where a denial of a denial leads to a new synthesis that transcends both the original thesis and the antithesis. From an existentialist perspective denying a predefined purpose or essence allows for the possibility of individuals to create their own meaning and existence. The line speaks to love as an infinite emotional state, one that transcends immediate gratification and endures through time, absence, and even death, resonating with the novel's larger themes of longing, loss, and the elusive nature of human connection.
  • “Forgive the cloud which knows not what it whispers” Luke 23:34 This line fits with the novel’s broader motifs of illusion, memory, loss, and the elusive nature of reality, where characters grapple with fragmented perceptions of existence and the blending of dream and waking life.
  • “I aspired to greater heights than most, so I fell a greater distance.” - This line occurs in a chapter where the narrator, Vera, and other characters grapple with their desires, failures, and the often painful gap between expectation and outcome, highlighting the complexity of human experience and the poignant cost of reaching beyond oneself.
  • “Forgive the secret none can tell. None can tell and live.” It is considered a classic riddle and the common answer is death. In a metaphorical sense it may refer to a profound or life-altering experience that can’t be adequately described in words. Or a secret that if revealed would lead to someone’s demise or ruin. The phrase captures the tension between the desire to disclose deep, painful truths and the necessity of silence for survival. It also suggests that some aspects of human experience, perhaps related to loss, guilt, or forbidden knowledge are too dangerous or profound to be openly shared. This interpretation aligns with the novel’s exploration of memory, secrecy, and the weight of unspoken suffering.
  • Steven Shaviro shared a comment from a Dalkey interview that according to Young Esther Longtree (at the end of the book) is the Mother of Us All which also happens to be an opera by Gertrude Stein about Susan B. Anthony. In that interview she also said Esther is the mother of us all and Mr. Spitzer is the father of us all.
  • “Death is love, and love is death…” It is a profound paradox since life, with its inherent drive for continuation, is ultimately defined by its end, death. Every living thing eventually dies making it the ultimate and unavoidable end. We experience life as a continuous present, however, everything is mortal. part of a natural cycle of birth, death, and decay. Even experience with death, the loss of a loved one, can have a profound effect on a person’s life. It can deepen one’s capacity for love and understanding. The death of self can involve the death of the ego or self-centeredness as one prioritizes the needs and well-being of another. Sacrificial love where one willingly puts themselves in harms way to protect another. The death of the old self allows for the emergence of a new, more compassionate and empathetic self. Even after death, love can endure through memories, experiences and the impact of a loved one to continue to live on. Love can be a source of strength and comfort. The love between two people can leave a lasting legacy. Contemplating death can highlight the preciousness of life and the importance of love. Experiences of loss can foster deeper empathy and appreciation for loved ones. Death can serve as a reminder to live fully, cherish relationships, and express love while we have the chance. The certainty of death raises questions about the meaning of life. Highlighting the complex relationship between individual life and the larger, overarching biological cycle. Some religions and philosophies offer concepts of an afterlife, reincarnation, or the idea that life continues through the legacy of one’s actions. Or love is seen as a force that can conquer death and offer a path through it. Some say that true love is immortal. Some works suggest that the intensity of love can be destructive, leading to a kind of “death” of the self or relationship. Others suggest that embracing the reality of death can lead to a more meaningful and authentic life. It encapsulates the novel's exploration of the cyclical, intertwined nature of these fundamental human experiences, suggesting that love and death are inseparable and that understanding one requires embracing the other. This paradox also underlines the novel's broader themes of illusion, memory, and the elusive nature of reality and identity. The phrase means that love and death are deeply connected realities; love inevitably involves loss and mortality, and death can be viewed as an extension or transformation of love, a theme that permeates the novel’s existential and metaphysical reflections.
  • “he who loves shall lose himself in love as in death” - Mathew 16:25 and John 12:25 The phrase aligns with the novel’s motifs of merging opposites (life and death, self and other, reality and illusion) and reflects the emotional and metaphysical struggles of the characters. The loss of self in love is not presented as purely tragic but as an essential part of the human condition and the search for connection beyond isolation.

Nan Shepherd in The Living Mountain examined what it meant to walk “around” the mountain. “To aim for the highest point is not the only way to climb a mountain.”
