Chapter 44

← Chapter 43 · Home · Chapter 45 →

Summary

Over the years, Mr. Spitzer pieces together fragments of Hannah's hidden life from her papers: letters, unreadable languages, evidence of a double existence. He recalls her deathbed talk of skirts and petticoats, strange from the great champion of bloomers, and her cry that false modesty killed her love. He wonders whether heroes are driven by a secret cowardice, and whether those who never loved know most of love.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Fear and Courage · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Love · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Heraclitus and Flux · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: Judaism · The Bible · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Mr. Spitzer reflects on the paradox of Cousin Hannah, a great feminist and enemy of restrictive fashion, calling for her skirt as she was dying. This paradox highlights the complexities and contradictions in her character. Though she battled societal constraints, at the end she seemed to long for something she had fought to discard. This mystery sets the tone for the chapter's exploration of illusion versus truth and the human vulnerability beneath heroic veneer.
  • Mr. Spitzer's gesture of bringing her snowdrops, delicate white flowers resembling snow, and her agony increasing upon seeing them melt in her hand is a poignant metaphor. It suggests the fragility of life and love, the melting away of hope, and the uncontrollable forces that govern human fate, forces akin to natural phenomena like avalanches and winds, that Mr. Spitzer likens to a musician losing control of his baton.
  • Cousin Hannah’s dying lament reveals a deep personal grief underlying her public persona. Her repeated cry about finding her skirt is both literal and symbolic, implying a search for identity, love, or completeness that was never fulfilled. This passage underscores the theme of lost love as a motivating force behind her suffrage battles and personal suffering.
  • Cousin Hannah’s words that “False modesty killed my love” and the declaration that there was “no man in all those mountains” or “one star looking down” evoke isolation and the absence of external validation or support. This passage deepens the existential solitude of her experience and suggests that internal struggles, not external enemies, may have been her greatest challenge.
  • As she questions whether her love and the love she received were true or false, the suffrage captain’s dying confession reveals the complexity of human emotions and relationships. This ambivalence illustrates that heroism and love are not clear-cut or absolute but often involve contradictions and inner conflict.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s reflection on the possibility that the greatest heroes might be driven by secret cowardice and that this inner failure propels them toward greater battles is philosophically profound. It questions traditional notions of heroism and valor, suggesting that vulnerability and fear are inseparable from greatness.
  • The chapter repeatedly returns to death as a process of transformation rather than an end: “flowers turning into birds, birds turning into flowers,” and “death was this eternal transmutation.” This idea challenges conventional finality of death, proposing a mystical continuity that blurs life and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s struggle to understand the suffragette’s life, filled with secret letters, unintelligible languages, and mysteries “greater than the Sphinx,” symbolizes the inscrutability of human motivations and emotions. Her heart is portrayed as “in darkness and terrifying whirlwind,” emphasizing that even the most public figures harbor private enigmas.
  • The paradox that Cousin Hannah had “never experienced” love, death, or marriage in a conventional sense, yet was the confidante of many secrets and the recipient of many whispered confessions, raises profound questions about knowledge, experience, and empathy. It suggests that knowing about human emotions can be distinct from living them.
  • The closing reflections ponder the nature of love and death as inseparable and universal experiences that “all who lived had already died” in some sense, and that the greatest love might be ineffable and unexpressed. Mr. Spitzer’s thoughts on the fate of all lives being “increased by this great mystery of death” provide a somber, philosophical conclusion to the chapter.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah / The Great Suffrage Captain

  • A once-celebrated suffragette whose public life was marked by courage and activism.
  • In private, she was vulnerable, haunted by lost love, and self-doubt.
  • Her death is poetic and symbolic, involving imagery of skirts, snowdrops, mountains, and clouds.

Mr. Spitzer

  • An old lawyer entrusted with handling Cousin Hannah’s affairs after her death.
  • Reflective, cautious, and rational, yet deeply affected by the mysteries he uncovers.
  • He struggles to reconcile the public image of Cousin Hannah with the private truths he learns.
  • Acts as Vera and interpreter of the suffragette’s life and legacy.

Research: Themes

Truth vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The chapter opens with the idea that truth in life is rare but powerful, like granite and sunlight amidst illusions (moonbeams). Mr. Spitzer slowly pieces together the fragmented truth of Cousin Hannah’s life, which is elusive and fleeting.
  • The suffragette’s public persona versus her private reality is a central tension. Though once celebrated, her fame has faded, and her true self remains mysterious and partly hidden.

Love and Loss

See: Love · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Despite being a fierce fighter for women’s rights, Cousin Hannah is shown to be deeply haunted by a lost love, which shapes much of her life and final moments.
  • Her dying cries for her "love," "little snowdrop," and her search for a "skirt" symbolize a yearning for something lost, possibly innocence, identity, or a personal connection.
  • The narrative suggests that her suffrage activism was motivated by personal heartbreak, intertwining public struggle with private grief 455.

Heroism and Cowardice

See: Fear and Courage

  • The chapter challenges traditional notions of heroism, suggesting that great heroes may be driven by secret cowardice or inner failures 456.
  • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as both a heroic figure and a vulnerable woman who doubted herself at the end.
  • Mr. Spitzer debates the nature of courage, recognizing that even the smallest, seemingly weak acts can be heroic, such as a moth’s desire to reach a star.

Death and Memory

See: Death and Mortality · Memory and the Past

  • Death is portrayed as a transformative and mysterious force, an eternal transmutation where forms change but essence remains.
  • Mr. Spitzer's reflections suggest that death does not erase a person but deepens the mystery of their existence.
  • The chapter explores how memory is fragile; great lives and deeds can be forgotten, and the true nature of a person might never be fully known.

Mystery and the Human Heart

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The suffragette is depicted as a repository of secrets and confidences, receiving the hidden sorrows and loves of others even as her own heart remains obscure.
  • The novel questions whether anyone can truly understand love, life, or ambition, suggesting these remain inscrutable mysteries.
  • The idea that knowing without experiencing, knowing love without loving, or death without dying, might be a deeper form of understanding is proposed.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Skirts, Laces, Petticoats

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Symbolize femininity, freedom, and perhaps the burden of societal expectations. Cousin Hannah’s paradoxical final request for her skirt contrasts with her life’s advocacy for shedding such encumbrances.

Snowdrops and Snow

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Roses and Flowers

  • Represent purity, fragility, and the coldness of death. The melting snowdrops in her hand symbolize fading life and lost love.

Mountains, Clouds, Icebergs

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Mountains · Clouds and Storms

  • Evoke the harshness and isolation of her inner world and struggles.
  • The iceberg imagery suggests overwhelming, unseen dangers and emotional coldness.

Music and Sound

See: Music and Instruments

  • Mr. Spitzer often parallels his thoughts to music, hearing the “roaring of the long-tongued surf” and “race-track music,” symbolizing the ongoing passage of time and memory.

The Whirlwind and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Clouds and Storms

  • Represent confusion, chaos, and the unknowability of the human heart.

Research: Resources

  • Lucy Stone and other suffragists adopted the Bloomer costume, which consisted of a knee-length skirt worn over trousers or pantaloons, in the early 1850s. Stone loved the comfort and practicality of the outfit and wore it both at home and in public for about three years. However, the Bloomer costume attracted significant public scrutiny and ridicule, and critics of the women's rights movement often focused on the reformers' attire rather than their arguments for suffrage and other reforms. By late 1853, many prominent suffragists, including Elizabeth Cady Stanton, abandoned the Bloomer costume due to the negative attention it generated. Stanton persuaded Stone to follow suit. Stone resumed wearing long skirts, although she never again wore the restrictive corsets and voluminous dresses of the fashionable style. Other notable suffragists like Susan B. Anthony also stopped wearing Bloomers around the same time. Amelia Bloomer, the editor of The Lily newspaper and namesake of the costume, continued to wear it until 1858. Only Elizabeth Smith Miller, who had helped popularize the style, continued to wear bloomers longer, until 1861.
  • There is a reference to “heart of darkness” again (book by Conrad that examines the horrors of Western colonialism). The phrase encapsulates both the personal anguish of Catherine and the broader existential themes of decay, loss, and the search for meaning in the novel.
  • “For false was my true love’s heart.” is used in folk songs like, A Brisk Young Sailor Courted Me, having some similarities to Madge’s subplot. Blackamoor - Hannah’s conscience may be similar to the Black Coachman for Catherine. It signifies the painful recognition that her idealized love was fundamentally flawed or deceptive, contributing to her sorrow and the novel’s ongoing exploration of illusion versus reality in human connections.
  • “eternal transmutation” - Transmutation is change and alchemy is a process of elevation. There is a subtle difference between the two and both are associated with the idea of turning lead into gold. They’re often used as a metaphor for spiritual or personal growth. With transformation it is inevitable because life is in a constant state of flux. People are in a perpetual process of becoming. Another way of pointing to Thales of Miletus and Heraclitus. This concept aligns with the novel’s broader themes of illusion, identity, and the blurred boundaries between life and death, reality and dream. It highlights the paradox of permanence in impermanence or the idea that while individual forms or lives may end or change, the process of transformation is ongoing and eternal.
  • “bearding the sleeping lion in its den” means to attack someone on their own ground or subject. The context of the novel, this expression highlights Mr. Spitzer's role as a persistent figure who, despite his cautious and reserved nature, must face the daunting and often confusing realities surrounding the Cartwheel family and their complex, dreamlike world. It suggests his courageous, though sometimes reluctant, engagement with the mysteries and challenges he encounters, especially concerning the enigmatic and troubled lives of the characters like Vera, her mother Catherine, and Miss MacIntosh.
  • The dedication Young gave the novel is in this chapter “For all dead loves and all remembered things. I have travelled through many seas.” The phrase reflects the novel’s overarching themes of memory, loss, and the blending of reality and dream, emphasizing that the journey through these "seas" is both personal and universal, touching on the shared human experience of love and remembrance.
  • “Judas cock” may refer to the Book of the Cock/Rooster which was probably written in the 400s or 500s in Arabic or Greek and used by Ethiopian Christians who have and use the text during Holy Week activities. It describes the final three days of Jesus's life, including a sequence where he reanimated a previously roasted rooster that He sent to spy on Judas Iscariot when he (Judas) was plotting to betray Jesus. The rooster informed Jesus and his disciples of the plan. Among other events, the Book of the Rooster describes Saul of Tarsus' participation in the arrest, abuse and crucifixion of Jesus, the betrayal of Jesus by a female relative of Judas, a debate between Pilate and Herod about the culpability of Jesus, Mary's grief, John the Evangelist witnessing the crucifixion of Jesus, the conversations Jesus had with the two thieves he was crucified alongside Gestas (Awsēmobyā) and Demas (Salikonilidākki) and references to other miracles that Jesus performed during his life. The rooster may be based on the Ziz of Jewish mythology, a giant bird. Like the Gospel of Judas from the second century, the Book of the Rooster attempts to explain the betrayal of Judas before the Last Supper, an act which is traditionally seen as abrupt or lacking reason.
  • Beau joueur is a person who shows a spirit of fairness and generosity in sport.
  • A chanticleer is another name for a rooster. It is also a character name in various works of fiction such as Reynard the Fox and The Nun’s Priest’s Tale in the book Canterbury Tales.
  • Albert Einstein was a German theoretical physicist who is best known for the theory of relativity. Relativity was a revolutionary idea that would change our understanding of the universe, but they were rarely able to explain any further. He said in a 1929 interview that, “The meaning of relativity has been widely misunderstood. Philosophers play with the word, like a child with a doll. Relativity, as I see it, merely denotes that certain physical and mechanical facts, which have been regarded as positive and permanent, are relative with regard to certain other facts in the sphere of physics and mechanics. It does not mean that we have the right to turn the world mischievously topsy-turvy.”
  • “there was no such thing as safety—not even for her— certainly none for him” This sentence encapsulates the idea that safety, in the absolute sense, is an illusion for all humans, even for the seemingly steadfast Miss MacIntosh and the cautious Mr. Spitzer, as they face the inexorable forces of fate, death, and the unknown. It is similar to Helen Keller’s quote from The Open Door, “Security is mostly a superstition. It does not exist in nature, nor do the children of men as a whole experience it. Avoiding danger is no safer in the long run than outright exposure. Life is either a daring adventure, or nothing.”

Chapter 56

Summary

Mr. Spitzer recalls dressing Peron's body in an elegant black suit cut like his own, and burying him with poker chips, dice, a playing card, and a red rose, while a one-armed violinist and a racetrack bugler played. Over the years he gave Peron's huge wardrobe away to the poor. He doubts reality, wonders who tailored his strange life, and carries a golden key to a door that no longer exists.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Great Tailor

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Madness and Sanity

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Clouds and Storms · Mirrors and Reflections · Music and Instruments · Roses and Flowers · The Sea and Water

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Gambling and Playing Cards · Music and Composers · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer meticulously arranges his brother’s funeral, dressing the corpse with the utmost sartorial elegance, symbolizing death as a formal occasion requiring proper attire and ritual. The detail about placing poker chips, dice, and a playing card in the grave represents the interplay of chance and fate in life and death. The presence of a violinist with an empty sleeve and an official track bugler who had played at renowned venues emphasizes the blending of the theatrical, the musical, and the ceremonial in mourning. Mr. Spitzer’s identity and grief are deeply intertwined with this performance of death, as he leaves only the red rose to Peron, symbolizing recognition at "the portals of the great city".
  • Peron is portrayed as an elusive, shape-shifting figure, likened to a squid that evades capture by producing an inky cloud, while Mr. Spitzer is the shadow to Peron’s substance. This metaphor illustrates their complex, intertwined identities. Mr. Spitzer clings to his threadbare suit as a sign of his enduring self amidst chaos, while recognizing that both brothers have become all others except themselves by reflecting on themes of identity dissolution and the fluidity of self.
  • The act of giving away Peron’s lavish wardrobe to the homeless and the poor is laden with symbolic significance. Clothing, representing identity and presence, is dispersed, highlighting the transience of life and the fading of memory. The detailed description of the various garments and hats, especially the jockeys' suits, connects Peron’s past life and interests to the present dispersal, symbolizing the scattering of a once vibrant existence into fragments of color and fabric.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s grief extends beyond personal loss to a cosmic mourning for all changing and ephemeral things: flowers, animals, natural phenomena, moments, and even the future. His grief is universal and diffuse, capturing an almost pantheistic sorrow for impermanence and transformation. The imagery of tides, stars, moths, and flowers conveys a deep connection between human sorrow and the natural world.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s philosophical reflections reveal his skepticism about reality, suggesting that what we call reality is merely appearances and dreams layered upon each other. He questions the existence of a stable self or a divine author, concluding that life and death might be inseparable or aspects of the same experience. The motifs of clothing, masks, and shadows reinforce the theme of identity as a fragile and mutable construct. Mr. Spitzer’s feeling of being a “dead man walking” clad in his black suit symbolizes his liminal state between life and death.
  • The imagery of Mr. Spitzer as a puppet, a tailor’s dummy, and a cloud with seams unraveling captures his fragmented existence and loss of agency. He is a “poor copy” of himself, patched and fragile, caught between madness and reality. His body and mind are portrayed as disconnected, with his identity slipping away like a dream or a reflection in a dark glass. This passage powerfully conveys the disintegration of self and the ephemeral nature of being.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates madness not merely as illness but as a state that blurs the boundaries between life and death, sustaining the semblance of health even as the mind is annihilated. This duality suggests that madness may be the only life possible for the dead, reflecting the profound ambiguity of existence in the aftermath of loss.
  • In the closing passage, Mr. Spitzer laments the absence of a guiding author or architect of being. The world is a place without an ordered design, and he carries the “golden key to the door that was no more,” symbolizing lost access to meaning or transcendence. The final image of the “dead musician” who lives despite attempts to silence him encapsulates the persistence of art, memory, or spirit amid chaos and decay.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is the grieving brother, depicted as a man shattered by loss, struggling with his identity and the nature of reality. He clings to his old, threadbare clothes as symbols of himself and his grief.

Peron

  • Peron is Mr. Spitzer’s deceased brother, described as eccentric with a flamboyant lifestyle, many coats and hats, and a lavish wardrobe. Peron’s death triggers Mr. Spitzer’s existential reflections.

The Tailor

  • The Tailor (mad tailor) is a metaphorical figure representing the forces shaping Mr. Spitzer’s identity and existence, questioning who "tailored" him in this strange life and afterlife.

Research: Themes

Death and Mourning

See: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Death is portrayed as a formal, solemn occasion requiring proper dress and ritual, exemplified by the funeral preparations and symbolic items placed with Peron (poker chips, dice, playing cards, racing forms).
  • Mr. Spitzer’s grief is all-encompassing, extending beyond his brother to encompass all things transient and ephemeral (flowers, moths, tides, stars, moments).
  • The boundary between life and death is blurred; Mr. Spitzer often questions whether he is alive or dead, and whether life and death are two sides of the same experience.

Identity and the Self

See: Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with his identity, feeling like a shadow or a poor copy of his brother, or even a puppet controlled by unknown forces.
  • He questions the nature of selfhood, pondering whether he might become his brother by adopting his clothing and mannerisms.
  • The metaphor of clothing is powerful: Peron’s elaborate wardrobe symbolizes identity and social roles, while Mr. Spitzer’s threadbare suit symbolizes decay, loss, and continuity of self.

Reality vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Reality is depicted as an illusion, a dream clothed in appearances.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s literal-mindedness causes him to confuse abstract qualities (love, beauty, truth) with physical objects, illustrating his disorientation.
  • He philosophizes that reality might be “unreal” and that existence is layered with dreams and shadows, making existence fragile and unstable.

Madness and Sanity

See: Madness and Sanity

  • Madness is presented ambiguously as both a form of death and a form of life, sustaining illusion and preventing the advance of time.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s mental state deteriorates as he questions who controls him, who “tailored” his existence, and whether he is merely a puppet or a phantom.
  • His inability to distinguish between reality and imagination is a symbol of his psychological collapse.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Clothing and Tailoring

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Represent identity, social roles, and continuity/death. Peron’s lavish suits contrast with Mr. Spitzer’s threadbare suit, symbolizing life and decay.

White and Red Roses

See: Roses and Flowers

  • The white rose worn by Mr. Spitzer symbolizes passing beyond life (death or transcendence), while Peron’s red rose is a signifier of identity and remembrance.

The Mirror and Reflection

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Symbolize self-perception and identity confusion; often Mr. Spitzer sees distorted or absent reflections.

Clouds, Sea, and Tides

See: The Sea and Water · Clouds and Storms

  • Recurring natural motifs representing impermanence, change, and the fluid boundary between life and death.

Music and Instruments

See: Music and Instruments

  • The funeral bugler and violinist evoke the ceremonial aspect of death and a connection to the past.

Animals and Nature

  • Moths, barnacles, starfish, whales, and birds symbolize fragility, transformation, and the natural cycle of life and death.

Chapter 53

← Chapter 52 · Home · Chapter 54 →

Summary

No instrument is wide enough for Mr. Spitzer's feelings. He contrasts Peron, a chameleon of many colors, with himself, a timid chess player who never made the final move. Since the death he has been mistaken for his brother and has come to know things only Peron knew: boxing records, gambling, speakeasies. He calls himself a pale replica, divided between himself and his twin.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Philosophy: Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Gambling and Playing Cards · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · Sir Walter Raleigh · The Bible · The Civil War · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Mr. Spitzer is described as a "lost musician with his unfinished song," struggling to find a way to express the vast range of his feelings and experiences, which surpass any available instrument or keyboard. His music is marked by many segnos and signs, suggesting incomplete or concealed meanings. This metaphor extends to his life itself, indicating a sense of incompletion and fragmentation, a yearning for unity and integration that remains unfulfilled.
  • A central motif is the blurring of identities between Mr. Spitzer (Joachim) and his brother Peron. Since Peron’s apparent suicide, Mr. Spitzer has been mistaken for Peron and struggles with the paradox of being a "pale replica," a mask or dream rather than flesh and blood. The reversal of roles with Joachim seeming to be Peron, exposes the fragile boundary between life and death, self and other, reality and illusion.
  • Time is portrayed as fluid and illusory. Mr. Spitzer contemplates the collapse of centuries into moments and the eternal cry of a lost child wandering in darkness. He is haunted by the feeling that he has "missed his brother by only a minute," symbolizing missed opportunities and the relentless passage of time. The imagery of trains passing by, always missing the right connection, reinforces this sense of temporal dislocation and existential solitude.
  • Peron’s life is described as volatile, colorful, and many-sided, like a chameleon changing colors, while Joachim’s is opaque, timorous, and marked by a search for equilibrium. Peron's life is a "crazy patchwork" of many identities and experiences, whereas Joachim is the "heart of darkness," withdrawn and selfless. This contrast underscores themes of individuality, fate, and the search for meaning in a fractured existence.
  • Death is depicted as the "heart of life," and yet life itself may be the "heart of death." Mr. Spitzer reflects on the inevitability of change, the impossibility of stasis, and the paradox of "changelessness" as a form of change. Love, represented by the blind god Cupid, is indifferent to distinctions between the living and the dead, blurring boundaries and questioning the significance of identity itself.
  • Mr. Spitzer is a solitary mourner, wandering through empty landscapes seeking his dead brother and a place where they might be reunited. His grief is diffused and pervasive, spreading like an ink blot over his unwritten music and his existence. The imagery of the black cloak, the ivory-headed cane, and the shadowed self accentuate the theme of mourning and existential alienation.
  • Through his late-blooming sympathies with his brother, who was involved in shady and illegal activities, Mr. Spitzer acquired unexpected knowledge of the underworld of gambling, speakeasies, boxing, billiards, and other sports and games. This knowledge, alien to his former life as a musician and lawyer, symbolizes the crossing of boundaries between worlds, the mingling of high and low, life and death, order and chaos.
  • Recurring images of chess, billiards, and card games illustrate life's strategic, repetitive, and sometimes futile nature. Mr. Spitzer sees himself as a timid chess player afraid to make a move that would mean his final defeat, highlighting the paralyzing fear of change and the interplay of fate and free will. The idea that he might have "missed his cue" in life or become a "dead man walking" underscores the theme of existential uncertainty and the search for selfhood.
  • The chapter closes with the idea that identity is fluid and that men are like chameleons or accidental conformations, changing with circumstances and perceptions. Joachim’s fixed, black-velvet pall identity contrasts with Peron’s many-colored, shifting persona. This evokes the essential ambivalence and mystery of human existence and the elusive nature of the self.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer (Joachim)

  • A composer and musician, burdened by an unfinished “song,” representing his incomplete life and unresolved feelings.
  • He is introspective, sensitive, and often alienated from the world. His reflections reveal a man caught between worlds like life and death, self and other, reality and illusion.
  • He wrestles with the sense of being overshadowed by his brother’s legacy and struggles with his own identity and place in existence.

Peron

  • Mr. Spitzer’s brother, a gambler and more flamboyant, volatile personality.
  • Peron’s life is described as colorful, many-sided, and seemingly successful, but also transient and elusive.
  • His death creates a “rift” in Spitzer’s life and intensifies Spitzer’s struggle with his own existence and identity.

Research: Themes

  • Identity and Duality The chapter explores the paradox of the two brothers’ overlapping identities. Joachim as the “pale replica” of Peron, and Peron as an elusive, many-personality figure. The idea that Joachim might be Peron and vice versa underlines the instability of self and questions the fixity of identity.
  • Life, Death, and Memory Mr. Spitzer contemplates death not as an end but a transformation and continuation beyond physical existence. The boundaries between life and death blur, as love and memory maintain connections beyond mortality. He mourns his brother, yet also mourns himself, reflecting on the theme of grief diffused over time.
  • Time and Eternity Time is depicted as fluid, collapsing moments, and shifting perspectives. Mr. Spitzer experiences a disorienting sense of timelessness, where centuries might seem like minutes, and events overlap or miss connections like trains passing at the wrong station.
  • Failure and Unfulfilled Potential Spitzer’s sense of failure pervades the chapter. His unfinished compositions, his timid nature, and his unrealized potential as a musician contrast with his brother’s more vibrant, reckless, life.
  • The Illusory Nature of Reality The narrative suggests that much of human experience is illusion or performance, with shifting roles, identities, and perceptions. Peron’s chameleon-like existence contrasts with Joachim’s desire for stability and order.
  • The Intersection of the Mundane and the Metaphysical Spitzer’s knowledge expands beyond his musical sphere to encompass gamblers, fighters, sportsmen, and other facets of earthly life, blending the terrestrial and the spiritual, the everyday and the eternal.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Music and the Unfinished Composition Symbolizes Spitzer’s incomplete life and emotional fragmentation. Music also represents the ineffable, the transcendent, and the ungraspable aspects of existence.
  • The Train and Missed Connections Represents lost opportunities, failed encounters, and the passage of time. The recurring image of trains passing the wrong station illustrates disjunctions in Spitzer’s life and identity.
  • Chess and Cards Symbolizes strategic life moves, fate, and chance. Spitzer’s timidness as a chess player echoes his fear of making irreversible decisions.
  • The Black Cloak and Ivory Cane Emblems of mourning, identity, and secondary intelligence. The cane serves as an extension of Spitzer’s self and his cautious, measured approach to life.
  • Sports and Fighters Represent struggle, endurance, defeat, and human frailty. Spitzer’s extensive knowledge of fighters and sportsmen symbolizes life’s battles and the inevitability of loss.
  • The Weather and Nature (Fog, Snow, Wind) Reflect Spitzer’s moods and the shifting, uncertain nature of reality. The snow’s color shifts (black, white) and the fog symbolize ambiguity and blurred perception.

  • The Boston Public Garden was the first public botanical garden in America. It was decorative and flowery from its inception, featuring meandering pathways for strolling.
  • Louis XIV did love pool and other games and encouraged gambling at Versailles to entertain and keep the nobles close to him. His Minister of France then was Jean-Baptiste Colbert. There is no reference to him gaining the position by beating Louis XIV at pool. Gambling was banned by Louis XIV for the general populace.
  • A cue-stick was also a mace and similar in shape to a cane. There is no reference for a cue-stick being called a baton. Cue-sticks could be very elaborate with jewels, inlays, and works of art. A baton was used in the military as a weapon and in heraldics.
  • Martin Luther, the Protestant Reformation founder, had a bowling lane built next to his house. Mr. Spitzer thought Martin Luther recommended bowling as an outlet for “...human aggression and the thirst for conquest…” Organized sports has been compared to simulated war and as a diversion for the populace.
  • The “queen of the desert” who played pool may refer to Cleopatra in Shakespeare's play Anthony and Cleopatra where she is bored and asks Charmian to play billiards.
  • Sir Walter Raleigh was beheaded but there is no mention of him playing cards with his executioners.
  • Skijoring is a winter sport in which a person on skis is pulled by a horse, dogs or a motor vehicle. Although skijoring is said to have originated as a mode of winter travel, it is currently primarily a competitive sport.
  • Sublunary means belonging to this world as opposed to a better or more spiritual one.
  • "Death rode a stumbling nag" - Revelation 6:8 "Death rode a pale horse," signifying the arrival of death and its accompanying consequences, but with an added emphasis on a slower, less forceful, or more uncertain approach. This imagery emphasizes a sense of the fragility or the unpredictable nature of death. It is a vivid metaphor conveying the imperfect, faltering, and perhaps unpredictable nature of death. The image of death riding a "stumbling nag" (a nag being an old or worn-out horse) suggests that death is not a graceful, certain, or dignified force but one that is awkward, uneven, and uncertain in its approach or effect. In the context of the chapter, which is deeply concerned with mysteries, dreams, identities, and the blurred boundaries between life and death, this metaphor emphasizes the theme that death is not a neat or final event but an ambiguous, elusive presence that stumbles through the lives of the characters. It aligns with the overall tone of the narrative that questions reality, identity, and the nature of existence itself. This metaphor also complements the broader imagery in the chapter of confusion, fading identities, and the overlapping of shadows and realities. Death, like the other great uncertainties and mysteries is portrayed as something that is at once inevitable and yet strangely unstable, not easily grasped or understood. It is part of the blurred, dreamlike world where distinctions between life and death, reality and dream, are not clear-cut
  • "behind the 8-ball" - refers to being in a difficult or disadvantageous position, often one from which it is hard to recover. The term originates from the game of pool, where being "behind the eight ball" means your cue ball is blocked by the eight ball, making it difficult to make a shot.
  • Pool is a series of cue sports played on a billiard table. The table has six pockets along the rails, into which balls are shot. Of the many different pool games, the most popular include: eight-ball, blackball, nine-ball, ten-ball, seven-ball, straight pool, one-pocket, and bank pool. Eight-ball is the most frequently played discipline of pool, and it is often thought of as synonymous with "pool". The generic term pocket billiards is sometimes also used, and favored by some pool-industry bodies, but is technically a broader classification, including games such as snooker, Russian pyramid, and kaisa, which are not referred to as pool games. There are also hybrid games combining aspects of both pool and carom billiards, such as American four-ball billiards, bottle pool, cowboy pool, and English billiards.
  • A playing card with 8 pips would be any of the 8 cards in a standard deck. Each suit (hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades) contains an 8 card with eight corresponding suit symbols (pips) on the face.
  • Boxing has 17 weight divisions for men and 17 for women, ranging from strawweight (lowest) to heavyweight (heaviest). These divisions ensure fair competition by grouping fighters of similar size and weight.
  • John Patrick Kilbane was an American featherweight boxer in the early part of the 20th century. He held the World Featherweight title from 1912 to 1923, the longest period in the division's history, having defended the title against four contenders during the reign. He was inducted into the Ring Magazine Hall of Fame in 1960 and the International Boxing Hall of Fame in 1995.
  • Tony Canzoneri held the world light-welterweight title for only 33 days in 1933.
  • Henry Jackson Jr. was an American professional boxer and a world boxing champion who fought under the name Henry Armstrong. He is the only fighter to ever hold world championships in three divisions (featherweight, lightweight and welterweight) simultaneously. Armstrong was one of the few fighters to win titles in three or more different divisions: featherweight, lightweight, and welterweight. He defended his welterweight title a total of 19 times.
  • Decameron is a collection of novellas by Giovanni Boccaccio.
  • In Genesis 32:22-32 Jacob wrestles with an angel.
  • In boxing, "leathers" is slang for boxing gloves, specifically those made of leather. It refers to the traditional material used for boxing gloves, which offers superior protection, comfort, and durability compared to synthetic alternatives.
  • On April 6, 1893, Andy Bowen and Jack Burke fought the longest fight in history. Bowen had originally scheduled the fight with another opponent, however after dropping out of the fight, Jack Burke, who was the latter's trainer, fought the bout instead. The fight took place at the same Olympics Club Bowen had defended his title from Carroll. The fight lasted 110 rounds over seven hours and 19 minutes (each round lasting three minutes). It was reported that the fight went on for so long that the spectators who stayed to watch the fight had fallen asleep in their seats. It was also recorded that at round 108, with no clear end in sight, referee John Duffy made the decision that if no winner had emerged in the next 2 rounds, the bout would be ruled a "no contest". With both men having become too dazed and tired to come out of their corners, Duffy declared the match a no contest. Burke broke all the bones in both of his hands and was bedridden for six weeks. He had considered retiring after the fight but chose to continue competing. Bowen fought four more times after the fight. The club where the fight took place would burn to the ground four years later.
  • The highest number of knockdowns recorded in a single professional fight involved Christy Williams, who was knocked down 42 times by Battling Nelson in a 1902 bout. Nelson himself was knocked down 7 times in that same fight, which he ultimately won by knockout in the 17th round. Another fight between Joe Jeanette and Sam McVey lasted for three and a half hours for forty-nine rounds in 1909 where Jeanette was knocked down twenty-seven times and McVey nineteen times. Jeanette won the fight. Jeanette was never given a shot at the world heavyweight title because he was African-American. At that time the rules did not state that when a fighter is knocked down the other fighter must go to a neutral corner.
  • Andy Bowen died at 27 years old after his 1894 fight with Kid Lavigne.
  • “He knew a man who had fought on when he had broken his hand” - It is part of a richly symbolic and dreamlike meditation on perseverance, struggle, and endurance despite injury or limitation. Though the passage is metaphorical and layered with ambiguity, this particular phrase likely illustrates the idea of continuing to strive or fight even when physically or emotionally impaired, suggesting resilience in the face of hardship. Within the broader context of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer reflects on various images of endurance, loss, and identity, often blending reality and dream. The mention of a man who fights on despite a broken hand can be read as symbolizing the human capacity to endure suffering and continue struggling even when "broken" or diminished. It resonates with the novel’s themes of fragmented identities, the persistence of hope or effort despite injury or loss, and the ambiguous boundary between life and death, reality and dream. The phrase embodies the motif of persistence in adversity, highlighting that even with an injury that should impair one's ability, the will to continue battling remains. It serves as a metaphor for the characters’ emotional or spiritual struggles, such as Mr. Spitzer’s own wrestling with loss and identity, or the suffragette’s relentless, though ultimately tragic, quest for love and meaning in a shifting, uncertain world. The phrase underscores resilience, the refusal to give up despite damage or limitation as a theme central to the novel’s meditation on human endurance amid mystery and loss.
  • Burke is said to have broken all the bones in both his hands during the fight with Bowen.
  • Referees have a ten count rule where the boxer must get to his feet, unaided, by that time. The count does not refer to the number of seconds since there have been times when a long count has resulted in a boxer having more than ten seconds. Modern boxing rules have a standing eight count.
  • Etude is a short practice piece in order to practice a particular musical skill.
  • Black keyboards where the sharps are white were found in harpsichords and fortepianos. The white keys with black sharps became the standard because it was easier to see the keys.
  • The fighter retired from the ring and lived in isolation believing he had killed his father’s ghost when he killed that opponent. This is similar to the plot line in the Shakespeare play Hamlet where the ghost is Hamlet’s dead father.
  • Bridge of Sighs is a bridge in Venice, Italy.
  • Bridge of Lies is a legendary pedestrian bridge in Sibiu, Transylvania, Romania.
  • Lake of fire is a place of after-death punishment in Egyptian and Christian religions.
  • Angels in all his angles may refer to a Latin pun attributed to Pope Gregory I when he saw pale skinned boys at the slave market.
  • Garrison may refer to William Lloyd Garrison who published a newspaper in Boston against slavery and was for women’s rights.
  • The two political parties in the United States switched roles in the nineteenth century.
  • Included is Althea Garrison because she was the first transgender person to be elected to a state legislature although she was not active in politics at the time Young wrote this novel.
  • A traditional Republican may refer to the original Republican Party that emerged in the 1850s, founded by anti-slavery activists who opposed the expansion of slavery into US territories. During the 19th century, the party was strongly associated with the abolition of slavery and the preservation of the Union.
  • The Marquis of Queensberry, John Douglas (9th Marquess of Queensberry), did establish the Queensberry rules that are the basis for rules in modern boxing.
  • John L. Sullivan was the first recognized heavyweight fighter and the last bare knuckle heavyweight fighter.
  • Gentleman Jim may refer to James J Corbett who revolutionized boxing and was the only man to beat John L. Sullivan. There is no reference to Corbett having diamond-studded teeth but after his boxing career he did star in low budget films. He was considered the first sports sex symbol of the era.
  • The Prince Albert suit is a frock coat with double-breasted, peaked lapels.
  • “Death danced with the lady” This phrase metaphorically captures the intimate, complex, and ambiguous relationship between the lady (the old suffragette) and death. The lady is portrayed as someone who has lived a life filled with paradoxes, mystery, and transformative journeys. She is described as both active and passive, as a traveler between realms of life and death, reality and dream. The imagery of dancing with death suggests a close, almost companionable engagement with mortality, as if death is not merely an end but a partner in the ongoing movement of existence and identity. The "dance" implies a dynamic, fluid interaction rather than a static or fearful state. The lady, having abandoned conventional roles (such as bride or wife), and having lived a life of wandering, disguise, and defiance (including climbing mountains, flying, and escaping societal norms), engages with death not as a final cessation but as an essential part of her being and journey. It reflects her liminal status: between life and death, reality and dream, presence and absence. This metaphor also aligns with the novel’s broader themes about the blurred boundaries between states of being, the elusive nature of identity, and the intertwining of love, loss, and mortality. The lady's dance with death is a poetic way to express that she has been inextricably linked to death, not just physically in dying but symbolically in how she lived, loved, and searched for meaning amid illusions and truths. It signifies the profound and enigmatic connection between the suffragette and death, highlighting the novel’s exploration of mortality as a dance, a continual movement where endings and beginnings coexist, and where death is not a distant stranger but a close and intimate partner.
  • It may refer to the artistic and literary theme of the Danse Macabre, also known as the Dance of Death. This theme, popular in the late medieval period, depicts death, often personified by a skeleton, leading people of all social classes in a dance to their graves. It serves as a reminder of the inevitability of death for everyone. This artistic and literary motif emerged in the late medieval period, particularly following the Black Death, to remind people of their mortality. Death is often portrayed as a skeleton or a figure of decay, leading people from all walks of life in a procession to the grave. The Danse Macabre highlights the idea that death is a great equalizer, affecting everyone regardless of social status or wealth. The theme is expressed in various forms of art, including paintings, woodcuts, and literature. Camille Saint-Saëns wrote the musical composition, "Danse Macabre," which is a symphonic poem inspired by the theme.
  • “leather punching bags, stuffed with sand or flour, were used thousands of years before the discovery of the New World, and the sandbag dummy was probably as old as human history” - It serves as a metaphorical reflection on ancient human practices and the continuity of certain tools or symbols throughout history. This statement highlights the deep historical roots of the sandbag dummy (an object used for training, practice, or perhaps symbolic combat) and suggests it has been part of human culture for as long as human history itself. By referencing leather punching bags stuffed with sand or flour used long before the discovery of the Americas, the text emphasizes the long-standing human engagement with forms of struggle, preparation, or perhaps confrontation, whether physical or symbolic. Within the broader context of the novel, which often blends reality, memory, dream, and myth, this line likely underscores themes of timelessness, endurance, and the persistence of human rituals or symbols across ages. It may also reflect on the idea that certain human experiences (like conflict, self-discipline, or preparation) are universal and ancient, transcending specific historical moments. This line connects the concrete image of the sandbag dummy to a vast temporal scale, reinforcing the novel’s motifs of history, memory, and the layering of time.
  • Evidence suggests that ancient Egyptians, Greeks, and Romans utilized various forms of punching bags for combat training. These bags were often crafted from materials like leather and filled with sand or other readily available materials. Ancient Chinese and Japanese civilizations also used animal skin punching bags filled with sand or grain for martial arts training. Indian wrestling traditions also employed practice equipment called "mukha dhanda," which were essentially hanging leather pouches filled with sand, pebbles, or grain.
  • “he knew the Jew who was knocked out by an angel” - It is an allusion rich with symbolic and possibly biblical meaning. Although the text does not provide explicit context for this phrase, it likely references the biblical story of Jacob wrestling with an angel, a well-known episode from the Book of Genesis 32. In that story, Jacob wrestles with a mysterious divine being (often interpreted as an angel or God himself) throughout the night and is physically and spiritually transformed by the encounter. The phrase "knocked out by an angel" suggests a powerful, overwhelming, possibly humbling or transformative experience. Within the context of chapter and the broader themes of the novel, the reference may symbolize a profound confrontation with truth, fate, or spiritual challenge. It could reflect a moment where a character is metaphorically 'knocked out' or overwhelmed by a higher power, a revelation, or an internal struggle. Given the novel’s dense and poetic style, filled with dreamlike, mythic, and spiritual imagery, this phrase serves as a metaphor for a transformative or decisive encounter that shakes the foundations of identity or belief.
  • This may refer to Genesis 32 that describes Jacob wrestling with a "man" throughout the night. In the Book of Hosea, this figure is explicitly called an "angel". During the struggle, Jacob is injured, specifically having the socket of his hip put out of joint. This injury left him with a limp. Jacob is considered a foundational figure in Judaism and the patriarch from whom the nation of Israel descends.
  • Cestus - In ancient Greece and Rome, the cestus (also spelled caestus) was a type of combat glove, similar to modern-day brass knuckles, used in boxing and gladiatorial combat. Early Greek cesti were primarily leather straps or thongs used to protect the hands during boxing matches. As they evolved, particularly in Roman gladiatorial contexts, they became more elaborate, incorporating metal studs, spikes, and even lead or iron to inflict greater damage.
  • Mary, Queen of Scots is considered to be one of the first women to play golf which she did in Scotland and France. She also caused a scandal when she played golf at St. Andrews just twelve days after her husband’s funeral in 1560.
  • “famous baseball player never made a come-back” - symbolizes a theme of loss, failure to return, or the impossibility of reclaiming a former glory or state. It metaphorically reflects characters or situations in the novel where someone or something once prominent or vital is unable to regain their previous status or vitality, much like a celebrated athlete who fails to return successfully after an absence or decline.
  • It may refer to Lou Gehrig. He was forced to retire from baseball in 1939 at the age of 36 due to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS), which became known as "Lou Gehrig's disease". He played his last game on April 30, 1939 and never played another major league game after taking himself out of the lineup on May 2, 1939, ending his consecutive game streak at 2,130. He died two years later in 1941.
  • Ancient Egyptian wrestling, depicted in tomb paintings and sculptures, showcased a variety of holds and techniques, many of which are still recognizable in modern wrestling styles. These depictions, particularly those at Beni Hasan, reveal over 4000-year-old techniques, including throws, takedowns, and ground grappling, emphasizing both athletic prowess and strategic combat training.
  • “hairless racing dogs” This can be interpreted as emblematic of vulnerability and exposed speed or urgency. The “hairless” aspect suggests a stripping away of protection or covering, implying nakedness, bareness, or exposure. The “racing dogs” evoke speed, pursuit, and perhaps desperation or a frantic chase. Together, this image conjures beings that are both vulnerable and driven forward rapidly, possibly symbolizing characters or forces in the narrative caught in a relentless, exposed pursuit of something: be it fate, love, or identity.
  • It may refer to Joseph-Armand Bombardier’s Tracked Vehicles, a precursor to the snowmobile.
  • “who vaulted the farthest distance” The phrase likely alludes to someone who has made the greatest leap (physically, emotionally, or spiritually) beyond ordinary limits or boundaries. In the context of the chapter's exploration of the suffragette's far-ranging adventures, both literal (mountain climbing, flying, traveling) and symbolic (crossing boundaries of gender, identity, time, and reality), “vaulting the farthest distance” can be understood as transcending conventional human experience or limitations. It suggests surpassing all others in attempting or achieving the impossible, going beyond the known world, or bridging the gap between life and death, reality and dream. This fits with the novel's recurring motifs of journeys through unknown realms, the blurring of reality and illusion, and the search for lost love or identity.
  • It may refer to Jesse Owens who held the men's long jump world record for twenty-five years. He achieved his record-breaking leap of 8.13 meters (26 ft 8 in) on May 25, 1935. This record stood for an impressive 25 years until it was broken by fellow American Ralph Boston in 1960.
  • “that early tennis balls were black” Historically, balls were either black or white, depending on the background color of the court.
  • "Tallyho" is a cry traditionally used in fox hunting to signal the sighting of the quarry (the fox). It's also used as an exclamation of excitement or triumph, particularly when hunting.
  • Archery - has been a crucial hunting method for millennia, with evidence of its use dating back to prehistoric times. Bows and arrows were also essential for warfare in many cultures throughout history. The widespread adoption of firearms, particularly flintlock weapons, by the 1800s led to a decline in the use of archery for hunting, especially in regions where firearms were readily available. However, archery did not disappear entirely. In fact, the 19th century saw a revival of archery as a sport and recreational activity, with the establishment of archery clubs and competitions in Europe and elsewhere. A notable example is the Toxophilite Society in London, founded in 1781. While firearms became more prevalent, archery continued to be used for hunting in some areas, particularly where firearms were not as accessible or by those who preferred the traditional methods. The "primitive" regions of the world continued using bows and arrows in warfare. Archery's cultural significance extended beyond its practical uses. It was often associated with spirituality, skill, and social status in various societies. The book "The Witchery of Archery" by the Thompson brothers, who took up archery after the American Civil War, is credited with inspiring a revival of the sport in the United States.
  • fistmele - refers to the brace height, which is the distance between the bowstring and the deepest part of the bow's grip, traditionally measured using a fist with the thumb extended. It's a critical measurement for traditional bows, impacting performance and noise levels.
  • "birdcage" typically refers to Chuck-a-Luck, a dice game played with a distinctive hourglass-shaped cage containing three dice. The game is also known as "birdcage" or "sweat rag". Players bet on the outcome of the dice roll after the dealer flips the cage and the dice come to rest.
  • "Flying Mare" or "Flying Horse" (also known as Kasek Neyja or Mare) is a throw where a wrestler rotates their opponent over their back using a rope grip, similar to a shoulder throw but with a focus on rotational momentum and a bending forward motion. This technique is used in various wrestling styles, including Cornish wrestling and Collar and Elbow wrestling. In professional wrestling, "flying" moves refer to aerial maneuvers like dives and leaps onto opponents.
  • “acorns, hearts, bells, and leaves” are associated with German-suited playing cards, a traditional card system used in Central Europe. These suits predate the more internationally recognized French suits (hearts, diamonds, clubs, and spades). German-suited cards typically feature 32 or 36 cards with these four suits. The acorns suit is one of the oldest. Leaves is another of the original suits. Hearts are the same in both the German and French systems. Bells are a distinctive German suit. German suits are believed to have influenced the development of the French suits. For example, the French "clubs" are thought to be derived from the German "acorns". German-suited cards are still used in many parts of Central Europe.
  • “medieval ladies snow balling” there are historical depictions of medieval ladies participating in snowball fights. A 15th-century fresco from Trento, Italy, portrays individuals engaged in a snowball fight, showcasing the postures and expressions of players. Snowball fights are also referenced in medieval chronicles.
  • In Greek mythology, the Argonauts were a group of heroes who, led by Jason, sailed on the ship Argo to retrieve the Golden Fleece from Colchis. The myth of the Argonauts is one of the most famous tales from Greek mythology.
  • Chinese kite fighting, also known as "fighter kite" flying, is a competitive sport where participants attempt to cut the strings of their opponents' kites using specially designed kites and string. The string is often coated with abrasive materials like glass or other substances to enhance its cutting ability. The last kite remaining in the air wins the contest. Kites date back to over two thousand years in China.
  • “turned to cross North Square” North Square is in Boston’s North End, where the Paul Revere House still stands. Built around 1680, it is the oldest house remaining in downtown Boston, and Revere lived there from 1770 to 1800.

Chapter 35

← Chapter 34 · Home · Chapter 36 →

Summary

Catherine imagines inviting Hannah back for a winter of card games. She reviews Hannah's suffrage career on every front, her conquests and her refusal of any memorial window, and all the things Hannah was not: no dancer, no hostess, no keeper of private confessions. She concludes that Hannah was married to the suffrage movement as if it were her husband. Mr. Spitzer notes Catherine's habit of always taking the opposite view.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Freedom and Escape · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Music and Instruments

Allusions: Greek Mythology · Napoleon and Wellington · The Civil War · The History of Opium · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, the narrative contrasts Cousin Hannah’s fiery spirit and audacity with Mr. Spitzer’s cautious, prideful, and somewhat pitiable nature. Mr. Spitzer is portrayed as ignorant of cards, jealous, embittered by failures and losses, and unable to compete or engage fully in life’s “games.” Cousin Hannah, in contrast, is described as a lively, dashing, and indomitable player who had outwitted everyone and had “played a mean game of cards” which metaphorically represents her boldness in life and politics. This contrast highlights themes of courage versus timidity, engagement versus withdrawal, and vitality versus stagnation.
  • The chapter extensively praises Cousin Hannah’s life and character. She is portrayed as a “great pioneer” and “great captain” in the suffrage movement, a woman who had no time for trivialities or passive existence. Her life was devoted to overthrowing male domination and advocating for women’s rights on every front, domestic and foreign, and even in unknown territories. The metaphorical imagery of her riding horseback through vast deserts, confronting dragons and minotaurs, and facing physical dangers portrays her as an almost mythic figure whose courage and commitment transcended ordinary limitations.
  • Cousin Hannah’s rejection of typical feminine roles and sentiments is a key passage. She had no time for “feminine wiles,” “self-pity,” or “intimate revelations.” Unlike the romantic or domestic aspirations often associated with women of her era, she was married to the suffrage movement itself. This passage emphasizes her total dedication, as well as the radical nature of her life and beliefs, setting her apart from both societal norms and from Catherine.
  • Catherine imagines Cousin Hannah returning as a ghost or spirit, invited to stay in the large, empty house with its many vacant rooms and servants. This passage is important as it reflects Catherine’s complex feelings of admiration, longing, and unresolved tensions. It also contrasts Cousin Hannah’s vivid, active presence with Mr. Spitzer’s “vacant face” and absence, underscoring the symbolic displacement of vitality by inertia and jealousy.
  • The chapter reflects on the idea that Cousin Hannah is “more vivid in death than she had been in life,” having “escaped this wide-meshed net of years.” This passage considers the nature of memory, legacy, and the afterlife, suggesting that Cousin Hannah’s spirit and influence endure powerfully even when forgotten by others. It contrasts the enduring flame of her character with the fading presence of others, including Mr. Spitzer.
  • Vera’s mother, Catherine, sees herself as fragmented with multiple partial selves and vague thoughts, compared to Cousin Hannah’s remarkable unity of character and steadfastness. This passage offers insight into the psychological complexity and self-reflection of Vera’s mother, emphasizing themes of identity, coherence, and internal conflict.
  • The chapter describes Cousin Hannah’s “hardy temper,” her unflinching courage in the face of threats, dangers, and opposition, and her refusal to compromise or surrender. Her willingness to face “greater dangers than most men know” and to cross forbidden boundaries symbolizes her heroic stature and her commitment to her cause.
  • Towards the end, Catherine is portrayed as “beautifully obtuse,” often taking contrary views, bewildered by familiar surroundings, and suffering from claustrophobia even when thinking of vast cosmic spaces. This reflects her emotional and mental state as conflicted and detached, yet proud of Cousin Hannah. The mention of their “day” being her “night” and their “winter” her “summer” encapsulates the theme of opposites and contrasts running through the chapter

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • A formidable, spirited woman and a leader in the suffrage movement.
  • Described as a “great captain,” “old New England suffragette,” “stone horseman,” and a pioneer who had traveled extensively and fearlessly.
  • Known for her strength, courage, and refusal to conform to traditional feminine roles.
  • She is remembered as someone who never sought pity or protection and who had no time for courtly graces or domestic bliss.
  • Her life was devoted to overthrowing man’s dominance, both socially and domestically.
  • She represents emancipation, freedom, and unyielding resolve.
  • Even in death, she remains vivid and influential, symbolized by images of snowy mountains and celestial journeys.
  • Refused memorial tributes like stained glass windows, showing her disdain for conventional commemoration.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Portrayed as cautious, timid, and jealous; he lacks the boldness and dynamism of Cousin Hannah.
  • He is ignorant of cards, suspicious of Cousin Hannah, and bears grudges linked to personal failures and family misfortunes.
  • His presence is seen as an obstacle to Cousin Hannah’s legacy and spirit.
  • Mr. Spitzer is described as “corporeal, fat, soft-jowled, many-valved, sleepy-eyed,” symbolizing inertia and lack of willpower.
  • He is contrasted sharply with the fiery and active Cousin Hannah.
  • Catherine believes Mr. Spitzer should no longer linger in the house or in memory, making room for Cousin Hannah’s continued influence.

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine holds a complicated view of both Cousin Hannah and Mr. Spitzer.
  • Proud of Cousin Hannah and sometimes wistful about their relationship.
  • She is reflective, sometimes “unreasonably proud” of Cousin Hannah and often alone, conversing with shadows and memories.
  • Her own life is described as fragmented, filled with multiple selves and illusions.
  • She contrasts with Cousin Hannah’s unity of character and decisiveness.
  • Catherine blends admiration, doubt, and longing.

Research: Themes

Freedom and Emancipation

See: Freedom and Escape

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the fight for women’s rights and freedom from traditional roles.
  • Her life is a metaphor for breaking boundaries: social, geographic, and existential.
  • The suffrage movement is portrayed as her husband, her master, and her true love.

Memory and Legacy

See: Memory and the Past

  • The chapter meditates on how people are remembered after death.
  • Cousin Hannah remains vivid in memory, more alive in death than in life.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s legacy is one of bitterness and inertia, suggesting that memory favors the bold.

Conflict and Opposition

  • The tension between Cousin Hannah and Mr. Spitzer symbolizes broader conflicts: between courage and timidity, action and passivity, truth and deception.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s jealousy and bitterness contrast with Cousin Hannah’s fearless spirit.

Isolation vs. Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Catherine’s isolation contrasts with Cousin Hannah’s active engagement with the world.
  • Despite physical distance and death, Cousin Hannah communicates and influences across time and space.

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Death is depicted not as an end but as a transformation.
  • Cousin Hannah’s death elevates her to a symbolic, almost mythic status.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s survival past her death is seen as a burden.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Cards and Games

See: Cards, Games, and Chance

  • The metaphor of cards and poker reflects strategy, risk, and deception.
  • Cousin Hannah is a “mean game” player; Mr. Spitzer distrusts her, believing she cheats.
  • This imagery symbolizes life’s gambits and the characters’ differing approaches to fate and challenge.

Nature and the Elements

  • Frequent references to snow, stars, deserts, mountains, and storms symbolize the harshness and grandeur of Cousin Hannah’s life.
  • Snow and ice often signify coldness, isolation, and purity.
  • The natural imagery links Cousin Hannah to timeless, elemental forces.

Music and Dance

See: Music and Instruments

  • Music is associated with Mr. Spitzer. It represents internal worlds and subtle emotional states.
