Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes an infanticide and a man fleeing a lynching.

Summary

Esther makes tiny clothes for no one and sets out crumbs for spirits. She tells of her first child, Walter. His father was a Black man who had escaped a lynching and came to her one night, then fled. Alone and frightened, she gave birth and pressed her thumb to still Walter's cry. Believing she had killed him, she hid him and ran. Yet she imagines him alive and growing somewhere, returning in visions to ask why she killed him and where his father is.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Walter

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Memory and the Past · Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Philosophy: Freud and Jung

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Lynching and Racial Violence · Pregnancy, Abortion, and Midwifery · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • Esther is deeply affected by the presence of spirits and the memory of her dead children. She engages in rituals like making little clothes for no one, setting out bread crumbs for spirits, and building a little house of straw in a tree for the spirit to come home to. This shows her ongoing connection to the lost children and her attempt to reconcile with the past.
  • Esther discusses her impending marriage but insists she will not marry until the child comes. This hesitation reflects her uncertainty about the child's paternity and her own feelings about love and responsibility. She contemplates the future of her progeny, hoping for strength and happiness despite her doubts.
  • A central and deeply moving passage details Esther's first-born, Walter, who she believes she "killed" but who lives on in some form, haunting her conscience and mind. Walter represents both her guilt and her love, a child who was born under tragic circumstances and then taken away, yet whose presence continues to torment her.
  • Walter accuses Esther of killing him and questions her about his father. Esther's guilt is palpable as she tries to reconcile her actions with her love for Walter, describing him as a "black mystery" and acknowledging the painful burden he places on her.
  • Esther distinguishes Walter from her many stillborn children, emphasizing that he was born alive and continues to grow. This passage highlights the profound difference between the living child and the numerous losses she has endured, all of which weigh heavily on her psyche.
  • The chapter provides a detailed narrative of how Walter was conceived by a "black stranger" in a night of love and how Esther was unprepared and frightened by the pregnancy. This passage is important as it contextualizes Esther's fear, shame, and the social consequences she faced, especially regarding race and societal judgment.
  • Throughout the chapter, Esther is described as perpetually pregnant, symbolizing her ongoing burden of guilt, loss, and hope. This "everlasting pregnancy" is a metaphor for her emotional state: caught between life and death, hope and despair.
  • Esther admits to having pressed her thumb to still Walter's birth cry, effectively killing him, but not without enduring lifelong remorse. She also recounts how she hid the body and fled to avoid detection. This revelation is crucial as it underlines the secret that haunts her and explains her psychological torment.
  • The chapter closes with Esther reflecting on her many miscarriages and stillborn children, the idea that life is filled with loss and unfinished stories. Despite everything, she clings to the memory of Walter, who symbolizes both her greatest sorrow and her deepest love.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • Esther is complex, embodying resilience, confusion, sorrow, and hope.
  • She is aware of her societal marginalization and her own perceived "madness" but embraces her unique perspective.
  • Her character oscillates between despair and defiance, as she laughs at her barrenness and mourns her losses simultaneously.
  • Her first-born child Walter who both haunts and defines her. He symbolizes her greatest loss and source of emotional torment.
  • Walter’s Father is a black man whose identity and fate are shrouded in mystery and racial tension.
  • Many transient men appear in her life, symbolizing fleeting connections and failed attempts at establishing lasting family bonds.

Walter

  • Walter is a profoundly complex and symbolic character. He is Esther Longtree's first-born child, a figure who embodies both literal and metaphorical dimensions of life, death, guilt, and memory.
  • Walter is described as a child whom Esther had "killed," yet paradoxically, he "lived." This duality makes him a ghostly presence; both alive and dead in the narrative reality. Esther hears his cries, feels his accusations, and wrestles with the burden of her guilt and regret that he represents. Walter's persistent questioning, “Mother, why have you killed me?” and “Where is my father?”, haunts Esther’s conscience, embodying her unatoned sin and unresolved emotional pain.
  • Walter acts as a relentless accuser who confronts Esther with her past actions and their consequences. His presence "keeps her working," making her scrub floors and endure long hours in the restaurant. He embodies the emotional and psychological torment that Esther cannot escape. His accusations are unanswerable, and he seems to have a cruel, hard heart, adding to Esther’s suffering.
  • Walter is portrayed with specific physical features, "black as my true love, black as my heart", reflecting his mixed racial heritage, which complicates Esther’s feelings toward him. His blackness symbolizes difference and alienation, as well as the social challenges unresolved in Esther's life. The fact that his father was black and a "prince of Africa" adds layers to Walter’s identity, evoking themes of race, social stigma, and forbidden love.
  • Walter represents the "beloved obstacle" to Esther’s life and future. His existence and the guilt attached to him prevent her from fully embracing motherhood and happiness. Esther’s many stillborn children and miscarriages contrast with Walter’s unique status as the one child who lived but remained emotionally inaccessible. Walter is both the cause of her endless pregnancies and the reason for her emotional isolation.
  • Walter is inseparable from Esther’s memories, a persistent shadow in her mind. He symbolizes a trauma that has not been resolved: her fear, shame, and the consequences of a youthful mistake. The narrator, Vera, reveals that Walter's presence is intertwined with Esther’s perception of time, reality, and self, blurring lines between life and death, memory and present.
  • Walter is central to the chapter’s meditation on birth, death, life’s incompleteness, and the mysteries of existence. Esther’s dialogue with Walter, his questioning, and his haunting presence articulate the theme that life is an ongoing negotiation between presence and absence, love and loss, guilt and redemption.
  • Walter is not merely a character but a symbolic force representing Esther’s guilt, lost motherhood, racial complexity, and the unresolved past that haunts her. He is a living accusation and a ghostly memory, a child who should have died but has instead become an eternal presence in Esther’s life, shaping her identity and destiny.

Walter’s father

  • Walter's father is portrayed primarily through Esther Longtree's memories, feelings, and the symbolic weight he carries rather than through direct characterization or actions.
  • Walter's father is described as a black man, "as black as the ace of spades," a "Negro, a Negro, a Negro," who came into Esther's life unexpectedly and left an indelible mark upon her. He is portrayed as a "stranger," a "poor fellow," "a tramp," "a fugitive," or even a "prince," which indicates Esther's ambivalence and the mystique surrounding him. This man came into her life in the darkness of a summer night, in an act that was "half of sleeping and half of waking," suggesting a blend of innocence, confusion, and inevitability in their union.
  • His blackness is significant in the narrative: Esther did not initially realize the racial difference at the moment of conception because "his face had been white" in the moonlight, and only "at dawn... she had seen that he was black". This racial difference introduces a complex dynamic of love, fear, and societal judgment. Esther’s heart turns "black with the years," and she recognizes her bond to him as something that makes her a "slave to his memory". His departure is framed not as Esther leaving him, but as him fleeing "for fear the white people would see him and kill him", underscoring the racial tensions and dangers of the time.
  • Walter's father is not depicted as a traditional or nurturing figure in Esther's life. He is absent after the conception, and Esther carries the burden of his memory, the pregnancy, and the consequences largely alone. Despite this absence, his presence haunts Esther, symbolizing both the origin of her deepest grief and the source of a love she treasured but could not fully realize. His identity as a black man in a racially divided society adds a layer of tragedy and alienation to the story.
  • Walter's father is a mysterious, absent figure whose racial identity and sudden disappearance shape Esther's life and psyche profoundly. He embodies the forces of love, loss, societal exclusion, and the lingering pain of an unfinished past that Esther cannot escape.

Research: Themes

Motherhood and Pregnancy

See: Motherhood, Pregnancy, and Birth

  • Esther is perpetually pregnant, both literally and metaphorically. Her body swells with pregnancies that often end in stillbirths or miscarriages, yet she carries an enduring hope for a living child.
  • The physical and emotional toll of her pregnancies is immense; she experiences nausea, swelling, and an overwhelming sense of waiting and expectation.
  • Pregnancy is symbolic of life, death, and the cyclical nature of existence. It is her "widow’s weeds," representing loss and continual renewal.

Guilt and Redemption

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Esther harbors deep guilt over her first-born son, Walter, whom she believes she "killed" by abandoning him at birth.
  • Despite her guilt, Walter is alive in her memories and visions, accusing her of her sins and questioning her about his father.
  • Her attempts to redeem herself manifest in her ongoing pregnancies and her hope that the new child will compensate for the past losses.

Race and Identity

See: Identity and the Self · Society, Class, and Race

  • Walter's father was a black man, described metaphorically as "the prince of Africa" and "as black as the ace of spades."
  • Esther’s shock and societal stigma over this interracial relationship and child profoundly impact her life.
  • Walter’s blackness is a symbolic and literal source of conflict, shame, love, and fear for Esther, reflecting broader themes of racial tension and identity.

Life, Death, and the Supernatural

See: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The narrative blurs boundaries between life and death, as Esther communicates with spirits and imagines an "other world" parallel to this one.
  • Her miscarriages and stillborn children are depicted as ghostly presences and delicate entities like moths, feathers, and snowflakes.
  • Walter exists both as a living child and a spectral presence haunting her conscience.

Memory and Time

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • Esther’s memory is fragmented, cyclical, and tinged with confusion as she recalls her past pregnancies, loves, and losses.
  • Time is fluid; events from years ago feel present and immediate, especially as she contemplates the "unfinished murder" of Walter.
  • The narrative explores how memory shapes identity and the persistence of past trauma.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Pregnancy is a central symbol representing creation, hope, and the possibility of life. However, in Esther's case, it also symbolizes loss, failure, and the burden of guilt, as she has experienced many stillbirths and miscarriages. Her "everlasting pregnancy" is not just physical but metaphysical, carrying the memory and shadow of her first child who died but also "lived" in a spiritual or haunting way. This duality of birth and death intertwined in her pregnancy reflects her conflicted emotions and the complexity of motherhood.
  • Walter, Esther's first-born, is a powerful symbol of both guilt and unresolved trauma. He is described as both dead and alive; he haunts her as a ghostly presence, accusing her of killing him, yet he "lives" and grows outside her. Walter’s contradictory existence symbolizes Esther’s inner turmoil, remorse, and the inescapable consequences of past actions. His blackness, in contrast to the white imagery surrounding Esther, also symbolizes otherness, racial difference, and social alienation.
  • The interplay of black and white is a recurring symbol throughout the chapter. Esther herself is dark-skinned, and her lover and child are black, while many surrounding images are white: white butterflies, white snow, white moonlight, white flowers, and the white detective. This contrast symbolizes racial difference, purity versus guilt, life versus death, and the blending or conflict of identities. The "black as the ace of spades" and white moonlight imagery evokes a sense of fate, mystery, and the intersection of love and tragedy.
  • Nature is used extensively to symbolize the cycle of life and death, the presence of spirits, and the passage of time.
  • Butterflies and moths symbolize fragile, ephemeral life and transformation.
  • Leaves stirring and falling evoke the whispering of spirits and the inevitability of decay.
  • Rain and umbrellas suggest cleansing, sorrow, and the connection between this world and the "other world" where spirits reside.
  • The moon and stars symbolize mystery, the unconscious, and the eternal presence of life beyond death.
  • Esther’s connection to nature signifies her role as a "go-between," mediating between life and death, reality and spirit.
  • The "Little Shadow Boxer" is a metaphor for the unborn child she carries now, representing hope and continuity but also uncertainty. The child is called a "shadow," indicating something not fully realized or tangible and a continuation of her past mistakes but also a potential for redemption. This image underlines the tension between reality and illusion, life and death.
  • Esther is described as "always knitting the invisible," a metaphor for her attempts to create and sustain life out of intangible dreams and memories. This symbolizes her efforts to reconcile with her past and to give form to what has been lost or broken. The invisible thread also suggests the fragile connections between generations, memory, and identity.
  • The Chicago Detective and Salesmen recurring characters symbolize societal judgment, surveillance, and the external pressures Esther faces. The white detective’s suspicions and the sterile salesmen represent the social forces that have failed to understand or accept her, adding to her isolation and guilt.
  • The knocking and Esther’s answering represent her confrontation with her past, her guilt, and the spirits of her children; both born and unborn. It symbolizes the inescapable nature of memory and conscience, and her role as the mediator between the living and the dead.
  • Walter is described as the "beloved obstacle" preventing her from moving fully into new relationships or new conceptions. This symbolizes how past trauma and guilt can block future happiness and freedom.
  • The "Cloud," "Shadow," and "Reflection" images symbolize ambiguity, duality, and the blurred boundaries between reality and imagination, life and death. Esther often reflects on these, questioning where the living and the dead reside, and suggesting her mental state blurs these distinctions.
  • The "Black Hand Laid Across the Womb" is a potent symbol of the legacy of her first child’s death and haunting presence. It represents both the physical and psychological obstruction preventing her from fully moving on, and the lasting impact of her guilt and loss.
  • The "White Bird on the Ice Floe" evokes both beauty and isolation, symbolizing the fragile hope and distance between Esther and what she desires or has lost. It suggests the elusiveness of her dreams and the coldness of her reality

Research: Resources

  • Esther Longtree is portrayed as a profoundly tragic and complex figure, embodying themes of maternal loss, guilt, and longing. Her character is suffused with a haunting sense of grief that permeates her existence, shaped by repeated pregnancies, stillbirths, and a particularly painful memory of her first-born child, Walter. Physically, Esther is described as a large, cross-eyed waitress who is perpetually pregnant or swollen, a physical manifestation of her inner burden and continuous state of expectation and sorrow. Her pregnancy is not merely biological but symbolic: it represents her ongoing attempt to atone for past mistakes and losses and to reclaim a maternal identity fractured by tragedy. A central aspect of Esther's character is her relationship with Walter, her first-born, who, despite being "killed" in a sense, has lived on outside her awareness. Walter is both a ghostly presence and a source of endless accusation and sorrow. He haunts her conscience, asking why she killed him and where his father is, embodying Esther’s unresolved guilt and the burden of an unfinished murder. Walter's existence outside her, his growth and vitality, contrasts sharply with the stillborn children and miscarriages that have otherwise defined her reproductive life. Her narrative reveals a deep, ambivalent love and a tragic recognition of her own limitations and mistakes as a mother, compounded by her youth, ignorance, and fear at the time of Walter’s birth. Esther’s story exposes the intersection of race and identity: Walter’s father was a black man, a "prince" from Africa, who was a fugitive and victim of racial violence. This adds layers of social and personal complexity to Esther’s grief, shame, and isolation. Her memories of this man are filled with shock and surprise, reflecting the racial tensions and prejudices surrounding her. Esther’s heart turning black metaphorically expresses her internalization of this complex legacy. Esther is shown as a woman caught between two worlds: the physical, harsh reality of her life as a waitress and the spiritual, shadowy world of her lost and unborn children, as well as the memory of Walter. She acts as a "go-between," navigating the liminal space between life and death, presence and absence, reality and dream. This is symbolized by her making a little house of straw for the spirit to come home to, answering every knocking, and feeding the spirits as if to soothe her conscience. Her repeated pregnancies and stillbirths symbolize not only personal tragedy but also a universal theme of loss and unfulfilled potential. Esther’s life is a continual cycle of hope and despair, birth and death, presence and absence. Her laughter, sometimes convulsive or mule-like, reflects a bitter acceptance of her fate, mingled with stubborn resilience. Esther Longtree is a figure of profound maternal suffering and endurance. She is marked by a deep, unresolved guilt and grief linked to her first child, Walter, whose living presence she both mourns and fears. Her story is one of tragic memory, racial and social complexity, and the haunting persistence of loss. She is a living embodiment of the liminal space between life and death, the seen and unseen, the known and the unknowable, and her narrative richly explores themes of motherhood, identity, and redemption within the novel.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes a deep and tragic history of racial and social injustice in the United States, particularly relating to the legacy of slavery, interracial relationships under oppressive conditions, and the ongoing consequences of systemic racism. Her story reflects the painful history of a black father, described as a "Negro, a Negro, a Negro, poor young fellow, black as the black bough, the ace of spades," who was a fugitive, possibly an ex-convict, victimized by white supremacy: "the white people there had tried to kill him because he was black and had wanted to sleep with a white woman... they had tried to hang him from a white-blossoming tree for revenge, but the rope had broken". This narrative evokes the historical reality of lynching and racial violence in the American South. Esther’s pregnancy with this black man’s child, her subsequent abandonment of the child, and her lifelong torment symbolize the fraught and often violent intersections of race, gender, and power in America. Her child, Walter, who is black and whom she both loved and feared, becomes a haunting presence in her life: a symbol of the legacy of interracial unions condemned and punished by society, and the personal and social consequences of such relationships. The repeated motif of Esther being "always pregnant," carrying the memory and burden of lost or stillborn children, reflects the cycles of trauma and loss imposed on black and mixed-race families by systemic racism and social rejection. Her incarceration in the "Greasy Spoon" restaurant, her social marginalization, and her sense of isolation also symbolize the economic and social disenfranchisement experienced by many African Americans and women in American history. Esther’s struggle with guilt and the haunting presence of her first child, who lives outside her physically but not emotionally, represents the unresolved historical wounds of slavery’s legacy: the unacknowledged and hidden suffering passed down through generations. Esther Longtree embodies the history of racial violence, forbidden and punished interracial love, maternal suffering, social exclusion, and the enduring scars of America's racial past. Through her narrative, Young confronts the complexity of identity, memory, and historical trauma in the United States.
  • Esther Longtree's character carries symbolic weight that can be interpreted in relation to the abortion debate in the U.S., although the symbolism is complex, multifaceted, and embedded within the novel’s rich, dreamlike narrative. Esther Longtree is portrayed as a woman who is "everlastingly pregnant," carrying many stillborn children, miscarriages, and unfulfilled pregnancies over the years. She is described as both "brilliant but dumb," "mulish," "big-footed," and “pregnant with doubtfulness,” yet also maternal, loving, and burdened by her mysterious, repeated losses. Her pregnancies are often linked to a haunting mystery involving many absent or sterile fathers and the ambiguous presence of children who are never fully born or recognized. The narrative suggests that Esther has tried repeatedly to give birth to a "child who lived" but is also surrounded by countless stillborn, ghostly children, and shadows: symbolizing loss, grief, and the elusive nature of life and creation. In this light, Esther Longtree can be seen as embodying the tensions surrounding abortion debates: the conflict between life and death, fertility and sterility, birth and loss, hope and despair. Her "everlasting pregnancy" and the repeated miscarriages may symbolize the ongoing societal struggle over reproductive rights, the moral and emotional complexity of abortion, and the societal judgment and silence that often surround it. The ambiguity about the paternity of her children, the legal threats she faces, and her isolation also reflect the politicized and often stigmatized dimensions of abortion in American society. Esther’s story touches on themes of bodily autonomy, societal control, guilt, and secrecy. She is pursued by a detective who accuses her of murder, threatened with legal action, and yet she remains evasive, protective of her secret “pregnancies,” and burdened by the consequences of societal judgments. This can be interpreted as symbolic of the legal and moral scrutiny women face in abortion debates, where personal agency conflicts with external control and societal norms. The novel frames Esther’s experiences within a broader cosmic and existential context, blurring lines between life and death, reality and dream, and individual and universal experiences. This deepens the symbolism, suggesting that the abortion debate is not simply a social or political issue but also a profound human and metaphysical dilemma about creation, destruction, and the meaning of existence. Esther Longtree may symbolize the abortion debate in the U.S., the detailed portrayal of her character’s perpetual pregnancies, miscarriages, societal judgment, and emotional complexity strongly suggests an allegorical reflection on the themes central to abortion discourse. Her story embodies the profound personal and societal conflicts surrounding reproductive rights, loss, and the nature of life itself.

Chapter 17

← Chapter 16 · Home · Chapter 18 →

Summary

Miss MacIntosh is bald, her skull gleaming like an ivory ball in the moonlight. Vera, shocked and half triumphant, cries out that she is a man. A struggle follows, real or partly imagined. Vera is knocked down, lifted, and laid on the bed, and drifts in and out of consciousness, wondering whether she is wrestling a dummy, a gladiator, or the angel Jacob met. In the morning her braids are neatly plaited, and the only scratches on her cheeks could have come from leafless branches.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Fear and Courage · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars

Allusions: Genesis

Key passages

From the research

  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed almost as a spectral, otherworldly figure standing by the tall windows with blowing curtains. Her corset stays resemble quills of a porcupine or rays of moonlight, and her head is replaced by a "cold and dented" moonlike dome. This surreal image evokes a sense of alienation and transformation, suggesting that she is no longer fully human or recognizable. The metaphor of her body being "more angular than curved" and "ready to meet the opponent" sets the tone of confrontation and tension.
  • The silence, the white curtains blowing like wings, and the "faint tappings of a spectral branch" create an eerie atmosphere, hinting at supernatural or psychological disturbance. This passage is important because it introduces the unsettling and uncanny presence of Miss MacIntosh, foreshadowing the dramatic events to follow.
  • A key moment is the revelation that Miss MacIntosh is bald "as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows," her face "absolutely impersonal and expressionless." This stark image symbolizes loss of identity, vitality, and femininity. Vera is horrified by this transformation, seeing her as a "monster" or a "phantasmagoric being," a "bald pretender" who deceives the senses.
  • The contrast with the memory of her "red, shining hair, tawny as an August sunset," her eyeglasses, and umbrella underscores the dramatic change, suggesting that this is either a ghostly apparition or a symbolic representation of death, decay, or betrayal.
  • This passage is crucial as it marks the psychological crisis of Vera, confronting a beloved figure who is now alien and threatening, evoking themes of identity, disguise, and existential fear.
  • Vera reflects on proverbs and parables, such as "the mountains shall never meet with the mountains," "you shall praise the bridge that carried you," and "man is not born to happiness." These reflections highlight the philosophical and existential underpinnings of the chapter, emphasizing themes of inevitability, loss, and the fragile nature of human happiness.
  • Vera struggles with the notion that either Miss MacIntosh has changed or they themselves have changed, questioning the nature of reality and perception. This self-doubt and questioning of identity deepen the psychological tension and ambiguity.
  • This extended passage details a physical and symbolic struggle between Vera and the bald figure (Miss MacIntosh or a phantom). The fight is described in vivid, almost cinematic terms, with references to boxing moves ("left jab," "straight right," "rabbit punch") and wrestling.
  • Vera experiences disorientation, pain, and a sense of duality ("my body seemed divided as if now there were two of us"). The imagery of stars falling "like dried seed pods," "dark horsemen," and a black "cloud extending from pole to pole" evokes apocalyptic or mythic grandeur.
  • Importantly, Vera questions the identity of the attacker, wondering if it is a "fallen angel," a "Christian knight," or merely a "sandbag dummy come to life." This uncertainty blurs the line between reality, dream, and hallucination.
  • This confrontation symbolizes an internal psychic battle, possibly reflecting trauma, fear of loss, or the struggle with self-identity and acceptance of harsh truths.
  • Vera describes being overpowered, feeling hair pulled out "by handfuls," yet experiencing no pain but a speculative wonder about being "snatched bald." This loss of hair symbolizes a profound loss of beauty, femininity, and power, likened to a "terrible mistake, God’s error."
  • Despite this, Vera notes that "the next morning, of course, my long braids were exactly braided down my back," suggesting the experience may have been a dream, vision, or hallucination, blurring reality and illusion.
  • This passage is significant as it encapsulates the chapter's themes of identity loss, transformation, and the ambiguous boundary between nightmare and waking life.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Initially described as a familiar and trusted figure, a nursemaid, a guardian.
  • Transforms into a bald, expressionless, ghostly figure, described as “bald as the egg or as the rock where nothing grows,” symbolizing loss, change, or an unsettling void.
  • Portrayed with contradictory imagery: both fragile and monstrously strong, spectral yet physically violent.
  • Vera struggles to reconcile this apparition with the Miss MacIntosh they knew, suspecting deception and a hidden identity.
  • Symbolizes a “bald pretender,” a false self, or a shadowy force challenging Vera.

Vera Cartwheel

  • A young girl, around fourteen years old, caught between terror and fascination.
  • Experiences a physical and psychological battle with the transformed Miss MacIntosh.
  • Reflects on memories, identity, and the nature of illusion versus reality.
  • Shows moments of wild laughter, despair, and confusion, indicating a complex emotional state.
  • Vera’s perception is unreliable or dreamlike, blending corporeal reality with surreal visions.

Research: Themes

Identity and Transformation

See: Identity and the Self

  • Miss MacIntosh’s sudden baldness and altered demeanor symbolize a profound change, calling into question the stability of identity.
  • Vera’s inability to accept this change reflects a struggle with understanding the self and others.
  • The motif of hair loss as a loss of femininity or vitality is potent and unsettling.

Illusion vs. Reality

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The chapter blurs the lines between waking life, dream, and hallucination.
  • Vera questions what is real, what is illusion, and the nature of perception.
  • The fight with the “bald opponent” may also be symbolic, reflecting an internal conflict or a confrontation with an aspect of the self.

Fear and Madness

See: Madness and Sanity · Fear and Courage

  • The setting at midnight, the eerie descriptions, and the “zero hour” evoke a sense of dread.
  • Vera’s fear escalates into a violent struggle, suggesting a descent into madness and trauma.
  • The chapter explores how strange events can “leave us mad” or shatter sanity.

Power and Vulnerability

  • Miss MacIntosh’s physical power contrasts with her ghostly, fragile appearance.
  • Vera, though young and vulnerable, refuses to be defeated quietly.
  • The battle becomes a metaphor for the fight between opposing forces within or external threats.

Memory and Perception

See: Memory and the Past

  • Vera recalls past moments with Miss MacIntosh, contrasting them with the present terrifying vision.
  • There is an awareness that memory and perception can deceive or change over time.
  • Vera’s reflections on proverbs and parables hint at larger philosophical questions.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Baldness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Represents loss, emptiness, exposure, and transformation.
  • Compared to “the egg,” “the rock where nothing grows,” “the rose stripped of all its petals,” and “bare as the winter winds,” emphasizing barrenness and desolation.

Moonlight and Darkness

See: Moon and Stars · Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The moonlight creates a cold, distant atmosphere.
  • The interplay of light and shadow symbolizes the tension between knowledge and ignorance, reality and illusion.

Corset and Armor

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Miss MacIntosh’s metallic corset is described like a battleship or wrestler’s gear, symbolizing restraint, protection, and conflict readiness.

Animal Imagery

  • Falada, Vera’s old horse, a present from Mr. Spitzer, represents loyalty and alertness but is powerless.
  • Vera’s comparison of Miss MacIntosh to a “codfish swept up upon a barren shore” and “old man” adds to the grotesque transformation.

Physical Combat

  • The fight is depicted with detailed boxing terminology (rabbit punch, jab, left hook), emphasizing the visceral and brutal nature of the struggle.
  • The encounter may also symbolize internal psychological conflict or a battle with one’s fears or identity.

Stream of Consciousness

  • The narration flows with intense, fragmented, and poetic sentences reflecting Vera’s emotional turmoil.

Surreal and Symbolic

  • The imagery is often dreamlike, blending the real with the fantastical.

Emotional Intensity

  • The tone fluctuates between terror, disbelief, wild laughter, and despair.

Use of Parables and Philosophical Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Vera contemplates proverbs and existential questions, adding depth and universality.

Further notes from the text

  • Miss MacIntosh first appears as a silhouette: corset stays sticking out like the quills of an angry porcupine, and in place of a head another moon, an ivory ball “such as perhaps a god should play with.”
  • The baldness arrives as a litany of similes, bald as the egg, as the rock where nothing grows, as the rose stripped of its petals, and then as a list of missing things: her red hair, her eyeglasses, her black umbrella, her Pilgrim’s Progress.
  • Vera’s first response is laughter and “a kind of wild triumph” at having been right all along in imagining Miss MacIntosh with a red curled mustache and in casting her as the bridegroom, a direct callback to the dream wedding in Chapter 10.
  • The figure Vera fears is the lurking rapist Miss MacIntosh had warned her about, the drunken sailor reeling out of the fog. The protector and the danger she warned against have become one figure in the dark.
  • The struggle is told in boxing language: the left jab, the straight right, the rabbit punch, the left hook, the southpaw. It is the sandbag dummy of Chapter 15 come to life, and also, Vera thinks, the angel with whom Jacob wrestled at Peniel.
  • Vera calls for help that cannot come: her mother, and Mr. Spitzer, who “was gone from Boston to Boston.” She tells us she will be asking the questions of this night long years afterward, when she is old and grey.

Research: Resources

  • King Magnus was an illegitimate son who became king of Norway and Denmark. He functions as a symbolic figure representing power, challenge, and the monumental nature of Vera's confrontation with Miss MacIntosh's transformed, imposing presence
  • The “holy angel with whom Jacob struggled at Peniel” is in Genesis 32:22-32 and Hosea 12:3-5 It symbolizes a universal confrontation with the self or with higher powers, embodying the challenges of self-knowledge, division within the soul, and the search for unity and resolution in a fragmented world.

Chapter 27

Summary

Vera grows exasperated with the adults who circle their problems endlessly. Mr. Spitzer carries calling cards and an old passport so that, if he is found dead, he will be identified as himself and not his brother. He wears Peron's accurate wristwatch, and has lately rediscovered his own identical watch, broken and stopped near the time of Peron's death, and wears it too. He is always late and always caught between streams of traffic. A stranger once asked him on a crowded street whether he wanted to die. He said no while nodding yes, and was led safely across.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Time

Symbols: Mirrors and Reflections · Opium · The Bus and the Journey

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a reflection on Catherine's persistent engagement with "ancient people" and her habit of living in an imaginative, surreal world rather than facing reality. She imagines herself as historical or fantastical figures (e.g., Catherine the Great) and engages in imagined dialogues, addressing absent entities. This highlights her detachment from actual life and the dreamlike, opium-induced nature of her thoughts. It sets the tone for understanding her as a figure caught between illusion and reality, embodying a perennial lack of faith that paradoxically makes everything possible for her.
  • In contrast to Catherine, Mr. Spitzer is portrayed as being more aware of his difficulties and realities. Yet, he is burdened by his isolation, preferring neutrality and distance from the competitive world. His existence is described as "intermittent," marked by memory lapses and confusion, symbolized by the possibility of walking "through a wall of shimmering glass" or forgetting destinations. This motif emphasizes his fragile grasp on reality and self-identity, as well as his struggle with time and memory.
  • The chapter deeply explores the symbolism of time through the motif of watches. Mr. Spitzer wears his dead brother’s fine, accurate watch, contrasting it with his own broken and rusted timepiece. The brother's watch marks "the course of the inaccurate planets" and embodies an elegiac music in memory of the brother. This duality of watches reflects the tension between order and chaos, memory and loss, and the elusive nature of time itself. The mention of the brother's death and Mr. Spitzer's confusion about timing around this event underscores the theme of temporal dislocation and the impossibility of fully grasping or controlling time.
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on the artifice of time, comparing it to Catherine's opium dreams and the "great coffin of stars" that might contain his love. This passage philosophically questions the reality of time, suggesting it is an artificial construct. The imagery of "jumping headlong into time with screaming stars" conveys a sense of fatalism and the overwhelming force of existence that defies human control.
  • Despite his solemn reflections, Mr. Spitzer is conscious of his external dignity, fearing ridicule and the loss of respect. The passage describing the humor in a "fat man slipping on a banana peel" humanizes him, showing his vulnerability and self-awareness. His concern with maintaining dignity despite physical and mental frailty illustrates a profound human struggle against decline and absurdity.
  • The motif of musical discord parallels the confusion and disorder in Mr. Spitzer’s life. This metaphor extends to his experience of reality, where signals, timing, and order are unreliable. The image of being caught between two traffic streams or crossing streets at wrong lights symbolizes his dislocation in time and place. The stranger who asks if he "wanted to die" and then guides him through chaotic traffic encapsulates his precarious existence, teetering between life and death, clarity and confusion.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A man burdened by his awareness of his difficulties and haunted by memories and illusions.
  • He is isolated, secretive, and struggles to reconcile his inner world with external reality.
  • His interactions with the Catherine’s and his own sense of time and self are central.
  • Mr. Spitzer rarely leaves his home except for business and is burdened by his fragmented memory and difficulties.
  • He wears his deceased brother’s watch as a memento and a symbol of time and loss.
  • Mr. Spitzer experiences dislocation in time and space: arriving early or late, encountering sudden weather changes, and experiencing shifts in scenery.
  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with the notion that life, time, and events are illusions, yet he continues to strive for dignity and order in his existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s clothes are always described and contain items from other people (Peron and Jock).

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • A woman lost in opium dreams and fantasies, disconnected from reality.
  • She imagines herself in surreal, historical, or symbolic roles, often interrupting conversations with remarks addressed to absent figures.
  • Her lack of faith paradoxically makes "all things possible" for her.
  • Catherine insists on assigning significant interpretations to minor details and ignores major events, suggesting her detachment from reality.

Research: Themes

Isolation and Alienation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Mr. Spitzer prefers solitude and neutrality, finding the competitive world burdensome.
  • Catherine is isolated in her opium-induced fantasies and mental state.
  • Both characters exhibit a disconnection from ordinary social interactions and time.

Perception of Reality and Imagination

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • Catherine confuses or replaces reality with elaborate fantasies (e.g., imagining herself as Catherine the Great).
  • Mr. Spitzer’s reality is complicated by his own fragmented memory and sense of identity.

Time and Memory

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • Time is portrayed as fluid, unreliable, and artificial.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s broken and inherited watches symbolize the fractured nature of time and memory.
  • The struggle with remembering and forgetting is a persistent motif, especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer’s brother's death.

Death and Existence

See: Death and Mortality

  • The idea of death is ever-present, especially concerning Mr. Spitzer’s brother.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates his own mortality and the notion of life as an illusion or transient state.

Dignity and Self-Image

See: Identity and the Self

  • Mr. Spitzer is deeply concerned with preserving his dignity and avoiding ridicule.
  • His physicality (notably his size) and the fear of losing control over his image are recurring concerns.

Music and Harmony

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Mr. Spitzer finds solace in musical metaphors: the "Pythagorean harmonies," "music of the silent spheres," and the discordant experiences of life.
  • Music represents both order and chaos, reflecting the tension in Mr. Spitzer’s internal state.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Watches (Mr. Spitzer’s and his Brother’s, Miss MacIntosh also has a watch given to her by her brother)
  • The brother’s unbroken, elegant watch contrasts with Mr. Spitzer’s broken, dust-clogged timepiece.
  • Watches symbolize the passage and distortion of time, memory, and connection between the brothers.

Opium Dreams and Fantasies

See: Opium

  • Catherine’s opium-induced visions illustrate altered perception and escapism.
  • These dreams blur the line between reality and imagination.

Phantasmagoric Facts

  • Catherine’s interpretation of Mr. Spitzer’s life is described as “phantasmagoric,” highlighting the surreal and distorted nature of her view.

Invisible Glass Wall

See: Mirrors and Reflections

  • Metaphor for Mr. Spitzer’s barriers between himself and the external world, also referencing an incident where he “walked through a wall of invisible glass,” symbolic of his fragile state.

Traffic and Crossings

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • Recurring images of Mr. Spitzer being caught in dangerous or confusing traffic symbolizes his existential confusion and vulnerability.

Further notes from the text

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s exasperation at “these ancient people,” forever turning on the same spiral problems, and at her mother imagining she is Catherine the Great in a bed with pillars of twisted amethyst rather than facing the living sunlight.
  • Mr. Spitzer objects less to Catherine’s “phantasmagoric facts” about his life than to her interpretation of them: she insists that minor details matter most and major events not at all.
  • His life, which should be continuous, is “intermittent.” He takes the wrong train, gets off at the wrong city, “the wrong station, the wrong star,” though he is painfully accurate and covered with exact reminders to himself.
  • Almost any fool, he admits, including himself, could tell him there is no time, that it is all artifice like Catherine’s opium dreams, and yet Peron’s watch is a convenient timepiece for a poor lawyer and musician.
  • Peron’s watch was made for clocking horses. Mr. Spitzer now uses it to time the breakers coming in with their foaming manes and tails, thinking of the long horse race of life.
  • His fear of losing his dignity runs alongside a frank admission that a fat man slipping on a banana peel is the funniest thing there is. See Comedy in Chapter 27.

Research: Resources

  • Epithalamiums are songs that celebrate a marriage while dirges are a lament for the dead.
  • Avoirdupois is a system of weights based on a pound of 16 ounces.

Chapter 73

Content note: The Esther Longtree chapters (72 to 81) deal with stillbirth and pregnancy loss, rape, infanticide, racist violence including lynching, and cruelty to children. This chapter describes stillbirths and the hidden remains of infants.

Summary

Esther describes her stillborn children as fragments: an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb, a snowflake. She hid them in streams, snow, and tree stumps, and the undertaker complains she brings him no business. Dying fathers write to ask whether their child lived, and she keeps their illusions intact. A Chicago detective circles her, and she fears arrest. The story of the boxer Joe Goldberg enters her tale.

Characters present

Esther Longtree · Joe Goldberg · Justice O’Leary · The Chicago Detective · Phoebe · Coleman Bluebough · Abigail Porter

Concepts present

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens and repeatedly returns to the motif of Esther’s “everlasting pregnancy,” a state in which she is perpetually carrying children who are never fully born or who are stillborn, described as fragments like “an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb”. This surreal condition embodies her maternal nature and the sorrow she carries, as well as her isolation and the mystery surrounding the fate of these children. Her swollen womb and the “whistle of the stillborn in her ears” symbolize this burden.
  • Throughout the chapter, the narrative emphasizes the letters sent to Esther by several dying men “the fathers” who inquire about the children they supposedly fathered with her. These men seek reassurance that their progeny live, clinging to hope at the moment of death. Esther’s silence in response to them, advised by her old, drunken doctor to preserve their vanity and peace, highlights her protective but tragic role. She cannot confirm their hopes because, in fact, the children are “snowflakes,” “marsh butterflies,” or other insubstantial forms.
  • A particularly poignant and detailed passage concerns Joe Goldberg, the champion featherweight boxer who wrote long, anguished letters to Esther as he wasted away from tuberculosis. He remembered her as the “peak of his existence,” the greatest “victory” among his battles, and begged for remembrance and forgiveness. Esther, however, cannot recall him clearly as his image is “lost in clouds” and like “the weight of a feather” in her mind, unlike the weaker men whose memories linger more distinctly. This contrast underscores themes of memory, loss, and the elusive nature of identity and connection.
  • Joe Goldberg’s memory of meeting Esther in a graveyard on a foggy, windy night is recounted in detail. This encounter, marked by violence and intimacy, he “had knocked off the nose of an angel” and “had taken her against her will”, is both haunting and symbolic. It situates their relationship amid death and decay, reinforcing the chapter’s motifs of mortality and the ambiguity of life and conception.
  • Repeatedly, the narrative returns to Esther’s silence and her solitary endurance of her condition. She neither confirms nor denies the existence of the children to the fathers and has no answers for the legal or emotional claims made upon her. Her silence is portrayed as a form of protection for herself and the dying men and as a reflection of the “imponderable answer” she cannot find.
  • One of the most emotionally charged passages describes a labor in which Esther endures all the pains of childbirth but delivers “nothing”. This “birth of nothing” symbolizes her profound loss and the futility she feels: her body is broken, her labor intense, but no child emerges. The passage conveys the deepest sorrow of her experience and her isolation in this repeated tragedy.
  • The chapter uses the image of an old mule, barren and mournful, as a recurring symbol of sterility and loneliness that “followed” Esther. Similarly, the white feather drifting down during her labor is interpreted as a possible “message from the silence,” a sign of hope amid despair. These symbols deepen the thematic exploration of fertility, loss, and the fragile boundary between life and death.
  • Esther faces the threat of legal inquiry and possible trial for “murder” due to the disappearance of her stillborn children, as the undertaker complains that she has not brought business to the graveyard. This introduces a grim social dimension to her plight, where her mysterious condition could be criminalized, adding to her burden of silence and secrecy.
  • Throughout, Esther struggles with memory: she cannot recall all the fathers or children, especially the strong featherweight champion, despite his vivid letters and pleas. This lapse underscores the chapter’s meditation on the instability of personal identity, the limits of memory, and the ephemeral nature of human connections.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Esther Longtree

  • Big-boned, slow-moving waitress, cross-eyed, with a deformed foot and swollen womb.
  • Maternal, compassionate, yet burdened by a mysterious, continuous pregnancy with stillborn children.
  • Silent and evasive when questioned by fathers, embodying endurance, sorrow, and resilience.
  • Symbolizes fertility, loss, and the complex intersection of memory and identity.

Joe Goldberg (Champion Featherweight)

  • A once-powerful boxing champion, now frail and dying of tuberculosis.
  • Writes long, emotional letters to Esther, hoping to be remembered and to claim his child.
  • Represents strength, vulnerability, and the tragic human fight against death.
  • His relationship with Esther is ambiguous, partly forgotten by her but deeply significant to him.

Old Doctor

  • A drunken, disillusioned physician who advises Esther to maintain silence with dying men.
  • Offers a philosophical perspective on death, illness, and the illusions surrounding conception and fertility.

The Fathers (Traveling Salesmen, Sterile Men)

  • Many are weak, sterile, or self-centered men who impregnated Esther but never took responsibility.
  • They symbolize failure, disappointment, and the social stigma attached to Esther's condition.

The Chicago detective

  • A symbolic figure representing societal judgment, scrutiny, and the external pressures faced by Esther Longtree. Though he appears only indirectly through Esther’s thoughts and fears, his presence is significant and multifaceted.
  • The detective symbolizes the potential legal and moral condemnation that Esther fears. She imagines a scenario where she might be arrested, tried, and accused of murder for the stillborn children she has carried and lost over the years. The detective’s investigation represents society’s attempt to impose order and assign blame on Esther for the tragic outcomes of her pregnancies, despite her innocence in her own mind.
  • The detective is described as "old" and "sterile," highlighting a contrast with Esther’s "everlasting pregnancy." He stands for the many fathers who impregnated Esther but who were unable or unwilling to assume responsibility for the children, especially since most of the children were stillborn or never fully born. The detective’s search for proof and evidence reflects a broader theme of male absence and desertion, with Esther bearing the burden alone.
  • Esther fears the detective’s inquiries, which might lead to public exposure of her condition and the stillborn children. She worries about appearing before a jury while visibly pregnant, the social humiliation involved, and the invasive nature of such an investigation. This fear adds to her isolation and suffering, emphasizing the harshness of societal judgment towards women in her position.
  • The detective’s efforts to find evidence of murder or wrongdoing are ultimately futile, as Esther has hidden the stillborn children in natural places (streams, fields, under snowdrifts) making proof elusive. This futility underscores the theme of invisibility and loss that permeates Esther’s life and the narrative. The detective’s inability to find tangible evidence mirrors Esther’s own uncertainty about the fate and existence of the children.
  • Through the detective’s imagined role, the narrator Vera explores themes of justice, mercy, and the limits of human understanding. Esther’s silence and refusal to answer inquiries, partly motivated by kindness to the dying fathers and partly by self-preservation, contrast with the detective’s probing. This tension raises questions about who is truly culpable and how society deals with grief and loss.

Phoebe

  • Phoebe is mentioned in the context of a graveyard, specifically as "the old washwoman’s grave" with a statue that has a bulbous nose, warts, wrinkles, and a sunbonnet. This description suggests she is a deceased figure remembered by the characters, particularly in relation to the environment surrounding Vera and her mother.
  • Phoebe's statue symbolizes one of the many tombs in the graveyard, representing the past and the presence of the dead in the narrative. She is part of the imagery of mortality and memory that permeates the story.
  • Phoebe is a symbolic figure within the narrative, evoking themes of death, memory, and the passage of time.

Coleman Bluebough

  • Coleman Bluebough is mentioned in the context of Esther Longtree’s story as a figure associated with old deaths and graves, specifically noted on a tombstone in a vegetable garden.
  • Esther Longtree recalls the name Coleman Bluebough, who died at the age of three, and his place is marked among other graves and memorials in the narrative.
  • The mention of Coleman Bluebough helps underscore themes of death, stillbirth, and loss that pervade Esther Longtree’s life and experiences, particularly her repeated pregnancies and the stillborn children she mourns.
  • Coleman Bluebough represents one of the many children who have died young or were stillborn, figures that are part of Esther Longtree's troubled memories and grief.

Abigail Porter

  • Abigail Porter is referenced as a person whose grave is marked in the graveyard, and she is among the many figures evoked in the narration that surrounds Esther Longtree's story.
  • The graveyard where she rests is described as a place filled with various symbolic elements like crosses, rustling owls, winged beings, inscriptions, and old statues. Abigail Porter is part of a broader meditation on death, memory, and loss within the narrative.

Research: Themes

  • Esther Longtree is a woman perpetually pregnant, carrying the memory and burden of many stillborn children: fragments such as an eye, ear, fingernail, cobweb, or snowflake rather than whole babies. This condition is both literal and symbolic, representing loss, unfulfilled motherhood, and isolation. Her pregnancy is a metaphor for enduring sorrow and hope intertwined.
  • Esther struggles to remember the fathers of her many lost children and even the details of conception, while the dying fathers vividly recall her and their supposed children. The featherweight champion Joe Goldberg, one of the few who wrote her, haunts her memory, but she cannot fully recall him, symbolizing the elusive and fragmented nature of memory.
  • Despite her perpetual pregnancy and maternal instincts, Esther is isolated, misunderstood, and burdened with silence. She mothered many children who never lived, and she bears the emotional weight alone, rarely responding to inquiries from dying fathers, protecting their illusions and her own fragile peace.
  • The novel explores the boundary between life and death, conception and loss. The children are often invisible and symbolized as feathers, snowflakes, or shadows which highlight the ephemeral nature of existence and the impossibility of closure or concrete answers.
  • Joe Goldberg represents a powerful figure in Esther's life and the narrative: strong and victorious in his prime, yet reduced to a frail, dying man battling God. His letters to Esther reveal his longing for remembrance and his hopes for their child, underscoring themes of memory, regret, and the human desire for legacy.
  • Esther faces potential accusations, including murder of her stillborn children, reflecting societal judgment and misunderstanding of her condition. She fears trial and public humiliation, but she remains protective of her silence and her unborn "little shadow boxer".

Research: Symbols and Imagery

  • Stillborn Children as Snowflakes, Feathers, Cobwebs These fragile, ephemeral images represent the children that Esther carries but never fully births. They highlight invisibility, loss, and the intangible nature of her motherhood.
  • The Graveyard The location of Esther’s encounter with Joe Goldberg symbolizes death, the boundary between life and afterlife, and the haunting memory of their union.
  • The Old Mule Represents sterility, loneliness, and the persistence of life without fruition. It is Esther's constant companion symbolizing the barrenness surrounding her fertility.
  • The Little Shadow Boxer The unborn child she feels under her heart, symbolizing hope, continuation, and the enduring mystery of life and death.
  • Blood-Stained Clothes and Bruises Signify the pain, violence, and social stigma Esther endures during her labors and life. They also underscore the physical and emotional toll of her condition.

Research: Resources

  • Esther Longtree emerges as a profoundly tragic and complex figure burdened by perpetual pregnancy and the sorrow of countless stillborn children. Her character is marked by an overwhelming maternal instinct intertwined with mystery, loneliness, and a haunting sense of loss. Esther is described as a "big, dumb-headed waitress," slow-moving and physically altered by her condition: one foot is deformed, her womb swollen, and her body constantly expanding with what she perceives as an "everlasting pregnancy." This physical state symbolizes her ceaseless burden and the weight of her unresolved grief. Her dark hair often drifts before her eyes, symbolizing both a literal and metaphorical veil between her and the world around her, emphasizing her isolation and internal confusion. Despite the numerous pregnancies resulting only in stillborns or incomplete births ("an eye, an ear, a long gold hair, a fingernail, a cobweb") Esther remains intensely maternal. She has mothered everything from her childhood thumb and big toe to a bullfrog, underscoring her nurturing nature even in the face of continual loss. This maternal impulse is paradoxical; she is both the source of life and a witness to death and absence, which causes her embarrassment and deep sorrow. Many men, termed "fathers," have impregnated her, yet none seem to have produced a living child. These men are generally weak, sterile, or dying, and several write to Esther as they face death, seeking acknowledgment of their supposed offspring. Esther, however, rarely answers these inquiries. She prefers to maintain silence to preserve the dignity and hope of the dying fathers, fearing the cruelty that truth would impose. This silence also protects her from the pain of confronting the truth about her stillborn children and the uncertain paternity of her current perpetual pregnancy. A significant figure in Esther’s narrative is Joe Goldberg, the champion featherweight boxer, who wrote to her desperately in his dying days. He remembers their encounter in a graveyard: a strange, violent, and intimate meeting where he "deflowered her" and left his seed. Despite his vivid memories and longing for recognition, Esther cannot recall him clearly, only the graveyard and the circumstances of their meeting. This failure to remember symbolizes her fragmented and overwhelmed state of mind. Joe represents the strongest of the fathers who becomes weak and ephemeral like a feather, and Esther’s inability to anchor him in her memory contrasts sharply with her vivid remembrance of the weaker men. Esther’s narrative is steeped in symbolic imagery: the stillborn children as snowflakes, feathers, cobwebs, and shadows; the old mule representing sterility and loneliness; the graveyard setting for the conception of Joe Goldberg’s child; and the recurring motif of silence as both protection and sorrow. Her "everlasting pregnancy" could be read as a metaphor for enduring grief, unfulfilled potential, and the human condition of bearing loss silently. Her story is riddled with ambiguity about reality versus memory, truth versus illusion, and life versus death. Esther is socially isolated, working alone in a restaurant with fewer and fewer customers, burdened by her physical state and the mystery of her pregnancies. There is an undercurrent of potential accusation against her, from a Chicago detective who suspects her in a forgotten murder of stillborn children to the threat of a public trial. This looming social judgment contrasts with Esther’s own self-view as a suffering, unselfish mother who has never demanded support or recognition from the fathers. Despite her suffering and the enormity of her loss, Esther exhibits resilience. She continues "waxing, waxing, never waning," embodying a strange, almost supernatural endurance. Yet there is also resignation and confusion: she cannot fully grasp her own condition, cannot remember many fathers, and exists in a liminal space between hope and despair, life and death. Esther Longtree is a figure of tragic maternal devotion, loss, and mystery. Her physical and emotional existence is defined by an endless cycle of pregnancy and stillbirth, a heavy silence toward the men who impregnated her, and a haunting ambiguity about what is real and remembered. Her story explores themes of fertility, death, memory, and the human tendency to shield others from harsh truths through silence. She stands as a poignant embodiment of suffering and endurance.
  • Esther Longtree symbolizes a complex and tragic history of loss, abandonment, and the elusive promise of fertility and continuity that can be read metaphorically as reflecting aspects of American history. Her character embodies the sorrow of countless lost hopes and unfulfilled potential: she is "everlastingly pregnant" yet only ever gives birth to stillborn children: fragments like "snowflakes," "cobwebs," "little feet," or "golden hair." These stillborns are the children of many fathers, most of whom are sterile or absent, and who only awaken a sense of conscience or responsibility at their deathbed, asking about the children they never knew. Esther’s silence toward these dying fathers symbolizes the unanswerable questions of lineage, legacy, and accountability in a fragmented, transient society where promises remain unfulfilled and where the past cannot be fully reconciled with the present. This condition can be interpreted as symbolic of the broader American experience, particularly the history of displacement, broken promises, and the elusiveness of the American Dream. Esther’s endless pregnancies with no living offspring reflect the cycles of hope and disappointment in a land marked by migration, loss, and the failure of paternal or institutional responsibility. The many "fathers" who impregnate her but then disappear or fail to support her children can be related to the many waves of settlers, immigrants, and transient individuals who have contributed to the making of America but whose legacies are uncertain or incomplete. The fact that Esther hides her stillborns "everywhere," in streams, under snow, in tree stumps, and yet is threatened with accusations of murder, can be seen as a metaphor for the buried or forgotten histories of marginalized people and the silenced suffering that underlies American progress. The undertaker’s complaint that she brings no business because she hides the evidence of death symbolizes the societal reluctance or failure to confront these hidden tragedies. Her life is also connected to a landscape marked by graveyards, broken fences, and natural elements like wind, snow, and autumn leaves, evoking the American frontier and the harsh realities faced by those living on its margins. Esther Longtree’s tragic and ambiguous history symbolizes the haunted, fragmented, and often unacknowledged history of America itself: a land of many fathers but few fulfilled legacies; a place where life and death, hope and despair, fertility and barrenness coexist; and where the true stories of loss and endurance are obscured by silence and the passage of time. Esther Longtree stands as a profound metaphor for the unresolved burdens and contradictions in American history (the tension between promise and loss, presence and absence, birth and death) that shape the nation's identity.
  • Materia medica (It encompasses ancient and medieval knowledge of remedies, with a foundational text being Dioscorides' De Materia Medica) refers to the comprehensive body of knowledge, historically cataloging the origins, properties, and preparation of substances used to treat diseases. They were indigenous to the regions of northern Iraq, southeastern Turkey, northeastern Syria and northwestern Iran, many have migrated to Western countries including the United States, Canada, Mexico, Australia, Sweden and Germany.   • Historical weight classes for boxing are: heavyweight at 200+ pounds, light heavyweight at 168-175 pounds, middleweight at 154-160 pounds, welterweight at 140-147 pounds, lightweight at 130-135 pounds, featherweight at 122-126 pounds, bantamweight at 115-118 pounds, flyweight at 108-112 pounds.
  • Phoebe may refer to several in Greek mythology or a first-century Christian woman mentioned by the Apostle Paul in his Epistle to the Romans, verses 16:1-2. Summary

Mr. Spitzer realizes that Hannah was also a secret mountain climber, of peaks real and of the mind. As her executor he takes her alpenhorn for his collection of instruments. He wanders a fog-bound city asking strangers whether they have seen her, and people take him for mad. A steeplejack answers him in paradoxes. The chapter ends with Hannah's last cry to the bright star of her love.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Identity and the Self · Love · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Fog and Mist · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Music and Instruments · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Allusions: Judaism · Romantic Poets

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens by portraying Cousin Hannah not merely as a suffrage leader but as a "valiant wanderer" who climbed "formidable mountains and supernumerary peaks" beyond physical realms such as mountains "greater than mountains," rising "Alp above Alp through consciousness" even after death. This metaphor suggests her spirit transcends earthly limits, linking her struggles and love to the eternal and the sublime. Her life is framed as an ascent beyond mortal boundaries, symbolizing a quest for immortal love and freedom.
  • Mr. Spitzer, acting as Cousin Hannah’s executor, finds and appropriates her alpenhorn, a heavy musical instrument twice her height. This alpenhorn is symbolic: though it cannot literally evoke the Alps in the lowlands, it serves as a poignant emblem of her spirit and the mountains she climbed. Mr. Spitzer reflects on how music arises from chaos and how the instruments of earth are linked to the heavenly realm, though none are truly "strung in paradise." This passage explores the tenuous relationship between art, memory, and transcendence.
  • The novel muses on how ghosts in dreams never appear naked but are always clothed in some form implying that all of life and death is a form of "mask" or "clothing." This metaphor conveys the idea that identity, beauty, and existence are layered, elusive, and perhaps illusory. Mr. Spitzer’s own music is described as a form of elegy or aubade that cannot quite awaken the dead but hints at the dreamlike quality of life and death.
  • A deeply philosophical passage appears as Mr. Spitzer contemplates the "power of a dead beauty, a dead love," and the "sterility which begets... all beautiful things." He asserts that no one truly knows the present moment because it is always "freighted with the past," suggesting that beauty and existence are ghosts of themselves, transitory and elusive. The cloud over beauty is beauty itself, so the veil of mystery remains intact. This suggests an acceptance of ambiguity and the unknowable as essential to human experience.
  • Despite her achievements, Cousin Hannah is described as being ashamed of her mountain-climbing accomplishments, preferring oblivion over fame. Mr. Spitzer reflects on how many famous people value a moment of oblivion more than lasting glory, as oblivion is paradoxically both what they flee from and what they seek. This passage reveals a tension between public success and private vulnerability, heroism and cowardice, and the human desire for both recognition and escape.
  • A haunting voice from an old steeplejack (a tall, church-like figure) speaks to Mr. Spitzer, embodying contradictions like "I live because I am dead," "I love because I love not," and the idea that all who have loved have died and drowned. Time is depicted as a cloud crossing a clock face that tells no time. This passage powerfully captures the theme of existence as filled with paradox, where life and death, love and loss are inseparable, and where time itself is an illusion.
  • After Cousin Hannah’s death, Mr. Spitzer wanders the fog-bound city asking strangers if they have seen her, despite being perceived as mad. This quest symbolizes the human search for meaning, connection, and remembrance in a world of loss and forgetting. It also reflects on how memory is fragmented and how one can be simultaneously lost yet followed suggesting the persistence of influence beyond death.
  • The chapter closes with Cousin Hannah’s dying cry, calling for a "bright star of my love" to find the "lightless star," signaling the mysterious journey beyond death. The imagery of mountains resurrecting before "the last great cataclysm" and her love "going down" evokes a cosmic, cyclical view of life and death, blending mythic and personal dimensions.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • A complex figure; a suffragette, a mountain climber, a symbol of liberation and love’s endurance. She is proud yet ashamed of her achievements, embodying contradictions of strength and vulnerability. Her death is portrayed almost mythically, with imagery of frost, mountains, and alpenhorns signaling her passage to another realm.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Vera and executor of Cousin Hannah’s estate, an old musician who is deeply introspective and symbolic. He is both observer and participant, grappling with loss, memory, and the meaning of life and death. His inquiries after Hannah’s death reveal his obsession and his quest for understanding the mysteries she embodied.
  • A steeple jack is a skilled tradesperson who works at great heights, primarily on tall structures like church steeples, chimneys, and towers, to perform repairs, maintenance, or construction. The profession has historical roots in the maintenance of ecclesiastical buildings.

Research: Themes

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Cousin Hannah’s death is described with vivid cold and frozen imagery, suggesting a transition into an eternal, timeless state, but one that still holds mystery and significance. There is an ongoing meditation on what it means to die and what survives beyond death, particularly love and memory.

Love Beyond Mortality

See: Death and Mortality · Love

  • Hannah's message is that love transcends mortal bounds, aiming for an immortal love. This idea recurs as Mr. Spitzer contemplates the power and persistence of love even after death, and the paradox that those who have loved have also died, and vice versa.

The Mountain as a Symbol

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • Mountains symbolize challenges, spiritual ascension, and the unknown. Cousin Hannah is portrayed as an unparalleled mountain climber not just of physical peaks like the Matterhorn or Mont Blanc, but of metaphorical mountains of consciousness and existence.

Memory and Oblivion

See: Memory and the Past

  • The chapter addresses how history, fame, and memory are fleeting. Cousin Hannah, despite her great achievements, is largely forgotten by the world, illustrating the tension between individual legacy and collective memory.

Music and Silence

See: Music, Sound, and Silence

  • Mr. Spitzer, a musician, reflects on music as a metaphor for life and death, where silence and sound intermingle. Music arises from chaos and holds a kind of ephemeral power, much like life itself.

Identity and Masks

See: Identity and the Self

  • The motif of masks and clothing in dreams suggests that identity is always layered, never fully naked or transparent. Ghosts and memories are always clothed in some form, and this applies to living beings as well.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Alpenhorn

See: Music and Instruments

  • Represents a call to lost love and memory; a connection to the mountains and the past. Its presence in a flat coastal landscape symbolizes the displacement of memory and the difficulty of preserving legacy in an unresponsive world.

Mountains and Snow

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter · Mountains

  • Mountains stand for the ultimate challenges and heights of spirit and consciousness. Snow and ice symbolize purity, death, and timelessness, as well as the coldness and isolation that often accompany great achievements or sacrifices.

The Dead Moon

See: Moon and Stars

  • A recurring symbol of deathless love and the eternal, especially in a world where stars have faded or fallen. It suggests a cosmic, timeless love that persists beyond human life.

Music and Bells

See: Music and Instruments

  • Music, especially the unplayed or unheard music, represents the ineffable aspects of life and death. Bells ringing without clear cause evoke mystery, transition, and the presence of the unseen.

Fog and Darkness

See: Fog and Mist · Lamps, Candles, and Light
