Summary

Vera describes the world as Catherine experiences it: drifting mirrors, ceilings that become floors, clocks striking impossible hours. She asks who the dreamer is. Catherine declares that order is a madman's dream. She still schemes to bring Hannah back, but Hannah will not return. Death has throttled her, and silence follows.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Fear and Courage · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Birds · Clouds and Storms · Eyes and Blindness · Fog and Mist · Horses and Carriages · Mirrors and Reflections · Roses and Flowers · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Aristotle · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Epicureanism · Existentialism · Freud and Jung · Nietzsche · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Schopenhauer · Stoicism · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory · Wittgenstein

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a surreal vision of a world where mirrors drift, the ceiling becomes a fluid floor, clocks strike inept hours, and dolphins bark unusually. This sets up the motif of a "mistaken dream" with no clear boundaries between heaven and hell, life and death. The question "But who was the dreamer?" introduces the existential uncertainty that pervades the chapter.
  • Vera recounts a discussion with her mother, Catherine, and Mr. Spitzer about the nature of order and chaos. Her mother insists that "Order...was a mad man’s dream," a "suicidal plan omitting the irrational elements," emphasizing the complexity and irrationality of life and the universe. This passage challenges the human desire for simple, orderly explanations.
  • Catherine is portrayed as someone living under the "pervasive influence of opium," caught in a half-conscious dream state where time is an illusion. Death is described not as an end but as an "immeasurable extension" of this dream, blending life and death indistinguishably. Catherine’s inability or refusal to awaken to this knowledge symbolizes human denial of mortality and oblivion.
  • The chapter describes numerous surreal reversals highlighting the instability of identity and perception. This underscores the theme that nothing is fixed or certain, not even one’s own self or reality.
  • Cousin Hannah, a strong suffrage figure, is presented as having passed beyond death in a way Catherine cannot accept. Her adventures contrast with Catherine’s passive existence. Hannah’s death is final and unescapable, symbolizing the inevitability of mortality despite human pride and strength.
  • Catherine fears complete extinction that "land of infinite greyness" without memory, ego, or voice. This fear keeps her "horizontal," an invalid clinging to life’s illusions rather than facing the void. This passage poignantly captures human dread of nothingness and the unknown beyond death.
  • The chapter closes with the recognition that no matter Catherine’s plotting or longing, Cousin Hannah will not return. Death has "throttled her," and the echoes of life and struggle fade into silence. Mr. Spitzer’s metaphor of hearing silence after the last requiem symbolizes acceptance of death’s ultimate finality.

Research: Resources

  • The philosophy of reversals consists of various philosophical ideas and concepts related to the notion of something being turned upside down or reversed. It explores the nature of reversals in different domains: time, causality, values, societal structures. It examines how these reversals impact our understanding of reality, ethics, and meaning. Reversals in literature and art are used to create suspense, irony, and thematic complexity. It can be used to challenge expectations, expose hidden truths, and engage audiences on a deeper level. Aristotle’s reversal and recognition, Baudrillard’s Principle of Reversal examines how oppositions and differences can be overturned, leading to new forms of understanding and meaning. The philosophy of reversals is a prominent theme that permeates the narrative, revealing a worldview where binaries dissolve and opposites interpenetrate, creating a complex and unstable reality. This chapter explores the idea that opposites, such as night and day, sun and moon, beginning and end are not separate entities but are deeply intertwined and often indistinguishable. The narrator, Vera, reflects on how "his night was his day, and his day was his night," and "his dawn was his twilight, and his moon was his sun, and his sun was his moon, and his beginning was his end, and his end was his beginning". These statements encapsulate the core of the reversal philosophy: the collapsing of distinctions that we usually take for granted. The narrative also conveys a sense that reality itself is fluid and mutable, with physical and metaphysical elements constantly changing places or merging. For example, "there should be these somersaultings as when the ceiling was the mirroring floor, trees of enormous crystal growing with their roots in the clouded sky, their branches under the earth". This imagery suggests a world where spatial and conceptual norms are inverted, challenging linear and stable perceptions of existence. The chapter touches on the paradoxical nature of life and death, love and its absence. Vera notes that "Love might wear the face of death, the grinning skull, as death might wear the face of love", emphasizing that what seem like opposites are reflections or transformations of each other. This complicates the understanding of identity and existence, as individuals may be "other than we seemed," with two forms "blended into one which was amorphous, being neither". The philosophy of reversals extends to the cosmic scale, where even celestial bodies and natural laws are subject to change and ambiguity. The narrative questions the fixity of time and space, suggesting that "there should be no harmony, no silent music like the music of the spheres" in the world beyond, because "nothing should be simple there because nothing was simple here". This reflects a skepticism of absolute order or finality in the universe. It presents a vision of a world and perhaps a universe where dualities are illusory, and existence is marked by continuous transformation and contradiction. This philosophy challenges conventional binaries and invites readers to consider a reality that is simultaneously unified and divided, stable and unstable, known and unknowable. This philosophy is central to the novel's exploration of existence, identity, and perception, illustrating a world where certainty dissolves and the dreamlike nature of reality is revealed.
  • Time, perception vs reality, distorted time perception, and time as a mental construct is described as an emergent property in physics. Einstein stated that the distinction between past, present, and future is only a “Stubbornly persistent illusion”. The implications of the illusion of time for humans is it would redefine reality, raise profound philosophical questions (about the nature of existence, consciousness, and the meaning of time), and lead to a shift in perspective encouraging people to focus on the present moment and appreciate the flow of experience. Carlo Rovelli proposes that time is not a fundamental aspect of reality, but rather an emergent phenomenon. He suggests that time may be a complex network of events, and our perception of its flow is a projection onto this network. The chapter presents time as a profound mystery deeply connected to themes of illusion, memory, mortality, and the blending of opposites. Time is not a fixed, measurable entity but a fluid and enigmatic force that shapes and is shaped by human perception, dreams, and the cosmos.
  • Life as a state of experience and potential - Socrates thought death might be a dreamless sleep or passage to another realm where one can converse with the dead. Existentialism believes death is an inevitable aspect of human existence and that it can lead to a heightened sense of self-awareness and responsibility. Epicureanism argues death cannot harm a person, as it’s either not yet experienced (while alive) or not experienced at all (once dead). Death is defined as the loss of the capacity to engage in vital activities and the cessation of consciousness. Wittgenstein said that death is not an experience in life. Schopenhauer believed that understanding death as the ultimate end of life can provide a perspective on the meaning of life itself. Freud thought the life instinct (Eros) and the death instinct (Thanatos) are fundamental forces in human behavior. The chapter depicts life as a state of ongoing experience and potential characterized by uncertainty, illusion, and transformation. It is not a fixed reality but a mutable and often paradoxical condition where life and death, truth and illusion, identity and multiplicity coexist and where human understanding is limited and provisional.
  • The meaning of life in relation to death - Stoicism emphasized that facing death can lead to a deeper understanding of life’s meaning and the ephemeral nature of earthly possessions. Nietzsche used the thought experiment of eternal return (recurrence) to encourage individuals to examine the meaning and value of their lives, given the possibility of living them again and again. The chapter conveys that the meaning of life is deeply connected to death, and that understanding or embracing this connection is part of the human condition. It suggests that love, life, death, and identity are bound in an intricate, often paradoxical relationship that transcends simple definitions, and that this profound ambiguity is central to our experience of existence.
  • The paradox of life and death - some philosophers see life and death as a continuous process, with life as a moment of lucidity within the vastness of existence. Others view death as a finality, a cessation of consciousness and experience. The chapter conveys that life and death are two sides of the same coin, eternally connected, and that understanding this paradox is beyond simple human comprehension, being filled with mystery, ambiguity, and endless transformation.
  • Descartes’ dream argument - He used the experience of dreaming to question the certainty of our perceptions and beliefs. He argued that if we cannot definitively distinguish between waking and dreaming, then our sensory experiences, which are the foundation of our knowledge, might be illusions. There is philosophical skepticism because the possibility of dreams may be genuine or a fabrication. It leads one to question the validity of knowledge of the external world. Freud believed dreams are a symbolic representation of unconscious thoughts and desires. Jung expanded on Freud’s ideas that dreams can also reveal universal, archetypal patterns in the human psyche. Some theories suggest dreams are a natural byproduct of the brain’s activity during sleep, possibly involving memory consolidation, emotional processing, or the clearing out of mental clutter. Neuroscience has provided insights into the physiological processes which in turn influences philosophical discussion about the nature and functions of dreams. Some philosophers think dreams are a way of accessing another realm of existence or experiencing different perspectives on reality. The chapter concludes that dreams are not simply illusions but fundamental to existence and consciousness, blurring distinctions between reality and unreality, life and death, self and other, and that this ambiguity is a central and inescapable part of human experience.

It’s not inherently determined by biology, but rather shaped by cultural norms, societal expectations, and historical contexts. This means gender is not fixed and can vary across cultures and time. Not a biological reality, socially created, varies across cultures, dynamic and fluid, individual identity, distinct from biological sex attributes. The earliest recorded philosophical thought on gender emerged in ancient Greece with Plato and Aristotle, also Mary Wollstonecraft, Judith Sargent Murray, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, John Locke, Pythagoras. The chapter and novel presents gender as a fluid and changeable construct rather than a rigid, innate fact, using metaphorical and dreamlike language to question fixed dichotomies between male and female, self and other, life and death.

Summary

Vera wakes at dawn in Miss MacIntosh's bed, half hoping the night was a dream. Before opening her eyes she reconsiders details she never questioned: the baseball cap, the evening ribbons, the veils over the whaler's hat, the umbrella indoors. Then she looks. The bald head lies on the pillow. The red wig hangs on the hat rack. Around the bare room are false teeth in a glass, a Bible chained to the table, a deuce of clubs, cards printed with Dutch windmills, and seaweed hanging on the barred door. Then she sees that one breast has been amputated.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Decay and Ruin · Dreams and Imagination · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Cards, Games, and Chance · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Roses and Flowers · The House · The Umbrella

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Music and Composers · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a meticulous depiction of Miss MacIntosh’s largely bare and austere bedroom. The room contains very few ornaments: a bust of Martin Luther, a large seashell used as a doorstop, and crumbling cherubim heads around a blackened fireplace, covered by cheese-cloth drapery. The room is described as "plain," "barely furnished," and showing signs of decay which metaphorically reflects Miss MacIntosh’s own physical and perhaps spiritual condition. This setting evokes a sense of austerity, fragility, and impermanence, mirroring the character’s struggle with her own vulnerabilities.
  • Vera observes Miss MacIntosh’s physical traits with a mix of curiosity and tenderness. Notable is the absence of her eyebrows, the rapid changes in the color of her skin, her habitual wearing of old caps or a baseball cap, and the ever-present whistle around her neck. The description of her headgear and her old black umbrella carried like a shield even indoors, suggests a defensive posture against the world or perhaps her own frailty. These details hint at a woman who is both physically fragile and psychologically guarded, living with an awareness of her own vulnerability.
  • A striking image is that of Miss MacIntosh’s bald head lying next to Vera's pillow, "cold as marble" and "seldom touched by sunlight." This evokes a sense of mortality and the harsh reality of illness or aging. Her red wig, compared to a "rare tropical bird," is carefully placed within reach, symbolizing a constructed identity or a protective mask she wears in public. The presence of her worn clothing, her corset stained and draped over a chair, and other personal belongings scattered around the room reinforce the theme of physical deterioration and survival. Vera’s detailed observation of these items underscores a deep intimacy and respect for Miss MacIntosh’s resilience despite her hardships.
  • Among the personal items is a set of translucent playing cards with Dutch windmills, with the upturned card being the deuce of clubs, described as "the test of tears" and "the omen of death." This is particularly poignant given Miss MacIntosh’s critical view of gambling as "the crafty Devil’s handiwork." The card’s presence symbolizes fate, mortality, and perhaps the inevitability of death. It also highlights the duality in Miss MacIntosh’s beliefs between her Christian faith, her honesty, and her rejection of "double motions" or duplicity in the heart. This passage deepens the psychological complexity of her character and sets a somber, reflective tone.
  • The description of the room’s decay continues, with cracked walls, stained ceilings, barred doors with seaweed and barnacles, mud tracks, grains of sand, and salt gleamings. These vivid natural and physical details evoke a sense of isolation, imprisonment, and the passage of time, suggesting that Miss MacIntosh’s life is enclosed, weathered by external elements and internal struggles. The imagery of the umbrella, still opened on the floor as if for protection during the night, reinforces the motif of defense and vulnerability. Vera’s discovery that one of Miss MacIntosh’s breasts has been amputated is a stark and intimate revelation, symbolizing loss and suffering, yet also the survival and endurance of the woman.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Bald head cold as marble, veined limbs, a missing breast (amputated), thin and ascetic face without any facial hair, red wig resembling a tropical bird, gnarled hands.
  • Wears a baseball cap or old caps in the morning and a green ribbon in the evenings.
  • Always carries a whistle around her neck.
  • Wears a veil-tied hat outdoors, sometimes layered with heavy veiling.
  • Carries an old black umbrella indoors and outdoors, like a shield.
  • Sleeps lightly, alert to the slightest noise.
  • Has a strong Christian faith, critical of gambling and superstition.
  • Exhibits physical and emotional contradictions: shifting skin color, blushing for no apparent reason, and trying to resist external forces (“buck[ing] against the broncho wind”).
  • The playing cards, especially the “deuce of clubs,” symbolize fate, death, or a trial by tears, despite her rejection of gambling.
  • Her patched clothing and worn items reflect hardship and resilience.

Vera Cartwheel

  • She describes their mind as "lucid as day" but simultaneously reveals a hesitation or reluctance to fully open their eyes and confront reality directly. This tension between clarity and avoidance suggests an internal conflict or a fragile psychological state. She seems caught between the realms of dream and waking, reality and imagination, as shown by their uncertainty about whether they are truly awake despite the vividness of the dawn light and surroundings.
  • She meticulously catalogues the objects and conditions in Miss MacIntosh’s bedroom, from the "crumbling heads of cherubim" to the "red wig, almost purple," and the "jeweled water glass" holding false teeth. This detailed observation indicates a careful, almost forensic attention to detail, suggesting a mind that seeks to understand and piece together the significance of the environment and the person within it.
  • There is a tone of gentle curiosity in Vera’s internal questioning about Miss MacIntosh’s peculiarities: her missing eyebrows, the changing colors of her skin, her habitual wearing of hats and a whistle, and the careful way she avoids showing vulnerability ("she was no deep sleeper wrapped in the sloth of sensuality"). These questions are posed with "studied detachment," as if Vera is trying to maintain emotional distance while simultaneously probing deeply into the character of Miss MacIntosh.
  • Despite this detachment, Vera’s sensitivity is apparent in their awareness of the "quiver of wind upon the high cheek bones," the "thin, ascetic mouth," and the "wet and stained" pillow. They notice intimate, tender details such as the "one breast had been amputated," describing what remains as "no bigger than a baby’s fist," which evokes a sense of vulnerability and loss. This reveals an underlying empathy and a recognition of Miss MacIntosh’s suffering and resilience.
  • Vera reflects on themes of fate, morality, and human frailty. This moral reflection suggests that she is not only attentive to physical details but also to symbolic meanings and ethical considerations, which adds a philosophical dimension to their character.
  • Vera’s detailed description of Miss MacIntosh’s room (with its broken, bare, and patched furnishings, barred door, and scattered personal effects) reflects a broader sense of isolation, hardship, and complexity. She seems attuned to this atmosphere of loneliness and endurance, which may mirror their own inner state or the broader themes of the narrative.

  • The Mental Hygiene Movement in the US was the organized treatment of mental illness which began in the early 19th century, a period when many states opened asylums to house individuals who at the time were understood to be suffering from insanity. Early advocates believed that asylums offered a controlled environment for the development of “cures” for various forms of mental illness, which at that time was thought to be a type of disease requiring expert medical treatment. Led by Dorothea Dix, proponents of asylums “confidently and aggressively asserted that properly organized institutions could cure almost every instance of the disease.” By the 1870s, however, the reformers’ vision had collapsed. Their notion that order and discipline could cure the “recently insane” proved inaccurate. Even individuals with less serious forms of mental illness did not respond as reformers had hoped, and for the more seriously ill, being sent to an asylum often ended up being a lifetime sentence. By the early 20th century, even as many state asylums changed their names to “hospitals” to underscore their ostensible commitment to “curing” mental illness, asylums had devolved into largely custodial institutions. A similar historical path was followed in Texas, which like many other Southern states began opening asylums just before or during the Civil War. Opened in 1861, the Texas State Lunatic Asylum was physically and programmatically modeled closely on the principles of the national movement for asylums. Renamed the Austin State Hospital in 1925, the institution suffered from overcrowding and underfunding through most of its existence.

Summary

Vera takes a last long look at Miss MacIntosh asleep: the scar, the missing eyebrows and lashes, a green ribbon looped over a bust of Martin Luther. She falls back asleep. When she wakes, Miss MacIntosh stands fully dressed, her red wig shining, in unusually good humor, and the room is tidy as if nothing happened. She says Vera has been sick and scolds her for dancing without a partner. She holds up the birthday dress Mr. Spitzer sent, declares it cannot be mended, and sends it to the ash bin.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Love

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Judaism · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • This opening passage is crucial because it establishes Vera's conscious perception of their companion (later identified as Miss MacIntosh) in her usual, seemingly strong and formidable state. The language ("shining armor," "scaled vizor," "rugged individualist," "triumphant") creates an image of someone powerful, decisive, and perhaps intimidating, contrasting sharply with the vulnerability revealed later. It sets up the central theme of appearance versus reality and the layers of disguise or perception that Vera navigates. The detail about the evening walk and the old dog grounds this potentially abstract description in a concrete, if slightly surreal, daily ritual.
  • The physical reality of the companion's baldness is explicitly revealed to Vera upon waking is a pivotal moment. Vera contrasts this "palpable disguise of the average man" (or perhaps, woman) with a sense of hidden "dead and vanished glory." The image of the "great baldness as of the moon sunken" is striking and suggests something vast, desolate, and perhaps beyond reach. Crucially, Vera interprets this physical revelation not as a simple lack, but as something that reveals a deeper truth about reality: that strength is intertwined with fragility, illusion, and disorder. This passage shifts the narrative from external observation to deep internal reflection on the nature of identity, love, and perception.
  • Vera's complex motivation is articulated after witnessing Miss MacIntosh's vulnerability. The "good intention" is to maintain a facade of normalcy for her sake, even if it requires Vera to "deceive her" about their own profound realization. Vera seems to want to protect her from the implications of the "glory" or "chaos" they perceived, wishing instead for her to see herself as ordinary, stable, and authentic. This reveals Vera's protective instinct but also highlights the inherent tension in their relationship and the burden of Vera's newfound knowledge. It introduces the theme of deliberate self-deception or mutual deception as a way to cope with difficult truths.
  • While seemingly a digression, it reinforces the chapter's themes of appearance vs. reality, disguise, and the difficulty of discerning truth. The companion's sayings about the Devil emphasize that evil can be deceptive, appearing in attractive forms ("charming," "handsome," "fine dancer," "God's ape"). This mirrors Vera's experience of seeing Miss MacIntosh's seemingly strong exterior peeled away to reveal a hidden reality, suggesting that what appears "normal" or even "good" might conceal something else entirely. It adds a layer of theological or philosophical depth to the personal revelation, implying that the struggle to understand her is part of a larger human struggle to understand complex, hidden realities. It also gives voice to Miss MacIntosh's own worldview.
  • This extended description is incredibly powerful and visceral. It moves beyond the initial shock of baldness to reveal a body marked by age, illness, and labor (the missing breast, scar, gnarled hands/feet). The imagery is both starkly realistic ("mouth open and toothless") and metaphoric ("Alpine frozen slopes," "wintry field," "polished marble," "barnacles"). The repetition of "pity" underscores Vera's overwhelming emotional response. The description emphasizes vulnerability, loss, and a stripping away ("denudement") of layers both physical and perhaps metaphysical. The comparison of this reality to something "less substantial than the wildest, saddest dream" suggests a profound disorientation for Vera, blurring the lines between waking life and nightmare, and making the revealed reality seem almost unbelievable despite its physical presence.
  • After the intense, detailed description of the vulnerable, sleeping figure, Miss MacIntosh is abruptly presented as the familiar, formidable "Miss MacIntosh," fully dressed and appearing exactly as she did the previous evening, complete with her shining red hair. Vera notes their lack of astonishment initially, highlighting how quickly the mind can revert to familiar perceptions, even after a profound revelation. However, Vera is astonished to find themselves in Miss MacIntosh's bed, introducing a new element of mystery and suggesting that the morning's events (or at least Vera's being there to witness them) are out of the ordinary. This passage reinstates the "disguise" or preferred appearance and raises questions about which reality is dominant or "true" – the vulnerable sleeping figure or the robust, familiar Miss MacIntosh.
  • This dialogue shifts the focus away from Miss MacIntosh's physical state to Vera's past and apparent recent illness or misbehavior. Miss MacIntosh's tone is parental ("sick and unusually stubborn," "mild reproach"), emphasizing their caregiver-dependent relationship. The mention of the "first birthday party" and the torn dress introduces a specific past event, possibly symbolic of a loss of innocence or a failed attempt at celebration. Most significantly, the passage presents a clear discrepancy: Vera sees no tear in the dress, but Miss MacIntosh insists it is irreparably damaged and must be discarded. This highlights a potential unreliability in the narrative, either on the part of Miss MacIntosh (perhaps deliberately misrepresenting the dress's condition) or Vera (perhaps unable to see the damage, literal or symbolic). The torn dress becomes a symbol of something broken or lost that cannot be fixed, but the disagreement about its state complicates its meaning and adds to the chapter's layers of uncertain reality. Miss MacIntosh's repetition of the "road to Hell" saying connects this conversation back to the earlier philosophical digression, grounding it in her practical, somewhat fatalistic worldview.

  • The King James Version of the Bible was not the first English language version of the Bible, but the culmination of extensive translation activity (some illegal!) in the 1500s. This began with the work of William Tyndale and the printing of the first English New Testament in 1526. Following a tumultuous 75 years, King James I came to power in 1603, unifying a divided England. Three main English Bibles were in use: the Bishops’ Bible (Church of England), the Geneva Bible (Protestants), and the Rheims New Testament (Roman Catholic Church), causing much confusion and dissension. To settle disagreements over reforms in the Church of England and respond to pressure from the Puritans, King James in 1604 approved a new translation of the Bible, primarily because he knew that it would reinforce his image as a political and spiritual leader. He appointed six committees, totaling 54 scholars, to prepare the new translation, using previous English Bible translation work, and using the best Hebrew, Greek, and Latin texts and manuscripts. The completed King James Version was first published in 1611. These first editions were large pulpit Bibles (folios) to be read in churches, but were followed within a year by the printing of smaller versions (quartos) for personal use. Though slow to be adopted in the English-speaking world and to replace the more popular Geneva Bible, from the mid-1600s to the late 20th century, the King James Version was the Bible of the English-speaking church. Though many recent modern translations have gained in popularity at the expense of the KJV, it remains the standard of measure for all new translations, and it still stands as the outstanding masterpiece of the English language.
  • The King James Only movement (also known as King James Onlyism or KJV Onlyism) asserts that the King James Version (KJV) of the Bible is superior to all other English translations of the Bible. Adherents of the movement, mostly certain Conservative Anabaptist, traditionalist Anglo-Catholic, Conservative Holiness Methodist and Independent Baptist churches, believe that this text has been providentially preserved as a perfect translation of the Bible into English. Followers of the movement assert that modern English Bible translations are corrupt, based on a distrust of the Alexandrian text-type or the critical texts of Nestle-Aland, and Westcott-Hort, sources for the majority of twentieth- and twenty-first-century translations. Instead, they prefer the Textus Receptus (which is mainly based on the Byzantine text-type, with some influences from other text-types). Some factions argue that the King James translation itself was divinely inspired. Others prefer the KJV simply because it is in the public domain in most countries (with the United Kingdom being a notable exception), which allows them to freely copy any amount of the translation without worrying about royalties or copyright.

Chapter 14

Summary

Vera comes to the grave of the black coachman, who once drove her grandfather's carriage with four white horses. Catherine is obsessed with that grave and its location. She questions Mr. Spitzer endlessly about the coachman's burial and the fate of the horses. Beneath this obsession, the story of the Spitzer twins comes out. Peron fell from a tall building, probably by suicide. Joachim has lived in the aftermath ever since, wearing his brother's cufflinks and being mistaken for him in the street. Catherine goes on talking long after Mr. Spitzer has left, asking about the grave of the other Mr. Spitzer, the one she loved, until dawn puts her to sleep.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer · The Black Coachman

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Duality and Doubles · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Horses and Carriages · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Kant and Hegel · Phenomenology · Plato and Platonism · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory

Allusions: Astronomy · Dante · Music and Composers · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Vera’s reflection on the grave of the black coachman, a figure who drove the family carriage with four white horses. Catherine, in her illness and hallucinations, obsessively wonders about the black coachman’s grave and whether he was buried with the carriage and horses as she had instructed, by the sea where one might still hear the sounds of hooves and carriage wheels. This passage sets the tone of uncertainty and haunting memory, questioning the final resting place and fate of the coachman and symbolizing the fragile boundary between life, death, and memory.
  • Catherine believes in “two Mr. Spitzers,” referencing a duality or doubling that permeates the narrative. Mr. Spitzer himself is portrayed as a figure caught between realities as possibly the survivor of a tragic loss, burdened by his brother’s death and his own diminished existence. His silence about the black coachman and other mysteries reflects his internal conflict and the blurring of identities, especially between himself and his deceased brother.
  • The narrative delves deeply into Mr. Spitzer’s troubled life: his failed law practice, his haunted memories, and the confusion between himself and his brother. He is pursued by people who mistake him for his dead brother, and he carries the burden of that mistaken identity. His life is marked by a sense of loss, failure, and existential ambiguity, symbolized by repeated motifs such as the playing cards (four aces), the silent music he composes, and his futile attempts to make sense of his past and present.
  • Catherine’s hallucinations and visions serve as a counterpoint to Mr. Spitzer’s silence. She imagines vast, surreal scenes (funeral gondolas, angels, floating faces, and shifting landscapes) reflecting her mental state and the dissolution of clear boundaries between reality and illusion. Her insistence on the black coachman’s significance and her questioning of Mr. Spitzer highlights the themes of memory, loss, and the search for meaning in chaos.
  • The idea of multiple Mr. Spitzers (four in total) and the tragic fate of one brother killing himself to erase the other introduces a metaphysical layer about identity, fate, and the cosmic balance between opposites (life and death, presence and absence, order and chaos). The chapter explores the instability of self and the universe, where even laws (human and divine) seem uncertain or contested.
  • Throughout the chapter, both Catherine and Mr. Spitzer grapple with what is real and what is illusion. Catherine challenges Mr. Spitzer on his stories of travel, on the whereabouts of the black coachman, and on the nature of the world around them, pointing out contradictions and impossibilities, suggesting that much of what is accepted as real is mutable and uncertain. Mr. Spitzer’s evasiveness and Catherine’s accusations of his lying deepen this uncertainty.
  • The description of the brother’s funeral, with its symbolic white roses and horse racing imagery, stands out as a poignant moment that crystallizes the theme of mourning and the loneliness of the surviving Mr. Spitzer. The image of the corpse as the only mourner is a powerful metaphor for isolation and the burden of memory.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s retreat into composing “silent music” “music not heard by living ears but meant for the dead symbolizes his withdrawal from the world and the limits of communication between the living and the dead, between reality and dream. This motif ties into the overarching theme of failed communication and the ineffability of certain experiences.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Ailing and often delirious, she is obsessed with locating the black coachman and understanding the fate of her family’s legacy.
  • She experiences visions and hallucinations, blurring the line between reality and fantasy.
  • She is deeply distrustful of Mr. Spitzer and concerned that her last wishes have been ignored or betrayed.

Mr. Spitzer (Joachim and Peron) · Peron Spitzer

Joachim Spitzer

  • Joachim Spitzer is depicted as one of two Mr. Spitzers (twins or doubles) each reflecting and haunting the other. The chapter explores the idea that there were "four Mr. Spitzers," due to reflections and mirrored images, and that the boundaries between them blur, creating a complicated identity crisis.
  • This duality extends to the notion that one Mr. Spitzer is "vacant and slow and smiling," while the other had died by suicide, attempting to "kill the Mr. Spitzer who was the pale reflection in his own heart."
  • The surviving Spitzer is burdened by his brother’s shadow, the "dark counterpart running through all his nights and days," which disrupts his peace and confounds his existence.
  • Joachim is portrayed as a man who has not achieved conventional success.
  • He is described as a "failure," living a "retired, unassuming life" in the shadow of his brother’s more colorful and gregarious personality.
  • Despite his literal-mindedness and conservative habits, he is haunted by self-doubt and confusion, often unsure of his own actions and memories.
  • Instances such as finding his brother’s belongings in his coat pockets, or the mysterious "second cup of coffee" he supposedly drank but cannot explain, illustrate his fragmented sense of self and reality.
  • Joachim’s relationship with Vera’s mother is complex. He is her lawyer, executor, and companion in her illness, yet she doubts his trustworthiness and resents his evasiveness and silence.
  • Catherine’s obsession with the black coachman (a symbolic figure representing continuity, memory, and conscience) serves as a foil to Joachim’s own failures and ambiguities.
  • She accuses him of neglecting or betraying the black coachman and the family’s legacy, suggesting that he may have "cheated the black coachman out of his employment and inheritance" and failed to honor her dying wishes.
  • Joachim’s inability or unwillingness to answer her questions about the black coachman and other matters deepens the tension and highlights his evasive nature.
  • Joachim is a man of silence and restraint, in contrast to his brother’s vibrant life.
  • He has ceased composing "oral music" and instead writes "silent music, a dirge for a dead clam," symbolizing his withdrawal from active life and communication.
  • This self-imposed silence and his "utter self-forgetfulness and selflessness" suggest a man resigned to obscurity and loss, attempting to protect himself and others from the chaos that surrounds him.
  • His life is overshadowed by the death of his brother, an event that has left him "hopelessly benumbed" and struggling to keep up with time and reality.
  • He is pursued by people who mistake him for his deceased brother, and he attempts to shield his brother’s memory, sometimes maintaining the illusion that the brother still lives.
  • This haunting presence causes him distress but also a certain pride in having "preferred the last footstep, the last doorway," indicating a preference for quiet endurance over dramatic exit.
  • Joachim is enveloped in mystery and ambiguity. His actions and whereabouts are uncertain; he is sometimes imagined wearing the black coachman’s livery, sometimes unable to explain trivial facts like train journeys.
  • His existence blurs the line between the living and the dead, the real and the illusionary.
  • He is a man "who could not know himself" and whose life is marked by "minor but palpable discrepancies" and "things which did not add up".
  • Joachim’s character is embedded in a cosmic framework where ordinary human concerns intersect with metaphysical questions.
  • He reflects on "the music of the spheres," "the silent music," and the "lawless image of the dream," suggesting a man grappling with the ultimate nature of reality and existence.
  • His legal work, particularly the "case of Spitzer versus Spitzer," symbolizes his internal conflict and the unresolved tensions of his identity.
  • Joachim shows a degree of faithfulness and compassion, particularly toward Catherine and Vera.
  • He visits Catherine regularly, tries to please her, and protects her interests "to the best of his present legal ability." However, his "slumberous inertia" and evasiveness frustrate her, revealing a gap between his intentions and her expectations.
  • Joachim Spitzer’s life is inextricably linked to the death of his brother Peron. The brother’s suicide or accidental death seems to have precipitated a crisis in Joachim’s identity and existence.
  • He is described as having taken up his brother’s mantle in some respects: wearing his brother’s cufflinks, carrying his cane, and even being mistaken for him by acquaintances. Yet he is also deeply burdened by the consequences, trying to protect his brother’s reputation while simultaneously being haunted by his brother’s unresolved, chaotic life.
  • This complicated relationship fuels Joachim’s feelings of inadequacy and fuels his tendency toward silence and withdrawal.
  • Clam-digger is the manservant of Mr. Spitzer.

The Black Coachman

  • A symbolic and somewhat mythical figure associated with the family’s carriage and horses.
  • Represents continuity, memory, and the link between life and death.
  • Catherine’s wish was for the black coachman to be buried with the carriage and horses so that she might continue to “go driving” even after death.

  • Catherine has also defined the Black Coachman as her conscience.

Chapter 20

Summary

In full dawn Vera studies the sleeping woman, thinking about God, about hair, and about what the night revealed. She makes her decision: she will act as though she never saw. She will iron the shirts more eagerly, learn the genealogies and ancient measures, and keep the secret. She will protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of herself. The chapter ends in a litany of biblical images for God.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Light and Darkness · The Search for Meaning

Symbols: Angels, Devils, and Myth · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Genesis · Judaism · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid depiction of dawn which paradoxically serves as both illumination and a force that has "already killed the heart of Miss MacIntosh" before her actual death. The light reveals wounds and deprivations that "would not heal with time," suggesting an exposure of deep, irrevocable suffering and loss.
  • A striking passage focuses on the physical absence of hair on Miss MacIntosh's head which symbolically represents a loss of feminine identity, vitality, and perhaps a history of mourning or trauma. Vera reflects on the significance of hair as beauty or terror and wonders about the circumstances of her hair loss, whether gradual or sudden, linking it to emotional or existential devastation.
  • Vera experiences a powerful tension between the recognition of Miss MacIntosh’s vulnerable, altered state and a desire to revert to ignorance for the sake of "common sense" and routine. There is a determined resolve to "go on as if I had never seen her," to protect her from the knowledge of herself, and to maintain the illusion of normalcy despite the stark reality of her condition.
  • The passage detailing Vera’s imagined daily routines contrasts sharply with the internal, almost mystical knowledge of Miss MacIntosh’s profound deprivation. Vera contemplates learning ancient measures, weights, and biblical geography, suggesting a search for meaning or order amid chaos and personal loss.
  • Toward the end, Vera muses deeply about mortality, identity, and divinity. The baldness and missing breast become metaphors for the exposed realities of life and death, while Vera questions the nature of God with rich biblical imagery and reflecting on God's multifaceted definitions as friend, refuge, crown, and shadow. This passage underscores the theme of confronting harsh truths and the limits of human understanding.
  • The final lines evoke a solemn recognition of the "image of life failing before his eyes," highlighting Vera’s acute awareness of mortality and the profound emotional weight of witnessing the decline of a once vibrant individual.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • A figure of strength and common sense, yet marked by profound physical and existential deprivation.
  • Described as “hale and hearty, a red-headed nursemaid” in the past, yet now revealed in a state of vulnerability and loss.
  • Her condition is a mystery to Vera, who struggles to reconcile her external robustness with the internal and physical ravages revealed by the light.
  • She embodies the tension between resilience and suffering, denial and revelation.

Vera Cartwheel

  • Exhibits complex emotions: pity, love, denial, and a protective instinct toward Miss MacIntosh.
  • Is philosophical and reflective, wrestling with large existential questions prompted by Miss MacIntosh’s condition.
  • Exhibits a desire to maintain normalcy and routine to shield both himself and Miss MacIntosh from harsh truths.

Research: Themes

Light as a Revealing and Destructive Force

See: Light and Darkness

  • Dawn and light symbolize both revelation and destruction. Vera suggests that light has “already killed the heart of Miss MacIntosh” before her physical death, exposing wounds that cannot heal and deprivations that are eternal.
  • The light strips away illusions, revealing the “fearful forehead” and the “bald and naked, cloudless summit” of Miss MacIntosh’s head, symbolizing a harsh unveiling of truth and vulnerability.
  • There’s also a paradoxical beauty in the light, described as “diamond dawn” and “celestial aureole,” which offers hope for redemption and healing, yet simultaneously exposes harsh realities.

Loss and Absence

See: Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Miss MacIntosh’s baldness is a potent symbol of loss: loss of hair as a “crowning glory,” loss of feminine nature, and the missing breast as a “door knob,” a stark reminder of what is absent.
  • Vera questions the cause and timing of this loss: was it gradual or sudden? Was it caused by heartbreak, mourning, or some unknowable trauma?.
  • This absence is not just physical but metaphysical, representing the stripping away of identity and vitality.

Mortality and the Inevitability of Decay

See: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin

  • Vera reflects on mortality, decay, and the “wounds in our sides” that light will bind up to prevent death like “Saul or Solomon or Sennacherib”.
  • There is a tension between the desire to protect Miss MacIntosh from the knowledge of her own condition and the inevitability of facing harsh truths.
  • The novel grapples with the idea that despite external appearances or the passage of time, some wounds and losses are timeless and unhealable.

Identity and Self-Perception

See: Identity and the Self

  • Miss MacIntosh’s self-awareness and common sense shield her from the deeper, visionary truths Vera perceives; she is “content with things just as they were” and would deny or not suspect the “empty vision” beyond the commonplace.
  • Vera’s internal conflict involves a desire to pretend normalcy to protect both Miss MacIntosh and herself from confronting the full reality of her condition.
  • There is also a complex emotional dynamic, where Vera simultaneously sees her as an “obstacle” to her happiness and as someone deeply significant, a secret lover or cause of his “vain pursuits”.

Spiritual and Existential Questions

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · The Search for Meaning

  • The narrative moves toward existential and spiritual reflection, pondering God’s nature, the problem of creation, and the place of suffering and imperfection in the divine order.
  • Vera likens the “baldness” and loss to a profound experience, possibly greater than mere mortal wisdom or aging, invoking biblical and mythological imagery.
  • The chapter closes with a meditation on life failing before one’s eyes and the idea of seeing something no one “should see and live to relate”.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Hair and Baldness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Hair symbolizes beauty, identity, and vitality; baldness represents loss, vulnerability, and exposure.
  • Absence of hair is described as a “barren, impoverished landscape without flower or bush or hedge”.

Light and Dawn

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Dawn is both “diamond” and “many-prismed,” a metaphor for clarity, revelation, but also a harsh revealer of truth.
  • The “Aurora Borealis” in her sparsely furnished bedroom suggests a surreal, otherworldly illumination, the “first experience of light” upon uncreated things.

Missing Breast

  • The missing breast is a stark physical symbol of loss and incompleteness, described as “like a door knob,” emphasizing its unnatural absence.

Biblical and Mythological References

See: Angels, Devils, and Myth

  • References to biblical figures (Saul, Solomon, Sennacherib) and ancient measurements, calendars, and places (Nisan, Jyar, Wady Feiran, Egypt to Canaan) ground the narrative in a spiritual and temporal history.
  • Quotes and allusions to Ovid and Greek perspectives on beauty and hair enhance the classical depth of the novel.

This fits the chapter's broader theme of transition from darkness and despair to illumination and acceptance, where the light is not only physical but also symbolic of understanding, compassion, and the end of suffering. The narrator, Vera, reflects on the fragility and pain of life, and here the phrase emphasizes a hopeful promise that wounds (whether physical, emotional, or spiritual) will be soothed and healed in time

Chapter 3

← Chapter 2 · Home · Chapter 4 →

Summary

After Catherine took to her bed, Mr. Spitzer hired Miss Georgia MacIntosh of What Cheer, Iowa, to raise Vera. Vera paints her in full: marcelled red hair, a broken nose, a black umbrella, a tight corset, sensible shoes, long walks along the shore in any weather, strict schedules, and a deep suspicion of anything imaginary. She is everything Catherine is not, the practical Middle West in one person. Vera recalls how Miss MacIntosh dealt with an Australian bushman, a head-hunter who visited Catherine’s bedside and was obsessed with the nursemaid’s head, and she mentions Miss MacIntosh’s brother, a missionary bishop lost among the islands. Then Vera returns to the loss. Miss MacIntosh’s clothes were found on the beach and her purse held two pennies. Her body was never found, and Vera blames herself. Mr. Spitzer always insists that she was a good and dependable woman who never wavered.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Catherine Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Light and Darkness · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Order, Chaos, and Discipline · Society, Class, and Race

Symbols: Birds · Cards, Games, and Chance · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fireflies · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella · Twins and Doubles

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Freud and Jung · Heraclitus and Flux · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: American Religious Movements · American Writers · Ancient Egypt · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Milton · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War · The History of Opium

Key passages

From the research

  • Miss MacIntosh is described as a “truer than the North star” guide to the bewildered child, Vera, someone who is steadfast in her moral principles and practical in her approach to life. She rejects fantasies, illusions, and the “phantoms thickening in the air” around others, especially Vera’s mother, Catherine’s hallucinatory environment. Her quick temper and no-nonsense attitude symbolize a force that dispels the fanciful and unreal.
  • The detailed imagery of Miss MacIntosh’s red hair shining like fire or sparks, her robust health sustained by sunlight and physical exercise, and her preference for outdoor life even in inclement weather emphasize her grounded, vigorous nature. She uses physical activity and connection with natural elements to keep herself strong and unclouded by fantasy or despair. This connection also reflects her philosophy that life is about facing realities, not escaping them.
  • Miss MacIntosh disdains fanciful dreams, luxury, and illusions such as the “golden apples” or “pearls” that Catherine dreams of. She insists on simplicity, honesty, and the acceptance of life’s hardships: “Life was made up, in short, of the necessary deprivations.” She believes in fulfilling one’s duties, avoiding self-pity, and not chasing impossible ideals. Her practical mindset is embodied in her tasks like mending clothes, preparing meals, and maintaining order.
  • Miss MacIntosh holds a stark, unromantic view of death as a final, dreamless sleep without illusions of heaven or afterlife grandeur. She rejects “six-winged seraphim” and “golden towers” as fanciful nonsense, insisting that if there is a heaven, it should be plain and unfurnished. This reflects her consistent rejection of fantasy and her focus on the tangible realities of mortal life.
  • Miss MacIntosh is brusque, solitary, and does not encourage intimacy or pity. Her past is largely unknown, and she has no friends, embodying a figure who compensates for others’ losses in a practical way. She has little patience for mental or emotional sorrows that lack physical cause, emphasizing courage in the face of actual trials. Her interactions with the Australian head-hunter highlight her disdain for affectation and false pretenses.
  • The Australian head-hunter serves as a foil to Miss MacIntosh’s grounded realism. She despises his semi-civilized, erratic behavior, his ambitions, and his inappropriate intimacy, seeing him as a symbol of confused and corrupt aspirations that contrast with her straightforward, honest life. Her reactions to him underscore her rejection of fantasy, deceit, and social pretense.
  • The chapter ends with the mystery of Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance, leaving behind her clothes and personal effects on the beach as if she had walked into the sea. Mr. Spitzer’s reflections underscore her enigmatic presence and the lasting impact she had on those around her. Despite her ordinariness, she was a “pearl of light” in a world of shadows and illusions, and her absence leaves an unresolved question about her fate.
  • Miss MacIntosh believes in honest work, self-discipline, and the acceptance of life’s hardships. She foresees a necessary revolution to overthrow the “powers of darkness” and strip away illusions and luxury. Her philosophy is one of immediate action and responsibility to others, emphasizing that life is short and should not be wasted in “the vain expectation of that which might never happen” or on “graven images.” This reflects a deep existential and moral seriousness.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The chapter opens with adults “like the shadows of grotesque puppets dancing on a wall,” and “The puppeteer they dreamed of did not exist although he moved the strings.” How does this image prepare for a nursemaid who believes only in what she can see?
  • Miss MacIntosh “could endure nothing that took its time,” and her days are filled with mending, hammering, sweeping, and running. What is she outrunning?
  • She and Vera “swept our footprints away from the sands before the waters crept over” them. Why might someone so committed to the present want to leave no trace?
  • Miss MacIntosh makes a lamp of fireflies when they are lost in the dark, “carrying the lamp up high like a lighthouse.” How does this moment complicate her refusal of anything fanciful?

Characters

  • Miss MacIntosh is “so usual” that her ordinariness becomes strange in Catherine’s house. Yet she has a broken nose, a receding brow, a past no one knows, and a cheek that throbs when her hand is touched. What clues does the chapter plant that she is not what she seems?
  • Mr. Spitzer remembers hiring “the shawled figure” he took for a brunette, whose “eyebrows were dark and beetling cliffs.” Why might the novel let him misremember the one person he chose so quickly?
  • The head-hunter tells Miss MacIntosh that she “had a greater imagination than anyone who lived.” Why does this compliment offend her more than any insult?
  • Miss MacIntosh preaches common sense, but her own sayings are full of contradictions: there is no heaven, yet God is a harness-maker; the sins committed are worse than those of omission, yet God has forgotten things. How does she hold her faith together?

Connections

  • In Chapter 2 Catherine lives only in dreams. In Chapter 3 Miss MacIntosh insists “If she dreamed, she would dream that she was running.” What does Vera inherit from each of these two mothers?
  • Miss MacIntosh believes in revolution, “the whole bird,” not the left wing or the right. How do her politics grow out of her years in “the dregs of the city”?
  • The chapter ends with clothes on the beach, two pennies under a rock, and a body never found. How does this loss reshape everything Vera has said about Miss MacIntosh up to that point? See The Search for Life, for Love, for Truth That Does Not Fail.

Reflection

  • “Who but I had killed her?” Vera asks. Why do children so often blame themselves for the losses of the adults around them?
  • Miss MacIntosh says “we knew now all we would ever know . . . of misery or happiness.” Is living wholly in the present a kind of courage, a kind of hiding, or both?

Research: Characters

Miss (Georgia) MacIntosh

  • A nursemaid who embodies practicality, common sense, and moral certainty.
  • Described physically with “marcelled red hair,” “greyish, greenish eyes,” and a robust constitution.
  • She is a symbol of stability, reality, and groundedness amidst chaos and confusion.
  • Rejects illusions, fantasies, and idle dreams; values labor, discipline, and the present moment.
  • Wears simple, durable clothing; disdains luxury and extravagance.
  • Has a brusque, rough demeanor, often compared to an old sailor.
  • She is industrious, always busy, and advocates physical exercise and self-forgetfulness.
  • Holds a strict moral code, emphasizing honesty, self-control, and acceptance of life’s hardships.
  • Originates from What Cheer, Iowa, a simple town, and contrasts sharply with the opulent, dreamlike environment of the household.
  • Maintains distance from others, avoids intimacy, and does not indulge in self-pity.
  • Ultimately disappears under mysterious circumstances, leaving behind only her clothes and belongings on the beach.
  • Mentions her brother, who went out as a missionary bishop to the Easter Islands and never returned.

Vera Cartwheel

  • A child who has escaped from her mother’s “opium paradise.”
  • Looks up to Miss MacIntosh as a guide and protector.
  • Observes and reflects on the strange atmosphere and characters around her.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Employer who hired Miss MacIntosh without much inquiry.
  • Holds a fondness and respect for her practical nature.
  • Believes Miss MacIntosh might have returned to the city’s “dregs” after disappearance.
  • Is uncertain about her fate but respects her memory and legacy.

The Head-Hunter (Australian Bushman)

  • An unwelcome visitor who comes each afternoon in a black-curtained cab to sit at Catherine’s bedside.
  • Seen by Miss MacIntosh as deceitful, semi-civilized, and culturally alien.
  • His presence and behavior clash sharply with Miss MacIntosh’s values.
  • Fascinated by Miss MacIntosh’s head, which he wants to sculpt, but she rejects his advances.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • Living in a surreal, opium-induced environment with grand illusions and fantasies.
  • Contrasted with Miss MacIntosh’s grounded reality.

Research: Themes

Reality vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh represents the harsh reality of life, while Catherine’s world is filled with dreams, illusions, and hallucinations.
  • The nursemaid’s disdain for luxury, fantasy, and self-pity underscores the value of facing life’s truths directly.

Discipline, Labor, and Practicality

See: Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Life is portrayed as a testing ground requiring discipline, hard work, and acceptance of necessary deprivations.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s emphasis on practical tasks (mending clothes, building fires) and physical exercise reflect this ethos.

Mortality and Transience

See: Death and Mortality

  • Frequent imagery of time running low, life’s brevity, and the inevitability of death.
  • The nursemaid’s disappearance and the uncertainty surrounding her fate emphasize the fragile nature of existence.

Isolation and Independence

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh is a solitary figure who keeps to herself, avoids intimacy, and values self-reliance.
  • Her rejection of social pretenses and false hopes highlights her independence.

Nature and the Elements

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The natural world (sea, wind, light, sand) is a constant presence and source of strength for Miss MacIntosh.
  • She prefers exposure to natural elements over sheltered luxury or confinement.

Social Order and Class

See: Society, Class, and Race · Order, Chaos, and Discipline

  • Miss MacIntosh rejects aristocratic airs and illusions of grandeur.
  • She advocates for the dignity of simple people and honest labor.

Faith and Doubt

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • While Miss MacIntosh acknowledges God, she does not believe in extravagant religious fantasies or promises of an afterlife.
  • She sees life itself as a sufficient test and believes in accepting one’s lot without illusions.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Black Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • Miss MacIntosh’s shield and sword against the elements and the unknown.
  • Represents her protection from illusions and external threats.

Fireflies in a Jar

See: Fireflies

  • Symbolize hope and guidance in darkness.
  • The moment when Miss MacIntosh uses them as a lamp suggests her role as a beacon of reason amid confusion.

Sea and Surf

See: The Sea and Water

  • Represent the uncontrollable forces of nature and time.
  • The beach is the boundary between worlds and the place where Miss MacIntosh’s disappearance occurs.

Two Pennies

See: Cards, Games, and Chance · Twins and Doubles

  • Found in her purse, symbolizes her humility and the little she possessed.
  • Also a poignant reminder of her mortality and disappearance.

Corset

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Represents discipline and the necessary constraints of life.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s tight corset is a physical embodiment of her moral and mental self-control.

Research: Resources

  • “like the shadows of grotesque puppets dancing on a wall”: In the allegory of the cave in Plato’s Republic, prisoners chained in the dark see only shadows thrown on a wall by figures carried past a fire, like a puppet show, and take the shadows for the whole of reality. Vera’s adults are the shadows, and “The puppeteer they dreamed of did not exist although he moved the strings.” See Plato and Platonism.
  • “Miss MacIntosh, my darling, truer than the North star”: Polaris, the North Star, stays nearly fixed above the North Pole while the other stars wheel around it, so sailors steered by it. Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar boasts, “I am constant as the northern star.” In Chapter 1 she was “the dead steersman.” See Moon and Stars.
  • “not even a game of chess as chess was the game of kings”: Chess has long been called “the royal game” and “the game of kings.” Its pieces are a feudal court, with the king who must be protected at all costs and the pawns who are sacrificed, which is why Miss MacIntosh finds the game undemocratic.
  • “her marcelled red hair fitting close like a helmet”: Marcelled hair is set in deep, regular waves with heated tongs, a method introduced by the Paris hairdresser Marcel Grateau in 1872 and most fashionable in the 1920s. See Marcelled hair (Ch 3).
  • “imaginary nightingales or turrets of ivory”: The Song of Solomon says, “Thy neck is as a tower of ivory” (7:4), and “Tower of Ivory” became a title of the Virgin Mary. By the nineteenth century an ivory tower meant a place of dreamy retreat from the world, which Miss MacIntosh will not allow. The nightingale is the bird of the Romantic poets, as in Keats’s “Ode to a Nightingale.”
  • “flower-crowned satyrs and moon-eyed minotaurs”: A satyr is a male nature spirit of Greek myth with the ears and tail of a horse, a follower of Dionysus given to wine, music, and dancing. Later Roman art gave satyrs the legs of goats, like Pan.
  • “giant periwinkle shells filled with mystic roarings”: The roar heard when a shell is held to the ear is not the sea but the sounds of the room around it, caught and amplified as they echo inside the shell’s spiral.
  • The problem with God and his attributes of omniscience (God’s complete and perfect knowledge, knowing everything past, present, and future), omnipotence (God’s unlimited power and ability to do anything), omnipresence (God is present everywhere at all times, not limited by space or time), and also added by some omnibenevolence (God has perfect or unlimited goodness) are that they create fallacies: god cannot be omnibenevolent and omnipotent in a universe in which evil exists (I.e. his creation suffers). Can god not prevent evil? Then he is not omnipotent. Does he not want to prevent evil? Then he is not omnibenevolent. If god can prevent evil, and god wants to prevent evil, then evil would not exist. Can god defy the laws of physics (create a rock so heavy even he can’t lift it? destroy himself? create a square circle? make himself not omnipotent?) If god is omniscient, then he has always known every single choice every human has ever and will ever make. Therefore, from his perspective, free will is impossible because there was only ever one choice any person who has ever or will ever exist could make. Any argument made from free will with an omniscient god is logically unsound. Any god that forces his followers to adopt illogical arguments to defend his existence in a universe very clearly explicable by logic is a malicious god, not a benevolent god.
  • “God had been her harness-maker, that He had hung her harness with tinkling bells so that it might always be known where she was”: The robe of the Hebrew high priest was hung at its hem with golden bells and pomegranates, “and his sound shall be heard when he goeth in unto the holy place” (Exodus 28:33-35). Miss MacIntosh’s bells ring on through the chapter: “her bells ringing so that I might know, through fog and mist and darkness, where she was.”
  • “labor was man’s lot upon this earth”: The Protestant work ethic, the Calvinist Work Ethic, or the Puritan Work Ethic is a work ethic concept in theology, sociology, economics and history that emphasizes that hard work, discipline, and frugality are a result of a person’s subscription to the values espoused by the Protestant faith, particularly Calvinism. The phrase was coined by the sociologist Max Weber in his book The Protestant Ethic and the Spirit of Capitalism (1904 to 1905). Weber asserted that Protestant ethics and values along with the Calvinist doctrine of asceticism and predestination gave birth to capitalism. See The Protestant Work Ethic (Ch 3) and The Protestant Ethic.
  • “If at night I heard the wings of time like angelic wings roaring faster and faster”: Andrew Marvell’s “To His Coy Mistress” says, “But at my back I always hear / Time’s wingèd chariot hurrying near.”
  • “the sleep of the innocent should be deep and dreamless”: Macbeth, after murdering the sleeping king, thinks he hears a voice cry that he has murdered sleep, “the innocent sleep, / Sleep that knits up the ravell’d sleave of care.” See Shakespeare.
  • “almost Tyrian purple in certain lights”: Tyrian purple is a reddish-purple dye made from the glands of murex sea snails, first in the Phoenician city of Tyre. Thousands of snails were needed for a single garment, so the color was worth more than gold, and in Rome it was reserved for emperors.
  • “knocking down ninepins and the old kingpin who should be leveled like the old king of Bulgaria”: Ninepins, the old form of bowling, is the game the ghostly crew plays in the mountains in Washington Irving’s “Rip Van Winkle.” The kingpin stands at the center. Bulgaria’s kings fell one by one: Tsar Ferdinand abdicated after defeat in the First World War in 1918, his son Boris III died suddenly in 1943, and in 1946 the monarchy was abolished and the boy king Simeon II sent into exile.
  • “no hawk’s-wing sea shell with a broken wing or broken great keyhole limpet or star sea shell dragging its broken foot”: Limpets are sea snails with simple cone-shaped shells that cling to rocks. The keyhole limpet has a small opening at the top of its shell, and the hawk-wing conch and star shells are other sea snails of warm waters. Miss MacIntosh “could endure nothing that took its time.”
  • “not venturing to do what the wisest man had failed to do”: When the oracle at Delphi said that no one was wiser than Socrates, Socrates concluded that his only wisdom was knowing that he knew nothing (Plato, Apology). The wisest man in the Bible, Solomon, ends Ecclesiastes with the same humility: “of making many books there is no end.”
  • “I should make a useful contribution to human society, which was composed of simple people”: The Greek word aretē means excellence or virtue, the fulfillment of something’s purpose, and for people the act of living up to one’s full potential. For Miss MacIntosh excellence means usefulness: a person lives up to her potential by serving “simple people.”
  • Miss MacIntosh’s philosophy could be compared to the Amish, Quakers, or Shakers. The Amish have a significant population in the Middle West and are known for simple living, plain dress, and reluctance to adopt many conveniences of modern technology. They educate their children up to the eighth grade and then they are apprenticed to work.
  • “these unusual luxuries which tempted no honest face”: The Theory of the Leisure Class (1899) is a treatise on economics and a detailed, social critique of conspicuous consumption. Its author, Thorstein Veblen, coined the phrase “conspicuous consumption” for the spending of money on and acquiring of luxury goods and services to publicly display economic power in order to attain or maintain social status.
  • “as if she were trying to placate it”: An old story told by the chronicler Henry of Huntingdon has King Canute set his throne on the shore and command the tide to stop, to show his flattering courtiers that even a king cannot rule the sea.
  • “rolling pea-souper”: A pea-souper was a thick, yellowish fog, named for its likeness to pea soup, especially the coal-smoke fogs of London. See Fog and Mist.
  • “wearing her salt-streaked mackintosh of almost faded plaids”: The mackintosh, the rubberized raincoat, is named for the Scottish chemist Charles Macintosh, who patented his waterproofing process in 1823, and Miss MacIntosh wears her name. See Charles MacIntosh (Ch 3).
  • “useful work for the benefit of others and strenuous physical exercise and self-forgetfulness prolonged one’s useful life”: In his speech “The Strenuous Life,” given in Chicago on April 10, 1899, Theodore Roosevelt said, “I wish to preach, not the doctrine of ignoble ease, but the doctrine of the strenuous life.” He advocated for a life of effort, hardship, and struggle over ease and idleness, arguing that it was essential for both individual character and national greatness. He believed that facing challenges, whether physical or moral, was the only way to achieve true success and national power in the coming century. The speech also reflected his views on American expansionism and the “strenuous” duty of the nation to take an active role in the world. Miss MacIntosh warns against “slothful ease.”
  • “on this old terra firma which was certainly no cloud”: Terra firma is Latin for “firm land,” dry ground as opposed to the sea.
  • “there was not much room for the individual, for those who should lift up their heads”: A Japanese proverb says, “the nail that sticks out shall get hammered down.”
  • “the mischief caused by those who did not work and yet were restless”: The saying that the devil finds work for idle hands is often thought to be biblical, but it comes from Isaac Watts’s hymn for children “Against Idleness and Mischief” (1715): “For Satan finds some mischief still / For idle hands to do.” Proverbs 16:27 has a similar thought: “An ungodly man diggeth up evil.”
  • “no time for the luxury of idle tears”: The phrase recalls Tennyson’s song from The Princess (1847): “Tears, idle tears, I know not what they mean, / Tears from the depth of some divine despair.”
  • “the dark prince charming who should carry me away and rescue me from this dark tower”: The dark prince is a symbolic figure representing an imaginary or idealized rescuer, a figure of hope and escape for Vera.
  • “this dark tower”: The phrase recalls Robert Browning’s “Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came” (1855), whose title comes from a line in King Lear. In Chapter 30 Catherine’s search for her lost husband ends where “Childe Roland had blown his horn before a dark tower.” See Childe Roland to the Dark Tower Came.
  • “Like the princess, I would let down my hair, and he should climb it as if it were a rope”: The image is Rapunzel’s, from the Grimm brothers’ tale of 1812: “Rapunzel, Rapunzel, let down your hair.” The Grimms took the story from Charlotte-Rose de La Force’s French tale “Persinette” (1698). Many scholars have interpreted “Maiden in the Tower” stories, which Rapunzel is a part of, as a metaphor for the protection of young women from premarital relationships by overzealous guardians. Scholars have drawn comparisons of the confinement of Rapunzel in her tower to that of a convent, where women’s lives were highly controlled and they lived in exclusion from outsiders. Scholars have also noted the strong theme of love conquering all in the story, as the lovers are united after years of searching in all versions after Persinette and are ultimately happily reunited as a family. The “Maiden in the Tower” archetype has drawn comparisons to a possible lost matriarchal myth connected to the sacred marriage between the prince and the maiden and the rivalry between the maiden, representing life and spring, and the crone, representing death and winter. See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “We should not nurture our grief at the breast of sorrow”: Miss MacIntosh allows no time for grief. Elisabeth Kübler-Ross later described five stages of grief in On Death and Dying (1969): denial, anger, bargaining, depression, and acceptance. See Grief, Loss, and Mourning.
  • “God, moving in His mysterious ways”: “God Moves in a Mysterious Way” is a Christian hymn written in 1773 by the English poet William Cowper, first titled “Light Shining out of Darkness.” The poem is the likely source for the phrase “God moves in mysterious ways,” although the first line of the poem actually runs “God moves in a mysterious way.” Cowper wrote it at Olney, and it is often said to have been his last hymn, written as he felt a period of deep depression coming on.
  • “Apples fell downward, not upward”: The best-known falling apple is Isaac Newton’s. Newton told his friend William Stukeley that the fall of an apple in his mother’s orchard at Woolsthorpe set him thinking about gravity, the force that keeps the moon in its orbit. Miss MacIntosh’s law of gravity is moral as well as physical: “All that fell upward were bound to fall downward.”
  • “not even should there be those golden apples of which my mother dreamed”: Catherine dreamed of the golden apples of the Hesperides in Chapter 2. The golden apple serves as a metaphor for the tension between illusion and reality, dreams and practicality, with Miss MacIntosh advocating for reality and practicality.
  • “the macintosh apple and the crab apple and the pippin and the russet”: The McIntosh apple grew from a seedling that John McIntosh found on his farm in Ontario in 1811. Pippins and russets are old English apple varieties; a russet has rough, brownish skin. The nursemaid named MacIntosh lists her own apple first.
  • “the path of the brave was narrow and girt about by thorns, and it was lonely, there being great solitude, for man was seldom good”: The passage turns on Matthew 7:13-14: “wide is the gate, and broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction, and many there be which go in thereat: Because strait is the gate, and narrow is the way, which leadeth unto life, and few there be that find it.”
  • “of fleshly pleasures and fleshpots of luxury, of dancing girls and headless men”: The fleshpots come from Exodus 16:3, where the Israelites in the wilderness long for Egypt, “when we sat by the flesh pots, and when we did eat bread to the full.” The dancing girl and the headless man recall Salome and John the Baptist from Chapter 2.
  • “none finding a celestial city”: The Celestial City is the goal of the pilgrim Christian in Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress, the heavenly Jerusalem at the end of his road. Miss MacIntosh’s travelers on the path of virtue never reach it.
  • “chasing a will-o’-the-wisp, a false light”: The will-o’-the-wisp, or ignis fatuus, “foolish fire,” is a faint light seen at night over marshes, probably caused by burning marsh gas. In folklore it lures travelers off the path and into the bog.
  • “no slug with its shell rudimentary and often buried in the mantle or wanting entirely”: The phrase reads like an entry from an old natural history or dictionary, which defined slugs as mollusks whose shell is small and hidden in the mantle or wanting altogether. Miss MacIntosh wants no child without a shell to carry.
