  • “my house would be well kept, and I should make my husband happy”: There has been important feminist criticism of marriage including: the effect that marriage has on individual liberty, equality between the sexes, the relation between marriage and violence, philosophical questions about how much control can a government have over its population, the amount of control a person has over another, the financial risk when measured against divorce/separation, and the questioning of the necessity to have a relationship sanctioned by government or religious authorities. There is also the emotional labor and management of the house that has been and is the unpaid work of mostly women.
  • “the numbers of tons of coal mined by coal-miners in distant mines”: Coal mining labor history in the United States is marked by dangerous work, exploitation, and the struggle for workers’ rights, driven by waves of immigration, the Civil War, and industrialization. Early laborers were diverse, including enslaved and free African Americans, and later, large numbers of immigrants from Great Britain, Ireland, and Eastern and Southern Europe were drawn to the industry by recruiters. The United Mine Workers of America (UMWA) was founded in 1890 to fight for better wages, safer conditions, and benefits, leading to significant labor conflicts and hard-won reforms like the eight-hour workday and pensions. The coal industry was marked by a series of violent conflicts and massacres, often stemming from labor disputes between striking workers (many of whom were immigrants) and mine owners who hired private security forces or leveraged local law enforcement to suppress union organizing efforts.
    • Lattimer Massacre (September 10, 1897): In Lattimer, Pennsylvania, a sheriff’s posse opened fire on a march of unarmed striking immigrant anthracite miners, mostly of Polish, Slovak, Lithuanian, and German descent. At least 19 miners were killed, and many more were wounded. The sheriff and his deputies were later tried but acquitted.
    • Battle of Virden (October 12, 1898): In Virden, Illinois, a gun battle erupted when the Chicago-Virden Coal Company attempted to bring in African-American strikebreakers with armed guards. Eight striking miners and at least four guards were killed.
    • Ludlow Massacre (April 20, 1914): During a major strike in Colorado, the Colorado National Guard and guards from the Colorado Fuel & Iron Company attacked a tent colony of 1,200 striking miners and their families. The assault resulted in the deaths of approximately 21 people, including women and children, many of whom were burned to death when the camp was set on fire.
    • Matewan Massacre (May 19, 1920): A deadly shootout occurred in Matewan, West Virginia, between Baldwin-Felts detective agency guards (hired by mine owners to evict striking workers from company-owned housing) and local residents, including the mayor and police chief, who supported the miners. Ten people died in the clash (seven detectives, two miners, and the mayor).
    • Battle of Blair Mountain (August/September 1921): The culmination of the West Virginia Mine Wars, this was the largest armed insurrection in U.S. history since the Civil War. Thousands of union miners fought against local law enforcement and company-hired forces. Federal troops were eventually sent in by President Harding to quell the uprising, which involved the use of airplanes to drop bombs. Estimates of the dead vary widely.
    • Herrin Massacre (June 21-22, 1922): In Herrin, Illinois, a violent confrontation occurred between union miners and strikebreakers at a strip mine. After a gunfight and a surrender under the promise of safe passage, union miners killed the mine superintendent and 19 strikebreakers and guards, and three union miners also died. The incident is considered one of the most violent labor disputes in U.S. history.
    • Columbine Mine Massacre (November 21, 1927): In Serene, Colorado, striking miners were met with machine-gun fire from the Colorado Rangers and guards from the Rocky Mountain Fuel Company during a strike, resulting in the deaths of six miners.
    These events, part of the broader “Coal Wars” (roughly 1890-1930), were pivotal in the struggle for better wages, safer working conditions, and the right to unionize in the U.S. coal industry.
  • “We dealt with the unjust circumstances under which Negroes were employed”: Miss MacIntosh’s lessons show her concern with social movements, the working class, and inequality, and she is repeatedly described as left-leaning. “Negro” was the standard term of the time. See Society, Class, and Race.
    • Ta-Nehisi Coates’ “The Case for Reparations” is a 2014 essay arguing that the U.S. owes African Americans compensation for centuries of systemic injustices, from slavery and Jim Crow laws to modern discrimination like redlining. The essay uses historical examples and personal accounts, like that of Clyde Ross, to trace how a legacy of stolen labor, land, and wealth created an enduring racial wealth gap. Coates argues that acknowledging and addressing this “moral debt” is necessary for both African Americans and the nation’s spiritual and economic healing.
    • The 1619 Project reframes American history by centering the consequences of slavery and the contributions of Black Americans, arguing that the country’s founding can be understood as beginning with the arrival of enslaved people in 1619. It explores how slavery has shaped modern America, including its economy, healthcare, and music, and challenges traditional narratives of American exceptionalism. The project originated as a New York Times Magazine special issue and has since expanded into a book and podcast series.
  • “the injustices done to the Africans working in diamond mines”: Diamond mining in Africa began in 1867 with the discovery of alluvial diamonds in South Africa, leading to a large-scale rush and the founding of De Beers Consolidated Mines by Cecil Rhodes in 1888. Subsequent discoveries of diamonds in kimberlite pipes enabled the transition from small-scale digging to industrial mining, which eventually consolidated into a monopoly by De Beers. Diamond mining then expanded to other countries, including Namibia, Botswana, Angola, and Sierra Leone, though its history is also marked by exploitation and conflict, such as the issue of “blood diamonds” which were sold to finance civil wars.
  • “We pitied the lighthouse keepers who had no union and no organization”: Lighthouse keepers lived for months at isolated stations, keeping the lamps lit and the lenses clean through every storm. In 1939 the United States Lighthouse Service was merged into the Coast Guard, and most lights were later automated.
  • The history of U.S. labor is a story of evolving unions fighting for worker rights, from the first trade unions in the late 18th century to the formation of national organizations like the National Labor Union and American Federation of Labor. Key events include the Great Railroad Strike of 1877, the Haymarket bombing, the Pullman strike, and the Triangle Shirtwaist factory fire, which led to significant safety reforms. The movement saw a peak in power between the late 19th century and mid-20th century, especially with the passage of protective legislation like the National Labor Relations Act during the New Deal, but has since faced a decline in membership while new organizing efforts continue.
    • 1794: The Federal Society of Journeymen Cordwainers (shoemakers) is formed in Philadelphia, marking the start of sustained trade union organization in the U.S.
    • 1866: The National Labor Union is founded, making the first national call for an 8-hour workday.
    • 1869: The Knights of Labor is established, becoming a major force in organizing skilled and unskilled workers.
    • 1886: The American Federation of Labor (AFL) is formed, focusing on a coalition of craft unions.
    • 1892: The Homestead strike occurs at a Carnegie Steel plant, and the Pullman strike takes place in 1894, highlighting the intense conflicts between labor and big business.
    • 1909: The New York shirtwaist strike, the “Uprising of the 20,000,” highlights the role of women in the labor movement.
    • 1911: The tragic Triangle Shirtwaist factory fire leads to a national outcry and a push for significant workplace safety reforms, inspired by eyewitness accounts and activism.
    • 1914: The Ludlow Massacre is a violent confrontation between coal miners and company guards, leading to further calls for reform.
    • 1920s: The rise of new industries leads to new labor-management challenges.
    • 1932: The Norris-LaGuardia Act is passed, limiting the power of courts to block strikes and other union activities.
    • 1933: The Wagner-Peyser Act creates a nationwide system of public employment offices.
    • 1935: The National Labor Relations Act (Wagner Act) is signed into law, giving workers the right to organize, bargain collectively, and strike.
    • 1937: A sit-down strike against General Motors in Flint, Michigan, results in the company recognizing the United Auto Workers (UAW).
    • Post-WWII: Labor unions begin to see a decline in membership and political influence, though they remain powerful in some sectors.
    • Late 20th Century: Globalization and a changing economy lead to further challenges for organized labor.
    • 2014: The Bureau of Labor Statistics reported that 11.1 percent of U.S. wage and salary workers belonged to unions, down from 20.1 percent in 1983, the first year of comparable figures.
  • “the united brotherhoods of the sleeping car porters”: The Brotherhood of Sleeping Car Porters (BSCP) was founded in 1925 by A. Philip Randolph and other porters to fight for better wages and working conditions against the Pullman Company. After a long and difficult struggle involving company opposition, the Great Depression, and internal community division, the BSCP gained recognition from the Pullman Company in 1937. It became the first African-American labor union to receive a charter from the American Federation of Labor (AFL) and went on to become a vital training ground for civil rights leaders and a significant force in the broader civil rights movement.
  • “the truck-drivers driving their trucks all night long”: The history of U.S. trucking labor is marked by early exploitation and the rise of powerful unions. Early drivers faced dangerous conditions and long hours, leading to the formation of the International Brotherhood of Teamsters (IBT) in 1903 to fight for better wages and conditions. In 1938 the federal government set the first limits on how many hours a truck-driver could drive, because tired drivers like the ones Miss MacIntosh pities were falling asleep at the wheel. The Federal-Aid Highway Act of 1956, which created the National Interstate and Defense Highways, spurred the industry’s growth.
  • “The shadow created the light, but the light created the shadow”: Light and darkness carry profound symbolic significance, reflecting the tension between reality and illusion, knowledge and ignorance, life and death. Miss MacIntosh, the practical and no-nonsense nursemaid, embodies a clear preference for reality and common sense or the “light” and is skeptical of illusions, dreams, and the “darkness.” She insists on facing life’s facts plainly, avoiding the “soporific luxury” of dreaming or indulging in fanciful visions. For her, the light symbolizes clarity, truth, and the tangible aspects of existence that must be accepted and dealt with. She values labor, self-forgetfulness, and living in the present moment, and she warns against chasing illusions or “things which the conditions of this mortal frame could not simply provide.” Conversely, darkness in this chapter is associated with illusion, uncertainty, and the unknown. It represents the realm of dreams, memories, and the ethereal, all of which are unstable and elusive. The darkness is also linked to death and the unconscious, a place where boundaries dissolve and individual identity blurs into a collective or universal soul. Vera’s mother, for example, lives in a twilight state between life and death, surrounded by shadows, dreams, and hallucinations, unable to firmly grasp reality. The interplay of light and darkness captures the novel’s thematic exploration of the fragility of human perception and the elusiveness of truth. The light is never fully stable or pure, there is always shadow and ambiguity and the darkness is not merely absence but a realm charged with mystery and the possibility of other forms of knowledge or existence. Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic insistence on the light and rejection of the darkness is thus a stance against the chaos and uncertainty that the darkness represents, but the novel complicates this by showing how darkness is also an inescapable part of life and consciousness. Light and darkness symbolize the conflict between the tangible, knowable world and the intangible, mysterious realms of dreams and death. Miss MacIntosh’s character aligns with the light, representing order and reason, while the darkness embodies the dreamlike, uncertain, and often threatening aspects of existence. This duality frames much of the novel’s meditation on human experience. See Light and Darkness.
  • “the light which came from within was the only light by which to steer our way”: The Quakers teach that every person holds the Inner Light, the light of God within, a surer guide than any outward authority. George Fox, who founded the Society of Friends in the 1650s, spoke of “that of God in every one.” See American Religious Movements.
  • “made a lamp by filling it with fireflies”: A firefly’s light comes from a chemical reaction between luciferin and the enzyme luciferase, and nearly all its energy is given off as light rather than heat, which is why it is called cold light. See Fireflies.
  • “This flat-footed Middle Westerner”: “Middle Westerner” encapsulates Miss MacIntosh’s essential nature as a pragmatic, strong, and no-nonsense woman, deeply rooted in the values and environment of the American Midwest. The term “Middle Westerner” emerged in the late 19th century, solidifying a regional identity for the area between the American East and West. This region, often called the “Midwest,” evolved through westward expansion and the development of transportation networks, particularly railroads. It became a distinct area with its own cultural and economic characteristics, influenced by both rural and urban landscapes. The Midwest, initially known as the “Northwest,” played a key role in westward expansion following the Louisiana Purchase. As the frontier moved further west, the term “Middle West” gained traction to define the area between the Northwest (Great Lakes region) and the Southwest (Oklahoma and Texas). The development of railroads significantly shaped the Midwest’s growth, facilitating trade and connecting disparate areas. A literary movement in the late 19th century focused on realistic depictions of Midwestern life, particularly in small towns and rural areas. The Midwest has been a significant force in American history, contributing to movements like the Granger movement (The Granger movement, also known as the Patrons of Husbandry, was a 19th-century agrarian movement that aimed to address the economic hardships faced by farmers, particularly those related to railroad and grain elevator monopolies. Founded in 1867 by Oliver Hudson Kelley, the movement grew rapidly in the 1870s, fueled by economic instability and the perceived exploitation of farmers by powerful industries.), the Progressive movement (The Progressive Movement was a period of widespread social and political reform in the United States, spanning roughly from the 1890s to the 1920s. It aimed to address the negative consequences of rapid industrialization, urbanization, and political corruption, seeking to improve society and government through various reforms.), and the development of industries and architecture. The Midwest uniquely combines urban industrial power with the conservatism of its rural hinterland. Miss MacIntosh’s Iowa was Granger country: in the 1870s Iowa had more Granges than any other state, farmers banding together against the railroads, which fits her concern for “those who were not the children of fortune.” The Midwest typically includes the following 12 states: Illinois, Indiana, Iowa, Kansas, Michigan, Minnesota, Missouri, Nebraska, North Dakota, Ohio, South Dakota, and Wisconsin.
  • “all those Romish graven images”: Graven images come from the Ten Commandments: “Thou shalt not make unto thee any graven image” (Exodus 20:4). Romish is an old, hostile Protestant word for Roman Catholic, and Miss MacIntosh distrusts the statues of saints.
  • “the whirling dervishes”: The whirling dervishes of the Mevlevi Order, founded by followers of the thirteenth-century poet Rumi in Konya, Turkey, are a Sufi order that practices whirling as a form of dhikr or remembrance of God.
  • “those sorrows bringing our grey hairs”: Jacob, fearing the loss of his youngest son, says his sons would “bring down my gray hairs with sorrow to the grave” (Genesis 42:38). See Genesis.
  • “this life being so short, so earnest, so full of woe”: Henry Wadsworth Longfellow’s “A Psalm of Life” (1838) declares, “Life is real! Life is earnest! / And the grave is not its goal,” and promises that great lives leave “Footprints on the sands of time.” Miss MacIntosh sweeps her footprints away. See American Writers.
  • “one should not place his faith in earthly things”: Colossians 3:2 reads, “Set your affection on things above, not on things on the earth.”
  • “She dismissed the insubstantial fabric of the dream”: The phrase echoes Prospero in Shakespeare’s The Tempest: “And, like the baseless fabric of this vision, . . . this insubstantial pageant faded, / Leave not a rack behind. We are such stuff / As dreams are made on.” See Shakespeare.
  • “those green pearls which had been manufactured by the secretive ear oyster”: The ear shell is the abalone, a sea snail named for its ear-shaped shell. Its rare pearls are green, blue, and violet like the shell’s lining.
  • “those pink pearls formed by the winged stromb”: Strombs are the conchs, sea snails whose shells flare into a wide lip, or wing. The queen conch of the Caribbean produces rare pink pearls with a shimmering, flame-like pattern. Like all natural pearls, they form around an irritant, which is why Miss MacIntosh says they “belonged to the sick oysters.”
  • “pearls of greater price, a pearl as big as her head”: Jesus compares the kingdom of heaven to a merchant who, “when he had found one pearl of great price, went and sold all that he had, and bought it” (Matthew 13:46). See Pearls and Jewels.
  • “those already rich as Croesus for whom all things had turned to gold, even his bed and his bread”: Croesus was the king of Lydia, in Asia Minor, in the sixth century B.C., renowned for his wealth. The golden bed and bread belong to another king, Midas, whose wish that everything he touched would turn to gold left him unable to eat. Croesus is significant as a metaphor for the fragile and illusory nature of material wealth and earthly glory, reinforcing the novel’s meditation on mortality, loss, and the contrast between external appearances and deeper truths.
  • “coats of golden fleece”: The Golden Fleece, the hide of a golden ram, was the prize Jason and the Argonauts sailed to Colchis to win. See Greek Mythology.
  • “the black-winged angels of mortality falling into the burning sea”: Revelation 8:8 tells how “a great mountain burning with fire was cast into the sea,” and Revelation 12:9 how Satan and his angels were cast out of heaven. See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “she was in the middle passage, as she would always say”: Miss MacIntosh means the middle of life’s voyage, the place Dante begins the Divine Comedy: “Midway in the journey of our life.” The Middle Passage also named the crossing of the Atlantic by slave ships from Africa, the deadliest leg of the slave trade, a darker meaning in a chapter about injustice.
  • “these end-of-the-world visions staining the atmosphere”: Miss MacIntosh notes that the Bible’s visions of the end “had appeared in the end and not in the beginning,” in the Book of Revelation, “and they had not been intended for daily life.” The philosophy of the end of the world, or “apocalyptic philosophy,” explores the concept of the world’s end, often involving catastrophic events, societal collapse, or human extinction, and examines its implications for ethics, meaning, and the understanding of existence. Philosophers have considered various end-of-world scenarios, from natural disasters to societal collapse, prompting reflection on human mortality, the nature of time, and the value of life.
  • “The sands of time . . . were running low”: The phrase “sands of time” is an idiom that refers to the passage of time, often emphasizing its relentless and irreversible nature. It originates from the imagery of an hourglass, where sand steadily flows from one chamber to another, symbolizing the continuous movement of time from past to future. The idiom is used to convey that time marches on, and moments are fleeting and irretrievable.
  • “Man was but a breath, a puff of smoke, and quickly gone. Time was short, growing always shorter just like a candle burning in the wind”: The Psalms say, “Man is like to vanity: his days are as a shadow that passeth away” (Psalm 144:4), and James asks, “For what is your life? It is even a vapour, that appeareth for a little time, and then vanisheth away” (James 4:14). Macbeth cries, “Out, out, brief candle!”
  • “we knew now all we would ever know, it was her opinion, of misery or happiness, all we would ever need to know. We must not waste our lives in the vain expectation of that which might never happen and had never happened and was impossible and would not be good for us if it did happen”: Matthew 6:34 counsels, “Take therefore no thought for the morrow: for the morrow shall take thought for the things of itself. Sufficient unto the day is the evil thereof.” The passage reflects the novel’s recurring themes of illusion versus reality, the elusive nature of truth, and the tension between dreams and the harshness of life. The narrator, Vera, and other characters grapple with these themes as they seek meaning amid suffering and loss. The passage encourages embracing what is real and immediate rather than being consumed by hopes that lead to despair or distraction.
  • “To kiss the rod”: To kiss the rod means to accept punishment meekly, like a child kissing the rod that beat it. Shakespeare uses it in The Two Gentlemen of Verona.
  • “than to imagine we were free and our own architects, building heaven”: In John Milton’s Paradise Lost, Satan, newly fallen into hell, declares, “The mind is its own place, and in itself / Can make a Heaven of Hell, a Hell of Heaven.” The line suggests that one’s inner state can transform the worst outward circumstances. Miss MacIntosh distrusts any such architecture of the mind. See Milton.
  • “We were the nestless birds”: Jesus says, “Behold the fowls of the air: for they sow not, neither do they reap” (Matthew 6:26), and also, “The foxes have holes, and the birds of the air have nests; but the Son of man hath not where to lay his head” (Matthew 8:20). The image symbolizes the characters’ and narrator’s profound estrangement from the world and themselves, their vulnerability, and the yearning for a refuge or truth that remains elusive.
  • “all these fine-feathered birds of paradise”: The birds of paradise of New Guinea reached Europe in the 1500s as trade skins with their feet removed, and naturalists concluded that they had no feet and lived their whole lives in the air, feeding on dew, until they fell to earth at death. Linnaeus named one species Paradisaea apoda, “footless.” See Birds.
  • “six-winged seraphim with crowns of gold”: In Isaiah’s vision of the throne of God, “each one had six wings; with twain he covered his face, and with twain he covered his feet, and with twain he did fly” (Isaiah 6:2). See Angels and Archangels.
  • “God was not a harlequin with a shaven head and a masked face and parti-colored tights and a sword of lath”: Harlequin is the acrobatic servant of the Italian commedia dell’arte, in a black half mask and a costume of colored diamonds, carrying a wooden bat or slapstick, the “sword of lath.”
  • “God was rather an old harness-maker or an old harpooner or a simple carpenter”: In Mark 6:3 the people of Nazareth ask of Jesus, “Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary?” Miss MacIntosh can imagine God only as a working man.
  • “the hard way which closed behind us, which had provided no way of turning back, of walking twice in the same path, of living once again in memory”: This is a take on the saying credited to Heraclitus that no man ever steps in the same river twice, for it is not the same river and he is not the same man. See “No man ever steps in the same river twice” (Ch 3).
    • The philosophy of impermanence or becoming, panta rhei, is best known in Western philosophy from the writings of Heraclitus. Panta Rhei is translated as everything flows. Heraclitus was famous for his insistence on ever-present change as being the fundamental essence of the universe. “No man ever steps in the same river twice.” See Heraclitus and Flux.
  • “we were given our opponent in order that we might struggle with him”: The struggle recalls Jacob, who wrestled through the night with a mysterious stranger and would not let him go until he was blessed (Genesis 32:24-30).
  • “She believed… in accepting the plain reality as it was, not in self-indulgence and these corrupting dreams of incorruptibility”: 1 Peter 1:23 speaks of being “born again, not of corruptible seed, but of incorruptible.” The statement emphasizes Miss MacIntosh’s practical, no-nonsense approach to life that values facing facts honestly and living with integrity, rather than indulging in self-delusion or fanciful ideals that deny human frailty and mortality.
    • Philosophical realists hold that the world exists independently of anyone’s mind and can be known as it is. Critics reply that even realists see through their own assumptions and biases. Miss MacIntosh’s realism is closest to the common-sense philosophy of the Scottish thinker Thomas Reid, who held that ordinary people know the world directly through their senses and that common sense is the foundation of all reasoning. American colleges taught his philosophy throughout the nineteenth century. In Chapter 1 she declares, “Common sense is the finest sense.” See Common Sense and American Pragmatism.
  • “those who died but once, those who could not afford to die twice”: Julius Caesar says in Shakespeare’s play, “Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.” See Shakespeare.
  • “these lute-players strumming in fields of asphodel above the stars”: The Asphodel Meadows were the part of the ancient Greek underworld where ordinary souls were sent to live after death. In this chapter it evokes the idea of an ethereal, liminal space of the afterlife or memory, highlighting the novel’s meditation on mortality, loss, and the persistence of the past.
  • “Her feet were too big a size, number eights, long and narrow, pointed outward”: In the 1940s the average shoe size for men was size eight like Miss MacIntosh. Women’s shoes were about half that size.
  • “this stout Admiral Dewey corset”: George Dewey was Admiral of the Navy, the only person in United States history to have held the rank. He is best known for his victory at the Battle of Manila Bay during the Spanish-American War, in 1898, where the American side lost only a single man. His name was given to streets, towns, products, and babies across the country, and Young’s corset, with its “girders as of a ship made to cut the Arctic ice,” is built like a battleship.
  • “the glassy shore covered with comb jellyfish like a mirror”: Comb jellies are not true jellyfish but ctenophores, clear sea animals that swim by beating rows of tiny hairs, the combs, which scatter light into moving rainbows.
  • “the chambered nautilus”: The nautilus builds its spiral shell one chamber at a time, sealing off each old room as it grows. In Oliver Wendell Holmes’s poem “The Chambered Nautilus” (1858), the shell becomes a lesson for the soul: “Build thee more stately mansions, O my soul.” See American Writers.
  • “Woman’s heart was folly”: Proverbs 9:13 says, “A foolish woman is clamorous: she is simple, and knoweth nothing.” The line can be interpreted as a recognition of the emotional vulnerability and the sometimes irrational nature of the human heart, especially as experienced through the female characters in the novel, caught between dreams and reality, love and loss.
  • “This earth was the testing ground even for God, often making His own mistakes which had perhaps been unavoidable as He had wished to leave man free”: Augustine, in On Free Choice of the Will, argued that God gave human beings free will, though they could misuse it, because a world with freedom is better than one without. This free-will defense remains one of the main answers to the problem of evil. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “the argument as to how many angels might stand on a needle’s point”: The question of how many angels can stand on a needle’s point is a philosophical and theological one, often used to illustrate the difference between physical and spiritual beings. If angels are understood as immaterial beings, an infinite number could potentially occupy the space of a needle’s point. However, if angels are considered to have physical bodies, then the number would be limited by the physical space available. It is also used as a metaphor for wasting time, debating topics of no practical value, or questions whose answers hold no intellectual consequence, while more urgent concerns accumulate. Medieval scholastics such as Thomas Aquinas did ask whether angels occupy space, but the needle’s point seems to come from later mockery of them; the English writer William Chillingworth asked in 1638 “whether a million of angels may not sit upon a needle’s point.”
  • “whether a camel shall enter through the needle’s eye or a rich man through the gates of heaven”: The image is a metaphor used in both the Bible and the Quran. It emphasizes the difficulty, or even impossibility, of a wealthy person achieving salvation through their own means. The phrase uses the image of a camel, a large animal, being unable to pass through the tiny eye of a needle to illustrate the immense challenge for a rich person to enter heaven. The saying appears in the Gospels of Matthew, Mark, and Luke, often in the context of Jesus speaking to a rich young man who is unwilling to give up his possessions to follow him. The Quran also uses this metaphor in Surah Al-A’raf (7:40), stating that those who reject God’s signs will not enter Paradise until a camel passes through the eye of a needle.
  • “we should rather be concerned with the anatomy of the clouds”: In 1802 the English chemist Luke Howard gave the clouds the Latin names still used today, cirrus, cumulus, and stratus, and Goethe wrote a poem in his honor. See Clouds and Storms.
  • “opportunity knocked but once at the door of the sleeper”: The proverb “opportunity knocks but once” was common by the nineteenth century, and John James Ingalls’s sonnet “Opportunity” gave it its best-known form: “I knock unbidden once at every gate! / If sleeping, wake.” The word “opportunity” comes from the Latin ob portum, “toward the harbor,” and the phrase uses personification to describe opportunity as something that comes to a person’s door.
  • “these empty husks”: In the parable of the prodigal son, the son who has wasted his inheritance “would fain have filled his belly with the husks that the swine did eat” (Luke 15:16).
  • “We were to be proved, and the truth was better than the lie, even should the lie seem truer than the truth, every lie containing a seed of truth in it, no doubt, but ours was the freedom to make a choice between the truth and the lie and the truth and the truth, to do what was good and right, leaving no uncertainty”: The passage underscores that while lies may be seductive and intertwined with truth, it is the conscious choice to pursue what is good and true that defines human freedom and moral integrity. Many cultures and thinkers have expressed the belief that, despite the potential pain or discomfort of truth, it ultimately offers a more beneficial and sustainable foundation than deception. A common African proverb states, “The bitter truth is better than a sweet lie.” This highlights the idea that even if the truth is difficult to hear, it is ultimately more valuable than a comforting falsehood. Writers and thinkers like Tolstoy have emphasized the importance of truth for moral clarity and authentic relationships. They argue that while lies might offer temporary comfort, they ultimately lead to unsustainable situations and undermine trust. Miss MacIntosh, who “could not endure a bare-faced lie or even the equivocal statement hovering between two truths,” would agree.
  • “a lighthouse for the blind”: The Lighthouse, founded in New York in 1905 by the sisters Winifred and Edith Holt as the New York Association for the Blind, gave its name to “lighthouses for the blind” across the country, agencies that trained blind people for work.
  • “a home for old sailors on shore leave”: Sailors’ Snug Harbor on Staten Island opened in 1833 as a home for “aged, decrepit and worn-out sailors,” paid for by the estate of the shipowner Robert Richard Randall.
  • “crack nuts on a rusted flatiron”: A flatiron was a heavy iron for pressing clothes, heated on the stove before electric irons. Upturned between the knees, it made a good anvil for cracking nuts.
  • “passing through the garden of the blind”: The garden is the one Catherine’s father planted for his blind wife in Chapter 2, with “neat and circling paths where was no obstacle.” See Eyes and Blindness.
  • “wallowing in a Slough of Despond, almost the gutter itself”: The Slough of Despond is a deep bog in John Bunyan’s allegory The Pilgrim’s Progress, into which the protagonist Christian sinks under the weight of his sins and his sense of guilt for them. It signifies a dark, painful phase in Miss MacIntosh’s life, highlighting both her resilience and the harsh realities she has faced before becoming Vera’s steadfast moral guide. See Miss MacIntosh in Intertextuality in MMMD.
  • “before, at last, I knew her, before I saw her plain”: The phrase echoes Robert Browning’s “Memorabilia”: “Ah, did you once see Shelley plain, / And did he stop and speak to you?” To see someone plain is to see the person as they really are, which no one in the house has done with Miss MacIntosh.
  • “a phosphorous light playing upon the darkened waters”: The glow sailors called phosphorescence in a ship’s wake is bioluminescence, light made by tiny plankton such as Noctiluca, “night light,” when the water is disturbed.
  • “She was neither a high brow nor a low brow but just . . . a plain middle brow”: The terms come from phrenology, which judged intelligence by the shape of the skull. Highbrow and lowbrow were in use by the 1900s, Van Wyck Brooks wrote “Highbrow and Lowbrow” in 1915, Virginia Woolf wrote an essay, “Middlebrow,” around 1932, and Russell Lynes’s “Highbrow, Lowbrow, Middlebrow” appeared in Harper’s in 1949.
  • “trying to steer her middle course between these jangling rocks”: Odysseus had to steer between Scylla, the six-headed monster, and Charybdis, the whirlpool, and the Argonauts passed through the Clashing Rocks that crushed ships between them. See Homer’s Epics.
  • “her British tan oxfords, her grey fedora”: The fedora, a soft felt hat with a creased crown, took its name from Victorien Sardou’s play Fédora (1882), whose heroine wore one, and was later taken up by men. Miss MacIntosh wears the men’s hat.
  • “armored always by her silver dollar watch”: Dollar watches were cheap, sturdy pocket watches. The Ingersoll company sold one for a dollar from 1896 and called it “the watch that made the dollar famous.” See Clocks and Watches.
  • “she could not see the purple hairstreak moths among the evening flowers”: The purple hairstreak is in fact a small butterfly, not a moth, that lives high in the tops of oak trees, where it is easily missed. See Butterflies and Moths.
  • “her good pin-striped grey serge with the shining elbows”: Serge is a type of twill fabric that has diagonal lines or ridges on both sides, made with a two-up, two-down weave. This choice of material aligns with Miss MacIntosh’s practical, no-nonsense character, emphasizing her plain, robust, and durable style of dress suited to her hardworking and sensible nature.
  • “made up of the bare necessities, as she would say, and no more”: Miss MacIntosh’s wardrobe is simple living in practice, with “not even a trimming of braid or a fichu of lace or an unnecessary button, for if there were an unnecessary button, it would be only one more button to lose.” Simple living encompasses a number of different voluntary practices to simplify one’s lifestyle. These may include: reducing one’s possessions, generally referred to as minimalism, or increasing self-sufficiency. Simple living may be characterized by individuals being satisfied with what they have rather than want.
  • “its pockets sagging because she had carried so many rocks, perhaps as ballast”: The novelist Virginia Woolf drowned herself in March 1941 by filling her pockets with stones and walking into the River Ouse, a few years before Young began writing this novel. See Virginia Woolf walked into the River (Ch 3) and Suicide in History and Literature.
  • “the known facts I had memorized as to the deaths of kings”: Shakespeare’s Richard II, facing his own fall, says, “For God’s sake let us sit upon the ground / And tell sad stories of the death of kings.” Miss MacIntosh thinks the deaths of kings “far less important than instructions in navigation.”
  • “Pilgrim’s Progress which she preferred to even the Word of God”: The Pilgrim’s Progress from This World, to That Which Is to Come is a 1678 Christian allegory written by John Bunyan. It is commonly regarded as one of the most significant works of Protestant devotional literature and of wider early modern English literature. It has been translated into more than 200 languages and has never been out of print. It appeared in Dutch in 1681, in German in 1703 and in Swedish in 1727. The first North American edition was issued in 1681. It has also been called the first novel written in English. According to literary editor Robert McCrum, “there’s no book in English, apart from the Bible, to equal Bunyan’s masterpiece for the range of its readership, or its influence on writers as diverse as William Hogarth, C. S. Lewis, Nathaniel Hawthorne, Herman Melville, Charles Dickens, Louisa May Alcott, George Bernard Shaw, William Thackeray, Charlotte Bronte, Mark Twain, John Steinbeck and Enid Blyton.” The lyrics of the hymn “To be a Pilgrim” are based on the novel. See John Bunyan’s Pilgrim’s Progress (1678) (Ch 3) and Pilgrim’s Progress.
  • “the Word of God was that which should be taken with a grain of salt”: To take something with a grain of salt, cum grano salis, goes back to Pliny the Elder, who described an antidote to poison to be taken with a grain of salt.
  • “the winds and their antiphon reminding me of all who had died”: An antiphon is a short chant in Christian ritual, sung as a refrain. It conveys the idea of voices or sounds answering each other, creating a haunting, ghostly chorus that surrounds the characters, particularly Vera and the nursemaid Miss MacIntosh, in a liminal space between reality and dream or life and death. The antiphonal quality of sounds evokes the mysterious and sometimes disorienting atmosphere of the novel, reflecting the characters’ internal and external conflicts.
  • “an Arctic tern stopping upon the rocks”: The Arctic tern makes the longest migration of any animal, flying each year from its Arctic breeding grounds to the Antarctic and back, and so sees two summers and more daylight than any other creature. See Birds.
  • “The sins we committed were worse than those of omission”: Christian teaching distinguishes sins of commission, wrongs done, from sins of omission, good left undone, as in the general confession of the Book of Common Prayer: “We have left undone those things which we ought to have done; And we have done those things which we ought not to have done.” Miss MacIntosh ranks the first as worse, yet elsewhere she speaks of “those things God in His haste had forgotten,” as if God, too, had sins of omission.
  • “What is the best time to plant corn? Which part of the ship is abaft the main-mast?”: Old farm lore says to plant corn when the oak leaves are as big as a squirrel’s ear, when the soil has warmed. Abaft means toward the stern, and starboard is the right-hand side of a ship facing forward.
  • “two pennies with which, she used to say, her eyes would be closed when she was dead”: Charon’s obol is the term for the coin placed in or on the mouth of a dead person before burial. Greek and Latin literary sources specify the coin as an obol, and explain it was used as a payment or bribe for Charon, the ferryman who conveyed souls across the river that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead. In later custom, coins were laid on the eyelids of the dead to keep them closed. It is a powerful symbol of passage, marking the threshold between the known world and the mysterious beyond, and reflects the novel’s preoccupation with mortality and the metaphysical journey that follows.
  • “that I would see America first”: The slogan returns from Chapter 1, where Miss MacIntosh’s advice sends Vera into the Middle West. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “better than all the principalities, all the powers of darkness”: Ephesians 6:12 reads, “For we wrestle not against flesh and blood, but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world.”
  • “What Cheer, Iowa, a small town like any other”: What Cheer is a real town in Keokuk County, Iowa, of about six hundred people. Its name is an old English greeting; the Narragansett people are said to have greeted Roger Williams in 1636 with “What cheer, netop?” (“What cheer, friend?”). In an interview Young said she had no idea there was a real town by the name of What Cheer, Iowa. She thought she had made it up. See What Cheer (Ch 3) and Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “Few ever saw Miss MacIntosh”: Social invisibility here signifies the overlooked yet vital presence of Miss MacIntosh, whose plainness and refusal to engage in illusion cause her to be unseen or ignored, representing those who labor quietly and faithfully without acknowledgment in a world filled with illusions and distractions. It also emphasizes themes of isolation, unrecognized labor, and the contrast between appearance and reality. Social invisibility occurs when a group or individual is consistently overlooked or excluded from social, political, or economic participation. Catherine’s visitors “cared not to inquire who the active servant was.”
  • “her admirer was a head-hunter. He was an Australian bushman”: In Australian English a bushman is someone at home in the outback, usually a white settler skilled in bush life, and the Bushmen contingents were Australian volunteers who fought in the Boer War in 1900. The word did not usually mean Aboriginal people. There is little evidence of head-hunting on the Australian mainland. He is a wild, primitive figure with a surprising touch of grace and aspiration. His obsessive admiration for Miss MacIntosh, coupled with his cultural and personal dislocation, make him a symbol of alienation and the tensions between civilization and savagery. Miss MacIntosh’s disdain and rejection of him underline her role as a practical, grounded counterpoint to the novel’s dreamlike and chaotic elements. This character enriches the novel’s exploration of identity, otherness, and the boundaries of social acceptance. The Australian Bushman symbolizes a primitive, untamed force, a disruption within the otherwise orderly and practical world that Miss MacIntosh represents. His “wild mien” and “calculated, incalculable eloquence” reflect a tension between civilization and savagery, rationality and irrationality. The chapter suggests that he is out of place in the refined and wealthy environment of the invalid’s house, likening his presence to a scandal or an intrusion on social norms. The bushman serves as a foil to Miss MacIntosh. While she embodies sobriety, practicality, and a clear-eyed acceptance of reality, he represents fantasy, confusion, and the disruptive power of illusion and unfulfilled ambition. His presence heightens the contrast between the grounded nursemaid and the fantastical, opium-induced world of the invalid and her acquaintances.
    • Miss MacIntosh’s head-hunter is a mixture. He is called an Australian bushman, a “wild, half-naked man of Borneo,” and a recent arrival from New Mexico, and her brother was lost in the Easter Islands. A bushman is easily confused with a bushranger, an outlaw of the bush; the most famous, Ned Kelly, was hanged in 1880, and some saw him as a champion of poor farmers against large landowners.
    • Head-hunting was practiced in the Torres Strait Islands, between Australia and New Guinea, including on Badu, where taking heads was tied to warfare and ceremonies honoring the dead. It was also practiced by the Dayak peoples of Borneo and in New Guinea, and the Māori of New Zealand preserved the tattooed heads of ancestors and enemies.
  • “his dreams . . . were that he might go over to Rome”: To “go over to Rome” was the English phrase for converting to Roman Catholicism, used of John Henry Newman and others in the Oxford Movement of the 1840s.
  • “nor was he even a good Presbyterian or Free Methodist or Shouting Baptist or Jehovah’s Witness”: Miss MacIntosh lists the plain Protestant churches of the Middle West. The Free Methodist Church was founded in New York in 1860 in protest against pew rents and slavery, and “shouting” describes the loud, ecstatic worship of revival meetings. See American Religious Movements.
  • “nor did he believe in total immersion, for he believed in sprinkling”: Churches have long divided over baptism. Baptists and many revival churches baptize adults by total immersion, while Catholics, Presbyterians, and Methodists usually baptize by sprinkling or pouring. Anabaptist groups are established in Iowa, including the Amish, the Mennonites, and the Old Order River Brethren, who baptize by immersion.
    • Baptism for especially early Christians was like being buried so that a person could rise to a new life. According to Paul, full immersion under water represents the believer’s death and burial in a watery grave with Christ, and the rising out of the water represents resurrection to a new life (Romans 6:3-4). Drownings during baptism have occasionally happened, and in the 1500s drowning was used as a punishment against the Anabaptists themselves: Felix Manz was drowned in Zurich in 1527, a mocking “third baptism.”
  • “as if he might even some day become the Pope wearing turrets of gold”: The papal tiara was a beehive-shaped crown of three tiers. Pope Paul VI was crowned with one in 1963 and then gave it away, and no pope since has worn it.
  • “walls of bones in beautiful designs like lace”: In the Capuchin Crypt beneath the church of Santa Maria della Concezione in Rome, the bones of some 3,700 friars are arranged in arches, rosettes, and chandeliers.
  • “the dead burying the dead until there were no more to bury”: Jesus tells a would-be follower who first wants to bury his father, “Follow me; and let the dead bury their dead” (Matthew 8:22).
  • “the primitive Christians of great works and little faith, not of great faith and little works”: The old quarrel between faith and works runs through Christianity. James 2:17 says, “faith, if it hath not works, is dead,” and Martin Luther, who taught salvation by faith alone, called the Epistle of James “an epistle of straw.”
  • “stopping to admire a broken Apollo”: Apollo is an Olympian deity in classical Greek and Roman religion and mythology. He is a metaphorical emblem of beauty, transformation, and the dualities inherent in life, drawing from classical mythology and natural imagery to deepen the novel’s exploration of human experience and perception.
  • “a dreaming Psyche”: The story of Psyche, told by Apuleius in The Golden Ass, is about the overcoming of obstacles to the love between Psyche and Cupid/Amor. Psyche in this context embodies the spiritual and psychological dimensions of human life, the inner reality behind outward appearances, and the continual transformation inherent in the human condition.
  • “a fat-stomached cupid with grapes in its hair and its nose broken when it had fallen from a Roman roof”: Roman palaces and churches lined their rooflines with stone statues of saints, gods, and cupids, so a broken cupid might well have fallen from a Roman roof. The roofs themselves were made of overlapping clay tiles, flat tegulae with curved imbrices covering the joints, a durable design still used across the Mediterranean.
  • “the wooden huntresses in ruined gardens”: Diana is a goddess in Roman and Hellenistic religion primarily considered a patroness of the countryside, hunters, crossroads, and the Moon. She is equated with the Greek goddess Artemis. The goddess Diana in this chapter serves as an archetype of feminine power, purity, and the sacred mysteries of birth and renewal amidst the novel’s broader themes of illusion, mortality, and transformation.
  • “born in his native bush among bush-whackers”: In Australia a bushwhacker is someone who lives in the bush or clears it. In the United States the word meant a guerrilla fighter, especially in the Civil War. See The Civil War.
  • The Catholic Church had an assimilation policy (as in many other colonized countries) which was used to break the spiritual and cultural identity of Aborigines (and indigenous cultures worldwide) by removing tens of thousands of children from their parents. They apologized to Aborigines for the “stolen generation”. Recently Canada (2008), Pope Francis (2022) and the United States (2024) have also apologized for this practice.
  • “the love songs of a lyre bird who had fallen in love with an Australian spinster and had built a tower of earth to her window”: The lyrebird is a ground-dwelling Australian bird famous for mimicking natural and artificial sounds, even chainsaws and camera shutters. The male builds mounds of earth on which he dances and sings to court the female. Rural Australia also has its Bachelors and Spinsters Balls, country dances where single men and women meet.
  • “an old Ritz menu . . . an Etruscan mirror and an ivory comb”: César Ritz opened the Hôtel Ritz in Paris in 1898 with the chef Auguste Escoffier, whose French menus set the standard of luxury dining. Etruscan mirrors were polished bronze hand mirrors, engraved on the back with scenes from myth.
  • It is interesting that the Head-hunter focuses on her head given what follows in later chapters. This also highlights a man’s feeling that he has the right to interrupt, surprise, and corner a woman when he is interested in her no matter how the woman is feeling. In feminist literature this behavior can be identified as a man who feels he is entitled, deserving, and owed a woman’s attention regardless of her feelings. He is the “hunter,” and she is his “prey.”
  • “he might still revert to the noble savage”: The phrase “noble savage” first appears in English in John Dryden’s play The Conquest of Granada (1672). It is often credited to Jean-Jacques Rousseau, who never used it, though he praised humanity in a natural state.
  • “the wild, half-naked man of Borneo”: “The Wild Man of Borneo” was a stock attraction of nineteenth-century freak shows, and P. T. Barnum exhibited men under that name.
  • “memories of Eskimos”: Eskimos are the Indigenous peoples who have traditionally inhabited the northern region from eastern Siberia to Alaska, Canada, and Greenland. Many now prefer their own names, such as Inuit and Yupik.
  • “cherubim, many-faced angels with plumes of gold”: In Ezekiel’s vision the cherubim each have four faces, of a man, a lion, an ox, and an eagle (Ezekiel 1:10).
  • “Charon on his great ferry boat crossing the dark river Styx”: In Greek and Roman mythology Charon is the ferryman of Hades who carries souls of the newly deceased across the river Styx and Acheron that divided the world of the living from the world of the dead.
  • “the ghost of Cheops”: Cheops is the Greek name of the Egyptian pharaoh Khufu, who built the Great Pyramid of Giza around 2560 B.C. See Ancient Egypt.
  • “St. Simeon the Stylite and what he had thought of this lower world”: St. Simeon the Stylite was a Syriac ascetic saint who achieved notability for living thirty-seven years on a small platform on top of a pillar near Aleppo. The significance of St. Simeon the Stylite lies in his representation of spiritual isolation and relentless pursuit of higher realities, contributing to the novel’s exploration of human suffering, transcendence, and the elusive nature of truth.
  • “Daniel encompassed by sleeping lions”: Daniel 6:22 tells how Daniel is saved from lions by the God of Israel. Symbolically, this reference typically evokes themes of courage, faith, endurance, and survival in the face of danger or adversity.
  • “the Appian Way and houses of the dead”: The Appian Way, begun in 312 B.C., is one of the earliest and most important roads of the Roman Republic. Its first miles outside Rome are lined with tombs, the “houses of the dead.”
  • “St. Augustine in the city of God”: The City of God is a book of Christian philosophy written in Latin by Augustine of Hippo after the sack of Rome in 410. The mention of St. Augustine’s “City of God” serves as a profound symbol of the contrast between earthly decay and spiritual aspiration, reflecting the characters’ inward struggles with faith, reality, and the hope for salvation or ultimate truth beyond the ephemeral world. See Augustine and Christian Theology.
  • “Georgian architecture”: Georgian architecture is the name given in most English-speaking countries to the set of architectural styles between 1714 and 1830, the reigns of the first four King Georges.
  • “Spode chinaware”: Spode is the English pottery founded by Josiah Spode in Stoke-on-Trent in 1770, famous for its blue-and-white transfer-printed ware.
  • “of Delft, of silver urns”: Delftware is the blue-and-white tin-glazed pottery made in the Dutch city of Delft from the seventeenth century, in imitation of Chinese porcelain.
  • “He could not digest the golden steeples and streets of gold”: The heavenly Jerusalem of Revelation has gates of pearl, “and the street of the city was pure gold, as it were transparent glass” (Revelation 21:21). See Revelation and the Apocalypse.
  • “these gaping cannibals”: Thomas Baker was a Methodist missionary in Fiji and is the only missionary in that country to be killed and eaten.
  • “Her own dear brother had gone out as a primitive Christian bishop from Iowa”: A bishop is an ordained member of the Christian clergy who oversees other clergy. See Richard MacIntosh.
  • “to convert the heathen of the Easter Islands”: Easter Island is an island and special territory of Chile in the southeastern Pacific Ocean. It is famous for its nearly 1,000 statues called moai. Its people are the Rapa Nui. Recent research has challenged the old story that an ecological collapse drove the islanders to war and cannibalism.
  • “the ladies mentioned by Plutarch”: Plutarch was a Greek Middle Platonist philosopher, biographer, and essayist, and a priest at the Temple of Apollo at Delphi, best known for his Parallel Lives of famous Greeks and Romans. Plutarch functions as a symbol of the mother’s intellectual and cultural anchoring amidst her drifting consciousness, representing a link to enduring human wisdom and the complexities of love, fate, and history that permeate her visionary world.
  • “the Protestant graveyard where Keats and Shelley slept and who after only one week in Rome had died of the marsh fever”: Keats and Shelley are buried in Rome’s Non-Catholic Cemetery near the Pyramid of Cestius. Marsh fever, or Roman fever, was malaria, whose name comes from the Italian mal aria, “bad air.” In Henry James’s “Daisy Miller” (1878), an American girl dies of Roman fever after a night visit to the Colosseum. See Romantic Poets.
  • “the best hotel would be the Quirinale”: The Quirinal Palace in Rome was a papal palace, then the royal palace, and is now the home of the president of Italy. It has housed thirty Popes, four Kings of Italy and twelve presidents of the Italian Republic. Rome also has a Hotel Quirinale, on the Via Nazionale.
  • “if he should not be admitted there, then he should try the Pantheon”: The Pantheon, completed about 125 A.D., was a temple to all the gods. Since 609 it has been a Catholic church, Santa Maria ad Martyres, and it holds the tombs of the painter Raphael and two kings of Italy, a strange hotel.
  • “mummery and flummery and junk”: Mummery is empty ritual or play-acting, from the masked mummers of folk plays. Flummery is a soft pudding, and so empty flattery or nonsense.
  • “For herself, she asked nothing”: Saint Teresa Margaret of the Sacred Heart, an eighteenth-century Carmelite nun of Florence, gave this counsel: “Always receive with equal contentment from God’s hand either consolations or sufferings, peace or distress, health or illness. Ask nothing, refuse nothing, but always be ready to do and to suffer anything that comes from His Providence.”
  • “even as the canker eats the rose, as gold and silver rust”: Shakespeare’s Sonnet 35 says “loathsome canker lives in sweetest bud,” the canker being a worm or blight. James 5:3 warns the rich, “Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you,” and Matthew 6:19 speaks of treasures on earth “where moth and rust doth corrupt.”
  • “a dead lobster or broken hermit shell or lion’s mane”: The lion’s mane is the largest known jellyfish, with a reddish bell and masses of long, stinging tentacles like a mane.
  • “There must be, in fact, a revolution”: In political science, a revolution is a fundamental and relatively sudden change in political power and political organization which occurs when the population revolts against the government, typically due to perceived oppression or political incompetence. Miss MacIntosh cannot wait for gradual change, “no more than for a glacier moving in the night,” and socialists of her time argued the same question, whether society should change by slow reform or by revolution.
  • “What had this Darwinian evolution ever done for anybody?”: Darwinian evolution, set out in Charles Darwin’s On the Origin of Species (1859), is a theory of biological evolution stating that all species of organisms arise and develop through the natural selection of small, inherited variations that increase the individual’s ability to compete, survive, and reproduce.
  • “God’s was the strength of the unicorn”: Numbers 23:22 and 24:8 say of God that “he hath as it were the strength of an unicorn.” The King James translators used “unicorn” for the Hebrew re’em, probably the wild ox. The phrase may be interpreted as a poetic way of emphasizing the ineffable, incorruptible power of the divine, which stands apart from the fragile, chaotic human condition depicted throughout the novel.
  • “were we not still in Egypt, the waste-howling wilderness”: Miss MacIntosh’s speech is a weave of scripture. God led Israel out of Egypt, and Deuteronomy 32:10 says he found Jacob “in the waste howling wilderness.” “I was shapen in iniquity” is Psalm 51:5, “the mystery of iniquity” is 2 Thessalonians 2:7, “the joy of the hypocrite but for a moment” is Job 20:5, and “In the sweat of thy face shalt thou eat bread” is Genesis 3:19. See The Bible.
  • “Honesty was surely, and it had always been, the best policy”: The proverb has been attributed to Sir Edwin Sandys, who used it in 1599, and it was later quoted by Benjamin Franklin and Thomas Jefferson.
  • “never to hide one’s head in the desert sands like the poor ostrich”: The belief that the ostrich hides its head in the sand goes back to Pliny the Elder. Ostriches actually lie low with their necks along the ground, or turn their eggs in the nest with their beaks.
  • “our good works should not live after us”: Miss MacIntosh reverses Mark Antony in Shakespeare’s Julius Caesar: “The evil that men do lives after them; / The good is oft interred with their bones.” See Shakespeare.
  • “not the left wing . . . not the right wing . . . but something more immense, an honest point of view, the whole bird”: Centrism is a political outlook or specific position that involves acceptance or support of a balance of a degree of social equality and a degree of social hierarchy, while opposing political changes which would result in a significant shift of society strongly to either the left or the right. Centrism has a specific meaning within the Marxist movement, referring to a position between revolution and reformism. Miss MacIntosh’s centrist position is a firm, pragmatic, and sober approach to life, emphasizing common sense, self-discipline, and the rejection of illusions as the best way to navigate a harsh and uncertain world. Miss MacIntosh’s centrism is not merely a political or social stance but a fundamental worldview that privileges order, clarity, and practical wisdom in a world otherwise engulfed by confusion and chaos. Catherine’s list in Chapter 2 included “the left-wing political movement, the right wing of the dove.”
  • “another sea-swept spar which, clothed with feathery goose barnacles”: Goose barnacles hang from driftwood on fleshy stalks, their feathery feeding legs looking like plumes. Medieval writers such as Gerald of Wales believed that barnacle geese hatched from them, since no one had seen the geese nest.
  • “without the dead body, there could be no proof of death in a legal sense”: In the common law, a person who has been missing without word for seven years may be presumed dead, but without a body or that long wait, a death cannot be proved.
  • “or even a lamp-lighter”: A lamplighter lit and tended candle or gas street lamps at dusk. Maria Susanna Cummins’s novel The Lamplighter (1854) was one of the great bestsellers of its century, and the lamplighter on his tiny planet in Antoine de Saint-Exupéry’s The Little Prince (1943) lights and puts out his lamp every minute. The lamplighter stands as a symbol of hope, constancy, and the pursuit of clarity in a world engulfed by darkness, illusion, and uncertainty.
  • “The wait-and-see policy had always been his”: “Wait and see” became a political catchphrase in 1910, when the British prime minister H. H. Asquith used it repeatedly in Parliament, and his critics made it his nickname.
  • “no man knew, unless it was Mr. Spitzer, the hour of his death”: “Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh” (Matthew 25:13).
  • “He had always preferred a dark lady”: The phrase recalls the Dark Lady of Shakespeare’s Sonnets, the dark-haired, dark-eyed woman of Sonnets 127 to 152, so unlike the fair beloved of convention. Miss MacIntosh, the redhead Mr. Spitzer remembers as a brunette, is the novel’s own dark lady.
  • “at the doors of an employment agency which was turning away the unemployed”: During the Great Depression, unemployment in the United States reached about a quarter of the workforce in 1933, and lines of jobless men waited outside employment offices and soup kitchens.
  • “under the sign of three golden balls of a pawn shop like golden apples”: The pawnbroker’s sign of three golden balls is often traced to the Medici of Florence, whose coat of arms bore balls, and to Saint Nicholas, patron of pawnbrokers, who gave three bags of gold to save three poor girls.
