Chapter 10

← Chapter 9 · Home · Chapter 11 →

Summary

Unable to picture her own wedding, Vera imagines other weddings and drifts into a dream of one. Mr. Spitzer is the veiled bride and Miss MacIntosh the bridegroom. The preacher’s marriage vows slide into a funeral service before he vanishes. Vera wakes troubled rather than amused. She realizes she has been thinking unkindly of Miss MacIntosh as colorless and unwanted, and she feels pity for a woman who gave her life to duty. She is hungry and wants to go to her, but she has been warned not to wander the house or the shore at night.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Miss MacIntosh · Solomon the Turtle

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Society, Class, and Race · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Roses and Flowers · The House · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Plato and Platonism

Allusions: Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Milton · Music and Composers · Romantic Poets · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • Vera dreams or hallucinates a surreal wedding ceremony in which Mr. Spitzer and Miss MacIntosh are paired, but the roles and identities are confused and inverted. The preacher’s words blur distinctions between man and woman, human and beast, and even marriage rites and funeral rites become intertwined. This dream culminates in an eerie meditation on death and the fleeting nature of life. The preacher’s speech shifts seamlessly from wedding vows to funeral liturgy, emphasizing the inseparability of marriage and death, union and dissolution. The dream ends with the unsettling image of Mr. Spitzer as the bride and Miss MacIntosh as the bridegroom, highlighting ambiguous identities and roles.
  • Following the dream, Vera reflects on Miss MacIntosh’s situation, age, and prospects for marriage. She is portrayed as a somewhat colorless, ordinary woman, past the prime of youth, who has resigned herself to loneliness. Yet Vera also feels a budding pity and empathy for her, contemplating the pain of being old and unloved and recognizing her human frailty.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a strong undercurrent of existential melancholy. The preacher’s speech invokes biblical imagery about the brevity of life, decay, and the inevitability of death. This generalizes human fate and questions the permanence of social institutions like marriage.
  • Vera’s hunger, both literal and metaphorical, is evident as she contemplates the absence of celebration and the lack of meaningful connection. She regrets not visiting Miss MacIntosh, wishing to reconcile and share intimacy, yet respects her privacy and limitations, underscoring themes of isolation and the human need for companionship.
  • The chapter is rich in symbolism. The wedding and funeral imagery combined suggests the cyclical nature of life and death. Mr. Spitzer’s twin iron bedsteads symbolize duality or fractured identity; the snow and ice evoke coldness and isolation; the locked bedroom door represents the boundaries of privacy and emotional distance. The preacher’s litany names biblical and mythic figures (Lucifer, Beelzebub, Gorgons, Hydras, Chimeras) and cosmic events, creating a vision of a chaotic universe where human rituals struggle for meaning.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The preacher does not seem “to know who was woman and who was man and who was beast and who was bird.” What does the dream undo?
  • Mr. Spitzer nods “negatively as he replied affirmatively.” What is he really saying?
  • When the stars light the scene, “this error was the error of the dream which had begotten nothing.” Whose error is it?

Characters

  • Vera gives Miss MacIntosh a waxed mustache and a silk hat, as she did in Chapter 9. What does Vera keep seeing in her?
  • Mr. Spitzer would marry “no one now but his brother worm.” What holds him to his dead brother?
  • Vera calls Miss MacIntosh “the most colorless” person in the world, then feels “the first embryonic emotion of pity.” What changes in one night?

Connections

  • Madge’s wedding was a funeral in Chapter 6, and here the preacher slides from one service to the other. Why does the novel keep joining weddings and funerals?
  • Miss MacIntosh’s locked bedroom door returns to the locked doors of Chapters 7 and 8. What is behind it?
  • The preacher recites the tribes of Israel as Miss MacIntosh made Vera recite them in Chapter 9. Why does the dream use her lessons?

Reflection

  • “One who could know us and yet love us was undoubtedly the truest love this world has ever seen.” Is it possible to be fully known and still loved?
  • “What would it be like to be old and unloved?” Is it harder to be young and unloved, or old?
  • Vera laughs at the dream, then feels ashamed. When does laughing at someone become wronging them?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • She is the central consciousness reflecting on marriage, dreams, and the strange events unfolding.
  • She is introspective, sensitive, and somewhat confused by the surreal experiences.

Mr. Joachim Spitzer

  • An older man, melancholic and resigned to his fate.
  • He is described with an old-fashioned elegance, symbolized by his clothes and the twin beds he shares (in memory) with his deceased brother.
  • His identity is ambiguous, shifting between bride and groom in the dream.

Miss MacIntosh

  • An older woman, practical and resigned to a life without love or marriage.
  • She is portrayed as colorless, ordinary in appearance, yet capable and domestically inclined.
  • In the dream, she assumes the role of bridegroom, further blurring gender and identity.

The Preacher

  • A mysterious figure who recites ritualistic and apocalyptic language blending wedding rites with funeral orations.
  • His speech is symbolic and confusing, reflecting the instability of the event.
  • His words come almost entirely from the Book of Common Prayer, the marriage service sliding into the Order for the Burial of the Dead, with verses from Job, Psalms, Corinthians, Jude, and Revelation spliced in.

Solomon the Turtle

  • He can be interpreted as a symbol of longevity, endurance, and ancient wisdom.
  • Turtles traditionally embody qualities such as patience, stability, and a slow, deliberate approach to life.
  • In the context of this chapter, where Vera confronts themes of mortality, the fleeting nature of existence, and the confusion between life’s ceremonies (weddings) and rites of passage (funerals), Solomon may represent a counterpoint to human transience and folly.
  • The turtle’s slow, deliberate presence contrasts with the chaotic, disordered, and surreal wedding-funeral rites, emphasizing the tension between the ephemeral and the enduring.
  • The turtle’s name, “Solomon,” evokes the biblical King Solomon, renowned for his wisdom and judgment. This further amplifies the symbolic weight of the turtle as a figure of insight and contemplation amidst the chaos and absurdity Vera perceives around her.
  • Solomon’s silent witness role amidst this disarray may suggest the presence of a wise, patient observer within Vera’s subconscious, hinting at a deeper understanding or acceptance of life’s contradictions and mysteries.

Research: Themes

Marriage and Identity

See: Identity and the Self · Women, Gender, and Marriage

  • The confusion and inversion of roles in the dream wedding hint at fluidity in gender and societal roles.
  • Marriage is portrayed ambiguously, blending union and separation, life and death.
  • The preacher’s confusing vows suggest the complexity and sometimes absurdity of social rituals.

Mortality and Impermanence

See: Death and Mortality

  • The wedding turns into a funeral, reflecting the inseparability of life and death.
  • Biblical and apocalyptic references underscore the transient nature of human life.
  • The preacher’s speech highlights human frailty and the inevitability of death.

Loneliness and Human Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh’s character symbolizes the loneliness of aging and societal neglect.
  • Vera feels pity and empathy, recognizing the shared human condition.
  • The dream’s isolation (few guests, symbolic objects) stresses the solitude underlying social ceremonies.

Dream versus Reality

See: Illusion and Reality · Dreams and Imagination

  • The blurred line between dream and waking life shows the instability of perception.
  • Vera’s hallucinatory experience reflects inner turmoil and existential questioning.

Social Roles and Expectations

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • Miss MacIntosh’s rejection of marriage and Vera’s reflections reveal societal pressures on women.
  • The notion that “none would have her” contrasts with Vera’s hope for unexpected companionship.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Twin Iron Bedsteads

See: The House · Twins and Doubles

  • Represent memory, duality, and the coexistence of past and present selves (Mr. Spitzer and his deceased brother).

Wedding/Funeral Ceremony

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Symbolizes the intertwined nature of beginnings and endings, union and separation.

Veil and Mustache

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Play with gender roles and identity, challenging traditional expectations.

Turtle Solomon

  • Symbolizes wisdom and endurance.

Red Geranium

See: Roses and Flowers

  • Might symbolize life, vitality, and domesticity.

Old Empty Shoe

See: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • Could represent emptiness, absence, or abandonment.

Research: Resources

  • “some other bride blushing like a red, red rose”: Robert Burns, “O my Luve’s like a red, red rose” (1794). See Romantic Poets.
  • “live happily ever after as in an old fairy tale”: The fairy-tale ending, “and they lived happily ever after.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “his brother worm who was under the ground”: Job says “to the worm, Thou art my mother, and my sister” (Job 17:14), and Hamlet says, “Your worm is your only emperor for diet” (Hamlet 4.3). See The Book of Job and Shakespeare.
  • “pots and pans jangling in my ears”: A shivaree, or charivari, was the old custom of banging pots and pans outside newlyweds’ windows on their wedding night. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “it was a funeral march which was played at a perfect wedding”: Chopin’s Funeral March (Piano Sonata No. 2, 1839) in place of Mendelssohn’s Wedding March (1842) or Wagner’s “Here Comes the Bride” (Lohengrin, 1850). See Music and Composers.
  • “we are gathered here in the sight of God and of this company to join man and woman together”: The Book of Common Prayer opens the marriage service, “Dearly beloved, we are gathered together here in the sight of God, and in the face of this congregation, to join together this man and this woman in holy matrimony.” See Weddings and Funerals.
    • The marriage vows and priestly blessing in the prayer book came from the Sarum rite, the medieval service of Salisbury Cathedral.
    • The Council of Carthage (398), also known as the Fourth Council of Carthage, did not explicitly define marriage in a single canon, but it addressed aspects related to marriage and divorce through various decrees. One notable aspect was the reinforcement of the canon against clerics marrying, and the enforcement of celibacy for those ordained. Additionally, the council addressed the issue of remarriage after consecration, deeming it similar to adultery and punishable by excommunication, while also stating that such marriages were valid. One canon of the council’s rulings had the bride and groom presented by their parents to the priest for a blessing.
  • “for the end of the world draweth nigh”: This echoes “The end of all things is at hand” (1 Peter 4:7) and “your redemption draweth nigh” (Luke 21:28). “Lightnings and thunderings and voices” come from Revelation 4:5, and “in the twinkling of an eye” from 1 Corinthians 15:52: “we shall all be changed, in a moment, in the twinkling of an eye.” The phrase echoes the novel’s recurring themes of mortality, judgment, and the struggle between hope and despair in the face of inevitable endings. See The Bible.
  • “when there shall be many gnashings of teeth, many wailings”: Matthew 8:12 reads, “there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth.” This phrase underscores themes of mortality, judgment, and the sorrow that accompanies human existence, blending the sacred with the tragic in Vera’s experience of the marriage ritual. See The Bible.
  • “a mighty hurricane is blowing in from the Canary Islands or Hebrides”: Atlantic hurricanes are born off West Africa, near the Canary and Cape Verde Islands. The Hebrides lie in the cold north of Scotland, where no hurricane begins.
    • The Canary Islands are a Spanish archipelago off the coast of northwestern Africa.
    • The Hebrides are an archipelago comprising hundreds of islands off the northwest coast of Scotland.
  • “this life is very short and full of mortal sorrow”: Job 14:1 reads, “Man that is born of a woman is of few days, and full of trouble.” This phrase serves as a sobering meditation on human finitude, the inevitability of death, and the sorrow that colors a brief life. See The Book of Job.
  • “Porpoises shall eat the drowned sailor. The waters of this world shall close over his head”: The preacher gives the bride and groom a sailor’s burial at sea. Milton’s “Lycidas” (1638) mourns a friend drowned in the Irish Sea, and Ariel sings of a drowned father in The Tempest: “Full fathom five thy father lies.” The line foreshadows Miss MacIntosh lost in the waves. See Milton, Shakespeare, The Sea and Water, and the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “Do either of ye know of an impediment to this marriage”: The phrase is from the Book of Common Prayer, which drew on the Sarum rite. It reads, “I require and charge you both, as ye will answer at the dreadful day of judgment when the secrets of all hearts shall be disclosed, that if either of you know any impediment . . . ye do now confess it,” and calls on anyone who knows a cause to “speak, or else hereafter for ever hold his peace.” See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “St. Michael and of all the holy angels”: The list comes out of Milton’s Paradise Lost, which gives Hell “Gorgons and Hydras, and Chimaeras dire” (2.628) and seats Chaos as umpire with “high arbiter Chance” who “governs all” (2.907-910). See Milton and Angels and Archangels.
    • St. Michael is an archangel, a spiritual warrior in the battle of good versus evil.
    • Lucifer “who was the brightest and is fallen farthest” is the name of different figures in folklore associated with the planet Venus. “How art thou fallen from heaven, O Lucifer, son of the morning!” (Isaiah 14:12). See the Chapter 7 resources.
    • Beelzebub is Baal-zebub, “lord of the flies,” god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2), and in the Gospels the prince of devils (Matthew 12:24).
    • Chaos is the void before the forming of the universe in Greek mythology.
    • Gorgons are creatures in Greek mythology. Medusa and her sisters had a gaze that turned men to stone.
    • Hydras are serpentine water monsters in Greek and Roman mythology. Heracles killed the many-headed Hydra as his second labor.
    • Chimeras are monsters made of different parts of animals in mythology. Bellerophon killed the Chimera, part lion, part goat, part serpent.
    • In Aristotle’s Physics, chance (automaton) works in nature and luck (tyche) in human affairs.
  • “the dreadful Day of Judgment”: The Day of Judgment belongs to eschatology, the part of theology that deals with the ultimate destiny of humans. It is found in Judaism, Christianity, Islam, and Zoroastrianism. The golden thrones and “the sea shall turn to glass” come from Revelation 4:4-6: “a sea of glass like unto crystal.” See The Bible.
  • “Unadvisedly or lightly, marriage should not be entered in”: The prayer book says marriage is “not by any to be enterprised, nor taken in hand, unadvisedly, lightly . . . but reverently, discreetly, advisedly, soberly.” See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “none shall take a wife of whoredoms”: God tells the prophet Hosea, “Go, take unto thee a wife of whoredoms” (Hosea 1:2). See The Bible.
  • “to have and to hold from this day forward”: The prayer book vows: “to have and to hold from this day forward, for better for worse . . . in sickness and in health, to love, cherish, and to obey.” Mr. Spitzer nods “negatively as he replied affirmatively.” See the Chapter 6 resources on “love, honor, and obey.”
  • “all corporeal and incorporeal hereditaments”: Appurtenances are accessories or other items associated with a particular activity or style of living. The preacher slips into the language of property deeds, which pass “hereditaments and appurtenances,” everything that can be inherited or that goes with an estate.
  • “Man that is born of woman”: The burial service opens, “Man, that is born of a woman, hath but a short time to live, and is full of misery.” The preacher adds the swollen stomach, from the trial of the jealous husband’s wife in Numbers 5:27. See The Book of Job.
    • “Her belly shall swell, and her thigh shall rot” (Numbers 5:27). This phrase encapsulates the complex interplay of physical condition and the spiritual or emotional state likely reflecting on the human condition’s heaviness and vulnerability as portrayed throughout the novel.
  • “the rites for the burial of the dead”: Funeral rites originated from Jewish and Roman customs. The Order for the Burial of the Dead in the Book of Common Prayer is the service the preacher slides into. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “He cometh up, and he is cut down”: Job 14:2 reads, “He cometh forth like a flower, and is cut down: he fleeth also as a shadow, and continueth not.” This phrase serves as a poignant reminder within the narrative of life’s impermanence and the inescapable presence of death even at moments of joy and union. The preacher quotes the burial service word for word: “He cometh up, and is cut down, like a flower; he fleeth as it were a shadow, and never continueth in one stay.” See The Book of Job.
  • “He has gone from Newport to Mystic, from Wellfleet to Buzzards Bay”: The preacher lists the coast of Rhode Island, Connecticut, and Cape Cod, the New England shore where Vera grows up.
  • “May God forgive us, for we know not who or where we are”: “Father, forgive them; for they know not what they do” (Luke 23:34). See The Bible.
  • “Spare us, Lord most holy, God most mighty, holy and merciful Savior”: The burial service prays, “spare us, Lord most holy, O God most mighty, O holy and merciful Saviour.”
  • “the archangel trumpeting the last trump”: “For the Lord himself shall descend from heaven with a shout, with the voice of the archangel, and with the trump of God” (1 Thessalonians 4:16). See Angels and Archangels.
  • “Why stand we in jeopardy every hour?”: Paul asks it in 1 Corinthians 15:30. The phrase conveys a broader theme in the novel of the tension between life and death, the known and the unknown, and the profound uncertainties that define human experience. It is a rhetorical question that underscores the fragile, often perilous journey of life that the characters navigate throughout the narrative. 1 Corinthians 15 is the lesson read at the burial service. See The Bible.
  • “Nothing thou hast brought into this world”: “For we brought nothing into this world, and it is certain we can carry nothing out” (1 Timothy 6:7), one of the burial service’s opening sentences. See The Bible.
  • “Gold and silver rust”: “Your gold and silver is cankered; and the rust of them shall be a witness against you” (James 5:3). See The Bible.
  • “What is man but a poor, two-legged animal?”: Plato defined man as a featherless biped, and Diogenes answered with a plucked chicken. Lear calls man “such a poor, bare, forked animal” (King Lear 3.4). See Plato and Platonism and Shakespeare.
  • “His beauty consumeth away, like as if it were a moth fretting a woolen garment”: “Thou makest his beauty to consume away, like as it were a moth fretting a garment” (Psalm 39:12, as the burial service gives it). See The Bible.
  • “In the morning it is green and groweth up, but in the evening it is cut down, withered”: “In the morning it is green, and groweth up; but in the evening it is cut down, dried up, and withered” (Psalm 90:6, in the burial service). See The Bible.
  • “All hearts shall melt to water”: “The hearts of the people melted, and became as water” (Joshua 7:5). See The Bible.
  • “The weak are the strong”: Paul writes, “for when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10). See The Bible.
  • “Selah, selah, selah”: In the Bible, the word “selah” typically signifies a pause, a time for reflection, or a musical interlude. It appears most often in the Psalms and Habakkuk, suggesting a moment to stop and consider what has just been said or sung.
  • “Where is Nepthalin? Where is Reuben who begot a horde? Where is Manasses?”: Nephthalim and Manasses are the King James spellings of Naphtali and Manasseh in Revelation 7:6, where twelve thousand of each tribe are sealed. See the Chapter 9 resources on the genealogies.
  • “Oh, death, where is thy sting? Oh, grave, where is thy victory?”: Paul’s words in 1 Corinthians 15:55, read at the burial service. The phrase encapsulates the struggle to find meaning beyond death and the hope or belief that death may not be the ultimate end. It reflects a yearning for transcendence, where death’s “sting” (its pain and finality) and the “victory” of the grave (the end of life) are questioned or denied. See The Bible.
  • “thy womb of morning”: “From the womb of the morning” (Psalm 110:3). See The Bible.
  • “Can these bones live?”: God asks Ezekiel in the valley of dry bones (Ezekiel 37:3). See The Bible.
  • “earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust”: The burial service reads, “Forasmuch as it hath pleased Almighty God . . . to take unto himself the soul of our dear brother . . . we therefore commit his body to the ground; earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust.” The preacher’s “brother to brother, deep calling to deep” adds Psalm 42:7. See the Chapter 1 resources.
  • “As it was in the beginning, is now, and ever shall be, world without end”: The Gloria Patri, the doxology sung at the end of the psalms.
  • “Where is Philemon?”: Philemon was a Christian of Colossae to whom Paul wrote his letter about Onesimus, a runaway slave, asking forgiveness for him. In Ovid, Philemon and Baucis are the old married couple who asked to die at the same hour and were turned into two trees, an oak and a linden. See The Bible and Greek Mythology.
  • “Where is Zipporah, a little bird?”: Zipporah was the wife of Moses. Her name means “bird” in Hebrew. See The Bible.
  • “Where are those wandering stars to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness forever?”: The preacher recites Jude 1:12-13: “clouds they are without water, carried about of winds; trees whose fruit withereth, without fruit, twice dead, plucked up by the roots . . . wandering stars, to whom is reserved the blackness of darkness for ever.” See The Bible.
  • “Strike up the music! On with the dance”: Byron’s “On with the dance! let joy be unconfined,” from the ball on the eve of Waterloo (Childe Harold’s Pilgrimage, Canto III). See Romantic Poets.
  • “the turtle Solomon and the red geranium and an old, empty shoe”: An old shoe was thrown after the bride or tied to the carriage for luck. See Weddings and Funerals.
  • “Her face was certainly not her fortune”: The nursery rhyme’s milkmaid answers, “My face is my fortune, sir, she said.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “She had stopped it only once, and that was in Spokane”: Miss MacIntosh’s broken nose from a bus in Spokane, from Chapter 9. See the Chapter 9 resources.
  • “the oldest fool was the greatest fool”: “There is no fool like an old fool” (John Heywood, 1546).
  • “she could be the helpmeet”: “I will make him an help meet for him” (Genesis 2:18). See The Bible.
  • “their numbers were legion”: “My name is Legion: for we are many” (Mark 5:9). See The Bible.
  • “Familiarity breeds contempt”: Chaucer’s Tale of Melibee is the most widely cited source for the phrase in English. Chaucer used the phrase “hoomlynesse” (familiarity) and “dispresisynge” (contempt). In St. Augustine’s Latin a similar idea, expressed as “vulgare proverbium est, quod nimia familiaritas parit contemptum” (meaning “it is a common proverb, that too much familiarity breeds contempt”), appears in St. Augustine’s writings from the fifth century. Some point to Srimad Bhagavatam as the ultimate origin, with the phrase being expressed in Sanskrit by the sage Narada Muni. This interpretation suggests the idea has been around for a much longer period.
  • “One who could know us and yet love us was undoubtedly the truest love this world has ever seen”: Psalm 139 begins, “O Lord, thou hast searched me, and known me.” The line suggests that the deepest and most genuine form of love is not blind or naive, but rather one that fully comprehends all aspects of a person (their strengths, weaknesses, flaws, and complexities) and loves them in spite of, or even because of, that complete knowledge. This statement highlights the theme of authentic love as acceptance and compassion for the whole person, including their imperfections and vulnerabilities. It contrasts with superficial or idealized love, which might only appreciate a partial or idealized image. The “truest love” is grounded in reality, acknowledging the full truth of the beloved. In the context of the chapter, Vera (the narrator) reflects on the nature of love and marriage, and the idea that true love involves a deep understanding and acceptance of the other person. Miss MacIntosh, who values common sense and reality, would likely agree with this view, emphasizing love based on truth rather than illusion or fantasy. The phrase captures a central insight into the nature of love as something that embraces the whole self (the light and the dark, the certain and the uncertain) and that this kind of love is the most meaningful and enduring.
  • “to waste one’s sweetness in the desert air”: Thomas Gray’s Elegy: “Full many a flower is born to blush unseen, / And waste its sweetness on the desert air.” See the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “The sands of time were always running low”: The hourglass, and the hymn “The sands of time are sinking” (Anne Ross Cousin, 1857).
  • “claws upon her forehead like the claws of a lobster”: The pain from shoulder to hand and the crab’s claws may foreshadow what Vera learns of Miss MacIntosh’s body. Cancer takes its name from the crab, the Greek karkinos.
  • “whirling dervishes”: The Mevlevi Sufis, followers of the poet Rumi, worship by whirling.
  • “good, true, beautiful”: Plato’s three highest ideas, the Good, the True, and the Beautiful. See Plato and Platonism.

Chapter 8

← Chapter 7 · Home · Chapter 9 →

Summary

The bus pushes through a cloudburst with a broken windshield wiper, the road barely distinguishable from the flooded fields. It stops at a fork near a hill of old tombstones, beside Beatrice Fitzgerald’s tin house in a yard of mud and wreckage. Madge calls Beatrice a common prostitute. Homer defends her: a hard worker who lost an eye to a boy’s arrow, whose son, rumored to be old Doc’s, joined the Navy. Lost in thought of drowning, Vera cries out for Miss MacIntosh. Moses brings word that old Josh Hathaway is dead and calls it murder, whoever turned the key. Moses delivers a long, dark meditation on death and medicine, insisting that no doctor could have saved Jacqueline. The bus enters a village at night. Its houses look like coffins under a skull-like moon, and Vera wonders whether she has arrived in a land of eternal night or a dream within a dream.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Moses Hunnecker · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn · Beatrice Fitzgerald · Jacqueline White · Miss MacIntosh · Justice O’Leary

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past · Society, Class, and Race · Time

Symbols: Birds · Keys, Doors, and Locks · Lamps, Candles, and Light · The Bus and the Journey · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology · Descartes and Dualism · Kant and Hegel · Plato and Platonism · Schopenhauer

Allusions: Dante · Don Quixote · Edgar Allan Poe · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Milton · Music and Composers · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid description of passing through violent weather: cloudbursts, thunder, rain like a deluge, darkness without illumination, the broken windshield wiper, and the road as a river. This stormy journey symbolizes a transition, perhaps even a metaphor for the passage from life to death or from one state of existence to another. Vera reflects, “Perhaps it was the beginning of creation. Perhaps we had said farewell to earth.” This sets a tone of mystery and existential reflection, indicating a crossing into an unknown or liminal space.
  • The bus stops at a place where the road divides near a graveyard hill, with old tombstones bearing faded names. One branch leads downward to an obscure village described as a “land of promise through eternity,” where time ceases, and life is eternal, “where the children would dance, where the young would not grow old, where the old would never die.” This passage contrasts the realm of death (graveyard) with the idealized vision of eternal life, emphasizing themes of mortality, hope, and the human yearning for immortality.
  • On the other side of the road is a decrepit tin house in a flooded yard, described in grim detail: mud, refuse, broken furniture, and wreckage. Here lives Beatrice Fitzgerald, an old woman shrouded in mystery and local gossip. The dialogue about her reveals the community’s harsh judgments, mingling myth and fact: she is called a “common prostitute,” yet also described as “royal,” with “blue blood” due to her name’s prefix “Fitz-.” Her tragic story includes losing an eye and having a son who joined the Navy and travels the world but still remembers her. This passage reflects themes of social ostracism, the complexity of human identity, and the enduring bonds of family amid decay and despair.
  • Moses delivers a long, rambling, and philosophical monologue about “old Doc,” a once-practicing physician now dismissed as mad and irrelevant. He talks about the futility of medical science against death and decay, expressing skepticism about doctors, cures, and even the existence of God or heaven. His words are laced with dark humor and bitterness: “There’s no hell, and there’s no heaven, and there’s no doctor.” He wrestles with mortality, the inevitability of death, and the human desire to resist it, but ultimately acknowledges the helplessness everyone faces. This passage is a meditation on aging, illness, and the limits of human control over life and death.
  • Moses’s speech includes vivid, symbolic imagery: “Alpha and Omega, beginning and end! Trunk, bole, hulk, skeleton,” and references to biblical and mythological figures: Leviathan, Julius Caesar, Hercules, and Charon. These evoke the grand, inescapable cycle of life and death, reinforcing the theme that no one escapes mortality. The passage blends the mundane and the cosmic, illustrating the universal human condition through both everyday and mythic lenses.
  • The chapter concludes with a haunting description of arriving at a village at night, described as “spectral,” with “upright houses like coffins,” “a pale, dented moon like a skull,” and “great spaces yawning between.” The imagery evokes death, emptiness, and silence, filled only with the voices of the past and the dead. Vera questions whether this place is real or a dream, a “dream within the dream,” underscoring the elusive nature of reality and the boundary between life and death.

Questions and observations

Reading closely

  • The road divides at the graveyard: one branch climbs to the tombstones, the other descends to the village of “promise through eternity.” Which branch does the bus take?
  • Madge leaves the light on so a man “cannot say he did not know,” while Beatrice puts the lights out. What does each woman want to be seen, or not seen?
  • Moses rattles off strings of words: “Barmy . . . screw loose, unhinged, off his head.” What is he trying not to say?

Characters

  • Homer calls Beatrice “royal,” and Madge calls her “the oldest prostitute in all this country.” What makes each of them see her as they do?
  • Moses says of old Doc, “you can’t help giving him your hand when he gives his hand to you.” Why can’t Moses let Doc go?
  • Beatrice’s son “never forgot her” and sends postcards from the world’s great ports. What has he escaped, and what has he kept?

Connections

  • Moses repeats “the key turned by itself” and Madge’s charge of murder from Chapter 7. Why does the novel keep returning to the locked door?
  • Vera wonders whether she relives “another’s” life, as the drowning are said to do. Whose face is “pillowed upon the oozy tides of time”?
  • The chapter ends on “that dream within the dream.” How has the whole journey come to feel like one?

Reflection

  • “You can’t prove it’s murder . . . you can’t prove it’s not, so you are right, whichever way you look at it.” Can a town live by that logic?
  • “There’s no hell, and there’s no heaven, and there’s no doctor.” What is left to Moses if he believes this?
  • “To come to a village at night may be never to know it.” What do people miss when they first meet a place, or a person, in the dark?

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • Her descriptions are richly metaphorical and poetic, often blending natural imagery with existential or mythic overtones.
  • She imparts a sense of transition or passage not just through physical space but through states of being or time.
  • She frequently distances herself from the events, perceiving them as if in a vision or dream.
  • She is grappling with realities that are elusive, fragmented, or overwhelming.
  • She contemplates mortality, memory, and identity. This reflects an engagement with themes of impermanence and the unknowability of ultimate fate.
  • While observing others on the bus, Vera remains somewhat apart, bearing witness to their stories and conflicts without fully participating.
  • Her grief and confusion suggest a loneliness or estrangement, emphasized by the eerie, almost spectral description of the village and its inhabitants.
  • Vera is positioned on the edge of the known and unknown, the living and the dead, the earthly and the eternal.
  • The stopping of the bus at a fork, one path leading to a graveyard hill and the other to a mysterious village of promise, serves as a potent symbol for her liminal condition. This reflects an internal or spiritual threshold, not merely a physical one.
  • Her tone is somber, contemplative, and at times skeptical or cynical, especially in the bus-driver’s monologue on medical science, mortality, and social decay. She absorbs this skepticism without endorsing it outright, contributing to a complex, layered narrative voice.

Moses Hunnecker (The Bus Driver)

  • An experienced, somewhat cynical man who knows the terrain well and sees the storm as routine.
  • He stops the bus at a graveyard hill, signaling a crucial moment in the journey.
  • He is skeptical of medical science and doctors, especially “old Doc,” whom he sees as out of touch and ineffective.
  • The bus-driver’s long monologue reveals his mistrust in institutions, the inevitability of death, and a complex view of life, health, and mortality.

Madge Capehorn

  • Madge condemns Beatrice Fitzgerald as “the oldest prostitute in all this country.”
  • Madge is outspoken and somewhat judgmental, suggesting that Beatrice tries to hide in darkness because of her ugliness and reputation.
  • Madge’s perspective contrasts with Homer’s more sympathetic view.

Homer Capehorn

  • Offers a more nuanced and sympathetic view of Beatrice Fitzgerald, describing her as hardworking, loyal, and even “royal” because of her name’s lineage.
  • He recounts stories of her past hardships and suggests a tragic background, including the loss of an eye and a son who joined the Navy.

Beatrice Fitzgerald

  • Described by some characters as an “old dirty thing,” “the ugliest old hag for miles,” and a “common prostitute,” highlighting the harsh judgment and stigma she endures.
  • Madge’s disdainful remarks emphasize how Beatrice is viewed through a lens of moral condemnation and social ostracism.
  • This negative perception is powerful enough that Beatrice is said to hide because she “puts out the lights” so “they won’t see her,” suggesting that she is conscious of her social invisibility and perhaps the shame imposed upon her by the community.
  • Contrasting with the harsh judgments, Homer provides a more sympathetic and respectful view of Beatrice. He notes that she “brings my mother’s laundry” and “washes the clothes so clean,” and that “no one ever worked so hard,” illustrating her role as a diligent, if marginalized, member of society.
  • The image of her pulling a little red sled over snow, with “Her face turns blue,” evokes a sense of endurance and hardship borne quietly.
  • This portrayal complicates the one-dimensional negative stereotype and suggests that beneath social condemnation lies a person who struggles to survive and maintain dignity.
  • Beatrice is noted to be “nearly blind” and losing “the other eye,” a physical manifestation of her vulnerability and decline.
  • This detail adds a layer of pathos to her character, symbolizing not only physical deterioration but also perhaps the metaphorical blindness of society toward her suffering.
  • The loss of her eye is somberly attributed to a childhood incident, where “a little boy shot at her with his bow and arrow,” an event she dismissed lightly, indicating either denial or stoic acceptance of suffering.
  • Homer refers to Beatrice as “royal,” citing her surname Fitzgerald and the idea that names beginning with “Fitz” are linked to royal bastardy (“the bar sinister”).
  • This rumor of noble blood contrasts sharply with her low social standing, suggesting a tragic fall from grace or a life marked by lost potential.
  • The community’s suspicion and gossip about her lineage add to the aura of mystery and complexity surrounding her identity.
  • Homer also speaks of a son Beatrice supposedly had with “old Doc,” a figure who “never claimed him.”
  • This son, who joined the Navy and travels the world, symbolizes a link to a life beyond the village and possibly a hope or legacy that Beatrice clings to.
  • The son’s absence and the fact that “no one ever worked so hard” to survive in the village underscore themes of abandonment and endurance.
  • The chapter uses Beatrice as a symbol of those who exist on the margins of society, invisible and judged yet enduring.
  • Her existence amidst “wreckage” and a “flooded yard oozing with mud and refuse” reflects her precarious social and material condition.
  • The bus-driver’s need to “change horses” at her house metaphorically suggests a pause or shift in the journey, highlighting Beatrice’s role as a waypoint in the narrative of this community’s life and death struggles.

Jacqueline White

  • Jacqueline is described as a “poor little Jacqueline” who evokes a poignant emotional response from the old bus-driver. The bus-driver reflects on her with a mixture of sympathy and sorrow, noting that “Death never entered her head” and calling her “kind of infatuated with life.”
  • He observes that she is “prettier now than she ever was,” and there is a hopeful anticipation that she will go “to see us all next Christmas, going to dance the light fantastic.”
  • This imagery conveys a youthful vitality and innocence, an almost naïve optimism or denial of mortality in the face of impending death.
  • Jacqueline is portrayed as vibrant and spirited, someone who clings to life and the joys it holds, despite the dark, foreboding atmosphere that envelopes much of the chapter.
  • The bus-driver’s reflection on Jacqueline contrasts with the grim and fatalistic tone that permeates his monologue about death, illness, and the futility of medical science.
  • He laments that “the best doctor couldn’t help her,” and that “Old Doc certainly couldn’t,” implying Jacqueline is suffering from an incurable condition.
  • This adds a tragic dimension to her character; she is full of life and hope, yet doomed by forces beyond her control.
  • The bus-driver’s lament underscores the helplessness felt by those who witness her decline and the inevitability of death, which no amount of medical intervention or human will can prevent.
  • Jacqueline’s brief mention is also thematically significant. Her character embodies the tension between life and death, hope and despair, youth and decay that runs throughout the chapter.
  • The contrast between her vitality and the decay and ruin described elsewhere in the chapter highlights the fragility of life and the relentless passage of time.
  • Jacqueline represents a fleeting glimpse of beauty and life amidst a landscape marked by death, desolation, and resignation.

Research: Themes

Mortality and Death

See: Death and Mortality

  • The graveyard hill, the bus-driver’s reflections, and the references to death throughout the dialogue emphasize the theme of mortality.
  • The bus-driver’s long rant on death, medical science’s limitations, and the inevitability of going “when the tide goes” frame death as an unavoidable reality.

Memory and the Passage of Time

See: Memory and the Past · Time

  • Vera reflects on the idea that drowning people relive their lives in moments before death, but here the memories seem fragmented and possibly belong to others.
  • The blending of past and present, and the uncertainty of reality and memory, permeate the narrative.

Isolation and Mystery

See: Isolation and Connection · Faith, God, and the Supernatural

  • The setting (a spectral village at night, broken fences, a flooded yard with refuse, and a mysterious woman who hides from strangers) creates a sense of isolation and secrets.
  • The village itself appears ghost-like, with empty streets, wooden geese, and flickering lights, symbolizing a place suspended between life and death.

Skepticism Toward Institutions

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • The bus-driver’s distrust of “old Doc,” politicians, and even the concept of God highlights disillusionment with traditional authorities and systems.
  • Medical science is portrayed as outmoded and helpless in the face of mortality.

Social Stigma and Reputation

See: Society, Class, and Race

  • Beatrice Fitzgerald’s character embodies themes of social judgment, stigma (being called a prostitute), and resilience.
  • The conflicting opinions of Madge and Homer reveal the complexity of social roles and the harshness of gossip.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

The Broken Windshield Wiper and Flooded Road

See: The Sea and Water · The Bus and the Journey

  • Symbolize vulnerability and the overwhelming forces of nature or fate that the characters cannot control.

The Graveyard Hill

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Represents the boundary between life and death, a literal and figurative crossroads on the journey.

The Old Tin House and Flooded Yard

See: The Sea and Water · The House

  • The dilapidated house and refuse-strewn yard symbolize decay, neglect, and the harsh realities hidden behind appearances.

Light and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • The dimming and raising of lights in the house reflect attempts to hide or reveal truth, beauty, and identity.
  • Madge’s insistence on keeping the light on contrasts with Beatrice’s hiding in darkness.

Names on Tombstones

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Names like Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, and others evoke lineage, memory, and the passage of generations, underscoring the permanence of death. Longtree is the last name of Esther, a character at the end of the novel.

The Locked Door and the Turning Key

See: Keys, Doors, and Locks

  • Suggest mysteries, secrets, or supernatural forces at play.
  • The locked door that “just locked by itself” hints at unseen powers or fate.

Birds (Woodpeckers, Bluejays, Mockingbirds)

See: Birds

  • Birds appear repeatedly, symbolizing nature, communication, and, perhaps, the persistence of life amid decay.

Research: Resources

  • “where the cape of the glacier had reached”: The last ice sheets covered northern and central Indiana and left behind the flat, rich till plains. See Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest.
  • “a white carbon lamp like a moon”: Carbon-arc lamps lit streets and grounds with a harsh white light from the 1880s into the 1920s.
  • “Stonecipher, Longtree, Thistlewaite, Chesterfield, Dalton, Grebe, Thomas, Whitehill”: The graves carry names of stone, tree, thistle, and hill, as Chapter 7’s dead carried names of stone. Longtree is the surname of Esther, who appears late in the novel.
    • Stonecipher means stone, swampy creek.
    • Longtree refers to the parish they came from in England.
    • Thistlewaite means thistle meadow.
    • Chesterfield means Roman fort, open country.
    • Dalton means from the valley town.
    • Grebe means digger of ditches or graves or engraver of seals.
    • Thomas is a common name meaning twin.
    • Whitehill is a Scottish name meaning white hill.
  • “a realm of visionary hypothesis or uncertain speculation”: Representationalism, or indirect realism, is the philosophical theory that argues that the mind perceives only mental images (representations) of the external world, not the world itself. It’s opposed to realism, which holds that the mind directly grasps objects as they are in the world. In his philosophy, Kant distinguishes between intuitions (immediate, sensory representations) and concepts (general, mediate representations). He also distinguishes between appearances (things as they appear to an observer) and things-in-themselves (the world as it is independently of anyone’s perception).
  • “I got to change horses”: Stagecoaches changed horses at stations along the road. Moses’s “last stage” is also a phrase for dying.
  • “that same old one-eyed Beatrice”: Beatrice is a name derived from the French name Béatrice, which came from the Latin Beatrix, which means “she who makes happy.” The popularity of the name spread because of Dante Alighieri’s poetry about the Florentine woman Beatrice Portinari. Dante presents Beatrice as being worthy of speaking for God, making her a holy individual. Beatrice “Bice” di Folco Portinari was an Italian woman who has been commonly identified as the principal inspiration for Dante Alighieri’s Vita Nuova, and is also identified with the Beatrice who acts as his guide in the last book of his narrative poem the Divine Comedy, Paradiso, and during the conclusion of the preceding Purgatorio. Within the Comedy, Beatrice is symbolic of divine grace and theology. Young’s Beatrice, a one-eyed washerwoman called a whore, is the opposite of Dante’s guide to heaven. Yet she too lives where the road divides, the graveyard on one side and the village of “promise through eternity” on the other. See Dante.
  • “Everything that begins with Fitz is royal in this country”: There is the belief that the last name Fitzgerald and every name that begins with Fitz is from royalty except that it is a bastard line in England. This belief is because of Charles II, who named his bastard son Fitzroy and the Duke of Clarence, later William IV, whose children by the actress Dorothea Jordan were named FitzClarence. Fitz comes from the Norman French fils, “son,” so Fitzgerald means son of Gerald. The Fitzgeralds were Norman lords in Ireland, the Earls of Kildare.
  • “It’s the bar sinister”: Bar sinister is the popular and erroneous term for bend sinister. Bend sinister is a diagonal stripe on a shield said to be a sign of bastardy.
  • “That’s where they learned to toboggan, too”: Toboggan is a sled. The word comes from the Mi’kmaq, and Madge uses it as a sly euphemism.
  • “See no evil”: The three wise monkeys are carved over a stable at the Tōshō-gū shrine in Nikkō, Japan (1636).
  • “Borneo, Singapore, Japan, the China Sea, the Rock of Gibraltar”: In the 1920s and 1930s the U.S. Navy’s Asiatic Fleet patrolled the China coast and its rivers, so a sailor could truly send postcards from these ports.
    • Borneo is the third largest island in the world.
    • Singapore is a sovereign island city-state.
    • Japan is an island country in East Asia.
    • The China Sea is the East and South China Seas, the waters off the coast of China.
    • The Rock of Gibraltar is a monolithic limestone promontory located in the British territory of Gibraltar, near the southwestern tip of Europe on the Iberian Peninsula. Its name is Arabic, Jabal Tariq, for Tariq ibn Ziyad, the Muslim general who landed there in 711 to invade Spain. The Prudential Insurance Company made the Rock its emblem in 1896, which is Homer’s “life insurance ad.”
  • “was it really true that one relived, in three minutes, all one’s life as the drowning are said to do”: Life review: In 1790, British naval officer Francis Beaufort nearly drowned and reported experiencing a life review. In 1847, a letter by Beaufort recalling the incident was published in the autobiography of Sir John Barrow, 1st Baronet. Wrote Beaufort: “Thought rose after thought with a rapidity of succession that is not only indescribable, but probably inconceivable, by any one who has not been in a similar situation. The course of those thoughts I can even now in a great measure retrace... our last cruise - a former voyage, and shipwreck - my school - the progress I had made there, and the time I misspent - and even all my boyish pursuits and adventures. Thus travelling backwards, every past incident of my life seemed to glance across my recollection in retrograde succession; not, however, in mere outline, as here stated, but the picture filled up with every minute and collateral feature. In short, the whole period of my existence seemed to be placed before me in a kind of panoramic review, and each act of it seemed to be accompanied by some reflection on its cause, or its consequences; indeed, many trifling events which had been long forgotten then crowded into my imagination, and with the character of recent familiarity. The length of time that was occupied by this deluge of ideas, or rather the shortness of time into which they were condensed, I cannot now state with precision, yet certainly two minutes could not have elapsed from the moment of suffocation to that of my being hauled up.” Vera finds herself remembering not her own life but “another’s ultimate face,” and she cries out for Miss MacIntosh, who was lost in the sea.
  • “I was sinking for the first, the second, the third time”: An old belief held that a drowning person rises three times before going down for good.
  • “Where was Miss MacIntosh, my darling, now aloud I cried?”: The novel’s title may echo the old ballad “Oh My Darling, Clementine,” whose Clementine is lost beneath the water. See Music and Composers.
  • “You can’t prove it’s murder”: A logical fallacy is a flaw in reasoning that makes an argument invalid. It’s an error in logic that can weaken or even defeat the conclusion of an argument. Fallacies can be either formal (related to the structure of the argument) or informal (related to the content or premises of the argument). Knowing them helps a reader spot weak or flawed arguments, argue more persuasively by avoiding them, and weigh information more critically. Moses commits the argument from ignorance: what cannot be proved false is taken as true.
  • “Who killed the old horse? Who killed the sparrows?”: The nursery rhyme asks, “Who killed Cock Robin? / I, said the Sparrow.” See Fairy Tales and Folklore.
  • “the influenza epidemic that struck us shortly after the Armistice”: The influenza pandemic of 1918 peaked as the war ended on November 11, 1918, and killed about 675,000 Americans. It reached the United States through Boston, and rumors blamed German agents for spreading it, hence Moses’s “German germs washed up in Boston Harbor.”
  • “Delirium tremens, mocking birds, snakes”: The shaking delirium of alcohol withdrawal often brings visions of snakes and crawling things. See Madness and Sanity.
  • “snatch me from the jaws of living death”: Tennyson’s “The Charge of the Light Brigade” (1854): “Into the jaws of Death, / Into the mouth of Hell.”
  • “me hanging by a thread”: The sword of Damocles hung over him by a single horsehair. In Chapter 5 Moses hangs on to life by “a single hair that would never break, a hair hanging between him and a star.” See the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “me trusting to a broken reed”: “Thou trustest in the staff of this broken reed, on Egypt” (Isaiah 36:6). See The Bible.
  • “going to dance the light fantastic”: John Milton’s poem L’Allegro (The Happy Man), written about 1631 and published 1645, has the lines “Come, and trip it as ye go / On the light fantastic toe.” It is a pastoral poem, which has from its first appearance been paired with the contrasting pastoral poem, Il Penseroso (The Melancholy Man), which depicts a similar day spent in contemplation and thought. L’Allegro is the poem of the happy man, and Moses gives its dance to the dying Jacqueline. See Milton.
  • “Barmy, old Doc is, screw loose, unhinged, off his head”: Moses’s strings of synonyms, mad words here and later “Trunk, bole, hulk, skeleton,” read like the lists in Roget’s Thesaurus (1852). See Madness and Sanity.
  • “Mad as a March hare”: Hares run wild in their March mating season. Lewis Carroll’s March Hare (1865) keeps the mad tea party. See Madness and Sanity.
  • “that old knight errant curing them all”: Don Quixote, the mad knight errant who rides out to help people who never asked to be rescued. See Don Quixote.
  • “A clean bill of health!”: A ship’s certificate that no disease was aboard when it left port.
  • “Galloping consumption, that churchyard cough”: Moses names Jacqueline’s tuberculosis. See the Chapter 6 resources.
  • “horse feathers”: 1920s slang for nonsense, and the title of a Marx Brothers film (1932).
  • “You got to go when the tide goes”: In Dickens’s David Copperfield, Barkis “goes out with the tide,” since, as Mr. Peggotty says, people along the coast “can’t die . . . except when the tide’s pretty nigh out.”
  • “Shallows, rocks, crossing the bar”: Tennyson’s “Crossing the Bar” again. See the Chapter 7 resources.
  • “Greatest kings have died. A turtle falling on your head”: The story goes that the playwright Aeschylus, father of tragedy, died when an eagle dropped a tortoise on his bald head. See Greek Mythology.
  • “three sheets to the wind”: Sailors’ slang for drunk. The sheets are the ropes that, let loose, leave a ship staggering.
  • “Yet you can’t help giving him your hand when he gives his hand to you”: Schopenhauer places compassion as the foundation of his ethical system, arguing that it is the only truly moral motive because it is based on a genuine concern for the well-being of others. He sees indifference as the opposite of this, something to be overcome in order to live a moral life. Compassion allows individuals to transcend their self-centeredness and act for the benefit of others, whereas indifference is a form of egoism that hinders moral conduct. Moses mocks old Doc and still pities him: “It kind of makes your heart give.” See Schopenhauer.
  • “Was old Lethe roaring, making you forget?”: Lethe means oblivion, forgetfulness, or concealment. Lethe is the river of forgetfulness in Hades, from which the dead drank to forget their lives. See Greek Mythology.
  • “How was old Charon that rowed the boat?”: Charon is the ferryman of Hades (the underworld). See the Chapter 5 resources and Greek Mythology.
  • “My age, my change of life!”: The change of life is menopause. Moses claims it for himself, as in Chapter 5 he would not be “my mother’s daughter.”
  • “Alpha and Omega, beginning and end!”: “I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the end” (Revelation 22:13). See The Bible.
  • “Man of straws where?”: A man of straw is a weak argument set up to be knocked down, another fallacy for Moses.
  • “bone of my bone”: Adam says of Eve, “This is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh” (Genesis 2:23). See Genesis.
  • “Render unto Caesar the things that are Caesar’s!”: “Render therefore unto Caesar the things which are Caesar’s; and unto God the things that are God’s” (Matthew 22:21). Moses turns it into “Render unto Doc.” See The Bible.
  • “Canst thou draw out leviathan with a hook?”: Moses recites God’s speech on Leviathan from Job 41:1-21 nearly word for word, then adds his own line, “He roareth like a great locomotive.” See The Book of Job.
    • “Or his tongue with a cord which thou lettest down?” (Job 41:1). This phrase metaphorically questions how one might access or influence the hidden, powerful depths of existence: whether within the self, nature, or the cosmos.
  • “What happened to Julius Caesar?”: Julius Caesar was a Roman general and statesman. He was stabbed in the Senate in 44 B.C. by conspirators including Brutus, his friend, and Shakespeare gave him the words “Et tu, Brute?” See Shakespeare.
  • “Hercules, what happened to Hercules?”: Hercules is a half-god in Greek and Roman mythology famous for his strength and adventures. He died through his wife, Deianira, who gave him a shirt soaked in the centaur Nessus’s poisoned blood, believing it a love charm. Burning with it, he built his own funeral pyre, a death by a wife and by fire, like old Josh’s. See Greek Mythology.
  • “Wormwood, dust, ashes”: The burial service commits the body “earth to earth, ashes to ashes, dust to dust” (Book of Common Prayer).
  • “Hewers of wood and drawers of water!”: The Gibeonites were made servants of Israel (Joshua 9:21). See The Bible.
  • “Was I not made to be the king of the earth?”: Genesis 1:26 reads, “let them have dominion over the fish of the sea, and over the fowl of the air.” This question is a poignant expression of human aspiration confronted by existential despair and the limitations imposed by mortality and circumstance. It highlights themes of lost potential, the transience of life, and the universal confrontation with death that pervades the novel. See Genesis.
  • “No partridges in these mountains”: David says Saul hunts him “as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” (1 Samuel 26:20). See The Bible.
  • “Roosevelt in the White House?”: Moses asks whether old Doc thinks he is Roosevelt, who seemed never to leave the White House. In Chapter 5 Moses swore not to cut his hair until Roosevelt was gone. It may also refer to the New Deal and Social Security as well as other programs. See the Chapter 5 resources.
  • “Don’t believe in free silver”: William Jennings Bryan ran for president in 1896 on free silver and his “Cross of Gold” speech, and Republicans held to the gold standard.
  • “Upon a thin steeple, a fish weather vane”: The fish, ichthys in Greek, was an early Christian sign for Christ.
  • “Cyclops, men whose heads do grow beneath their shoulders”: Othello tells of “the Anthropophagi, and men whose heads / Do grow beneath their shoulders” (Othello 1.3). The Cyclops is the one-eyed giant of the Odyssey, like one-eyed Beatrice. See Shakespeare and Greek Mythology.
  • “dead souls”: This may echo Gogol’s Dead Souls (1842), whose hero buys up the names of dead serfs.
  • “that dream within the dream”: This may refer to Edgar Allan Poe’s poem “A Dream within a Dream” (1849), which says, “All that we see or seem / Is but a dream within a dream.” This dream within a dream is a recurring theme throughout the book. The idea that life is a dream goes back to Plato, Aristotle, and Descartes. The first stanza ends with that statement, and the last stanza turns it into a question: “Is all that we see or seem / But a dream within a dream?” This symbolizes the recursive, elusive quality of existence in the novel: a reality constantly refracted through multiple dreamlike states that challenge the notion of a fixed, singular truth. See Edgar Allan Poe.

Chapter 69

← Chapter 68 · Home · Chapter 70 →

Summary

Vera's room is marked Fire Escape. It has a corn-husk mattress, a "Forget me not" picture of a church steeple, and a slop jar holding someone else's hair combings. The landlord points out the other guests on the way: Moses, a knitting girl named Tillie, an old woman with enormous canaries, and Mr. Weed's shadow. All night, through the thin wall, old Dr. Justice O'Leary rages at Sarah, his dead sister, lists every disease he knows, and mentions his strangest case, a woman who is always pregnant. Vera finally screams at Sarah to go.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · The Tavern Landlord · Mr. Weed · Justice O’Leary · Sarah O’Leary

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Decay and Ruin · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Madness and Sanity · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Birds · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Fire · The House

Allusions: Alice in Wonderland · Ecclesiastes · Genesis · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Shakespeare · The Bible · The Book of Job

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a vivid description of the protagonist's room marked "Fire Escape," featuring a narrow bed stuffed with corn husks, a picture of a silver church steeple with the words "Forget me not," and unsettling details such as a slop jar with sediment and blonde hair combings. This sets a bleak, eerie atmosphere and introduces motifs of decay, memory, and forgotten lives. The reflection of only the eyes in the warped mirror symbolizes fragmented identity or perception. The creaking rocking chair suggests unseen presences, hinting at the spectral or psychological elements in the narrative.
  • The landlord is depicted as a colorful, loquacious man with tattoos, a rich past, and contradictory traits: strong yet faded in color, worldly yet tied to this dilapidated hotel. His monologues reveal a layered personality and provide backstory on Mr. Weed and other characters like Moses and “Tillie,” a young girl who knits baby hoods. The landlord’s tales weave together local myths, histories, and the odd coexistence of the living and dead in the hotel. His perspective contrasts with Mr. Weed’s silence and introduces themes of memory, reputation, and the passage of time.
  • The landlord’s comments about Mr. Weed and his “shadow” who speaks for him reveal a symbolic duality. Mr. Weed himself is cautious and reserved, while his shadow is outspoken and more intriguing. This duality might represent the tension between public persona and hidden truths, or between the living and the spectral. Mr. Weed’s reputed success in his enterprises and his role in the local community add complexity to his character.
  • The most emotionally intense passages are the doctor’s anguished soliloquies and interactions with "Sarah," a ghostly, haunting figure who disrupts his life. The doctor mourns the loss and disgrace Sarah represents, reflecting on death, memory, and human frailty. His repeated curses ("God damn it, Sarah!") and the description of Sarah as a “baby” and “senile” with cold breath and sores evoke themes of decay, madness, and the inescapability of death. The doctor’s anguish over his professional failures and the burden of his memories gives a tragic depth to his character.
  • Across these passages, there is a pervasive meditation on death, both literal and symbolic. The doctor’s reflections on Sarah’s death, Mr. Weed’s shadow, and the hotel’s other inhabitants (like the chained turkey buzzards and the silent old people) create a liminal space where life and death intermingle. The chapter explores how memory can be both a blessing and a curse, how the past haunts the present, and how human dignity is fragile in the face of time and mortality.
  • The room’s designation as a “Fire Escape” and the landlord’s references to the hotel as a “good enough port for a man in a storm” symbolize refuge and escape but also confinement and decay. The hotel is a microcosm of a decaying world where ghosts, literal or metaphorical, linger, and where the characters’ histories are inscribed in the physical and social environment.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Vera

  • A reflective observer who notices the eerie attributes of the room and the unfolding drama next door.

The Landlord

  • A loquacious, colorful figure with a tattooed, lion-like chest, who shares stories of Mr. Weed, the hotel’s history, and his own varied past as a sailor, performer, and soldier. He is knowledgeable but somewhat cynical, providing a bridge between reality and the supernatural elements.

Mr. Weed and His Shadow

  • Mentioned as mysterious figures, Mr. Weed is a man of few words, while his shadow is more outspoken and unsettling. The landlord distinguishes between the two, adding layers to the mythos of the hotel.

Dr. Justice O’Leary

  • An aging, embittered physician who is haunted by "Sarah," a ghost or symbolic figure representing death, disgrace, and the burden of his past. He is portrayed as mad, desperate, and filled with sorrow and rage.

Sarah O’Leary

  • A ghostly, troubling figure who haunts Dr. O’Leary’s room and mind. She is described variously as a dead woman, a baby, a spiteful presence, and a symbol of decay and disgrace. Her interactions with the doctor reveal themes of memory, loss, and the inescapable presence of death.

Other Figures

  • The bus driver, Imadaisy (Imadaisy is described as someone that Esther Longtree knew. Ima: Derived from Hebrew, means "mother" and is associated with qualities of nurturing and care. Daisy: The English word for the flower, which is often associated with innocence, purity, and new beginnings. The flower's name originally comes from the Old English for "day's eye," referring to its petals that open at dawn. When put together, the name suggests a "motherly flower" or "motherly purity." The combination likely refers to the caring and pure qualities associated with motherhood, with a historical origin in the family names of its bearers.), and various clients of the doctor add depth to the setting’s community. Tillie is a young girl who lives in the hotel where the narrator, Vera, is staying. The landlord describes her as "a very young girl" who will knit a baby hood for Vera. He mentions her casually while showing Vera the corridors of the hotel, specifically pointing to the door opposite Vera’s room. The landlord’s description suggests that Tillie is a quiet presence in the hotel, possibly involved in simple, caring tasks like knitting. This detail appears amid the landlord’s rambling about the hotel’s other eccentric inhabitants, such as the old woman who keeps canaries as big as turkey buzzards and the hangman’s shadow. The landlord seems to treat Tillie as a benign, almost innocuous figure within this strange and lively environment.

  • “The bed was narrow, the mattress stuffed with corn husks” corn husks were used from the Colonial era to the 19th century.
  • “slop jar” were used along with a pitcher and basin in hotels until the 1950s.
  • loquacious means talkative or tending to talk a great deal.

It was a special, richly decorated robe given to him by his father Jacob, symbolizing his favoritism, which fueled his brothers' jealousy, leading them to sell Joseph into slavery and present the bloody coat to Jacob as proof he was dead. The garment, likely a regal tunic with long sleeves, signified Joseph's special status and set him apart, though it also provoked envy, highlighting themes of favoritism, betrayal, and God's guiding purpose through hardship.
  • "Naked, we come into this world, and naked, we go out of it." The quote comes from the Bible, found in both Ecclesiastes 5:15 and Job 1:21. The phrase reflects the inevitability of human vulnerability at birth and death, stripping away all pretenses or material concerns, which is a poignant theme running through the novel’s exploration of mortality, identity, and human frailty.
  • “circus fat lady” The "fat lady" in the U.S. circus was a prominent sideshow attraction from the 19th to mid-20th centuries, embodying spectacle, curiosity, and sometimes exploitation, with famous figures like Lottie Whitlock, billed as the original "Fat Lady," and later stars like Alice from Dallas and Celesta Geyer (Dolly Dimples) who gained fame and fortune before some dramatically lost weight, highlighting societal views on size and health. These performers, part of the "freak show" tradition, used their size to build successful careers, often achieving celebrity status within the circus world, though facing exploitation and objectification.
  • “lamer ducks” an official (especially the president) in the final period of office, after the election of a successor; an ineffectual or unsuccessful person or thing.
  • Phineas Taylor Barnum was an American showman, businessman, and politician, remembered for promoting celebrated hoaxes and founding the Barnum & Bailey Circus with James Anthony Bailey. Barnum went on to create America's first aquarium and to expand the wax figure department of his museum. His Seven Grand Salons demonstrated the Seven Wonders of the World which claimed 850,000 curiosities.
  • “Fire Escape” emerged in the U.S. from the 1800s, driven by deadly urban fires, initially as simple ladders and later evolving into complex external stair systems, with Anna Connelly's 1887 patent for a bridge-like design becoming foundational; they became common after laws following disasters like the Triangle Shirtwaist Factory fire but faded in new construction after the 1960s as modern sprinklers, alarms, and improved firefighting equipment made them less essential, though they remain iconic features in older cityscapes.
  • “Hardening of the arteries” atherosclerosis, is a widespread issue in the U.S., a slow-developing disease where plaque (fat, cholesterol) narrows arteries, significantly contributing to heart attacks and strokes, the leading causes of death, affecting roughly half of Americans aged 45-84, often silently until serious events occur, with risk factors including high blood pressure, smoking, high cholesterol, and diabetes.
  • “Maybe I was surprised by the hangman’s confessions” The passage explores themes of death, violence, and respectability, highlighting the banality and repetitiveness of horror, and the unsettling coexistence of brutality and normalcy in the hangman’s life. The gruesome crimes serve as a backdrop to the hangman’s enigmatic identity and the eerie atmosphere of the setting.
  • “model dairy farms” modernization started in the 1879 and continued to World War II.
  • The Last War may refer to World War II since World War I was referred to as the Great War.
  • “Intelligence during the Last War” Before WWII, the United States had virtually no permanent, non-departmental peacetime foreign intelligence services. The war effort necessitated the rapid creation and expansion of intelligence services globally, characterized by several key developments. The Office of Strategic Services (OSS) was established in 1942, the OSS was the U.S.'s first full-fledged organization for intelligence and secret operations, coordinating espionage behind enemy lines for all U.S. armed forces. Its functions included intelligence gathering, propaganda, subversion, and post-war planning. The OSS was dissolved at the end of the war, but its veterans became the foundation of the post-war intelligence community, including the CIA. The FBI played a central role in U.S. counterintelligence efforts, operating a significant foreign intelligence collection effort in the Western Hemisphere from 1940-1947. Its Special Intelligence Service (SIS) identified hundreds of Axis spies and propaganda agents, confiscating secret radio stations and even using enemy networks to feed false information back to Nazi Germany. Signals Intelligence (SIGINT) and Codebreaking made a strategic contribution to the Allied victory, particularly in the Battle of the Atlantic (breaking German Enigma codes) and at the Battle of Midway (breaking Japanese military codes). While human intelligence (HUMINT) and codebreaking were vital, up to 80% of the intelligence for major operations like D-Day came from aerial photo reconnaissance. WWII ushered in an "intelligence revolution" due to rapidly advancing military technology and the need for new methods of collection and analysis. The war led to an unprecedented international willingness to share intelligence and accelerated advances in technical collection means. The end of WWII marked a pivotal moment in the history of intelligence, leading to the creation of a permanent peacetime intelligence structure to address the emerging Cold War.
  • The OSS was disbanded and replaced temporarily by the Strategic Services Unit (SSU) and the Central Intelligence Group (CIG). The National Security Act of 1947 established the independent Central Intelligence Agency (CIA) to coordinate and provide objective intelligence analysis for policymakers. The State Department's Bureau of Intelligence and Research (INR) emerged as the initial civilian component of the intelligence community, and military intelligence components were restructured as well. This period essentially formalized intelligence as a continuous, critical function of government, rather than a temporary measure solely for wartime use.
  • “Frenchies” is an informal and sometimes derogatory term used describing French people.
  • Remember the Marne may refer to Remember the Maine! To hell with Spain! after the USS Maine. It was a United States Navy ship that sank in Havana Harbor on February 15, 1898, contributing to the outbreak of the Spanish–American War in April 1898. Although the USS Maine explosion was not a direct cause, it served as a catalyst that accelerated the events leading up to the war.
  • "Hun" was used during WW2 to refer to Germans, a pejorative nickname revived from WW1 propaganda, linking them to the barbaric, nomadic Huns of antiquity known for cruelty under Attila, especially after Kaiser Wilhelm II's 1900 speech encouraging similar savagery in China; Allied propaganda effectively used this to portray Nazis as barbaric, though terms like "Fritz" or "Jerry" (British) and "Heinie" (American) were also common for German soldiers.
  • Hagenbeck’s out of Berlin may refer to The Tierpark Hagenbeck zoo in Stellingen, Hamburg, Germany. The collection began in 1863 with animals that belonged to Carl Hagenbeck Sr., a fishmonger who became an amateur animal collector. The park itself was founded by Carl Hagenbeck Jr. in 1907. It is known for being the first zoo to use open enclosures surrounded by moats, rather than barred cages, to better approximate animals' natural environments. Among his collections, however, were also human beings whom he exhibited in "human zoos". The private zoo is still run by the Hagenbeck family.
  • “mad as March Hare” is an idiom meaning extremely silly, eccentric, or crazy, originating from the frenzied, unpredictable behavior of European hares during their spring breeding season (March), which includes frantic chases, high leaps, and "boxing" matches where females swat males away to discourage unwanted advances. This phrase was popularized by Lewis Carroll's Alice's Adventures in Wonderland, featuring the eccentric March Hare at the Mad Hatter's tea party, though the behavior itself is a real, albeit misunderstood, part of hare mating rituals, not actual madness.

  • “Oh, God! Let this cup pass from him…” from Matthew 26:39 where Jesus is asking God if he has to go through with this. This moment is part of a larger, surreal and symbolic interaction filled with themes of death, memory, disgrace, and the passage of time, as the doctor grapples with his own mortality and the ghostly reminders of a troubled past.
  • “My God! Why hast thou deserted me?” From Psalm 22, according to the Gospels, Jesus spoke these words during the Crucifixion, after he had suffered on the cross for three hours. It is a cry of abandonment and despair, reflecting Dr. O’Leary’s inner turmoil as he confronts death, loss, and the haunting past.

It's similar to "You can't get blood from a stone" and signifies the futility of demanding something unavailable.
  • Mayo Clinic originated with the medical practice of William Worrall Mayo, M.D. who immigrated to the United States in 1846. He had two sons. The Mayo brothers were financially successful and professionally prominent. The Mayo Clinic is still in the US and has opened branches in several countries.

  • “Lady Gonorrhea” was first documented in ancient Greece by Galen, who used the term from the Greek words gonos (semen) and rhoia (flow) to describe what he mistakenly called an "involuntary ejaculation of semen". The name "the clap" emerged in the 1500s, originating from the French "les clapiers," a term for brothels where the disease was common. While medieval and early modern records describe symptoms, the specific bacterium, Neisseria gonorrhoeae, wasn't identified until 1879 by Albert Neisser, though the connection to women's health was sometimes misunderstood.
