Chapter 49

← Chapter 48 · Home · Chapter 50 →

Summary

In the longest of his meditations, Mr. Spitzer moves through a frozen cosmos of the mind. He mourns Martha, the last passenger pigeon, who died at the Cincinnati Zoo in 1918, weeping for others who did not weep for him. He lists the contradictions of his existence, dying through life and living through death. He wonders whether he is one man or two, bound so closely to his brother that he cannot tell which he is.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Martha the Passenger Pigeon · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Identity and the Self · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

Symbols: Birds · Fireflies · Mirrors and Reflections · Moon and Stars · Music and Instruments · Shadows · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Aristotle · Augustine and Christian Theology · Buddhism · Descartes and Dualism · Empiricism (Locke, Berkeley, Hume) · Kant and Hegel · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Plato and Platonism · Spinoza · Taoism and Zhuangzi · The Problem of Universals · Time, Physics, and Chaos Theory · William James and Pragmatism

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Angels and Archangels · Astronomy · Deafness and Sign Language · Genesis · Greek Mythology · Judaism · Music and Composers · Revelation and the Apocalypse · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible

Key passages

From the research

  • Mr. Spitzer experiences a profound disorientation where he "was disoriented by his great experience of living when he was dead, waking only when he was sleeping, sleeping in a watery grave or in an ice hole". This passage encapsulates the paradoxical state of existence and non-existence, blurring the boundaries between life and death, wakefulness and sleep.
  • The imagery of landscapes and continents being lost or carried away like feathers or lace handkerchiefs symbolizes the transient, fragile, and mutable nature of reality itself.
  • Mr. Spitzer contemplates vast cosmic elements: "Ice had frozen so hard that it was like a dome or like the shell of an egg... Ice was frozen into shapes of frozen roofs over the winding rivers and the seas and the lakes... ice piled up like weird spires and minarets and bell towers". This grand imagery conveys a frozen, timeless cosmos, a metaphor for stasis, death, or suspended animation of existence.
  • The passage also reflects on the impossibility of finding solid ground or stable meaning in a world dominated by illusions and transformations.
  • Mr. Spitzer mourns the death of Martha, the last passenger pigeon, noting the poignant historical moment: "Martha, who expired September 14, at one o’clock in the afternoon just as the clock was tolling one, 1918, A.D., at the Cincinnati zoo". This event symbolizes the extinction of a species and, metaphorically, the loss of innocence, beauty, and connection to nature.
  • His grief for Martha becomes a symbol for his own loneliness and the universal sorrow at loss and disappearance: "He wept for others who wept not for him".
  • The novel frequently questions the nature of the self: "He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image... one of whom no unitary statement could be made". This reflects a fragmented identity, the multiplicity of selves, or even the illusion of a stable self.
  • The motif of doubling and mirrored selves recurs: "how often he had nearly collided with himself though this would seem impossible". This evokes existential ambiguity and the fluidity of personal identity across time and space.
  • Mr. Spitzer embraces a paradoxical philosophy: So he had come "to trust only the false... For why... should he trust the truth which had already failed him if the false would never fail". This reflects a deep skepticism about knowledge, reality, and the reliability of perception or memory.
  • The passage suggests that constancy is found only in inconstancy, and that faith in truth is always tentative and fraught.
  • The chapter emphasizes the unreliability and fragmentation of memory: "His memory... had omitted so much, perhaps the whole content of mortal life, of certain death".
  • Time is portrayed as fluid, uncertain, and perhaps even illusory: "Perhaps there was no time... What calendar keeps the sea of the months flowing into the months...?".
  • Reality is likened to a dream or a fog: "the fog concealed the barnacle, the rose, the wing, the star... obliterated the obvious differences between the living and the dead".
  • Mr. Spitzer reflects on the interrelatedness of life’s opposites: "He died through sickness, died through health... died through happiness which should have saved him, died through sorrow, sorrow by which he lived, died by not dying, died by living, lived by dying".
  • Love is depicted as immortal and paradoxical: "when love lived, it died—but having died, it lived and could not die".
  • The text repeatedly returns to Mr. Spitzer’s profound loneliness and his longing for understanding and communion: "He trusted those who had lost... all those who were dispossessed and wandering through the storm of years as he was. They drew him nearest to the city. They were all his loves because he could not love or could love only by indirection".
  • His existential isolation is underscored by the metaphor of walking "through the rain of the city where the rain of the city drummed upon the dark or golden porches and roofs" and feeling himself "oblivious to them”.
  • Water, ice, and the sea are pervasive symbols throughout the chapter, representing both life and death, fluidity and stasis, memory and oblivion: He was like a shipwreck, "his hull broken... paying out more water than the seas contained". The rising waters symbolize overwhelming forces beyond control and the engulfing nature of death and oblivion.
  • Near the end, Mr. Spitzer is described as "the living lighthouse at that one moment when he saw his light, moment when he was dying... his own light shining, shining from him". This image captures the simultaneous presence of life and death, light and darkness, as well as the enduring, though fragile, spark of consciousness amid cosmic dissolution.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • A complex figure symbolizing the human struggle with mortality, memory, and meaning.
  • Described metaphorically as a shipwreck, a shadow, a lighthouse, a phantom, and a musician whose music is unheard.
  • His physical ailments (e.g., irregular pulse, short breath) parallel his metaphysical disintegration and confusion.
  • He functions as a “mourner” and witness to extinction, loss, and the fading of worlds.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s paradoxical existence of alive yet dead, remembering yet forgetting makes him a liminal, almost mythical figure.

The Old Caretaker

  • Represents skepticism, finality, and the harsh reality of extinction.
  • His views on Martha the passenger pigeon emphasize the finality of death and the absence of spiritual continuation.

Martha (Passenger Pigeon)

  • Symbolizes lost beauty, extinction, and irretrievable loss.
  • Her death is mourned as the death of a species, a cosmic event, and a personal loss for Mr. Spitzer.

Research: Themes

Life, Death, and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Mr. Spitzer’s state blurs the boundary between living and dead. He lived “when he was dead, waking only when he was sleeping”.
  • Death is portrayed as a paradox: he “died at his zenith because he was at his nadir, died at his nadir because he was at his zenith”.
  • The text questions the reality of death and life, suggesting both may be illusions: “He knew there was no death because there was no life”.
  • The theme of immortality is paradoxical, with Mr. Spitzer’s spirit existing in a liminal state, neither fully present nor gone.

Memory and Forgetfulness

See: Memory and the Past

  • Mr. Spitzer struggles with remembering and forgetting, his past and identity constantly shifting.
  • His “forgetfulness veiling his forgetfulness” and “oblivion hiding behind his oblivion” illustrate layers of fading consciousness.
  • He questions the reliability of memory, pondering if he ever truly lived or if life was just a “mistaken dream”.

Identity and Self-Perception

See: Identity and the Self

  • There is a profound ambiguity regarding Mr. Spitzer’s identity, “He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image”.
  • The motif of doubling, shadows, and reflections recurs, contributing to his fragmented self-understanding.
  • He often quarrels with himself or his shadow, suggesting an internal conflict and fractured self.

The Natural World and Extinction

See: Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The extinction of the passenger pigeon, Martha, serves as a poignant symbol of loss and mourning.
  • Nature is depicted as vast, mystical, and fragile all subject to decay and disappearance.
  • The natural world mirrors the human condition as being both transient, vulnerable, and caught in cycles of life and death.

The Cosmic and the Mystical

See: Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos

  • The cosmos, stars, and celestial imagery permeate the text, emphasizing vastness, mystery, and the unknowable.
  • Mr. Spitzer imagines his existence woven into universal patterns, yet feels lost and disoriented within them.
  • The narrative contemplates the idea of multiple dimensions, alternate realities, and the eternal recurrence of life and death.

Isolation and Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Despite being surrounded by crowds, Mr. Spitzer experiences profound solitude and alienation.
  • His relationships are ambiguous since he mourns lost loves, mourns a lost species, and even quarrels with his own shadow.
  • The idea of failed communication and the search for understanding pervade, especially in his interactions with the blind and deaf.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Water and Ice

See: The Sea and Water · Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Recurring images of frozen waters, ice domes, and watery graves symbolize stasis, death, and the frozen moment between life and death.
  • Water also represents fluidity, dream states, and the passage between worlds.

Stars and Celestial Bodies

See: Moon and Stars

  • Stars represent memory, the soul, and cosmic order, yet are also fading, crumbling, or melting snowflakes.
  • The interplay of light and shadow among stars mirrors the ambiguities of life and death.

Shadows and Reflections

See: Mirrors and Reflections · Shadows

  • Shadows emphasize duality, absence, and the elusive nature of identity.
  • Reflections question reality versus illusion, with Mr. Spitzer sometimes chasing shadows or reflections rather than reality.

Birds (Pigeons, Blackbirds, Fireflies)

See: Birds · Fireflies

  • Birds symbolize life, freedom, and the passage of souls.
  • The extinction of the passenger pigeon is a metaphor for loss and the fragility of existence.
  • Fireflies and moths symbolize faint, fragile light, hope, memory, or the soul’s flicker.

Music

See: Music and Instruments

  • Music is a metaphor for existence, memory, and communication.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s music is “unspoken,” “unheard,” and a “barcarolle” rocking on waves, symbolizing the elusive nature of his life and thoughts.

Research: Resources

  • “grace note” is a musical ornament, a brief note that precedes and embellishes the main note in a musical passage. It means a small, delicate, and ornamental component of a larger composition of life and death as a metaphor for the subtle, transient experiences and nuances that enrich the human condition but are often overlooked or not fully grasped.
  • “surrey lumbering under Alpha and the long-necked horses flying under Omega” This is a richly symbolic and poetic image that evokes a cosmic and mystical scene blending earthly and celestial elements. A surrey is a type of horse-drawn carriage that moves slowly and heavily ("lumbering"), here symbolizing a grounded, earthly presence or journey. The long-necked horses flying under Omega contrasts with the surrey by introducing a sense of ethereal or spiritual ascent, as Omega is the last letter of the Greek alphabet and often symbolizes the end or ultimate limit, while Alpha (the first letter) symbolizes the beginning. Together, this imagery suggests a movement or journey that spans from the beginning (Alpha) to the end (Omega), from the earthly to the cosmic or spiritual realm. The surrey’s slow, heavy pace represents the physical, tangible world, while the flying longnecked horses under Omega evoke a transcendent, perhaps heavenly or otherworldly dimension. This juxtaposition reflects themes of transition, the passage of time, and the connection between mortal life and the infinite or eternal. In the broader context of the novel, which often blurs the boundaries between reality, dreams, life, and death, this phrase encapsulates the interplay between the material and the spiritual, the finite and the infinite. It evokes the sense of a journey through different realms or states of being, moving from the concrete to the mystical as part of the narrator’s or characters’ passage through life and beyond. The phrase poetically envisions a liminal space where earthly life (the surrey) and cosmic or spiritual forces (the flying horses under Omega) coexist and interact, marking the continuum of existence from beginning to end.
  • “miaowed” is the spelling before 1842. It is still used in Spanish, German, and French. Cats in Ancient Egypt were called Mau.
  • “a road not taken” may refer to the famous Robert Frost poem, The Road Not Taken. In the chapter it is a profound metaphor about life's uncertainties, the passage of time, and the elusive nature of reality, memory, and identity.
  • “causes which were perhaps never popular in any public sense but of which he had been an unsolicited and unelected representative, a minority representing a majority, a hidden majority like those sleeping in the churchyard” This refers to Mr. Spitzer's role as a defender or advocate of unpopular or overlooked causes. This means that Mr. Spitzer, the character in question, has taken it upon himself to represent issues or people that society at large does not openly support or acknowledge. Although these causes are unpopular publicly, they might actually concern a large, silent majority: people who are marginalized, ignored, or forgotten, symbolized here as the "hidden majority like those sleeping in the churchyard." The churchyard metaphor emphasizes the invisibility and silence of this group, much like the dead who lie quietly without public recognition. Mr. Spitzer acts as an advocate for those unseen or unheard in society, standing for "minority" causes that actually affect many more people than is apparent. His representation is unsolicited and unelected, indicating that he has not been formally chosen or asked to take on this role but has done so out of conviction or necessity.
  • “But why should any man weep if the heavens wept for him?” Found in Islamic, Ancient Egyptian, and Jewish tradition, it is a metaphorical way to express profound sorrow and the impact of a loss on a cosmic scale. Moses 7, Jeremiah 8:19, Genesis 6:6, John 11:35 It reflects a profound meditation on sorrow, mourning, and the vastness of grief that transcends individual human experience. This rhetorical question suggests that if the heavens themselves are mourning a person’s fate, then the individual weeping might seem redundant or insignificant in comparison. It evokes the idea that cosmic forces or the universe acknowledge and encompass the sorrow of human lives on a scale far greater than any one person could express. This notion ties into the novel’s theme of the interconnectedness of human suffering with the natural and cosmic order. The mourning of the heavens symbolizes a universal sympathy and recognition of loss, making individual grief a part of a larger, perhaps more meaningful, cosmic process. It also hints at the shared destiny of all beings, where personal sorrow is enveloped within the universal cycles of life and death. The question serves to elevate the concept of mourning beyond the personal, suggesting that human tears are part of a grander, universal lamentation that the heavens themselves embody. It invites the reader to contemplate the scale of grief and the place of individual suffering within the vastness of existence.
  • “To weep for himself would seem an excess since he was already dead or dying to this world, this world dying. He wept for others who wept not for him.” Luke 23:28 It reflects the deep existential sorrow and isolation experienced by the character Mr. Spitzer. This means that Mr. Spitzer feels that mourning for himself would be excessive or unnecessary because, in a profound sense, he is already "dead" or fading away from the world: a world itself in decline or death. His own life or presence is diminishing, so grieving for his own condition seems redundant to him. Instead, he directs his sorrow outward, feeling grief for others who, ironically, do not mourn him in return. This expresses a poignant loneliness and the idea that he is disconnected from reciprocal human care or recognition. It highlights his role as a solitary mourner and witness, caught between life and death, mourning not only his own fading existence but also the indifference or absence of mourning from others. It also suggests the theme of unshared or unacknowledged sorrow, and the idea that while he is "dead" in a metaphysical or emotional sense, the world around him is also dying, creating a shared but unreciprocated experience of loss.
  • “Hallo, halloo!” is used to incite dogs to chase during a hunt.
  • “He knew not whether he was himself or an image contained within an image” It reflects Mr. Spitzer’s profound confusion about his own identity and existence. It conveys his sense of being caught in layers of reality and illusion, unable to distinguish the true self from reflections or copies of himself. This uncertainty symbolizes a deeper metaphysical dilemma about the nature of selfhood and reality, where Mr. Spitzer feels like he might be a mere reflection or shadow within multiple layers of perception. This theme is consistent throughout the novel, where characters often grapple with fragmented identities, blurred realities, and the coexistence of life and death. Mr. Spitzer’s experience of not knowing if he is the original or just an image demonstrates his alienation and the dissolution of a fixed sense of self, emphasizing the novel’s exploration of illusion, memory, and the elusive nature of personal identity.
  • “the last passenger pigeon known to earth” On a monument to the Pigeon by Aldo Leopold, 1947. It refers to the extinction of the passenger pigeon species, symbolizing the theme of loss, impermanence, and the passing of an era. The last known passenger pigeon, named Martha, died in 1918, and this event is used in the novel as a poignant metaphor for finality and the irrevocable nature of death. Mr. Spitzer, a character deeply preoccupied with memory, loss, and mortality, mourns Martha as the last of her kind, reflecting on the broader human experience of loss and the fleeting nature of life. The passage emphasizes the idea that once something is lost (whether a species, a person, or a moment in time) it cannot be recovered, no matter how much one might hope or search. Martha’s death marks the end of a natural lineage, and the mourning for her is akin to mourning for all that is irretrievably gone. This metaphor extends beyond the extinction of the pigeon to encompass the novel’s larger exploration of bereavement, memory, and the ephemerality of existence. The last passenger pigeon becomes a symbol of the finality of death and the sorrow that accompanies the loss of anything precious and irreplaceable.
  • “How precious then was life, this fleeting moment, and all things illegal as the dreamer and the dream of this continuing life, as all who were destroyed by politicians and lawyers and the great powers” It reflects a meditation on the fragility and transience of life. Here, life is described as a brief, precious moment (fleeting and ephemeral) emphasizing how temporary and delicate human existence is. The phrase suggests that much of what sustains life or is intertwined with it (perhaps desires, hopes, or actions) might be seen as illicit or forbidden, metaphorically “illegal” in the grand scheme of existence. The dreamer and the dream symbolize the ongoing illusion or ephemeral nature of life itself, where reality and illusion blend. The reference points to the harsh realities and external forces, such as political authority, legal systems, and powerful institutions that often oppress, limit, or ultimately destroy individual lives and freedoms. It underscores a theme of human vulnerability not only to the passage of time but also to the societal and political structures that shape and sometimes devastate lives. This passage expresses the preciousness of life despite its fragility and the dangers posed by external powers, while also acknowledging the illusory, dreamlike quality of existence itself.
  • “If there were no pigeons, could there be people or pigeon people or the pigeon-colored dawn, rose and blue and silver and gold mottled like the pigeon’s wing, the twilight of this hour which was Mr. Spitzer’s dawn? He had lost all sense of the hour.” The passenger pigeon’s story is a powerful symbol of the consequences of human actions, overexploitation, and habitat destruction. It uses pigeons as a symbolic motif representing life, presence, and continuity in the world. Pigeons are intertwined with the imagery of dawn and twilight, symbolizing the passage of time and the subtle transitions between states of being: night and day, life and death, consciousness and oblivion. The “pigeon-colored dawn” evokes a richly mottled, variegated light that suggests complexity and ambiguity rather than a clear-cut moment in time. For Mr. Spitzer, the pigeons and the pigeon-colored dawn reflect his disorientation and loss of temporal bearings. The phrase “He had lost all sense of the hour” indicates his detachment from conventional time and reality. His sense of time is fractured, much like his identity and existence, which are key themes in the novel. The pigeons, as a natural and persistent presence, contrast with Mr. Spitzer’s drifting consciousness and his fading grasp on reality and temporality. This passage metaphorically expresses Mr. Spitzer’s state of confusion, alienation, and the blurring of boundaries between moments, where even the dawn, usually a clear marker of time, is uncertain and indistinct to him.
  • Mark which may refer to Mark Catesby who painted pictures of animals including the passenger pigeon.
  • “three trinitarian minutes. Father, Mother, Son.” It refers to a deeply symbolic and religiously resonant moment tied to the concept of the Holy Trinity in Christian theology, which comprises the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit. Here, the narrator uses "three trinitarian minutes" to mark a precise and solemn moment of time: three minutes that carry the weight and significance of the Trinity. This moment is described as the exact time emphasizing a sacred and profound point of transition between life and death. The invocation of "Father, Mother, Son" not only echoes the Christian triad but also ties into themes of family, birth, death, and spiritual passage that permeate the novel. The phrase captures the intertwining of temporal measurement with spiritual meaning. It suggests that the passing was not merely a physical event but also a metaphysical one, framed within the religious and cosmic order that the book often reflects upon. The mention of these "three trinitarian minutes" underscores the gravity and sanctity of the passage of life into death, as well as the complex fusion of earthly and spiritual elements.
  • threnodies is a lament.
  • “only the female endures” - Women are often depicted as enduring various forms of hardship, including prolonged stress and instability, without succumbing to their circumstances. Some believe that societal expectations and responsibilities, like caregiving, can contribute to women developing a strong ability to persevere through difficulties. This concept is reflected in literature and cultural narratives, where women are often portrayed as resilient characters who face challenges with strength and fortitude. While men often dominate in shorter, more intense endurance events, women demonstrate strong performance in longer distances, particularly ultra-endurance activities. This is partly attributed to potential physiological advantages, such as efficient fat utilization and greater fatigue resistance in women during prolonged exercise. Psychological factors like strong mental resilience and consistent pacing strategies are also believed to contribute to women's success in these events. It's important to acknowledge that the experiences of endurance and resilience differ based on individual circumstances and intersectional factors like race and culture. For instance, Black women in horror narratives are described as "Enduring Women" who face different and more persistent threats than the traditional "Final Girl" trope, highlighting the complexities of navigating misogynoir and societal challenges. It is crucial to recognize the importance of understanding resilience within the context of women's lived experiences and the societal factors that influence their well-being. It underscores a contrast between the fleeting, fragile nature of life and the sustaining, enduring role of the female, whether literally through reproduction or metaphorically as a symbol of lasting strength and continuity in a world marked by change, decay, and death.
  • “Every Martha must have her Mary” may refer to Mary and her sister Martha from the Bible. They appear in Luke 10:38 and John 11. It reflects a symbolic and thematic contrast between two archetypal figures, drawing from the biblical story of Martha and Mary, sisters of Lazarus. Martha is often associated with active service, practical duties, and worldly concerns, while Mary represents contemplative devotion, spiritual insight, and inner life. The phrase suggests that for every practical, perhaps burdensome, figure like Martha, who is engaged in the material and often difficult tasks of life, there is a corresponding Mary, who embodies a more spiritual, gentle, or receptive aspect. The phrase highlights the duality in human experience in general: the coexistence of worldly struggle and spiritual or emotional depth. It also points to the idea that even those who carry heavy burdens (Marthas) have their counterpart in those who nurture and embody grace and hope (Marys). This symbolic reference underscores themes of loss, maternal suffering, spiritual yearning, and the interplay between external realities and inner lives that run throughout the narrative.
  • “to all those beauties which never should have been expressed” then he would be “threatened with the Federal pen”. It has been customary even with non-violent actions of protest or resistance that the federal government starts their prison term charges at 35 years. In at least one instance this led to Aaron Swartz committing suicide. It refers metaphorically to the intangible, elusive, and perhaps forbidden or hidden aspects of life, art, or existence: those subtle, delicate, or ineffable qualities that are difficult to fully reveal or communicate. These "beauties" could symbolize hidden truths, deep emotions, or mysterious experiences that the characters or the narrator encounters, which are beyond ordinary perception or societal acceptance. When it says that he would be “threatened with the Federal pen,” this means that if he were to openly express or expose these hidden truths or forbidden beauties, he would face serious consequences from legal or governmental authorities. The “Federal pen” symbolizes the power of law enforcement or government censorship that could punish or suppress such revelations. Metaphorically, it conveys the idea that revealing certain profound or secret realities could be dangerous or forbidden, with threats of punishment looming over those who dare to disclose them.
  • “Boston, the Great Hub” may refer to “The Hub” a nickname derived from Oliver Wendell Holmes’s description of the State House as “the hub of the solar system” in his 1858 essays, The Autocrat of the Breakfast Table.
  • “It is possible that we are illusions in the light-streaked fog.” It reflects a deep philosophical and existential uncertainty permeating the novel.   • Problem of Universals - The problem of universals is an ancient question from metaphysics that has inspired a range of philosophical topics and disputes. "Should the properties an object has in common with other objects, such as color and shape, be considered to exist beyond those objects? And if a property exists separately from objects, what is the nature of that existence?” The problem of universals relates to various inquiries closely related to metaphysics, logic, and epistemology, as far back as Plato and Aristotle, in efforts to define the mental connections a human makes when they understand a property such as shape or color to be the same in nonidentical objects. Universals are qualities or relations found in two or more entities. As an example, if all cup holders are circular in some way, circularity may be considered a universal property of cup holders. Further, if two daughters can be considered female offspring of Frank, the qualities of being female, offspring, and of Frank, are universal properties of the two daughters. Many properties can be universal: being human, red, male or female, liquid or solid, big or small, etc. Philosophers agree that human beings can talk and think about universals, but disagree on whether universals exist in reality beyond mere thought and speech.
  • William James - Though James certainly agreed with Peirce and against Berkeley that general ideas exist as a psychological fact, he was a nominalist in his ontology: “From every point of view, the overwhelming and portentous character ascribed to universal conceptions is surprising. Why, from Plato and Aristotle, philosophers should have vied with each other in scorn of the knowledge of the particular and in adoration of that of the general, is hard to understand, seeing that the more adorable knowledge ought to be that of the more adorable things and that the things of worth are all concretes and singulars. The only value of universal characters is that they help us, by reasoning, to know new truths about individual things.” William James, The Principles of Psychology (1890). There are at least three ways in which a realist might try to answer James' challenge of explaining the reason why universal conceptions are more lofty than those of particulars: the moral–political answer, the mathematical–scientific answer, and the anti-paradoxical answer.   • There are many philosophical positions regarding universals (also found in Indian and Buddhist philosophy):
  • Platonic realism is the view that universals or forms in this sense, are the causal explanation behind the notion of what things exactly are which is that universals are real entities existing independent of particulars.
  • Aristotelian realism is the rejection of extreme realism. This position establishes the view of a universal as being that of the quality within a thing and every other thing individual to it which is that universals are real entities, but their existence is dependent on the particulars that exemplify them.

  • Realism - Realists tend to argue that universals must be posited as distinct entities in order to account for various phenomena. A common realist argument said to be found in Plato's writings, is that universals are required for certain general words to have meaning and for the sentences in which they occur to be true or false. Take the sentence "Djivan Gasparyan is a musician" for instance. The realist may claim that this sentence is only meaningful and expresses a truth because there is an individual, Djivan Gasparyan, who possesses a certain quality: musicianship. Therefore, it is assumed that the property is a universal which is distinct from the particular individual who has the property.
  • Nominalism - Nominalists assert that only individuals or particulars exist and deny that universals are real. Four major forms of nominalism are predicate nominalism, resemblance nominalism, trope nominalism, and conceptualism. One with a nominalist view claims that we predicate the same property of/to multiple entities, but argues that the entities only share a name and do not have a real quality in common.Nominalists often argue this view by claiming that nominalism can account for all the relevant phenomena, and therefore, by Occam's razor, and its principle of simplicity,nominalism is preferable, since it posits fewer entities. Different variants and versions of nominalism have been endorsed or defended by many.
  • Conceptualism - Conceptualism is a position that is meshed between realism and nominalism. Conceptualists believe that universals can indeed be real, but only existing as concepts within the mind. Conceptualists argue that the "concept" of universals are not mere "inventions but are reflections of similarities among particular things themselves." For example, the concept of 'man' ultimately reflects a similarity amongst Socrates and Kant.

There is a division between perception of an object and how an object really is. What does existence mean and what is the difference between perception and reality?
  • Mr. Spitzer cried when he thought of the last passenger pigeon named Martha. It was named after First Lady Martha Washington. Records have her dying at the Cincinnati zoo at one o’clock in 1914. It is still on display and is a symbol of the threat of extinction.

This theme of chaos versus order is central in the novel.
  • Pigeons embody the fragile boundary between life and death, presence and absence, and the haunting nature of what has vanished but is not forgotten.
  • Mr. Spitzer hears a bell tolling. Bells are a powerful motif for mortality, memory, and the threshold between presence and absence, sound and silence, life and death.   • The passenger pigeon or wild pigeon is an extinct species of pigeon that was endemic to North America. Its common name is derived from the French word passager, meaning to pass by, due to its migratory habits. Passenger pigeons were hunted by Native Americans, but hunting intensified after the arrival of Europeans, particularly in the 19th century. Pigeon meat was commercialized as cheap food, resulting in hunting on a massive scale for many decades. There were several other factors contributing to the decline and subsequent extinction of the species, including shrinking of the large breeding populations necessary for preservation of the species and widespread deforestation, which destroyed its habitat. A slow decline between about 1800 and 1870 was followed by a rapid decline between 1870 and 1890. The last confirmed wild bird is thought to have been shot in 1901. The last captive birds were divided in three groups around the turn of the 20th century, some of which were photographed alive. Martha, thought to be the last passenger pigeon, died on September 1, 1914, at the Cincinnati Zoo. The eradication of the species is a notable example of anthropogenic extinction or extinction of species directly due to human activity.

From the colonial period through the founding of the United States and continuing in the twentieth century, this has entailed torture, terror, sexual abuse, massacres, systematic military occupations, removals of Indigenous peoples from their ancestral territories, forced removal of Native American children to military-like boarding schools, allotment, and a policy of termination. The letters exchanged between Bouquet and Amherst during Pontiac's War, in which Amherst wrote to Bouquet stating that blankets should be used to spread the smallpox virus in order to exterminate Indians. This is part of a broader genocidal attitude that was frequently displayed to Native Americans during the colonization of the Americas. When smallpox swept the northern plains of the U.S. in 1837, the U.S. Secretary of War Lewis Cass ordered that certain Indian tribes not be given smallpox vaccinations, which were provided to other tribes in other areas. The United States has to-date not undertaken any truth commission nor built a memorial for the genocide of indigenous people. It does not acknowledge nor compensate for the historical violence against Native Americans that occurred during territorial expansion to the west coast. American museums such as the Smithsonian Institution do not dedicate a section to the genocide. In 2013, the National Congress of American Indians passed a resolution to create a space for the National American Indian Holocaust Museum inside the Smithsonian, but it was ignored by the latter. In 1970 the Family Planning Services and Population Research caused the sterilization of an estimated 25% of fertile Native American women within 6 years. In 1977, Marie Sanchez, chief tribal judge on the Northern Cheyenne Indian Reservation told the United Nations Convention on Indigenous Rights in Geneva, that Native American women suffered involuntary sterilization which she equated with modern genocide.
  • “...the fisherman was caught in his net, his net going down, he being caught as if he were the great haddock for whom he had fished…” It is a metaphor reflecting the idea of being trapped by one's own actions or fate. Here, the fisherman, who is usually the one capturing fish with a net, ironically becomes the one ensnared in his own net, symbolizing a reversal of roles or the inevitability of being caught by the consequences of one's own deeds. The comparison emphasizes that he falls prey just like the fish he sought to catch, suggesting a loss of control and the inescapability of destiny or self-entrapment. This metaphor fits the novel's broader themes of fatalism, the blurring of roles, and the complex interplay of life and death, where boundaries between hunter and hunted, captor and captive, are often ambiguous or reversed.
  • “You drown in your own drowning, burn in your own burning like that one spark which never will go out though under seas of darkness. Or say you survived the storm, dear sir, and are life’s castaway—you sink in the calm. Greatest shipwreck is this… to sink when there is no storm, for no sadder survivor may there be than this, dear sir, whom now you see or whom I see.” This conversation mirrors the tales of the Tavern landlord in the later chapters. This reflects the novel's broader themes of illusion, suffering, and the ambiguous boundaries between life, death, and existence, and it echoes the complex emotional and existential struggles of the characters.

Her body was frozen in a block of ice and sent to the Smithsonian Institution in Washington, where she was mounted and displayed, so Mr. Spitzer’s visit is a pilgrimage to her remains.

Chapter 68

← Chapter 67 · Home · Chapter 69 →

Summary

At night the bus finally stops. Vera watches Madge and Homer walk away, never to be seen again. She waits to check into the Tavern, a decaying hotel built in 1827, while the landlord talks at the bar with Mr. Weed, a Christian hangman. Mr. Weed's first wife, Marie, hanged herself from a peach tree for fear of another pregnancy. His second wife, Julia, has the mind of a child. His children play at hanging. He carries a pen given to him by a condemned man, a Jew's harp, and a black poker chip of unknown origin, and he considers himself a humanitarian. No clock strikes.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Moses Hunnecker · Mr. Weed · Marie Weed · Julia Weed · The Tavern Landlord · Madge Capehorn · Homer Capehorn

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Fate and Chance · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Guilt, Innocence, and Justice · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · Dogs · Eyes and Blindness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Music and Instruments · Shadows · Snow, Ice, and Winter · Weddings and Funerals

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Existentialism · Phenomenology

Allusions: American Religious Movements · Angels and Archangels · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Genesis · Lynching and Racial Violence · Romantic Poets · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening passage reflects on how coming into a village at night changes one's perception permanently, with shadows that never lift and reality that must be accepted no matter what it is. Vera emphasizes that reality, whether joyful or bleak, is real and must be confronted. This sets a tone of melancholy and philosophical reflection about the nature of existence and perception.
  • The detailed description of the Tavern and the surrounding town conveys a sense of decay, emptiness, and abandonment. The Tavern, despite its sign proclaiming it was built by "God’s servants," appears as just another commercial establishment, run-down and shadowy. This contrasts with Vera's later realization of the Tavern's deeper, more mysterious interior life.
  • Moses’s complex relationship with his old mother, who is sick and deluded, is a poignant metaphor for duty, denial, and the boundaries between love and obligation. Moses obeys "traffic rules" even in the "bridal chamber" with his mother, symbolizing his refusal to engage fully with her fantasies or to take her place.
  • Vera reveals a deep inner fear of their own "defective character," which loves imperfections, distortions, and the dead more than the living reality. This passage underscores a theme of alienation and longing for something unattainable or lost.
  • The arrival and conversation with the professional hangman introduces a major symbolic figure who embodies death, justice, and mercy. Mr. Weed’s reflections on his job, the nature of crime, punishment, and the human conscience provide a grim but humane perspective on life and death.
  • Mr. Weed’s narrative about his first wife who hanged herself, his children who play at hanging themselves, and his deep internal conflict reveals the toll his work takes on his personal life and psyche. His dreams of cooking live pigs, his vegetarianism, and his haunted conscience highlight the paradox of his profession.
  • Mr. Weed’s observations about criminals acting like sleepwalkers, the subtlety of some murders, and the idea that many crimes remain undiscovered underscore the themes of human fallibility and the complexity of justice. His story about the man who killed his wife because of jealousy over cats is a striking example.
  • The black poker chip, found near a severed woman’s head but ultimately meaningless, symbolizes the confusing and often contradictory clues in the search for truth and justice. Mr. Weed carrying the chip unknowingly for years suggests the persistence of unresolved mysteries.
  • The dialogue between Mr. Weed and the landlord, including the landlord’s impatience and Mr. Weed’s acceptance of his monotonous life, humanizes both characters and closes the chapter with a mix of resignation and quiet dignity.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Vera

  • Vera is introspective, haunted by memories and dreams, struggling with the boundary between reality and illusion.
  • Vera reflects on personal loss, especially of Miss MacIntosh, and experiences fear of their own imperfect character and fate.

Moses

  • A figure representing avoidance and detachment, Moses goes home to a mother who believes he is her bridegroom, but he maintains distance, obeying "traffic rules" metaphorically to avoid emotional entanglement.
  • His “old mother”
  • The bus driver feels obligated to care for his mother, who he says thinks he is "a baby crying in her arms". He made a promise to never leave her. This sense of responsibility, whether real or imagined, weighs heavily on him and contributes to his anxieties.
  • The bus driver's mother exists in a dreamlike state, much like the characters Vera encounters throughout her journey which blurs the lines between reality and fantasy.
  • The bus driver's mother is sometimes depicted as young and beautiful, with breasts filled with milk. This suggests a longing for an idealized past, a time of innocence and maternal comfort. She is associated with the potential, yet ultimately unfulfilled, union.
  • The bus driver's relationship with his mother can be interpreted as a symbol of his internal conflict between his desire for freedom and his sense of obligation. He dreams of escaping his mundane life as a bus driver. However, his commitment to his mother, whether self-imposed or externally enforced, keeps him tethered to his present circumstances.
  • The bus driver says that he will not cut his hair as long as "the Democrats were running us", and that he has made a promise to his mother to never cut his hair. It seems as though the bus driver's long hair is a symbol of his commitment to his mother and his abstinence from the more modern world.

Mr. Weed (The Christian Hangman)

  • Central to the chapter, Mr. Weed is a professional executioner who views his work as a mission to provide a painless death.
  • He is a deeply complex character: a good father, haunted by personal tragedy (his wife Marie’s suicide), and tormented by memories and dreams.
  • He discusses his profession with a mix of bitterness, humor, and philosophical insight, revealing his tolerance and humanity despite his grim role.
  • Mr. Weed recounts various cases of crime, murder, and the inefficiency or cruelty of some executions, highlighting the moral ambiguities of justice.
  • He is associated with symbolic objects (a Jew’s harp, a Parker fountain pen, and a black poker chip) each with narrative significance.

Parker Fountain Pen

  • The pen symbolizes death. Vera learns that the condemned man gave the pen to the hangman's grateful relatives. Additionally, the hangman is described as signing the hotel register with the pen.

Black Poker Chip

  • The black poker chip is found near the head of a murdered woman wearing rose-colored sunglasses, but it's a clue that can never be connected to the crime.
  • Even though it seems like it should be important, it ultimately has no bearing on solving the murder. The black poker chip plays a great part in the case but is a clue which led nowhere, nowhere at all, like a business man’s address book which was found in the hollow of a nearby oak tree. It was simply confusing.
  • Mr. Weed later finds a black poker chip in his coat pocket, but he claims he never gambles and has no idea how it got there. This adds another layer of mystery and confusion.
  • The Hangman finds the poker chip in his oldest suit, the suit he said that he wears to hangings and to church.
  • The black poker chip represents the often confusing and ultimately meaningless details that can arise in investigations, and it highlights the limitations of human understanding in the face of complex and tragic events.

Jew’s Harp

  • The hangman is described as always playing his Jew's harp, particularly when taking the shortcut home through the orchard 854. This suggests the Jew's harp is part of his routine, a habit he performs after a hanging.
  • The Jew's harp, often associated with folk music and simple pleasures, contrasts sharply with the hangman's profession. This incongruity highlights the hangman's attempts to reconcile his role as an executioner with his self-perception as a good, peace-loving man.
  • Despite his constant playing, the Jew's harp ultimately fails to console the hangman from the troubles and darkness within his life, particularly the disturbing events involving his children. The music seemingly cannot penetrate the deeper issues plaguing him.
  • The hangman makes a point of saying, "A Jew's harp is not Jewish". This statement may symbolize the way the hangman himself is often misunderstood. He is a man whose profession is death, yet he sees himself as a humanitarian who brings a painless end to suffering.
  • Mr. Weed's profession as a hangman directly symbolizes capital punishment and the administration of justice. He embodies the often-unseen figure who carries out the state's ultimate punishment.
  • Despite the grim nature of his work, Mr. Weed is portrayed as an ordinary, even respectable, individual, a family man who attends church. This highlights the moral ambiguity and societal complicity in the death penalty, suggesting that even those who carry out such acts can be integrated into mainstream society.
  • Mr. Weed's constant connection to death and crime, as well as his troubled dreams, symbolize the burden of the past and the lingering presence of violence and injustice in American history.
  • The juxtaposition of Mr. Weed's morbid occupation with his mundane, everyday life (his family, his farm) reflects a common theme in American literature and art: the grotesque and the mundane coexisting, often uneasily, in the same space.
  • Mr. Weed's interest in the innocence of children and his fear of corrupting them could symbolize a lost sense of American innocence, the idea that the nation has been tainted by violence and injustice.
  • Mr. Weed's wide-brimmed Western hat and his matter-of-fact attitude may evoke the spirit of the American frontier, where violence and justice were often intertwined.
  • Just as Mr. Weed is the man who makes it all painless, the rest of the people are silent accepters of death.
  • While not explicitly stated, Mr. Weed's statement that he does not hang women and the reference to a Negro who was wrongly accused and hanged in Kentucky may allude to the racial injustices prevalent in American history, particularly in the South.

Marie Weed, his first wife who hanged herself

  • Marie Weed, the first wife of the hangman, is a character defined by her tragic end and the haunting impact she has on her husband's life.
  • Marie dies by suicide, hanging herself from a peach tree in their orchard. This act is driven by her fear of another pregnancy and the overwhelming sense of a "meaningless woe expressed by flesh and blood".
  • Her death profoundly affects her husband, the hangman, turning him into a tormented figure. He is haunted by the memory of cutting her down "a split second too late", and he sees her children playing at hanging themselves, symbolizing his guilt and the inescapable presence of death in his life. The grief and guilt transform him into a man who, despite his profession, is deeply averse to violence.
  • Marie's character is primarily revealed through the hangman's recollections and descriptions, creating a sense of mystery and incompleteness. Vera pieces together her image through the hangman's stories of his past. She is characterized by her absence and the powerful effect she has on those left behind.
  • Marie's death and subsequent presence in the hangman's memories symbolize the destructive power of despair and the enduring consequences of loss. The image of her hanging from a tree laden with peach blossoms represents the juxtaposition of beauty and tragedy, life and death.
  • The hangman’s stories of Marie may be connected to Vera's quest for meaning in the lives of marginalized people. The hangman himself is a marginalized character who is haunted by the past, similar to Vera and other characters she encounters.
  • Marie, while not directly present in the narrative, is a crucial figure in understanding the hangman and the themes of death, guilt, and the search for meaning.

Julia Weed, his second wife

  • Julia Weed is the second wife of the hangman. Her relationship with him is marked by a sense of his past deeds and the shadow they cast on their present life.
  • Julia's position as the second wife is complicated by the circumstances of the first wife's death, which was a suicide. She is sometimes found wearing the clothes of his first wife, Marie.
  • Julia is described as having "the mind of a child". Her understanding of the hangman's work and the events surrounding his first wife's death seem limited.
  • She is seen as someone who does not "think things through". This suggests a lack of depth or introspection, contributing to the perception of her as somewhat naive or unaware of the darker aspects of her situation.
  • She is connected to a history of sorrow and death, not only through her husband's profession but also through the tragic end of his first wife. This association highlights the theme of the past's inescapable influence on the present.
  • There's a contrast between her apparent innocence and the knowledge she possesses, or lacks, about her husband's profession and the events of the past. This tension adds to the complexity of her character.
  • The narrative suggests that Julia, in her innocence and limited awareness, is a victim of circumstances, a woman drawn into a situation she may not fully comprehend.
  • Julia Weed is portrayed as a simple, somewhat naive woman caught in the web of her husband's dark profession and the tragic history of his past. Her character serves as a vehicle to explore themes of death, guilt, and the burden of memory.

The Landlord

  • The Tavern’s landlord is pragmatic, skeptical, and somewhat cynical.
  • He interacts with Mr. Weed with a mixture of humor and impatience, grounding the scene in everyday reality.
  • His references to “turkeys and chickens” and dismissive attitude toward Mr. Weed’s stories add a humanizing, mundane contrast to the heavy themes.
  • The "Remember the Marne" tattoo suggests he is a veteran who experienced the horrors of World War I.
  • His world-weariness and the suggestion that his hotel "sinks every night" reflect the disillusionment and cynicism that followed World War I.
  • His background in intelligence implies knowledge of hidden truths and clandestine operations.
  • He listens to the troubles of all kinds of people, suggesting that he represents the common man and those who have been forgotten by society.
  • The mix of old and new, the presence of both a "lieutenant governor of Indiana" and "freaks" at the hotel, allude to a changing and increasingly diverse America.
  • He is a complex figure whose symbolism reflects the disillusionment, hardships, and changing social landscape of America in the first half of the 20th century.

Research: Themes

Reality and Perception

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Vera reflects on the nature of reality, emphasizing that whatever is experienced or perceived is "real," whether it is a dream, a memory, or a physical object.
  • Reality is not confined to conventional or positive experiences but includes shadows, decay, and the unreal or rejected (e.g., abandoned objects, shadows on the hills).
  • This theme is introduced early on, where the village at night is described as a place where shadows never fade, suggesting persistent darkness or hidden truths.

Death and the Inevitability of Fate

See: Death and Mortality · Fate and Chance

  • The chapter dwells heavily on death, especially through the experiences and reflections of the Christian hangman, who symbolizes the finality of mortality.
  • Mr. Weed’s profession is portrayed with a paradoxical humanity; he is portrayed as a missionary of painless death, emphasizing efficiency and compassion within a grim role.
  • Death is also symbolized as a "marital knot" or a binding connection that cannot be undone, suggesting an eternal union with mortality.

Memory, Loss, and the Past

See: Memory and the Past · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Vera recalls memories of lost loved ones, such as Miss MacIntosh, whose disappearance haunts Vera.
  • Memories blur with dreams and reality, suggesting a struggle to reconcile the past with the present.
  • Mr. Weed’s personal history, including the hanging of his first wife and his children’s strange behaviors, deepens the motif of loss and haunting memories.

Human Imperfection and Guilt

See: Guilt, Innocence, and Justice

  • Characters are deeply flawed and haunted by guilt, failures, and secrets (e.g., Mr. Weed’s reflections on the imperfect hanging, criminals who act unknowingly, and the failure to prevent tragedies).
  • Mr. Weed discusses the subtlety of crime and how even well-planned acts can betray the perpetrator by small, unnoticed details.
  • The narrative suggests a tension between the desire for justice and the complexity of human nature.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Shadows and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light · Shadows

  • Represent the unknown, death, and the persistent presence of the past.

The Tavern

  • A microcosm of decay, secrets, and transience; symbolizes a crossroads between life and death.

The Hanging/Marital Knot

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • Symbolizes the irreversible bond with death and the complexity of human relationships.

The Black Poker Chip

See: Cards, Games, and Chance

  • A meaningless yet persistent clue symbolizing the confusing and elusive nature of truth and justice.

The Jew’s Harp

See: Music and Instruments

  • Symbolizes Mr. Weed’s attempt at harmony and control amidst chaos.

Winter Weeds in Spring

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • Symbolize resilience and survival in a decaying environment.

The Blindfolded Dog

See: Dogs · Eyes and Blindness

  • Innocence and cruelty intertwined, reflecting on blindness to suffering.
  • The village is described as dilapidated and eerie, with details like rusted machinery, broken wheels, and a sign "Gentle Incline — Bride Ahead" which is a false reading for "Bridge Ahead," evoking a sense of decay and death.
  • The Tavern, built in 1827 by "God’s servants," is a gloomy, sprawling hotel with mildewed brick, claw-like vines, and a haunting presence. Its interior surpasses Vera’s imagination, filled with human-faced wasps and thin walls that seem to hear everything.
  • The atmosphere is filled with silence, shadows, and a slow, suffocating sense of inevitability, preparing the reader for the philosophical and existential meditations that follow.
