Chapter 57

← Chapter 56 · Home · Chapter 58 →

Summary

A bill keeps arriving from the tailor who made Peron's funeral suit, though the tailor and his shop cannot be found. Mr. Spitzer follows directions from his dreams and searches city directories in the library. There he meets a Confederate soldier who believes the South won, and readers debating immortality. He imagines a rose named for both brothers, red and white on a single bush.

Characters present

Joachim Spitzer · Peron Spitzer

Concepts present

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · Clocks and Watches · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Roses and Flowers · Twins and Doubles · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology · Iowa, Indiana, and the Midwest · Judaism · The Civil War

Key passages

From the research

  • The recurring motif of the great tailor, possibly mad or non-existent, who supposedly tailored the black funeral suit and sends an incessant bill to Mr. Spitzer, symbolizes Mr. Spitzer’s unresolved debts, guilt, and identity crisis. Despite having paid the funeral expenses, Mr. Spitzer is haunted by the tailor’s persistent demand, which can be interpreted as a metaphor for the burdens of the past that Mr. Spitzer cannot escape. The fact that the suit is associated with his dead brother (Peron) who wore it at the funeral adds layers of grief and identity confusion, as Mr. Spitzer wonders if he himself might be the dead man or the other way around. This passage reveals the theme of blurred boundaries between life and death, self and other, reality and dream.
  • Mr. Spitzer repeatedly dreams of searching for the tailor’s shop, traveling through confusing, shifting streets and cities that resemble a storm-tossed sea or a surreal landscape. This endless, futile search reflects his psychological torment and the elusive nature of truth and memory. The tailor's shop is described as empty or nonexistent, reinforcing the idea that what Mr. Spitzer pursues may be an illusion or a part of himself lost in time and space. The dream imagery (revolving doors, escalators, pigeons, and contradictory directions) emphasizes disorientation and the fractured nature of his existence.
  • Mr. Spitzer consciously allows for distortions, reversals, and opposites in his search, knowing that dreams operate by opposites: dark is fair, life is death, man is woman. This recognition of duality and the unreliability of sensory impressions underscores the philosophical meditation on reality’s instability and the fluidity between contradictory states. This theme is crucial for understanding Mr. Spitzer’s predicament; he is caught between worlds, identities, and states of being.
  • The scenes in the library reading room, where Mr. Spitzer consults city directories and old newspapers, highlighting his attempt to anchor himself in reality through facts and records, but his efforts are futile, no tailor or street exists. The presence of eccentric characters debating immortality and reconstructing alternate histories (such as the Confederate soldier who claims the South won the Civil War) adds to the surreal atmosphere and reflects Mr. Spitzer’s own existential doubts and confusion about time, history, and death.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s inner desire for absolute certainty and immortality contrasts with his awareness of doubt and confusion. His longing to interrupt the argument about the soul’s existence but refraining out of fear of rejection reveals his loneliness and the human desire for definitive answers about life after death, which remain elusive. This passage deepens the existential questioning central to the chapter.
  • Toward the end of the chapter, Mr. Spitzer’s observation of the twilight sky filled with colorful clouds and shapes (skulls, hands, birds) culminates in the image of a rose that changes from red to white. This rose symbolizes constancy, memory, and perhaps reconciliation of the living and the dead (the two brothers). Mr. Spitzer’s wish for a rose named after him and his brother encapsulates his yearning for remembrance, identity, and peace amid the instability of his existence.
  • Throughout the chapter, Mr. Spitzer struggles to distinguish his dreams from his waking life. He encounters impossible events (dropping a handkerchief in Pisa despite never having been there) and perceives his reflection as a shadow or a pigeon’s murmur. This ambiguity highlights the chapter’s central concern with the fluid boundary between life and death, memory and forgetting, reality and illusion.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is grappling with grief, guilt, and confusion after his brother’s death. He is introspective, haunted by recurrent dreams, and obsessed with settling an ambiguous tailor’s bill related to his brother’s funeral suit. He represents the struggle between reality and illusion, life and death.

Peron

  • Peron, Mr. Spitzer’s deceased brother, is described as a gambler and a man of dignity in death. Peron’s identity is intertwined with mystery and symbolic imagery (black suit, red rose, bright red necktie), representing a life ended but still profoundly present in Mr. Spitzer’s mind.
  • The Great Tailor may have made the black funeral suit for Peron. He symbolizes unresolved debts, both financial and psychological, and the elusive nature of truth and memory.
  • Various strangers and characters Mr. Spitzer encounters, including a Confederate soldier who claims contradictory historical facts, a librarian, and others who contribute to the dreamlike, surreal atmosphere.

Research: Themes

  • Mr. Spitzer’s identity is fluid and fragmented. He sometimes confuses himself with his brother, dreams of being the tailor, or living a double existence. His struggle to reconcile these selves reflects the complexity of human identity, especially after trauma or death.
  • The persistent tailor’s bill symbolizes the unpayable debts of the past and the burden of memory. Mr. Spitzer’s attempts to pay or deny the debt represent his inability to move beyond grief and the past.
  • The narrative blurs the line between waking life and dream, with Mr. Spitzer experiencing continuous, overlapping realities. The chapter questions what is real and what is illusion, emphasizing the instability of perception.
  • Discussions on the soul, the afterlife, and the persistence of the dead in memory permeate the text. Mr. Spitzer’s desire for certainty about immortality contrasts with others’ doubts, highlighting existential uncertainty.
  • The chapter reflects on the passage of time, both personal and historical, with references to changing cities, lost histories, and the impossibility of retracing steps exactly. Time is portrayed as fluid and unstable.

Chapter 30

Summary

Catherine and Mr. Spitzer discuss unreal persons as if they were real, especially Eustace, an invisible visitor who takes many shapes. Then Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden enters through memory. She was a Boston suffragette, archer, duelist, climber, and traveler who crossed deserts disguised as an Arab king, and she seemed to foresee assassinations. She is now dead and buried. She never cared for the Spitzer twins. Catherine longs for her company and imagines sending her to search the Alps for Jock, Catherine's husband, who vanished while mountain climbing.

Characters present

Catherine Cartwheel · Eustace · Joachim Spitzer · Cousin Hannah · Jock Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Faith, God, and the Supernatural · Freedom and Escape · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Nature, the Sea, and the Cosmos · Women, Gender, and Marriage

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Moon and Stars · Mountains · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Sea and Water

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Astronomy · Dante · Exploration and the Poles · Napoleon and Wellington · Shakespeare · The Bible · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Catherine and Mr. Spitzer endlessly discussing unreal persons, treating the dead as if they were alive and present. Catherine converses with an invisible figure named Eustace, who takes on many forms symbolizing the fluidity and multiplicity of identity, and the suspension of natural laws in her mental state. This passage highlights her detachment from the tangible world and immersion into a dreamlike or hallucinatory realm.
  • Catherine imagines inviting ancient relatives and historical personages to play card games. Cousin Hannah, a figure of vast duplicity and adventurous spirit, is considered an ideal partner. This fantasy reflects Catherine’s desire for companionship and the bridging of past and present through imagination, as well as her yearning for connection beyond loneliness.
  • A substantial portion of the chapter is devoted to a vivid, expansive biography of Cousin Hannah. She is depicted as a fearless, resourceful, and mercurial adventurer who defied conventional limits of gender and geography. Her life spans numerous cultures and eras symbolically: an archer, dueler, mountain climber, yachtsman, and traveler through remote deserts and cities. Her knowledge of global politics, secret whispers, and historical assassinations underscores a mystical or prescient quality. Importantly, Cousin Hannah embodies a rebellious spirit dedicated to overthrowing dreams and illusions, including those of Catherine.
  • Despite facing numerous mortal dangers Cousin Hannah survives through her prescience and determination. The narrative contrasts her survival with the fate of others lost to the elements or violence. Her life is portrayed as a continuous journey through perilous lands, reinforcing themes of resilience and the confrontation of fate.
  • Catherine romanticizes and mourns her lost husband, Jock Cartwheel, imploring Cousin Hannah to search for him in the Alps and other remote places. This longing underscores Catherine’s refusal to accept finality and death, blending memory, fantasy, and hope. The imagery of snow-capped peaks, dark valleys, and silent towers evokes a haunting atmosphere of loss and the persistence of love beyond death.
  • Catherine imagines herself sailing two ships simultaneously, one for the living and one for the dead, symbolizing a liminal existence between life and death, consciousness and unconsciousness. The dialogue with the star watchman, reflecting on stars, tides, and the nature of shore and shorelessness, deepens the metaphysical dimension of the chapter, contemplating the mysteries of existence, transition, and the cosmos.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Catherine Cartwheel (Vera’s mother)

  • Portrayed as a figure lost between reality and fantasy.
  • Engages in conversations with unreal or invisible persons such as “Eustace” who changes forms and identities.
  • She seems to live in a dreamlike state, haunted by memories and by the presence of the dead.
  • Experiences sudden emotional outbursts and imagines elaborate scenarios involving historical and mythical figures.
  • Wishes for company and distraction, often imagining card games with ghostly or imaginary partners.
  • Struggles with loss, particularly the absence of her husband, and clings to hope that he might still be found or returned.

Eustace

  • An invisible, multi-faceted figure in Catherine’s mind.
  • Takes on various guises: a mocking bird, an old woman, an old bearded man, a Venetian valet, a murdered gentleman, a blind astronomer, even Wellington.
  • Represents the fluidity of identity and the suspension of natural laws in Catherine's opium dreams.

Mr. Spitzer

  • A companion to Catherine, often silent and seemingly unable to anchor her in reality.
  • His presence is uncertain, described as an abstraction yawning like cosmic ideas.
  • Catherine often ignores or addresses him tentatively.

Cousin Hannah Freemount-Snowden

  • In stark contrast to Catherine, she is a robust, adventurous, and mercurial woman.
  • Known for her vast, almost mythical experiences across the globe, including deserts, mountains, and ancient cities.
  • Has a reputation for prescience, having foreseen many historical assassinations and events.
  • Skilled in various martial and survival arts: archery in Persia, dueling in France, mountain climbing, horseback riding, balloon ascensions.
  • Has traveled extensively in disguise, infiltrated hostile territories, and defied dangers.
  • Represents a force of action, clarity, and determination, dedicated to overthrowing dreams and illusions.
  • Symbolizes a bridge between myth and history, reality and fantasy, embodying strength and resilience.

Jock Cartwheel

  • Late husband of Catherine who is described as a philanderer who enjoyed dogs, yachts, and mountain climbing.
  • He disappeared while mountain climbing.

Research: Themes

Reality vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Catherine’s conversations with invisible and shifting figures highlight the tension between what is real and imagined.
  • The suspension of natural laws around Eustace suggests the fluidity of identity and reality within opium dreams.
  • Cousin Hannah’s practical and adventurous life contrasts with Catherine’s dreamlike existence, yet even Hannah’s life borders on legend.

Memory and the Past

See: Memory and the Past

  • The narrative dwells on historical figures and events (e.g., Russian czar’s murder, archdukes’ assassinations, Saladin, Solymon the Magnificent).
  • Cousin Hannah’s knowledge spans centuries and cultures, emphasizing the weight of history and memory.
  • Catherine’s longing for her lost husband and her imaginary invitations for card games with ancestors suggest an attempt to connect with the past.

Death and Immortality

See: Death and Mortality

  • Catherine imagines the dead as still living and interacting.
  • Cousin Hannah’s death is ambiguous, with no clear date or place, emphasizing the elusive nature of mortality.
  • Catherine’s hope that her husband still exists somewhere reflects denial of death and the desire for immortality.

Adventure and Escape

See: Freedom and Escape

  • Cousin Hannah embodies the spirit of adventure, traveling to forbidden places and surviving countless dangers.
  • Her life serves as a counterpoint to Catherine's static, opium-induced dreaming.
  • The recurring imagery of ships, deserts, mountains, and deserts emphasizes journeys both physical and metaphysical.

The Feminine and the Skirt

  • Repeated references to skirts, including the loss of a skirt as symbolic sorrow and redemption.
  • Cousin Hannah’s life is linked metaphorically to skirts, suggesting themes of femininity, identity, and transformation.

  • Eustace is a name of Greek origin that means fruitful or abundant in grain. It can also mean steadfast or stable. Eustace may be Saint Eustace since she mentions “golden-antlered stags.” St. Eustace converted to Chrisitanity while out hunting after seeing a cross between the deer’s antlers and hearing the voice of God.
  • Young is described as calling out to dead authors and poets while she was teaching a class for them to come join in.
  • “white plume of cowardice” - is a reference to the White Feather Campaign during World War I where women in Britain gave white feathers to men they perceived as shirking their duty to enlist in the war effort, symbolizing cowardice. The white feather symbolism borrowed the idea of a white feather in a game bird’s tail being a sign of inferior breeding. It became a symbol of cowardice and a way to shame men who did not volunteer for service. Women would publicly give white feathers to men in civilian dress, implying they were cowards for not enlisting. The campaign was a powerful tool in the propaganda efforts of the time, aiming to mobilize men into the war effort before conscription was introduced in Britain. The white feather campaign also had an impact on the understanding of masculinity and gender roles during the war. It was also a representation of conscientious pacifism in AEW Mason’s 1902 book, The Four Feathers. It symbolizes the visible sign of choosing the easy, cowardly path rather than the difficult path of bravery and virtue.
  • A white skirt often symbolizes purity, innocence, mourning (in some cultures), new beginnings, versatility, symbol of femininity. As far as suffragettes they wore white as a symbol of the movement to represent purity and unity. The white skirt is a richly symbolic image representing a lost love, the ideal of purity and womanhood, and the spiritual journey through life, death, and memory. It is less a physical object and more a poetic emblem of the suffragette’s inner life, loss, and the mystery that surrounds her final moments.
  • The white women’s suffrage movement, primarily organized and led by middle-class educated white women, focused on gaining voting rights for white women, culminating in the passage of the 19th amendment in 1920. The movement came out of the abolitionist movement with leaders being: Elizabeth Cady Stanton, Susan B. Anthony, Alice Paul, CArrie Chapman Catt, and Sojourner Truth (who played a significant role in the movement’s background). Suffragists employed various tactics, including lobbying, organizing marches and parades, and civil disobedience. After decades of activism, the 19th Amendment to the US Constitution was ratified in 1920 granting some women the right to vote. The 19th Amendment did not include women of color. It wasn’t until the Voting Rights Act of 1965 until all women’s voting rights were protected.

They represent authority, conquest, and legacy, but also the futility and ephemeral nature of power.   • Salah ad-Din Yusuf ibn Ayyub or Saladin was the founder of the Ayyubid dynasty. Hailing from a Kurdish family, he was the first sultan of both Egypt and Syria. The legendary decadence of Sardanapalus later became a theme in literature and art, especially in the Romantic era.
  • Seleucus I Nicator was a Macedonian Greek general, officer and successor of Alexander the Great. He went on to found the Seleucid dynasty.
  • Seleucus II Callinicus was a ruler of the Hellenistic Seleucid Empire. His reign was a time of great turmoil and fragmentation of the Seleucid Empire.
  • Seleucus III Ceraunus was the eldest son of Seleucus II Callinicus and Laodice II and for a few years was king of the Seleucid Empire. He was assassinated in Asia Minor by courtiers during a campaign against Attalus I of Pergamon.

The epithet Philometor means “mother-loving” and in the Hellenistic world usually indicated that Catherine acted as co-regent for the prince. He was killed by his mother in order to advance his younger brother, Antiochus VIII to the throne.
  • Young's inclusion of women engaged in various sports and non-traditional roles for their time carries significant thematic weight. This imagery reflects the novel’s broader exploration of gender roles, identity, and societal expectations, particularly highlighting the contrast between conventional femininity and more liberated or unconventional expressions of womanhood. The detailed references to women participating in sports such as tennis, skiing, horseback riding, and even archery, as well as wearing attire adorned with sports motifs, underscore a break from the traditional, passive roles often assigned to women in earlier eras. These women vividly illustrate an active, robust female presence engaged in physical and public life, which was unconventional at the time. This challenges the era’s typical expectations of women’s domestic confinement and passive social roles. Miss MacIntosh’s advocacy for physical exercise such as bowling, horseshoes, and skipping ropes, and her disdain for luxury and affectation, emphasize a robust, self-reliant female identity that contrasts with the fragile, dreamlike femininity embodied by Vera’s mother, Catherine. The active, sporty women serve as a symbol of independence and agency, affirming a woman's right to self-determination and physical presence in the world. The references to sporty and athletic women suggest an ideal of physical health, vitality, and engagement with life, counterbalancing the decay, passivity, and dream states that afflict other characters. By incorporating women in roles and activities traditionally reserved for men, Young subtly reflects the social transformations occurring in the early 20th century, including the women’s suffrage movement and the gradual expansion of women’s rights and public roles. This is echoed in the figure of Cousin Hannah, a suffragette and adventurer who defies conventional female roles through her militant activism and boundary-crossing journeys, contrasting with the passive, isolated femininity of other characters. It also emphasizes the complexity of female identity. These external symbols of activity and engagement contrast with internal struggles over self-perception, societal acceptance, and the tension between appearance and reality, which are central themes in the novel. Young’s references to women in various athletic and unconventional roles serve to critique restrictive gender norms, celebrate female strength and autonomy, and reflect the complex, often contradictory realities of womanhood. They help to illuminate the novel’s central concerns with reality versus illusion, freedom versus confinement, and the evolving social landscape for women during the period.

chapter-32:
Chapter 32

← Chapter 31 · Home · Chapter 33 →

Summary

Catherine remembers Hannah as a storm of a woman with a saber scar and burning eyes, who tried to break up Catherine's wedding by beating the bridegroom with her white umbrella and carrying the bride away. Catherine's marriage itself is spectral: a faceless bridegroom, a wedding to a sailboat, a porpoise, a star, a church bell. Hannah died old and alone and never married, though Catherine believes she still visits. Catherine always wanted to die while traveling, believing that death comes from partial knowledge.

Characters present

Cousin Hannah · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer · Vera Cartwheel · Madge Capehorn

Concepts present

Symbols: Clothing, Hats, and Skirts · Horses and Carriages · Lamps, Candles, and Light · Snow, Ice, and Winter · The Bus and the Journey · The Umbrella · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Ecclesiastes · Exploration and the Poles · Fairy Tales and Folklore · Greek Mythology

Key passages

From the research

  • The opening lines immediately establish Cousin Hannah as a dominant, unyielding figure: "Cousin Hannah , a lady who had forcefully expressed herself, a lady who had never drawn in the reins or paused to hear another person’s nugatory opinion...". This sets the stage for her powerful presence.
  • Her dedication is described in almost mythical terms: "...had fought against vanquished competitors when there were none except those of my mother’s drugged dreams... For this consanguineous relative had been interested in her overwhelming suffrage battles for woman on every front, her conquests which could never have been satisfied by temporary victories or the overthrow of man in this world." This passage is crucial because it introduces her primary cause (woman's suffrage) but simultaneously casts doubt on the reality of her battles, linking them to Catherine's internal, dreamlike state. It also suggests her ambitions were absolute, perhaps even unattainable or self-defeating ("the ultimate victory would have been the ultimate defeat").
  • The novel explicitly contrasts Cousin Hannah with Catherine: "Cousin Hannah, unlike my mother with her superfluity of bewildering pretenses... was not one to drag her standards in the dust... She was not one to invite her enemy to a banquet... Cousin Hannah had preferred to take the offensive, to advance by open hostilities...". This highlights Cousin Hannah's directness, unwavering principles, and aggressive approach, standing in stark opposition to the mother's evasiveness, dissimulation, and passive nature. This contrast is fundamental to their dynamic throughout the chapter.
  • Vera questions if Cousin Hannah could be a "misogynist" or "woman hater" despite describing herself as a "high-souled lover of woman, whom she had come to rescue from slavery to man". This paradox is explored through her opposition to traditional feminine "frivolities" like elaborate hats, silks, veils, and parasols.
  • A significant passage describes her urging women to adopt a more combative stance: "...had urged woman to use her parasol as her sword or her shield, her greatest weapon of offense or defense—had often urged woman to take off her great hoop skirts flounced with ribbons and lace, to show her little bird feet, to fly her skirts as her banners in her war against tyrannical man...". This passage vividly illustrates her radical vision of female empowerment, demanding a rejection of conventional femininity and an adoption of martial imagery and action.
  • Catherine's perception of Cousin Hannah is key: "My mother believed that Cousin Hannah had been the image of that past which never was, that future which might never be realized. She had been extemporal, sudden and abrupt... brief and meteoric, hastening through this life as if it were a journey one should make with the utmost quickness and dispatch...". This portrays Cousin Hannah as existing outside normal time and reality, a fleeting, powerful force that appears and disappears unpredictably, emphasizing her almost mythical status in Catherine's mind.
  • Her association with storms and cold further emphasizes her disruptive power: "She was certainly the greatest courier of every storm... The barometer dropped when she came, it was colder than a sea of the icebergs..." Her presence is linked to dramatic, chilling environmental changes, underscoring the profound, unsettling impact she had on Catherine's world.
  • The description of Cousin Hannah's death is perhaps the most important passage, as it drastically re-frames her life: My mother "still believed—that Cousin Hannah’s should have been a hero’s death... But she had died in no foreign war... She had suffered for years from frostbite. She had died after many years of semi-invalidism—in her old age confessing to my mother that she no longer believed in the glory of these foreign conquests—that these great battles had been as nothing to her... The greatest battles were fought in the domestic wars by those who had never left home... It was always an unequal battle, for woman reigned supreme." This passage subverts the heroic narrative built throughout the chapter. The mighty warrior dies quietly after years of decline, revealing a profound shift in her understanding of life's true conflicts. The declaration that domestic wars are the greatest and that woman reigns supreme within them is a startling conclusion from the champion of public, external battles.
  • The possibility that Catherine's visit to the dying Cousin Hannah occurred only in a dream, or even after death, is stated explicitly: "...my mother had visited her only in a dream when she was riding in her carriage driven by the dead black coachman... Mr. Spitzer asked vaguely... Perhaps a visit was all the reality there was... One was dead, and one was dying... He certainly hoped that my mother’s visit had not occurred after she was dead." This passage dissolves the boundary between reality and Catherine's internal landscape, suggesting that the most significant interactions, including the deathbed confession, may have occurred entirely within her mind or dreams, reinforcing the subjective and possibly unreliable nature of the narrative.
  • The chaotic wedding scene where Cousin Hannah intervenes is highly symbolic: "Cousin Hannah, beating with her white umbrella upon the bridegroom, screaming like ten thousand demons... had tried to cause havoc, a riot... She had tried to intrude, to carry my mother away as the robber bridegroom carries the swooning bride...". This passage portrays the wedding as a battleground, where Cousin Hannah attempts to rescue (or abduct) Catherine from a phantom marriage, using her signature white umbrella as a weapon. It encapsulates her lifelong fight against Catherine's entanglement with (or illusion of) men and traditional roles.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Cousin Hannah

  • Cousin Hannah is portrayed as a powerful, uncompromising woman who never concedes or softens her standards, even for strategic reasons. She advances by open hostility and brandishes her symbolic sword like a cane, even when there is no opponent.
  • She is deeply committed to the cause of women’s suffrage and liberation from male oppression. Cousin Hannah fights against man as the cruelest oppressor of beauty and womanhood, advocating for women to use their own "weapons" such as parasols and skirts as symbols of resistance.
  • She is described as a swift, meteoric figure, always on the move and engaged in battles and journeys that span deserts, mountains, and foreign lands. She is likened to a great courier of storms and a weathervane signaling change.
  • Despite her vigor, Cousin Hannah is also seen as ancient, worn by time, and somewhat removed from the natural cycles of life and love. She is described as never having fully experienced youth, romance, or the mating seasons of life.
  • She dies not on a distant battlefield but in obscurity after years of semi-invalidism caused by frostbite. Her deathbed confession reveals a shift in belief that the greatest battles are fought domestically, in the struggles between man and woman at home.

Catherine (Vera’s mother)

  • Catherine is described as bedridden, veiled in white lace and surrounded by an atmosphere of drifting snowflakes, candle flames, and reflections. She is physically confined and vulnerable, a "creature of such fragility" who is easily overwhelmed by the presence of Cousin Hannah and the harshness of reality. Her bed is a "floating swan bed in a dazzling cloud," which evokes both fragility and an ethereal, almost otherworldly quality. This imagery underscores her physical and emotional weakness.
  • Catherine’s essential loneliness and isolation is emphasized. She is abandoned by the "mysterious bridegroom” and all her loves are imaginary: pharaohs, captains, and other ethereal figures who "had left her, and they had never been". This abandonment extends to emotional desolation, as no one, "not even Cousin Hannah," has ever truly touched her "cold heart," which is "cold and hard as the mountain rock". This coldness suggests an emotional deadness or protective numbness born from pain.
  • Catherine lives largely in a world of dreams, illusions, and shifting realities. She imagines weddings to phantoms, sailboats, stars, and icebergs, reflecting a detachment from conventional life and relationships. Her marriage is portrayed as an ambiguous event, possibly symbolic or imaginary, rather than a concrete historical fact. The wedding imagery ("blushing behind her billowing wedding veils," "married to a phantom") conveys a sense of being caught between life and death, reality and fantasy.
  • Catherine's mental state is described as "changeful and capricious," with a wandering attention and vague memories. She is inconsistent in her accounts and perceptions, which may be interpreted as a symptom of her illness, age, or psychological state. This instability contrasts strongly with Cousin Hannah’s forceful and direct manner, highlighting Catherine’s passivity and internal turmoil.
  • Catherine’s relationship with Cousin Hannah reveals much about her character. Hannah is vigorous, militant, and confrontational, while Catherine simulates emotions she does not feel and "dissembles her feelings" when Hannah visits. Catherine’s indifference masks inner panic and vulnerability. Whereas Hannah is a symbol of active struggle and outward battle, Catherine is an embodiment of internal retreat and quiet suffering. Yet, Catherine admires Hannah’s energy and persistence, even as she is overshadowed by it.
  • Catherine is associated with death-like sleep and a liminal state between life and death. The novel suggests that she is "already dead" in a metaphorical sense, living in a "pretense of death". Her life is marked by a profound stasis, and she may be seen as a "sleeping lady" awaiting awakening or final rest. The imagery of snow, cold, and fading light reinforces this theme of suspended animation and the passage between worlds.
  • Catherine’s marriage and attitude toward men are ambiguous. She married "that great traveller who never would return," possibly to defy Cousin Hannah’s militant feminism or to assert independence, but the marriage was doomed. Her symbolic wedding to various natural and mystical entities rather than a man suggests rejection or transcendence of traditional romantic or marital relationships.
  • Catherine is depicted with a strong aesthetic sensibility: her fingers wear jewels that "gleam like northern lights," and her surroundings are rich in poetic symbolism (flutes, harps, snowflakes, candle flames). She is a "beautiful femme fatale," but her beauty is cold and distant, more a vision than a presence. This artistic and ethereal quality adds to her complexity as a character who inhabits a realm between reality and dream.

Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer serves as the "only go-between" between Cousin Hannah and Catherine, facilitating communication during times when direct contact was difficult or impossible. This intermediary role is underscored by his musical whispering ("musically whispering as he had thought what to say, what not to say") which suggests a careful, delicate handling of sensitive matters and emotions. His interactions hint at an awareness of the emotional and existential weight carried by these women, especially Cousin Hannah nearing the end of her life.
  • Mr. Spitzer appears as a figure who exists somewhat on the threshold between life and death, reality and dream. The chapter notes that Catherine had visited Cousin Hannah only in a dream, riding a carriage driven by a "dead black coachman," evoking an otherworldly atmosphere. Mr. Spitzer's presence in this liminal space, with his dark cape and snow "like ermine upon his collar," symbolizes a mediator between the living and the fading, between the tangible and the ephemeral. This imagery suggests that Mr. Spitzer is linked to the inevitable passage of time and mortality that frames the chapter.
  • There is a tone of respect and perhaps even reverence in Mr. Spitzer’s attitude toward Cousin Hannah. He "certainly hoped that my mother’s visit had not occurred after she was dead," indicating his sensitivity to timing and propriety in moments of transition between life and death. His role is not intrusive but rather one of discreet support and careful facilitation.
  • While Cousin Hannah and Catherine are enmeshed in their struggles (whether political, personal, or metaphysical) Mr. Spitzer’s character represents a connection to the external, practical world. His visits to the mansion, his knocking and waiting in the vestibule, contrast with the dreamlike, shifting realities inhabited by the women. This contrast shows him as a bridge between the ordinary and the extraordinary, the real and the imagined.

Research: Themes

  • The novel explores the feminist theme through Cousin Hannah’s militant suffrage activism and her advocacy for women to wield traditional symbols of femininity as weapons in their fight for freedom.
  • Catherine’s life is marked by dreams, illusions, and a sense of unreality, contrasted with Cousin Hannah’s dramatic, tangible battles. The blurred line between dream and reality is emphasized by descriptions of ghostly visits, fading cities, and spectral imagery.
  • Both women embody different aspects of solitude: Cousin Hannah through her relentless battles and eventual physical decline, and Catherine through her emotional coldness and unfulfilled romantic desires.
  • The imagery that weddings are funerals and funerals are weddings suggests a cyclical transformation between life and death, union and separation. Catherine’s ambiguous marriage to a phantom reflects this theme.
  • Cousin Hannah is seen as ancient and time-worn, while Catherine’s memory of her is vague and fleeting. The passage of time is also symbolically represented by the changing weather, candle flames, and shifting landscapes.
  • The confession that the greatest battles are fought at home between man and woman reframes the traditional idea of heroism and war, placing emphasis on personal and domestic struggles rather than grand military conquests.
  • Swords, battles, sieges, and military metaphors are used extensively to describe Cousin Hannah’s activism and life philosophy.
  • Snowflakes, winter winds, desert storms, and migrating birds symbolize the passage of time, change, and emotional states.
  • Candle flames, reflections in mirrors, and the interplay of light and dark underscore the theme of illusion and the duality of the characters.
  • Journeys to foreign lands, the Pony Express metaphor, and references to faraway cities emphasize Cousin Hannah’s restless spirit and Catherine’s longing for escape or transformation.
  • Catherine’s wedding veils, billowing skirts, and parasols symbolize both concealment and empowerment, linking femininity with both fragility and strength.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Cousin Hannah as a Warrior and Adventurer

  • Cousin Hannah is depicted as a forceful, uncompromising woman, a "great captain" who "brandishing her sword like a cane even when there was no one" and preferred "the strident clash of arms, the pitched battle against man".
  • Her sword symbolizes her militant feminism and unyielding fight against patriarchal oppression. The sword, usually a weapon of war and honor, here is also described metaphorically as a cane, suggesting both her authority and perhaps a certain defiance despite solitude. The image of her as a “veteran of so many winter campaigns, desert marches through burning sands” evokes the harshness of her battles, both literal and metaphorical.

Winter, Snow, and Cold Imagery

See: Snow, Ice, and Winter

  • The persistent references to coldness, snow, frostbite, and icicles create a chilling atmosphere that underlines both Cousin Hannah’s harshness and isolation and the emotional coldness surrounding the characters. For example, the barometer dropping "colder than a sea of the icebergs," and “great icicles hanging from the ceiling” during Cousin Hannah’s visits symbolize the emotional frost and the chilling impact she has on Catherine.
  • Snow and ice also symbolize purity, whiteness, and unattainable beauty, reflecting Cousin Hannah’s idealized vision of womanhood as “unsullied honor” and beauty “as white as virginal snow”.

The Riderless White Horse and Rider Imagery

See: Horses and Carriages

  • The image of a riderless white horse "white as snow" coming through the window, bringing snow and cold with it, is a powerful symbol of death or the passing of Cousin Hannah.
  • The white horse traditionally symbolizes a harbinger of death or a psychopomp figure in literature, and here it represents the transition from life to death for this warrior woman. Its entrance is supernatural, blending reality and dream, reinforcing the theme of liminality between life and death.

The Veils, Parasols, and Skirts as Symbols of Femininity and Defense

See: The Umbrella · Clothing, Hats, and Skirts

  • The chapter richly describes feminine accouterments like “great garden hats decked with billowing plumes,” “secretive veils,” “frilled parasols,” and “great hoop skirts flounced with ribbons and lace”. These symbolize traditional femininity, societal expectations, and also the subtle weapons and shields women use in social and gender conflicts.
  • Cousin Hannah’s urging for women to wield their parasol “as her sword or her shield” and to “fly her skirts as her banners in her war against tyrannical man” transforms these delicate objects into instruments of rebellion. The parasol becomes a metaphor for female agency in a world dominated by men.

The Journey and the Northwest Passage

See: The Bus and the Journey

  • Cousin Hannah’s life is described in terms of vast, almost mythical journeys through “desert cities,” “impregnable Asiatic fortresses,” “the great Wall of China,” “Manitoba, Hudson’s Bay,” and “ten thousand singing islands of snow and ice”. This geographical imagery symbolizes her relentless quest for freedom and truth, as well as the impossibility of fully conquering the patriarchal world.
  • The reference to the “Northwest Passage” metaphorically represents the ultimate, elusive goal of life or freedom or “that which cannot be found”. It connotes a spiritual or existential journey, echoing themes of quest and discovery.

The Contrast Between Cousin Hannah and Catherine

  • Catherine is portrayed as fragile, veiled in lace and illusions, “bed-ridden,” “cold heart, cold and hard as the mountain rock,” and largely passive. In contrast, Cousin Hannah is active, combative, and direct. This contrast is symbolized by Catherine’s white umbrella and lace, symbols of delicacy and retreat, versus Cousin Hannah’s white umbrella that she “beat with” like a weapon.
  • Catherine’s world is one of dreams, illusions, and absence, while Cousin Hannah’s is one of harsh realities and confrontations.

Death as a Wedding and Wedding as Death

See: Weddings and Funerals

  • The narrative blurs the boundaries between life milestones and death: “weddings are funerals, and funerals are weddings”. This imagery underscores the theme of transformation and loss inherent in marriage and life.
  • Catherine’s vague, elusive descriptions of her marriage (to a phantom, a porpoise, a star, an iceberg) symbolize the illusory or absent nature of her union and love. Marriage here is a symbolic death of the self or an eternal separation, while death is the final union.

The Ethereal and Dreamlike Atmosphere

The chapter often blurs reality and dream

  • visits occur “only in a dream,” and there are “ambient ghosts of all dead loves”.
  • The use of mirrors, candle flames, flickering stars, and shifting reflections invokes a dreamscape where time and space are fluid. This imagery conveys the fragile mental and emotional state of Catherine and the elusive, almost mythical nature of Cousin Hannah.

The Military and Siege Imagery

  • Cousin Hannah’s life is described metaphorically as a “long siege” with strategic withdrawals and renewed assaults. This symbolizes her relentless struggle for women’s rights and independence, never defeated but always adapting.
  • The castle symbolizes societal structures opposed to her, and the sea eroding the shore suggests slow but inevitable change wrought by persistent effort.

The Symbolism of Light and Darkness

See: Lamps, Candles, and Light

  • Cousin Hannah is described as “standing in a beam of sudden light,” a figure of revelation and defiance.
  • Yet there are also references to “dark cape,” “shadowed faces,” and “clouded looks” symbolizing mystery, obscurity, and the unknown. This interplay of light and dark reflects the duality of her character and the ambiguous outcomes of her life’s battles.

Research: Resources

  • Northwest Passage is a book by Kenneth Roberts. “On every side of us are men who hunt perpetually for their personal northwest passage, too often sacrificing health, strength, and life itself to the search; and who shall say they are not happier in their vain but hopeful quest than wiser, duller folks who sit at home, venturing nothing and, with sour laughs, deriding the seekers for that fabled thoroughfare?” It functions as a rich symbol of adventurous exploration, loss, and the quest for elusive truths. It aligns with the thematic concerns of Roberts’ book but is integrated into the novel’s unique mystical and psychological landscape, emphasizing human vulnerability and the unknowability of fate.
  • “She had been the veteran of so many winter campaigns…” - Reminds one of the painting, Liberty Leading the People, with the bird being the bald eagle. This phrase captures the essence of Cousin Hannah’s life as one of heroic endurance, battling through the metaphorical winters of life and fate, and serves to underline her strength and the epic scale of her personal journey.
  • Ecclesiastes 1:18 “For in much wisdom is much grief: and he that increaseth knowledge increaseth sorrow” The paradox of knowledge - challenges the common belief that knowledge is always a positive thing. It acknowledges that wisdom, while valuable, might also bring greater awareness of the problems, and limitations of human existence. It serves to underscore the novel's exploration of wisdom as a double-edged sword: enlightenment brings clarity but also increases one's sensitivity to life's tragedies and existential sorrows. It expresses the tragic insight that knowledge and sorrow are intimately linked, and that to be truly wise is to be deeply aware of life's inherent griefs. The verse encapsulates a key philosophical reflection in the novel: that the pursuit of wisdom and knowledge, rather than providing comfort, often exposes one to the profound sorrows of human existence.
  • Death and partial knowledge - Our incomplete understanding of life, death, and the universe can lead to poor decisions and actions that ultimately contribute to our own demise. It uses Mr. Spitzer’s introspective and metaphysical musings to convey that death is not a simple event but a complex, multifaceted experience deeply connected to memory, identity, and the limits of human understanding. It portrays death as both an ending and a continuation, filled with ambiguities that challenge the very notions of self and reality.
  • Consanguineous means people who are descended from the same ancestor.
  • A misogynist is a person who dislikes, despises, or is strongly prejudiced against women. Female misogynists (internalized sexism/oppression) are characterized by exalting the feminine ideal, in favor of traditional gender roles, looks down on women who are not feminine, has self-loathing for herself and other women, believes she is superior to other women and/or in constant competition with other women. There is a three tiered system for patriarchy. Patriarchy is the system of social organization that favors and empowers men. Sexism is the code of conduct or rules that are established for women. Misogyny is the policing or enforcement of these rules on women. Thus women can be misogynist if they are helping to police or enforce what women can and cannot do. Looking at all of this it can be determined that no, Cousin Hannah, was not misogynist for wanting women to have independence or the right to vote.
  • A Message to Garcia is an essay by Elbert Hubbard about the value of individual initiative and conscientiousness in work. It invokes the ideal of dutiful action and responsibility amid the novel's complex interplay of dreams, realities, and fragmented identities. Miss MacIntosh exemplifies the essay’s virtues, serving as a counterpoint to the novel’s more ambiguous and elusive characters, and reinforcing the theme that despite the chaos and illusion surrounding them, there remains a call to purposeful engagement with life.

  • This characterization of Catherine resembles the folktale of Sleeping Beauty which is a classic fairy tale about a princess who is cursed to sleep for a hundred years by an evil fairy, to be awakened by a handsome prince at the end of that time. The good fairy, realizing that the princess would be frightened if alone when she awakens, uses her wand to put every living person and animal in the palace asleep, to awaken when the princess does. Early origins and versions of the tale involve rape, incest, cannibalism and Sleeping Beauty giving birth to children while she is asleep (similar to non-canical books that depict Eve being raped by angels and giving birth). Catherine embodies the Sleeping Beauty archetype as a woman caught in a protracted, enchanted sleep between life and death, isolated in a dreamlike world filled with phantoms, awaiting an uncertain awakening. Her physical stillness, the symbolic presence of the bird, the grand but empty house, and the thematic concerns with time, death, and unfulfilled love strongly evoke the folktale’s motifs and deepen the novel’s exploration of illusion versus reality. Through Catherine, Young reimagines the Sleeping Beauty myth, using it to probe themes of mortality, memory, and the elusive boundary between waking life and dreams.

Chapter 13

← Chapter 12 · Home · Chapter 14 →

Summary

Vera announces in advance that on this night of her fourteenth birthday she will lose her last certainty. Miss MacIntosh will become a stranger in her eyes, though she does not yet say how. She wanders the garden of the deaf, where life-sized chessmen move on a board of light and shadow among statues and gargoyles. The chapter then turns to Catherine and Mr. Spitzer. Catherine insists that the ear and the heart are dead, that sound has fled the universe, and that this is why his music is silence.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Catherine Cartwheel · Joachim Spitzer

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Illusion and Reality · Memory and the Past · Music, Sound, and Silence

Symbols: Cards, Games, and Chance · Silence and Deafness · Snow, Ice, and Winter

Philosophy: Aristotle · Astrology, Alchemy, and Esoterica · Augustine and Christian Theology · Epicureanism · Heraclitus and Flux · Marguerite Young on Her Craft · Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres

Allusions: Deafness and Sign Language · Homer’s Epics · Shakespeare · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a poignant farewell to Miss MacIntosh, a figure who had seemed ordinary and unchanging but is now revealed to be mysterious and complex. Vera reflects on having taken her for granted, washing and ironing her clothes without understanding who she truly was. This passage symbolizes the moment of awakening to the deeper, often hidden realities beneath familiar aspects. The metaphor of the weary traveler crossing the frozen but never fully frozen Lake Constance powerfully conveys the shock of realizing that what seemed solid and known is actually fragile and deceptive. The traveler’s death upon comprehending the impossible crossing parallels Vera’s own transformation in perception. This passage marks the loss of innocence and the beginning of a more complex understanding of life and people.
  • Following the initial farewell to Miss MacIntosh, Vera bids farewell to the stability of past certainties: the "old moralities," "proverbial wisdom," and the "fabric of self-deception" that both she and Miss MacIntosh had lived by. This passage underscores a profound existential rupture where the past, reason, purpose, and future become unreliable, even illusory. The imagery of cherry blossoms, peach orchards, and dusty lanes as if they were lies evokes a sense of disillusionment with the world as it was once understood. This farewell is not just to a person but to an entire worldview, highlighting the theme of awakening to a more ambiguous and unsettling reality.
  • Vera wanders through a surreal, neglected garden that is described as "the garden of the deaf," a place where “the ear is dead.” This garden is filled with vivid, ghostly images: statues, flowers that fly away like moths, chessmen moving invisibly, and the presence of historical figures such as Dr. Galen and Dr. Harvey. The garden symbolizes a realm where sound and communication are absent, reflecting a profound isolation. The metaphor of the "deaf ear" extends into the relationship between Vera’s mother and Mr. Spitzer, emphasizing themes of silence, unhearing, and the inability to connect or be heard. Catherine’s insistence that the ear is dead and the world is soundless captures the tragic condition of isolation and the fading of meaningful communication.
  • The exchanges between Vera’s mother and Mr. Spitzer are significant for illustrating the tension between reality and perception. Mr. Spitzer represents a figure trying to engage with the world, arguing the possibility of sound and communication despite Catherine’s firm belief in their absence. Their dialogue about whose ear is dead (literal or metaphorical) introduces the theme of death not only of the physical ear but also of the heart and spirit. This passage deepens the motif of silence and the loss of voice, highlighting human suffering and the struggle to maintain connection amid internal and external voids.
  • Throughout the chapter, there is a recurring motif of things appearing familiar but becoming "increasingly unfamiliar," such as the Venus statue "bearded by patriarchal fog," flowers that fly away when touched, and shadows cast by barnacle-formed cherubim faces. These images evoke the fragility of memory and the instability of reality as perceived by Vera, underscoring how the past and present intertwine in confusing ways. The luminous yet ghostly descriptions of the garden and the figures within suggest a world where the boundaries between life and death, reality and dream, presence and absence blur.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Vera Cartwheel

  • She begins with a poignant farewell to the "last certitude," including the tender moment of their fourteenth birthday and the figure of Miss MacIntosh, who had been a constant presence for seven years.
  • This farewell symbolizes a significant psychological and emotional shift: a departure from innocence and an acknowledgement that the familiar is no longer certain or reliable.

Catherine Cartwheel

  • The recurring motif of the "dead ear," especially in relation to Mr. Spitzer and Catherine, underscores a world where communication fails and the essence of existence is isolated from meaning.

  • Catherine’s fear of the silence "unbroken by the sound" and her particular dread "when a frog screamed" indicate deep psychological distress. Mr. Spitzer

  • Mr. Spitzer is described as "pompous" and "beclouded," suggesting a man who carries a certain self-importance or authority, yet his thoughts and arguments are somewhat confused or unclear. While Mr. Spitzer physically experiences a kind of internal "roaring" in his right ear, a noise which "did not come from this world," he is metaphorically deaf to true communication or sound in the broader existential sense described by Catherine.

This frames him as a figure caught between the rational world of law and argument and a deeper, more profound silence that challenges or negates those faculties.

Mr. Spitzer tries to argue against the idea that his ear is dead, pointing out that his dead brother’s ear was not buried on the estate, yet Catherine remains insistent that "the ear was dead," emphasizing a metaphysical or symbolic deafness beyond just physical hearing.
  • Mr. Spitzer’s character embodies the tragic human predicament of isolation and the failure of communication. The novel suggests that even in his legal profession, where voice and argument are paramount, his voice is unheard in the cosmic or existential sense. This heightens the pathos of his character as someone who functions in society but is fundamentally cut off from true connection or understanding.

Chapter 63

Summary

The novel returns to Vera and Miss MacIntosh. Vera confronts her about the hollow pretense between them. Miss MacIntosh takes off her wig and speaks more openly than ever about her past, her body, her loneliness, and her coming end. She tells Vera that "nobody knows anybody," and that she suffers especially when there are rainbows.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection

Symbols: Fog and Mist · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Lamps, Candles, and Light · The Umbrella

Philosophy: Augustine and Christian Theology · Marguerite Young on Her Craft

Key passages

From the research

  • Early in the chapter, Miss MacIntosh is described as a figure of unwavering common sense and moral clarity amid chaos and illusion. She is portrayed as the “Rock of Ages in a land where all things crumbled,” the “surefooted Pilgrim,” and the “one person never dreaming where all might dream.” This passage highlights her steadfastness and practical nature, contrasting with the fog and illusions surrounding them.
  • A substantial and vivid passage details Miss MacIntosh’s intense dislike for electric lights, reflecting her preference for natural darkness and simplicity. She associates electric lights with loss of privacy, artificiality, and moral decay. This passage also reflects her nostalgia and resistance to the encroachment of modern technology and the disruption of natural rhythms.
  • A critical dialogue occurs between Vera and Miss MacIntosh, where Vera confronts her about the “hollow pretense” of their living situation and demands honesty about the nature of their relationship. Vera accuses Miss MacIntosh of deception and questions whether they are truly bound to each other, expressing a desire to understand what she wants and lacks. This exchange is charged with emotional intensity and existential questioning.
  • One of the most poignant moments is when Miss MacIntosh removes her wig, revealing her baldness, which she describes as a source of deep personal embarrassment and symbol of her vulnerability and the “burned wig” shielding her from life’s harsh elements. This act strips away illusion and forces a confrontation with bare reality, emphasizing themes of identity, appearance versus essence, and mortality.
  • Miss MacIntosh offers a bleak yet humorous meditation on life’s disappointments, the inevitability of death, and the “system of mutual deception” that love often entails. She speaks with a mixture of bitterness and dark humor about her past, the failures of God and creation, and the futility of illusions.
  • Miss MacIntosh discusses the umbrella as a symbol of equality and protection, tracing its history from the Orient to England and its social implications. She also mentions the raincoat as a practical item for the poor, underscoring her concern for everyday realities and the working classes. This passage blends historical anecdotes with social commentary.
  • Toward the end of the chapter, despite all the darkness and despair, Miss MacIntosh exhorts Vera to “be of good cheer,” acknowledging that “we are pilgrims” with a long day ahead. She urges living each day as if it were the last, knitting body and soul together even as they unravel. This passage encapsulates the chapter’s tension between despair and endurance, illusion and reality.
  • In the final lines, Miss MacIntosh offers a sober reflection that “people are never quite what they seem” and “nobody knows anybody,” underscoring the chapter’s themes of uncertainty, deception, and the limits of human understanding,

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Miss MacIntosh is described as the "Rock of Ages" in a crumbling world, a symbol of stability, clarity, and common sense.
  • She embodies straightforwardness, rejecting illusions and fantasies, and insists on living within a "framework" of reality.
  • Her physical appearance symbolizes her internal struggle: her ruddy hair like a "sunset burning with bees," a broken nose, and eventually revealed baldness, all reflecting her life's hardships and resilience.
  • The black umbrella she carries is a protective shield, symbolizing her defense against the "fog" of confusion, dreams, and illusions.
  • Miss MacIntosh is a moral mentor and nursemaid figure who values practicality over imagination.
  • She is skeptical of dreams, illusions, and modern distractions, such as electric lights, which she believes disturb natural life rhythms and privacy.
  • She is combative and sharp, not hesitating to scold even divine figures like Emperor Constantine or God Himself for what she sees as excess or failure.
  • Despite her stern exterior, she has a deep, incorruptible sense of humor and reveals moments of vulnerability, especially when discussing her baldness and personal losses.

Research: Themes

Reality vs. Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • Miss MacIntosh represents a rejection of illusions, emphasizing the importance of common sense and "what is immediate and near".
  • Vera struggles with this perspective, feeling trapped between dreams and the harshness of reality.
  • The fog surrounding them symbolizes ambiguity, confusion, and the shifting nature of perception.
  • The electric lights symbolize modern artificiality, disturbing natural darkness and the "dreamless sleep" necessary for authentic living.

Mortality and the Human Condition

See: Death and Mortality

  • The chapter grapples with death, impermanence, and the fragility of life. Miss MacIntosh openly discusses her own mortality, symbolized by her baldness and physical deterioration.
  • She speaks candidly about the "burned-out wick" and the "empty breast," metaphors for loss and the fading of vitality.
  • The idea that "life is very short" and "the spirit dwells not long in any place" underscores a sense of existential urgency 784.
  • Vera's confrontation with Miss MacIntosh about their relationship and existence reflects a deeper search for meaning and honesty in the face of death.

Isolation and Connection

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Despite Miss MacIntosh's role as a caretaker, there is a profound emotional distance and complexity in their relationship.
  • Vera demands honesty and openness, revealing a desire for genuine connection beyond social roles and appearances.
  • Miss MacIntosh's admission of her past struggles and loneliness highlights the theme of isolation in human experience.

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness
