This breakthrough quickly revolutionized medicine, allowing doctors to see inside the body for the first time without surgery, leading to rapid adoption for diagnosing fractures, though the dangers of radiation weren't understood early on. Over time, safety measures, digital imaging, and advanced techniques like CT scans evolved, building on this foundational discovery to create modern radiology.
  • Broadway's history began with Dutch settlement, named for its width, evolving from a trade route to New York's entertainment heart, moving uptown with the city, embracing vaudeville, and exploding into a musical powerhouse during its Golden Age (1940s-60s) with Rodgers & Hammerstein, then revitalizing in the 1990s with mega-musicals and Disney, cementing its global fame for polished, diverse productions today, notes Dance Informa Magazine.
  • Skid Row originated from Seattle's logging days as "skid roads" where logs were dragged (skidded) down hills to mills, evolving into a term for impoverished urban areas where transient, often unemployed men ("down-and-outs") congregated due to cheap lodging, cheap liquor, and missions, especially during the Great Depression, with Los Angeles's Skid Row becoming famous for its massive homeless population, cheap hotels, and social services. The history reflects shifts from resource extraction to urban poverty, the impact of economic crises, and evolving policies towards the homeless, becoming synonymous with large concentrations of unhoused people, addiction, and mental health challenges.
  • Naphtha is a flammable liquid hydrocarbon mixture, a key intermediate in petroleum refining, used widely as a solvent, cleaner, and feedstock for gasoline, jet fuel, and petrochemicals, derived from crude oil or natural gas, varying from colorless to reddish-brown with a gasoline-like odor, and known for its volatility and potential health risks like irritation and CNS effects with overexposure.
  • Diogenes of Sinope, also known as Diogenes the Cynic, was a controversial ancient Greek philosopher and founder of the Cynic school of thought. He lived a life of asceticism, rejecting societal norms and material possessions in favor of nature and simple pleasures. Diogenes was known for his provocative actions and sharp wit, which aimed to expose hypocrisy and greed in society and intellectual circles.
  • The Franklin Stove, invented by Benjamin Franklin in 1742, was a revolutionary cast-iron heating device designed to be a more efficient, less smoky alternative to open fireplaces, using less wood to provide more heat by circulating air and radiating warmth in all directions, functioning as an early furnace for its era's climate crisis and wood shortage. It worked by drawing smoke and heat through a hollow baffle and an "inverted siphon" to extract more warmth before exiting, though it was sometimes difficult to draft and required less wood for better comfort.
  • George III was King of Great Britain and Ireland from 25 October 1760 until his death in 1820. The Acts of Union 1800 unified Great Britain and Ireland into the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland, with George as its king. George III is often accused of obstinately trying to keep Great Britain at war with the rebels (American Revolution), despite the opinions of his own ministers.
  • Poor Richard's Almanack was a popular annual publication by Benjamin Franklin (under the pseudonym "Richard Saunders") from 1732 to 1758, known for its calendar, weather forecasts, and witty proverbs promoting thrift, industry, and self-reliance, which became a cornerstone of American culture and values. It was a bestseller in the American colonies, selling around 10,000 copies yearly, and served as a vehicle for Franklin's practical wisdom for the common people.
  • Benjamin Franklin "tampered with God’s nest egg and most private creation keeping us up all day and half the night" metaphorically refers to Franklin's invention and promotion of electric lighting. Miss MacIntosh expresses a strong aversion to electric lights, which she sees as an unnatural and disruptive force in human life.
  • These jobs have evolved or declined significantly due to technological advancements, mass production, changes in consumer habits, and modern logistics.
  • Ship chandlers are specialized suppliers for the maritime industry, providing everything from food (provisions) and cleaning supplies to technical equipment, safety gear, and deck stores (ropes, anchors) for ships and their crews, acting as crucial logistical partners to keep vessels operational and crews supplied globally.
  • An ironmonger (British English) is a retailer or shop that sells hardware, tools, household items, and metal goods, like hinges, locks, pans, and garden tools, essentially a traditional hardware dealer in American English.
  • Many umbrella repairmen, or "mush-fakers," were mobile, going from house to house or setting up on streets to mend umbrellas. They would often make one good umbrella out of parts scavenged from several broken ones. A popular song in 1938, "The Umbrella Man" recorded by the Kay Kyser Orchestra, highlighted this common occupation. Frankford Umbrellas started in 1898 in the U.S. as a door-to-door repair service and grew into a manufacturing and repair company in Philadelphia. They repaired various types of umbrellas, including patio and beach umbrellas as well as rain umbrellas. Beehler Umbrella Factory was located in Baltimore, Maryland, this was the first umbrella factory in the U.S., founded in 1828. Baltimore became a hub for umbrella manufacturing, shipping over 1.5 million umbrellas annually by the early 20th century. Uncle Sam Umbrella Shop was a New York City staple, founded in 1866, provided sales and repairs for decades, serving notable figures like Charlie Chaplin and President Franklin D. Roosevelt. Umbrella repair was a necessary trade when umbrellas were durable, often made with quality materials like whalebone (early on) and later steel ribs, designed to last and be repaired. The "throwaway society" eventually led to the decline of the repair business, as mass-produced, inexpensive umbrellas made it easier for people to buy a new one rather than fix an old one.
  • Tin roofers specialized in installing tin-plated iron/steel sheets, a popular, affordable, fire-resistant material that rose in the 19th century with the Industrial Revolution, evolving from imported tinplate to domestically produced, corrugated, and galvanized sheets (tin over iron/steel) for homes, barns, and factories, offering better durability and ease of installation than older methods, though often called "tin" roofs, they were actually steel coated in tin.
  • Rag pickers (or rag-and-bone men) were vital urban scavengers, primarily poor immigrants in the 19th/early 20th centuries, who gathered discarded textiles, bones, metal, and glass from streets and dumps to sell to middlemen for processing into new materials, forming an essential, albeit low-status, part of early recycling and industrial supply chains, especially for paper and textiles, surviving on meager earnings from this dirty work.
  • The questions Miss MacIntosh poses about monsoons (a rainy period in South and Southeast Asia between May and September), mackerel skies (a sky filled with rows of high-altitude cirrocumulus or mid-level altocumulus clouds that form a rippling, wavy pattern, resembling the scales of a mackerel fish. This formation indicates moisture and atmospheric waves, often signaling approaching weather changes, leading to the old saying, "Mackerel sky, not twenty-four hours dry"), the Bering Strait (is a narrow waterway separating Asia (Russia) from North America (Alaska), connecting the Pacific Ocean's Bering Sea to the Arctic Ocean, famous as the site of the Ice Age land bridge (Beringia) for human migration and currently a vital wildlife corridor with a US-Russia boundary, known for cold, stormy waters and the time-bending Diomede Islands), and Hyperborean lights (refers to the poetic or mythical descriptions of the sun and continuous daylight in the legendary land of Hyperborea, a paradisiacal realm in Greek mythology) are metaphorical and educational, suggesting a vast, perhaps overwhelming world of knowledge and challenges that must be faced. She challenges Vera on whether she has learned the necessary practical and worldly lessons (geography, arithmetic, nautical science, household management, even hunting) implying that without such knowledge and preparedness, one is condemned to "darkest ignorance," which is especially unfit for a poor man's wife after the "wedding feast" is over. This metaphor extends to life beyond the initial excitement or illusion of marriage or beginnings, where reality and hard work set in. It emphasizes Miss MacIntosh’s role as a stern moral guide who insists on facing life's harsh realities head-on, rejecting illusions or dreams. This passage reflects Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic, somewhat severe worldview, emphasizing survival, knowledge, and preparation in a harsh, unforgiving world.
  • Vera reflects on feelings of alienation and disconnection from the practical, external world that Miss MacIntosh inhabits. Vera is expressing that she cannot share Miss MacIntosh’s interests in the concrete, factual, and often technical matters of the world around them: the complexities of the Stock Exchange (whether in bearish or bullish markets), high finance, Australian shipping, cup racing, and even such details as the marriage of salmon or bowling and pitching. These topics symbolize the practical, "man’s world" that Miss MacIntosh is grounded in, a world of commerce, order, and routine. Vera’s own world is described as "the world within," an internal, emotional, and perhaps more mystical or dreamlike realm. She feels like she is trembling "at the threshold of life," meaning she is on the verge of experiencing life but is still overwhelmed and unprepared. Vera does not connect with or care for the physical and external landmarks and systems like the Brooklyn Bridge, the various types of buoys marking harbors, and the vast impersonal forces symbolized by these technical and navigational details. These things cause her confusion, headache, and a sense of overwhelming noise ("ears roar with distant reverberations"). This passage highlights the divide between Miss MacIntosh’s pragmatic, external engagement with the world and Vera’s inward, uncertain, and emotional experience of life. Vera feels out of place in the practical world and is more concerned with her interior struggles and the mysteries of existence, rather than the factual or logistical details that Miss MacIntosh cares about. The passage conveys Vera’s sense of estrangement from the practical, rational concerns of Miss MacIntosh and her own immersion in a more internal, emotional, and uncertain world.
  • "Heaven preserve you from a beardless man. Heaven preserve you from a hairy woman." This opening line is a warning against unnatural or incomplete identities, possibly alluding to the disruption of traditional gender roles or the loss of conventional human distinctions. The "beardless man" might symbolize immaturity or failure to fulfill societal or spiritual masculinity, while the "hairy woman" could indicate a departure from expected femininity or an overwhelming, chaotic force. The invocation of "Heaven preserve you" is a religious appeal for divine protection from these unsettling or undesirable conditions. "Consider well, my dear, if you mean what you are saying, if this is your infinite desire for nothing." Miss MacIntosh challenges the listener (Vera) to reflect carefully on whether their longing for "nothing", a void, emptiness, or perhaps death or nihilism is truly what they want. It suggests a deep questioning of desire, existence, and meaning. “She clapped the air with one hand. ‘A screech owl flew by just then. Did you not see it, hear it?’” The screech owl is a traditional symbol of death, omens, or the supernatural. Its sudden appearance emphasizes the gravity and ominous tone of the warning. The rhetorical question underscores awareness and perception, suggesting that profound or unsettling truths may go unnoticed. "The sun and the moon will shine in the same sky, and yet the earth will not be lighted but will be wrapped in darkness like the night." This line juxtaposes the presence of celestial bodies (sun and moon), which symbolize light, guidance, and life, with the paradoxical image of the earth being wrapped in darkness. It could imply a world where natural order and illumination exist but fail to reach or enlighten humanity, reflecting spiritual darkness despite physical light. "All earth will be made bare like this. No birds will sing in the tree-tops ever again. There shall be bare and ruined choirs." The "bare and ruined choirs" is a direct allusion to John Milton's Sonnet 7 ("...the bare and level plains, / The ruin of the ancient cities..."), evoking desolation, decay, and the loss of harmony or divine order. The silence of birds, which often symbolize the soul or spiritual joy, suggests a profound loss of life or spirit. "The flower will perish while it is still in the seed. The tides will not return what the tides take out." These images symbolize premature death or failure to reach potential ("flower perishing in the seed") and irreversible loss ("tides will not return what the tides take out"). They evoke the idea that some losses are final and natural cycles of renewal are broken. "There will be only, my dear, the dream." The closing line suggests that after all the destruction and loss, only the "dream" remains, possibly illusion, memory, or an insubstantial reality. It can be interpreted as a reflection on the ephemeral nature of life and the dominance of subjective perception or fantasy when the physical world fails. The invocation of "Heaven" and "Heaven preserve you" draws on Judeo-Christian imagery. The allusion to "bare and ruined choirs" connects to Milton, whose work is steeped in Christian theology and themes of the Fall and apocalypse. The presence of the sun, moon, and the view of the earth wrapped in darkness resonates with biblical apocalyptic imagery, such as the darkening of the sun and moon in the Book of Revelation signaling the end times. The repeated themes of loss, desolation, and the finality of death align with Christian meditation on mortality, sin, and the hope or despair beyond life. This passage is a somber meditation on loss, identity, and the tenuous hold on reality, filled with symbolic and religious imagery that suggests a spiritual or existential crisis. Miss MacIntosh’s words warn of the dangers of embracing "nothingness" or illusion without acknowledging the profound reality of life and death.
  • "Nonsense, oh, nonsense which kills us" reflects Miss MacIntosh’s frustration and pain at what she sees as Vera's fanciful or idealistic thinking ("it is you who dream...my life away"). Miss MacIntosh contrasts imagination and dream with the harshness of actual life: "imagination is nothing. The life is what counts." She insists on the primacy of tangible reality over illusions or fantasies, underscoring her role as a grounded, practical figure in the novel. Her rhetorical questions about "turn the spade over the living heart" and covering her with illusions suggest a rejection of any false comfort or denial of the painful truth of her existence. She acknowledges the inevitability of death and disappearance ("I shall surely disappear as surely as the sun sets"), emphasizing that this fate is her own choice and beyond Vera’s control. The enigmatic lines "What are two and two but one? What are four and four but three? Who holds the cards?" seem to point to the confusing and paradoxical nature of life and death, fate, and relationships: things that defy simple logic or arithmetic and are governed by forces beyond human understanding or control. Her mention of historical and mythical figures like Emperor Constantine and King Canute, both known for their symbolic struggles against fate or time, reinforces the theme of human limitation in the face of inevitable mortality and the futility of trying to control or change fundamental truths. The passage also touches on the tension between dreaming and reality, permanence and impermanence, and the existential loneliness of individual human experience. Miss MacIntosh’s pain, her trembling, and her questioning about where her father is, or whether this place is heaven or hell, reveal her deep inner turmoil and the gravity of the moment. Vera’s trembling wrist and her wish to undo her words or apologize indicate her recognition of the seriousness of Miss MacIntosh’s suffering and the potential irreversibility of their confrontational exchange. There is a sense that Miss MacIntosh’s presence is central to Vera’s life, and the thought of her disappearance evokes a profound fear of loss and guilt. This passage is a poignant exploration of the clash between imagination and reality, the inevitability of death, and the complex, painful dynamics of human relationships. Miss MacIntosh’s declaration and Vera’s reaction highlight the novel’s themes of mortality, truth, and the struggle to find meaning in a world filled with uncertainty and loss.
  • King Canute or Cnut was king of England, Norway, and Denmark. Miss MacIntosh invokes King Canute, who commanded the tides to stop, to illustrate the futility of "waste our lives in the vain expectation of that which might never happen". Canute, who despite being king, could not control the natural world, serves as a reminder that one must not dream of "what was not, of what would never be". He represents the limitations of human power against the forces of nature and the folly of arrogance. Catherine also mentions King Canute when she is lost in her opium-induced dreams. This further connects him with the realm of illusion and the rejection of reality that Miss MacIntosh so vehemently opposes. The story notes her mention of the "drowned pearl-diver rising to the surface, the griffin with folded wings, the centaur with its long-lashed eyelids closed," alongside her comment that James, the chauffeur, could be depended upon. Miss MacIntosh is said to be able to "do away with bodiless phantoms and monsters, with imaginary nightingales or turrets of ivory or turrets of gold or turrets of brass". King Canute, as used by Miss MacIntosh, directly contrasts with Catherine's "opium paradise." He embodies the futility of attempting to control the uncontrollable, while Vera's mother indulges in dreams that defy reality. Miss MacIntosh emphasizes that the "opium paradise was never God's way of life". The references to King Canute, particularly by Miss MacIntosh, serve as a critique of those who dwell in idealistic or unrealistic notions. He is a symbol of misplaced faith in one's ability to alter the fundamental realities of the world.
  • Crispin or Saints Crispin and Crispinian are the Christian patron saints of cobblers, curriers, tanners, and leather workers. They were beheaded during the reign of Diocletian.
  • Clarence may refer to the Duke of Clarence which is a substantive title traditionally awarded to junior members of the British Royal Family.
  • Cuthbert may refer to Cuthbert of Lindisfarne who was an Anglo-Saxon saint of the early Northumbrian church in the Celtic tradition. He was a monk, bishop and hermit, associated with the monasteries of Melrose and Lindisfarne in the Kingdom of Northumbria, today in north eastern England and South Eastern Scotland.
  • “harebells” Campanula rotundifolia, the harebell or common harebell, Scottish bluebell, or bluebell in Scotland, is a species of flowering plant in the bellflower family Campanulaceae.
  • This is a profound and poetic meditation by Miss MacIntosh, reflecting on the harsh realities of life, death, and the human condition. Through vivid imagery and metaphor, she expresses a sense of existential weariness and resignation, while also touching on themes of identity, loss, and the illusions we maintain. Miss MacIntosh begins by describing a place or state that feels like a "No Man’s Land," symbolizing isolation, emptiness, or a barren emotional or spiritual landscape. The physical sensations she describes water pouring from her skin, her nose lengthening, eyes watering which reflect intense anguish or transformation. She speaks of being "killed" repeatedly, not just physically but emotionally and spiritually, mourning not herself but others, which suggests deep empathy and sorrow for collective human suffering. She reflects on her body's frailty (her baldness, scars, missing breast), and the metaphor of being a skeleton wandering through endless waters. This imagery conveys both a literal and metaphorical stripping away of illusions and defenses, revealing vulnerability and the inevitability of death. The passage of "invisible assassin" and "one’s own heart which has no other enemy" suggests internal conflict, self-doubt, or self-inflicted suffering. It highlights the idea that much of human pain comes from within, from our own hearts or minds. Miss MacIntosh discusses the loss of her hair and wig, symbols of vanity and identity, revealing her head, "naked of all its illusion of planetary glory" is a metaphor for shedding false pride or external appearances. She acknowledges the "vain, shallow pretense" of life that fools might see through, exposing the emptiness behind social facades. She references the Spitzer brothers and their conflicting choices, suggesting that life’s paths are often confusing, contradictory, and beyond full control. The phrase "Time moves us when we move not" captures the inexorable passage of time regardless of human action. Miss MacIntosh feels "rooked" or cheated by God, lamenting the failure of divine promises or plans. She portrays herself as "God’s poorest and lowest," stripped of glory and dignity. This expresses a profound spiritual crisis or disillusionment. Moving from the personal to the social, she recounts the history of the umbrella as a symbol of equality: once a royal privilege, now a common man’s protection. The umbrella represents practical innovation that democratizes protection and privacy, disrupting old hierarchies (e.g., coachmen, nobility). This illustrates her practical, grounded view of life and society amidst the existential turmoil. At the end, Miss MacIntosh calls for "celestial navigation," urging a broader perspective and wisdom to navigate life’s complexities rather than being bogged down in fragmented, superficial knowledge or emotional despair. This suggests a desire to find meaning or direction despite the chaos. This passage reveals Miss MacIntosh’s complex character: a woman deeply aware of suffering, mortality, and the illusions of life, yet also practical, historically informed, and resolute. She embraces her imperfections and losses, including her baldness and physical scars, as part of her identity. She challenges Vera (the narrator) to see beyond appearances and illusions to the stark truths beneath, while also acknowledging the need to carry on with life’s "mournful business" despite the sorrow and emptiness. This passage encapsulates the novel’s themes of death, identity, illusion versus reality, and the struggle to live meaningfully in a world that often seems indifferent or hostile.
  • “No Man’s Land” disputed ground between the front lines or trenches of two opposing armies.
  • Ursa Major is also known as the Great Bear and is a constellation in the northern sky, whose associated mythology likely dates back into prehistory.
  • Charles’ Wain or the Big Dipper. A folk etymology holds that this derived from Charlemagne, but the name is common to all the Germanic languages and the original reference was to the men's wagon, in contrast to the women's wagon, the Little Dipper.
  • Charybdis and Scyllal are sea monsters in Greek mythology. To be "between Scylla and Charybdis" therefore means to be presented with two opposite dangers, the task being to find a route that avoids both.
  • Jonas Hanway was an English merchant, writer and philanthropist. He was the first male Londoner to carry an umbrella and was a noted opponent of tea drinking. Hanway created seventy-four printed works, mostly pamphlets, on a wide variety of subjects. Of literary importance is the Historical Account of British Trade over the Caspian Sea, with a Journal of Travels, etc. (London, 1753). He is also cited frequently for his work with the Foundling Hospital in London, particularly his pamphlets detailing the earliest comparative "histories" of the foundation versus similar institutions abroad.
  • Jonah from the Book of Jonah was swallowed by a large fish where he prays to God for three days. He is then released. The story of Jonah in the Bible teaches about God's universal mercy and grace, showing that his compassion extends to all people, not just the Israelites. It also highlights the dangers of disobedience and prejudice, as the prophet Jonah attempts to flee God's command to preach to the hated city of Nineveh. The story is a lesson for both individuals and nations, showing how even those closest to God must grapple with his love and mercy for those they consider enemies.
  • Noah is the last of the pre-flood patriarchs of the Book of Genesis. He builds an ark and takes pairs of animals in order to survive the great flood. The biblical story of Noah's Ark signifies a profound message about divine judgment, mercy, and salvation. It illustrates that God judges wickedness and sin but also provides a way for salvation for those who are righteous, like Noah, and those who have faith. The story highlights themes of God's faithfulness through the covenant of the rainbow, and in Christian theology, the ark is often seen as a foreshadowing of Christ as the ultimate source of salvation.
  • "Upon a primrose bank I lie. Cheerio, my dear, and fare thee well until we meet again if ever that may be which is not!" This opening line evokes an image of death or rest ("upon a primrose bank I lie") and a farewell that is uncertain ("if ever that may be which is not"), expressing the ephemeral and uncertain nature of life and afterlife. The phrase "cheerio" is a casual, almost ironic goodbye, hinting at resignation or acceptance of mortality. She admits to having come from hardship (sleeping in doorways, lost in the city without guidance) and to having been "broke," both financially and perhaps spiritually. She saved on electric lights, symbolizing her desire for simplicity or darkness over artificial illumination. Her physical appearance (baldness, missing breast, crooked wig) is revealed as a mark of her struggles and losses. This physical unveiling represents a shedding of illusions or pretenses, an invitation to Vera to see her true self beyond facade and social roles. Miss MacIntosh reflects philosophically that words cannot capture the fullness of flesh and blood reality, nor can they "harness the winds." This underscores the themes of communication’s limits and the gap between language and lived experience. She suggests that real life is often silent, and that love, too, is shrouded in silence and mutual deception. She cynically calls love "a system of mutual deception," revealing her guarded and perhaps disillusioned view of intimacy, likely shaped by her personal history of rejection and scorn. This could also reflect her role as a protector and moral guide: aware of human frailty and illusion. Miss MacIntosh muses that life might have been easier had she been a man, reflecting on the limitations imposed on women ("I could have slipped unnoticed through the crowds," "No one would have laughed"). This speaks to gender dynamics and her alienation from the roles expected of her. The removal of her wig is a powerful symbol of vulnerability and honesty. Baldness, a source of personal embarrassment, is revealed as a core truth she can no longer hide. It represents stripping away social masks and confronting reality, no matter how harsh. Miss MacIntosh contemplates mortality with a mixture of resignation and dark humor, acknowledging that life is short and filled with blows ("Life brings many blows"). She speaks of death openly and almost cheerfully, urging Vera to "live each day as if it were the last," emphasizing the preciousness and fragility of life. She calls them "pilgrims," suggesting life is a journey with an uncertain destination. The image of knitting bones together "though they unravel faster than we knit" evokes the struggle to maintain coherence and meaning in life despite decay and loss. Miss MacIntosh asserts that "people are never quite what they seem. Nobody knows anybody," highlighting the inscrutability of human beings and the limits of understanding others even in close relationships, such as marriage. Her closing remark about suffering "especially when there are rainbows" This poignant line suggests that moments of beauty or hope ("rainbows") can intensify her pain or sense of loss, perhaps because they contrast sharply with her own suffering or the stark realities she faces. This passage is a profound meditation on identity, loss, and the human condition. Miss MacIntosh, unveiling her bald head and revealing her painful history, challenges Vera to see beyond surface illusions to the raw truths of life and death. She speaks to the inevitability of disappointment and the limits of understanding others, urging a stoic acceptance of life’s brevity and complexity. Despite its somber tone, she ends with a call to face the day bravely, knitting body and soul for the journey ahead. This moment is crucial as it deepens the emotional and philosophical texture of the narrative, revealing the nursemaid’s inner life and her role as a moral and existential anchor amid the story’s shifting dreams and realities.
  • Poverty is a form of stress that research has shown alters a person’s behavior and development. The Great Depression would have been recent history for the characters in this story and Marguerite Young herself. The average American family lived by the Depression-era motto: “Use it up, wear it out, make do or do without.” Many tried to keep up appearances and carry on with life as close to normal as possible while they adapted to new economic circumstances. Households embraced a new level of frugality in daily life. They kept kitchen gardens, patched worn-out clothes and passed on trips.
  • The philosophy of ambiguity is not just a theme but a structural and stylistic principle that permeates every level of the novel. Characters defy easy categorization and are often contradictory. Mrs. Hogden embodies both vulgarity and a strange, disconcerting serenity. She seems both real and unreal, present and absent, and Vera struggles to grasp her true nature. Even Miss MacIntosh, who initially appears as a figure of steadfast common sense, is revealed to have hidden depths and a past that complicate her seemingly simple persona. This challenges the reader's ability to form definitive judgments about these characters. Characters are not fixed entities but rather fluid and shifting identities, reflecting the novel's broader exploration of the instability of the self. Mr. Spitzer is perhaps the prime example, constantly questioning his identity and blurring the lines between himself and his deceased twin brother. Vera also undergoes a transformation, as she struggles to reconcile her childhood perceptions with the complexities of the adult world. Vera's narration is filtered through her subjective consciousness, which is itself prone to hallucination, memory distortions, and dreamlike states. This makes it difficult to discern objective truth from Vera's personal interpretations, further contributing to the novel's ambiguity. The narrative voice itself is constantly shifting, blurring the boundaries between narrator and character. The novel is steeped in a dreamlike atmosphere, where the boundaries between reality and illusion become increasingly blurred. Events unfold in a non-linear fashion, and the narrative is filled with surreal imagery and symbolic motifs that resist easy interpretation. This dreamlike quality reflects the novel's exploration of the unconscious mind and the subjective nature of experience. Young employs a rich tapestry of symbolism and metaphor that invites multiple interpretations. Objects, places, and events often carry symbolic weight, but their meanings remain open to interpretation. For example, the sea, a recurring motif in the novel, can represent both the source of life and the threat of destruction, reflecting the inherent ambiguity of nature. The novel’s cyclical structure reinforces its themes of ambiguity and uncertainty. Events and motifs recur throughout the narrative, but with slight variations, suggesting that history repeats itself but never in the same way. This cyclical structure also creates a sense of timelessness, blurring the boundaries between past, present, and future. The novel ultimately rejects the notion of definitive truths or easy answers. The novel suggests that reality is inherently ambiguous and that our understanding of the world is always incomplete and provisional. By embracing ambiguity, Young challenges the reader to question their own assumptions and to accept the inherent uncertainty of human experience. The novel's exploration of ambiguity is not merely a stylistic choice but a reflection of Young's philosophical vision. She suggests that embracing ambiguity is essential for understanding the complexities of human existence and for appreciating the richness and diversity of experience.

Chapter 16

Summary

Vera rides her old black pony, Falada, through the dark grounds, laughing and whispering secrets into his ear. She decides not to bring a real horse into her mother's dream-filled bedroom. Instead she rides him up the stairs of the great house, past mosaic emperors, a funeral gondola, and tapestries of angels healing the blind and the deaf. They reach Miss MacIntosh's door, always barred from inside, and it swings open. In the moonlight Miss MacIntosh stands by the window, greatly changed, unbelievably not herself, and yet Vera recognizes her instantly.

Characters present

Vera Cartwheel · Miss MacIntosh · Falada

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Dreams and Imagination · Freedom and Escape · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Memory and the Past

Symbols: Horses and Carriages · Moon and Stars · The House · The Sea and Water · Weddings and Funerals

Allusions: Fairy Tales and Folklore

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter begins with a powerful, almost dreamlike description of Vera Cartwheel riding her black pony, Falada, on the night of her fourteenth birthday. This passage captures the fierce pride and exhilaration of youth, the connection between rider and horse, and the blurring of reality and fantasy. The pony, though old and worn, moves with a spirit and grace that transcends its physical limitations, symbolizing both endurance and the imagination's power to transform the mundane into the magical. This sets the tone for the chapter’s exploration of innocence, freedom, and escape.
  • As Vera and Falada ride through the dark allees, the narrative paints a haunting picture of the estate: burned trees, untended gardens, broken statues, faded tennis courts, gargoyles, and fountains. This imagery evokes decay, neglect, and the passage of time, contrasting with Vera’s youthful vitality. The garden as “the garden of the blind” metaphorically suggests blindness to the present or to reality, deepening the theme of lost grandeur and forgotten history.
  • Vera’s intimate bond with Falada is a central passage. She confides her deepest secrets to the horse about her orphanhood, her dislike for Miss MacIntosh, her hopes for the future. This reveals Vera’s vulnerability and longing for understanding and companionship. The horse is not just a companion but almost a confidant and extension of her inner world. The symbolic act of tying blue ribbons on Falada’s tail and whispering secrets reflects her need for connection and expression.
  • Another significant passage is the explanation of Falada’s pedigree and the importance Mr. Spitzer places on names. Falada is linked to an old Arabic fairy tale horse whose head spoke oracles after death, and also to historical influences on furniture design. Summary

The breakfast continues. Miss MacIntosh denounces vain man, the Emperor Constantine, and Caesar, declares that history lies, and professes her faith in common sense and the middle way. Then she settles on Benjamin Franklin, whose experiments with lightning led to electric light and the end of privacy. Darkness, she argues, once protected marriage and the poor and the ugly. Vera realizes what the tirade is for: a woman who was just seen without her wig is arguing that no one should have to be seen. The chapter ends with Miss MacIntosh quoting Job and crying that the stars have always lit the heavens.

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with a profound meditation on the futility and vanity of human aspirations, as expressed through the character’s reflections on Emperor Constantine and the "Slough of Despond." The metaphor of life as a marshland filled with brambles and weeds sets a somber tone about the human condition and the closing of the heart from within, emphasizing internal barriers to understanding or connection.
  • This passage questions history and knowledge, asserting that "history lies, and geography is uncertain," underscoring the unreliability of accepted truths and the elusive nature of identity in modern times.
  • The character expresses a strong belief in common sense as the "middle brow," the middle way, and the average life, asserting it as a rare and valuable quality. This passage reveals an internal tension between embracing ordinary life and the cosmic or remote issues that also preoccupy her.
  • The comparison of dwarves dreaming they are giants and giants dreaming they are dwarves illustrates the relativity of perception and ambition, hinting at the complexity of human identity.
  • One of the most extended and important passages is the critique of electric lights, attributed ironically to Benjamin Franklin, who paved "the way for electric lights" and thereby disrupted natural rhythms of day and night. The character laments how electric illumination invades privacy, disturbs sleep, and ruins traditional human experiences such as marriage by exposing flaws that darkness once concealed.
  • This passage deeply mourns the loss of darkness, which once provided refuge and mystery, and contrasts it with the artificial brightness that "keeping us up all night like Roman soldiers," contributing to social ills like divorce and loneliness.
  • The nostalgia for "bayberry candles" and natural starlight versus intrusive modern electric lights highlights a tension between technological progress and preservation of human dignity and natural order.
  • The character reflects on the role of darkness in protecting the sacredness and mystery of marriage, allowing spouses to be "modest" and sheltered from immediate judgment. The electric light, by exposing all, undermines this protective veil, leading to disillusionment and social problems.
  • This meditation extends to a broader social commentary on how modern illumination disrupts traditional human relationships and perceptions.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s practical, unadorned manner of dress and demeanor symbolize her serious approach to life, rejecting frivolity, dreams, and illusions. She lives fully in the present reality, "for no other life," and is skeptical of sentimental or metaphysical distractions.
  • This passage highlights her grounded nature and possibly her resistance or inability to engage with deeper or more cosmic concerns that transcend ordinary experience.
  • Vera reflects on how Miss MacIntosh’s frequent evocations of cosmic phenomena (creation, tides, stars) serve to mask her own human limitations and inner absences. These grand themes conceal what she does not wish to reveal about herself.
  • This passage suggests a tension between the vastness of universal mysteries and the intimate realities of human life.
  • The chapter ends with a meditation on the coming of winter, the changing of seasons, and the narrowing spectrum of colors in the natural world, symbolizing transition, loss, and endurance. The imagery of crystalline snow, dimmed colors, and the "luminous colors of the winter sea" evokes both harshness and beauty in nature’s cycles.
  • This passage metaphorically connects the natural world’s rhythms to human experience, emphasizing acceptance and preparation for inevitable change.
  • The concluding words question why light should be given to those in misery and darkness, affirming the enduring value of natural starlight and rejecting artificial electric light. The character’s exclamation, "Electric lights, fiddlesticks! The stars have lighted the heavens from pole to pole," reaffirms a preference for natural order over human tampering.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • Miss MacIntosh is portrayed as fiercely grounded in what she calls "common sense," valuing the "middle brow," the "middle way," and the "average life", a disposition she prides herself on as her "greatest love," even if others despise it.
  • This common sense coexists with a pervasive skepticism toward accepted truths such as history, geography, and law, which she dismisses as unstable, uncertain, or outright falsehoods.
  • She challenges grand narratives, like that of Caesar crossing the Rubicon or the veracity of historical figures, suggesting that time has neither accumulated nor taught wisdom.
  • This skeptical realism reveals a character who questions the foundations of knowledge and human pretensions but does so without despair; rather, she seems to accept human limitations with a certain weary humor and irony.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s discourse centers on her criticism of modern inventions, especially electric lights. She associates electricity, notably Benjamin Franklin’s experiments, as a disruptive force that has destroyed natural rhythms, privacy, and the quietness of night. She laments electric lights for erasing darkness, which she sees as essential for sleep, privacy, and even mystery in human relationships, particularly marriage. Electric lights, she argues, expose flaws and imperfections that were once safely hidden in darkness, thereby damaging marriages and social harmony.
  • Her detailed critique extends to "electric trains," "electric irons," "fluorescent lamps," and "two-way lighting systems" as unnatural intrusions into life’s natural order.
  • This stance encapsulates her resistance to tampering with "old, damaged creation" and her preference for simpler, older ways such as "bayberry candles," "snuffers," and natural starlight. Her view is that the modern world’s brightness is a form of extravagant excess that impoverishes human experience and dignity.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s practical nature is emphasized by descriptions of her appearance and habits. She dresses plainly, in worn, practical clothing: a grey baseball sweater with a ravelling sleeve, stout shoes, and a patched salt-and-pepper tweed coat.
  • She carries her "rigging" everywhere, including an old black umbrella likened to a sail and a whale-boned ice-breaker corset, symbolizing her preparedness and no-nonsense approach to life on a “rough shore.”
  • She rejects frivolities such as filmy dresses or adornments, even on significant occasions like weddings or funerals, signaling her seriousness and focus on the immediate, tangible world rather than on dreams or illusions.
  • Despite her talk of cosmic and remote issues like glaciers, submerged continents, and the first days of creation, Miss MacIntosh reveals little of her personal emotions or vulnerabilities.
  • She claims her consciousness ceases during sleep and that she cannot remember dreams, not even her own, suggesting a detachment from inner emotional life or a guardedness.
  • Her conscience "kept guard" as a "lonely vigil," indicating solitude and perhaps a self-imposed emotional isolation.
  • She evades personal disclosures and remains impassive, almost austere, in her demeanor.
  • This emotional reserve contrasts with the vastness of the cosmic themes she invokes, highlighting a tension between the grand and the personal.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections often shift from the mundane to the cosmic and from daily life and societal critiques to the “first starfish upon the first beach” and “the first moon drawing the first tide.” This oscillation suggests that she perceives human life as part of a vast, impersonal natural order that transcends immediate existence.
  • She uses cosmic imagery to mask what she does not want to reveal: her fears, losses, or inner life.
  • This duality makes her a somewhat enigmatic figure, connecting the earthly and the universal while remaining personally elusive.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s thoughts about the coming winter, the colorlessness of the world under snow and ice, and the need to prepare with warm clothing and supplies reveal a keen awareness of mortality and the cycles of life.
  • Winter symbolizes death or hardship, and her sober preparation indicates acceptance rather than fear. Yet, she also acknowledges the subtle beauty of winter’s muted colors, reflecting a nuanced appreciation of life’s phases and transitions.
  • Her concern with time’s passing, the loss inherent in change, and the persistence of “dimmed colors” in hardship underscore a mature, grounded philosophy.
  • Throughout her discourse, Miss MacIntosh repeatedly condemns human vanity, illusions of grandeur, and false hopes.
  • She refers to "vain man" in multiple historical and contemporary contexts, from Emperor Constantine and Caesar to Benjamin Franklin, pointing out the futility of human pretensions to immortality or mastery.
  • She warns against illusions, falsehoods that may mask other truths, and the human tendency to stumble blindly in the "broad daylight which God has lighted."
  • Her repeated invocation of vanity and illusion underscores a theme of human limitation and the importance of humility and realism.

  • War of the Currents - in the US there was a serious debate about which to use, AC or DC current, and that may be what is referred to in the novel The war of the currents was a series of events surrounding the introduction of competing electric power transmission systems in the late 1880s and early 1890s. It grew out of two lighting systems developed in the late 1870s and early 1880s: arc lamp street lighting running on high-voltage alternating current (AC), and large-scale low-voltage direct current (DC) indoor incandescent lighting being marketed by Thomas Edison's company. In 1886, the Edison system was faced with new competition: an alternating current system initially introduced by George Westinghouse's company that used transformers to step down from a high voltage so AC could be used for indoor lighting. Using high voltage allowed an AC system to transmit power over longer distances from more efficient large central generating stations. As the use of AC spread rapidly with other companies deploying their own systems, the Edison Electric Light Company claimed in early 1888 that high voltages used in an alternating current system were hazardous, and that the design was inferior to, and infringed on the patents behind, their direct current system. In the spring of 1888, a media furor arose over electrical fatalities caused by pole-mounted high-voltage AC lines, attributed to the greed and callousness of the arc lighting companies that operated them. In June of that year Harold P. Brown, a New York electrical engineer, claimed the AC-based lighting companies were putting the public at risk using high-voltage systems installed in a slipshod manner. Brown also claimed that alternating current was more dangerous than direct current and tried to prove this by publicly killing animals with both currents, with technical assistance from Edison Electric. The Edison company and Brown colluded further in their parallel goals to limit the use of AC with attempts to push through legislation to severely limit AC installations and voltages. Both also colluded with Westinghouse's chief AC rival, the Thomson-Houston Electric Company, to make sure the first electric chair was powered by a Westinghouse AC generator. By the early 1890s, the war was winding down. Further deaths caused by AC lines in New York City forced electric companies to fix safety problems. Thomas Edison no longer controlled Edison Electric, and subsidiary companies were beginning to add AC to the systems they were building. Mergers reduced competition between companies, including the merger of Edison Electric with their largest competitor, Thomson-Houston, forming General Electric in 1892. Edison Electric's merger with their chief alternating current rival brought an end to the war of the currents and created a new company that now controlled three quarters of the US electrical business. Westinghouse won the bid to supply electrical power for the World's Columbian Exposition in 1893 and won the major part of the contract to build Niagara Falls hydroelectric project later that year (partially splitting the contract with General Electric). Chapter 64

← Chapter 63 · Home · Chapter 65 →

Summary

Solomon the turtle is missing. Bald and unguarded, Miss MacIntosh tells Vera her life story: childhood baldness, wigs made of stolen horsehair, boys trying to hook her wig with fishing lines, a phrenologist who admired her skull, a Gaelic prince among her ancestors. As a matron of orphans she cared for a forger, who later wrote to her from Alcatraz, and for Lorena, a dancing girl she loved. Vera sees her as she cannot see herself and begins to compose an elegy. Their last month together begins.

Characters present

Miss MacIntosh · Vera Cartwheel · Solomon the Turtle · Lorena

Concepts present

Themes: Death and Mortality · Grief, Loss, and Mourning · Identity and the Self · Illusion and Reality · Isolation and Connection · Love

Symbols: Fog and Mist · Hair, Wig, and Baldness · Shadows · The Sea and Water · The Umbrella

Allusions: Ancient Egypt · Ecclesiastes · Genesis · Judaism · Music and Composers · Suicide in History and Literature · The Bible · The Civil War · Women’s Suffrage

Key passages

From the research

  • The chapter opens with Vera noticing Solomon’s absence and feeling a newfound appreciation for his presence, symbolizing the theme of unnoticed value and loss.
  • Miss MacIntosh reveals she loved only once, a beautiful dancing girl named Lorena, whose life was marked by escape and tragedy. This passage adds layers to Miss MacIntosh’s character, showing her vulnerability and past connections to those society might reject.
  • A significant portion of the chapter is devoted to Miss MacIntosh’s lifelong baldness. She explains that she was born bald, wore a toupee as a child, and has never had hair, making her different and marginalized. Her baldness symbolizes loneliness, alienation, and the human condition of exposure and vulnerability.
  • The story of the barber who could do nothing for her bald head illustrates the hopelessness of her condition and her acceptance of it as an intrinsic part of her identity. The barber’s eloquence about his inability to grow even a single hair underscores the finality of her condition.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s resourcefulness and desperation are shown through her making a wig from stolen horses’ hairs, symbolizing her attempt to mask her difference and blend in, yet also emphasizing her isolation and the futility of this attempt.
  • The chapter describes how boys tried to hook her wig with fishing lines and how she was afraid of many things, including animals and people, which highlights her deep-seated fear and social alienation from a young age.
  • Miss MacIntosh claims descent from a Gaelic prince who was also bald and lost his crown, presenting a tragic nobility that contrasts with her humble, marginalized existence. She rejects the idle rich and social pretensions, affirming her identity rooted in practicality and resilience.
  • Throughout the chapter, there are poetic meditations on mortality, the ephemeral nature of beauty and life, and the essential loneliness of the human condition. Miss MacIntosh’s baldness becomes a metaphor for universal mourning and the stripping away of illusions.
  • Near the end, she is portrayed as a firm, solid woman who, despite her internal dissolution, stands for stability and common sense in a shifting world, symbolized by her black umbrella and practical nature.
  • Miss MacIntosh challenges established religious narratives (e.g., Emperor Constantine’s changes to the calendar) and extols the humble macintosh (raincoat) as a symbol of practical, unpretentious survival, contrasting with grand but empty imperial and religious traditions.

Questions and observations

Research: Characters

Miss MacIntosh

  • The central figure of the chapter, an orphanage matron who has suffered lifelong baldness.
  • She is portrayed as a strong yet vulnerable woman, bearing the weight of loneliness and social alienation.
  • Her baldness is both a physical condition and a metaphor for her isolation and difference from others.
  • Miss MacIntosh evolves from a figure shrouded in mystery to a deeply human character marked by resilience and vulnerability.
  • Her storytelling reveals layers of her personality, from pride and courage to sadness and regret.

Vera Cartwheel

  • A person who cares deeply for Miss MacIntosh, showing compassion and love.
  • Through their eyes, we see the complexity of Miss MacIntosh’s character and her struggles.
  • Vera’s growing understanding and affection for Miss MacIntosh deepen the reader’s empathy.

Solomon (pet turtle)

  • Mentioned briefly as a lethargic creature absent at the beginning, symbolizing a kind of comfort or presence that is missing.

Lorena

  • Lorena is depicted as a beautiful dancing girl, dark and fat, with long hair described like a "midnight curtain concealing the star until the star was revealed." She first encountered Miss MacIntosh when the latter was working in an orphanage.
  • Lorena laughed at Miss MacIntosh and then ran away, eventually becoming a strip-tease dancer. Years later, Lorena was paroled to Miss MacIntosh’s care, but she ran away again, and Miss MacIntosh could not pursue her due to her role as parole officer.
  • Lorena symbolizes a more flamboyant, elusive, and perhaps tragic aspect of femininity and life experience, contrasting sharply with the sober, practical, and grounded Miss MacIntosh. While Miss MacIntosh is associated with order, responsibility, and a no-nonsense approach to life, Lorena embodies escape, performance, and the allure of the spotlight.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s relationship with Lorena is tinged with affection and regret with they were “very dear friends” for a time, but Lorena’s life took a path of repeated flight and apparent self-destruction, as she “slept with many men” and aged into baldness, a fate that mirrors Miss MacIntosh’s own physical barrenness and loneliness.
  • Miss MacIntosh reflects on Lorena’s invitation to join her in the strip-tease, suggesting Lorena believed Miss MacIntosh would have made a sensational artist in that world. This highlights the tension between Lorena’s world of public display and Miss MacIntosh’s private, concealed existence (especially with her baldness and wig).
  • Lorena’s life is marked by a search for light and visibility, “danc[ing] in the spotlight,” while Miss MacIntosh sought the shadow, the hidden, and the protective fog.
  • Lorena enriches the narrative by providing a foil to Miss MacIntosh’s character by showing a different trajectory of womanhood, freedom, and loss. Lorena’s story also deepens the themes of love, disappointment, and identity, as Miss MacIntosh mourns not only her own solitude but also the loss of a connection that might have been different if circumstances had allowed.
  • The mention of Lorena evokes a poignant sense of fragmented relationships and missed possibilities in the world the novel inhabits.

A forger

  • The forger is a minor but symbolically significant figure mentioned in the context of Miss MacIntosh’s past connections with orphans under her care. The forger is one of only two orphans with whom Miss MacIntosh maintained contact after they left the orphanage, the other being Lorena, the dancing girl.
  • He was incarcerated at Alcatraz, a notorious prison, and despite his criminal status, he maintained a connection with Miss MacIntosh by sending her beautifully decorated Christmas cards every year. These cards showcased his skill in penmanship, as he was able to imitate signatures ranging from Abraham Lincoln to William Jennings Bryan with remarkable artistry. His ability to produce such forgeries suggests a complex character capable of both criminality and refined craftsmanship.
  • Miss MacIntosh’s relationship with the forger reflects her enduring, if fraught, loyalty and care for those she once supervised. It also illustrates the theme of lost or broken lives touched by her, emphasizing her role as a maternal figure to children who ultimately faced harsh fates. The forger’s death marks the end of one such connection, underscoring the transient and often tragic nature of Miss MacIntosh’s attachments.
  • Symbolically, the forger embodies the blurred lines between authenticity and imitation, truth and falsehood, mirroring Miss MacIntosh’s own struggles with identity, appearance (notably her baldness and wigs), and the facades people maintain. His skill in forgery contrasts with her straightforward, no-nonsense character, highlighting the tension between illusions and reality pervasive in the novel.

Research: Themes

Loneliness and Isolation

See: Isolation and Connection

  • Miss MacIntosh’s baldness sets her apart physically and socially, causing her to feel like an outsider.
  • Her wandering through life, changing jobs, and lack of lasting relationships underline a profound sense of isolation.

Identity and Difference

See: Identity and the Self

  • Baldness symbolizes not only her physical appearance but also her difference and the struggle to be accepted.
  • Her attempts to wear wigs and create a semblance of normalcy reflect the universal human desire to fit in.

Resilience and Endurance

  • Despite her hardships, Miss MacIntosh exhibits strength and dignity.
  • She fights against despair and maintains a firm stance in the face of adversity, symbolized by her unwavering grip on her black umbrella.

Mortality and the Human Condition

See: Death and Mortality

  • The narrative meditates on the inevitability of death and the transient nature of beauty and life.
  • Baldness becomes a metaphor for universal human vulnerability and the “essential loneliness” each person must face.

Love and Loss

See: Love · Grief, Loss, and Mourning

  • Miss MacIntosh’s reflections on Lorena and her own life reveal deep emotional wounds.
  • The absence of romantic fulfillment and the loss of connections highlight themes of regret and yearning.

Reality versus Illusion

See: Illusion and Reality

  • The chapter contrasts the harsh realities of Miss MacIntosh’s life with her dreams and the illusions she once held.
  • Vera’s love and understanding challenge the idea of superficial appearances.

Research: Symbols and Imagery

Baldness

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • Represents vulnerability, difference, and mourning. It is a physical manifestation of Miss MacIntosh’s inner loneliness and social alienation.

Wig

See: Hair, Wig, and Baldness

  • The wig symbolizes the mask people wear to hide their true selves and conform to societal expectations. Miss MacIntosh’s frequent removal and replacement of the wig depict her struggle with identity.

Black Umbrella

See: The Umbrella

  • Serves as a protective shield against the world’s harshness and symbolizes Miss MacIntosh’s resilience and steadfastness.

Fog and Shadows

See: Fog and Mist · Shadows

  • Reflect confusion, concealment, the unknown, and the liminal space between reality and dreams.

Sea and Water Imagery

See: The Sea and Water

  • Symbolize life’s constant movement, change, and the inevitability of death.

the-novel-as-a-liberal-arts-education:
Miss MacIntosh, My Darling as a Liberal Arts Education

Readers who return to Miss MacIntosh, My Darling again and again often come away with the sense that the novel has been educating them. Every chapter sends the curious reader somewhere else: to scripture, to Greek myth, to Roman history, to geometry and the stars, to Shakespeare and the Persian poets. Followed faithfully, those references add up to something close to a traditional liberal arts education, gathered inside a single story.

The seven liberal arts

From late antiquity through the Middle Ages, a liberal education meant the seven liberal arts. The first three, the trivium, were grammar, logic, and rhetoric, the arts of language and argument. The other four, the quadrivium, were arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy, the arts of number. Boethius, the Roman philosopher Young draws on in several chapters, gave the quadrivium its name.

Miss MacIntosh, My Darling touches all seven. Its characters argue in paradox and fallacy, count and measure, hear music in everything, and read the stars, and its long, looping sentences and torrents of questions are lessons in how language carries thought. See Nearly Four Thousand Questions, Pythagoras and the Music of the Spheres, On musica universalis and Boethius (Ch 38), and On Boethius and the Consolation of Philosophy (Ch 51).

The course catalog at the end of this page sorts the novel’s references into subjects that grow out of those seven arts, with each chapter’s topics listed under its subject.

A traditional writer

Young claimed the word for herself. When Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs pressed her on the label “experimental,” she answered:

I see myself as traditional even though I know you see my work as experimental. I don’t really consider Sterne, Joyce, and Proust experimental either because the tradition of their writing goes back a long way. Traditional. The Grand Tradition. Clear back to Don Quixote.

Marguerite Young, in Ellen G. Friedman and Miriam Fuchs, “A Conversation with Marguerite Young,” The Review of Contemporary Fiction (Fall 1989)

In the same conversation she named the books that formed her: Saint Augustine’s City of God, Tristram Shandy, Gogol’s Dead Souls, Dickens, Poe, and “the poetry of the Mormons.” Her own schooling was classical. At the University of Chicago she studied the epic under Robert Morss Lovett and the structure of the novel under Ronald S. Crane, with whom she read Tom Jones thirteen times. A tradition that runs from the Church Fathers through Cervantes, Fielding, and Sterne is the old humanist curriculum, and it is the one she wrote from. See the Friedman and Fuchs conversation and Reading Miss MacIntosh, My Darling for Its Structure.

Young denied any debt to T. S. Eliot. There are “no echoes of Eliot” in her work, she said, only “echoes of the things that influenced him.” Even so, his 1919 essay “Tradition and the Individual Talent” describes the kind of tradition she meant. A writer with a true historical sense, Eliot argued, feels “that the whole of the literature of Europe from Homer” has “a simultaneous existence and composes a simultaneous order.” That is close to the sense of time running through Young’s novel, in which every moment seems equally present.

Critics have since given a name to the line she placed herself in. In 1976 Edward Mendelson called it the encyclopedic narrative: a work that tries to hold the whole knowledge of a culture inside a story. His examples run from Dante’s Divine Comedy and Cervantes’s Don Quixote, the book Young named as the start of the Grand Tradition, to Goethe’s Faust, Melville’s Moby-Dick, with its chapters on the science of whales, Joyce’s Ulysses, and Pynchon’s Gravity’s Rainbow. When the 1965 reviewers reached for Melville and Joyce to describe Miss MacIntosh, My Darling, this is the company they were placing it in.

The teacher inside the book

Young taught for most of her life, from a high school classroom in Indianapolis to the Iowa Writers’ Workshop and the New School. The novel teaches the way a good teacher does. It does not lecture. It hands the reader a name, an allusion, or a half-remembered line and trusts the reader to go and find out. She was known for welcoming every arriving idea into her classroom with “Oh, come in,” and the novel does the same. See On ‘Oh, come in’: Young’s classroom (Ch 39).

Mr. Spitzer is almost a student in that classroom: always attending, often confused, and learning, as Chapter 43 puts it, only when “it was too late to do anybody good.” The essay The Novel as Classroom looks at how the book teaches its own craft of writing. This page is about the other education it gives, an education in the world.

Using this site as a course

Each chapter page in To All My Darlings is built to make the novel’s education usable:

  • Research: Resources explains the allusions, history, and ideas in the order they appear in the chapter.
  • Vocabulary gives short definitions of unfamiliar words.
  • The Dictionary gathers those words across the whole book, with every chapter where each one appears.
  • Questions and observations offers reflection questions for reading alone or in a group.

The course catalog below shows which chapters are complete so far.
